The outbreak also sparked widespread discussion on social media platforms. Fear-inducing and uncertain information about CHIKF circulated rapidly online, which may complicate risk communication and outbreak management efforts. In this study, we assessed the content characteristics, video quality, information reliability, transparency, and engagement of CHIKF-related short videos across the two platforms. We searched TikTok China and Bilibili using the term "chikungunya fever" and included the top 100 videos from each platform on October 9, 2025 (N = 200). Video quality was assessed using the Global Quality Scale (GQS) and the Video Information and Quality Index (VIQI); information reliability was evaluated using the modified DISCERN (mDISCERN); transparency was measured using the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) benchmark criteria; and engagement was quantified using platform-based interaction metrics. Statistical analyses were performed to compare video characteristics across platforms and uploader categories, and to evaluate associations between these characteristics and quality scores. Videos from TikTok China showed higher JAMA benchmark scores, whereas videos from Bilibili achieved comparatively higher mDISCERN scores. Subgroup analyses indicated no statistical differences in engagement metrics across uploader categories, whereas quality scores differed significantly. In addition, engagement metrics showed weak correlations with video quality or reliability. The quality and reliability scores for CHIKF-related short videos on the two platforms were relatively low. The results support careful consideration of whether video quality and information reliability should be more explicitly incorporated into platform governance and content distribution strategies.

Epidemiological, clinical, and diagnostic characteristics of a large-scale upsurge of dengue in the rohingya refugee camps and host communities in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, 2021 to 2024: A retrospective study.
BACKGROUND: Dengue emerged as a new public health threat in the Rohingya refugee camps in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, in 2021 and expanded into large-scale upsurges in subsequent years. Evidence on dengue epidemiology and clinical presentation in protracted refugee settings remains limited, despite the need for stronger outbreak preparedness and case management in these contexts. OBJECTIVES: To describe the epidemiological, clinical, and diagnostic characteristics of the dengue upsurge among Rohingya refugees and surrounding host communities in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, and to identify predictors of inpatient admission and diagnostic positivity patterns. METHODS: This retrospective observational study used anonymized surveillance data from the International Organization for Migration (IOM) dengue patient database. Rapid diagnostic test (RDT)-confirmed dengue cases identified across 36 IOM-supported health facilities in Ukhiya and Teknaf between 1 October 2021 and 31 December 2024 were included. Demographic, epidemiological, clinical, and laboratory variables were summarized using descriptive statistics. Weekly case counts were aggregated by epidemiological week and calendar year, and epidemic growth and decay phases were modelled using phase-specific Poisson regression. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with inpatient admission, while separate models examined associations between delay in presentation and RDT positivity patterns, adjusting for age and sex. RESULTS: A total of 35,581 RDT-confirmed dengue cases were reported, of which 90.2% occurred among Rohingya refugees. The median age was 17 years (IQR 7-30), and 46.0% of cases were among children aged 0-14 years. Annual caseload increased from 1,011 in 2021-11,752 in 2022, 10,669 in 2023 and 12,149 in 2024, with seasonal peaks during the monsoon period and progressively later peaks and longer epidemic tails over time. Poisson models showed decreasing growth rates across years (r = 0.449 in 2021 to r = 0.091 in 2024) with increasing doubling times, while decay rates remained broadly comparable (halving time ~4.4-6.0 weeks). Overall, 8.0% of cases required inpatient admission, 1.3% were referred, and four deaths were reported (case fatality <0.1%). In multivariable analysis, inpatient admission was associated with older age (≥60 vs 0-14: aOR 2.48), delayed presentation (aOR 1.06 per day), refugee status (aOR 1.43), fever ≥38°C at presentation (aOR 1.13), presence of any WHO warning sign (aOR 28.87), and chronic co-morbidity (aOR 6.63). Males had lower odds of admission than females (aOR 0.87). CONCLUSION: Sustained dengue preparedness is required in Cox's Bazar, including strengthened surveillance, community-based early referral, targeted monitoring of high-risk groups, environmental vector control, and phase-appropriate use of NS1 and IgM/IgG diagnostics to reduce missed diagnoses and prevent progression to severe disease. These findings highlight the need for a policy shift from episodic outbreak response toward sustained dengue preparedness in humanitarian settings, including strengthened surveillance systems, integrated diagnostic strategies, community-based early referral, and coordinated vector control interventions.

Vector competence of Aedes albopictus and Culex quinquefasciatus for Oropouche virus.
Oropouche virus (OROV) is an arthropod-borne virus transmitted mainly by Culicoides paraensis midges in Latin America and the Caribbean, though evidence suggests occasional transmission by mosquitoes. Oropouche fever has been reported primarily in the Amazon Basin since the 1950s. In 2024, the number of Oropouche fever cases rose sharply and spread beyond the Amazon region, which has been associated with the emergence of a new reassortant OROV strain. We assessed whether increased case numbers could be explained by enhanced replication or transmission of the reassortant strain in peri-urban Culex quinquefasciatus and Aedes albopictus. Laboratory colonies established from Salvador, Brazil were orally exposed to the ancestral OROV strain BeAn 19991 or the contemporary strain 240023 (10⁴-10⁶ PFU/mL), and viral replication was quantified in bodies, legs, and saliva. To evaluate the influence of mosquito genotype on infection outcomes, infection rates were compared between Ae. albopictus from Salvador City (Brazil) and Houston (USA). In Cx. quinquefasciatus, the outbreak strain replicated less efficiently than the historical strain at low viral doses but not at high infection doses. Regardless of strain or dose, vector competence was extremely low, with only 0-1% of mosquitoes exhibiting infectious OROV particles in their saliva after extrinsic incubation. Conversely, Ae. albopictus showed consistently higher body infection rates for the 240023 strain than for BeAn 19991 at both low and high doses. However, overall transmission potential remained limited: only 0-6.4% of leg or saliva samples were positive across OROV strains and doses. The higher infection rates of the 240023 strain was consistent across both Ae. albopictus genotypes, but infectious saliva was detected only in mosquitoes from the Salvador line (up to 20%) and not in the Houston line (0%). Taken together, this suggests that the recent geographic expansion of OROV is unlikely to be driven by a vector shift from midges to these mosquitoes. Importantly, our findings do indicate higher infectivity of the 240023 strain in Ae. albopictus across different mosquito lines which may have future implications for further adaptation to OROV.

Immunoinformatics and reverse vaccinology design of self-amplifying RNA vaccine against marburg virus with structural dynamics and immune simulation analysis.
Marburg virus disease (MVD), a deadly zoonotic illness in humans, is caused by the Marburg virus (MARV), a single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the Orthomarburgvirus genus of the Filoviridae family. There are currently no approved vaccines or efficient antiviral therapies for MARV, despite high morbidity and fatality rates of the virus, particularly in Africa. Recognizing its epidemic potential and its inclusion on the WHO list of blueprint priority pathogens, an immunoinformatics approach was used to design novel multi-epitope saRNA vaccine candidates (MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII) targeting the viral GP, NP, VP40, and VP35 via CD8 + , CD4 + , and B cell epitopes. These epitopes were derived from target protein sequences and incorporated into MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII after validation for antigenicity, non-allergenicity, non-toxicity, and conservation. Additionally, the selected epitopes were conjugated to suitable adjuvants via various linkers, thereby enabling the design of a potentially stable vaccine. Additionally, the designed MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII were incorporated into the standard saRNA model, in which ORF-2 encodes the target vaccine peptide. Moreover, biophysical analyses unveiled that the developed vaccines are basic (pI < 7), soluble (GRAVY < 0), and stable (aliphatic index < 80). Subsequently, docking of MB-saVaxI to TLR2 (-938.3) and TLR4 (-902.4), and MB-saVaxII to TLR3 (-1485.4) and TLR7 (-1543.6) demonstrated significant affinity, with detailed hydrogen-bond interactions validated by MM-GBSA and molecular dynamics simulations. Furthermore, MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII were effectively cloned in-silico into Escherichia coli, and immune simulations indicated that the vaccines triggered robust innate and adaptive immunity, with a sustained memory response and TH cell activation, as evidenced by IFN-γ and IL-2 production. Additionally, the mRNA structure of MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII remained stable throughout the expression pathway in the host. However, extensive in-vitro and in-vivo studies are needed to establish the safety and efficacy of this vaccine candidate conclusively.

First evidence of measles virus detected from exhaled breath in humans.
OBJECTIVES: Measles is among the most transmissible human infections, yet direct capture of measles virus from an infected person's exhaled breath has not been described. We assessed whether measles virus RNA can be detected from exhaled breath using facemask sampling (FMS). METHODS: We studied a 23-year-old unvaccinated woman with laboratory-confirmed measles (throat-swab RT-qPCR positive on day 5 post symptom onset). From day 10 post symptom onset, longitudinal sampling was performed for six consecutive days with duplicate specimens collected at each timepoint from the throat, face, cutaneous lesions and exhaled breath using a surgical mask fitted with polyvinyl alcohol sampling strips (FMS). Dissolved mask strips and swab eluates underwent RNA extraction followed by RT-qPCR targeting measles nucleoprotein and haemagglutinin genes, with human RNase P as a sample adequacy control. Quantification was derived from nucleoprotein-gene standards and normalised per strip or per 100 μL of swab eluate. RESULTS: Measles virus RNA was consistently detected in exhaled breath captured by FMS and remained >10ˆ4 genome copies per sampling strip despite sampling beginning 10 days after symptom onset. During FMS collection, the participant reported no respiratory symptoms and did not vocalise. RNA kinetics differed by sampling site: throat and facial swabs increased even after complete rash resolution, whereas cutaneous-lesion swabs yielded comparatively low RNA levels. FMS kinetics diverged from throat swabs over time, suggesting distinct patterns of virus emission across compartments. CONCLUSIONS: This study provides the first empirical evidence that measles virus RNA can be captured directly from the exhaled breath of an individual with measles. Although RNA detection does not confirm infectious virus, persistent high-level exhaled RNA supports FMS as a practical, non-invasive tool to study measles respiratory emission and may inform understanding of transmission and the duration of potential contagiousness. Empirical sampling of different respiratory compartments may help refine infection-prevention guidance during resurgent outbreaks.

Seroprevalence of measles virus antibodies among residents of Kavaratti, Lakshadweep: assessing the immunity gap.
Despite India's progress toward measles elimination, serological data from isolated communities such as Lakshadweep remain limited. We conducted a community based cross-sectional serosurvey in selected wards of Kavaratti in September 2022. Of 368 samples collected, 299 participants with complete demographic data were analyzed. Measles-specific IgG was measured by commercial ELISA, and age- and sex- related patterns were assessed. IgG levels correlated positively with age, and serological status differed significantly across age groups (p < 0.001). Median levels were higher in females, but not significantly (p = 0.190). Negative or equivocal results clustered among younger participants, supporting surveillance.

Monkeypox on a disc: Portable centrifugal microfluidic platform for multi-assay colorimetric LAMP.
Monkeypox is currently the most important orthopoxvirus infection in humans. The increase in the number of cases, combined with its potential social impact and international spread, led the World Health Organization (WHO) to classify it as the most recent Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC). Although mainly endemic in resource-limited countries, quantitative Polymerase Chain Reaction (qPCR) remains the gold standard for detection but is challenging due to the need for specialized instrumentation. To address this, we propose an instrument-friendly molecular assay based on colorimetric Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP), performed on a multi-assay polystyrene-toner (PST) centrifugal device. The new analytical device was designed to include chambers for loading the LAMP mixture and samples, interconnected channels for mixing them, and separate chambers for simultaneous LAMP amplification and visual detection of each sample. When evaluated in a panel of real clinical samples, compared to qPCR, the assay based on visual detection demonstrated 100.00% specificity, 91.67% sensitivity, and 95.83% accuracy, which increased to 100% accuracy when digital image analysis was employed, with a total analysis time of approximately 60 min. The relative simplicity of the assay may facilitate its implementation in resource-limited settings and contribute to expanding access to molecular detection of monkeypox.

In silico conservation and HLA-binding profiles of HMPV F and G protein epitopes: implications for universal vaccine development.
BACKGROUND: Human metapneumovirus (HMPV) is a significant cause of respiratory infection, yet no licensed vaccine exists. Variability across viral subgroups, particularly in the attachment (G) protein, can complicate universal design. We assessed the immunogenetic regions in the fusion (F) and G proteins to identify stable vaccine targets. METHODS: We analyzed N = 324 Pittsburgh and N = 655 global HMPV genomes (2017-2022) for genome diversity per viral subgroup. Previously identified epitope sequences were obtained from the Immune Epitope DataBase (IEDB) for F and G proteins and sequence similarity was determined. Using NetMHCpan-4.1, we identified and computed inferred human leukocyte antigen (HLA) binding affinities for 15 epitope variants (1 or 2 substitutions) against universally common human alleles. RESULTS: The F protein was highly conserved across all subgroups (>96% amino acid sequence identity). In the G protein, we identified a conserved epitope cluster (G3-G7) where epitope G7 was present in 91% of A2 genomes. Functional modeling of the G-protein epitope variants revealed that the majority of HLA alleles maintained or gained binding affinity, a subset exhibited diminished binding (escape), suggesting these regions are subject to ongoing antigenic drift. B-genotypes showed fewer retained binders and were notably underrepresented in the current epitope databases. CONCLUSION: The conserved F protein remains an optimal target for neutralization, while the G3-G7 cluster provides a robust secondary target for T-cell mediated immunity. A bivalent vaccine strategy could pair the stable F protein with these high-frequency G-protein epitopes to elicit an immune response. This approach addresses the A2 subgroup, and incorporating B-genotypes through ongoing surveillance and epitope mapping will be essential to achieve comprehensive, multi-antigen coverage across circulating HMPV strains.

Epigallocatechin gallate inhibits rabies virus glycoprotein‑mediated infection in vitro.
Rabies is one of the most lethal zoonotic disease and causes approximately 60,000 human deaths annually. The high cost of immunoglobulin prophylaxis and the need for cold chain maintenance highlight the need for accessible antiviral strategies, particularly in resource-limited settings. Epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), the major polyphenolic compound of Camellia sinensis, has broad-spectrum antiviral activity. We therefore investigated its activity against Rabies virus (RABV). Because RABV requires BSL-3 containment, we first used a recombinant Vesicular Stomatitis Virus pseudotyped with RABV glycoprotein (pRABV) as a surrogate. EGCG inhibited pRABV infection in a concentration-dependent manner, with an EC50 of approximately 0.15 µg/mL and a selectivity index > 551.72. Time-of-addition, attachment, and entry assays showed that EGCG reduced pRABV infectivity when present during viral adsorption or after pre-incubation with viral particles, whereas no inhibition was observed when cells were treated before infection or after virus internalization. Viral infectivity remained almost completely abolished in a virucidal assay even after EGCG was diluted below its effective antiviral concentration, supporting a direct and irreversible effect on viral particles. EGCG activity was further confirmed using authentic RABV and disease-relevant cell types, including myotubes and neurons. Overall, these findings indicate that EGCG inhibits early stages of the RABV replication cycle, primarily by interfering with viral attachment and directly affecting viral particles. Further studies are needed to define the molecular basis of this interaction and assess the therapeutic potential of EGCG against RABV.

Rise of Lower Respiratory Tract Infections Other than Respiratory Syncytial Virus in the Emergency Room: Results from the Season (2024/25) of the RISE Study.
INTRODUCTION: Acute respiratory infections (ARI) are a major cause of pediatric emergency department (ED) visits and hospitalizations. Although respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), influenza, and rhinovirus (RV) are common etiological agents, pathogen-specific data from pediatric emergency settings remain limited. METHODS: This prospective surveillance study quantified ARI-related ED visits, described pathogen-specific epidemiology, and assessed attendance and hospitalization rates as well as the distribution of lower versus upper respiratory tract infections (LRTI/URTI) in children younger than 60 months in two pediatric EDs in Berlin between November 1, 2024 and May 31, 2025. Respiratory pathogens were identified using nasopharyngeal swab samples tested by multiplex real-time RT-PCR (QIAstat-Dx® Respiratory Panel Plus). RESULTS: Within the study period 4042 ARI-related ED visits occurred. A total of 310 children were enrolled in our study (median age 18 months); 115 (37.1%) had LRTI and 195 (62.9%) URTI. At least one respiratory pathogen was detected in 271 children (87.4%). The attendance rate for RSV was 24.4% (66 cases), for FLU 25.8% (70 cases), and for RV 29.5% (80 cases). Overall, 93 children (30.0%) were hospitalized, including 65 with LRTI and 28 with URTI. Hospitalization rates were highest for RSV infections (26/65, 40.0%) and RV infections (28/65, 43.1%), and lower for FLU infections (13/69, 18.8%). Hospitalization due to LRTI predominated among children with RSV (24/26, 92.3%) and RV infections (20/28, 71.4%), whereas FLU infections were less frequently observed (7/13, 53.9%). Furthermore, younger age, a history of pneumonia, a history of bronchiolitis, and the absence of breastfeeding were associated with hospitalization. CONCLUSIONS: In contrast to the previous season, in which RSV was associated with the highest attendance and hospitalization rate, we observed a high burden of RV infections in the 2024/2025 season. These findings may impact surveillance strategies, clinical management, and future public health strategies.

Possible Pediatric Autoimmune Neuropsychiatric Disorders Associated With Streptococcal Infections (PANDAS) Presenting in Late Adolescence and Early Adulthood: A Case Series.
PANDAS-like syndromes may rarely occur beyond childhood. Although these patients may meet criteria for PANS, recognizing a possible streptococcal-triggered subgroup remains important for diagnosis, future biomarker discovery, and refinement of disease classification. Clinicians should consider post-infectious autoimmune neuropsychiatric syndromes in older patients with abrupt-onset OCD or tics following pharyngeal illness.

Molecular characterization of carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales from Peshawar City, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan.
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: The dissemination of multidrug-resistant Enterobacterales poses a critical public health challenge, particularly in resource-limited regions with high antimicrobial use and limited surveillance. We analysed the phenotypic and genotypic resistance profiles of carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales collected in 2023 from three tertiary care hospitals in Peshawar, Pakistan. METHODS: We performed antimicrobial susceptibility testing on 32 Enterobacterales isolates suspected of carbapenemase production using disk diffusion, gradient diffusion, and broth microdilution according to EUCAST guidelines. We conducted whole-genome sequencing to identify resistance genes, sequence types, and mutations associated with reduced susceptibility to novel β-lactams. RESULTS: The collection comprised 16 Escherichia coli, 13 Klebsiella pneumoniae, and 3 Proteus mirabilis isolates. The predominant carbapenemase gene was bla NDM-5 (90.6%), frequently combined with bla OXA-48-like variants (46.9%). ESBL genes, mainly bla CTX-M-15, were common (78.1%), while CMY-type AmpC β-lactamases were detected in 28.1% of isolates. Insertions in the PBP3-encoding gene ftsI and CMY co-production were associated with elevated aztreonam-avibactam MICs in E.coli. Reduced cefiderocol susceptibility was observed mainly among NDM-producing E. coli ST2 isolates carrying cirA disruption and ftsI insertions. All isolates remained susceptible to colistin, most of them to gentamicin (84.4%), and exhibited wild-type MIC-distributions for tigecycline, and eravacycline. Genomic analysis identified clustering of high-risk clones, suggesting ongoing local transmission. Notably, 11/13 K. pneumoniae ST147 isolates carried multiple virulence-associated genes consistent with hypervirulence. CONCLUSIONS: High-risk NDM-producing Enterobacterales with increasingly complex resistance and virulence mechanisms are circulating in Pakistan, including determinants compromising last-line β-lactams. Strengthened genomic surveillance is essential to guide therapy and limit further spread.

Maxillary sinusitis due to Burkholderia cepacia mimicking fungal sinusitis.
Chronic maxillary sinusitis is a frequently encountered condition in otorhinolaryngology practice, with bacterial pathogens playing a critical role. The most commonly isolated pathogens include Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Isolation of Burkholderia cepacia complex (Bcc) from sinonasal infections is rare, particularly in immunocompetent individuals. It comprises a group of genetically distinct, aerobic, non-fermenting Gram-negative bacilli that are widely distributed in soil and water environments. Over the past few decades, Bcc has emerged as an opportunistic pathogen, particularly noted for causing severe infections in patients with cystic fibrosis (CF), chronic granulomatous disease, and other compromised immune states. In patients with CF, chronic pulmonary colonization by Bcc is strongly correlated with a rapid decline in lung function and increased mortality. In contrast to Burkholderia pseudomallei, which is known to cause life-threatening melioidosis, the major challenge of Bcc is its intrinsic resistance to multiple antimicrobial agents, including aminoglycosides, quinolones, polymyxins, and several beta-lactams, through various mechanisms, including active efflux pumps, reduced outer membrane permeability, and robust biofilm formation. Consequently, eradicating Bcc infections is notoriously difficult, often requiring culture-directed systemic therapy in combination with definitive surgical intervention.

Postmortem Artifacts Caused by Freshwater Crab Scavenging on Human Remains in Sri Lanka: A Case Series.
Artifacts from aquatic animal scavenging can disfigure human remains, making identification difficult, obscuring or mimicking antemortem injuries, and destroying evidence. Although freshwater crabs are common scavengers in tropical freshwater, literature describing their effects on human remains is limited. This case series describes postmortem scavenging by the freshwater crabs Oziotelphusa ceylonensis and Ceylonthelphusa rugosa in Sri Lanka, highlighting their forensic significance. Three adult males who died in separate incidents of accidental drowning were recovered from shallow freshwater streams in Sri Lanka. Freshwater crabs were observed scavenging on the bodies at the scene or recovered with the bodies during autopsy. The lesions consisted of superficial soft-tissue defects on the eyelids, lips, nose, ears, neck, chest, feet, and external genitalia. The injuries lacked vital reaction and were oval, elongated, or irregular in shape with scalloped margins and crater-like appearances, exposing underlying subcutaneous tissues or muscles. Internal examinations were consistent with drowning. Collected crab specimens were morphologically identified as Oziotelphusa ceylonensis in 2 cases and Ceylonthelphusa rugosa in one case. Freshwater crabs can produce characteristic postmortem artifacts that may mask or mimic antemortem injuries. Recognition of these artifacts is important for expressing accurate medico-legal opinions in cases involving human remains recovered from freshwater environments.

Invasive Meningococcal Disease in Hospitalized Children in Argentina, 2020-2024: Clinical, Epidemiologic and Molecular Findings From a Multicenter Active Surveillance Study.
BACKGROUND: Invasive meningococcal disease (IMD) is a low-incidence but high-impact infection associated with substantial mortality and sequelae. Following MenACWY vaccine introduction into Argentina's National Immunization Program in 2017, updated data on residual disease burden are needed. METHODS: A multicenter active hospital-based surveillance study was conducted in 6 pediatric sentinel units in Argentina (January 2020-December 2024) in children younger than 15 years with suspected IMD. Cases were confirmed by culture and/or polymerase chain reaction from a normally sterile body site. Hospital discharge rates were calculated per 10,000 discharges. Whole-genome sequencing and genetic Meningococcal Antigen Typing System were used to characterize strains and estimate theoretical 4CMenB coverage. RESULTS: Among 234,264 pediatric hospital discharges, 27 confirmed IMD cases were identified (overall rate: 1.2 per 10,000; 95% confidence interval, 0.8-1.7). Annual rates showed no consistent pattern between children younger than 2 years and those 2 years or older. The case-fatality rate was 14.8% (4/27); all deaths occurred in previously healthy children younger than 5 years and were associated with sepsis and a fulminant course (hospital stay ≤1 day). Of 20 cases with a determined capsular group, 19 (95%) were B and 1 (5%) was C; no capsular group Y or W cases were identified. Theoretical 4CMenB coverage by genetic Meningococcal Antigen Typing System was 77.3%, driven by ST-162 clonal complex predominance. CONCLUSIONS: IMD in Argentina continues to predominantly affect young children and is associated with elevated case-fatality amid fulminant sepsis. Serogroup B predominates in the post-MenACWY era, and high estimated 4CMenB coverage supports evaluation of serogroup B vaccination as a complementary prevention strategy.

Recasting Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance Through Contemporary Analytical Frameworks: An Integrated Analysis Using the WHO Bacterial Priority Pathogens List 2024 and AWaRe Classification in a Tertiary Care Hospital of Saurashtra, Western India.
BACKGROUND: Indian antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance rarely uses contemporary global frameworks, and Saurashtra is under-represented in the national evidence base. We applied the WHO Bacterial Priority Pathogens List (BPPL) 2024 and the WHO AWaRe (Access-Watch-Reserve) classification to institutional surveillance data, with national and global benchmarking. METHODS: Cross-sectional analysis of 2,195 non-duplicate clinical bacterial isolates (May-October 2024) at a 1,200-bed government tertiary care teaching hospital. Susceptibility testing followed CLSI M100-S33 (VITEK 2 Compact; Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion); multi-drug resistance (MDR) followed Magiorakos criteria. Isolates were assigned to BPPL 2024 tiers by resistant phenotype, and agent-level resistance was grouped by AWaRe 2023 category. MDR correlates were explored by multivariable logistic regression. The isolate was the unit of analysis; proportions describe cultured isolates, not infections or patients. RESULTS: Isolates meeting Critical-priority phenotypes numbered 1,192 (54.3% of the isolate pool): third-generation cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales (n = 1,086; 49.5%; ceftriaxone resistance 78% in E. coli and 61% in K. pneumoniae) and carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (n = 106; 4.8%). High-priority phenotypes accounted for at most 228 isolates (10.4%). Within the Access group, Enterobacterales resistance was high to ampicillin (89.7% in E. coli) and amoxicillin/clavulanic acid (77-83%) but lower to gentamicin (22-33%); Watch-group fluoroquinolone resistance was 47-73%. Meropenem resistance in E. coli (1%) and K. pneumoniae (7%) was markedly lower than ICMR AMRSN 2023 national estimates (40% and 54%). MDR was present in 58.6% of isolates and was independently associated with ICU admission, age >60 years, tracheal-aspirate specimens, and surgical-department admission. CONCLUSIONS: Reading isolate-level surveillance data through the BPPL 2024 and AWaRe frameworks adds a priority- and stewardship-oriented layer to the conventional antibiogram. These proportions describe cultured isolates, not the frequency of resistant infection in patients. The low Enterobacterales carbapenem resistance relative to national benchmarks warrants multi-center, consumption-linked confirmation.

Clinical Characteristics, 90-Day Functional Outcomes, Antimicrobial Susceptibility, and Exploratory Genomic Analysis of Invasive Human Streptococcus suis Infection: A Multicenter Retrospective Study in China.
BACKGROUND: Streptococcus suis is a zoonotic pathogen; survivors of invasive infection may have persistent auditory or vestibular sequelae. To address limited multicenter evidence from China, we characterized 90-day outcomes, antimicrobial susceptibility, and exploratory genomic findings. METHODS: We retrospectively studied 34 patients with invasive S. suis infection at eight hospitals in four Chinese provinces (2017-2025). Unfavorable outcome was defined as death within 90 days or persistent sequelae at day 90. Minimum inhibitory concentrations were reinterpreted using CLSI viridans-group streptococcal surrogate breakpoints; six recoverable isolates underwent whole-genome sequencing. RESULTS: Acute cochleovestibular involvement occurred in 11/27 (40.7%) patients with meningitis and 0/7 with nonmeningitic bacteremia/sepsis. Unfavorable outcomes occurred in 17/34 (50.0%) patients, including two deaths; 12/32 (37.5%) survivors had hearing-related sequelae. Acute cochleovestibular involvement was more frequent among patients with unfavorable outcomes (64.7% versus 0%; P < 0.001). All evaluable isolates were susceptible to penicillin (21/21), cefotaxime (19/19), and ceftriaxone (5/5). Resistance was observed in 17/20, 16/20, and 20/20 isolates tested for erythromycin, clindamycin, and tetracycline, respectively. Sequence types were ST1 (n = 3), ST7 (n = 2), and ST25 (n = 1); epf and sly were each detected in five isolates, and mrp in four. CONCLUSIONS: Substantial hearing-related morbidity supports structured audiological follow-up. Clinical associations and genomic findings remain exploratory and do not establish independent prognostic value or genotype-phenotype causality.

A Link Between Immunoglobulin M Levels and Overwhelming Post-Splenectomy Infection Risk in a National Asplenia Cohort.
BACKGROUND: Overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI) is a rare complication of asplenia that is frequently fatal. OPSI risk remains elevated in patients with asplenia who receive the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP)-recommended vaccines, suggesting additional variables influence OPSI risk. OBJECTIVE: To identify clinical and immunologic factors associated with OPSI in individuals with anatomic or functional asplenia. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was conducted of 2,992 individuals with physician-confirmed anatomic or functional asplenia and identified 47 OPSI cases. Demographic, clinical, and laboratory variables were analyzed to identify independent risk factors for OPSI. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis assessed predictive values of immunoglobulin levels, and time from asplenia index date to OPSI was summarized among cases. RESULTS: Streptococcus pneumoniae accounted for 89% of OPSI episodes. Prior to OPSI, most patients had documented receipt of asplenia-targeted vaccines corresponding to the bacterial species causing their specific infections. IgM <61.5 mg/dL was present in 86.7% (39/45) and 15.0% (164/1093) of patients with and without OPSI, respectively (p<0.001). In adjusted analysis, IgM <61.5 mg/dL (aOR 26.05 [9.28-73.13], p<0.001) was associated with OPSI. Serum IgM discriminated between patients with and without (AUC 0.92) with a cutoff of <61.5 mg/dL demonstrating an 86.7% sensitivity and 85.0% specificity for OPSI. CONCLUSION: Low serum IgM was strongly associated with OPSI and may help identify patients requiring closer surveillance and management.

Cholera rapid diagnostic test performance at the host-microbe interface: a prospective longitudinal study in Bangladesh.
BACKGROUND: Effective cholera outbreak response requires accurate bedside rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) because of poor laboratory access. Formative studies suggest that cholera diagnostics have multiple vulnerabilities, including target degradation by virulent bacteriophage (phage) specific to Vibrio cholerae and antibiotics. Our study objectives were to evaluate the performance of RDTs as a function of these antimicrobials to improve deployment and guide future diagnostic development. METHODS: In this prospective longitudinal study, participants were enrolled at seven hospitals across Bangladesh from March 13, 2018, to April 9, 2019. Inclusion criteria were participants aged 2 months or older with uncomplicated diarrhoeal disease. Exclusion criteria were the presence of severe comorbidity or the absence of participant or guardian consent or assent. Stool samples were analysed using culture, quantitative PCR (qPCR), and mass spectrometry. The primary outcome was RDT performance (eg, sensitivity and specificity) as a function of phage detection. Exploratory outcomes were the effects of antibiotics and disease severity on RDT performance. FINDINGS: 2574 participants were enrolled, and for 2078 samples, all assays were completed for analysis of the primary outcome. 394 samples without RDT data and 102 samples without qPCR data were excluded. Using the current gold standard of culture or qPCR positivity for V cholerae, we found that phage detection had no effect on RDT performance. When the diagnostic criteria were expanded to include phage detection, RDT sensitivity decreased from 0·46 (95% CI 0·41-0·51) to 0·38 (0·34-0·43), and the odds of RDT positivity among patients with cholera decreased with phage exposure (odds ratio 0·428; 95% CI 0·296-0·613). Antibiotics were detected in more than 80% of samples using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, limiting assessment of their effects on RDT performance. Among patients with moderate and severe dehydration, large increases in sensitivity and specificity were observed. We estimated that restricting RDT use to patients with severe dehydration and no reported antibiotic exposure increased sensitivity by 50% compared with unrestricted RDT use. If the presence of phage is considered a diagnostic proxy for V cholerae infection, then RDTs might not detect an additional 17% of cholera cases. INTERPRETATION: Cholera RDTs have limitations that require consideration during global deployments. Inclusion of phage detection in diagnostic criteria might improve case detection, although this requires further research in diverse settings. The implications of these findings likely extend to other diseases in which diagnostics share similar vulnerabilities. FUNDING: Wellcome Trust (DFID grant), NIH, and Thrasher Research Fund.

Phylogeographical structure and genetic introgression in Salmonella enterica serotype Napoli: a genomic epidemiology study.
BACKGROUND: Salmonella enterica serotype Napoli (S Napoli), a non-typhoidal Salmonella serotype that has been emerging in Italy, Switzerland, and France since the mid-1990s, has an unusual epidemiological profile that suggests a role for the environment in the transmission of these bacteria. The genomics of S Napoli has been inadequately characterised; we, therefore, aimed to provide a robust genomic framework for S Napoli surveillance. METHODS: In this genomic epidemiology study, we performed short-read sequencing of 1145 S Napoli isolates from national surveillance in four European countries (Italy, Switzerland, France, and Spain) and complemented this dataset with 175 additional genomes (174 published and one unpublished). We used the EnteroBase core genome multilocus sequence typing (cgMLST) scheme and its associated Hierarchical Clustering algorithm, along with other genome-based bioinformatics approaches such as single nucleotide variant-based phylogenetic analyses, ResFinder, PlasmidFinder, and RefSeq genomes, to characterise population structure, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) prevalence, and differences in gene content among genetic lineages. FINDINGS: We analysed 1320 S Napoli genomes, collected between April, 1945, and September 14, 2022, from human (n=1088, 82·4%) and non-human (n=232, 17·6%) sources in Italy (n=317, 24%), Switzerland (n=181, 13·7%), France (n=773, 58·5%), and Spain (n=48, 3·6%), confirming that the rising prevalence of S Napoli is driven by a single monophyletic serotype within cgMLST superlineage HC2000_1289. However, this serotype displays considerable genetic diversity (15 lineages falling into 12 HC900 clusters), strong spatial structuring, and a low frequency (2%) of AMR determinants. We also detected genetic introgression between S Napoli and the sympatric, closely related Salmonella enterica serotype Veneziana. INTERPRETATION: Unlike successful non-typhoidal Salmonella serotypes, for which globalisation has had a homogenising effect, S Napoli forms distinct lineages isolated by geographical distance. This study suggests that the persistence of S Napoli as a geographically structured metapopulation, causing localised human infections, could reflect the natural ecology of Salmonella before the rise of agribusiness. Future research should investigate the environmental reservoirs and transmission pathways of S Napoli. FUNDING: Fondation Le Roch-Les Mousquetaires, Institut Pasteur, Santé publique France, Investissement d'Avenir programme, Laboratoire d'Excellence 'Integrative Biology of Emerging Infectious Diseases', and Institute of Health Carlos III 'Acción Estratégica de Salud Intramural'.

Q fever in Spain: Epidemiology and demographic characteristics of hospitalized patients (2016-2023).
BACKGROUND: Q fever, caused by Coxiella burnetii, is a zoonosis with significant public health implications. This study described the epidemiology, demographic and clinical characteristics, clinical and hospitalization burdens, and geographical distribution of hospitalized Q fever patients in Spain from 2016 to 2023. METHODS: We conducted a nationwide, retrospective study using a nationwide registry between 2016 and 2023. We analyzed temporal trends, demographic data, comorbidities, complications, and mortality. RESULTS: We identified 3358 hospitalizations for Q fever, representing an overall hospitalization rate of 0.89 per 100,000 population. The median patient age was 56 years, and the cohort was predominantly male (72%). The median hospital length of stay was 9 days (IQR 6-15). The overall mortality rate was 2.4%. The most common complication was pneumonia (32%). The highest hospitalization rates in the Canary Islands, and La Rioja. CONCLUSION: The risk of hospitalization increases with age and the presence of predisposing conditions. The marked regional heterogeneity and high frequency of complications such as pneumonia underscore the need for enhanced surveillance and a strengthened One Health approach to control this zoonosis.

Dual activities of lysis and capsule degradation enable the bacteriophage protein Lys33795 to effectively disrupt Streptococcus suis biofilms.
Streptococcus suis (S. suis) is an encapsulated zoonotic pathogen that can form recalcitrant biofilms. Bacteriophage-derived endolysins and depolymerases represent promising antibiofilm agents, but currently, no report has described protein which displays both of lytic and capsule degradation activities simultaneously. Here, we mined the porcine gut virome and identified Lys33795, a dual-activity antibacterial protein that degrades both capsule and peptidoglycan of S. suis. Lys33795 consists of an N-terminal GH25_muramidase domain and a C-terminal cell wall binding domain (CBD). However, translational reinitiation at an internal start codon (M217) in the Lys33795 sequence generates an additional CBD that may assembles with the full-length protein to form an oligomeric complex. Interestingly, the GH25 muramidase truncation fragment of Lys33795 not only retains its classical function as a peptidoglycan hydrolase for degrading bacterial cell walls but also exhibits degradation activity towards capsule. This discovery contrasts sharply with the traditional functional understanding of the GH25 family. In addition, the CBD alone has a stable dimer and, as a nonstandard depolymerase without any classical polysaccharide-degrading catalytic domains, retains its degradation activity against S. suis capsule. We elucidated the molecular mechanism of Lys33795 exhibiting dual activity by combining mutagenesis, lysis, and capsule degradation activity assays. In addition, the results of in vitro and in vivo experiments showed that Lys33795 can effectively prevent and clear S. suis biofilms, and is more effective than single active mutants, and has a enhance effect when used in combination with antibiotics. This study describes the first multimeric bacteriophage protein with dual activities of lysis and capsule degradation against S. suis, encoded by a single gene. These findings provide valuable insights for designing potent antibacterial proteins targeting encapsulated pathogens.

Efficacy and safety of fluoroquinolones in the treatment of human brucellosis: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
INTRODUCTION: Brucellosis is a major zoonotic infection worldwide, with the highest burden reported in the Mediterranean region. The therapeutic role of fluoroquinolones in this disease continues to be controversial. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of fluoroquinolone-containing regimens compared with standard non-fluoroquinolone regimens for the treatment of human brucellosis. METHODS: In accordance with PRISMA recommendations, this systematic review and meta-analysis assessed the efficacy and safety of fluoroquinolone-based regimens for treating brucellosis. It was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251142019). A comprehensive search of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library was carried out, including studies published through August 2025. Randomized controlled trials comparing fluoroquinolones with conventional therapies (such as doxycycline with streptomycin or rifampicin) were included. Therapeutic failure, relapse, adverse events, and time to defervescence were the main outcomes. To compute pooled risk ratios and mean differences with 95%CIs, data were analyzed using STATA v18. The GRADE method and the RoB 2 tool were used to evaluate the risk of bias and the certainty of the evidence. RESULTS: The analysis comprised 9 clinical studies with 602 brucellosis patients. When compared to standard regimens, fluoroquinolone-based regimens were linked to a significantly higher risk of therapeutic failure (RR = 2.11, 95% CI: 1.26-3.51; P = 0.004) and a higher, though not statistically significant, risk of relapse (RR = 1.88, 95% CI: 0.94-3.74; P = 0.07). No statistically significant between-study heterogeneity was observed for either outcome (I² = 0%). Subgroup analyses showed a significantly increased risk of therapeutic failure in patients with uncomplicated brucellosis and in studies with treatment durations >8 weeks, although between-subgroup differences were not statistically significant. On the other hand, no statistically significant difference in adverse events was observed between fluoroquinolone-based and standard regimens under the random-effects model (RR = 0.62, 95% CI: 0.29-1.33; P = 0.22). Although the point estimate favored fluoroquinolone-based regimens, the confidence interval included the null effect. Fluoroquinolone-based regimens were also associated with a significantly longer time to defervescence compared with standard regimens (MD = 1.20 days, 95% CI: 0.66-1.74; P < 0.001). The certainty of evidence was moderate for therapeutic failure, and time to defervescence, and low for relapse and adverse events according to the GRADE evaluation. CONCLUSION: Compared with conventional doxycycline-based combinations, fluoroquinolone-based regimens were associated with a higher risk of therapeutic failure and longer time to defervescence, while the overall risk of relapse did not differ significantly. No significant difference in adverse events was observed with the random-effects model, although the point estimate favored fluoroquinolone-based regimens. Overall, these findings do not support the routine use of fluoroquinolones as first-line therapy for adult brucellosis. Further well-designed randomized controlled trials are needed.

Health, workforce, and cost trade-offs of HIV programme prioritization strategies in Malawi.
BACKGROUND: Malawi has achieved substantial progress towards HIV epidemic control, reaching the UNAIDS 95-95-95 targets. However, declining external financing and health-workforce constraints threaten sustainability. Programme reconfiguration is being considered to reduce resource use. METHODS: We used the Thanzi La Onse (TLO) individual-based health system simulation model to evaluate HIV programme changes in Malawi from 2025 to 2050. HIV testing, treatment monitoring, prevention interventions, and tuberculosis preventive therapy (TPT) were assessed individually and in combination, and compared against a Status Quo scenario with service delivery fixed at end-2024 levels. RESULTS: Changes that weakened diagnosis or treatment monitoring produced the largest adverse effects. Reducing HIV testing by 50% increased HIV/AIDS deaths by 55 200 (95% uncertainty interval 35 100-78 000) and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) by 3.28 million (2.41-4.54 million), while releasing 26.45 million healthcare-worker-hours and reducing total programme costs, including human resources for health and consumables, by USD 538.9 million. Removing viral load monitoring increased HIV/AIDS deaths by 21 460 (12 400-31 700) and DALYs by 1.17 million (0.58-1.69 million), with little change in workforce requirements but cost savings of USD 108.9 million. Reducing prevention services produced smaller savings with uncertain effects on mortality or DALYs. Combining reductions in testing, monitoring and prevention generated the largest cost savings (USD 812.0 million) but increased HIV infections by 1070 (990-1160), HIV/AIDS DALYs by 4.56 million (3.67-5.37 million) and AIDS deaths by 80 960 (66 240-93 640). CONCLUSION: Reducing HIV diagnosis or treatment monitoring risks undermining epidemic control. These services should be maintained if HIV programmes are reconfigured.

Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Parasitology: A holistic perspective from diagnosis to therapeutics.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being investigated to address challenges in parasite detection, disease surveillance, and therapeutic development. This narrative review examines current and emerging AI applications in parasitology across diagnostics, drug discovery, genomics, epidemiology, education, and public health decision-making, with particular emphasis on diagnostic applications. Machine learning and deep learning methods support automated parasite detection, classification, and quantification in microscopic images, alongside medical image analysis and arthropod identification. Applications are discussed for malaria, leishmaniasis, schistosomiasis, cystic echinococcosis, soil-transmitted helminth infections, and intestinal protozoal infections. Beyond diagnosis, AI-assisted approaches support compound screening, drug repurposing, toxicity prediction, and prioritization of potential therapeutic targets. Genomic and transcriptomic analyses also offer opportunities to investigate parasite biology and predict drug resistance. Surveillance models may inform outbreak forecasting and targeted control, although their operational value requires evaluation in the intended settings. Educational applications remain emerging, and the benefits of digital learning should be distinguished from those attributable specifically to AI. Across these domains, performance on curated datasets does not establish clinical utility or generalizability. Major barriers include limited representative datasets, insufficient external and prospective validation, infrastructure constraints, and concerns regarding privacy, bias, and accountability. Future progress requires reproducible evaluation, experimental validation of therapeutic candidates, and assessment of clinical and public health benefits. AI is therefore best positioned as a complementary tool that supports parasitological expertise, with responsible implementation guided by transparency, equitable access, and human oversight.

The medical and surgery outcomes of pulmonary hydatid cyst disease: A 12-year multidisciplinary experience.
BACKGROUND: Pulmonary hydatid cyst disease (PHCD) remains a significant public health problem in endemic regions. AIMS: To evaluate the demographic, serological, radiological, and surgical characteristics of patients with PHCD and to identify factors associated with hepatic involvement and postoperative outcomes. METHODS: This retrospective study included 515 consecutive patients who underwent surgical treatment for PHCD at Dicle University Faculty of Medicine between 2013 and 2025. Demographic characteristics, cyst features, indirect fluorescent antibody (IFA) test results, concomitant hepatic involvement, surgical procedures, postoperative outcomes, and complications were analyzed. RESULTS: Among 515 patients, 275 (53.4%) were male and 240 (46.6%) were female. Female patients were significantly older than male patients (28.0 ± 18.0 vs. 23.8 ± 18.4 years, p = 0.002). Hepatic involvement was significantly associated with positive IFA test results (p < 0.001), bilateral pulmonary disease (p < 0.001), multiple pulmonary cysts (p < 0.001), female sex (p = 0.045), and left-sided pulmonary involvement (p = 0.019). Blood group distribution was not associated with hepatic involvement (p = 0.773), although IFA positivity differed significantly among ABO blood groups (p = 0.006). Larger cyst size was associated with longer hospital stay (r = 0.130, p = 0.003) and prolonged drainage duration (r = 0.094, p = 0.034). Perforated cysts were associated with increased hospital stay (r = 0.180, p < 0.001) and drainage duration (r = 0.139, p = 0.002). Pediatric patients had significantly larger cysts than adults (p = 0.007). CONCLUSIONS: Positive IFA results, multiple pulmonary cysts, and bilateral lung involvement are associated with concomitant hepatic hydatid disease. Cyst size and perforation status significantly influence postoperative recovery, particularly hospital stay and drainage duration. Surgical treatment provides excellent outcomes with low reoperation rates and no disease-related mortality in experienced centers.

Parasitic diseases of marine fishes and their impact on human health: focus on the Egyptian biosphere: A review.
Recently, food deficiency has become the most critical problem and a major global challenge. Rapid population growth requires increased food production to meet the resulting demand. High meat and chicken prices prompted the world to focus on fish production to meet ongoing food needs. Seafood is rich in vitamins, minerals, and omega-3s. Fish-borne parasitic diseases are primarily found in people in most countries, causing severe illness and death. This review article will focus on the most important parasites affecting marine fishes and the most popular parasitic diseases affecting fish globally and locally, with an overview of their effect on human health. The survey of the most effective parasitic species that could attack marine fish species found nine groups: protozoans, myxozoans, monogeneans, digeneans, cestodes, nematodes, acanthocephalans, hirudineans, and crustaceans. Each group has several species that can cause severe damage to hosts, depending on the site of parasitism, which may be external or internal. Most previous parasitic species could transfer to humans and cause severe illnesses, leading to death. Important zoonotic diseases caused by marine parasites, such as Protozoa (Amoebiasis, Giardiasis, Cryptosporidiosis, Toxoplasmosis, and Microsporidiasis), could affect humans in two ways: through fish handling or through consumption of contaminated fishmeal containing protozoal cysts. The common signs appear as severe abdominal pains combined with general weakness and weight loss. Helminths, the largest group of zoonotic parasite species, cause severe damage to their final hosts, humans. Diagnosing such infections usually involves identifying the eggs, which are considered diagnostic when released with feces. The appropriate treatment of zoonotic parasites usually depends on the parasite species; intestinal disinfectants are recommended for mild infections, while anthelmintic drugs are recommended for severe cases. Surgical ablations are necessary if the infections are uncontrolled and life-threatening.

Lonely, but not the same: Exploring associations of emotional and social loneliness with psychological distress in older adults - A gendered perspective.
Emotional and social loneliness contribute to psychological distress in older adults. Gender differences may moderate these associations. This study investigates how emotional/social loneliness and gender relate to psychological distress. A postal survey was conducted with 3108 older adults (>60 years) in Erlangen, Germany, using Kessler Psychological Distress Scale, De Jong Gierveld Loneliness Scale, and additional psychosocial/health measures. Multiple regressions examined associations between psychological distress and loneliness, gender and psychosocial/health factors. The regression model explained 45% of psychological distress variance (adjusted R2 = 0.449). Emotional and social loneliness, satisfaction with life, changes in psychological and physical health, and access to routine medical care were significant predictors for psychological distress. A gender interaction showed a stronger association between emotional loneliness and psychological distress for women; no such interaction was found for social loneliness. These findings underscore the importance of gender-sensitive interventions targeting emotional loneliness to reduce psychological distress.

Strategies to strengthen childhood vaccination uptake: a qualitative study exploring Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander families' perspectives.
INTRODUCTION: Childhood vaccination is a highly cost-effective public health strategy, yet routine immunisation rates have declined yearly across Australia since the COVID-19 pandemic, especially among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children. Survey instruments used to understand drivers of vaccination have not been developed with or validated for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and families and may not reflect their lived experiences or priorities. This study aimed to understand factors shaping access to and acceptance of childhood vaccination from Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander family perspectives to inform targeted strategies and potential culturally appropriate survey tools. METHODS: Family focus groups were conducted in the Hunter New England region of New South Wales and the Northern Territory with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander parents and carers of children aged 5 years and under. Indigenous social and research yarning methods were used to explore families' views and experiences of childhood vaccination. Data were analysed using inductive content analysis led by Aboriginal researchers to ensure cultural integrity and uphold Indigenous data governance principles. RESULTS: Families participating in the study generally expressed support for routine childhood vaccination as a way of protecting children. Negative experiences and misinformation during COVID-19 increased concerns about adult vaccines, while participants generally remained supportive of routine childhood vaccination. Findings are presented across four key domains: (i) vaccine knowledge and information sources, participants wanted clearer, culturally relevant information explaining the diseases and how vaccines work in plain English and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages; (ii) vaccine decision-making, trust was strengthened through cultural connection, continuity of care and respectful communication with healthcare workers; (iii) access barriers, including restricted clinic hours, inflexible booking systems, miscommunication and transport difficulties; and (iv) strategies to improve access, including reminder and recall systems, outreach services and transport support. CONCLUSIONS: Families described a range of structural and health service barriers that made childhood vaccination harder to access, highlighting that childhood vaccination coverage is shaped by more than attitudes towards vaccines. Improving childhood immunisation coverage requires culturally grounded communication that puts families at the centre, builds trust with healthcare providers and addresses structural access barriers.

Inflammatory Biomarkers as Predictors of In-Hospital Mortality in Critically Ill COVID-19 Patients: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
BACKGROUND AND AIM: Inflammatory biomarkers have been proposed as prognostic indicators in COVID-19; however, their prognostic associations within critically ill ICU-admitted patients remain of interest. This study aimed to evaluate the associations of selected inflammatory biomarkers with in-hospital mortality and their discriminatory performance among critically ill COVID-19 patients. METHODS: In this retrospective cohort study, 244 adult patients with confirmed COVID-19 pneumonia admitted to the ICU between August 2020 and June 2021 were analyzed. Disease severity was assessed using the ISARIC 4 C Mortality Score. Associations between inflammatory biomarkers and mortality were evaluated using univariable and multivariable logistic regression, and discriminatory performance was assessed using ROC curve analysis. RESULTS: The in-hospital mortality rate was 90.6%. ESR and LDH levels were significantly higher in non-survivors. In a biomarker-restricted multivariable logistic regression model, ESR (OR 1.023 per 1 mm/h increase; 95% CI 1.004-1.042; p = 0.016) and LDH (OR 1.002 per 1 U/L increase; 95% CI 1.000-1.003; p = 0.009) remained significantly associated with in-hospital mortality after mutual adjustment for the other prespecified inflammatory biomarkers. LDH demonstrated good discriminatory performance (AUC 0.725; 95% CI 0.645-0.805). ESR showed modest discriminatory performance (AUC 0.646; 95% CI 0.559-0.732). CONCLUSION: ESR and LDH remained significantly associated with in-hospital mortality after adjustment for the other prespecified inflammatory biomarkers. These findings suggest that ESR and LDH may provide adjunctive prognostic information in critically ill ICU patients; however, they should be interpreted in the context of the biomarker-restricted model and the limited adjustment set. Confirmation in larger prospective studies incorporating established clinical prognostic factors is warranted.

Impact of COVID-19 restrictions on emergency bellwether procedures in South and Southeast Asia.
INTRODUCTION: Around the time COVID-19 was declared a global pandemic, various restrictions and measures were implemented at all levels to limit disease spread and preserve healthcare capacity. Data are lacking in many low- and middle-income countries on how these measures impact healthcare utilisation and outcomes. This study aims to determine the impact of COVID-19 restrictions on volumes of the three emergency bellwether procedures in South and Southeast Asia. METHODS: This was an interrupted time series study of patients who underwent any of the three emergency bellwether procedures (caesarean section, laparotomy and open fracture fixation) from 1 January 2018 to 31 December 2021 at one of eight institutions in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, India and Vietnam. We compared the weekly volumes, baseline characteristics and outcomes of each procedure across different time periods in each institution defined by different levels of COVID-19 restrictions using selected indicators from a city-level and hospital-level response index. RESULTS: Weekly volumes of emergency caesarean section decreased significantly in Guwahati Neurological Research Centre (GNRC) (p=1.62×10-5) and Ulin General Hospital (UGH) (p<2.2×10-16) but increased in Adam Malik Hospital (AMH) (p=1.45×10-5). For laparotomies, volume increased in Singapore General Hospital (p=2.38×10-5) but decreased in Military Hospital 175 (p=6.30×10-7). The volume of open fracture fixations decreased in GNRC (p=3.08×10-8), AMH (p=1.68×10-6) and UGH (p=8.15×10-6). CONCLUSIONS: COVID-19 restrictions on the city and hospital level were associated with a decrease in surgical volumes of the three bellwether procedures in some of the institutions. There was some suggestion of surgical capacity limitations in UGH and Military Hospital 175 during periods of more stringent COVID-19 restrictions.

Urotensin II: A Key Role in Hormonal and Inflammatory Cytokine Regulation in COVID-19 Patients.
The COVID-19 pandemic exhibits a wide spectrum of severities and pathophysiological mechanisms. The virus targets angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptors, disrupting the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) balance, which may explain various symptoms and risk factors. Fibrosis of the small airways is pivotal in the emergence of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Understanding these complex pathophysiological mechanisms is crucial for developing effective treatments and personalized approaches for COVID-19 patients. The present study is aimed at analyzing the concentrations of the clinical and laboratory parameters-such as hematological, biochemical, serological, angiotensin II (ANG II), endothelin-1 (ET-1), urotensin II (UII), and cortisol parameters-in patients with SARS-CoV-2 and evaluating the elevation of these parameters related to the pathogenicity. The study included two distinct groups: a healthy control group (n = 25) and a COVID-19 patient group (n = 75) during the period from August 2021 to January 2022. Cytokine levels were evaluated using commercially available enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits. The comparative analysis revealed that severe cases of COVID-19 have a significant elevation in the concentrations of hematological, biochemical, serological, and hormonal levels such as ANG II, ET-1, UII, and cortisol, as well as a substantial decline in the concentration of LYM%, in comparison with mild cases of COVID-19 and the control groups. Based on these findings, we concluded that ET-1, ANG II, and UII may be associated with COVID-19 pathophysiology and are linked to endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and thrombosis.

Impact of SARS-CoV-2 vaccination on cancer trends: a nationwide interrupted time series study.
BACKGROUND: A recent population-based cohort study of Seoul residents in South Korea reported increased incidence of several cancers within one year of SARS-CoV-2 vaccination. We examined whether a short-term, population-level change in cancer incidence trends was detectable at the national vaccination rollout, using a design that does not compare vaccinated with unvaccinated individuals. METHODS: We conducted an interrupted time series analysis of Korea National Health Insurance Service data for 36,024,394 individuals born between 1955 and 2004, covering February 2011 to September 2025 (176 months). The intervention point was August 2021, when cumulative first-dose coverage exceeded 50%. Monthly incidence of 13 cancer categories defined by ICD-10 code ranges and of four site-specific cancers (stomach, colorectum, lung and prostate) was compared with counterfactual forecasts from ARIMA/SARIMA models, and segmented regression estimated immediate level and trend changes (significance threshold P < 0.01). The placement of the intervention point was varied from 0 to 18 months, and the resulting estimates were compared with those obtained at 30 placebo points in the pre-pandemic period. RESULTS: Overall, 89.3% of the population received at least one dose. No immediate level change (relative risk 0.923-1.072) or trend change (0.995-1.005) reached significance for any of the 13 categories, and none reached significance for the four site-specific cancers. Across the lag grid, 2.0% of estimates met the threshold, compared with 4.1% at placebo points. The 99% confidence limits excluded immediate increases larger than 8.9% to 23.0% across the 13 categories and 8.1% to 23.4% across the four site-specific cancers. CONCLUSIONS: The national SARS-CoV-2 vaccination rollout in South Korea was not accompanied by a detectable short-term, population-level change in cancer incidence trends over the 50 months that followed. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Not applicable.

Predictive and operational artificial intelligence in emergency radiology for early risk stratification in acute care settings: a scoping review.
INTRODUCTION: Emergency departments face increasing overcrowding, resulting in diagnostic delays, higher mortality, and rising healthcare costs. Early risk stratification is essential to optimise clinical decision-making. Although medical imaging plays a central role in initial assessment, workload pressures and operational constraints have driven the development of artificial intelligence (AI) tools to support triage and prioritisation in emergency radiology. OBJECTIVE: To map and synthesise evidence on the applications, performance, and limitations of AI in emergency radiology for early risk stratification in acute care. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A scoping review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidelines and Joanna Briggs Institute recommendations. The protocol was developed a priori and registered in the Open Science Framework. A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science identified studies published between 2015 and 2025 that evaluated AI applications in medical imaging in acute care settings. Evidence was synthesised using conceptual mapping and thematic analysis. RESULTS: Seventy-one studies were included. Computed tomography was the most frequently evaluated modality, followed by radiography and ultrasound. Major domains included neurovascular disease, acute cardiopulmonary conditions, trauma, COVID-19, and acute aortic syndromes. Studies reported high diagnostic performance and potential workflow benefits; however, evidence was predominantly retrospective and internally validated, with limited prospective evaluation, external validation, or evidence of improved patient-level outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: AI applications in emergency radiology show promising diagnostic and workflow-support capabilities. However, current evidence largely reflects early-stage development, with limited prospective validation, scarce real-world impact assessment, and insufficient evaluation of clinically meaningful outcomes. KEY POINTS: Question How clinically mature are AI applications designed to support early risk stratification and prioritisation in time-sensitive emergency radiology workflows? Findings Most studies report high diagnostic performance in time-sensitive conditions, yet evidence remains predominantly retrospective with limited external validation or prospective real-world implementation. Clinical relevance AI may support earlier identification and prioritisation of critical imaging findings, but routine adoption requires prospective external validation and evidence of meaningful effects on clinical decisions and patient outcomes.
