Direct and indirect entomological efficacy of Targeted Indoor Residual Spraying against Aedes aegypti in Iquitos, Peru.
BACKGROUND: Control of Aedes aegypti, the primary vector of dengue and other Aedes-borne viruses, is challenged by insecticide resistance, limited efficacy of existing tools, and that control activities often occur in the context of large dengue epidemics that overwhelm control programs. Targeted Indoor Residual Spraying (TIRS), a modification of traditional indoor residual spraying focused on Ae. aegypti resting sites, has demonstrated promising results, yet its indirect community-wide effects remain underexplored. METHODOLOGY/PRINCIPAL FINDINGS: We conducted an entomological cluster-randomized controlled trial in Iquitos, Peru, to evaluate the direct and indirect entomological impacts of TIRS using pirimiphos-methyl. Thirty clusters were randomized to receive either TIRS (15 clusters, 898 structures) or standard Ministry of Health vector control activities (15 clusters, 1,018 structures). Aedes aegypti indoor densities were assessed in the 45 days pre-intervention and at four time points up to 255 days post-intervention using Prokopack aspiration. Generalized linear mixed models with a negative binomial link were used to estimate incidence rate ratios (IRRs) and calculate efficacy (1-IRR) for houses that received TIRS (direct effect) and untreated houses in TIRS clusters (indirect effect). Direct efficacy reached a 96% decrease in Ae. aegypti captured in sprayed houses at 15 days post-spraying and remained significant (40%) at 255 days post-spraying. Indirect efficacy reached 69% at 15 days and declined to 7% by 255 days post-spraying. Despite only 57% household-level TIRS coverage, both direct and indirect impacts on Ae. aegypti were significant during early post-intervention surveys, and after 8 months in TIRS clusters. CONCLUSIONS/SIGNIFICANCE: TIRS provided substantial and sustained reductions in indoor Ae. aegypti density, including measurable indirect effects in untreated homes within intervention clusters. These findings demonstrate the entomological value of TIRS even at moderate coverage levels and highlight its potential for both preventive and reactive vector control programs and should be considered for implementation by Ministries of Health in dengue-endemic urban settings as well as by the U.S. military when deployed to tropical or subtropical locations.

Temporal trends in reported vector-borne diseases in China before and after the onset of COVID-19 from 2004 to 2023.
BACKGROUND: Vector-borne diseases (VBDs) continue to pose a public health burden in China. However, changes in the reported incidence and mortality of VBDs during the COVID-19 period remain insufficiently characterized. METHODS: We analyzed five major VBDs-typhus, dengue, leishmaniasis, malaria, and epidemic encephalitis B (EEB)-in China from 2004 to 2023. Province- and age-specific surveillance data for 2004-2020 were obtained from the Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention, whereas national aggregate data for 2021-2023 were obtained from the National Health Commission. Accordingly, spatial and age-specific analyses were restricted to 2004-2020, while national trend analyses were extended through 2023. Annual trends were evaluated using Joinpoint regression, monthly seasonal patterns were assessed using STL decomposition, monthly changes after January 2020 were evaluated using interrupted time-series analysis, and expected monthly trajectories for 2020-2023 were estimated using SARIMA models trained on pre-COVID data. RESULTS: From 2004 to 2020, incidence and mortality of VBDs declined significantly, especially for malaria, dengue, and EEB, and spatial hotspots were concentrated mainly in southern provinces. Compared with 2013-2019, overall incidence and mortality during 2020-2023 were 59.86% lower (95% CI: -60.36 to -59.36; P < 0.001) and 83.72% lower (95% CI: -87.86 to -78.18; P < 0.001), respectively. Malaria and EEB showed the largest reductions, whereas typhus and leishmaniasis changed less markedly. However, these declines should be interpreted cautiously because they may reflect a combination of COVID-19-era public health measures, pre-existing long-term trends, disease-specific control programs, and possible surveillance disruption. CONCLUSIONS: During the COVID-19 period in China, reported VBD incidence and mortality decreased substantially. However, it would be overly simplistic to attribute these changes entirely to COVID-19-related interventions, as other factors were also likely involved. These findings highlight the need for reliable surveillance and reporting during public health emergencies, together with forecasting tools that can be adapted to changing conditions, to support future vector-borne disease control.

Global and regional burden of measles and vaccine coverage among children under 5 years, 1990-2023: a Global Burden of Disease Study.
Measles remains a leading cause of vaccine-preventable burden among children, particularly in low-income settings. Despite decades of progress, there are indications of measles resurgence due to stagnation in vaccine coverage. Here, using the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries and Risk Factors Study (GBD) 2023, we systematically assessed measles incidence, mortality, disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) and vaccine coverage (measles-containing vaccine 1 (MCV1) and measles-containing vaccine 2 (MCV2)) among children under 5 years of age across 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023. Between 1990 and 2019, global measles incidence and mortality declined by approximately 80% and 90%, respectively, but rebounded sharply after 2020, with 15.6 million cases and 118,000 deaths estimated in 2023 (+40% and +12% increases, respectively, between 2019 and 2023). Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia continue to bear the highest burden. Global MCV1 coverage rose from 67.2% in 1990 to 83.6% in 2019 but stalled and declined slightly to 81.0% by 2023; MCV2 coverage increased from 14.4% in 1990 to 68.4% in 2019 and reached 71.4% by 2023. Several regions remain well below the Immunization Agenda 2030 (IA2030) target of 90% coverage. The recent measles resurgence underscores the fragility of global immunization progress and the urgent need to restore routine vaccination, close immunity gaps and strengthen outbreak preparedness.

Analytical Validation of MethyLiverDx-Sigma, a Plasma cfDNA Methylation Assay for Hepatocellular Carcinoma Detection.
Hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance relies on ultrasonography and alpha-fetoprotein, both limited in sensitivity for early-stage disease; aberrant methylation of circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) offers a promising blood-based approach. Reported here is the analytical validation of MethyLiverDx-Sigma (MLDx-s), an assay that detects methylated RNF135 and DNMT3A in bisulfite-converted plasma cfDNA by methylation-specific PCR with high-resolution melting (HRM), with GAPDH as an endogenous control. Performance was evaluated following CLSI EP05-A3, EP07, EP12-A2, and EP37. Precision of quantification cycle (Cq) and melting peak temperature (Tm) was assessed by variance-component analysis within one site and across two sites and two operators. Because precision studies used bulk bisulfite-converted reference DNA, the reported coefficients of variation (CVs) primarily characterize the PCR-HRM detection module; end-to-end variability in clinical plasma specimens may be higher. Interference and cross-reactivity were evaluated in low-positive and contrived-negative samples against reproducibility-derived limits, with dose-response testing of reactive substances. Detection was 100% at both levels, and every run met control-validity criteria. Cq repeatability CVs ranged from 0.53% to 1.68%, and total reproducibility CVs ranged from 1.10% to 2.37%; all Tm CVs were ≤0.20%. All 18 interferents and 16 microbial cross-reactants evaluated in low-positive samples met the predefined acceptance criteria. In negative samples, hemoglobin, SARS-CoV-2, and measles virus produced concentration-dependent non-specific amplification, and dose-response testing established their respective no-effect concentrations. These findings characterize the analytical precision and multisite reproducibility of the PCR-HRM detection module and the analytical specificity of MLDx-s, complementing its previously reported clinical performance for plasma-based HCC detection.

Global mpox outbreak dynamics during and after the 2024-2026 public health emergency.
The second WHO Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) for mpox was declared on 14 August 2024 after clade Ib monkeypox virus emerged in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and spread rapidly across Africa and internationally. The PHEIC ended on 5 September 2025, and the Africa CDC Public Health Emergency of Continental Security was lifted on 22 January 2026. This study characterised global and Africa-specific mpox epidemiology across the full second PHEIC cycle and immediate post-emergency period, from January 2024 to February 2026. A retrospective surveillance analysis was conducted using the WHO Global Mpox Trends dashboard exported data, supplemented by WHO situation reports S32-S64 and international and national surveillance reports. Analyses included negative binomial segmented regression, travel-linked pathway analysis, exploratory analysis of documented secondary transmission after travel-linked detection, and descriptive statistics. Models used reported case counts with log population offsets; reported case-rate ratios therefore reflect reported case rates rather than true infection incidence. Between January 2024 and February 2026, 82,738 confirmed cases and 306 deaths were reported to WHO globally (case fatality ratio 0.37%). The PHEIC period accounted for 74.0% of cases, peaking at 7,405 cases in May 2025. In total, 163 clade-specific importation or travel-linked detection events were documented across 41 countries within the primary analytic cutoff; documented secondary transmission occurred in 25 (15.3%) events across 16 countries. Within DRC, 200 health zones recorded 144,035 total reported cases and 2,047 deaths (case fatality ratio 1.42%); these aggregate suspected/clinically compatible and confirmed cases. The top 20 health zones accounted for 45.4% of national burden. Reported transmission declined after the May 2025 peak but persisted beyond PHEIC termination. Emergency termination marked an administrative transition, not the end of mpox transmission. The post-emergency period requires sustained surveillance, maintained diagnostic capacity, targeted response in persistent transmission settings, and equitable access to vaccines and countermeasures.

Characterization of norovirus GI.3 and GII.12 variants detected in wastewater: proof-of-concept for integrating phenotypic insights in wastewater-based epidemiology.
UNLABELLED: Norovirus is the leading cause of acute gastroenteritis, responsible for 685 million cases and 200,000 deaths annually. Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) enables not only global surveillance of dominant strains but also the detection of cryptic and emerging viral variants. An important question, however, is how to link genomic diversity to clinical impact and phenotypic traits of the strains detected in wastewater. In the Global Urban Wastewater Project, phylogenetically distinct norovirus GI.3 and GII.12 lineages were detected in wastewater from Cameroon. In this study, we characterized their host- and tissue-binding specificity and antigenic makeup in comparison with other GI.3 and GII.12 lineages using a luciferase immunoprecipitation system-based assay, alongside sequence analysis of the VP1 P2 subdomain. We observed intra-genotype variation among GI.3 variants. GI.3 Cameroon/2017 shared phenotypes with its closest reference strain (GI.3 Mexico/2016), and their histo-blood group antigen (HBGA)-binding profiles suggested a narrower susceptible population compared to other GI.3 lineages. Conversely, GII.12 strains showed no significant differences in HBGA binding, antigenic profiles, and tissue attachment. Together, these results reveal distinct patterns of phenotypic diversity between the two genotypes. While GI.3 variants exhibited lineage-specific traits, the GII.12 strains appeared phenotypically conserved across lineages. These findings highlight the feasibility and importance of integrating phenotypic analysis with WBE to assess potential public health risks posed by novel viral variants. IMPORTANCE: While detection of norovirus through case-based surveillance is limited to variants causing symptomatic infection, wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) allows for detection of cryptic and emerging variants. However, validation, such as phenotypic characterization, is needed to assess the clinical importance of a variant detected in WBE. In this study, we investigated the phenotypic traits of genetically distinct GI.3 and GII.12 lineages detected in wastewater from Cameroon. We utilized NanoLuc luciferase immunoprecipitation system (N-LIPS)-based assays to assess binding specificity and antigenicity. Compared to traditional methods involving virus isolation and virus-like particle production, N-LIPS-based assays are considerably less laborious and faster. This allows for rapid characterization of novel variants, making the timely assessment of phenotypic changes of such variants for outbreak or pandemic preparedness feasible. Finally, by integrating insights from phenotypic assays, we showed the possibility of expanding the public health value of wastewater surveillance in assessing the risk of novel viral variants.

End-of-life care of patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and home mechanical ventilation: the national population-based DISCOVERY study.
Background: Home mechanical ventilation (HMV), including noninvasive ventilation (NIV) and invasive ventilation (IV), is increasingly used in people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (pwALS), but its impact on end-of-life care remains unclear. Objective: To examine whether ventilation pathway (NIV or IV) influences symptom prevalence and relief during the final week of life in pwALS. Secondary objectives were to assess end-of-life discussions, place and cause of death, and anticipated death. Methods: This national, population-based retrospective cohort study included pwALS using HMV in the Swedish National Quality Registry for Respiratory Failure (Swedevox), cross-linked with the Swedish Register of Palliative Care, which contains staff-reported end-of-life data, and other national registries. Results: Among 652 pwALS, 609 received NIV (mean age 66 years, 42% female) and 43 IV (mean age 60 years, 42% female). Anxiety and breathlessness were more common in the NIV group (76% vs 48% and 72% vs 31%, both p < 0.001), while prevalence and relief of other symptoms were similar between groups. Most patients had end-of-life discussions (NIV 87%, IV 92%). NIV patients more often died in specialized palliative wards (22% vs 7%, p = 0.023). Most deaths were due to ALS (96%) and were anticipated (NIV 94%, IV 88%). Conclusions: In pwALS with HVM, NIV was associated with higher rates of anxiety and breathlessness in the final week of life, but the ventilation pathway did not influence overall symptom relief. End-of-life communications and cause of death were similar; place of death differed by ventilation pathway; however, most deaths were anticipated.

Association of advanced age with liver function and inflammatory response in patients with malaria in Luanda, Angola.
Malaria remains a leading cause of mortality in sub-Saharan Africa, yet its clinical profile in older adults is poorly characterised. We therefore conducted a cross-sectional study of 518 hospitalised malaria patients aged ≤50 and >50 years in Luanda, Angola, between January 2023 and December 2024, comparing liver function, inflammatory markers, and leucocyte parameters. Older adults represented 9.8% of patients. Parasitaemia, sex, residence, and HbS genotype did not differ by age group. Older adults however showed distinct liver biomarker profiles, lower C-reactive protein positivity, lower inflammatory scores, and higher lymphocyte counts despite similar parasite density. Moderate and high inflammatory scores were inversely associated with advanced age, whereas lymphocyte count was positively associated, thus supporting the need for age-adapted clinical assessment, monitoring, and management strategies to improve outcomes in malaria.

Sevuparin in children with severe malaria: a phase I safety and dose-finding trial.
Mortality rates for African children with severe malaria remain high. Sevuparin, a heparin-like compound, as an adjunctive treatment, may improve outcomes due to its effects on Plasmodium falciparum-infected erythrocytes. A Phase I dose-finding trial in Kenyan and Zambian children with severe malaria aimed to identify the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) of sevuparin, given as three infusions (at 0, 8 and 16 h post-enrolment) using the continual reassessment method (ISRCTN32271864). The primary endpoint was dose limiting toxicity (DLT) defined as Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT) > 95 seconds (2.5x upper limit of normal) across 1.5-6 mg/kg doses. Secondary endpoints were lactate clearance, parasite half-life, APTT at 24 h and grade 3-4 serious adverse events. Twenty-three children were enroled; 20 were included in the primary analysis, across 10 cohorts. A data monitoring committee followed model recommendations, leading to dose escalation from 1.5 mg/kg through all doses to 6 mg/kg when 2 DLTs occurred. During de-escalation, DLTs occurred at 5 mg/kg and 4 mg/kg. The final dose was therefore 3 mg/kg. There was 1 death (1/23 (4.3%)), 1 readmission and 1 grade 3 non-DLT adverse event: all judged unrelated to sevuparin. MTD of 3 mg/kg sevuparin in each of three infusions at 0, 8 and 16 h was identified for future investigation.

The growing repertoire of putative pathogen interaction genes in the Biomphalaria glabrata vs Schistosoma mansoni system.
Schistosomiasis is major neglected tropical disease of humans that is caused by trematodes in the genus Schistosoma. Humans are infected during contact with water in which schistosomes are being shed from their intermediate hosts, freshwater snails. Snail control is effective at reducing transmission, but can be expensive and ecologically problematic. Therefore, there is substantial interest in understanding the genetic mechanisms behind variation in snail resistance to infection by schistosomes, with the goal of leveraging that information to reduce transmission at the snail stage. Biomphalaria glabrata is an important host snail for transmission of S. mansoni in the New World. Here we reanalyzed an older Genome-Wide Association Study (GWAS) dataset from Biomphalaria glabrata snails challenged by the trematode, Schistosoma mansoni. We identified two new regions of association with resistance to infection, named LG5R and LG11L. LG11L contains a cluster of genes for a diverse set of secreted lectins, which could be involved in some type of recognition. LG5R contains a cluster of genes for what appear to be membrane-bound receptors. These genes are very similar to those identified in an adjacent genomic region by a recent GWAS on the African snail, B. sudanica challenged by S. mansoni. Clusters of genes for single-pass transmembrane proteins also characterize two other genomic regions of association with resistance to S. mansoni that were previously described for B. glabrata (the PTC1/GRC and PTC2 regions). We hypothesize that the proteins coded for in such clusters of genes are involved in some type of matching polymorphism that may explain the ubiquitous parasite-population by snail-population interaction in compatibility that characterizes the B. glabrata-S. mansoni system. We discuss our results in light of the state of the field of genome-wide mapping studies on Biomphalaria sp., and discuss what types of loci found to date would be the best targets for reducing transmission in natural populations.

Schistosoma haematobium infection among school age children in two peri-urban areas of Lusaka, Zambia: A cross-sectional study.
BACKGROUND: Schistosomiasis is one of the most prevalent neglected tropical diseases in sub-Saharan Africa, causing substantial morbidity and millions of disability-adjusted life years (DALYs). Although the WHO aims to eliminate schistosomiasis as a public health problem in several countries by 2030, current epidemiological data on schistosomiasis in Zambia are insufficient to adequately characterize transmission patterns, identify priority intervention areas, and inform the planning and evaluation of control programmes. METHODS: We assessed the prevalence of urogenital schistosomiasis among school-age children in two peri-urban districts of Lusaka (Chongwe and Kafue). A total of 208 participants were enrolled, and infection status was determined using urine filtration microscopy, ELISA, and quantitative PCR (qPCR). RESULTS: Urogenital schistosomiasis prevalence was significantly higher in Chongwe than in Kafue, as determined by both microscopy and qPCR. By microscopy, 34 of 48 positive cases (70.8%) were from Chongwe and 14 (29.2%) from Kafue (χ² = 4.84; P < 0.05). Similarly, qPCR revealed a prevalence of 73.9% in Chongwe and 28.9% in Kafue (χ² = 13.52; P < 0.01). No significant association was observed between sex and infection status. However, infection was significantly associated with age across the study population. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings demonstrate that urogenital schistosomiasis remains highly prevalent in the peri-urban districts of Chongwe and Kafue in Lusaka Province, Zambia, highlighting ongoing transmission and the need for strengthened surveillance and control efforts. These results provide updated information on the epidemiological situation of urogenital schistosomiasis in Zambia and will support planning and implementation within the WHO NTD agenda.

"I will not accept to bury my pig": Taenia solium, WASH, and gender roles in the smallholder pork value chain in Southern Province, Rwanda.
Taenia solium is a zoonotic cestode and the causative agent of human taeniasis/cysticercosis and porcine cysticercosis. The burden in Rwanda is significant, including death and disability in people and income losses across the pork sector. Despite widespread recognition on the need for multi-sectoral and inclusive T. solium control programming, little is known about water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) access and gendered disease exposure among rural smallholders involved in the formal and informal pork sectors. This study aimed to characterize gender roles and WASH access in the Nyamagabe District (Southern Province) pork value chain (PVC) to better inform future interventions for disrupting T. solium transmission. We conducted Focus Group Discussions with 23 men and 21 women across five nodes of the PVC (farmers, animal health workers, butchers, vendors, consumers) and interviewed six key informants. Audio-recordings were transcribed verbatim, translated into English and coded as part of inductive thematic analysis. PVC participants identified numerous biosecurity gaps in the Nyamagabe PVC, such as free-range pig production, re-use of human waste, lack of prevention services (deworming, vaccination), informal slaughter, and consumption of infected and/or undercooked pork. Traditional gender roles were prevalent, with women managing domestic roles related to pig husbandry and men managing roles related to building pens, buying/selling pigs and slaughtering/butchering. Water and sanitation facilities were frequently inadequate, causing serious lapses in human and pig hygiene. Participants identified poverty as a major barrier for implementing T. solium control but demonstrated enthusiasm for receiving information and resources to support this goal. Altogether, these findings support the need for One Health programming to reduce the burden of T. solium and other zoonotic diseases in people and pigs in Rwanda. Gendered norms among rural smallholders indicated a need for gender transformative information campaigns targeting specific recipients along the PVC nodes.

Dual colored phenotypic switching and interaction-driven heterogeneity in clonal Candida auris clinical isolates.
Candida auris is an emerging multidrug-resistant pathogen designated by the World Health Organization as a critical priority due to its persistence, transmissibility, and association with healthcare outbreaks. Despite its clinical significance, the contribution of phenotypic heterogeneity to pathogenicity and treatment response remains poorly understood. In this study, we identified dual white (W) and pink (P) morphotypes in seven of 278 clinical isolates screened on CHROMagar™ Candida Plus and characterized their genetic relatedness, antifungal susceptibility, and phenotypic switching behavior. Whole-genome sequencing and internal transcribed spacer (ITS) analyses confirmed that paired morphotypes were clonally related (0-57 SNPs divergence) and belonged to Clade I, indicating within-host diversification rather than co-infection with distinct strains. All isolates carried identical ERG11 Y132F mutations and wild-type FKS1 sequences across both morphotypes, demonstrating that morphotype variation occurs independently of primary antifungal resistance determinants. Phenotypic profiling demonstrated comparable resistance profiles and aggregation capacity between paired morphotypes, with pseudohyphal formation as the principal differential trait. Systematic switching analysis across CHROMagar, yeast peptone dextrose (YPD), and sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) under multiple temperature and population conditions identified three principal patterns: interaction-dependent switching, in which mixed subpopulations generated enhanced or novel phenotypes not reproduced in pure cultures; morphotype-driven switching, dominated by a single subpopulation; and intrinsic switching capacity retained independently by both morphotypes. Switching dynamics were strongly modulated by temperature, growth medium, and incubation duration. These findings establish phenotypic switching in C. auris as a dynamic, environmentally modulated process driven in part by intercellular interactions within clonal populations. This plasticity may contribute to persistence and virulence without altering antifungal resistance profiles, underscoring the need to recognize and separately evaluate distinct C. auris morphotypes for antifungal susceptibility, particularly in persistent or treatment-refractory infections.

Reaching the last mile towards malaria elimination in Chhattisgarh, India.
BACKGROUND OBJECTIVES: While malaria incidence has decreased across India, Chhattisgarh continues to harbour a major proportion of national caseloads. Within the 11-state Global Fund evaluation framework (37,976 households), this study evaluated community intervention utilization, care-seeking timelines, topographic road tortuosity, and spatial clustering in southern Chhattisgarh to guide last-mile elimination. METHODS: A multi-stage cross-sectional cluster survey evaluated 4,041 households (18,184 individuals) across 40 primary sampling units in five high-endemic districts (Bastar, Bijapur, Dantewada, Narayanpur, Sukma) during peak transmission. Spatial autocorrelation (Global Moran's I , LISA) and multivariable Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE) identified determinants of prompt care seeking, febrile morbidity, and confirmed malaria, incorporating geodesic distances and road tortuosity. RESULTS: Net ownership covered 93.3% (92.4% state-procured, 81.5% intact), sleeping compliance exceeded 97% in vulnerable groups, and 99.1% sought care at public facilities. Diagnostic blood testing reached 99.2% of febrile patients, with village Mitanins (ASHA workers) performing 60.4% of tests. Spatial clustering was confirmed (Moran's I = 0.539, p = 0.001), with 5 Low-Low cold spots in Bastar demonstrating transmission interruption feasibility. Conversely, IRS acceptance was 30.1%, and 28.8% of confirmed cases ceased radical cure prematurely due to symptom resolution (65.8%). Below Poverty Line status reduced prompt care seeking (< 24 hours) by 66% ( AOR = 0.34, p = 0.043), and road tortuosity averaged 1.44 (peaking at 2.78 in Dantewada). INTERPRETATION CONCLUSION: High commodity coverage coexists with care-seeking friction, premature treatment cessation, and focal clustering. Achieving elimination requires micro-stratified hotspot targeting, Mitanin-supervised directly observed therapy, terrain-calibrated mobile outreach, and wage-loss compensation.

Natural products shape microbial ecology and disease in the cystic fibrosis airway.
Covering up to 2026Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a life-shortening autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by mutation in the gene encoding the CF transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR). Dysfunction in CFTR leads to the accumulation of thick and dehydrated mucus in the respiratory tract, which serves as a substrate for a complex microbiota that includes commensal oral and respiratory bacteria and opportunistic pathogenic bacteria and fungi. During chronic infections, these microbes persist in the airways and contribute to progressive lung tissue damage, ultimately leading to respiratory failure and premature death. Within this environment, microbes synthesize a diverse repertoire of natural products, including antimicrobials, siderophores and other metallophores, signaling molecules, toxins, and other virulence factors. In this review, we thoroughly discuss natural products produced by members of the CF airway microbiota, primarily the bacterial pathogens Burkholderia spp., Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Staphylococcus aureus and the fungal pathogens Aspergillus fumigatus and Scedosporium spp. When known, we describe the biosynthesis and roles of these natural products in microbial persistence, interspecies interactions, and virulence in the CF airway. When these roles are unknown, we infer potential roles based on evidence from the literature in different disease contexts. Finally, we briefly highlight natural products produced by the CF microbiota as novel sources for developing new antimicrobials and as drug targets to treat disease.

Assessment of Candida attributes under in vitro repeated exposure to hydrogen peroxide.
Fungal infections have emerged as a significant concern in healthcare, due to the development of antifungal resistance and the limited availability of diagnostic and therapeutic options. The Candida species represent a category of particular importance with regard to fungi. Therefore, the implementation of infection prevention and control measures, such as hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) disinfection, is imperative in healthcare settings. In consideration of the existing literature, which demonstrates that repeated exposure to H2O2 does not compromise microbial tolerance to the disinfectant, the expression of virulence attributes may be altered under the influence of external selective pressure.The present study aims to evaluate the effect of repeated exposure to H2O2 on antifungal susceptibility profiles, catalase production, and biofilm formation on Candida strains in a phenotypic assessment of the microbial behaviour.In previous studies, strains of C. albicans, C. parapsilosis, and C. auris were repeatedly exposed to different H2O2 concentrations and evaluated for their susceptibility to the disinfectant over 30 days. The present study demonstrated that repeated exposure to H₂O₂ resulted only in minor fluctuations of the antifungal susceptibility of C. albicans and C. parapsilosis, but not of C. auris. Repeated exposure to H₂O₂ demonstrated no variation in catalase production or alteration in biofilm formation for the evaluated species.In conclusion, repeated exposure to H₂O₂ resulted in only minor fluctuations in antifungal susceptibility in C. albicans and C. parapsilosis strains, demonstrating that utilization of H2O2 as a daily disinfectant is safe in relation to microbial adaptation. However, environmental surveillance is advised to prevent the inadvertent development of antifungal resistance.

Molecular survey of zoonotic protozoa in free-ranging marmosets (Callithrix penicillata) from Central Brazil: implications for One Health surveillance.
Urban expansion and environmental fragmentation have intensified contact among wildlife, domestic animals, and humans, reshaping infectious disease dynamics at the human-wildlife interface. Non-human primates (NHP), particularly the black-tufted marmoset (Callithrix penicillata), readily adapt to anthropogenic landscapes and may serve as sentinel hosts for zoonotic pathogens. This study investigated the occurrence of Leishmania spp., Plasmodium spp., Toxoplasma gondii, and Trypanosoma cruzi. in 232 free-ranging C. penicillata found dead in urban and peri-urban areas of the Federal District, central Brazil, between 2018 and 2023. Liver samples were analyzed by quantitative PCR. Plasmodium spp. was not detected (0/232). In contrast, 39.7% (92/232) of marmosets were positive for T. gondii, 32.4% (69/213) for Leishmania spp., and 21.1% (47/223) for T. cruzi. Overall, 71.6% of the animals tested positive for at least one protozoan agent, and 21.2% had coinfections, most commonly Leishmania spp. plus T. gondii. Positive cases were widely distributed across administrative regions, with evidence of spatiotemporal clustering in some urbanized areas. Parasitic loads varied substantially, and most infected animals showed no lesions attributable to these infections. These findings demonstrate the widespread circulation of zoonotic protozoa in free-ranging marmosets inhabiting anthropized environments and reinforce their epidemiological relevance within a One Health framework. Surveillance of urban NHP populations can contribute to understanding transmission networks and environmental contamination, thereby supporting public health strategies for the prevention and control of zoonotic diseases in central Brazil.

Genomic dynamics and macrolide resistance in Bordetella pertussis: implications for surveillance and rapid visual detection.
BACKGROUND: The post-COVID-19 resurgence of pertussis has raised concerns regarding shifts in circulating Bordetella pertussis populations and increasing macrolide resistance. This study aims to characterize the population dynamics and clinically relevant genomic changes of B. pertussis in China and globally, and to develop a rapid visual assay for detecting the macrolide resistance-associated 23S rRNA A2047G mutation. METHODS: In this cross-sectional genomic epidemiology study, 22 recent clinical isolates were sequenced and analyzed with 7322 publicly available B. pertussis genomes. Global population structure was assessed using 7344 genomes, and Bayesian phylodynamic analysis was performed on 1054 temporally informative Chinese genomes selected from 1292 isolates collected during 1951-2024. We designed and optimized an allele-specific loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) assay incorporating a 3'-terminal artificial mismatch and a neutral red indicator for detection of the macrolide resistance-associated 23S rRNA A2047G mutation. Its analytical sensitivity and specificity were evaluated alongside quantitative PCR (qPCR) using serially diluted plasmids and 39 contrived DNA samples. RESULTS: The macrolide resistance of B. pertussis in China, defined by the 23S rRNA A2047G mutation, reached 98.9% (88/89; 95% CI 93.9-100) among available genomes in 2024, concurrent with the rapid clonal expansion of the ptxP3-MT28 sub-lineage. Among the available Chinese isolates, the proportion of predicted Prn-deficient strains increased to 31.46% in 2024, with 12 distinct prn inactivation mechanisms, predominantly IS481-mediated insertions. The optimized LAMP assay differentiated mutant and wild-type alleles within 50 min at 65°C, with a neutral red visual limit of detection (LOD) of 10 copies/μL, compared with 100 copies/μL for qPCR. The results of LAMP-based differentiation were consistent with those obtained by qPCR for all 39 contrived samples. CONCLUSIONS: B. pertussis populations have undergone marked genomic shifts characterized by antigenic variation and macrolide resistance, although the evolutionary drivers underlying these temporal and genomic patterns remain to be determined. The visual LAMP assay provides a proof-of-concept analytical evidence for rapid A2047G allele discrimination and may have future point-of-care potential following validation with prospective clinical respiratory specimens. These findings support continued genomic surveillance and further evaluation of vaccine antigen matching and antimicrobial resistance.

Antiviral activity of lapachol and synthetic hydroxynaphthoquinone derivatives against Mayaro virus.
The Mayaro virus (MAYV) is an arbovirus belonging to the Togaviridae family, genus Alphavirus. MAYV causes several sporadic outbreaks, affecting regions of the Americas. There are no specific antivirals for treating the disease. Therefore, studies are increasingly needed to discover effective antivirals against these neglected viruses. Thus, our study investigates the antiviral potential in vitro of a natural hydroxynaphthoquinone (QHM0001 - lapachol) and its synthetic derivatives (QHM0011, 0020 and 0110) against CMV-MAYV-nanoluc. We observed that the compounds QHM0001, 0011, 0020 and 0110 interfered with the post-entry stages (2 h.p.i.) of the CMV-MAYV-nanoluc, suggesting an effect on the viral genome replication stage. QHM0001, 0011 and 0020 showed high percentages of inhibition in late stages (4, 6 and 8 h.p.i.) of CMV-MAYV-nanoluc replication cycle. Thus, our study highlights the potential of the tested hydroxynaphthoquinones as promising candidates for new broad-spectrum antivirals.

Dengue virus disease phenotypes in C57BL/6N Ifnar1-/-Ifngr1-/- mice.
Dengue virus (DENV) remains a major global health problem, and experimentally tractable animal models are essential for investigating severe dengue pathogenesis and antiviral or vaccine strategies. However, whereas interferon receptor-deficient mouse models are used, the disease phenotype in C57BL/6N Ifnar1-/- Ifngr1-/- double-knockout (DKO) mice has not been sufficiently characterized. Here, we generated and characterized C57BL/6N-based DKO mice deficient in both type I and type II interferon receptors (Ifnar1-/- Ifngr1-/-). We first assessed susceptibility to DENV-2 NGC infection in wild-type, single-knockout, and DKO mice and found that combined Ifnar1 and Ifngr1 loss was required for rapid and severe disease. DENV-2 NGC-infected DKO mice exhibited marked weight loss, severe clinical manifestations, and 100% mortality. We then performed phenotypic screening using selected DENV serotype 1-4 strains under strain-specific inoculation conditions. This revealed strain- and condition-dependent differences in disease outcomes, and DENV-2 NGC was selected for further characterization based on the rapid lethal disease observed under the conditions used. Detailed characterization of DENV-2 NGC infection demonstrated progressive viral RNA accumulation in multiple organs, including the liver, brain, spleen, and large intestine, and infectious virus was detected in selected peripheral tissues. Histopathological analyses revealed multi-organ tissue alterations with inflammatory changes and vascular abnormalities, and Evans blue extravasation assays demonstrated increased vascular permeability in infected tissues. Collectively, these findings establish a C57BL/6N-based Ifnar1-/- Ifngr1-/- mouse platform for studying DENV-2 NGC-induced severe disease phenotypes and provide a practical framework for future mechanistic and preclinical studies on antiviral or vaccine strategies.

Retrospective serological evidence of exposure to selected equine viruses in horses from Indigenous communities of Costa Rica, 2011.
Horses are essential for transportation and livelihoods in Indigenous communities of Costa Rica. However, information on their exposure to viral pathogens remains scarce. We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional serosurvey using samples collected from horses from four Indigenous communities (Alto Pacuare, Amubre, Paso Marcos, and Vereh) sampled between March and October 2011 (n = 278). Sera were tested in 2014 using commercial immunodiffusion or ELISA assays for antibodies against West Nile virus (WNV), equine herpesviruses 1 and 4 (EHV-1 and EHV-4), influenza A virus, equine arteritis virus (EAV), and equine infectious anemia virus (EIAV). Seroprevalence estimates and Wilson 95% confidence intervals were calculated, and differences among communities were assessed using Pearson's chi-square or Fisher's exact tests, as appropriate. The number of tested sera differed across assays due to sample availability. Serological evidence compatible with WNV exposure was detected in 58.9% (139/236) of horses, with the highest proportion in Amubre (83.3%). EHV-4 showed consistently high seropositivity (91.2%, 125/137), whereas EHV-1 seroprevalence was low (6.6%, 9/137). Antibodies to influenza A virus and EAV were detected at low frequencies (5.1%, 12/237, and 3.0%, 7/236, respectively). EIAV seroprevalence reached 16.6% (35/211), with the highest proportion in Paso Marcos (23.8%). Significant differences among communities were observed for WNV, influenza A virus, and EHV-4 seropositivity. These findings represent historical serological evidence of exposure in 2011 and should not be interpreted as reflecting current viral circulation. Nevertheless, they provide a retrospective baseline for comparison with future surveillance and highlight the value of including underserved Indigenous equine populations in disease-monitoring and prevention programs.

Interacting climatic, environmental, biologic and socio-economic drivers of the global dengue expansion.
Dengue is the most rapidly expanding mosquito-borne viral disease worldwide. The worst year on record was 2024, with over 100 countries reporting 14.4 million cases and over 11,000 deaths. Since then, and up to August 2026, another 7.4 million cases and over 5000 deaths have been reported. The region of the Americas was impacted the most, followed by South-East Asia and the Western Pacific. Both the spread of dengue viruses (DENV) and their primary vectors, Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, are driven by several factors. Globalization has accelerated vector dispersal, particularly through international trade and transportation networks. The movement of desiccation-resistant eggs in used-vehicle tyres and the inadvertent transport of adult mosquitoes via trucks and passenger vehicles have enabled the establishment of vector populations in previously uncolonized regions. Human mobility and unplanned urbanization further contribute to dengue emergence by introducing DENV into susceptible populations where competent vectors circulate. Climate change has enhanced dengue transmission potential by altering temperature and rainfall patterns that influence mosquito survival, reproduction, biting behaviour and viral replication. Containing or even reversing this global dengue expansion will require a complementary set of interventions that rely on proven and novel control strategies, including sterile insect techniques, Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes, virus-resistant mosquito strains through CRISPR-Cas9 gene drive, vaccines, antiviral drug prophylaxis and urban interventions that eliminate Aedes habitats. Building climate-resilient urban environments through sustainable development to minimize the urban heat island effect and advancing climate-informed early warning systems are long-term strategies for effective dengue control.

Hantaviruses as Emerging Zoonotic Pathogens: Molecular Biology, Epidemiology, Therapeutics, vaccine, and Pathogenesis.
Hantaviruses are globally distributed zoonotic pathogens belonging to the family Hantaviridae and are responsible for two major human diseases, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). Despite substantial progress in hantavirus research, important challenges remain in understanding the interactions among viral evolution, reservoir ecology, environmental change, transmission dynamics, and host immunopathology. This review provides an integrated One Health perspective that connects molecular virology and host-virus interactions with transmission ecology, global epidemiology, and the mechanisms underlying vascular leakage and severe disease. In addition to summarizing established knowledge, we highlight recent advances in hantavirus taxonomy, genomic and molecular surveillance, ecological and transmission modeling, and the identification of hantavirus circulation in previously underrecognized regions. Particular emphasis is placed on the role of reservoir host dynamics, climate and environmental change, habitat disturbance, and human-wildlife interactions in shaping spillover risk, as well as on endothelial dysfunction, immune dysregulation, and coagulation abnormalities as interconnected mechanisms of disease severity. We also identify persistent knowledge gaps concerning host susceptibility, viral persistence, determinants of differential virulence and tissue tropism, interspecies transmission, and the development of effective antiviral therapies and vaccines. By integrating these complementary perspectives, this review provides a framework for understanding hantavirus emergence and pathogenesis while identifying priorities for future surveillance, prevention, and therapeutic research.

Hypertensive Intraventricular Hemorrhage in a Chinese Population: Clinical Characteristics, Treatment, and Outcomes.
OBJECTIVE: Intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) is associated with high mortality and poor outcomes in survivors. This study described the clinical characteristics and treatment outcomes of patients with hypertensive IVH (HIVH) in a large single-center Chinese cohort. METHODS: We conducted retrospective analysis of prospectively maintained stroke registry at a tertiary medical center in China from September 2018 to January 2026. Patients with hypertensive IVH were included, while those with vascular-structural lesions or trauma were excluded. Demographic data, clinical treatments, and outcomes were analyzed. RESULTS: In total, 489 patients with HIVH were enrolled, including 49 (9.9%) with primary IVH (pIVH) and 440(90%) with secondary IVH (sIVH). Panventricular hemorrhage was the most common overall HIVH pattern (31%), and 170 patients (35%) received external ventricular drainage (EVD). The overall 30-day mortality rate was 26%, and the 90-day mortality rate was 29%, respectively. Multivariate analysis showed that larger hematoma volume (OR=1.02, p=0.001), lower admission GCS score (OR=1.37, p<0.001), and older age (OR=1.03, p=0.011) were independent risk factors for 90-day mortality in patients with HIVH. Subgroup analysis showed that the EVD group had significantly lower 90-day cumulative mortality risk than the non-EVD group (HR=0.57, 95%CI 0.41-0.79, p<0.001), but no significant difference in favorable functional outcome at 90 days [modified Rankin Scale (mRS) 0-2: 22% vs 27%, p=0.265]. Additionally, the EVD group had significantly prolonged hospital stay (21 days vs 13 days, p<0.001). Furthermore, there was no significant difference in 90-day mortality risk between pIVH and sIVH (HR=0.94, 95%CI 0.51-1.75, p=0.848), but pIVH had significantly higher favorable functional outcome rates (mRS 0-2: 65% vs. 21%, p < 0.001). CONCLUSION: Parenchymal brain injury was the predominant factor associated with prognosis in patients with HIVH. EVD was associated with lower mortality but did not improve functional outcomes.

Mapping and analysis of the knowledge graph on the current status and key issues in global research on Norovirus infections in children over the past 28 years.
BACKGROUND: Norovirus (NoV) is a major pathogen responsible for acute gastroenteritis and outbreaks of diarrhea in humans. Children, due to their underdeveloped immune systems and higher risk of exposure, constitute a population with a relatively concentrated incidence of infection and disease burden. In recent years, research on NoV infections in children has been growing globally; however, there remains a lack of systematic quantitative analysis regarding the evolution of research themes, models of international collaboration, and future development directions in this field. Therefore, this study employs bibliometric methods to conduct a visual analysis of the knowledge structure, research hotspots, and development trends in the global field of NoV infection research in children, providing a reference for future scientific research and the formulation of prevention and control strategies. METHODS: This study retrieved literature on pediatric NoV infections published between January 1998 and December 2025 from the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) database. Using CiteSpace, VOSviewer, and Bibliometrix software, we conducted a visual analysis of annual publication trends, countries/regions, institutions, authors, journals, keywords, and references to reveal the research trajectory, knowledge base, and cutting-edge directions in this field. RESULTS: This study included a total of 2,161 relevant publications. The results show that research on NoV infections in children worldwide has generally followed a steady upward trend, with activity remaining high in recent years. The United States, China, and Japan are the leading contributors to research in this field, with the United States exerting significant influence through international collaboration. The University of Tokyo, Emory University, and Chiang Mai University are the research institutions with the highest number of publications. Vinje, Jan; Ushijima, Hiroshi; and Khamrin, Pattara were the most prolific core authors, while Atmar, Robert L.; Lindesmith, Lisa C.; and Patel, Manish M. demonstrated strong academic influence. Keyword analysis revealed that research in this field primarily focuses on viral molecular characteristics, epidemiological features, and clinical manifestations in children, and is gradually expanding toward disease burden assessment, global prevention and control strategies, and vaccine development. CONCLUSION: Global research on NoV infections in children has evolved into a Multi-Disciplinary research framework driven by virology, epidemiology, clinical medicine, and public health. Current research focuses primarily on molecular epidemiology and genetic diversity, as well as epidemiological characteristics and outbreak transmission mechanisms, while the assessment of disease burden and the optimization of global prevention and control strategies are gradually emerging as key future research directions. In the future, international collaboration, multicenter surveillance, and interdisciplinary research should be further strengthened to advance research on pediatric NoV infection from describing disease characteristics toward precision surveillance, proactive prevention, and comprehensive control and prevention measures.

Assessment of Tidal Volume in Patients Undergoing Noninvasive Ventilation: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
OBJECTIVES: Noninvasive ventilation (NIV) is widely used in acute respiratory failure (ARF), yet the association between high tidal volume (Vt) and clinical outcomes remains incompletely defined. We evaluated the association between Vt and NIV failure overall and by ARF type, and its relationship with respiratory and clinical outcomes. DATA SOURCES: MEDLINE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Web of Science, and Latin American and Caribbean Health Science Literature (1976 to September 2025). STUDY SELECTION: Observational studies of adults with ARF treated with NIV reporting Vt or Vt normalized to predicted body weight (Vt/PBW) in NIV success and failure groups. DATA EXTRACTION: Three pairs of reviewers identified studies and extracted data independently. Random-effects meta-analysis was performed. Risk of bias and certainty of evidence were assessed using Risk of Bias In Nonrandomized Studies of Interventions and Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation. DATA SYNTHESIS: Eleven studies (1136 patients) were included. Vt/PBW was higher in NIV failure vs. success (mean difference [MD], 1.02 mL/kg [95% CI, 0.60-1.45 mL/kg]), whereas absolute Vt did not differ (MD, 1.30 [-33.31 to 35.91]). In hypoxemic ARF, Vt/PBW remained higher in NIV failure (MD, 0.89 mL/kg [95% CI, 0.04-1.73 mL/kg]); no data were available for hypercapnic ARF. Post hoc analyses showed that higher Vt/PBW was associated with increased mortality (odds ratio, 9.11; 95% CI, 3.88-21.37), higher respiratory rate (RR; MD, 3.14 breaths/min [95% CI, 1.36-4.92 breaths/min]), and lower Paco2 (MD, -2.38 mm Hg [95% CI, -4.16 to -0.5938 mm Hg]), but no with pressure support (PS) level (MD, 0.24 [95% CI, -0.81 to 1.29]). Certainty of evidence ranged from very low to moderate. CONCLUSIONS: In adults with ARF treated with NIV, higher Vt/PBW was associated with NIV failure and worse outcomes. These findings reflect prognostic associations rather than causality, and interventional studies with systematic Vt monitoring are needed. Importantly, elevated Vt/PBW, higher RR, lower Paco2, and increased mortality, without differences in PS, collectively implicate elevated respiratory drive as a driver of increased mortality (PROSPERO [CRD42024584977]).Findings: Higher Vt/PBW was associated with NIV failure, particularly in hypoxemic respiratory failure; post hoc analyses showed associations with increased mortality, higher respiratory rate, and lower Paco2.

Australian Rotavirus Surveillance Program: Annual Report, 2025.
This report from the Australian Rotavirus Surveillance Program (ARSP) describes the circulating rotavirus genotypes identified in children and adults during the period 1 January to 31 December 2025. In 2025, the ARSP saw a continuation of a high burden of rotavirus disease in the Australian population. During this period, 2,419 faecal specimens were referred to the National Rotavirus Reference Centre (NRRC) for rotavirus G- and P-genotype analysis; of these samples, 2,288 were confirmed as rotavirus positive. This represents the highest number of referred samples and the highest number of positive samples recorded in a single surveillance year in the NRRC's more than 20-year history. Of the 2,288 samples confirmed rotavirus positive, 2,071 (90.5%) were identified as wildtype rotavirus; 215 (9.4%) were identified as the Rotarix vaccine-like strain; and two G1P[8] samples could not be confirmed as wildtype or vaccine-like due to inadequate sequence quality. The equine-like G3P[8] variant was the dominant genotype nationally (87.7%; n = 1,816/2,071). Other genotypes were identified at low frequencies, including wildtype G1P[8] (0.3%; n = 6/2,071), G2P[4] (2.0%; n = 42/2,071), G3P[8] (2.4%; n = 50/2,071), G8P[8] (0.5%; n = 10/2,071), G9P[4] (0.3%; n = 6/2,071), G9P[8] (2.2%; n = 46/2,071) and G12P[8] (0.3%; n = 6/2,071). Genotype distribution was consistent nationally, with equine-like G3P[8] the dominant genotype in all jurisdictions. Consistent with observations in recent years, a small number of samples with unusual genotypes were identified (3.7%; n = 77/2,071). Of these unusual genotypes, the most frequently detected was equine-like G3P[6] which accounted for 26.0% of unusual samples (n = 20/74) and 1.0% of all positive wildtype samples (n = 20/2,071). The high number of rotavirus positive samples received by the program reflected the notifications for rotavirus disease reported to the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance Service (NNDSS). Across Australia, 9,520 notifications were recorded, which is the second highest annual total reported since rotavirus became nationally notifiable in 2018. Outbreaks were reported in the Northern Territory, Western Australia and Queensland. The ability to monitor the genotypes of rotavirus strains causing disease across ages and jurisdictions provides important data to aid in assessing the performance of the national rotavirus vaccination program and to inform public health interventions during outbreaks. The ARSP also provides important data to monitor annual variations in genotypes circulating in the population. Understanding the diversity of genotypes in circulation and the emergence of variants provides important context for any changes observed in disease epidemiology in the community. The ARSP provides diagnostic laboratories with valuable feedback on laboratory data quality by reporting incidences of wildtype, vaccine-like, and/or false positive rotavirus results.

Nationwide survey of testing practices for respiratory viruses in Australia in the post COVID-19 pandemic era.
BACKGROUND: In the wake of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, there have been dramatic changes in the testing protocols for respiratory illness. Laboratory identification of respiratory pathogens causing clinical symptoms has become more important in the post-COVID-19 era, both for epidemiological and clinical reasons. This is particularly the case for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) where a number of preventatives are at the point of clinical translation. The laboratory diagnosis is one of the critical elements in understanding the disease burden of respiratory pathogens and the effectiveness of preventatives. The aims of this study were to understand current laboratory testing and reporting practices across Australia. METHODS: We undertook a cross-sectional survey of Australian NATA (National Association of Testing Authorities) accredited laboratories to collect data on patterns of laboratory testing, the methods used and their reporting processes. The survey asked participants to report on testing of respiratory samples for 2022 as well as current respiratory multiplex testing in 2023. OUTCOMES: In total, 45 out of 193 eligible laboratories (23%) completed the online survey. The majority of laboratories were from Victoria and New South Wales (31% and 27%, respectively) and most were hospital-based clinical diagnostic laboratories. Overall, 40% of responding laboratories (18/44) reported that > 80% of all tests in the molecular laboratory in 2023 were respiratory multiplex. Influenza viruses, RSV and SARS-CoV-2 were tested most frequently on respiratory multiplex PCR panels. RSV typing (RSV A or RSV B) was included in under a quarter of panels (9/43; 21%), compared to almost two-thirds for influenza typing (influenza A or influenza B: 29/44; 66%). There was considerable variability in testing platforms used, with thirty-seven laboratories using 87 different platforms (18 unique platforms). GeneXpert® (Cepheid) was the most commonly used platform; with a higher concentration of this instrument in laboratories from the eastern states (New South Wales, Queensland, Victoria). Forty percent of laboratories reported changes to respiratory testing procedures/panels in 2023 compared to the previous year. Laboratories were most likely to report results directly to the referring doctor (96-100%) followed by notifying their jurisdictional Department of Health.

Preliminary study on expression and functions of Toxoplasma gondii SRS67 and SRS20A proteins.
BACKGROUND: Toxoplasma gondii surface proteins play critical roles in parasite invasion, proliferation, and host immune modulation, and represent promising targets for anti-toxoplasmosis intervention. SRS67 and SRS20A are poorly characterized surface proteins of T. gondii, and their biological functions and host regulatory effects remain largely unclear. METHODS: In the present study, we prepared recombinant SRS67 and SRS20A proteins and generated corresponding polyclonal antibodies to explore their functional characteristics and protective potentials. RESULTS: Immunofluorescence analysis localized both proteins as punctate signals surrounding the parasite membrane, indicating their involvement in surface-associated biological processes. In vitro phenotypic assays demonstrated that the prepared polyclonal antibodies significantly inhibited host cell invasion and intracellular proliferation of T. gondii. In vivo animal experiments further showed that antibody treatment effectively alleviated T. gondii-caused pathological injuries in mice. In the acute RH infection model, single or combined protein immunization increased the survival rate of mice by approximately 60%, and combined immunization delayed mortality by 1-2 days. In chronic PRU infection, antibody intervention reduced brain cyst burden by over 85% and markedly attenuated meningeal thickening and neuronal necrosis. Mechanistically, SRS67 upregulated the expression of Th1 cytokines (TNF-α, IL-18) during acute infection, while both proteins downregulated IFN-γ to limit excessive immune-mediated tissue damage. The elevated glutathione (GSH) level suggested the participation of these proteins in antioxidant regulation. During chronic infection, combined immunization synergistically enhanced superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity to resist oxidative stress, and decreased IFN-γ expression contributed to the maintenance of immune homeostasis. CONCLUSIONS: Collectively, this study systematically characterizes the biological functions of SRS67 and SRS20A, and demonstrates that their polyclonal antibodies exert potent inhibitory effects against T. gondii infection by directly blocking parasite biological behaviors and indirectly regulating host immune responses and antioxidant status. Our findings provide novel insights into the functional mechanisms of SRS family proteins and support the development of SRS-targeted anti-Toxoplasma strategies.

Skull Base Osteomyelitis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Epidemiology, Microbiology, Diagnosis, and Treatment Outcomes.
BACKGROUND: Skull base osteomyelitis (SBO) is a life-threatening infection arising predominantly from necrotizing external otitis, producing progressive osteitis of the temporal and central skull base. Originally described in elderly diabetic patients, its demographic profile has broadened to encompass immunocompromised hosts of diverse etiologies. Although historical mortality exceeded 50%, advances in imaging, microbiology, and antimicrobial therapy have improved prognosis substantially. OBJECTIVES: To systematically review the epidemiology, microbiology, clinical features, diagnostic modalities, therapeutic strategies, and outcomes of SBO and to identify evidence gaps requiring further investigation. METHODS: A comprehensive search of PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library (inception to March 2025, updated to March 2026) was performed. Studies reporting primary data on SBO (n >=5 patients) with defined diagnostic criteria, microbiological findings, treatment protocols, and outcome measures were included. Two independent reviewers screened records, extracted data, and assessed quality using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Findings are presented as a narrative synthesis per PRISMA 2020 guidelines. For the outcomes most consistently reported in primary cohorts, a random-effects meta-analysis of pooled proportions (DerSimonian-Laird, logit scale) was additionally performed. RESULTS: Forty-five studies encompassing 1,628 patients met inclusion criteria. The median patient age was 68 years (IQR 57-76); diabetes mellitus was present in 74.2%. Pseudomonas aeruginosa predominated (62.4%), with ciprofloxacin-resistant strains identified in 11.3% of post-2000 series. Fungal SBO, principally Aspergillus spp., accounted for 7.8% of cases and was consistently associated with higher mortality across reported series. Gallium-67 scintigraphy demonstrated the highest sensitivity (94%) for treatment monitoring; FDG-PET/CT sensitivity exceeded 96%. Combined fluoroquinolone-based therapy yielded a cure rate of 71.4%. Evidence for adjunctive hyperbaric oxygen therapy remains limited to uncontrolled series and a single small comparative study, with no randomized trials, so its efficacy is unproven. The overall mortality was 15.3%. In a proportion meta-analysis of primary cohorts, pooled estimates were: diabetes 82.4% (95% CI 68.2-91.1), Pseudomonas aeruginosa 55.6% (48.4-62.6), clinical cure 84.7% (74.6-91.2), cranial nerve involvement 28.0% (16.1-43.9), and mortality 8.4% (4.3-15.8). CONCLUSIONS: SBO remains a serious condition requiring multimodal diagnostic evaluation and prolonged antimicrobial therapy. Emerging fluoroquinolone resistance constitutes a pressing clinical challenge. Standardized diagnostic criteria, prospective multicenter trials, and consensus treatment protocols are urgently required.

Patterns and determinants of antimalarial drug use and treatment adherence in Osun State, Southwestern Nigeria: a cross-sectional study.
BACKGROUND: Malaria remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in Nigeria. Artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) are first-line treatments, but adherence is suboptimal and resistance is emerging. This study assessed patterns, determinants and barriers related to antimalarial drug use and adherence in Osun State, southwestern Nigeria. METHODS: A community-based cross-sectional household survey was conducted between October 2024 and September 2025. Using multistage sampling, 1500 residents aged ≥15 years across three senatorial districts were enrolled. Data on sociodemographics, recent antimalarial use, adherence, knowledge and access barriers were collected via structured questionnaires. Descriptive and inferential statistics, including binary logistic regression, were used to identify factors associated with treatment completion. RESULTS: The mean age of participants was 26.7 (±10.7) years; 77.0% were female. Among 713 recent antimalarial users, 70.5% completed the full course. Persistent chloroquine use was reported by 46.0% of users. Cost (40.5%) was the most cited access barrier. In adjusted analysis, treatment completion was significantly associated with tertiary education (adjusted OR (aOR)=1.85, 95% CI 1.32 to 2.59), urban residence (aOR=1.55, 95% CI 1.10 to 2.18), formal drug sources (aOR=2.20, 95% CI 1.55 to 3.12) and awareness of drug resistance (aOR=1.95, 95% CI 1.42 to 2.68). CONCLUSIONS: Suboptimal adherence, persistent use of discontinued drugs and high out-of-pocket costs threaten malaria control and may accelerate drug resistance. Public health strategies should enforce prescription policies, institute basic universal health coverage to subsidise ACTs, implement behaviour change communication and address drug unavailability in rural areas to mitigate resistance risks.

Temporal Trends in Invasive Pulmonary Aspergillosis Among Critically Ill Patients: Serum Galactomannan Testing Intensity and Host Risk Status.
OBJECTIVES: We evaluated temporal trends in invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA) incidence in relation to serum galactomannan (GM) testing intensity and compared outcomes by classical host-risk status. METHODS: Adults with ICU stays ≥72 hours during 2017-2024 were retrospectively screened for proven/probable IPA. Consensus EORTC/MSGERC and FUNDICU definitions defined the primary cohort. Modified criteria were exploratory. Negative binomial and Cox regression assessed incidence and 30-day mortality. RESULTS: Among 11,707 ICU stays, 135 patients met consensus definitions; 55 (40.7%) lacked classical host risk factors, rising to 48.9% under modified criteria. IPA incidence increased over time (IRR/year 1.40; 95% CI 1.06-1.85). After adjustment for serum GM testing intensity, the calendar-year IRR was 0.73 (95% CI 0.54-0.98), whereas testing intensity was strongly associated with measured incidence (IRR 6.15; 95% CI 2.81-13.43). Patients without classical host risk factors received antifungal therapy less often (12.7% vs 67.5%) and had higher crude 30-day mortality (58.2% vs 36.2%). The adjusted host-status association was attenuated (aHR 1.48; 95% CI 0.82-2.66). CONCLUSIONS: The temporal rise in measured IPA incidence was associated with serum GM testing intensity, underscoring diagnostic ascertainment. Patients without classical host risk factors were treated less often and had higher mortality, although the adjusted association was attenuated.

Clinical and dermatological findings associated with Leishmania spp. test-positivity in shelter dogs of Kastamonu, Black Sea region of Türkiye: an exploratory cross-sectional study.
Canine leishmaniosis (CanL) has a broad clinical spectrum, with cutaneous abnormalities among its most frequent manifestations. We characterised clinical and dermatological findings in 200 stray dogs admitted to the municipal shelter of Kastamonu, Türkiye, and explored associations with Leishmania test positivity, lymphadenopathy, age, sex, sampling month and geographic origin. Blood samples were examined by thin blood-smear microscopy and a lateral-flow serological rapid test. Nine dogs (4.5%) met the study's combined definition of test positivity. Above-normal body temperature, lymph-node abnormalities and skin abnormalities were recorded in 33.5%, 16% and 15% of dogs, respectively. Abnormal skin status was significantly associated with test positivity (microscopy p<0.001; combined positivity p=0.031, OR 5.08, 95% CI 1.28-20.15; Fisher exact tests), consistent with a rank-correlation analysis. All four microscopy-positive dogs had abnormal skin (4/30), whereas rapid/combined positivity occurred in 4/30 dogs with abnormal skin and 5/170 with healthy skin. Lymph-node status differed by sex in an exploratory Mann-Whitney analysis (U=4363.50; p=0.026). Skin-health ranks differed across recorded ages (Kruskal-Wallis χ²=31.797; df=10; p<0.001) and sampling months (χ²=13.541; df=5; p=0.019), but sparse older-age strata, uneven monthly sampling and an association between month and age limited inference. The data did not support a bimodal age distribution or an autumn-winter increase in skin abnormalities. Because diagnostic and lesion-specific confirmation were limited, these findings are interpreted as exploratory clinical associations and provide a baseline for molecularly confirmed prospective surveillance in the Black Sea region.

Clinical and laboratory predictors for differentiating visceral leishmaniasis from hematological malignancies in adults with pancytopenia.
Visceral leishmaniasis (VL) is a systemic, life-threatening zoonotic disease. VL and hematological malignancies (HMs) may present with overlapping clinical and laboratory features. The primary endpoint of our study was to identify the clinical and laboratory parameters for differentiating VL from HMs in adult patients with pancytopenia. The secondary endpoint was to evaluate the clinical and laboratory findings in patients with VL. In this 15.5-year retrospective case-control study, adult patients with pancytopenia who were diagnosed with VL or HMs at a tertiary referral hospital in Antalya were included. A total of 53 patients were included (VL, n = 24; HMs, n = 29). The VL group was younger and presented with a significantly longer duration from symptom onset to hospital admission compared to the HMs group (each, p 13.75 cm (AUC: 0.945, sensitivity: 92%, specificity: 93%), followed by CRP >33.5 mg/L (AUC: 0.817, sensitivity: 83%, specificity: 83%) and symptom duration >52.5 days (AUC: 0.799, sensitivity: 67%, specificity: 86%). VL should be considered in the differential diagnosis of adults with pancytopenia, particularly in endemic regions. We believe that our findings may contribute to earlier and more accurate diagnosis of VL. Prolonged symptom duration, hepatosplenomegaly, elevated AST, elevated CRP, hyperproteinemia, hypoalbuminemia, and reversed albumin-globulin ratio necessitate a high index of clinical suspicion for VL compared to HMs.

Absence of Validated and Candidate Plasmodium falciparum Kelch13 Markers of Artemisinin Resistance and Low Frequency of a Pfcoronin Mutation in Igombe, Mwanza Region, Tanzania.
Tanzania recently identified partial artemisinin resistance in the Kagera region bordering Rwanda and Uganda, where resistance is established. Monitoring neighboring regions is critical to guide containment strategies. We, therefore, conducted molecular surveillance of Plasmodium falciparum Kelch13 (pfk13) and Plasmodium falciparum actin-binding protein coronin (pfcoronin; P76S) mutations in Igombe in Mwanza region. In a health facility-based cross-sectional study in 2025, P. falciparum DNA from patients with uncomplicated malaria was analyzed using polymerase chain reaction, Sanger sequencing, and allele-specific melting curve assays. Among 121 sequenced isolates, no validated or candidate pfk13 mutations were detected. The nonsynonymous, nonvalidated pfk13 variant N489K occurred in 2.5%. The pfcoronin P76S mutation was observed at low prevalence (3.6%). Despite proximity to Kagera hot spots, validated pfk13 markers have not yet been established in the Mwanza region. The presence of pfcoronin P76S, albeit at low levels, requires careful monitoring. Continued molecular surveillance is essential to support the early detection and containment of emerging artemisinin resistance in Tanzania.

Identification of Novel CD52+ Fibroblasts in Nodular Prostatic Hyperplasia.
BACKGROUND: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and lower urinary tract symptoms are strongly associated with chronic prostate inflammation and stromal remodeling, yet the stromal cell programs that emerge during inflammatory, nodular remodeling remain incompletely defined. A Toxoplasma gondii infection model produces persistent inflammation and nodular formations, providing an experimentally tractable system to map inflammation-linked stromal states. METHODS: We performed single-cell RNA sequencing of prostates from control and chronically infected male CBA/J mice harvested at 28 days post-infection (DPI). Stromal subset reprogramming was assessed by cluster-resolved pseudobulk differential expression and Ingenuity Pathway Analysis. Stromal expansion and Cd52+ fibroblast subset changes were validated by whole-section immunofluorescence at 28 and 60 DPI using a CellposeSAM-based tissue cytometry pipeline. To assess human relevance, CD52+ fibroblasts were evaluated in FFPE human prostate sections by comparing inflamed versus non-inflamed stromal regions. RESULTS: Whole-prostate single-cell profiling resolved stromal, epithelial, immune, and seminal vesicle compartments. Infection increased immune-cell abundance and increased stromal representation among non-immune cells (53.1% in controls to 69.0% in infected prostates). Stromal reclustering identified eight subsets, including a Cd52+/Ccl5+ immune-reactive fibroblast population that showed the strongest selective expansion during infection. Whole-section imaging supported overall stromal expansion over time, and Cd52+ fibroblasts were higher during infection at 60 DPI (270% increase, p = 0.0507), whereas Cxcl13+ fibroblasts remained rare and stable across conditions. Pathway analysis indicated immune-like stromal reprogramming during infection, with antigen-presentation programs enriched in larger fibroblast subsets and interferon/JAK-STAT signaling most consistently concentrated in the Cd52+/Ccl5+ subset. In human prostate tissue, CD52+ VIM+ CD45- fibroblasts were significantly enriched in inflamed regions compared with paired non-inflamed regions within the same specimen (paired Wilcoxon p = 0.0026). CONCLUSIONS: Chronic, pathogen-driven inflammation produces selective, program-specific stromal remodeling rather than uniform fibroblast activation. An interferon-reactive Cd52+ fibroblast state expands during infection in mice and marks inflamed stromal microenvironments in human prostate, supporting discrete immune-reactive fibroblast programs as a prominent feature of inflammation-associated prostate remodeling.

Changes in patient concentration and accessibility across 5 Pediatric Emergency Departments in Daegu, Korea.
BACKGROUND: The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic has substantially altered Pediatric Emergency Department (PED) utilization. However, longitudinal changes across multiple PEDs after major policy transitions remain unclear. PURPOSE: This study aimed to evaluate changes in utilization, patient distribution, accessibility to pediatric emergency care, and clinical characteristics across 5 participating PEDs in Daegu, Korea. METHODS: This multicenter retrospective study analyzed 140,017 visits among patients aged <16 years between January 2019 and May 2023. Concentration was assessed using monthly institutional shares and the Herfindahl- Hirschman Index (HHI), while the segmented interrupted time-series regression incorporated the Prais-Winsten correction and seasonal terms. The door-to-emergency room (door-to-ER) distance was defined as the WGS84 geodesic distance between the residential administrativedong centroid and fixed coordinates of the visited PED. We also evaluated the Korean Triage and Acuity Scale (KTAS) score, proportion of ambulance arrivals, and Emergency Department length of stay. RESULTS: Median monthly population-standardized visit rates were 580.9, 315.8, and 500.1/100,000 child personmonths in the pre-COVID, COVID, and post-COVID periods, respectively (P<0.001); the post-COVID rate did not differ significantly from the pre-COVID rate after Bonferroni adjustment. Center D's share increased from 25.7% in the pre-COVID period to 44.4% in the post-COVID period. The HHI showed no immediate level change but increased in slope after May 2022 (β=0.00437/mo; 95% confidence interval, 0.00072-0.00801; P=0.020). Median door-to-ER geodesic distance increased from 6.44 to 8.68 km, and visits originating ≥20 km away increased from 16.8% to 20.9%, with a more pronounced distance increase among Daegu residents. The proportion of KTAS level 3 visits increased from 44.9% to 60.5%, and that of KTAS levels 1-2 from 3.0% to 4.3%. CONCLUSION: These findings indicate patient redistribution across the 5 participating PEDs serving Daegu and Gyeongsangbuk-do. Visit volume recovered after the COVID period, whereas patient distribution became increasingly concentrated with longer door-to-ER distances and greater reliance on emergency medical services, suggesting reduced accessibility.

Aedes vittatus in Haiti: continued expansion across the Caribbean and implications for the Americas.
BACKGROUND: Aedes vittatus, an emerging invasive species and arboviral vector with high ecological plasticity and dispersal capacity, is expanding in the Caribbean, being detected in the Dominican Republic, Cuba, and Jamaica and recently in Yucatán, Mexico. OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to provide evidence of the establishment of Ae. vittatus in Haiti. METHODS: Larval surveys were conducted in 18 localities within 12 municipalities in the North and Northeast departments of Haiti. Specimens were identified morphologically and confirmed by COI-based DNA barcoding. FINDINGS: We report, for the first time, the detection of the invasive vector Ae. (Fredwardsius) vittatus in Haiti, confirmed morphologically and molecularly, with the species detected in half of the municipalities sampled. Phylogenetic analyses placed Haitian specimens within a Caribbean/American group, closely related to sequences from Mexico. Additional mosquito species were identified, including first records of Culex garciai and Culex interrogator in Haiti.
