It further summarizes the major oncolytic virus platforms, recent preclinical and clinical advances, emerging combination strategies, current translational challenges, and future directions expected to advance precision oncolytic virotherapy and expand its role in modern cancer treatment.

Financial toxicity and the economic burden of Chagas disease: a scoping review.
This scoping review mapped, synthesized, and critically analyzed the evidence on financial toxicity in Chagas disease, focusing on its determinants, impacts, and management strategies. Financial toxicity refers to the financial burden and distress experienced by individuals and their families as a result of healthcare expenses. The review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Comprehensive searches were conducted across seven electronic databases and the gray literature. Studies were selected and data extracted independently using the population-exposure-outcome framework, and 14 studies included. Most studies described indicators of the economic burden of Chagas disease rather than directly measuring patient-level financial toxicity. Substantial indirect costs were associated with absenteeism, productivity loss, and premature mortality, accounting for 44% to 75% of total costs. The findings also indicated that financial hardship may be intensified by structural vulnerabilities, including extreme poverty, lack of health insurance, and precarious migration status. Available evidence suggests that individuals affected by Chagas disease are at increased risk of healthcare-related financial hardship. However, studies directly assessing financial toxicity are scarce, with most relying on indirect economic indicators. This highlights an important gap in the literature and underscores the need for validated measures to evaluate financial toxicity in this population. Interventions that reduce financial barriers and strengthen access to healthcare services may help mitigate the economic consequences of Chagas disease. Future research should prioritize patient-centered assessments of financial toxicity to better inform policies and strategies aimed at reducing the financial burden associated with the disease.

Clinical and epidemiological aspects of coinfection with American tegumentary leishmaniasis and HIV/AIDS in South American countries: a systematic review.
Leishmaniasis is one of the 10 leading neglected tropical diseases (NTDs), and cutaneous leishmaniasis is endemic in 19 countries in the Americas. This study aimed to systematically review the epidemiological and clinical characteristics, diagnostic methods, and outcomes associated with coinfection with American tegumentary leishmaniasis (ATL) and HIV in South American countries. This review was registered in the International Prospective of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; CRD42023138800). Searches were conducted in the following electronic scientific databases: the Biblioteca Virtual em Saúde, Literatura Latino-americana e do Caribe em Ciências da Saúde, SciVerse Scopus, the US National Library of Medicine (PubMed) and Web of Science, using subject headings from the Descritores em Ciências da Saúde and Medical Subject Headings in Portuguese, English and Spanish for studies published from 1987 to 2025. Two independent reviewers performed study selection. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal Checklists. Overall, 417 participants from 32 studies were included in this systematic review. Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Paraguay and Peru reported concurrent ATL and HIV. In 29 studies (90.6%), the diagnosis was established based solely on clinical criteria. Diagnostic methods for ATL included culture and the Montenegro skin test, whereas those for HIV included Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay, Western blotting, and indirect immunofluorescence. Approximately 68% of the analyzed data were derived from case reports, limiting the overall level of evidence. Strengthening integrated surveillance is needed to improve the clinical management of patients with ATL-HIV coinfection and expand access to health services.

Paroxetine activity against Trypanosoma cruzi: in vitro and in vivo studies.
BACKGROUND: Chagas disease (CD) lacks effective therapy. However, the long time and high financial investments for the development of new drugs are limiting obstacles. The repositioning of drugs is an interesting approach for novel antiparasitic medicines. Previous results suggest that paroxetine (PXT) may represent a promising anti-Trypanosoma cruzi agent. OBJECTIVES: Our aim was to evaluate the activity and cellular targets of PXT on T. cruzi infection in vitro and in vivo. METHODS: PXT and benznidazole (BZ) were assayed against intracellular and bloodstream forms for different periods of incubation by colorimetric and light microscopy analysis. Bloodstream forms were exposed to PXT and observed by transmission electron microscopy. PXT alone and in combination with BZ was evaluated as an acute mouse model of T. cruzi infection. FINDINGS: PXT is active (EC50 = 2.18 μM) against amastigotes of T. cruzi (Tulahuen-β gal strain), resulting in > 99% suppression of parasitism after 168 h of drug exposure. Upon bloodstream forms (Y strain), PXT was effective, displaying EC50 values of 8.90 and 4.27 μM after 2 and 24 h of incubation, respectively, revealing a rapid trypanocidal activity. PXT triggered ultrastructural alterations on trypomastigotes, including cytoplasmic disorganization, numerous contractile vacuoles besides damage on the mitochondria and paraflagellar stem. The proof of concept using a mouse model of acute T. cruzi infection demonstrates that although the parasitaemia was suppressed, PXT was unable to protect against mortality. MAIN CONCLUSIONS: Our findings demonstrate the activity of PXT against T. cruzi and reinforces the relevance of drug repositioning for CD.

Range expansion of two Triatominae species in Oaxaca, Mexico: first report and molecular identification of Triatoma barberi and Triatoma dimidiata in the Cañada regionFIRST REVIEW ROUND - REVIEWERS' COMMENTSREVIEWERS' COMMENTS.
BACKGROUND: Chagas disease (CD) is a chronic, disabling vector-borne disease caused by Trypanosoma cruzi and transmitted to humans by infected triatomine insects during blood meals. CD is currently endemic in 21 Latin American countries and the United States of America, with factors such as climate change, urbanisation, and migration contributing to the expansion of the vector's range from endemic to non-endemic regions. Globally, 44 countries have reported CD cases, indicating that it is an important public health problem. OBJECTIVES: To document the presence and geographic distribution of Triatoma dimidiata and Triatoma barberi in previously unreported areas, and to assess their epidemiological relevance for CD. METHODS: Molecular, entomological, and spot pattern analyses were performed. DNA was extracted from triatomines, the ITS2 region amplified, cloned, and sequenced. An extensive search for reports on triatomine in Oaxaca was conducted from 2019 to 2024, and a distribution map was generated. FINDINGS: We report the range expansion of two species to communities in La Cañada region. The CD vector range expansion poses an increased risk of infection in newly affected communities, given the higher prevalence of CD in Oaxaca. MAIN CONCLUSIONS: Awareness of triatomine distribution is essential to prevent the spread of CD into non-endemic areas and to identify emerging endemic zones for epidemiological surveillance and disease control.

Isavuconazole: Real-World Data and Clinical Considerations for Pediatric Patients.
Isavuconazole (ISAV) is a broad-spectrum triazole antifungal approved for the treatment of invasive aspergillosis and mucormycosis and has recently received approval for use in children ≥1 year of age. Pediatric approval was based on limited registration data, underscoring the importance of real-world evidence to better define efficacy and safety in children and adolescents. In this manuscript, we reviewed pediatric registration trials and real-world studies evaluating ISAV, with a focus on treatment and prophylaxis indications, pharmacokinetics, and safety. The literature review was conducted using PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane databases to identify relevant real-world and clinical studies published between January 1, 2005, and October 31, 2025. Studies reporting ISAV use in patients <18 years of age, including registration trials, observational cohorts, case series, and pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic studies, were included. Twenty-six real-world publications and two clinical registration trials met inclusion criteria. Among the real-world publications, ISAV was used for treatment in 23 studies and for prophylaxis in 5 studies, while 17 studies evaluated drug exposure or pharmacokinetics (several studies involved more than one mode of administration). Most patients had underlying hematologic or oncologic conditions. Across heterogeneous study populations and outcome definitions, complete or partial response was reported descriptively in approximately 72% of evaluable patients treated for invasive fungal disease, with breakthrough fungal infections reported in approximately 10% of patients receiving prophylaxis. Adverse events were generally mild and predominantly consisted of reversible hepatic laboratory abnormalities; serious drug-related toxicity, including one reported case of acute liver failure, was rare. Pharmacokinetic data demonstrated predictable exposure and achievement of target plasma concentrations in the majority of patients. Taken together, current evidence, although limited and derived largely from retrospective and salvage-treatment cohorts, suggests promising clinical activity and generally favorable tolerability of ISAV for invasive mold infections in pediatric populations. Real-world data support its use as a therapeutic option in selected patients, while underscoring the need for prospective studies to confirm efficacy, optimize dosing, and assess long-term safety.

Retrospective analysis of genetic diversity, clinical manifestations and risk factors, during outbreak of lumpy skin disease virus.
Lumpy skin is a highly host-specific, contagious, transboundary, notifiable disease affecting cattle (Bos taurus and Bos indicus) and water buffalo (Bubalus bubalis), and also reported in some wild ruminants. The spread and reporting of Lumpy skin disease (LSD) in the past five years in disease-free countries, mainly in Pakistan, has highlighted the threat of its emergence and re-emergence in neighboring areas. Notably significant outbreaks of this disease have been reported in the neighboring countries of Pakistan during the last decades and are thought to be the reason for the first reported outbreak of LSD in Pakistan in the year 2021-22. This study targeted seven locations and collected samples and clinical data of LSD-suspected animals, focusing on clinical presentation, farm-level risk factors, and molecular characterization via PCR and subsequent phylogenetic relatedness of sequenced isolates. Out of the collected samples (n = 285), 117 cases were found positive for LSDV. The most frequent clinical signs included fever (83.7%), skin nodules (94.8%), emaciation (88.0%), and snoring (83.7%), all of which were statistically significant (p ≤ 0.05). Significant farm-level risk factors associated with LSDV positive cases included the use of shared water sources (64.9%), treatment by quack practitioners (79.4%), improper handling of manure (22.2%), and lack of disinfection (15.3%), with significant p-values ≤0.05. Molecular confirmation of LSDV was performed by PCR amplification of a 554-bp fragment of the RPO30 gene, a commonly used molecular marker for LSDV detection and characterization. The sequenced isolates showed close genetic similarity to strains reported from India, Bangladesh, and China, indicating a regional genetic relatedness among circulating LSDV strains. The study highlights that enhanced biosecurity, farmer education, vaccination, and veterinary guidance can prevent disease spread, improve livestock health, and reduce economic losses.

The cow udder as an influenza mixing ground.
Bovine mammary tissue can support infection and replication of diverse influenza A viruses and may provide an environment in which different viral strains can co-infect cells.

The next generation of maternal vaccines: scientific advances, regulatory readiness, and strategic planning in Europe.
With the recent approval of maternal RSV vaccines and late-phase trials underway for a GBS vaccine, Europe is entering a new era of maternal immunisation. Yet scientific progress is outpacing pregnancy-specific evidence and preparedness for equitable implementation. Pregnant women are often excluded from early vaccine trials, while national recommendations, surveillance and delivery vary across Europe, even after regulatory authorisation. Without coordinated planning, new maternal vaccines risk reproducing the delays and inequities seen with influenza, pertussis and COVID-19 vaccination. In this Review, we examine scientific advances in the next generation of maternal vaccines, including mRNA, protein conjugate, nanoparticle and combination approaches, and candidates against emerging and other priority pathogens. We discuss barriers to including pregnant women in trials, assess regulatory and pharmacovigilance readiness, and identify health-system and vaccine-confidence risks to equitable rollout. We offer strategic recommendations for Europe's maternal immunisation roadmap, from research investment to policy integration, provider education, and equity-centred planning. Realising this potential will require integrated action across research, regulation, implementation, and communication. This is the final paper in the Series on the future of maternal vaccination in Europe and synthesises its findings into a framework for Europe and beyond.

Defining trauma-informed approaches and their purpose in nursing education: A scoping review.
BACKGROUND: A focus on nursing student trauma has increased since the COVID-19 pandemic. Scholars have turned to trauma-informed approaches to understand how nursing students can be better supported in their education and mitigate the effects of past, current, and future trauma exposure. AIM: To examine the current published literature on how trauma-informed approaches to nursing education are described in the literature. DESIGN: We conducted a scoping review following the Joanna Briggs Institute framework. We used the PRISMA-ScR guidelines for reporting of findings. METHODS: We performed searches in June 2024 and then again in June 2025 in Medline via OVID, CINAHL via EBSCO, ERIC, PsycInfo, Education Research Complete, and Scopus. We included literature published in English in any year that focused on nursing students and/or nurse educators, included a definition of a trauma-informed approach (TIA) and involved any education context. RESULTS: 35 sources were included, published between 2020 and 2025. Study types included 11 descriptions of implementing a TIA and 6 unstructured reviews supporting its implementation. 10 sources were primary research. Findings included descriptive categories of definitions of a TIA, sources of nursing students' exposure to trauma (in their education, personal lives, and specifically COVID-19), and the purpose of a TIA (success in education and the creation of a future workforce). CONCLUSIONS: TIA to support student learning and develop the future nursing workforce are increasingly prevalent and recommended in the nursing education literature. Terminology and definitions of TIA varied but often shared commonalities, with some specifically addressing structural inequities. Differences between definitions that highlight structural inequities specifically need to be examined for how they differ from more common definitions. The student perspective on resilience and TIA effectiveness is needed. Conceptualizations of TIA must also address how they might reinforce power structures within educational institutions, thereby avoiding the reproduction of inequities.

Nationwide surveillance, mitochondrial genetic diversity, and associated microorganisms of Lipoptena fortisetosa collected from cervids in the Republic of Korea.
BACKGROUND: Deer keds are blood-feeding ectoparasites of cervids and can carry diverse microorganisms of veterinary or potential zoonotic relevance. Nationwide information on their distribution, mitochondrial diversity, and associated microorganisms has been lacking in the Republic of Korea (ROK). This study investigated deer keds collected from cervids across the ROK and characterized their species identity, COX1 diversity, and sequence-confirmed microorganisms. METHODS: A total of 405 deer keds were opportunistically collected from 116 cervids made available through ongoing regional wildlife management activities across nine provinces of the Republic of Korea, including Korean water deer (Hydropotes inermis) on the mainland and Siberian roe deer (Capreolus pygargus) on Jeju Island. All 405 specimens were examined morphologically, and 186 were analyzed using cytochrome oxidase subunit 1 (COX1) sequencing for molecular confirmation and population-genetic analysis. Selected viral, bacterial, and protozoan microorganisms were screened using pooled qPCR/qRT-PCR or conventional PCR, followed by individual conventional PCR and Sanger sequencing for confirmation. Host-level clustering was evaluated using binomial generalized linear mixed models when sufficient confirmed detections were available. RESULTS: All 405 deer keds were identified morphologically as Lipoptena fortisetosa, and all 186 COX1-sequenced specimens were molecularly consistent with this identification. The 617-bp COX1 dataset comprised 29 haplotypes (Hd = 0.681 ± 0.038; π = 0.01262 ± 0.00101). AMOVA showed significant mitochondrial differentiation between Jeju Island and mainland samples (ΦST = 0.615, P < 0.001), although host species and geography were completely confounded. Sequence-confirmed microorganisms included Bartonella spp. in 94/405 deer keds (23.21%), Theileria spp. in 40/405 (9.88%), Coxiella-like organisms in 4/405 (0.99%), and Anaplasma capra in 2/405 (0.49%). No sequence-confirmed Babesia spp., Ehrlichia spp., Borrelia spp., Hepatozoon spp., or SFTSV were obtained. Bartonella detection showed very strong host-level clustering and a marked Jeju-mainland contrast, whereas Theileria detection did not differ significantly between regions after accounting for host clustering. CONCLUSIONS: Lipoptena fortisetosa was widely associated with the cervids examined across the ROK and showed substantial mitochondrial genetic structure between the sampled Jeju and mainland groups. Bartonella spp. were the most frequently sequence-confirmed microorganisms, followed by Theileria spp. Molecular detection alone does not establish vector competence, and the geographic and host-species effects in the present sampling design cannot be separated. Standardized longitudinal sampling and host-vector-microorganism interaction studies are required to clarify transmission ecology and population structure.

Mortality dynamics of West Nile virus and Lyme disease in the United States: Temporal, spatial, and socioeconomic dimensions (2003-2021).
BACKGROUND: West Nile virus (WNV) and Lyme disease pose a growing public health threat in the United States. This study investigated spatial and temporal mortality trends of WNV and Lyme disease and evaluated associations with individual and county-level factors. METHODS: We utilized National Center for Health Statistics data to identify WNV- and Lyme-related deaths (2003-2021), including demographics and the decedent's county of residence. County-level insurance status was sourced from the U.S. Census Bureau, and urbanicity was defined using the 2013 National Center For Health Statistics classification. We applied negative binomial regression models to identify predictors of mortality. RESULTS: Our analysis of 3694 deaths (WNV: 2,628 [71.2%]; Lyme: 1,066 [28.8%]) revealed WNV peaks occurred in 2003 (246 deaths, 9.4% of WNV deaths) and 2012 (281 deaths, 10.7%), and an increasing trend for Lyme (103 deaths, 9.7% in 2021). Overall, deaths were highest in 2012 (343, 9.3%) and lowest in 2009 (105, 2.6%). Age ≥65 (rate ratio [RR] = 1.5, confidence interval [CI] = 1.27, 1.48), male sex (RR = 1.2, CI = 1.04, 1.26), and White race (RR = 1.7, CI = 1.37, 1.73) were associated with increased mortality. Spatial analysis indicated high WNV mortality in California, Colorado, Arizona, and Texas, and states along the Mississippi River. In contrast, Lyme disease deaths were concentrated in the Northeast and the Upper Midwest. CONCLUSION: Our results suggest that age, sex, race, and urbanicity are important factors influencing mortality from WNV and Lyme disease. More research is needed to link exposures and incidence to mortality of WNV and Lyme to better understand the drivers of regional variation, given the spatial and temporal variability.

Analysis of Laboratory Testing for Imported Dengue Fever in the Republic of Korea, 2020-2025.
Objectives: Dengue fever is an acute, mosquito-borne disease that is widely endemic in tropical and subtropical regions. While no autochthonous cases have been reported in the Republic of Korea, imported cases continue to occur. This study analyzed laboratory testing data from 2020 to 2025 to support the surveillance of imported mosquito-borne infections. Methods: A total of 2,904 laboratory test requests for dengue fever submitted to the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency and 17 provincial Institutes of Health and Environment were reviewed. Laboratory diagnosis was performed using real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) and immunoglobulin M (IgM) enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). The analysis focused on annual trends, presumed countries of infection, and the distribution of dengue virus (DENV) serotypes. Results: Of the 2,904 test requests, 613 cases were confirmed positive, with an overall positivity rate of 21.1%. The number of positive cases was lowest in 2021, with three cases, but increased after international travel resumed, reaching 177 cases in both 2023 and 2024. Most infections were presumed to have been acquired in Southeast Asia, particularly in Indonesia, the Philippines, and Vietnam. DENV-2 was the most common serotype, followed by DENV-1, DENV-3, and DENV-4; all four serotypes were detected. Conclusions: Imported dengue fever increased following the recovery of international travel, with infections concentrated in Southeast Asia. Presumed countries of infection were mainly associated with four Southeast Asian countries (73.1%), with cases concentrated during the summer vacation season. Because reinfection with a different DENV serotype may increase the risk of severe dengue, individuals who travel repeatedly to dengue-endemic countries should exercise particular caution.

Efficacy, Effectiveness, and Immunogenicity of the Respiratory Syncytial Virus Prefusion F Vaccine Administered During Pregnancy: Protocol for a Living Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
BACKGROUND: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of lower respiratory tract disease in infants, with the highest burden in the first 6 months of life. Maternal immunization with the bivalent (RSV-A and RSV-B) prefusion F (RSVPreF) protein subunit vaccine (ABRYSVO) is a recently recommended strategy for preventing RSV-related outcomes in infants. First licensed for use in pregnancy in 2023, the RSVPreF vaccine demonstrated efficacy in a single pivotal randomized trial (Maternal Immunization Study for Safety and Efficacy; MATISSE); postlicensure real-world evidence on vaccine effectiveness across settings, seasons, and subgroups and on antibody durability and transplacental transfer remains limited and has not been synthesized in a continuously updated framework, motivating this review. OBJECTIVE: This living systematic review and meta-analysis will synthesize emerging postlicensure data on the efficacy, effectiveness, and immunogenicity of the RSVPreF vaccine in real-world settings. METHODS: We will conduct, in real time, a living systematic review and meta-analysis following Cochrane methods and PRISMA-P (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Protocols) guidance, including randomized clinical trials and postlicensure real-world studies (eg, cohort, case-control, test-negative, and quasi-experimental studies). Primary objectives are evaluation of vaccine efficacy and effectiveness in preventing RSV-specific and all-cause respiratory disease and immunogenicity in infants and pregnant individuals. Vaccine effectiveness outcomes include RSV laboratory-confirmed infection, RSV acute respiratory illness, RSV lower respiratory tract disease, RSV hospitalization, RSV complications, all-cause lower respiratory tract disease and hospitalization, and antibiotic use in infants with RSV infection. Immunogenicity outcomes include maternal neutralizing antibody titers, maternal-infant transfer ratios, infant titers over time, and RSV viral load. We will search MEDLINE, Embase, the Cochrane Library, LILACS, Science Citation Index Expanded, Chinese biomedical and citation databases, clinical trial registries from January 2023 onward with no language restrictions, updating at least monthly. Two investigators will independently select studies, extract data, and assess risk of bias. Adjusted estimates will be standardized to vaccine efficacy and effectiveness. Certainty will be graded using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) system. RESULTS: This living systematic review was funded in June 2025. Searches began in January 2023 and will continue with surveillance updates at least monthly until April 2028. As of January 2026, 837 records were screened, 105 (12.5%) were assessed in full text, and 12 (1.4%) met the inclusion criteria, of which 10 (1.2%) contributed extractable data. Data collection and analysis are ongoing and displayed on an interactive dashboard. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, conferences, and a real-time dashboard, with the first effectiveness estimates available in July 2026. CONCLUSIONS: This living systematic review and meta-analysis will provide a continuously updated synthesis of real-world evidence on maternal RSVPreF vaccination to inform clinical and policy decisions.

Klebsiella pneumoniae pyogenic liver abscess mimicking hepatic malignancy in a non-diabetic patient: A case report from Kazakhstan.
Pyogenic liver abscess is an infectious condition associated with significant morbidity and mortality, with Klebsiella pneumoniae emerging as a major pathogen. We report a case of Klebsiella pneumoniae pyogenic liver abscess in a 76-year-old woman from Kazakhstan, representing one of the first indexed reports from Central Asia. The patient presented with prolonged fever, jaundice, and constitutional symptoms without diabetes mellitus. Initial ultrasound revealed a large heterogeneous hepatic mass with a solid, tumor-like appearance, raising concern for malignancy in the setting of chronic hepatitis B infection. MRI and contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated diffusion restriction, multiloculated architecture, and mild peripheral and septal enhancement without arterial hyperenhancement or venous washout, favoring hepatic abscess over hepatocellular carcinoma. The solid, tumor-like ultrasound appearance, atypical for a pyogenic abscess in its resemblance to hepatic malignancy, posed the primary diagnostic challenge, underscoring the value of multimodal imaging in characterizing hepatic lesions. Additionally, KPLA should be considered in the differential diagnosis even in the absence of classical metabolic risk factors and in regions with limited epidemiological data.

Epidemiological modeling of African swine fever in wild boars-A systematic review.
African swine fever (ASF) is a viral disease that poses a major threat to swine production, with wild boars contributing to virus persistence and transmission. We systematically reviewed global epidemiological modeling studies published from 2014 to 2024 to assess modeling approaches, transmission pathways, methodological patterns, and factors associated with ASF occurrence and spread in wild boar populations. Fifty-four studies from twenty-nine countries were grouped into five categories based on research objectives. Risk-factor and spatiotemporal analyses were the most common approaches, supporting targeted surveillance and risk mapping. Carcass-mediated transmission, wild boar density, movement, habitat conditions, and seasonal variation were important factors influencing ASF occurrence and spread. As modeling approaches differ in their assumptions, data requirements, and applicability, we developed a framework linking model choice to surveillance capacity, outbreak stage, data availability, and management objectives. This framework provides a structured basis for selecting appropriate approaches to strengthen ASF surveillance and control strategies.

Risk map for high pathogenicity avian influenza in 2022-2023 winter season in Japan.
For high pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI) outbreaks at poultry farms, both farm and regional characteristics have been reported as risk factors. Because the regional-level component of outbreak risk may reflect the level of virus contamination in the surrounding area, it may also serve as a proxy for exposure risk potentially shared by poultry farms and sympatric wildlife. We examined associations between HPAI outbreaks at chicken farms in Japan during October 2022-April 2023 and both farm factors (flock size, production type, and peripheral water bodies) and regional factors (land cover, meteorological conditions, and topography); we also estimated the regional-level component of outbreak risk and developed an HPAI risk map. We conducted a nationwide cross-sectional study using data from 68 affected chicken farms and 5496 unaffected farms, excluding remote southern islands. Multivariable analyses were performed using stochastic partial differential equation models accounting for spatial autocorrelation. Farm factors were forced into all models, and combinations of regional factors aggregated on 10-km grids were selected using wAIC. Models with ΔwAIC <2 were combined by stacking. Among the 59 models retained for stacking, four contributed to the final stacked prediction. Coefficient estimates from these models suggested that lower elevation, lower forest cover, and high TWI were associated with higher HPAI outbreak risk. Although further investigation is warranted to examine other factors potentially affecting HPAI outbreaks and to validate the regional risk index in wildlife, the regional-level component of outbreak risk may provide a useful basis for mapping HPAI risk potentially shared by poultry farms and sympatric wildlife.

Polyclonal breast milk-derived secretory IgA confers broad antiviral protection against multiple respiratory viruses.
Passive immunization is an important tool for protecting individuals with primary immune deficiencies from infectious diseases and offers a rapid response strategy for protecting vulnerable populations, particularly during the interval between pathogen emergence and vaccine deployment. Current approaches rely on intravenous delivery of IgG-enriched plasma or monoclonal antibodies, which limits accessibility, scalability, and effectiveness at mucosal surfaces, the primary entry point for respiratory viruses. Here, we tested LCTG-001, a polyclonal secretory IgA preparation derived from pooled human breast milk, to address these limitations. LCTG-001 demonstrated broad antiviral activity against clinically relevant respiratory viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and influenza A virus. LCTG-001 effectively recognized both group 1 and group 2 influenza A subtypes, including the highly pathogenic H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b, and engaged nonneutralizing effector mechanisms such as neuraminidase inhibition and neutrophil activation. When administered intranasally, LCTG-001 conferred complete protection against influenza A challenge in both immunocompetent and antibody-deficient murine models, preventing morbidity and mortality through a transient early reduction in viral burden followed by sustained improvements in lung pathology and lung barrier integrity. These findings highlight the potential of breast milk-derived secretory IgA as a scalable, mucosa-targeted passive immunization strategy capable of addressing both endemic and emerging respiratory viral threats.

Avian cholera causes mass mortality at penguin mega-colonies amid H5N1 HPAI outbreaks in Antarctica.
The characterization of pathogens affecting Antarctic wildlife has been historically limited and sporadic. With the introduction of H5N1 high pathogenicity avian influenza virus (HPAIV) in Antarctica in the austral summer 2023/2024, concerns about the health of Antarctic seabirds and mammals prompted immediate surveillance efforts. In March 2024, we visited the Danger Islands archipelago, that hosts two mega-colonies of Adélie penguins, and observed an unusual mortality estimated in thousands of Adélie penguins and other species. Swabs and tissues were collected for molecular detection of infectious agents from 49 carcasses, and additional tissues for histology from a selection of 9 carcasses. We detected Pasteurella multocida DNA in 46 of 49 individuals, and diagnosed avian cholera as the cause of death of most of these animals. By shotgun sequencing, we retrieved the first genomic sequences of the P. multocida strain from this region, and the phylogenetic analysis showed a close relation with strains from other locations retrieved during the same expedition and with strains previously reported in the Southern Ocean area. This study confirms avian cholera as a relevant cause of mortality in the Antarctic, and overall highlights the importance of considering this disease in the differential diagnoses during mortality events in Antarctica.

A one health visual analytics approach for syndromic surveillance.
Effective syndromic surveillance requires integrating diverse data streams while maintaining transparency and interpretability to support timely and informed public health action. Traditional surveillance approaches often rely on single-domain data, such as clinical reports or environmental measurements, or employ black-box models that limit stakeholder trust and validation. To address these challenges, we present a One Health visual analytics framework that integrates heterogeneous surveillance signals with complementary predictive models and interactive model analysis, enabling systematic comparison of data contributions, model configurations, and predictive uncertainty across infectious disease surveillance tasks. The framework integrates mixed-effects models, Transformer-based deep learning architectures with spatiotemporal embeddings, and interactive dashboards to balance predictive performance with explainability in a white-box environment. We demonstrate the framework's utility through three mixed-effects case studies and the complementary Transformer forecasting experiment: (i) prediction of influenza and RSV cases in Arizona, (ii) modeling of COVID-19 cases and deaths in Arkansas, and (iii) prediction of COVID-19 hospitalizations in Oklahoma using wastewater, animal health, and environmental data. Across the case studies, integrating multi-source signals improved predictive accuracy for most configurations, although the incremental value of individual streams proved species- and configuration-dependent, while hierarchical random effects (e.g., county, month, age group) captured contextual variation and enhanced robustness. For longer-term forecasting, Transformer models with spatial and spatiotemporal embeddings outperformed baseline statistical models, highlighting the value of contextual information. By transforming complex modeling outputs into interpretable visual tools, the framework supports proactive decision-making, enhances public health preparedness, and strengthens One Health collaboration across human, environmental, and animal health domains. This work introduces a generalizable One Health approach for transparent, data-driven syndromic surveillance with direct implications for health security and community resilience. The novelty of this work is the integration of heterogeneous One Health signals with complementary modeling strategies and interactive model provenance so that prediction and interpretation can be examined together across health domains.

Oropouche virus attack rate in an urban setting outside the Amazon Basin: findings from a post-outbreak seroprevalence survey.
BACKGROUND: Oropouche virus (OROV) is transmitted by the biting midge Culicoides paraensis. Historically, it was restricted to small outbreaks in the Amazon region. Since 2023, genomic reassortment and human-environment interactions facilitated its geographic expansion, including into urban areas. We estimate the OROV attack rate and identify factors associated with infection in an urban area outside the Amazon. METHODS: A randomised cross-sectional serosurvey in the urban area of Baturité, Brazil. Households were selected using stratified probability sampling proportional to census tract population; one resident per household was randomly chosen. Participants completed a questionnaire, and serum samples were tested for OROV IgM using MAC-ELISA. Associations were estimated using prevalence ratios (PR) with 95% confidence intervals from Poisson regression with robust variance. Spatial clustering of seropositives was assessed using kernel density and nearest-neighbours. FINDINGS: Of 392 participants, 212 were seropositive (54·0%). Most infections were asymptomatic/oligosymptomatic (72·6%-154/212). Living near rivers (PR = 1·80; 95% CI: 1·20-2·50) and working from home (PR = 1·70; 95% CI: 1·30-2·30) were associated with higher prevalence of infection. Clustering of seropositivity was found in census tracts close to cultivated and forested areas, and in central urban neighbourhoods. INTERPRETATION: We show large-scale urban OROV transmission, with attack rates exceeding 50%. The high proportion of infections among low mobility individuals suggests peridomestic transmission and vector adaptation to urban microenvironments. Results highlight the need to incorporate OROV into routine surveillance, outbreak preparedness, and differential diagnoses of acute febrile illnesses. FUNDING: Health Surveillance Secretariat/Brazilian Ministry of Health, and Japan International Cooperation Agency.

Clinical and virological characterisation of Oropouche, dengue, and chikungunya during simultaneous co-circulation in the State of Espírito Santo, Brazil: a retrospective observational study.
BACKGROUND: Dengue (DENV), chikungunya (CHIKV), and Oropouche (OROV) viruses co-circulate in Brazil and present with overlapping acute febrile syndromes, complicating clinical differentiation. Comparative data integrating clinical phenotyping and viral load dynamics across these arboviruses are limited. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective observational study using linked surveillance and laboratory databases from Espírito Santo State, Brazil (2024-2025). We aimed to compare DENV, CHIKV, and OROV infections and to explore their virological correlates. Cycle threshold (Ct) values, used as a relative semi-quantitative proxy for viral RNA levels, were analysed within each virus to characterise temporal dynamics and clinical expression. Multinomial logistic regression identified clinical features associated with arboviral infection; associations between Ct values and clinical domain scores were assessed using multivariable linear regression adjusted for age, sex, and time since symptom onset. FINDINGS: Among 10,793 cases (4058 DENV, 2508 CHIKV, 4227 OROV), Oropouche affected older individuals (median age 49 years, interquartile range [IQR] 43-56) and was characterised by near-universal fever (97·8%), headache (96·2%), and intense arthralgia (86·4%), with fewer gastrointestinal and mucocutaneous manifestations. After adjustment for age, sex, and time since symptom onset, increased odds of arthritis (OR 5·22, 95% CI 4·08-6·68) and rash (OR 2·39, 95% CI 1·83-3·12) were observed for CHIKV versus OROV. Conversely, nausea (OR 2·98, 95% CI 2·52-3·53), vomiting (OR 2·54, 95% CI 2·01-3·21), and retro-orbital pain (OR 8·00, 95% CI 6·69-9·56) were positively associated with DENV versus OROV. Dengue and chikungunya showed progressive Ct increases over time, consistent with viral decay. Oropouche displayed a non-monotonic, with lower Ct values and higher systemic and musculoskeletal domain scores after adjustment for age, sex, and time since symptom onset. INTERPRETATION: The distinct clinical and temporal patterns identified provide descriptive foundations that may inform future development of diagnostic algorithms and sampling strategies, pending formal predictive validation. FUNDING: This study was partially funded by the Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa e Inovação do Espírito Santo (FAPES), with additional institutional support from the Brazilian Ministry of Health and the Government of the State of Espírito Santo.

Measuring enteric pathogen force of infection through antibody responses in children.
Enteric pathogens account for a substantial global disease burden, yet population-based surveillance remains limited by the transient nature of pathogen shedding, which constrains the sensitivity of stool-based molecular testing to a narrow detection window. Detection of IgG responses in serological surveys could enable new insights into enteric pathogen transmission, but benchmarking serological measures relative to stool-based measures of infection remains a critical evidence gap. We compared measures of disease transmission in longitudinal birth cohort samples using multiplex IgG (1,575 dried blood spots, 369 children) and PCR assays (2,229 stool samples, 369 children) that overlapped for nine pathogens (norovirus GI/GII, Shigella /enteroinvasive Escherichia coli (EIEC), Campylobacter spp., enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (LT-ETEC), Salmonella enterica , Giardia spp., Cryptosporidium spp., Entamoeba histolytica ). Campylobacter and LT-ETEC ranked highest while E. histolytica and S. enterica ranked among the lowest by both IgG and PCR measures of infection. Measures of infection were less aligned for norovirus GI, norovirus GII, Cryptosporidium , Shigella /EIEC, and Giardia . Despite this, for most pathogens, and across both measures, force of infection was lowest in the urban city of Esmeraldas and substantially higher in more rural populations, with relative risks in assay measures (seroconversion rate and PCR detected prevalence) of approximately 2.0 for pathogens with the largest differences ( Shigella /EIEC and norovirus GI). Together, our results suggest that although absolute levels of infection differed between assays, IgG and PCR captured consistent relative risk of infection across geographic strata, suggesting either method can identify high-versus low-transmission settings.

Diisonitrile Chalkophore Structure and Function in Mycobacterial Copper Acquisition.
Tuberculosis, the disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, is a leading cause of death worldwide. While first-line treatments are effective for many patients, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis poses a continued threat to global public health, and new approaches are needed to provide effective chemotherapy against drug-resistant disease. Diisonitrile lipopeptide chalkophores are a novel class of natural products that play critical roles in copper homeostasis and virulence in M. tuberculosis by supplying copper to the heme:Cu oxidase of the respiratory chain. However, the molecular mechanisms by which the bacteria use diisonitriles to mediate copper homeostasis are poorly understood. Herein, we investigate structure-activity relationships of synthetic diisonitriles to identify structural features required for biological function in mycobacterial copper acquisition. We have developed a modular synthetic approach that allows efficient construction of diisonitrile natural products and diverse analogues. We confirmed that a short-chain analogue of the natural products binds tightly to Cu(I) and Cu(II), but not Zn(II), and estimated its Cu(I) binding affinity. We then used these analogues to probe the impacts of diisonitrile acyl chain length, amino acid backbone, and C-terminal motif on the rescue of M. tuberculosis and Mycobacterium marinum growth in copper-restricted conditions. The observed structural preferences align with current knowledge of the corresponding natural product structures in these bacteria, but both species also exhibited surprising flexibility in accepting diverse diisonitrile analogues for this function. This work provides new insights into the structural features of diisonitrile chalkophores required for function in mycobacterial copper homeostasis, and the distinct structural preferences between species, while suggesting some structural plasticity in their cellular copper acquisition systems.

Poor mental health days and depressive disorders comparing non-caregivers, informal non-cancer caregivers, and informal caregivers of cancer patients: BRFSS 2022-23.
PURPOSE: Informal caregivers are increasing in number, especially those caring for cancer patients, and caregiving can affect both patient outcomes and caregiver well-being. This study sought to elucidate whether the mental health outcomes differed among informal cancer caregivers, informal non-cancer caregivers, and non-caregivers. METHODS: Data from 2022 and 2023 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance Surveys (BRFSS) were analyzed for 24 states administering the caregiving module. The sample included non-caregivers(n = 157,539), informal non-cancer caregivers (n = 39,047), and informal cancer caregivers (n = 3,078). Logistic regressions identified factors associated with frequent mental distress days (FMD; ≥ 6 days of poor mental health in the last 30 days) and lifetime depression diagnosis. Models included caregiver status, reporting ≥ 14 poor physical health days monthly, exercise in the previous month, age, sex, marital status, education, employment, and rural/urban status, adjusted for U.S. region and year. RESULTS: In unadjusted comparisons, informal caregivers differed significantly from non-caregivers across several sociodemographic and health characteristics and were more likely to report FMD or a lifetime depression diagnosis. After adjusting for sociodemographics, year, U.S. region, physical health, and exercise, informal cancer caregivers had significantly higher odds of FMD than non-caregivers (aOR = 1.89, 95%CI = 1.58-2.26). Informal non-cancer caregivers had significantly higher odds of a lifetime depression diagnosis (aOR = 1.44, 95%CI = 1.36-1.52) than non-caregivers. CONCLUSION: Cancer caregiving was more strongly associated with frequent mental distress than with lifetime depression. Integrating clinical screening into patient visits and informal caregiver supports could help identify caregiving distress during periods of increased burden and facilitate timely supportive care.

Emergence of the GI-23 lineage of infectious bronchitis virus in Brazilian backyard poultry.
Infectious bronchitis virus (IBV) remains a major threat to poultry production worldwide, with the GI-23 lineage emerging as one of the most epidemiologically relevant variants in recent years. Although GI-23 has been reported in Brazilian commercial poultry, its occurrence and genomic characteristics in backyard poultry remain poorly understood. This study investigated the molecular epidemiology and evolutionary features of IBV circulating in backyard poultry from São Paulo State, Brazil. Samples from 893 backyard birds were screened for IBV using RT-qPCR targeting the 5' untranslated region (5'UTR). Positive samples were further characterized by lineage-specific RT-PCR assays, S1 gene sequencing, virus isolation, and whole-genome sequencing, followed by phylogenetic, phylogenomic, and recombination analyses. IBV was detected exclusively in chickens, with an overall prevalence of 13.8% (42/304 swab pools; 95% CI: 10.1-18.2). Among RT-qPCR-positive samples, 23.9% were identified as belonging to the GI-23 lineage, while GI-1 and GI-11 lineages were not detected. Phylogenetic analysis of partial S1 gene sequences revealed multiple GI-23 sublineages circulating in Brazil, indicating different viral introductions. Whole-genome sequencing of a Brazilian GI-23 isolate showed high identity to a virus identified in Mexico and revealed recombination events involving European and Middle Eastern IBV lineages. These findings provide the molecular and genomic evidence of IBV GI-23 circulation in Brazilian backyard poultry and highlight the importance of monitoring viral evolution and supporting effective disease control strategies.

Questioning the cost of convenience: a mixed methods study of the impact of a telehealth service delivery on pharmacists' work.
OBJECTIVES: Telehealth represents a fundamental change to the health care delivery process. Despite the burgeoning literature on the rapid expansion of telehealth services during the COVID-19 pandemic, the consequences of these changes for clinicians' workload are seldom examined. This study addresses that gap by describing the interactions between patient activity, work processes and pharmacists' experience of an Australian hospital outpatient telepharmacy service that was rapidly upscaled during the pandemic to ensure all patients continued to access pharmaceutical care. METHODS: A three-phase explanatory mixed methods design was used: (1) a retrospective audit quantified changes to patient use of telepharmacy before (August 2019-March 2020) and during (March-September 2020) COVID-19 lockdowns; (2) process mapping to visualise and compare all the work steps involved in delivering telepharmacy and its face-to-face equivalent; (3) interviews with pharmacists (n = 10) to explain the patterns of patient use identified in the audit data and explore the impact of telepharmacy on their work. RESULTS: Telepharmacy occasions of service (N = 1442) increased 6-fold during COVID-19 lockdown, with a significant increase in metropolitan and express deliveries. Comparing the process maps reveals the inherent efficiencies of face-to-face care, as remote dispensing involved substantially more administrative steps than in-person encounters. Three themes emerged from the interviews that illuminate pharmacists' experience of delivering telepharmacy: increased and less satisfying work; shifting responsibility for medication management from patients to pharmacists; and questioning the cost of convenience. CONCLUSIONS: Telepharmacy successfully maintained access to pharmaceutical care for highly immunocompromised outpatients during, and long after the COVID-19 pandemic, but this came at the cost of increased administrative workload and reduced professional satisfaction for pharmacists. As telehealth becomes embedded in routine care, service models must account for these hidden workload consequences and ensure telehealth is targeted to settings where it delivers value rather than just convenience.

Hydrolytic Disruption of Viral Envelopes for Broad-Adaptive Antiviral Protection by an Esterase-Mimicking Nanozyme based on Copper Imidazole-Carboxylate Coordination.
Viral infections pose a persistent challenge to global public health and cause millions of infections and substantial mortality each year. There is therefore an urgent need for effective antiviral strategies to limit the transmission of viruses such as influenza A virus and SARS-CoV-2. In this work, we report a copper imidazole-carboxylate coordinated nanozyme (Cu-ImCar) with high esterase-mimicking activity and potent antiviral performance. Mechanistic studies reveal that Cu-ImCar nanozyme catalyzes the hydrolysis of lipid components in the viral envelope, leading to structural disruption and rapid loss of viral infectivity. In addition, the nanozyme demonstrates excellent catalytic stability and tolerance to extreme conditions. When functionalized onto fabrics, Cu-ImCar nanozyme efficiently inactivated influenza virus and SARS-CoV-2 pseudovirus over a wide temperature range (-20 to 37 °C). Notably, at a moderately elevated temperature of 50 °C, it reduces viral titers to undetectable levels within 5 min, even at the low loading level (6.25 μg cm-2). These findings establish Cu-ImCar as a robust antiviral nanozyme with broad environmental adaptability and highlight the potential of esterase-mimicking catalysis as an effective strategy for viral inactivation and transmission control.

Human epidemiological data of Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever, 2014-2023: scoping review over one decade.
Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (CCHF), a severe emerging viral tick-borne disease, poses a global threat. The virus, endemic to Africa, the Middle East, Asia, and the Balkans, is being detected in new regions. This study aimed to summarise available human CCHF epidemiological data and determine whether scientific literature, surveillance system reports, and public health authorities' disease notifications offer uniform and sufficiently useful data to timely detect changes in epidemiological trends. We conducted a systematic PubMed search (2017-2023) using relevant CCHF MeSH and entry terms (e.g. CCHF and epidemiology). We reviewed ProMED reports and publicly available public health authorities' notifications on CCHF (2014-2023). We extracted case characteristics, reporting date, and transmission routes from these reports. The review includes 88 PubMed articles, 309 ProMED reports, and 44 public health authorities' notifications, reporting on 7073, 4169, and 3749 confirmed cases respectively, mostly from endemic regions. The number of ProMED reported cases did not increase significantly over one decade (p = .281). The case-fatality rate was significantly higher in the African and Southeast Asian Regions compared to the European and Eastern Mediterranean Regions. The risk appeared elevated in people working with animals and in healthcare workers. Tick exposure was the most frequently reported transmission route. None of the three data sources provided a complete overview of CCHF epidemiology. A more accurate CCHF monitoring system is needed to detect epidemiological changes timely. Addressing current gaps, such as inconsistencies in reporting frequency, requires coordinated, standardised data collection and sharing using standardised reporting frameworks to strengthen global preparedness and response.

Catalytic Immunoassay with Fluorescence-Colorimetric Dual Readout for Highly Sensitive Zika Virion Detection.
Zika virus (ZIKV) infection may induce severe neurological disorders and congenital malformations in pregnant women and fetuses, posing a substantial threat to global public health. Therefore, sensitive, accurate, and convenient detection strategies are essential for early ZIKV diagnosis to block viral transmission and mitigate adverse clinical complications. Herein, a robust fluorescence-colorimetric dual-modal immunoassay was successfully developed for high-performance ZIKV detection based on dual-functional fluorescence nanoprobes grafted with ZIKV antibodies and catalase. The elaborately designed nanoprobes can generate stable fluorescence signals to realize precise fluorescence-based quantitative detection. Meanwhile, the modified catalase can efficiently decompose hydrogen peroxide, thereby modulating the morphological transformation of gold nanoparticles and achieving naked-eye visible plasmonic colorimetric analysis, with a low limit of detection down to 0.85 PFU/μL. Benefiting from the complementary dual-signal outputs and mutual verification mechanism, the proposed method effectively avoids signal interference and detection errors inherent to conventional single-mode assays. Clinical specimen validation verified that this dual-modal immunoassay achieves 100% diagnostic accuracy in practical ZIKV detection. Integrating high sensitivity, visual readout, excellent anti-interference ability, and reliable quantitative performance, this dual-modal sensing platform provides a promising strategy for early clinical diagnosis and epidemiological surveillance of ZIKV infections.

Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis after Measles Outbreaks, the Philippines, 2007-2022.
Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a delayed, almost uniformly fatal complication of measles. The Philippines had measles outbreaks in 2010-2011, 2013, and 2018-2019; the last was the largest in the World Health Organization Western Pacific Region. Published SSPE data from the Philippines end in 2015. We reviewed all 20 children admitted with SSPE to a tertiary pediatric hospital in Quezon City during 2007-2022 and estimated year of measles infection. Median patient age was 6.2 years at hospital admission and 0.7 years at reported measles illness. Five (25.0%) of 20 admissions occurred in 2022, and estimated infection dates placed 4 patients within the 2018-2019 outbreak; all were admitted during 2020-2022. Given the multiyear latency of SSPE, additional cases might emerge over coming years. Reported measles history could not be established in one quarter of patients. Strengthened measles surveillance and sustained 2-dose vaccination coverage are needed.

Cryptococcal Infection in Advanced HIV-Associated Immunosuppression-Case Series.
Background and Clinical Significance: Cryptococcal meningitis remains a life-threatening complication of advanced HIV infection. Its recognition can be challenging when neurological manifestations are nonspecific or cerebrospinal fluid inflammation is limited. This case series illustrates the diagnostic variability and therapeutic challenges encountered in five patients managed at a regional HIV/AIDS center in northeastern Romania. Case Presentation: Five men aged 26-69 years were hospitalized between November 2022 and March 2025 with HIV-associated cryptococcal disease involving the central nervous system. All had profound immunosuppression, with CD4+ T-cell counts of 6-31 cells/mm3. Clinical manifestations included headache, confusion, altered consciousness, and focal neurological deficits. Cerebrospinal fluid opening pressures were elevated, while inflammatory findings ranged from lymphocytic pleocytosis to an almost acellular profile. Microbiological investigations included direct microscopy, fungal culture, and molecular testing, according to availability. In one patient, culture confirmed Cryptococcus neoformans despite negative India ink microscopy and absent documented pleocytosis. Antifungal treatment included liposomal amphotericin B and fluconazole-based regimens, with treatment selection constrained by drug availability and organ dysfunction. Three cases had fatal outcomes during hospitalization. Conclusions: Cryptococcal meningitis should remain a diagnostic consideration in profoundly immunosuppressed patients with neurological symptoms, even when initial microscopy is negative or cerebrospinal fluid inflammation is minimal. These cases emphasize the importance of complementary microbiological investigations, assessment and management of intracranial pressure, reliable access to recommended antifungal regimens, and appropriate timing of antiretroviral therapy.

Not Just a Fluke: A One Health review on Schistosoma japonicum and Fasciola spp. in Malaysia.
Zoonotic trematodes Schistosoma japonicum, Fasciola hepatica and Fasciola gigantica are neglected tropical diseases imposing significant health and livestock burdens in Asia. Control remains uneven due to complex host-parasite-environment interactions and fragmented surveillance. Both species utilise aquatic snail intermediates and hepatobiliary tropism, presenting common challenges for diagnosis, treatment, and control. Agricultural intensification and landscape change reshape human-livestock-environment interfaces, facilitating transmission. Despite progress, diagnostics remain constrained by low sensitivity, variable performance, and limited scalability. This review synthesises advances in parasite biology, transmission ecology, and socioecological drivers, with Malaysia as an illustrative case, and identifies One Health opportunities. We evaluate emerging integrated strategies, persistent barriers, and outline priorities for harmonised diagnostics, strengthened multisectoral surveillance, and community-centred interventions.

A base-editing and auxotrophic selection platform for linking epigenetic regulators to silent biosynthetic gene clusters in Aspergillus nidulans.
Filamentous fungi harbor numerous silent biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs), representing an underexplored reservoir of natural products. Chemical inhibition of epigenetic regulators is an effective strategy for activating silent BGCs, but it often lacks specificity and cannot readily link activated clusters to their cognate regulators. Here, we developed a coupled cytosine base editing and auxotrophic selection platform in Aspergillus nidulans to systematically identify epigenetic regulators of silent gene clusters. An sgRNA library targeting 24 core epigenetic regulators was introduced, together with a cytosine base editor, into 21 pyrG-based PKS reporter strains, enabling growth-based selection and direct sgRNA recovery by Sanger sequencing. This screen identified five regulator-cluster activation pairs, including known interactions and two previously uncharacterized mechanisms. Specifically, KdmB represses the AN7084 gene cluster by erasing promoter H3K4me3, whereas Kmt5 silences the cichorine core pks gene through H4K20me3 deposition. This scalable platform enables rapid matching of silent BGCs with their epigenetic regulators and advances chromatin-guided fungal genome mining.

Intracellular SCARB2 mimicry overcomes decoy failure to broadly inhibit enteroviruses.
Enterovirus A71 (EV-A71) and coxsackievirus A16 (CV-A16) are leading causes of severe hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD) with high childhood mortality and no specific antiviral therapy. SCARB2 is the essential uncoating receptor, yet extracellular SCARB2-Fc decoys fail to block infection, representing a decade-old paradox in enterovirus therapeutics. Here, we overcome this limitation by engineering RMP(R8), a cell-penetrating SCARB2 mimetic peptide comprising the minimal VP2-binding domain (W146-K166) fused to an octa-arginine transporter. RMP(R8) shows potent antiviral activity (EC50 = 0.156 μg/mL), outstanding safety (selectivity index > 2003), and excellent aqueous solubility, a critical asset for clinical translation. It broadly inhibits genetically divergent EV-A71 isolates and CV-A16 in intestinal and neural cells by blocking viral entry. In a lethal neonatal mouse model, RMP(R8) increases survival against EV-A71 and CV-A16 challenge in vivo. Intracellular receptor mimicry thus establishes a generalizable strategy for viruses refractory to extracellular intervention. RMP(R8) is a promising clinical candidate to address the unmet need for targeted anti-enterovirus treatment, and our findings redefine how to drug virus-receptor interactions that act inside cells.

Cardiac injury in children with severe hand, foot and mouth disease: risk factors and clinical outcomes.
PURPOSE: To determine the risk factors and clinical outcomes of cardiac injury in pediatric patients with severe hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD). METHODS: We conducted a multicenter retrospective study at two tertiary children's hospitals in southern Vietnam, including hospitalized patients with severe HFMD and suspected cardiovascular complications. Cardiac injury was identified according to cardiac enzyme results and findings from electrocardiography and echocardiography. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were used to identify risk factors associated with cardiac injury. RESULTS: A total of 395 patients were included, with a male predominance, and 96.5% were younger than 36 months. Typical skin rash and herpangina remained the most common clinical manifestations. Intensive care unit admission was required in 72.2% of cases, and 50.9% required endotracheal intubation with mechanical ventilation. Cardiac injury was identified in 7.3% (29/395) of severe HFMD cases with suspected cardiovascular complications. Fever ≥ 39 °C (aOR 10.5, 95% CI 3.4-32.6, p 20 mg/L (aOR 3.3, 95% CI 1.3-8.4, p = 0.012), and aspartate aminotransferase > 40 U/L (aOR 4.1, 95% CI 1.7-9.8, p = 0.002) were independent risk factors for cardiac injury. Patients with cardiac injury had higher mortality, longer hospital stays, and a greater incidence of neurological sequelae compared with those without cardiac injury. CONCLUSIONS: Cardiac injury in pediatric patients with severe HFMD is associated with adverse clinical outcomes, underscoring the need for early risk stratification and comprehensive cardiac assessment.

Biosecurity implementation in indoor and outdoor-access broiler production systems in the Netherlands.
Good biosecurity practices on poultry farms can improve animal health, welfare, and productivity, but implementation varies considerably between farms. Recurrent highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) outbreaks and the expansion of higher-welfare systems with outdoor access have raised concerns about potential differences in exposure risk. However, it remains unclear to what extent biosecurity implementation differs between production systems. A cross-sectional comparative study was conducted to assess HPAI-related biosecurity practices and risk factors in Dutch broiler farms, comparing intensive systems (indoor-only) and extensive systems (slower-growing broilers with covered outdoor access). The study included 78 farms (63 intensive and 15 extensive). Biosecurity was assessed using a harmonized subset of the Biocheck.UGent survey. From 40 comparable variables, 28 were selected based on relevance to HPAI introduction and transmission pathways. Differences between production systems were evaluated using Bayesian logistic regression with horseshoe priors. Most biosecurity measures did not differ substantially between systems, with considerable variation observed within both intensive and extensive farms. The largest estimated differences involved carcass storage cleaning, stocking density, and chick delivery frequency, although the statistical support for these differences varied. Stocking density and delivery frequency reflected structural differences between systems, whereas carcass storage cleaning reflected differences in management practices. These findings suggest that interventions targeting farm-specific weaknesses, supported by tailored biosecurity plans and on-site coaching, are likely to be more effective than system-based recommendations alone.

Binding Free Energy Landscape of Different SARS-CoV-2 Nsp1 Variants Interacting with NXF1-RRM: Insights from Molecular Dynamics Simulations and Markov State Models.
The interaction of the SARS-CoV-2 Nsp1 protein with the host NXF1-RRM domain plays an important role in host gene expression, which influences virus replication and host immune surveillance. Thus, understanding the key factors that determine their binding affinity, such as mutations, is of great interest. In this work, we investigated the effects of three Nsp1 mutants─D33K/E36K/E37K/E41K, L27D/V28D, and R124E/K125E─on its binding to the NXF1-RRM domain using structural and energetic analysis. To quantify the affinity changes, we developed a computational framework for calculating the free energy landscape of protein-protein binding based on the Markov state model (MSM). Our approach is based on fluctuations of the radius of gyration and the root mean square deviation (RMSD) from a reference state. We found that the D33K/E36K/E37K/E41K mutant exerts the strongest destabilizing effect, resulting in greater structural deviation, reduced compactness, and a significant loss of intermolecular hydrogen bonds. In contrast, the L27D/V28D and R124E/K125E mutants retain structural and dynamical properties closer to those of wild-type Nsp1 (WT), indicating that these mutations have a more limited impact on the stability of the Nsp1-NXF1-RRM complex. These results are in good agreement with the previous experimental work. We also used the molecular mechanics Poisson-Boltzmann surface area (MM-PBSA) method to estimate the binding free energy of these complexes, yielding results consistent with the MSM analysis and experimental data. However, the binding free energy values obtained from the MSM method are more realistic compared to the MM-PBSA method, which tends to overestimate binding free energy values or produce unphysically negative results. Therefore, the MSM approach provides a useful framework for characterizing mutation-induced changes in the structural stability and binding energetics of Nsp1-NXF1-RRM complexes.

Knowledge, attitudes and practices about dengue vaccines in Latin America and the Caribbean: a scoping review.
Dengue remains a major public health concern in Latin America and the Caribbean, where vaccination has emerged as a key strategy to reduce severe disease. However, its successful implementation depends on population knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP). This study aimed to synthesize available evidence on KAP related to dengue vaccination in the region. A scoping review was conducted following JBI guidelines. Searches were performed in international and regional databases, including MEDLINE/PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, SciELO, and the Virtual Health Library. Original studies were included without language or date restrictions. Study selection and data extraction were conducted independently and in duplicate. Sixteen studies were included. Most studies reported limited knowledge regarding vaccine availability, safety, and mechanisms of action. In contrast, attitudes were generally favorable, with high acceptance and willingness to pay, estimated at approximately USD 23 for a three-dose regimen. However, willingness to participate in clinical trials remained low due to safety and trust concerns. Evidence from a study conducted in Puerto Rico indicated that the COVID-19 pandemic was associated with increased intention to receive the dengue vaccine. Practices were less studied, and findings showed low completion of vaccination schedules, indicating a gap between attitudes and uptake. Despite generally favorable attitudes, important knowledge gaps and implementation challenges persist. Strengthening educational strategies and promoting qualified communication between healthcare professionals and the population - particularly during the introduction of new vaccines and in the context of adverse events - may support informed decision-making and improve dengue vaccine uptake.

Acute macular neuroretinopathy: is the name still appropriate?
BACKGROUND: Acute macular neuroretinopathy (AMN) is a rare but increasingly reported retinal disorder that predominantly affects young women and is characterized by acute-onset paracentral scotomas and distinctive parafoveal macular lesions. Following its first report in 1975 as an inner retinal disease, a considerable body of work has been produced, expanding on its clinical presentation and systemic associations. Aim of this review is to synthesize the current understanding of AMN, including existing controversies on nomenclature. METHODS: A literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE for English-language articles published up to 31 July 2025. Search terms included "acute macular neuroretinopathy" and "acute macular outer retinopathy". Additional relevant sources were identified through manual screening of reference lists and targeted updating of the literature through 28 August 2025. Relevant articles were selected for inclusion in this narrative review based on the authors' judgment of relevance to the review aims. RESULTS: Multiple cases of AMN in association with a variety of ocular and systemic conditions have been reported. Reported associations include viral illnesses such as influenza, Dengue fever, oral contraceptive use, vasoconstrictive agents, non-ocular trauma, and vaccination. An increased incidence of AMN was reported at a single center during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. Advances in multimodal retinal imaging, particularly optical coherence tomography (OCT) and OCT angiography, have led to a more precise localization and insight into the pathogenesis of the disease in the outer retinal layers. These findings have prompted some authors to suggest renaming the condition acute macular outer retinopathy (AMOR) to better reflect the anatomical involvement. CONCLUSIONS: AMN appears to primarily affect the outer retinal layers, with current evidence suggesting a role for underlying vascular impairment in its pathogenesis. Although "AMOR" may offer a more anatomically precise description, AMN remains widely used in the academic literature and continues to be both appropriate and accepted. Further research is needed to elucidate the underlying pathophysiology, precisely localize the site of vascular impairment, and explore potential therapeutic strategies. In this context, consistent terminology is essential, and the continued use of the acronym "AMN" is supported by both clinical and historical considerations.

Presumed herpes simplex virus keratouveitis in a 2-year-old child: a case report.
BACKGROUND: Ocular herpes simplex virus (HSV) disease is uncommon in very young children and may be difficult to recognize because history and examination are limited and early manifestations can resemble bacterial conjunctivitis. Pediatric disease may involve multiple corneal layers, extend into the anterior chamber, recur, and threaten visual development. We describe presumed HSV keratouveitis in a 2-year-old child. CASE PRESENTATION: A 2-year-old girl presented with a two-month history of right-eye pain, photophobia, and tearing after an episode diagnosed elsewhere as HSV blepharoconjunctivitis. Previous topical treatments, including antibiotics, had produced little improvement. Examination revealed right eyelid edema, conjunctival congestion, and an inferior geographic epithelial defect involving one-third of the cornea; the anterior chamber was quiet. Suspected HSV epithelial keratitis was treated with topical acyclovir 3% ointment, moxifloxacin, and lubrication. Although the epithelium healed, stromal edema, infiltration, and endotheliitis developed. Topical prednisolone acetate and therapeutic-dose oral acyclovir were commenced after normal renal function was confirmed. Serological testing showed reactive cytomegalovirus (CMV) IgG and IgM; Epstein-Barr virus IgG and IgM, HSV-1 IgG, HSV-2 IgG, rubella IgM, and Toxoplasma IgG and IgM were non-reactive. Initial improvement was followed by acute recurrence one week after transition to prophylactic acyclovir. Examination under anesthesia revealed a recurrent 3-mm epithelial defect, diffuse stromal edema and infiltration, 2+ anterior chamber cells, and right-eye intraocular pressure of 29 mmHg; no keratic precipitates, iris atrophy, synechiae, or posterior-segment abnormalities were identified. Ocular-surface HSV-1/HSV-2 polymerase chain reaction (PCR), obtained after four weeks of topical and three weeks of systemic acyclovir, was negative, and bacterial cultures showed no growth. Ocular CMV and varicella-zoster virus testing was not performed, and the parents declined aqueous-humor sampling. The child received intravenous acyclovir (10 mg/kg every 8 hours) and methylprednisolone (1 mg/kg/day) for five days, with topical anti-inflammatory, cycloplegic, pressure-lowering, lubricating, and initially empirical antibacterial treatment. At discharge, the eye was quiet, intraocular pressure had normalized, and a 4-mm paracentral stromal opacity remained. At six months there was no recurrence; intraocular pressure was 15 mmHg, refraction was stable, and no fixation preference or ocular misalignment was observed. CONCLUSIONS: The sequential unilateral epithelial, stromal, endothelial, and anterior uveal involvement favored HSV, but absent aqueous-humor testing and negative post-treatment surface PCR precluded virological confirmation. This case supports longitudinal assessment of persistent unilateral corneal inflammation in young children and surveillance for recurrence, corneal sequelae, and impaired visual development.

Integrated miRNA expression dataset in ruminant hosts naturally infected with cystic echinococcosis.
Cystic echinococcosis is a zoonotic infection caused by the larval stage of Echinococcus granulosus sensu lato and remains endemic in several livestock-producing regions. This article describes a dataset of microRNA (miRNA) profiles obtained using Echinococcus cyst material collected from naturally infected sheep, cattle, and water buffalo in southern Italy, providing a valuable resource for the characterization and comparative analysis of miRNA profiles across different ruminant host species. The dataset includes 38 samples obtained from different cyst matrices, including 10 protoscoleces (PSCs), 11 fertile and 17 sterile germinal membranes. Total RNA was extracted and processed using high-throughput sequencing technology. Raw sequence data, quality-filtered reads, and annotated miRNA entries are provided. A total of 168 mature molecules were identified using standardized bioinformatics workflows, including quality control, adapter removal, sequence alignment, annotation against reference databases, normalization procedures, and differential expression analysis. Raw fastq files are publicly available in the Sequence Read Archive under accession SUB16008388. Supplementary Tables provide raw and normalized counts for each sample, together with information on host species, cyst localization, biological matrix, fertility status, and sample quality parameters. Sequencing metrics include raw reads, retained reads following processing and adapter trimming, percentage of reads retained, and the number of mature miRNAs detected. Differential expression results are also provided for fertile vs sterile membranes, PSCs vs fertile membranes and PSCs vs sterile membranes. Overall, this dataset provides a comprehensive small RNA-Seq resource supporting studies of parasite developmental biology, host-associated variation, molecular marker discovery, comparative omics analyses, and the development of bioinformatics workflows.

Newcastle disease virus: Insights into molecular epidemiology, dynamics of distribution and diagnostics.
AbstractThe Newcastle disease virus (NDV) is the etiological agent of a highly transmissible avian disease, first recognized in 1926. The virus continues to pose a substantial threat to both commercial and domestic poultry farming globally, causing major outbreaks with high mortality rates and resulting in considerable economic losses. Despite the widespread use of vaccines and other control measures outbreaks persist.
