UShER-TB: scalable, comprehensive, accessible phylogenomic analysis of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Background. Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the bacterium responsible for tuberculosis, remains a leading cause of global infectious disease deaths. While genomic epidemiology is essential for understanding transmission dynamics and the rise of antibiotic resistance, significant computational limitations currently prevent comprehensive phylogenetic analysis of the vast number of publicly available M. tuberculosis genomes.Methods. We developed UShER-TB, a comprehensive collection of community resources, including a computational analysis pipeline designed for scalable phylogenomic analysis of M. tuberculosis. To demonstrate this system's utility, we processed 129,312 genomes to construct a global phylogeny. We evaluated the system's accuracy in transmission cluster reconstruction, its ability to identify novel genetic lineages and its performance in placing ancient DNA samples within the global tree.Results. The pipeline successfully constructed a global phylogeny capturing genomic diversity from over 129,000 samples. UShER-TB achieved high accuracy in reconstructing transmission clusters, reaching an adjusted Rand index of 0.95 when compared to conventional phylogenomic methods. This tool also facilitated the identification of putative novel lineages and sublineages. Furthermore, the platform enabled the successful phylogenetic placement of ancient samples. The system allows for real-time analysis of new genomes to reveal transmission dynamics and introduction patterns on a global scale.Conclusions. This approach overcomes longstanding computational barriers in genomic surveillance. UShER-TB provides researchers with efficient tools for tuberculosis monitoring, particularly for resource-limited settings where the disease burden is highest.Trial registration. Not applicable.

Malady in motion: Effects of chronic wasting disease on host movement.
Pathogens can have significant impacts on host movement and behavior with consequences for ongoing transmission. For example, chronic wasting disease (CWD) causes severe nutritional deficiencies and neurologic changes, which may alter white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) movement and subsequent transmission risk. Our objectives were to test for changes in movement and habitat selection in deer affected by CWD, and determine the timing of any changes we observed. We leveraged comprehensive movement and mortality data from a large study of free-ranging deer in southwest Wisconsin, a region with high prevalence of CWD. We used necropsy data to identify end stage CWD cases with movement data leading up to death (n = 44), and sex-, date-, and age-matched test-negative controls. Using GPS collar data, we identified extra-home range excursions and tested for differences in excursion rates, distances, and durations between cases and controls. We evaluated movement characteristics (e.g., movement rates, weekly range sizes) and habitat selection for the two groups, using change point analysis to determine when behavior changes occurred during disease progression. Excursion distances were reduced for CWD cases but were otherwise largely unaffected by infection status. However, CWD cases moved at slower rates and maintained smaller ranges than controls. Habitat selection varied minimally between cases and controls, though CWD cases had an increased preference for proximity to forest edges. While changes in case movement rates and range sizes were detected at or before 6 months prior to death, other movement and habitat selection changes appeared about 2 months prior to death. In addition, CWD cases were frequently in good body condition even within 6 months prior to death, implying that clinically apparent changes occur very late in the disease progression. Our results suggest the occurrence of subclinical and clinical phases of infection, beginning around 6 and 2 months prior to death, respectively. Public communication may therefore benefit from emphasizing that CWD-infected deer are infectious long before they appear sick. Further, because most movement changes occur for very short periods relative to the infectious period of CWD, typical healthy deer movement is likely adequate for representing transmission dynamics for surveillance and management planning.

Cross-sectional surveillance of bluetongue virus, epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus, and chronic wasting disease in wild cervids in Nebraska.
Bluetongue virus (BTV) and epizootic hemorrhagic disease virus (EHDV) are Culicoides-transmitted orbiviruses, while chronic wasting disease (CWD) is an enzootic prion disease affecting North American cervids, primarily transmitted through contact with prions shed in bodily secretions and excretions. Recent work has shown the potential of retropharyngeal lymph nodes (RPLNs) for virus surveillance in addition to CWD and concurrent surveillance of these distinct diseases is limited. During the 2025 Nebraska hunting season, 780 RPLN samples were tested for CWD, BTV, and EHDV. Overall, 25.0% (195/780) were positive for CWD, followed by 17.9% (140/780) for BTV and 11.9% (93/780) for EHDV. For BTV, fawns (aOR = 1.64; p = 0.042) and yearlings (aOR = 1.63; p = 0.032) had greater odds of detection than adults, whereas mule deer had lower odds than white-tailed deer (aOR = 0.34; p < 0.001). Mule deer also had lower odds of EHDV detection (aOR = 0.43; p = 0.013). Co-detection of two or more pathogens was identified in 9.9% (77/780) of animals, most commonly BTV and EHDV (4.2%; 33/780), whereas 1.4% (11/780) were positive for all three pathogens. Spatially, pathogen detection and co-detection rates varied across counties, with hotspots identified in southern Nebraska, particularly in Adams and Harlan counties. These findings demonstrate concurrent circulation and spatial clustering of prion and vector-borne viral pathogens, highlighting the need for integrated surveillance to better understand disease transmission dynamics in cervid populations.

A high-quality telomere-to-telomere lumpy skin disease virus genome assembly.
Lumpy skin disease virus (LSDV) is an emerging livestock capripoxvirus (CaPV) that continues to cause substantial economic losses across Africa, Asia and Europe. However, important uncertainties remain regarding LSDV genome structure, particularly at the telomeric inverted terminal repeats (ITRs) that are central to host interaction, replication and adaptive evolution. Structural variation at the ITRs is driven by recombination during virus replication. Previous assemblies have relied primarily on short-read sequencing, which provides limited resolution of repeat-rich telomeric regions and propagates structural ambiguities into downstream annotation and comparative analyses. Here, we present a high-quality telomere-to-telomere assembly of the LSDV Oman 2009 isolate, generated using a hybrid approach that integrates short Illumina reads with higher-accuracy long Nanopore reads. The resulting 151,091 bp genome contains 157 annotated ORFs and fully resolves complex repeat-rich structures at both ITRs. This new reference corrects misassemblies present in earlier LSDV genomes and confirms clade-specific gene truncations. This genome provides a robust foundation for improved genomic surveillance, accurate read mapping, mutation detection and evolutionary inference of LSDV and demonstrates the value of long-read approaches for resolving complex CaPV genome structures.

Sigma-1 Receptor-Targeting Compounds Show Antiviral Activity Across Multiple Coronavirus Models.
Over the past two decades, coronaviruses have caused three major public health crises, including the epidemics of SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and SARS-CoV-2. Following the outbreak of SARS-CoV-2, several antiviral drugs have been approved for the treatment of COVID-19. However, the high mutation rate of SARS-CoV-2 has led to the emergence of multiple variants, some of which can escape vaccine-induced immunity and develop resistance to virus-targeted drugs. Viruses rely on host cell mechanisms to complete replication and transmission. Host-directed therapy is an emerging strategy that inhibits infection by targeting host cell factors essential for pathogen replication. Interventions targeting host factors have been proven effective in limiting viral infections and have the potential to reduce the risk of drug resistance. Our previous study found that the sigma-1 receptor (σ1R) is involved in the autophagic process mediated by the SARS-CoV-2 non-structural protein NSP6, suggesting that σ1R may serve as a therapeutic target against SARS-CoV-2. In this study, we found that the σ1R antagonists BD-1047 and σ1RA1 inhibited SARS-CoV-2 and its variants in vitro and showed antiviral activity in vivo. At the cellular level, these compounds also inhibited porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV) and infectious bronchitis virus (IBV), indicating cross-model antiviral activity. BD-1047 further showed antiviral activity against HCoV-OC43 in both in vitro and in vivo models. In addition, Ocaperidone, identified through computer-aided screening, exhibited protective effects against SARS-CoV-2 and HCoV-OC43 in both cell-based and mouse models. Collectively, these findings support σ1R as a host-associated antiviral target candidate and provide several compounds for further optimization and mechanistic investigation.

An Immuno-Epidemiological Model of Foot-and-Mouth Disease (FMD) in the African Buffalo Population with Carrier Transmission.

Endemic persistence of FMD in buffalo populations is facilitated by chronic infections in carrier hosts: Upon exposure to the virus, buffalo become acutely infected, followed by either viral clearance and recovery with immunity, or persistent infection for several months. In our model, we divide the infectious population based upon these two stages, acute and carrier infection, so that we can dynamically capture the immunological characteristics of both phases of the disease to better understand the carriers' role in disease transmission. We first define the epidemiological basic reproduction number, R 0 , depending on the viral-immune kinetics from acute and carrier infected hosts. Then, we show that R 0 is a threshold condition for the local stability of the disease free equilibrium and for the existence of the endemic equilibrium. Later, by using a sensitivity analysis (SA) approach developed for multi-scale models, we assess the impact of the acute infection and carrier phase immunological parameters on R 0 . Interestingly, our numerical results show that the viral and immunological parameters from a carrier infected host and the susceptible individual recruitment rates play significant roles in disease persistence, which are consistent with experimental and field studies.

Avian influenza overview June-August 2026.
Between 5 June and 28 August 2026, 110 highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) A(H5N1) virus detections were reported in domestic (7) and wild (103) birds in 12 countries in Europe. The number of detections remained at a seasonal low throughout the summer, continuing the decline observed since spring. In contrast to previous years, fewer colony-breeding seabirds were affected, and the geographical range of detections was more limited. Further sporadic detections of HPAI A(H5) virus were reported in wild terrestrial carnivores and pinnipeds. Outside Europe, the epidemic continued in the Americas, where also the HPAI A(H7N3) subtype was detected in Mexico. Following its first introduction to mainland Australia, HPAI A(H5N1) virus spread within local wild bird populations and spilled over to terrestrial carnivores and marine mammals. In the US, the number of dairy cattle farms reportedly affected by HPAI A(H5N1) increased, while detections in captive American minks were reported for the first time. Between 5 June and 31 August 2026, 15 cases of avian influenza virus infection were publicly reported in humans (no fatal cases) in three countries and territories: Bangladesh (one A(H5N1) case), Cambodia (one A(H5N1) case) and China (13 A(H9N2) cases). All human cases reported exposure to poultry or a poultry environment prior to detection or onset of illness. Human infections with avian influenza viruses remain rare and no sustained human-to-human transmission has been documented. The risk posed by avian influenza A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b viruses currently circulating in Europe remains low for the general public in the European Union/European Economic Area (EU/EEA) and low-to-moderate for those occupationally or otherwise exposed to infected animals or contaminated environments.

Detection of highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) virus, clade 2.3.4.4b, genotype B3.13 in placentas from aborted bovine fetuses.
Infection by highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) A(H5N1) virus (family Orthomyxoviridae, taxon species Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae), clade 2.3.4.4b, genotype B3.13, was first diagnosed in dairy cattle in the United States in March 2024. Study to assess mothers' knowledge regarding immunization of their under-five children in Al-Andalus Primary Health Care Center, AL-Ramadi city.

Although coverage rates are high, vaccine-preventable diseases remain a concern, particularly in regions where gaps in mothers' knowledge exist. To assess the extent of maternal knowledge regarding immunization and to determine the full immunization status of the children according to maternal characteristics and other determinants. BACKGROUND: Dysmenorrhea affects daily life, mental health, and productivity, raising economic and social concerns. It also significantly affects women's productivity and quality of life. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid unravels brucellosis in a patient with chronic lung disease and venous thrombosis: A case report.
BACKGROUND: Brucellosis is a re-emerging zoonosis in Xinjiang, China. Pulmonary involvement and thrombotic complications are rare but can be life-threatening. In patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), unexplained respiratory worsening poses a diagnostic dilemma: is it an acute exacerbation of IPF, community-acquired pneumonia, or a zoonotic infection? METHODS: A 57-year-old male farmer with IPF presented with progressive dyspnea and hypoxemia (SpO₂ 77% on room air). Serum Brucella agglutination test (SAT) and mNGS of BALF were performed. Clinicians should also be aware that severe infection and hypoxemia are risk factors for venous thrombosis.

Global evolutionary dynamics of peste des petits ruminants virus reveals geographic lineage structuring and clade-defining mutational signatures.
Peste des petits ruminants virus (PPRV) is recognized as one of the most economically significant transboundary pathogens affecting small ruminants. However, despite the increasing availability of whole-genome sequences, comprehensive global analyses integrating evolutionary history, phylogeography, and genome-wide lineage-defining molecular markers remain limited. This study investigated the global genomic diversity, evolutionary history, and molecular characteristics of PPRV using whole-genome sequences. A total of 212 temporally informative whole-genome sequences, retrieved from GenBank (between 1969 and 2025) representing all four recognized PPRV lineages, were analyzed using comparative genomics, Bayesian time-scaled phylogenetic reconstruction, and genome-wide candidate phylogenetic marker; single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) analysis and codon-based selective-pressure analyses. The results demonstrated high genomic conservation across all genomes despite their broad geographic distribution. Bayesian analysis estimated a mean evolutionary rate of 5.07 × 10-4 substitutions per site per year (95% HPD: 4.79 × 10-4 to 5.35 × 10-4) and dated the most recent common ancestor of PPRV to 1839 (95% HPD: 1829 to 1848) which likely reflects the ancestry of currently sampled viral diversity rather than the historical emergence of PPRV. Lineage IV, the predominant contemporary lineage, was further subdivided into four geographically structured subclades: A, B.1, B.2a, and B.2b. A total of 125 subclade-associated fixed SNP signatures were identified, primarily within the L gene, with most variants resulting in nonsynonymous substitutions. The overlapping P, V, and C coding regions underscored the complex functional consequences of lineage-defining mutations. Gene-wide dN/dS values were below 1 for all six genes, indicating predominant purifying selection, while functional mapping identified several SNP related amino acid substitutions within experimentally characterized antigenic regions; however, these substitutions were not supported as positively selected in the present analyses. These results provide a comprehensive genomic framework for understanding PPRV evolution and identify candidate phylogenetic markers for lineage discrimination to support genomic surveillance, molecular epidemiology, and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)-World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) Global PPR Eradication Programme.

Climate-driven shifts in lumpy skin disease risk across Iran: Insights from ensemble species distribution models.
This study aimed to identify the environmental determinants influencing the distribution of lumpy skin disease and to predict changes in its spatial distribution risk and potential geographic range across Iran under future climate change scenarios using ensemble Species Distribution Models (SDMs). To this end, following data cleaning and quality control of 3654 disease occurrence records, a total of 2849 presence points recorded between 2013 and 2024 were retained for model development. The CTA, GAM, GBM, and RF algorithms were implemented within an ensemble modelling framework. The final ensemble model (EMca) achieved a True Skill Statistic (TSS) score of 0.85, an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.96, and a Boyce index of 0.96 during calibration. For the validation data, the corresponding scores were 0.66, 0.89, and 0.93, respectively. The model therefore demonstrated broadly consistent predictive performance across calibration and validation based on these three evaluation metrics. Future projections were generated using three General Circulation Models (GCMs) HadGEM3-GC31-LL, MIROC6, and MPI-ESM1-2-HR under the SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 climate scenarios for the 2021-2040 and 2041-2060 time periods. The results indicated that hydrological, anthropogenic, and climatic variables were the three primary determinants of the spatial distribution of lumpy skin disease. Among the predictor variables, distance to rivers, distance to roads, and annual precipitation were identified as the most influential factors governing disease distribution, respectively. Furthermore, the risk maps revealed that western and northwestern Iran, together with the Zagros Mountain Range, which currently represent the principal disease hotspots, are projected to remain the major potential hotspots under future climate change scenarios. Range size analysis further indicated that although a proportion of the currently suitable areas for lumpy skin disease is projected to be lost under future climate conditions, the emergence of newly suitable areas is expected to largely offset these losses. Consequently, the net change in the disease's potential range is predicted to be minimal during the 2021-2040 period (-0.98%). However, this decline is projected to increase to -4.34% under the SSP2-4.5 scenario and -8.01% under the SSP5-8.5 scenario during the 2041-2060 period. Overall, the findings suggest that, in the near future, climate change is more likely to drive a spatial reorganization of disease risk hotspots than to cause a substantial expansion of the disease's potential distribution. These findings provide a robust scientific basis for targeted surveillance, strategic vaccination, and the development of early warning systems for the effective management of lumpy skin disease in Iran.

Environmentally relevant glyphosate exposure increases susceptibility to tilapia lake virus through disruption of antiviral immunity in Nile tilapia.
Fish in aquatic environments face numerous stressors, including temperature fluctuations, toxins, pollutants, and infectious pathogens, such as bacteria, viruses, water molds, fungi, and parasites. Exposure to environmental chemicals can influence the susceptibility to infectious pathogens, including tilapia lake virus (TiLV), which leads to high morbidity and mortality in both wild and farmed tilapia. This study aimed to investigate whether glyphosate exposure could increase Nile tilapia susceptibility to TiLV infection and to determine how glyphosate affects the infection process and disease development. To thoroughly assess glyphosate and TiLV as stressors, detailed analyses were conducted, including clinical sign observations, histopathological examinations, viral load measurements, and assessments of innate immune gene expression across various tissues. The key finding was that oral exposure to glyphosate at environmentally relevant sediment concentrations (1 mg/kg) for 14 days altered the expression of innate immune genes (irf3, ifn, and mx), thereby increasing tilapia susceptibility to TiLV infection. Exposure to glyphosate also worsened TiLV infection in tilapia as early as 6 days post-infection, evidenced by significantly higher viral loads, downregulation of innate immune genes (irf3, ifn, and mx), increased inflammation, and more extensive histopathological damage in critical immune and target organs. Overall, this study provides valuable insights into the environmental risk factors associated with TiLV infection and highlights the role of glyphosate as a chemical stressor that can increase fish susceptibility to this infectious disease. Finally, the findings may help in developing environmentally sustainable aquaculture practices that prioritize the health of tilapia.

N70 S/Y155H combined mutation of neuraminidase of avian influenza H9N2 virus confers oseltamivir and zanamivir resistance and pathogenicity to mice.
Recently, H9N2 avian influenza virus (AIV) poses a significant threat to both the poultry industry and public health. Therefore, investigating the impact of its neuraminidase mutations on susceptibility to neuraminidase inhibitors (NAIs) is of great importance for clinically preventing potential cross-species transmission of H9N2. In this study, our results revealed that NAI resistance-related mutations of most H9N2 viruses isolated from China during 1998 to 2024 mainly occurred at positions N70S, E119 A/D/G/V, Q133K, Q136A, D151E, Y155H, I222V, R224K, E276D, R292K, N294S, and R371K. Among them, the combined N70S and Y155H mutations are common characteristics of H9N2 viruses circulating in recent years. In vivo experiments demonstrated that these H9N2 viruses harboring the combined N70S and Y155H mutations exhibit high pathogenicity to BALB/c mice without prior adaption. In vitro neuraminidase inhibition assays confirmed that these H9N2 viruses bearing the N70 S/Y155H mutations exhibited greater reduced inhibition than their counterparts bearing the N70S or Y155H single mutation to oseltamivir and zanamivir, but remained highly sensitive to peramivir. Notably, the in vivo protective effect of NAIs against H9N2 virus with combined N70S and Y155H mutations is limited, possibly due to the restricted ability of these drugs to ameliorate the excessive inflammatory responses. Therefore, there is an urgency to strengthen research on epidemiological surveillance and prevention strategies for avian influenza H9N2 harboring these mutations.

One Health preparedness for Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus: lessons from the 2026 outbreak centred in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The 2026 outbreak of Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD), caused by Bundibugyo virus (BDBV), involved limited international exportation but remained centred in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). The outbreak tested whether earlier institutional mobilisation translated into timely field delivery. We conducted a structured narrative review of peer-reviewed research, official reports and operational guidance on epidemiology, diagnostics, medical countermeasures (MCMs), One Health surveillance, clinical care, infection prevention and control (IPC), community engagement and cross-border preparedness. Key institutional mechanisms for emergency decision-making, coordination and MCM prioritisation were activated earlier than during the 2013-2016 Ebola virus disease epidemic in West Africa, widening the window for action. Field delivery nevertheless remained uneven: the model-adjusted median onset-to-sampling delay was 4.8 days among 129 confirmed patients, while insecurity posed additional challenges for field response. Preparedness was further constrained by uncertainty about reservoir ecology, limited clinical validation of BDBV-specific diagnostics and the absence of MCMs with established efficacy in BVD. We therefore propose a One Health alert-to-action pathway linking human, animal, environmental and community signals to BDBV-inclusive confirmation, safe care, IPC, cross-border continuity, accountable governance and feedback-informed adaptation. Earlier activation is a preparedness gain, but protection depends on whether that advantage is carried through reliable, traceable and equitable operational hand-offs.

Need-based Compared to Guidelines-based Fluid Administration in Dengue Patients with Warning Signs: An Open-label Randomized Study.
INTRODUCTION: Fluid therapy is fundamental in dengue management. We evaluated an individualized, hemodynamic parameter-guided fluid strategy compared with standard World Health Organization (WHO) guideline-based care in dengue patients with warning signs. METHODS: In this open-label randomized controlled trial conducted at a tertiary care hospital in New Delhi (December 2019-October 2023), 80 adult dengue patients with warning signs were randomized (1:1) to receive either WHO guideline-based fluid therapy (control) or need-based therapy guided by noninvasive cardiac output monitoring (NICOM) and point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) (intervention). The primary outcome was hemodynamic stability assessed by systolic blood pressure (SBP), pulse pressure (PP), and mean arterial pressure over 48 h. Secondary outcomes included hospital stay, progression to severe dengue, and mortality. RESULTS: Baseline characteristics were comparable across groups. The intervention arm demonstrated higher mean PP at 8 h (45.2 ± 11.6 mmHg vs. 39.8 ± 8.7 mmHg), 12 h (45 ± 11.3 mmHg vs. 38.9 ± 8.1 mmHg), and 24 h (44.1 ± 9.6 mmHg vs. 39.1 ± 6.6 mmHg) (P < 0.05). SBP was higher at 8 h (P = 0.02). However, progression to severe dengue (17.5% in both groups), hospital stay (5.4 vs. 5.5 days; P = 0.87), and mortality (none) were similar. CONCLUSION: Although NICOM/POCUS-guided fluid therapy improved selected hemodynamic parameters, it did not translate into measurable improvements in clinical outcomes compared with WHO guideline-based care. Larger, multicenter studies powered for clinical endpoints in high-risk subgroups are warranted.

The UK Health System's Response to the Monkeypox Outbreak of 2022: A Scoping Review.
INTRODUCTION: The 2022 mpox outbreak represented a major shift in transmission dynamics, with sustained community spread occurring in several nonendemic countries, including the United Kingdom. Examining how nonendemic health systems responded to this outbreak is essential for strengthening preparedness for future emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases. METHODS: A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic and Meta-Analysis Extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines to synthesize evidence on the UK healthcare system's response to the 2022 mpox outbreak. Electronic databases and gray literature sources were searched for publications released between January and December 2022. RESULTS: Evidence was mapped across seven World Health Organization-aligned intervention domains relevant to outbreak preparedness and response. Eleven sources were included, comprising peer-reviewed studies and policy-relevant gray literature. Evidence was most frequently reported for infection prevention and control (n = 7), systems for identifying emerging and re-emerging infections (n = 6), and rapid data sharing and risk communication (n = 5). Moderate evidence addressed community engagement (n = 5) and vaccine and therapeutic capacity (n = 5). In contrast, only one source examined laboratory systems (n = 1), and no studies described structured surge capacity training for healthcare workers. CONCLUSION: The UK response to the 2022 mpox outbreak demonstrated timely coordination, effective surveillance, and implementation of infection prevention measures in a nonendemic setting. However, important limitations remain, particularly in workforce surge capacity, domestic vaccine manufacturing, and evidence on postexposure vaccination effectiveness. Addressing these gaps is essential for strengthening health system resilience and preparedness for future outbreaks.

Rapid Identification of Antibiotic-Resistance Mutation in Bordetella pertussis Using a One-Pot Isothermal System.
Rapid and accurate genotyping of Bordetella pertussis (BP) is essential for guiding antimicrobial therapy and epidemiological surveillance. However, existing genotyping methods often involve multistep workflows and postamplification handling, increasing the risk of aerosol contamination and limiting their applicability in resource-limited settings. Here, we present a closed-tube, one-pot strategy that integrates loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) with an enzyme-free catalytic hairpin assembly (CHA) circuit for the simultaneous detection and genotyping of wild-type BP and the antibiotic-resistance A2047G mutant. In this platform, LAMP provides rapid and efficient isothermal amplification, while the CHA circuit directly converts amplification products into fluorescence signals and enables single-nucleotide discrimination through sequence-specific recognition, thereby improving genotyping accuracy without increasing assay complexity. The integrated assay combines rapid detection, high specificity, and a simple closed-tube workflow with minimal instrumentation requirements, making it well suited for point-of-care testing and applications in resource-limited settings.

Multiplexed Detection of Foodborne Pathogens and the Antibiotic Resistance Genes Based on the CRISPR/Cas System with Engineered LwaCas13a.
Foodborne pathogens represent a persistent threat to global public health, necessitating the development of point-of-care testing (POCT) platforms that integrate rapidity, ultrahigh sensitivity, cost effectiveness, and operational simplicity. Herein, we developed a system for high-specificity identification of foodborne pathogens and associated antibiotic resistance genes, which is a dual-modal diagnostic platform integrating recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with an engineered LwaCas13a variant. By leveraging the CRISPR/Cas13a system, the platform establishes a multiplex fluorescence array that simultaneously detects four major foodborne pathogens (Salmonella enterica serovar typhimurium, Listeria monocytogenes, Escherichia coli, and Staphylococcus aureus) and their corresponding critical antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), including mecA, blaCTX-M, mcr-1, ermB, and tet(M). Notably, the system retained robust trans-cleavage activity in complex biological matrices, achieving a remarkable limit of detection (LOD) at 100 copies/mL. Furthermore, the CRISPR/Cas13a system is coupled to an instrument-free lateral flow assay (LFA) for the detection of L. monocytogenes and tet(M), which effectively circumvents matrix-induced viscosity and ionic inhibition in egg and milk samples. Moreover, our developed platform was validated using samples from 40 household refrigerators, which drastically reduces assay time and thereby circumvents the inhibitory effects that constrain qPCR in food matrices and achieves 100% diagnostic agreement compared with the gold-standard methods. Collectively, this dual-modal strategy provides a promising paradigm with point-of-care capability for food safety surveillance and antimicrobial resistance monitoring.

Environmental surveillance: harnessing environmental sample data to protect animal health.
Infectious diseases in domestic animals-including those with zoonotic potential-impose a substantial global burden on food security, livelihoods, and public health. Environmental surveillance (ES) offers a critical complement to conventional animal-level diagnostics by detecting pathogens or their genetic signatures directly in the matrices through which they persist and spread: water, soil, air, manure, fomites, and arthropod vectors. This review synthesizes evidence across three analytical dimensions-matrix suitability, detection method performance, and wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE)-for 15 viral, bacterial, and parasitological diseases of domestic animals. Key findings reveal that matrix choice profoundly governs detection sensitivity: surface water and wetland sediments support infectious avian influenza virus isolation; pooled environmental feces and slurry outperform individual animal sampling for Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis (MAP); and electrostatic dust cloths enable simultaneous detection of peste-des-petits ruminants virus (PPRV) and capripoxviruses at livestock markets. Molecular methods, principally quantitative RT-PCR and droplet digital PCR, consistently outperform conventional culture in sensitivity and turnaround time, though viability-linked assays remain an important unresolved need. WBE is increasingly applied beyond human pathogens: piggery effluent surveillance for Japanese encephalitis virus and wastewater metagenomics for antimicrobial resistance exemplify its veterinary potential. Interpretive limitations persist, including matrix-driven inhibition, absence of harmonized protocols, and the challenge of equating nucleic-acid signals with infectious risk. Realizing the full promise of ES within a One Health framework requires standardized, field-validated sampling workflows, viability-linked molecular assays, and formal integration of environmental signals into routine veterinary surveillance and outbreak-response systems.

Epidemiological update on spatial and space-time clusters of African swine fever in the Philippines.
African swine fever (ASF), particularly the highly contagious Genotype II strain, is a transboundary viral disease causing up to 100% mortality in swine and threatening food security across the Asia-Pacific region. Since 2019, control strategies in the Philippines have relied on depopulation and strict administrative zoning to limit contiguous, land-based spread. However, the long-term effectiveness of these approaches within the country's fragmented archipelagic landscape remains poorly understood, complicating evidence-based resource allocation and preparedness for regional vaccination campaigns. Here we show that the endemic trajectory of ASF was highly non-uniform across the three main island groups of the Philippines from October 2022 to October 2024. Spatiotemporal analysis of a national surveillance dataset comprising 8,213 barangay-level events revealed twelve statistically significant retrospective space-time clusters-with radii up to 183.2 kilometers-and highly asynchronous regional epidemic waves across Luzon, the Visayas, and Mindanao. Although crude case volumes were highest in Luzon (52.10%), followed by the Visayas (31.69%) and Mindanao (16.21%), accounting for swine population density reshaped the spatial distribution. Spatial mapping and a Getis-Ord Gi* hotspot analysis consistently identified the highest burden of reported ASF events within Regions IV-A, IV-B, and VI, specifically peaking on Mindoro Island and in the Western Visayas. Together, these findings demonstrate that maritime borders fail to provide natural biosecurity isolation against transboundary viral transmission. Consequently, region-specific interventions and resources must be dynamically allocated to address this heterogeneous spatial burden. These spatiotemporal results provide the evidence-based framework necessary to transition toward targeted sub-national surveillance and to systematically evaluate the epidemiological impact and guide live-attenuated vaccine implementation in the Philippines and analogous archipelagic settings throughout the Asia-Pacific.

Phospholipid codes at virus-host membrane interfaces: mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities in animal viral diseases.
Animal viruses depend on host membranes at every stage of infection, yet membrane lipid states are often treated as background rather than as causal determinants of virus-host interactions. This Review develops a phospholipid-code framework in which headgroup identity, acyl-chain chemistry, leaflet topology, and lipid flux define infection-stage-specific membrane states. Evidence from Newcastle disease virus, infectious bronchitis virus, avian influenza virus, porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus, African swine fever virus, Senecavirus A, Japanese encephalitis virus, and porcine epidemic diarrhea virus shows that these states can control attachment, endosomal progression, growth of replication organelles, viral protein allostery, budding, virion infectivity, ferroptotic tissue injury, and delivery of vaccines or antivirals. Comparative evidence from human and plant virus systems is used only to identify transferable membrane mechanisms that require validation in animal-virus models and natural host species. The framework distinguishes viral lipid demand from host defense and tissue damage and explains why total-cell lipidomics or broad metabolic inhibitors rarely establish causality. We argue that the most promising interventions will target viral protein-lipid interfaces, virus-specific recruitment of lipid-transfer machinery, transient leaflet transitions, virion envelopes, or pathological lipid oxidation rather than globally suppressing essential lipid metabolism. Species-relevant primary cells, organoids, virion lipidomics, topology-resolved assays, acute perturbation, rescue experiments, and animal challenge models will be required to translate causal phospholipid biology into safe and practical antiviral strategies for livestock and poultry health.

The role of African Canadian immigrant Midwives: A historical perspective on community homebirth.
PROBLEM: There is limited scholarship on homebirth practices and social networks of African Canadian immigrant community midwives during times of strained healthcare. BACKGROUND: Community care planning left gaps both during Canada's historic nation building phase and the recent COVID-19 pandemic. METHODS: Semi-structured interviews were held with Afrodescendant family members and storytellers who knew community midwives who practiced between 1800-1960 in Nova Scotia, Ontario, Saskatchewan and Alberta. Transcripts were triangulated with archival searches and key community informant consultations with genealogists and historians. FINDINGS: Participants, key informants and archival searches provided evidence for eleven migrating community midwives who provided culturally inclusive care in Nova Scotia, Ontario, Saskatchewan, and Alberta settlements between 1800-1960. Themes that emerged included: the Ancestral Community Midwife Role, Drivers of Community Birth, Drivers Promoting Access, and Migration Resilience. Midwives used homebirth to help immigrants access culturally inclusive responsive care in isolated, low-resourced immigrant communities in Canada. DISCUSSION: Common sub-themes were midwives' survival, resistance and prioritising health of the community. The Ubuntu or communitarianism framework ties individual health closely to community health, which is highly valued by many immigrant families and midwives. Findings support current midwifery trends where culturally sensitive and integrated care are offered as interventions to facilitate flourishing in immigrant communities. CONCLUSIONS: We concluded that community midwifery provided access to homebirth and mitigated the challenging healthcare gaps during Canada's historical and current healthcare crises. We encourage continued deployment of midwives, especially during the current times of scarcity.

Infection prevention and control considerations in invasive group A streptococcus outbreaks.
Invasive Streptococcus pyogenes (group A streptococcus, GAS) infection is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality and has shown a notable resurgence in several countries since late 2022, including the United Kingdom (UK) and Ireland. Healthcare-associated cases, particularly in maternity and acute hospital settings, present significant infection prevention and control (IPC) challenges due to the organism's high transmissibility, potential for asymptomatic carriage among patients and healthcare workers, and the rapid progression of invasive disease. Even a single healthcare-associated case may signal unrecognised transmission within the clinical environment and therefore requires prompt investigation. This IPC Toolkit article summarises practical approaches to recognising, investigating, and managing GAS outbreaks in acute healthcare settings. Current UK guidance from the UK Health Security Agency and the British Infection Association is reviewed alongside recent outbreak reports and emerging evidence relevant to hospital practice. Key operational considerations include early case recognition, structured outbreak management through an incident management team, epidemiological investigation, and microbiological characterisation of isolates, including the use of whole genome sequencing to establish transmission pathways. The article also discusses patient isolation, environmental control measures, healthcare worker screening, and the role of targeted chemoprophylaxis for high-risk contacts. Recent literature emphasises the growing role of genomic epidemiology in outbreak confirmation and highlights the operational challenges associated with healthcare worker screening and contact management. Emerging population-level data may also influence future approaches to chemoprophylaxis for contacts. This article provides a practical framework to support clinicians and IPC teams in responding effectively to suspected or confirmed healthcare-associated GAS outbreaks.

Secondary Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis Mimicking Sepsis in Adults: A Case Series.
Background and Clinical Significance: Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) is a life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome that can closely resemble sepsis in adults, potentially delaying recognition and treatment. Because infection may trigger or coexist with HLH, persistent or disproportionate inflammation despite appropriate antimicrobial therapy should prompt reassessment for concomitant HLH and investigation of the underlying trigger; Case Presentation: We describe three adults initially managed for presumed sepsis or severe infection at a referral hospital in Colombia. All developed persistent fever, cytopenias, organomegaly, and marked hyperferritinemia. HScore values were 222, 246, and 248, respectively; the score in Case 3 was calculated retrospectively from available pretreatment data. Bone marrow hemophagocytosis was demonstrated in Cases 1 and 2 but not in Case 3. The underlying triggers were acute myeloid leukemia, disseminated histoplasmosis in the setting of advanced HIV infection, and visceral leishmaniasis. The malignancy-associated case had an unfavorable outcome. Both infection-associated cases improved after pathogen-directed therapy combined with corticosteroids to control hyperinflammation, without escalation to an etoposide-based regimen; Conclusions: Sepsis and secondary HLH should not be regarded as mutually exclusive diagnoses. Persistent or disproportionate inflammation accompanied by progressive multilineage cytopenias, splenomegaly, markedly elevated or rising ferritin levels, hypertriglyceridemia, and/or decreasing fibrinogen should prompt early HScore calculation, assessment of HLH-2004 criteria, and concurrent investigation for an underlying trigger. Recognition of the clinical pattern and individualized treatment of both the trigger and hyperinflammatory state may facilitate timely management.

Recombinant Antigen for Newcastle Disease Virus Vaccine Focusing on Currently Circulating Virus Variants.
Newcastle disease virus (NDV) causes a highly contagious avian infection and is characterised by its high genetic diversity and mutation rate. Currently applied vaccines are based on NDV genotypes I and II, which are considerably distinct from the circulating pathogenic genotypes, of which genotype VII is predominant, and therefore, they may not provide complete protection for birds or stop virus transmission. This work is a proof-of-concept study aiming to develop a genotype VII-focused recombinant antigen for a vaccine targeting relevant NDV strains. The research primarily focuses on novel antigen design based on the bioinformatics analysis of recent circulating isolates. Haemagglutinin-neuraminidase (HN) is one of the two main NDV antigens. Two HN fragments ("1"-341-368 aa and "2"-239-257 aa) were selected due to the presence of linear neutralising epitopes. An approach focusing on using a number of selected-fragment variants simultaneously was applied for the first time. The resulting antigen Castle1 encompasses the sequence diversity of most circulating isolates. Preliminary immunological evaluation showed that antibodies from Castle1-immunised animals possessed haemagglutination inhibition activity and interacted with NDV of genotypes I and VII. That makes Castle1 a promising antigen for the further development of a vaccine for preventing ongoing and incoming NDV outbreaks.

Lack of evidence for arthropod or vertical transmission of Hepacivirus bovis in a persistently infected dairy herd.
Hepacivirus bovis (BovHepV) has been detected globally since its initial description in 2015, but its transmission routes remain largely unknown. Arthropod-borne or vertical transmission is a common route for several livestock viruses, including Rift Valley fever virus and bluetongue virus. Moreover, many members of the genus Orthoflavivirus (family Flaviviridae) are transmitted by hematophagous arthropods, raising the possibility that hepaciviruses such as BovHepV, which also belongs to the Flaviviridae family, could share similar transmission routes. In this study, we examined possible transmission routes of BovHepV, including the involvement of mosquitoes, hematophagous flies, biting midges, and mites. Arthropods were collected on a dairy farm with documented circulation of BovHepV genotypes 1 and 2 and were subsequently tested for the presence of BovHepV RNA by quantitative real-time PCR. Furthermore, multiple bovine sample types were examined for the presence of BovHepV RNA. To assess local spread, serum samples from cattle on a neighboring farm within flight range of stable flies and mosquitoes were analyzed. Potential vertical transmission was evaluated by testing serum samples from 20 calves and 20 young heifers. None of the analyzed samples tested positive for BovHepV RNA. However, BovHepV was detected in blood samples collected for bovine herpesvirus 1 (BoHV-1) surveillance one month after the arthropod collection periods in both 2022 and 2023, confirming ongoing virus circulation on the farm. Under the conditions investigated, no evidence was found to support transmission via arthropods or vertical transmission. However, rare transmission events or low-prevalence vector involvement cannot be excluded and warrant further investigation.

Non-Coding Transcripts From Diversified Members of IgLec Family Protect Antiviral Effectors From Viral miRNA.
Immune gene families frequently produce numerous non-coding transcripts, yet their biological functions remain largely unexplored. Here, using the arthropod immunoglobulin domain-containing lectin (IgLec) family as a paradigm, we provide evidence that this complexity may reflect a critical defensive function for non-coding transcripts in antiviral immunity. IgLec is restricted to decapod infraorders (Brachyura and Astacidea), and a structurally related bacterial homolog suggests its origin may involve horizontal gene transfer. The IgLec family generates extraordinary transcript diversity through three mechanisms, multi-locus duplication, inter-locus recombination, and extensive alternative splicing, yielding both protein-coding and non-coding transcripts. Protein-coding IgLec variants restrict viral replication by inducing antimicrobial peptide expression. Upon white spot syndrome virus infection, non-coding transcripts (e.g., intron-retaining transcripts) are preferentially targeted by virus-encoded microRNA-N48, thereby protecting protein-coding isoforms from repression. Loss of these decoy transcripts compromises antiviral defense and increases host mortality. Collectively, these results reveal a decoy-based antiviral strategy in which non-coding transcripts safeguard immune effectors from pathogen subversion, uncovering an unrecognized layer of innate immunity.

Liver Viscosity Imaging and Disease Severity in Alcohol-Associated Hepatitis: A Prospective Cross-Sectional Pilot Study.
Background: Alcohol-associated hepatitis (AH) is an acute inflammatory phenotype of alcohol-associated liver disease associated with substantial short-term mortality. Established clinical scores quantify disease severity but do not directly characterize liver tissue mechanics. Ultrasound-derived viscosity-related measurements may provide complementary, non-invasive information on viscoelastic tissue behavior, although their biological determinants remain incompletely defined. Objective: We aimed to evaluate the association between liver viscosity and AH through the Sound Touch Visco-elastography Imaging (STVi) parameter and inflammatory, biochemical, and MDF-defined severity measures, and to explore its discriminatory performance. Methods: This prospective, single-center, cross-sectional pilot study included 62 patients with clinically diagnosed AH and 30 healthy volunteers. Participants underwent multiparametric ultrasound assessment using the Resona A20 platform with STVi, liver stiffness measurement, and attenuation imaging. Results: The viscosity-related parameter was higher in patients with AH than in healthy volunteers and was associated with liver stiffness, inflammatory markers, and MDF-defined severity. The exploratory AH-versus-healthy comparison yielded an AUC of 0.873 (95% CI, 0.797-0.934). Within the AH cohort, 28 patients had severe AH (MDF ≥ 32) and 34 had non-severe AH. For MDF-defined severe AH, the AUC was 0.863 (bootstrap 95% CI, 0.756-0.955). At the Youden-derived cutoff of 2.8 Pa·s, sensitivity was 78.6% and specificity was 94.1%. Conclusions: STVi provides a model-derived, platform-dependent viscosity-related parameter associated with inflammatory measures and clinical severity in AH. These preliminary findings suggest that liver viscosity imaging may represent a valuable new avenue for the non-invasive assessment of AH. However, standardized acquisition, longitudinal assessment, histological correlation, and external validation are required before clinical implementation.

Leprosy mimicking lymphoproliferative disorders: a case report and structured literature search.
OBJECTIVES: Leprosy is a chronic infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae that remains endemic in several regions, including Brazil. The disease predominantly affects the skin and peripheral nerves, but atypical presentations dominated by systemic symptoms such as fever and lymphadenopathy, particularly when accompanied by nonclassical cutaneous findings, are rare and may be mistaken for lymphoproliferative disorders. This study aim to raise clinical suspicion for atypical leprosy among health care providers in endemic areas, complemented by a structured literature search of comparable published cases to better characterize this diagnostic pitfall. METHODS: This study was conducted in two steps. First, we reported an index case of multibacillary borderline leprosy in accordance with the CAse REport (CARE) guidelines. Second, we performed a structured literature search across MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library to identify published case reports and case series describing leprosy presenting as, or mimicking, lymphoma or another lymphoproliferative disorder. CASE PRESENTATION: We describe a 44-year-old woman from southern Brazil with a 1-year history of progressive, initially painful, generalized lymphadenopathy (inguinal, cervical, and axillary), a diffuse pruritic erythematous eruption, and systemic B symptoms (fever, night sweats, and 9 kg of unintentional weight loss). An outside skin biopsy had been read as psoriasiform dermatitis, and the patient had been treated unsuccessfully with methotrexate. One year later, skin and lymph node biopsies subsequently demonstrated acid-fast bacilli on Ziehl-Neelsen staining and histopathology consistent with Hansen's disease, establishing a diagnosis of multibacillary borderline leprosy. The patient was started on multidrug therapy (rifampicin, clofazimine, dapsone). Skin lesions progressively improved and constitutional symptoms resolved with treatment, although residual neuropathic symptoms persisted. Household contact investigation identified a sister with compatible skin lesions. RESULTS: Of 785 records screened, 20 underwent full-text assessment; 13 case reports described a comparable diagnostic pitfall. The closest parallels involved generalized lymphadenopathy with a full constitutional syndrome misattributed to tuberculosis or lymphoma (Bagla, Mahajan, Singh, Herekar, Kiran, and especially Reis et al., a Brazilian case with an almost identical systemic symptom profile); a second group mimicked lymphoma cutaneously (Gunawan, Nawalerspanya, Rodríguez et al.). Taken together, our structured literature search identified relatively few reports combining, as our patient did, disseminated multi-chain lymphadenopathy and a full constitutional syndrome. This combination underscores both the rarity of such a comprehensive presentation and the persistent risk of diagnostic delay when leprosy is not considered in patients from endemic regions presenting with lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms, reinforcing the educational aim of this case report and structured literature search. CONCLUSION: This case and accompanying structured literature search highlight leprosy as an important, underrecognized mimicker of lymphoproliferative disorders when it presents with systemic symptoms and lymphadenopathy. Increased clinical awareness, particularly in primary care and endemic settings, along with systematic contact tracing, is essential to reduce diagnostic delay and interrupt transmission.

Molecular evolutionary dynamics of Coxsackievirus A16 in Shenzhen, China, 2012-2022.
OBJECTIVES: To investigate the epidemiological and genetic characteristics of Coxsackievirus A16 (CVA16) associated with hand, foot and mouth disease (HFMD) in Shenzhen, China. METHODS: CVA16 was examined by a real-time RT-PCR method. Complete VP1 gene sequences of CVA16 strains were determined, and sequence analyses were performed using a series of bioinformatics programs. RESULTS: Of 6436 mild HFMD specimens collected between 2012 and 2022, 1395 (21.7%) were CVA16-positive, with annual detection rates ranging from 4.1% to 45.4% and peaking in 2018. Molecular phylogenetic analysis revealed the circulation of three CVA16 sub-genotypes (B1a, B1b and B3) in Shenzhen, China. The major sub-genotype was B1b from 2013 to 2019, while the sub-genotype B1a predominated in 2020-2022. Phylogenetic and sequence homology analyses suggested that re-emerging CVA16 B1a strains in Shenzhen originated from Vietnam and Thailand. The mean evolutionary rate of CVA16 strains circulating in Shenzhen was estimated at 3.604 × 10-3 substitutions per site per year. Distinct amino acid mutations in VP1 correlated with temporal shifts in Shenzhen's dominant CVA16 sub-genotypes: N14S/L23M for B1b, and T164K/V251I for the 2017-2022 re-emergent B1a. CONCLUSION: In the post-EV-A71 vaccine era, CVA16 remains one of the major pathogens of HFMD in Shenzhen. Over the study period, the CVA16 sub-genotype in Shenzhen underwent a B1a→B1b→B1a turnover, which was associated with both imported lineages and local adaptive evolution. This study underscores the critical importance of continuous molecular surveillance for CVA16.

Genomic characterization of highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b into wild seabirds from coastal Ecuador.
INTRODUCTION: Highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) clade 2.3.4.4b has spread widely across South America, but its genomic diversity and patterns of introduction into Ecuador remain poorly characterized. METHODS: In this study, we report and characterize four genomes of A(H5N1) viruses detected in four individuals of two Ecuadorian seabird species: two magnificent frigatebirds (Fregata magnificens) and two blue-footed boobies (Sula nebouxii) sampled in 2023. RESULTS: These genomes represent confirmed detections of avian influenza in wild birds in the country. The viruses were assigned to genotype B3.2. Global phylogenetic analysis showed that the Ecuadorian wild-bird viruses formed groups distinct from viruses detected in domestic birds in Ecuador. Subsequent phylogenetic and phylogeographic analyses within the South American dataset placed our samples in two distinct clusters, each closely related to viruses previously detected in Peru. These findings highlight the genetic diversity of genotype B3.2 viruses detected in Ecuador and their relationship to viruses circulating in the region. FluServer screening identified 29 amino acid substitutions previously associated with virulence, antigenic change, host specificity, polymerase activity, or antiviral resistance. DISCUSSION: These findings provide genomic evidence of repeated H5N1 introductions into Ecuador as part of the regional spread of the virus along the eastern Pacific coast. They also support sustained surveillance across wildlife, animal-health, and public-health sectors.

In silico analysis of pH stabilising mutations of hemagglutinin of influenza A virus H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b.
Highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) viruses are expanding their host range among mammals, raising concerns about their pandemic potential. Building on recently published deep mutational scanning data1, we show that hemagglutinin retains structural plasticity to increase acid stability through independent mechanisms, including modulation of electrostatic interactions, hydrogen-bonding networks and hydrophobic packing that may facilitate human adaptation. These findings illustrate how structural analyses can strengthen genomic surveillance for pandemic risk assessment.

Establishment of an indirect competitive ELISA for detection of antibodies against goose astrovirus genotype 1 based on ORF2 protein.
Goose astrovirus genotype 1 (GAstV-1) is a major causative agent of visceral gout in goslings, leading to substantial economic losses across Chinese poultry farms. Currently, no commercial vaccine is available, rendering early serological surveillance essential for disease control. In this study, a sensitive and specific indirect competitive enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ic-ELISA) was developed using a monoclonal antibody (mAb) targeting the ORF2 capsid protein of GAstV-1. Following optimization of antigen coating concentration, serum dilution, mAb concentration, and incubation time, the assay demonstrated a detection limit at a serum dilution of 1:160 and showed no cross-reactivity with antisera against other avian pathogens, including H9N2 avian influenza virus (H9N2-AIV), avian reovirus (ARV), goose parvovirus (GPV), goose astrovirus genotype 2 (GAstV-2), and Tembusu virus (TMUV). The cutoff percent inhibition (PI) value was established at 25%, based on 40 GAstV-negative sera. Intra- and inter-assay coefficients of variation (CV) ranged from 0.41 to 0.88% and 3.12-6.95%, respectively, confirming excellent reproducibility. Evaluation of 35 clinical serum samples revealed an 88.6% (31/35) concordance with virus neutralization tests (VNT), with a kappa value of 0.77. These findings indicate that the ORF2-based ic-ELISA is a reliable, cost-effective, and high-throughput tool for seroepidemiological investigation and post-vaccination monitoring of GAstV-1 in geese.

Neonatal mpox in Pakistan: a case study in infection prevention and control gaps and opportunities for improvement.
BACKGROUND: In 2026, a cluster of neonatal deaths from mpox clade Ib was identified in Khairpur, Sindh, marking Pakistan's first pediatric mpox mortality and its first detection of clade Ib. The country had previously recorded only imported clade IIb cases. The cluster mirrors earlier iatrogenic pediatric human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) outbreaks in Ratodero, Mirpur Khas, and Taunsa, and recurrent nosocomial Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever (CCHF) outbreaks. METHODS: A structured comparative clinical and case review reports analysis of six infectious disease outbreaks in Pakistan (2019-2026) was conducted. Peer-reviewed literature was identified through PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar (January 2021-September 2026) using outbreak-specific terms combined with "Pakistan," "iatrogenic," "nosocomial," "infection prevention and control," and "International Health Regulations (IHR)." Gray literature was retrieved from World Health Organization (WHO) country and joint-mission reports, Pakistan's National Institutes of Health advisories, provincial acquired immunodeficiency syndrome control program dashboards, ProMED-mail, and named journalistic investigations where peer-reviewed evidence was not yet available. Outbreaks were compared against IHR 2005 core capacities and the tripartite One Health framework. Infection prevention and control (IPC) failures were assessed by cross-referencing outbreak reports with WHO minimum IPC requirements and the 2025 IPC Assessment Framework assessments in Sindh. RESULTS: Across the six outbreaks, more than 2050 children were affected between 2019 and 2026. The Khairpur cluster (26 confirmed cases, 50% infants under six months, eight neonates) is consistent with maternal-infant vertical transmission and healthcare-associated amplification, not with adult sexual networks. A separate Karachi cluster (n = 8) demonstrated sustained human-to-human transmission from an index case with recent travel to Central Africa. Points-of-entry syndromic screening missed clade Ib because concealed lesions evade visual assessment. Cross-cutting failures include syringe reuse by unregulated practitioners, driving pediatric HIV; personal protective equipment and isolation shortfalls causing fatal nosocomial CCHF among staff each Eid-ul-Azha; and absent integrated One Health surveillance. CONCLUSION: The 2026 neonatal deaths reflect unreformed clinical practice, not a novel pathogen. Priorities include enforceable provincial IPC audits, a ban on unregulated practitioners, molecular-epidemiology-linked points-of-entry surveillance, a clinical pathway for mpox in pregnancy and in neonates, regional-language risk communication, and Modified Vaccinia Ankara - Bavarian Nordic for Mpox and antiviral stockpiling.

Investigation and Response to a Single Cat Injuring Multiple People - Shandong Province, China, 2026.
WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ABOUT THIS TOPIC?: Rabies is an almost universally fatal zoonosis; dogs remain China's main human exposure source. Cats are generally not persistent rabies reservoirs; most feline infections result from spillover from rabid dogs or wildlife. However, feline rabies has been documented worldwide. WHAT IS ADDED BY THIS REPORT?: This report describes a laboratory-confirmed incident in which one stray cat successively attacked two people in Shandong Province, China, in 2026. Rabies virus nucleic acid was detected in cat brain and saliva specimens; whole-genome sequencing showed extremely high homology with two canine-derived strains from Henan. WHAT ARE THE IMPLICATIONS FOR PUBLIC HEALTH PRACTICE?: Large-scale canine vaccination and strengthened dog source management, including registration, confinement or tethering, and collection and sheltering of strays, should remain core interventions for blocking rabies spillover at its source. Cats should also be formally incorporated into rabies prevention and control systems.

Epidemiological Characteristics and Spatial Clustering of Single-Dog-Induced Multiple Human Exposure Events - Chongqing, China, 2016-2025.
INTRODUCTION: Single-dog-induced multiple human exposure events can result in multiple potential rabies exposures within a short period, with substantial public health and economic costs. In China, these events are managed under nationally standardized procedures and require a coordinated public health and animal health response. This study analyzed the epidemiological characteristics, post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), and response gaps associated with these events in Chongqing from 2016 to 2025. METHODS: Data on events, offending dogs, and exposed persons were collected from investigation reports submitted by district and county CDCs. Human rabies surveillance data for Chongqing were obtained from the China CDC Information System. Spearman correlation analysis was used to assess the association between annual event counts and the number of human rabies cases reported, and cross-correlation function (CCF) analysis was used to assess the temporally lagged association. Joinpoint regression was used to evaluate temporal trends, and global and local Moran's I statistics were used to assess spatial clustering. Statistical significance was defined as P<0.05. RESULTS: A total of 124 events involving 649 exposed persons were reported, including 3 human rabies deaths. Annual event counts were positively correlated with the number of human rabies cases reported during the same period (r=0.782, P<0.01), and CCF analysis showed positive correlations across all lag months, with the correlation being strongest with a 2-month lag (r=0.426, 95% CI: 0.355, 0.629, P<0.001). The annual number of events declined during the study period (average annual percent change=-19.0%, P<0.01), with a rapid decline between 2016 and 2022 and a nonsignificant increase between 2022 and 2025. Most events (74.2%) occurred in rural areas. Spatial clustering was detected in 2016-2017, 2018-2019, and 2024-2025. Category III exposures accounted for 82.7% of exposed persons. Rabies vaccine coverage was 98.9%, and rabies immunoglobulin was administered to 87.5% of persons with Category III exposure. No deaths occurred among those who received standard PEP, whereas mortality was 2.6% among those who did not (P<0.01). Stray dogs accounted for 66.9% of offending dogs. Only 7 canine specimens were tested from the 124 offending dogs (5.6%), and all were positive for rabies virus antigen by direct fluorescent antibody test using brain tissue. CONCLUSIONS: From 2016 to 2025, single-dog-induced multiple human rabies exposure events in Chongqing declined overall and showed localized clustering. Most events occurred in rural areas, with Category III exposures predominating. In this group, no deaths occurred among standardized PEP recipients, whereas 3 deaths occurred among individuals who did not receive standardized PEP. To reduce human rabies, event monitoring and standardized PEP should be strengthened.

The Epidemiological Characteristics of 55 Multiple-Victim Incidents Involving Bites from a Single Dog - Shandong Province, China, 2025.
WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ABOUT THIS TOPIC?: Rabies is a zoonotic infectious disease caused by rabies virus infection and was classified as a Class B notifiable infectious disease in China. Events involving multiple victims bitten by a single dog represent a distinct category in rabies epidemiological surveillance and risk assessment. These incidents indicate high-probability point-source exposure to potentially rabid animals and thus pose urgent public health threats. WHAT IS ADDED BY THIS REPORT?: This study analyzed the epidemiological characteristics of events involving multiple victims bitten by a single dog in Shandong Province in 2025 and evaluated the effectiveness of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) implementation. WHAT ARE THE IMPLICATIONS FOR PUBLIC HEALTH PRACTICE?: This study highlights the severity of events involving multiple victims bitten by a single dog in Shandong Province and validates the effectiveness of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) strategies, providing robust evidence for the formulation of rabies prevention and control strategies.

Prebassianins from Akanthomyces araneicola: Discovery, Biosynthesis, and a Rare OYE-SDR Fusion Enzyme.
Two new 4-hydroxy-2-pyridone alkaloids, prebassianins F (5) and G (6), featuring a rare 1,4-cyclohexanediol moiety, were isolated from rice cultures of Akanthomyces araneicola GY29011. Genome mining and heterologous expression of the corresponding biosynthetic gene cluster (pre) in Aspergillus nidulans afforded six additional new analogues (3-4 and 7-10), along with two known compounds (1-2). Combinatorial expression and substrate feeding experiments enabled the elucidation of the biosynthetic pathway and functional assignment of the tailoring enzymes. Notably, PreC was identified as a rare bifunctional fusion enzyme comprising old yellow enzyme (OYE) and short-chain dehydrogenase (SDR) domains. Truncation of PreC led to the accumulation of a key intermediate (10), supporting its role in sequential reductions. cDNA analysis confirmed that PreC is encoded as a single open reading frame containing four introns, including a rare GC-AG intron. Compounds 3 and 4 exhibited antibacterial activity against Bacillus subtilis (MIC = 16 μg/mL). These findings expand the structural diversity of 4-hydroxy-2-pyridone alkaloids and provide new insights into the enzymatic logic and evolution of fungal biosynthetic pathways.

Discovery and Biosynthesis of Brasilanes G-L: N-Acetylglucosamine-Decorated Sesquiterpenoids with Anti-Inflammatory Activity.
N-Acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc)-decorated natural products represent a structurally unique class of metabolites that possess diverse biological activities. Through the genome mining of Coccidioides sp. CMB-TN39F, we identified a GlcNAc transferase-encoding terpene synthase gene cluster brc. Heterologous expression of this cluster in Aspergillus nidulans enabled the characterization of seven GlcNAc-adorned brasilane-type sesquiterpene glycosides, including six previously undocumented compounds, brasilane G-L (1-6), and one known compound, brasilane A (7). Functional characterization revealed that the cytochrome P450 BrcC functions as an epoxidase, catalyzing a stereoselective epoxidation of 7 to form 1. Compound 1 can undergo non-enzymatic conversions to generate compounds 2-5 under mildly acidic conditions. Pharmacological evaluation demonstrated that compounds 1-6 effectively downregulate the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α) in LPS/IFN-γ-stimulated THP-1-derived macrophages. Notably, 1, which features an epoxide moiety, exhibits superior anti-inflammatory activity compared to its biosynthetic precursor 7, with an IC50 value of 30.4 μM against IL-6. This study expands the chemical space of GlcNAc-conjugated terpenoids and showcases a biosynthetic logic in which enzymatic tailoring is coupled with nonenzymatic reactions to amplify both structural diversity and biological properties.

A comprehensive high-throughput detection strategy: an indirect ELISA for serodetection of the novel aMPV/C in ducks.
INTRODUCTION: Avian metapneumovirus subtype C (aMPV/C), a re-emerging and widespread epidemic in China, causes hydrosalpinx fluid syndrome (HFS) in laying ducks, resulting in significant economic losses to the poultry industry. In the absence of any licensed vaccines or antiviral drugs for aMPV/C, accurate diagnosis and timely eradication of the infected ducks remain the primary control measures, underscoring the urgent need for reliable and effective detection methods. METHODS: In this study, the purified whole novel aMPV/C was used to develop an indirect enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (iELISA) for the detection of aMPV/C antibodies in ducks. RESULTS: The cut-off value of the iELISA was determined to be 0.258. No cross-reactivity was observed with duck sera positive for antibodies against H5 AIV, NDV, DTMUV, BTV, DHAV-3, DPV, EDSV, MDPV, or GPV, demonstrating good specificity. Both intra-assay and inter-assay coefficients of variation were less than 10%, and the detection sensitivity of the iELISA reached a serum dilution of 1:102400. A total of 216 clinical serum samples from three duck breeds were tested via the established iELISA, of which 129 (59.7%) were positive. The concordance rate between the iELISA and an indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA) was 100% (53/53). CONCLUSION: Overall, this cost-effective iELISA provides a reliable tool for the detection of aMPV/C antibodies in clinical diagnostics and epidemiological surveillance.

Seroprevalence and associated factors of foot-and-mouth disease virus antibodies in cattle in Africa and Asia: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
BACKGROUND: Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) is a highly contagious transboundary animal disease that continues to threaten livestock production and trade, particularly in endemic regions. Cattle are among the principal livestock species affected. However, comprehensive assessments of regional variation in FMDV antibody seroprevalence and its associated epidemiological factors remain limited. This study aimed to systematically evaluate FMDV antibody seroprevalence in cattle across Asia and Africa and to identify potential factors associated with variation in serological exposure. METHODS: A systematic literature search was conducted in seven databases (PubMed, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, CNKI, WanFang, CAB Abstracts, and VIP) to identify studies published up to 16 October 2024 that reported FMDV antibody seroprevalence in cattle from Asia and/or Africa. Eligible studies were selected according to predefined criteria, and study quality was assessed using a standardized scoring approach. Random-effects meta-analysis, sensitivity analysis, assessment of publication bias, and subgroup analyses were performed to estimate pooled FMDV antibody seroprevalence and explore potential sources of heterogeneity. RESULTS: A total of 67 studies were included. The pooled FMDV antibody seroprevalence in cattle across Asia and Africa was 26.86%. However, extremely high between-study heterogeneity was observed (I² = 99.3%), and the pooled estimate should therefore be interpreted cautiously as an overall epidemiological summary of FMDV antibody exposure. Regional analysis showed that FMDV antibody seroprevalence was significantly higher in Africa (35.37%, 95% CI: 26.35-45.55) than in Asia (16.36%, 95% CI: 10.82-23.96). Unvaccinated herds exhibited a significantly higher FMDV antibody seroprevalence (37.59%, 95% CI: 23.55-54.07) than vaccinated herds (14.39%, 95% CI: 5.45-32.91). Among the FMDV serotypes evaluated, serotype O showed the highest pooled FMDV antibody seroprevalence (47.16%, 95% CI: 23.45-72.24), with significant differences among serotypes. Mixed-serotype antibody positivity was also observed (8.80%, 95% CI: 3.82-18.99). CONCLUSIONS: FMDV antibody seroprevalence was substantial among cattle populations across Asia and Africa, with considerable regional variation and higher levels of serological exposure observed in Africa. Higher FMDV antibody seroprevalence was observed among unvaccinated herds, whereas serotype O exhibited the highest pooled FMDV antibody seroprevalence among the serotypes evaluated. These findings highlight the importance of sustained serological surveillance, region-specific vaccination strategies, appropriate vaccine matching, and strengthened biosecurity measures to support evidence-based FMD prevention and control.

Highly sensitive detection and identification of six viruses in shrimps by universal primer based multiplex PCR.
The global expansion of shrimp aquaculture faces severe threats from viral disease outbreaks, which cause substantial economic losses and create an urgent demand for rapid, accurate diagnostic tools. To address this need, we developed a universal primer-mediated multiplex PCR (UP-M-PCR) assay for the simultaneous detection of six major shrimp-infecting viruses: Taura syndrome virus (TSV), hepatopancreatic parvovirus (HPV), infectious hypodermal and hematopoietic necrosis virus (IHHNV), Penaeus monodon-type baculovirus (MBV), and yellow head virus (YHV), white spot syndrome virus (WSSV). The assay employed a strategy of combined usage of a universal primer and chimeric primers who had a universal primer tail at the 5'-end of each virus-specific primer to increase analytic specificity and sensitivity. The assay specifically detected the six viruses and demonstrated exceptional sensitivity, with limits of detection (LODs) of 5 copies/μL for TSV, WSSV, and IHHNV, and 50 copies/μL for HPV, MBV, and YHV. In testing of 1180 shrimp samples in 236 pools of 5, the assay detected a calculated overall viral positivity rate of 8.17% at the individual shrimp level, with IHHNV showing the highest prevalence (5.91%), followed by WSSV (1.93%) and HPV (0.08%), and WSSV-IHHNV coinfections were identified in 0.26% of samples. This UP-M-PCR assay allows for the concurrent detection and differentiation of multiple shrimp viral pathogens with excellent analytical and diagnostic performance, supporting its good application potential for viral surveillance in shrimp aquaculture.

When fear meets knowledge: The effects of risk aversion and policy information on sustainable pig carcass disposal under government regulation.
Against the backdrop of recurrent African swine fever (ASF) outbreaks, this study establishes a behavioral baseline for carcass governance under China's pre-crisis regulatory environment. Integrating the fear appeal framework with mental accounting theory, we draw on unique household survey data to estimate how farmers' risk aversion toward command-and-control policies and their policy information acquisition ability shape sustainable disposal behavior. Our results show that fines exert limited deterrent effects, likely because they are encoded as manageable operating costs. Conversely, risk aversion toward detention significantly increases compliance. Furthermore, information acquisition ability directly promotes sustainable practices and amplifies the deterrent effect of detention. By establishing these micro-foundations, we identify detention and information navigation as central behavioral mechanisms within the regulatory toolkit under normal pre-ASF conditions. This provides a benchmark reference for capturing psychological processing mechanisms underlying responses to command-and-control policies and offers a robust pathway for advancing sustainable waste management in developing contexts.
