Given the limited number and low methodological quality of the studies, caution is recommended when applying these findings.

Comparative Evaluation and Optimization of a CRISPR/Cas-Based Assay for Rapid Detection of Tilapinevirus tilapiae (TiLV) in Indian Isolates, Validated Against Conventional Nucleic acid Detection Methods.
UNLABELLED: Tilapia lake virus (Tilapinevirus tilapiae; TiLV) remains a significant threat to global tilapia aquaculture, underscoring the urgent need for rapid, sensitive, and field-ready diagnostic approaches. In this study, we developed a CRISPR-Cas12a assisted reverse transcriptase-recombinase polymerase amplification assay (Cr-TiLV) targeting a conserved region of segment 6 of the TiLV genome. The integration of RT-RPA with Cas12a significantly enhanced analytical sensitivity, enabling the detection of viral RNA at levels as low as 10 copies. Diagnostic assessment using 40 clinical samples demonstrated that the Cr-TiLV assay achieved sensitivities of 86.67% and 82.29%, and accuracies of 90% and 85%, respectively, relative to semi-nested PCR and RT-qPCR, with specificity approaching 99.9% for both benchmark methods. Although less sensitive than RT-qPCR for samples with low viral loads, the assay consistently detected low to moderate viral concentrations and showed substantial concordance with semi-nested PCR. Operating isothermally at 39 °C and requiring minimal laboratory resources, the Cr-TiLV assay offers a rapid and field-deployable diagnostic solution with strong potential for routine TiLV surveillance in resource-limited aquaculture settings. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s12088-026-01550-y.

Emergence of novel highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza in slender-billed gulls (Chroicocephalus genei) and gull-billed terns (Gelochelidon nilotica) at Dukan Lake, Iraq.
BACKGROUND: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 continues to cause severe mortality among wild birds globally. AIM: The present study aimed to investigate the mass mortality in Slender-billed Gulls (Chroicocephalus genei) and Gull-billed Terns (Gelochelidon nilotica) at Dukan Lake, Iraq, during the 2024 breeding season. METHODS: Field monitoring was conducted at breeding colonies, and dead carcasses were collected for necropsy, histopathology, and molecular analysis. Virus detection and genetic characterization were performed by reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction and sequencing. In addition, the viral lineage was inferred by phylogenetic analysis of the hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) genes. RESULTS: More than 3,200 gulls and terns were found dead, exhibiting severe neurological signs and systemic illness. Necropsy and histopathological investigations indicated significant multi-organ damage, with gulls showing more pronounced visceral lesions than terns, while terns exhibited greater neurological damage. Molecular characterization confirmed the virus as HPAI H5N1, and analysis of the HA and NA genes revealed that the strain from Dukan Lake falls within clade 2.3.4.4b, displaying a high genetic resemblance (>98%) with the recently identified H5N1 strain isolated from Mute swans in Kazakhstan. The virus showed multibasic cleavage sites characteristic of high pathogenicity but maintained receptor-binding specificity for avian hosts. Moreover, the results demonstrate the recent introduction of the virus via migratory flyways and the significance of gulls and terns in the disease ecology of HPAI virus (HPAIV). CONCLUSION: This outbreak is the first recorded mass mortality of gulls and terns due to HPAI H5N1 in Iraq. The results emphasize the need for improved surveillance at migratory stopover and breeding sites to observe viral evolution, host susceptibility, and potential risks for cross-species transmission.

The evolutionary landscape and serotypic dynamics of avian infectious bronchitis virus from spike protein.
Avian infectious bronchitis virus (IBV), a gammacoronavirus with substantial agricultural impact, offers a tractable model for dissecting coronavirus evolution. Here, we integrated 20 years of epidemiological surveillance with whole-genome sequence analysis of 624 IBV strains, including 136 newly isolated field samples, to investigate the evolutionary and structural dynamics of N-linked glycosylation at the spike protein. We identified three dominant glycosylation haplotypes defined by residues 51 and 77 of spike protein, which correlate with receptor-binding interfaces, clinical phenotypes, and spatiotemporal transmission patterns. Molecular modeling and docking analyses provided insights into potential mechanistic links between glycan positioning and Neu5Acα2-3Galβ1-3GlcNAc receptor engagement. Complementing these findings, we developed a proof-of-concept machine learning model that shows potential for predicting clinical serotypes directly from the spike protein sequence, achieving high accuracy on a preliminary independent validation set. These findings support the use of glycosylation motifs as structural-genomic markers and highlight the potential of sequence-based serotype prediction. Our work establishes a scalable genomic-structural framework that leverages glycosylation motifs and sequence features as evolutionary markers, providing a powerful approach for forecasting coronavirus adaptation and informing vaccine design and outbreak preparedness.

Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza H5N1 in Missouri: Current Situation and Pandemic Potential.
Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1, which has caused severe disease in poultry since 1996, has become panzootic in wild birds and recently has spread to dairy cattle and other mammalian species in the United States. Although few human cases have been reported, devastating HPAI H5N1 poultry outbreaks and massive dieoffs in wild birds and in some mammals raise concern about pandemic potential. Surveillance, early detection, public health interventions, farm biosecurity measures, and next-generation vaccines may reduce the risk of a future HPAI H5N1 pandemic.

Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Emerging Viral Zoonotic Diseases, 2016-2026.
Emerging viral zoonoses-infections caused by viruses that cross the species barrier from animal reservoirs into human populations-account for the majority of emerging infectious disease (EID) events and now constitute a defining threat to global health security. Over the past decade the tempo of these spillovers has increased, propelled by land-use change, agricultural intensification, wildlife trade, and climate change, while reverse zoonosis-the transmission of human pathogens back into animal populations-has created novel animal reservoirs capable of seeding future outbreaks. Against this backdrop, we systematically reviewed and meta-analyzed epidemiological evidence on emerging viral zoonoses from January 2016 through June 2026, searching five bibliographic databases and synthesizing 312 included studies. Annual high-consequence spillover events increased by 4.98% (95% CI 3.22%-6.76%), and the decade saw five Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) declarations, alongside other high-consequence spillovers such as the 2026 Bundibugyo virus outbreak (case fatality rate [CFR] 30.9%) and the expansion of H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza into dairy cattle. Bat-origin viruses exhibited the highest pooled CFR (29.86%), whereas primate-origin viruses demonstrated greater transmissibility, supporting a virulence-transmissibility trade-off. Land-use change emerged as the dominant anthropogenic driver, increasing zoonotic host diversity by 18%-72%. White-tailed deer SARS-CoV-2 seroprevalence reached 32.7% (95% CI 21.4%-46.1%), with confirmed deer-to-human spillback. Nonpharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) collectively reduced the effective reproduction number by up to 82%, and prevention-oriented One Health strategies yielded returns exceeding 1100% on investment. Viral zoonoses are accelerating under anthropogenic pressure, and upstream prevention with integrated One Health surveillance represents the most cost-effective pandemic preparedness strategy.

Difference between initial ventilation strategies in patients seen in the emergency department during the first and second waves of the COVID-19 pandemic.
OBJECTIVE: COVID-19 infection has led to changes in known treatment strategies, mainly with respect to its critical form, that is, the presentation of acute respiratory distress syndrome, which requires the use of mechanical ventilation. METHODS: Ventilation strategies were compared between the first and second wave of patients with COVID-19 who were treated in the emergency department and who required endotracheal intubation. RESULTS: Of the 62 patients treated in the emergency department, invasive mechanical ventilation was started in the second group 7.9 hours earlier than in the first group (95%CI: -11.65 to -4.19; p < 0.001). The use of prone position was greater up to 50% in the second group (95%CI: 0.17-0.85; p = 0.009). The second group used 3 cmH2O less PEEP (95%CI: -4.17 to -1.87; p < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Changes in ventilation strategies were evident in patients with severe COVID-19. Although they did not show a significant difference, it can be inferred that 28-day mortality in the second group decreased due to the change in the use of PEEP, early intubation, and prone position.

Effectiveness of Quality Improvement Strategies in Preventing Healthcare-Associated Infections Among Neurosurgical Patients Admitted to Intensive Care Units: A Systematic Review.
BACKGROUND: Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) remain a major and largely preventable cause of morbidity, excess mortality, prolonged hospitalization, and escalating healthcare costs in intensive care units (ICUs) worldwide. Neurosurgical patients are particularly vulnerable because of frequent exposure to invasive devices such as external ventricular drains (EVDs), central venous catheters, urinary catheters, and mechanical ventilation, combined with impaired neurological status and prolonged ICU stays. Although quality improvement (QI) strategies have been widely implemented across critical care settings, evidence specific to neurosurgical and neurocritical care populations remains fragmented. OBJECTIVES: To systematically evaluate the effectiveness of QI interventions in reducing HAI incidence among neurosurgical and neurological ICU patients and to assess their impact on secondary outcomes including ICU length of stay, device utilization, and bundle compliance. METHODS: A comprehensive search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science from January 2010 to May 2026, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Eligible studies for the primary evidence synthesis included randomized controlled trials, quasi-experimental studies, and observational cohort studies evaluating structured QI interventions for HAI prevention in neurosurgical or neurological ICU populations, or mixed ICU settings with extractable neurocritical care data. Systematic reviews identified during screening were retained for contextual interpretation and reference screening but were excluded from the primary evidence synthesis to avoid duplication of overlapping primary data. Risk of bias was assessed using ROBINS-I, Cochrane RoB 2, and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale according to study design. RESULTS: Seventeen primary studies from 14 countries met eligibility criteria and were included in the primary narrative synthesis. Three systematic reviews were retained for contextual interpretation. Structured QI interventions consistently reduced device-associated infection rates across studies. The strongest evidence was observed for EVD-specific care bundles, with EVD-related infection rates decreasing from 14.35 to 3.21 per 1,000 catheter-days following bundle implementation, and one study reporting 20 consecutive infection-free months after interprofessional bundle adoption. Device-associated infection prevention bundles also demonstrated clinically meaningful reductions, including VAP rates decreasing from 68.2 to 47.4 per 1,000 ventilator-days and CAUTI rates from 24.9 to 13.4 per 1,000 catheter-days following structured educational interventions. CLABSI rates declined substantially following standardized central venous catheter bundle implementation, reaching zero in one study with sustained monitoring. Risk of bias was predominantly low to moderate across included primary studies. CONCLUSIONS: Structured QI interventions, particularly EVD-specific care bundles, device-associated infection prevention protocols, and staff education programs with compliance monitoring, consistently reduce HAI incidence in neurosurgical and neurological ICU settings. Although the evidence base is predominantly non-randomized, findings are directionally consistent across diverse healthcare systems and institutional contexts. Universal adoption of evidence-based infection prevention frameworks in neurocritical care is strongly supported.

Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis: An Underrecognized Complication of Pediatric Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever.
AIM: Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (sHLH) is a potentially life-threatening hyperinflammatory complication of Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever (CCHF), yet pediatric data remain limited. This study aimed to characterize the clinical phenotype of pediatric CCHF-associated sHLH and to identify early clinical features associated with sHLH development. METHODS: PCR-confirmed pediatric CCHF cases from four tertiary centers in Türkiye (2018-2025) were retrospectively analyzed, and clinical characteristics, laboratory findings, treatment, and outcomes were compared between children with and without sHLH. RESULTS: Of 79 patients, 27 (34.2%) fulfilled the diagnostic criteria for sHLH. Compared with children without sHLH, these patients more frequently presented with hemorrhagic findings (44.4% vs. 11.5%, p = 0.002), diarrhea (37.0% vs. 7.7%, p = 0.004), and bradycardia (25.9% vs. 1.9%, p = 0.002), and had lower platelet and fibrinogen and higher ferritin, AST, ALT, and LDH concentrations at diagnosis. On multivariable analysis, bradycardia (OR 11.1, 95% CI 1.7-126.3), hemorrhagic findings (OR 7.1, 95% CI 2.1-26.5), and diarrhea (OR 6.4, 95% CI 1.6-29.0) remained independent predictors; hemorrhagic findings and diarrhea preceded the sHLH diagnosis, whereas bradycardia was identified concurrently. Ferritin and aPTT worsened progressively only in children with sHLH, whereas platelet count declined in both groups. Despite more frequent immunomodulatory therapy and transfusion, no deaths occurred. CONCLUSIONS: Secondary HLH should be actively considered in pediatric CCHF, particularly with hemorrhagic findings, diarrhea, or bradycardia preceding full laboratory evolution to facilitate earlier diagnosis and timely therapy.

Molecular Prevalence and Genotype Detection of Babesia microti in Multiple Wild Rodent Species and Suncus murinus From Subtropical Mountainous Regions of South-Central Zhejiang, China.
Human babesiosis, an emerging zoonosis with ongoing geographic expansion, is primarily caused by Babesia microti, a tick-borne apicomplexan parasite that resides within host erythrocytes. While small mammals serve as its recognized reservoir hosts, the relative contribution of sympatric wild rodents and shrews in subtropical mountain endemic areas of Eastern China remains poorly characterized. In South-central Zhejiang, an endemic focus of human babesiosis, systematic data on local small-mammal hosts remain limited. In this study, 630 small mammals, comprising six rodent species and the shrew Suncus murinus, were captured across six counties in Zhejiang Province of China. Host identity was confirmed by morphological examination and mitochondrial cytochrome b (cytb) barcoding. Whole-blood DNA was screened for B. microti by TaqMan real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR); positive specimens were further analyzed by nested PCR (NPCR) targeting the 18S rRNA gene, followed by sequencing for genotype identification. The overall qPCR-positive rate was 3.0% (19/630). Geographically, B. microti infections were detected in four out of six surveyed counties, with Jinyun County showing the highest prevalence of 6.9%, followed by Qingyuan (4.0%), Wencheng (3.2%), and Qingtian (3.0%); no positive samples were identified in the Yunhe and Jingning counties. Among the sampled species, Niviventer lotipes showed the highest prevalence (11.7%, 12/103), followed by S. murinus (3.8%, 2/52), Alexandromys fortis (3.7%, 3/81), Apodemus agrarius (1.0%, 1/99), and Rattus norvegicus (0.5%, 1/222). No positive results were detected in R. tanezumi (n = 62) or Leopoldamys edwardsi (n = 11). Fifteen of the 19 samples yielded positive amplification by NPCR and were successfully sequenced. All 15 sequenced isolates were assigned to the Kobe genotype and exhibited close genetic relatedness to previously reported local human-derived and tick-derived strains. The dominance of a single haplotype (n = 14) across host species and counties indicates genetically homogeneous circulation of the Kobe genotype within local small-mammal communities, with host species rather than sampling county as the significant determinant of infection risk. These findings suggest that N. lotipes may be an important reservoir host in this region, and shrews may represent understudied secondary hosts, supporting the inclusion of both rodents and shrews in regional babesiosis surveillance.

Within-Host Evolution of Foot-and-Mouth Disease Virus From Persistently Infected Cattle and Buffaloes in Vietnam.
Foot-and-mouth disease virus (FMDV) persists endemically through carrier animals that maintain infection >21 days postdetection. We characterized within-host FMDV evolution in persistently infected cattle (n = 168) and buffalo (n = 16) from northern Vietnam using longitudinal oropharyngeal sampling (3-4 month intervals) under non-outbreak conditions. Animals remained rRT-PCR positive without clinical FMD. Persistent infections were defined by 5% divergence between sequential samples. From 120 sequences across 38 persistently infected hosts (PIHs), 13.3% of apparent carriers (rRT-PCR positive >21 days) were actually serially infected with distinct strains. This emphasizes the need for sequence confirmation alongside OPF positivity when estimating carrier prevalence in high-diversity settings. True persistent infections (n = 33 animals) showed rapid VP1 evolution (0.081 mutations/nt site/yr), with diversifying selection strongest in VP1 and VP3 capsid regions. Serotype O PIH exhibited higher VP3 mutation rates than serotype A. Interserotypic recombination was also detected, consistent with carrier animals serving as viral mixing vessels. These field data confirm high evolutionary rates and recombination within FMDV carriers under natural conditions, extending experimental superinfection findings to endemic systems. Results support targeted PIH detection and management to disrupt FMDV persistence and evolution in resource-limited regions.

Detection and Characterisation of The 'A' Variant of Rabbit Haemorrhagic Disease (RHDVa, GI.1a) Over a Decade (2013-2023) in Italy.
Since the 1980s, highly pathogenic and hepatotropic Lagovirus species have significantly impacted rabbit populations, including Rabbit Haemorrhagic Disease Virus (RHDV, genotype GI.1), its variant RHDVa (genotype GI.1a), and RHDV type 2 (RHDV2, genotype GI.2). Non-pathogenic Lagovirus strains such as Rabbit Calicivirus (RCV, genotypes GI.3 and GI.4), which mainly replicate in the gastrointestinal tract, have also been identified. Recombination between pathogenic and non-pathogenic strains, particularly at the junction between non-structural (NS) and structural genome regions, is a major driver of the emergence of new variant strains. In the context of the widespread and predominant circulation of RHDV2, we analysed 51 RHDVa strains collected from domestic rabbit farms across Italy between 2013 and 2023 to assess their genetic and antigenic variability. Phylogenetic analyses were performed using full and partial genome sequences, and antigenic characterisation was conducted using a panel of RHDVa-specific monoclonal antibodies (MAbs). Phylogenetic analysis showed no evidence of recombination involving the Italian RHDVa strains. Nucleotide and amino acid identities with the reference strain RHDVa_Pv97 ranged from 95% to 98% and 97%-99%, respectively, confirming high genetic stability. The antigenic study indicated overall stability, consistent with the genetic results, but the few mutants found allowed us to map at least two epitopes located on the outer loops of the VP60 protein, which constituted a large part of the virus surface. In particular, the substitution at position N414S leads to the loss of MAb 2B4 binding to the RHDV/Italy/FG2014_1 strain, and the N348S mutation, which is present in five strains, results in the acquisition of binding to the MAb 2A10. Despite the global predominance of RHDV2, RHDVa persists to be detected sporadically in various Italian regions, especially within commercial rabbit farms. Continuous molecular and antigenic monitoring of Lagovirus strains remains essential to detect potential co-circulation and recombination events that could lead to the emergence of novel strains with distinct genomic and antigenic traits.

Serosurveillance and Postvaccination Seromonitoring of Peste Des Petits Ruminants in Small Ruminants in Central Gondar Zone, Northwest Ethiopia.
Peste des petits ruminants (PPR) is a highly contagious transboundary viral disease of small ruminants caused by the PPR virus (PPRV). Despite Ethiopia's goal of eradicating PPR by 2027 through a risk-based vaccination strategy, the disease remains endemic, with 554 outbreaks reported nationwide. This cross-sectional study was conducted in the North Gondar Zone, Ethiopia, between June 2024 and February 2025 to evaluate antibody responses in vaccinated small ruminants and estimate PPRV seroprevalence in unvaccinated flocks. A multistage cluster sampling design was used to select the study sites, while individual animals were selected using a haphazard sampling approach to approximate random sampling. A total of 600 serum samples were collected, including 300 from vaccinated and 300 from unvaccinated small ruminants; samples from vaccinated animals were obtained ~28 days postvaccination. All samples were tested for anti-PPRV antibodies using competitive enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (c-ELISA). Overall individual-level seropositivity in the vaccinated population was 75%, comprising 75.73% in sheep and 72.1% in goats, serving as a proxy measure of flock immunity. In unvaccinated animals, PPRV seroprevalence was 14.33% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 10.6%-18.82%). Multivariable logistic regression identified age and flock size as the main risk factors influencing seropositivity. Adult animals were 2.89 times as likely to be seropositive as young animals (95% CI: 1.17-7.15; p = 0.022), and animals in medium-sized flocks were more likely to test positive than those in small flocks (AOR = 2.26; 95% CI: 1.11-4.63; p = 0.026). No significant differences were observed across districts, species, sex, production systems, newly introduced animals, or animal movement (p > 0.05). The observed seropositivity was slightly below the commonly used 80% population immunity target associated with reducing transmission under the PPR eradication framework. The detection of PPRV antibodies in unvaccinated animals indicates previous exposure to PPRV and highlights the need for strengthened surveillance to assess whether active virus circulation persists in the area. To achieve effective control and eventual eradication of PPR, intensified vaccination programs combined with active surveillance are needed. Furthermore, refining vaccination strategies in alignment with global and national eradication plans is essential to establish PPR-free zones in these districts.

Seroprevalence of Epizootic Hemorrhagic Disease Virus in Cattle, Sheep, and Goats in New York State From 2022 Through 2025.
Epizootic hemorrhagic disease (EHD) virus (EHDV) is a vector-borne virus transmitted by Culicoides midges that infects domestic and wild ruminants. EHDV causes high mortality in white-tailed deer (WTD) and oral lesions mimicking foot and mouth disease (FMD) in cattle. Small ruminants (e.g., domestic sheep, domestic goats) seroconvert but do not typically develop disease. In 2021, ~2100 WTD deaths were attributed to EHD in New York (NY) State. That same year, an EHD outbreak at a NY dairy resulted in a foreign animal disease (FAD) investigation to rule out FMD, and EHDV was detected in a captive bison herd in NY. In response to the EHD outbreak affecting wildlife, agricultural, and exhibition animals, serum samples from cattle, sheep, and goats submitted to the Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine Animal Health Diagnostic Center (AHDC) were tested for EHDV antibodies. The samples tested in our surveillance study included samples collected during and after Culicoides vector activity (July-January) over three seasons from 2022 to 2025. A total of 5698 samples comprising 4874 cattle and 824 small ruminants were tested using the agar gel immunodiffusion assay (AGID). Season 1 had 0.6% seroprevalence (10/1719), season 2 had 0.7% seroprevalence (15/2021), season 3 had 0.5% seroprevalence (9/1958) with an overall seroprevalence of 0.6%. Neutralizing antibody (NA) titers were determined on all AGID positive samples for EHDV serotypes 1, 2, and 6. There were 20 samples positive for EHDV serotype 2 (NA titers from 1:40 to ≥ 1:1280); 11 samples positive for EHDV serotype 6 (NA titers from 1:10 to 1:640); and three animals with cross-reaction amongst serotypes. Of the 34 positive samples, 31 were from cattle and 3 were from sheep. Nineteen samples were from counties with large numbers of WTD deaths attributed to EHDV in 2021 or counties with cases of EHDV in cattle. This data indicates that EHDV serotypes 2 and 6 subclinically infected a small number of domestic ruminants in NY from 2022 to 2025.

Synergistic Effect of Newcastle Disease Virus and Hydroxyurea in Apoptosis of Human Hepatocellular Carcinoma Cells (HepG2).
INTRODUCTION: Despite widespread use, chemotherapy often leads to adverse effects and resistance. Hydroxyurea (HU) is commonly used in combination with other chemotherapeutic agents. Efforts have been made to enhance its efficacy and reduce associated toxicity. Combination therapy appears to be the most effective approach for targeting cancer cells through multiple mechanisms. Newcastle disease virus (NDV) has recently been investigated as a potential cancer therapy. This is the first study to evaluate the combined cytotoxicity of NDV and HU in HepG2 cells. MATERIALS AND METHODS: The effects of the nonvirulent oncolytic LaSota strain of NDV and HU (alone and in combination) on human liver cancer cells were assessed using MTT, annexin/PI, AO/EtBr staining, scratch and transwell assays, colony formation, quantitative real-time PCR, and Western blot for gene and protein expression. The combination results were analyzed using the Chou-Talalay method. RESULTS: The combination of HU and NDV at IC30 doses resulted in approximately 65%-70% cell death, which is significantly greater than that observed with either monotherapy (p = 0.0006). The annexin V/PI assay showed that the combination induced 36.8% apoptosis, whereas monotherapy with HU or NDV induced only about 17% (p < 0.05). Cell migration was significantly impeded in all treated groups, with the combination resulting in a 65% decrease in migration relative to the control (p = 0.009). With HU + NDV, colony formation was reduced by about 60%, and with HU alone, it was reduced by about 43% (p = 0.0005). The mRNA expression of VEGF-A was markedly diminished in all treated groups; but, on the contrary, the cleaved caspase 9 was boosted at the protein level. These data collectively confirm a synergistic inhibitory effect on the proliferation, migration, and survival of HepG2 cells. CONCLUSION: The combination of the common chemotherapeutic agent HU with the nonpathogenic LaSota strain of NDV as virotherapy showed a synergistic effect on HepG2 cells in vitro. The results suggest a possible therapeutic benefit by suppressing cancer cell proliferation, inhibiting growth, and inducing cell death. However, these results are restricted to in vitro tests and may not fully represent the complexity of liver cancer in humans; additional in vivo research is required to assess the approach's safety and clinical applicability. Additionally, this combination might serve as a foundation for further research on multidrug resistance.

Evolutionary and Spatiotemporal Dynamics of Foot-and-Mouth Disease Virus in Ethiopia (1957-2025): A Molecular Perspective on Serotype Persistence and Emergence.
Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) represents a significant global economic burden and remains the primary constraint on Ethiopia's livestock economy and international trade. This desk review synthesized 60 years of data (1957-2025) using a structured, multidatabase search across four domains: disease, genotype/lineage, geographic spread, and temporal context. Data were stratified into three periods: Period I (1957-1980), Period II (1981-2000), and Period III (2001-2025). Results indicate that Period I saw the identification of serotypes O, A, and C, though serotype C has not been detected after 1983. Period II was marked by the continued circulation of serotypes O and A, and the first emergence of Serotype SAT 2 near the Kenya-Ethiopia border, which temporarily disappeared until its major re-emergence in 2007. Period III is characterized by a significant intensification and modernization of FMD virus (FMDV) outbreak investigation that provided more granular data on viral activity in the country. The period saw four major endemic serotypes O, A, SAT 2, and SAT 1, SAT one being confirmed for the first time during this period, circulate simultaneously and covering the entire country. Molecular analyses revealed a heterogeneous landscape: serotype O is dominated the serotype distribution in the country by its O/EA-3 and O/EA-4 topotypes, while serotype A involving complex lineages (Africa G-I, G-IV, and G-VII) follows in serotype O and precedes serotype SAT 2 in distribution. Notably, serotype SAT 2 has historically comprised four topotypes (IV, VII, XIII, and XIV), with the recent dominance of the re-emergent SAT 2/XIV topotype. The global biosecurity threat posed by FMDV SAT 2 topotype XIV stems from its unprecedented transcontinental dissemination into immunologically naive regions, rather than inherent lethality. This expansion highlights the complex evolutionary dynamics of the virus and the vulnerability of current surveillance system. The global dissemination of emerging lineages, such as SAT 2 topotype XIV, underscores the complex evolutionary dynamics and environmental plasticity inherent across all FMDV serotypes. The rapid shift of these viruses into nonendemic territories highlights critical vulnerabilities in existing biosecurity. Ultimately, these dynamics necessitate a shift toward adaptive, multiserotype surveillance and integrated control frameworks to address the continuous antigenic evolution and geographical expansion of the virus. Advancing Ethiopia along the progressive control pathway (PCP-FMD) is critically contingent upon evaluating the protective efficacy of current trivalent vaccines against rapidly evolving field strains. Immediate intervention is required to address diverged genotypes that jeopardize both national herd health and international market access.

Live Attenuated Vaccines for African Swine Fever: Perspectives on Their Use and Strategic Directions.
African swine fever (ASF) continues to cause substantial economic and production losses in affected countries. Although biosecurity and conventional control measures remain essential, the challenges of ASF control underscore the need for safe and effective vaccines as additional tools, particularly in endemic settings. Live attenuated vaccines (LAVs) are the most advanced ASF vaccine platform, providing the most consistent protection to date and remaining the only ASF vaccines to reach commercial deployment. Field experience with licensed products has shown encouraging safety, immunogenicity, and disease-control outcomes. However, the introduction and spread of recombinant genotype I/II strains may reduce vaccine effectiveness and contribute to limited vaccine uptake. Together with the detection of vaccine-like variants of uncertain origin, these issues have generated contrasting perspectives: a precautionary view focused on risks associated with replication-competent vaccine viruses, and a benefit-risk view emphasizing the consequences of continued ASFV circulation without effective vaccination. This review contrasts these perspectives, draws lessons from other live vaccines, and frames the responsible use of ASF LAVs within a benefit-risk approach. Experience with human and veterinary LAVs shows that persistence, transmission, genetic instability, reversion to virulence, and recombination are inherent biosafety concerns of LAVs, yet such vaccines remain important when alternative platforms do not provide equivalent protection. Their use therefore requires identifying, monitoring and minimizing residual risks in relation to expected benefits. Accordingly, ASF LAVs should be avoided in ASF-free regions but may be justified in endemic settings when licensed products are used within coordinated programs integrating adequate coverage, biosecurity, surveillance, and molecular monitoring. Future vaccine development should focus on improving safety in growing pigs and breeding animals, broadening protection against emerging ASFV strains, validating DIVA tools and developing safer next-generation platforms, while continued reassessment ensures that vaccine use remains appropriate to epidemiological conditions, emerging evidence, and disease-control needs.

Early African Swine Fever Dynamics in Wild Boar After Reemergence in Catalonia, Spain: Surveillance-Based Estimates of Initial Spread.
African swine fever (ASF) reemerged in free-ranging wild boar in Catalonia, northeastern Spain, in November 2025, representing the first detection in Spain since 1994. We described the initial outbreak phase using surveillance data collected from 25 November 2025 to 23 February 2026. ASF virus (ASFV) positivity by real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) was estimated overall and by surveillance stream; mortality timing was reconstructed probabilistically from estimated death-date intervals; and early front displacement was analyzed using leading-edge cumulative minimum convex polygons (MCPs), linear and generalized additive models (GAMs), segmented regression, and directional modeling. Among 1483 wild boars with definitive qPCR results, 201 were ASFV qPCR-positive, giving an overall qPCR positivity of 13.6% (95% confidence interval [CI] 11.9-15.4). Positivity was substantially higher in enhanced passive than in active surveillance (28.2% vs. 0.9%; positivity ratio [PR] 32.11, 95% CI 15.21-67.78; p < 0.001). A probabilistic cumulative mortality curve based on 198 positive carcasses indicated that, by the date of the first detected carcass, expected cumulative mortality had already reached 25.8 deaths (13% of reconstructed total mortality). Leading-edge analysis estimated an apparent mean radial front-displacement rate of 0.042 km/day (95% CI 0.029-0.055). The surveillance-derived distance-time relationship was nonlinear, indicating that the apparent front-displacement rate varied over the study period, with a segmented-regression breakpoint at 119 days and higher apparent front-displacement thereafter (0.106 vs. 0.021 km/day). The exploratory directional analysis indicated the fastest predicted advance toward the South-Southwest sector. These surveillance-derived estimates describe the observed leading edge under the surveillance and control conditions operating during the study period and should not be interpreted as direct estimates of ASFV transmission speed. These findings support an adaptive, risk-based response that prioritizes carcass search and removal and incorporates directional spread information to refine surveillance and zoning as the outbreak evolves. The analytical framework, combining reconstruction of estimated dates of death with simple descriptors of early epidemic spread, may support early epidemiological assessment of ASF incursions in other newly affected settings.

Investigation of deaths from ill-defined causes and probable scarlet fever outbreak among schoolchildren, São João del-Rei, 2023.
OBJECTIVE: To investigate deaths from ill-defined causes and a probable scarlet fever outbreak among schoolchildren in São João del-Rei between September and October 2023. METHODS: This was a descriptive study of children hospitalized with sepsis symptoms and a case series of schoolchildren with pharyngotonsillitis and scarlet fever. Data from medical records and interviews were used to calculate absolute frequencies and measures of central tendency. RESULTS: Six healthy children (1-10 years old, of White/mixed race skin color) were hospitalized with sepsis symptoms, presenting fever, purpura, bruising, and odynophagia. Streptococcus sp. was identified in oropharyngeal swabs in three of the six children, but blood cultures were negative. Three children died, three were discharged, and two attended the same school. Among the schoolchildren, 873 records of absenteeism were identified; of these, 212 met the definition of pharyngotonsillitis and 87 were interviewed. Of the 87,7 also met the criteria for scarlet fever, 47 were female, and 78 were aged 5-13 years. Symptoms included malaise (62/87), throat plaques (49/87), and body rash (26/87). Antibiotics (58/75) and analgesics/antipyretics (32/75) were prescribed for treatment. During renovations at the school, small poorly ventilated adapted containers were used as classrooms. Twelve students did not use individual drinking glasses, and 53/87 did not use masks when symptomatic. CONCLUSIONS: Suspected invasive streptococcal disease deaths were caused by septic shock, without confirmation of the etiological agent. Streptococcus sp. may have contributed to the probable scarlet fever outbreak. Recommendations were made to alert the population and professionals about hygiene practices and staying away from school, in addition to training health teams to diagnose and manage re-emerging diseases.

WHO statement on notification of withdrawal of the United States
WHO regrets the United States’ notification of withdrawal from WHO – a decision that makes both the United States and the world less safe. The notification of withdrawal raises issues that will be considered by the WHO Executive Board at its regular meeting starting on 2 February and by the World Health Assembly at its annual meeting in May 2026. As a founding member of the World Health Organization (WHO), the United States of America has contributed significantly to many of WHO’s greatest achievements, including the eradication of smallpox, and progress against many other public health threats including polio, HIV, Ebola, influenza, tuberculosis, malaria, neglected tropical diseases, antimicrobial resistance, food safety and more. WHO therefore regrets the United States’ notification of withdrawal from WHO – a decision that makes both the United States and the world less safe. The notification of withdrawal raises issues that will be considered by the WHO Executive Board at its regular meeting starting on 2 February and by the World Health Assembly at its annual meeting in May 2026. WHO takes note of statements from the government of the United States that say WHO has “trashed and tarnished” and insulted it, and compromised its independence. The reverse is true. As we do with every Member State, WHO has always sought to engage with the United States in good faith, with full respect for its sovereignty. In its statements, the United States cited as one of the reasons for its decision, “WHO failures during the COVID-19 pandemic”, including “obstructing the timely and accurate sharing of critical information” and that WHO “concealed those failures”. While no organization or government got everything right, WHO stands by its response to this unprecedented global health crisis. Throughout the pandemic, WHO acted quickly, shared all information it had rapidly and transparently with the world, and advised Member States on the basis of the best available evidence. WHO recommended the use of masks, vaccines and physical distancing, but at no stage recommended mask mandates, vaccine mandates or lockdowns. We supported sovereign governments to make decisions they believed were in the best interests of their people, but the decisions were theirs. Immediately after receiving the first reports of a cluster of cases of “pneumonia of unknown cause” in Wuhan, China on 31 December 2019, WHO asked China for more information and activated its emergency incident management system. By the time the first death was reported from China on 11 January 2020, WHO had already alerted the world through formal channels, public statements and social media, convened global experts, and published comprehensive guidance for countries on how to protect their populations and health systems. When the WHO Director-General declared COVID-19 a public health emergency of international concern under the International Health Regulations on 30 January 2020 – the highest level of alarm under international health law – outside of China there were fewer than 100 reported cases, and no reported deaths. In the first weeks and months of the pandemic, the Director-General urged all countries repeatedly to take immediate action to protect their populations, warning that “the window of opportunity is closing”, “this is not a drill” and describing COVID-19 as “public enemy number one”. In response to the multiple reviews of the COVID-19 pandemic, including of WHO’s performance, WHO has taken steps to strengthen its own work, and to support countries to bolster their own pandemic preparedness and response capacities. The systems we developed and managed before, during and after the emergency phase of the pandemic, and which run 24/7, have contributed to keeping all countries safe, including the United States. The United States also said in its statements that WHO has “pursued a politicized, bureaucratic agenda driven by nations hostile to American interests”. This is untrue. As a specialized agency of the United Nations, governed by 194 Member States, WHO has always been and remains impartial and exists to serve all countries, with respect for their sovereignty, and without fear or favour. WHO appreciates the support and continued engagement of all its Member States, which continue to work within the framework of WHO to pursue solutions to the world’s biggest health threats, both communicable and noncommunicable. Most notably, WHO Member States last year adopted the WHO Pandemic Agreement, which once ratified will become a landmark instrument of international law to keep the world safer from future pandemics. Member States are now negotiating an annex to the WHO Pandemic Agreement, the Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing system, which if adopted will promote rapid detection and sharing of pathogens with pandemic potential, and equitable and timely access to vaccines, therapeutics and diagnostics. We hope that in the future, the United States will return to active participation in WHO. Meanwhile, WHO remains steadfastly committed to working with all countries in pursuit of its core mission and constitutional mandate: the highest attainable standard of health as a fundamental right for all people.

Timor-Leste certified malaria-free by WHO
The World Health Organization (WHO) has certified Timor-Leste as malaria-free, a remarkable achievement for a country that prioritized the disease and embarked on a concerted, nation-wide response shortly after gaining independence in 2002. “WHO congratulates the people and government of Timor-Leste on this significant milestone,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. “Timor-Leste’s success proves that malaria can be stopped in its tracks when strong political will, smart interventions, sustained domestic and external investment and dedicated health workers unite.” With today’s announcement, a total of 47 countries and 1 territory have been certified as malaria-free by WHO. Timor-Leste is the third country to be certified in the WHO South-East Asia region, joining Maldives and Sri Lanka which were certified in 2015 and 2016 respectively. Certification of malaria elimination is granted by WHO when a country has proven, beyond reasonable doubt, that the chain of indigenous transmission has been interrupted nationwide for at least the previous three consecutive years. “We did it. Malaria has been one of our most relentless enemies – silent, persistent, and deadly. We lost too many lives to a disease that should be preventable. But our health workers never gave up, our communities held strong, and our partners, like WHO, walked beside us. From 223 000 cases to zero – this elimination honours every life lost and every life now saved. We must safeguard this victory with continued vigilance and community action to prevent malaria's re-entry,” said Dr Élia António de Araújo dos Reis Amaral, SH, Minister of Health, Government of Timor-Leste. A rapid shift from high burden country to malaria-free Since gaining independence in 2002, Timor-Leste has made remarkable strides in the fight against malaria – reducing cases from a peak of more than 223 000 clinically diagnosed cases in 2006 to zero indigenous cases from 2021 onwards. Timor-Leste’s success in eliminating malaria was driven by the Ministry of Health’s swift action in 2003 to establish the National Malaria Programme, a dedicated programme for planning, implementing, and monitoring malaria control efforts nationwide. With only two full-time officers initially, the programme was able to lay the foundation for progress early on through strong technical leadership, managerial capacity and attention to detail. Within a few years, the country introduced rapid diagnostic tests and artemisinin-based combination therapy as part of the National Malaria Treatment Guidelines and began distributing free long-lasting insecticide treated nets to communities most at risk. In 2009, with support from the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria, Timor-Leste scaled up nationwide vector control efforts through the distribution of long-lasting insecticide-treated nets and indoor residual spraying. Malaria diagnosis was also expanded using microscopy and rapid diagnostic tests at the point of care across all local health posts. Facing the challenges of severe shortages of health workers and doctors, Timor-Leste made investments and developed its three-tier health system – comprising national hospitals, reference hospitals, community health centers (CHCs), and health posts – to ensure most residents can access care within an hour's walk. Additionally, citizens are provided with free health services at the point of care, as part of the government’s policy on free universal health care. Monthly mobile clinics and community outreach programmes further enhance health services in rural areas. Timor-Leste’s success in combating malaria highlights the importance of country leadership and strong collaboration between the Ministry of Health, WHO, local communities, non-governmental organizations, donors, and multiple government sectors. A real-time integrated case-based surveillance system ensures rapid data collection and response, while trained health workers ensure timely detection and screening of malaria cases, including at borders. These integrated efforts have paved the way for the country to be officially certified malaria-free. "Timor-Leste’s malaria-free certification is a defining national triumph – driven by bold leadership, tireless efforts of health workers, and the resolve of its people. As a young nation, Timor-Leste stayed focused – testing, treating, and investigating swiftly. Ending transmission and maintaining zero deaths takes more than science; it takes grit. This victory protects generations, present and future, and shows what a determined country can achieve,” said Dr Arvind Mathur, WHO Representative to Timor-Leste. Note to the editor WHO malaria-free certification The final decision on awarding a malaria-free certification is made by the WHO Director-General, based on a recommendation by the Technical Advisory Group on Malaria Elimination and Certification and validation from the Malaria Policy Advisory Group. More on WHO’s malaria-free certification process .

African Union and World Health Organization renew strategic partnership to drive impact and strengthen health systems in Africa
The World Health Organization (WHO) and the African Union (AU) Commission renewed their longstanding strategic partnership today with the signing of an updated Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on the sidelines of the 78th World Health Assembly in Geneva. This renewed agreement reaffirms the joint commitment to advancing health security, universal health coverage, and sustainable development across the African continent at a time of unprecedented financial challenges in the global health landscape. It further underscores the African Union’s leadership in fostering collective action, inclusive partnerships, and regional resilience, and positions the Department of Health, Humanitarian Affairs, and Social Development of the AU Commission at the heart of the continent’s health policy implementation efforts. The agreement was signed by Her Excellency Ambassador Amma Adomaa Twum-Amoah, Commissioner for Health, Humanitarian Affairs and Social Development, on behalf of His Excellency Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Chairperson of the African Union Commission, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. It marks a defining moment for primary health care and universal health coverage. Commissioner Twum-Amoah emphasized the strategic importance of the agreement and the AU’s leadership in shaping Africa’s health landscape: “This Agreement marks a new chapter in AU–WHO cooperation. By working together more closely, we can better respond to the health needs of our populations and ensure that no one is left behind. The African Union values WHO’s central and leading role in global health and looks forward to deepening this strategic partnership in support of our shared goals. We need to move from budgeting for survival to planning for health sovereignty,” she added. Building on the foundation of the 2019 MoU, the renewed agreement streamlines and strengthens collaboration across all AU entities. It aligns efforts in support of Africa’s health priorities and sets the stage for enhanced cooperation between WHO and the AU. It also reaffirms WHO’s central technical and normative leadership role in global and regional health, and its commitment to supporting the AU and its institutions in achieving health-related Sustainable Development Goals. “This renewed agreement comes at a critical time, as cuts to bilateral aid imperil the health of millions in Africa,” said Dr Tedros. “It reflects our determination to translate our partnership into tangible results for the people of Africa, and support countries to leave behind the era of aid dependency and transition to sustainable self-reliance. We are proud to stand with the African Union in driving forward the health priorities of the continent.” The Memorandum outlines five key areas of collaboration: health systems strengthening : including regulatory harmonization, support for local pharmaceutical manufacturing, traditional medicine, domestic health financing, workforce development, and digital health innovation; reproductive, maternal, neonatal, child, and adolescent health (RMNCAH) : with continued support for the Campaign on Accelerated Reduction of Maternal Mortality in Africa (CARMMA Plus 2021–2030) and advancement of the reviewed Addis Ababa Declaration on Immunization (ADi); disease prevention and control : supporting the implementation of AU frameworks on communicable and noncommunicable diseases, including efforts to end AIDS, tuberculosis, and malaria; eliminate neglected tropical diseases (NTDs); and address the burden of viral hepatitis in line with WHO strategies; nutrition and food security : strengthening the nutrition agenda through implementation of the Africa Nutrition Strategy 2015–2025 and related WHO strategies; and health in emergency settings : by strengthening joint responses to humanitarian crises, conflicts, and climate-related emergencies. The timing of the renewed agreement is significant. It reflects the African Union’s elevated voice in global health governance – bolstered by its G20 membership – and highlights WHO’s ongoing key role as a trusted technical and operational partner. The renewed MoU marks new momentum for regional and multilateral cooperation to address Africa’s most pressing health challenges and deliver meaningful, lasting results on the continent. Frank, in-depth discussion as Belgium and WHO map ahead priorities for collaboration
In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies. The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape. In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies. The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape. The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe. "After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together." Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success. Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation. Universal Health Coverage (UHC) Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care. The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas. WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. The Canadian underage substance use prevention (CUSP) trial: Amended protocol for a hybrid effectiveness-implementation cluster randomized trial of PreVenture.
BACKGROUND: Adolescent substance use remains a significant public health concern, particularly among youth with elevated personality-based risk profiles. PreVenture is a brief, personality-targeted intervention shown to reduce substance-related behaviours in prior randomized trials. OBJECTIVE: The Canadian Underage Substance Use Prevention (CUSP) trial was designed to evaluate the effectiveness and implementation of PreVenture under routine school conditions. METHODS: CUSP is a three-arm, parallel-group, hybrid effectiveness-implementation cluster randomized controlled trial in public secondary schools across three Canadian provinces. Schools were randomized to: (1) PreVenture via a Train-the-Trainer model; (2) PreVenture Train-the-Trainer plus Implementation Facilitation; or (3) treatment-as-usual control. Grade 10 students completed baseline screening using the Substance Use Risk Profile Scale (SURPS); those scoring above predefined SURPS thresholds were invited to participate in PreVenture workshops and included in primary analyses. The primary outcome is screening positive for substance-related problems (CRAFFT score ≥ 2). Secondary outcomes include binge drinking, cannabis, illicit drug, and non-medical prescription drug use. Implementation outcomes include fidelity, reach, uptake, acceptability, and sustainability. CONCLUSIONS: Data collection is complete, but outcome analyses have not yet been conducted. The trial was affected by the COVID-19 pandemic and other implementation challenges, resulting in substantial attrition at both the student and school levels. This protocol documents modifications to the design and analytic plan, also reflected in the updated trial registration (NCT04198974), to ensure transparent reporting of findings. The pre-specified Statistical Analysis Plan, provided as an online supplement, was finalized and accepted by the trial steering committee prior to unblinding. In this study, we screened a library of 2,620 small molecules enriched for reported inhibitory activity against cellular and viral helicases to identify phenotypic inhibitors of a biologically contained virus, Ebola∆VP30 virus, in Vero cells stably expressing VP30 protein. Seven compounds significantly reduced virus titers at least 100-fold with minimal cytotoxicity and demonstrated low IC50 values. Two of these compounds completely inhibited EbolaΔVP30 virus infection, interfering with either virus entry or replication. Although these preliminary screening hits require further optimization and in vivo validation, their identification opens new avenues for anti-Ebola virus drug discovery.

External Ventricular Drainage for Refractory Intracranial Hypertension in Traumatic Brain Injury: Efficacy, Safety, and Outcomes.
INTRODUCTION: External ventricular drainage (EVD) is commonly used to manage refractory intracranial hypertension following traumatic brain injury (TBI), yet its efficacy, timing, and prognostic value remain uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate the short-term efficacy of EVD in controlling intracranial hypertension in TBI patients. PATIENTS AND METHODS: We conducted a retrospective, observational, single-center study including consecutive adult patients with TBI who underwent EVD placement for refractory intracranial hypertension between 2020 and 2024. Demographic, clinical, radiological, surgical, and ICP data were collected. Trauma severity was assessed using the ISS and the SOFA score. EVD efficacy was defined as a sustained reduction in mean ICP below 20 mmHg for at least 24 hours. Functional outcome was assessed at 1 year using the Glasgow Outcome Scale (GOS). RESULTS: Fifty-three patients were included (51±18 years; 75% male). Median ICP significantly decreased after EVD placement (30 [25-35] vs. 15 [10-35] mmHg; p<0.01). Sustained ICP control was achieved within the first 24 hours in 25 patients (47%), whereas 28 (53%) did not reach control, including 8 patients (29%) with transient improvement. Patients with uncontrolled ICP had higher pre-EVD ICP values and greater injury severity scores. Normal basal cisterns were more frequent in the controlled group. One-year mortality was 70%, and 32% of the patients with controlled ICP had a GOS 4 at 12 months. EVD-related complications occurred in four patients (8%). CONCLUSION: EVD significantly reduces ICP in selected TBI patients, but sustained control occurs in fewer than half of cases and appears associated with baseline injury severity. Prospective studies are needed.

Effect of Relaxation Techniques Combined With Cognitive Behavioural Therapy on Depression, Anxiety and Quality of Life Among Pulmonary Tuberculosis Patients in Northern Ethiopia: Multicentre Cluster Randomized Controlled Trial.
OBJECTIVE: Depression and anxiety are prevalent among subjects with pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB), especially in lower-middle-income countries. CBT and RT are widely recognized psychological interventions. The study aimed to assess the effect of Relaxation Techniques (RT) combined with Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) on depression and anxiety symptoms and quality of life among patients with PTB. METHODS: A multicentre cluster randomized controlled trial was employed among participants. Hospitals were randomly divided into two equal groups using a computer-generated algorithm. The intervention had seven sessions lasting for 3 months. Outcomes were measured at baseline, 7-week and 3-month post-randomization for both groups with the same measures. A Linear Mixed-Effect Model (LMM) was utilized for data analysis, with 95% CI and p value < 0.05. RESULTS: A total of 121 samples were included in the final analysis. The LMM findings indicated a significant Group*Time interaction across all outcomes (p < 0.001). At 3-month follow-up, the RT-CBT group demonstrated reduced depression scores compared with the control group (Mean difference (MD) = -4.95, 95% CI: -6.98, -2.92, p < 0.001; Cohen's d = -0.93). Significant reductions were also observed in anxiety scores among RT-CBT groups (MD = -3.62, 95% CI: -4.30, -2.92, p < 0.001; Cohen's d = -1.14). Similarly, participants in the intervention group compared to control had greater improvements in quality of life (MD = 16.21, 95% CI: 12.93, 19.47, p < 0.001; Cohen's d = 1.08) and treatment adherence (MD = 2.40, 95% CI: 1.84, 2.96, p < 0.001; Cohen's d = 0.93). CONCLUSION: The study demonstrated that RT-CBT is effective for decreasing depression and anxiety and promoting improvements in quality of life and treatment adherence for individuals with PTB attending treatment follow-up. The results support the integration of RT-CBT into routine tuberculosis treatment clinics. TRIAL REGISTRATION: The trial has been registered on 'Pan African Clinical Trials Registry' with trial number: PACTR202412822674360, registered on December 24, 2024, available at https://pactr.samrc.ac.za/.

Molecular detection of pathogens in Rhipicephalus ticks collected from companion animals in Bejaia province, northern Algeria.
Ticks are increasingly recognized as important vectors of pathogens affecting animals and humans worldwide. In northern Algeria, data on tick-borne pathogens (TBPs) in ixodid ticks collected from companion animals are still scarce. This pilot study is the first molecular investigation of TBPs in ixodid ticks collected from companion animals in Bejaia province, bordering the Mediterranean Sea. A total of 100 ticks were collected from 75 dogs, 11 cats, and one tortoise. Rhipicephalus sanguineus was the predominant tick species identified (99/100; 99%; 95% CI: 94.0-100.0), whereas a single tick collected from the tortoise was identified as Hyalomma aegyptium (1/100; 1%; 95% CI: 0-6.0). Ticks were tested for Rickettsia spp., Bartonella spp., Anaplasma phagocytophilum, Ehrlichia canis, Piroplasmida, and Hepatozoon spp. Only Rickettsia spp. (11/100; 11%; 95% CI: 6.1-18.8), Hepatozoon spp. (6/100; 6%; 95% CI: 2.5-12.7) and Piroplasmida (2/100; 2%; 95% CI: 0.1-7.4) were detected. Rickettsia spp. (11/88; 12.5%; 95% CI: 7.0-21.2) and Piroplasmida (2/88; 2.3%; 95% CI: 0.1-8.4) were found only in ticks from dogs, while Hepatozoon spp. was found in both ticks from dogs (3/88; 3.4%; 95% CI: 0.8-9.7) and cats (3/11; 27.3%; 95% CI: 9.2-57.1). Further molecular characterization revealed R. massiliae and R. conorii, as well as H. canis, Babesia vogeli, and Cytauxzoon spp. Phylogenetic analysis supported species identification. These findings highlight the presence of TBPs in ticks from companion animals and their potential relevance to One Health, particularly for zoonotic Rickettsia spp.

The detection paradox: How COVID-19 surveillance patterns shifted from lower-income to more affluent neighborhoods in Miami-Dade County.
Passive disease surveillance systems may systematically undercount burden in low-resource minority neighborhoods, yet fine-scale evidence of this phenomenon remains limited. We examined spatiotemporal patterns of reported COVID-19 cases across Miami-Dade County's diverse neighborhoods and investigated which socioeconomic and demographic characteristics predicted areas of elevated and suppressed case rates. In an ecological, cross-sectional analysis of 491,769 geocoded cases across 1,831 census block groups from March 2020 to May 2021, we applied negative binomial regression with spatial eigenvector filtering and Getis-Ord Gi* hot spot analysis across five pandemic periods aligned with major policy shifts. The analysis revealed a detection paradox. Early hot spots concentrated in lower-income census block groups (median household income: $52,022-$55,676), but by September 2020, hot spots had shifted to more affluent areas (median: $77,069). Historically Black neighborhoods along the I-95 corridor emerged as persistent cold spots despite multiple structural risk factors: lower incomes, reduced insurance coverage, and limited healthcare access. From Period 3 onward, predominantly Black census block groups showed significantly lower reported rates (incidence rate ratio [IRR]: 0.991-0.995, p < 0.001). Household overcrowding was tested but retained in no final model. These paradoxical patterns suggest that as testing expanded, surveillance increasingly tracked healthcare utilization rather than transmission. What appeared as neighborhood "protection" likely reflected barriers to testing access shaped by transportation constraints, work schedule inflexibility, and historical relationships with medical institutions. Census block group analysis revealed these dynamics obscured at broader geographic scales. The findings challenge the assumption that reported case rates approximate true disease burden and have direct implications for emergency response planning: surveillance systems require complementary detection streams, risk-adjusted monitoring for underdetection, and targeted outreach where poverty and limited access to testing are concentrated but reported rates are low.

Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and control measures on type 2 diabetes care among South Asians: the perspective of healthcare providers in British Columbia, Canada.
BACKGROUND: British Columbia is one of the most ethnically diverse provinces in Canada, with South Asians emerging as one of the fastest-growing ethnic minority groups, burdened by a high incidence of type 2 diabetes. During the COVID-19 pandemic, many healthcare services shifted to virtual care to minimize infection transmission. Given the limited understanding of how primary care physicians in BC adapted their diabetes care approaches and the consequent impact on patient experience, this qualitative study aims to explore the effects of pandemic-related control measures on primary care diabetes services in BC from the perspectives of general practitioners, focusing particularly on their South Asian patients. METHODS: We conducted semi-structured interviews with ten primary care physicians serving large South Asian patient populations. Interviews explored the pandemic's effects on care delivery, provider adaptations, and consequences for South Asian patients with diabetes. Sessions were held in person or via Zoom/Teams and transcribed verbatim. Transcripts underwent thematic content analysis to identify recurring themes and insights regarding barriers, adaptations, and recommendations to improve diabetes care. FINDINGS: The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted diabetes care, shifting services to virtual care and interrupting routine monitoring. This transition impacted specific aspect of diabetes care that can best be provided in-person (e.g., foot examinations, blood pressure checks and lifestyle counselling). The pandemic compounded existing issues, e.g., cost, concerns with side effects, and medication compliance among South Asian patients. Physicians also observed a general rise in anxiety and depression during the pandemic among their patients. Older South Asian patients faced additional cultural, language, and digital barriers; physicians struggled to obtain timely Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) tests. For many patients, a significant reliance on pharmacists embedded within certain physician's clinics, ensured an uninterrupted access to diabetes medication and supplies. CONCLUSION: The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted diabetes care, with some groups facing additional cultural, language, and digital barriers. Our findings highlight the need for primary care reforms: improved telemedicine and EMR infrastructure, and policies to support virtual care. Bridging the digital divide and implementing targeted supports are essential to minimize care disruption for vulnerable populations during future pandemics or similar crises and ensure equity.

Mindful Awareness and Stress Associations Among People Living With the Effects of Stroke and their Partners: Findings From a Daily Diary Study.
OBJECTIVE: Stroke is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality, significantly affecting the health of individuals post stroke and their partners. Both people living with the effects of stroke (PLWS) and their partners experience elevated stress. Therefore, this daily diary study examined day-to-day variations in stress and its association with mindful awareness as a potential protective factor against stress within and between PLWS and their partners. METHODS: Eighty-six community-dwelling couples (67±10 y old, 50% female) in Canada, with one partner living with the effects of stroke, reported their daily stress, their partners' stress, and their own mindful awareness every evening for up to 14 days. RESULTS: Distinguishable dyads models showed that individuals reporting that their partners felt more stressed (daily and overall), and whose partners felt more stressed (daily and overall) reported more daily stress themselves. In contrast, when individuals reported more mindful awareness (daily and overall), they reported less daily stress. PLWS also reported less daily stress when their partners reported more overall mindful awareness. However, this dyadic association was not found in the other direction or for daily mindful awareness. CONCLUSIONS: Results suggest dyadic associations of daily stress between partners and indicate that mindful awareness may reduce daily stress within individuals. Within the dyad, PLWS seemed to benefit from their partners' mindful awareness. Results highlight the significant role of the partner for PLWS and emphasize the need to consider how interpersonal dynamics vary, particularly in couples managing medical conditions. REGISTRATION: The study was preregistered at OSF (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/XTV2H).

Mental Health Burden and Vulnerability Among Long-Term Care Facility Residents During the COVID-19 Pandemic: A Systematic Review With Exploratory Prevalence Meta-Analysis.
BackgroundOlder adults in long-term care facilities (LTCFs) faced social and care disruptions during COVID-19, but evidence on mental health burden and vulnerability remains fragmented.ObjectiveTo synthesise evidence on mental health outcomes among LTCF residents during the pandemic and identify resident- and facility-level vulnerability and protective conditions.MethodsMEDLINE, Embase and PsycINFO were searched for English-language peer-reviewed studies published from January 2020 to January 2025. Findings were narratively synthesised, and exploratory random-effects meta-analyses were conducted where at least three studies reported extractable resident-level prevalence.ResultsThirty-two studies were included as follows: 24 quantitative, six qualitative and two mixed-methods. Most reported high prevalence, deterioration, or qualitative evidence of depression, anxiety, loneliness, isolation, or related distress. Pooled prevalence was 55.6% for depression, 51.4% for anxiety and 54.5% for loneliness, with substantial heterogeneity. Vulnerability reflected clinical, social and facility-level factors; consistent staffing, social connection and family communication were potential protective conditions.

CRISPR/Cas13a-Based Nucleic Acid-Functionalized Discrete Floating-Gate Field-Effect Transistor for Amplification-Free Rapid Nipah Virus Detection.
Nipah virus (NiV) is a highly lethal zoonotic pathogen, and existing rapid diagnostic tools are scarce and reliant on nucleic acid amplification. In this study, we designed and fabricated a thin-film field-effect transistor with an IGZO channel and, for the first time, combined a discrete AuNP floating gate with the CRISPR/Cas13a system to achieve amplification-free detection of NiV. A pair of partially complementary nucleic acid reporter probes was used to attach AuNPs onto the channel, forming a nucleic acid-functionalized discrete floating gate. Under positive gate voltage, the AuNPs electrostatically induce mirror charges in the IGZO channel, amplifying the sensing signal. Additionally, the electrons can be injected from AuNPs into the channel via the Fowler-Nordheim tunneling effect under negative gate voltage, as a potential complementary sensing mechanism. The AuNPs are immobilized via nucleic acid strands, ensuring good biocompatibility. CrRNA was designed and the CRISPR system was optimized for compatibility with the FET, achieving amplification-free detection of NiV standards down to 10° copies/μL within 10 min. This study not only provides a reliable and rapid detection tool for NiV but also establishes a biosensing framework applicable to other pathogens.

Genotypic and phylogenetic characterization of Salmonella Minnesota ST548 strains with potential risk to public health.
Salmonella Minnesota ST548 has emerged as an important serovar in the poultry industry and has been detected in food products. Five nonclonal S. Minnesota isolates from poultry in southeastern Brazil were characterized using whole-genome sequencing (WGS), and 263 database sequences were analyzed for virulence genes, antimicrobial resistance genes, and phylogenetic relationships. Among the analyzed sequences, 191 multidrug-resistant (MDR) strains carried antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) conferring resistance to aminoglycosides (aac(6')-Iaa, aph(3')-Ia and aadA1), quinolones (qnrB19), tetracycline (tetA), sulfonamides (sul2), and beta-lactams (blaCMY-2, blaCTX-M-8, blaCTX-M-55 and blaTEM-126). Furthermore, several genes associated with virulence factors were identified, including adherence (faeC, faeE, and fimB), fimbrial adherence determinants (pegA, staA, fimA, and csgD), magnesium uptake (mgtB and mgtC), macrophage inducible genes (mig-14), toxin (cdtB) and secretion system (ssaM, sseE and sseJ). Twenty-five plasmid replicons and 53 distinct prophages were identified in the analyzed sequences. Phylogenetic analysis showed close relationships between nonclonal S. Minnesota poultry isolates from southeastern Brazil and S. Minnesota sequences associated with human outbreaks from other sources and countries. These findings highlight the need for surveillance of this serovar in both public and veterinary health.

Antimicrobial susceptibility of E. coli isolated from dairy cow milk in Egypt and antibacterial activity of selected nanomaterials against MDR strains.
Escherichia coli (E. coli) is a significant livestock and foodborne pathogen. This study was designed to isolate E. coli from raw cow milk, evaluate its antimicrobial susceptibility, and investigate the antimicrobial activity of silver nanoparticles (nAg), zinc oxide nanoparticles (nZnO), and Moringa nano-emulsion (MNE) against multidrug resistant (MDR) strains. A total of 146 individual milk samples were obtained from dairy cows in Egypt. E. coli were isolated by standard culture methods and pathotyped using molecular techniques. The antibiotic resistance of the isolates was determined, and the antimicrobial activity of the selected nanomaterials was evaluated using the broth microdilution method on the identified MDR strains. E. coli was detected in 54.8% (80/146) of the samples; 42 out of 80 (52.5%) were virulent strains, including STEC (15/42; 35.7%), ETEC (12/42; 28.57%), EPEC (12/42; 28.57%), and AE-STEC (3/42; 7.1%). The isolated strains showed the highest resistance rate to sulfa-trimethoprim (52.5%), tetracycline (45%), and ampicillin (42.5%); and the lowest against marbofloxacin (8.75%) and ceftiofur (27.5%). Overall, 42.5% of the E. coli strains exhibited MDR, including virulent and non-virulent strains at 45.2% (19/42) and 39.47% (15/38), respectively. The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) values against MDR E. coli isolates were lowest for nAg (1.56-12.5 µg/mL), followed by nZnO (12.5-50 µg/mL).
