BACKGROUND: The global spread of extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Enterobacterales in livestock poses critical threats to human and animal health, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. This study investigated the prevalence, antibiotic resistance profiles, and genetic determinants of ESBL-producing Enterobacterales in healthy chickens from poultry farms in Grand-Abidjan and Korhogo, Côte d'Ivoire, alongside antibiotic use practices in the sector. METHODS: A semistructured questionnaire assessed veterinary practices across 26 farms, whereas chicken fecal samples from 27 farms were screened for third-generation cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales. Phenotypic and genotypic characterization of ESBL producers was performed, along with antimicrobial susceptibility testing against 12 antibiotics. RESULTS: All farmers reported antibiotic use, primarily tetracyclines (76.9%), macrolides (69.2%), polymyxins (61.5%), aminoglycosides (57.7%), and sulfonamides (53.8%), mainly for disease prophylaxis (65.38%) and often without veterinary supervision. ESBL-producing Enterobacterales were detected in 96.3% (26/27) of fecal samples, yielding 90 isolates identified as clinically relevant species: Klebsiella pneumoniae (42.2%, 38/90), Escherichia coli (38.9%, 35/90), and Enterobacter spp. (18.9%, 17/90). Overall, 74.8% (63/90) of isolates were resistant to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and 57.8% to amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, whereas no resistance to carbapenems was observed. Molecular characterization revealed the presence of bla CTX-M, bla SHV, and bla TEM genes, with bla CTX-M being the most prevalent (77.8%, 70/90), followed by bla SHV (54.4%, 49/90) and bla TEM (31.1%, 28/90). These genes were coexpressed in half of all isolates, predominantly in K. pneumoniae and Enterobacter spp. CONCLUSION: This study highlights the widespread dissemination of ESBL-producing Enterobacterales in poultry farms in Côte d'Ivoire, emphasizing the role of poultry as a reservoir for resistant bacteria and underscoring the urgent need for integrated surveillance and antimicrobial stewardship within a One Health framework.

Beware the Muscle: Silent Exercise-Induced Aminotransferase Elevation as a Diagnostic Pitfall in Hepatology and Pretreatment Screening-A Report of Two Cases.
BACKGROUND: In clinical hepatology practice, pretreatment liver enzyme screening plays a key role in making management decisions, such as initiation of antituberculosis therapy or surveillance of chronic hepatitis B. Unrecognized extrahepatic sources of aminotransferase elevations can lead to misdiagnosis, inappropriate treatment alteration, and unnecessary invasive or costly investigations. CASE PRESENTATION: We present two cases of active young males who were undergoing liver biochemical testing for therapeutic decision-making for other underlying illnesses. Patient one was undergoing baseline liver enzyme testing prior to first-line antituberculosis treatment initiation while patient two was undergoing surveillance for e-antigen-negative hepatitis B infection. Both patients had asymptomatic aminotransferase elevations mimicking acute hepatocellular injury. There was a marked and disproportionate elevation of aspartate aminotransferase (AST) relative to alanine aminotransferase (ALT), in the setting of otherwise normal cholestatic and synthetic parameters. Targeted history revealed heavy resistance weight training prior to testing. Measurement of serum creatine kinase (CK) confirmed exercise-induced muscle injury, demonstrating elevated CK concentrations that paralleled the AST trajectory. Cessation of strenuous training led to rapid normalization of aminotransferases and a decline in CK levels, without interruption of tuberculosis management or unwarranted antiviral initiation. CONCLUSION: Clinically silent exertional muscle injury is an underappreciated mimicker of acute liver injury. In patients presenting with isolated or disproportionate AST elevation, confirming a myogenic enzyme source via CK quantification can prevent misdiagnosis, eliminate unnecessary liver-directed workup, and avoid inappropriate modification or initiation of essential pharmacotherapy.

Molecular epidemiology and resistance mechanisms of carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacilli in a referral hospital in Lima, Peru.
BACKGROUND: Carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacilli (CR-GNB) represent a significant public health threat, as they are associated with high mortality in healthcare settings. Carbapenemase production is the predominant resistance mechanism, and horizontal gene transfer drives the rapid dissemination of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to characterize the phenotypic and genotypic AMR profiles of CR-GNB isolated from patients at Arzobispo Loayza National Hospital (Lima, Peru) between October 2021 and January 2022. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional study and collected clinical and epidemiological data from patients with bacterial infections. MALDI-TOF identified pathogens, and antimicrobial susceptibility was interpreted according to CLSI guidelines. A subset of isolates underwent whole-genome sequencing (Illumina) to determine genomic resistance markers. RESULTS: A total of 159 patients were included (median age = 54 years; 66.7% male); 72.3% had confirmed clinical infections, and 66% were admitted to the ICU. The most frequent infection types were pneumonia, urinary tract infection and bacteraemia. Overall, 97.5% of isolates were classified as XDR. Carbapenem resistance approached 100% (imipenem 99.4%, meropenem 98.7%). Whole-genome data revealed clonal diversity among Klebsiella pneumoniae (ST13/ST15) carrying bla NDM-1; Acinetobacter baumannii uniformly harboured bla OXA-23; and Pseudomonas aeruginosa included high-risk clones ST357 (bla IMP-93) and ST111 (bla IMP-18, bla VIM-2). CONCLUSIONS: These findings demonstrate a critical burden of XDR-GNB and the presence of multiple carbapenemases (NDM, IMP, KPC and VIM) associated with clinically relevant high-risk lineages. Strengthening molecular surveillance, optimizing antimicrobial stewardship and reinforcing infection-control measures are urgently needed to contain CR-GNB in critical-care settings in Peru.

Nationwide Q Fever Hospitalizations in Italy, 2014-2023: Evidence of Underrecognition and a Sardinian Hotspot.
BACKGROUND: Q fever is a zoonotic disease caused by Coxiella burnetii. In Italy, serologic evidence shows exposure in humans and livestock, but surveillance data are sparse, and underreporting is likely. We aimed to characterize Q fever-related hospitalizations in Italy during 2014-2023 and examine environmental risk correlates. METHOD: We conducted a nationwide retrospective study using the Italian National Hospital Discharge Database. Hospitalizations with ICD-9-CM code 083.0 as primary or secondary diagnosis were included. We calculated hospitalization rates by age, sex, and region and described clinical characteristics. We linked hospitalizations with climatic, livestock, and land-use data; for Sardinia, we fitted Bayesian spatial regression models including bovine, ovine, and caprine density, temperature, precipitation, and land use. RESULTS: We identified 428 hospitalizations (67% male), corresponding to a rate of 0.07 per 100 000 person-years. Rates were highest in children and older adults. The overall case fatality ratio was 2.4%. The most frequent Q fever-related concomitant diagnosis was pneumonia. Sardinia had the highest case count and adjusted hospitalization rate, 7-fold the national rate (0.55 vs 0.07). Spatial models for Sardinia showed hotspots in the north of the island and a 12% increase in spatial hospitalization risk per 10 bovine heads/km2 (adjusted relative risk 1.12, 95% credible interval 1.03-1.24). CONCLUSIONS: Q fever causes an underrecognized burden of hospitalizations in Italy, with marked regional heterogeneity and a Sardinian hotspot associated with high cattle density areas. Clinical awareness, surveillance, and One Health interventions are warranted in high-risk areas.

Global, regional and national burden of pertussis in 1990-2023: a Global Burden of Disease study.
Despite long-standing immunization programs, pertussis remains a major cause of vaccine-preventable mortality, particularly among infants. Here we present a primary assessment of global pertussis incidence, mortality and disability-adjusted life years across 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023. We show that despite short-term pandemic-period fluctuations, the dominant global pattern from 1990 to 2023 was long-term decline: age-standardized mortality decreased by 61.2% and age-standardized incidence by 41.6%. Relative to the anomalously low pandemic-period estimates, incidence and mortality rebounded by 102.6% (95% uncertainty interval, 77.0-128.2%) and 66.1% (95% uncertainty interval, 2.4-174.5%), respectively, between 2020 and 2023. In 2023 alone, we estimated 18.9 million cases and 115,000 deaths attributable to pertussis. This burden remains profoundly inequitable and inversely correlated with the sociodemographic index; sub-Saharan Africa now accounts for roughly 65% of global deaths, with the highest population-adjusted risk concentrated among infants younger than 6 months. Our findings highlight a modeled geographic concentration of pertussis mortality and support strengthening timely infant vaccination, maternal immunization where recommended and feasible and robust surveillance in highly susceptible regions.

Analysis of the impact of naturally-acquired immunity on Shigella vaccine performance to inform clinical trials: A simulation-based modeling study.
BACKGROUND: Effective vaccines against Shigella, the leading bacterial cause of diarrheal disease globally, could prevent morbidity and mortality from shigellosis as well as limit antibiotic resistance. Several Shigella vaccine candidates are in late stages of development, and the design of large Phase 3 trials in target populations is underway. In high incidence settings, children are expected to rapidly accrue natural immunity such that after repeated pathogen exposure, unvaccinated infants may have similar levels of immunity as vaccinated infants. For this reason, in these settings estimates of vaccine efficacy (VE) may underestimate expected efficacy in a fully naïve population. To set expectations and support optimal planning of future Shigella vaccine trials, we aimed to quantify the potential impact of this phenomenon on VE estimates under different surveillance strategies and assumptions about Shigella immunity. METHODS AND FINDINGS: We simulated Shigella vaccine trials in low-, medium-, and high-burden settings under different assumptions about vaccine- and infection-conferred immunity. We estimated VE against severe, Shigella-attributable disease and any Shigella-attributable diarrhea under six trial designs: active surveillance for Shigella infection or symptom-based reporting paired with single-outcome, stratified recurrent outcome, or crude recurrent-outcome Cox proportional hazards models. In each scenario, we evaluated bias, 95% confidence interval (CI) coverage, and the false negative rate. Only the trial design using active surveillance for infection and single outcome models was consistently unbiased across all examined scenarios. The other five designs underestimated VE by up to an absolute 20%, with a single outcome model paired with symptom-based reporting performing least poorly. Bias generally was worse at higher-burden sites. For realistically sized trials, the 95% CI coverage and false negative rate were also worse at higher-burden sites. The results were sensitive to input parameters which depended on assumptions about Shigella natural history based on limited published data. CONCLUSIONS: The observed VE in Shigella vaccine trials is likely to underestimate true VE, though the magnitude of underestimation described here is conditional on the simulation's inputs and assumptions. Careful trial design is needed to minimize this underestimation.

Initial empiric carbapenem versus non-carbapenem β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor therapy in sepsis across simplified SENECA phenotypes: a retrospective study of two independent cohorts.
PURPOSE: Whether initial empiric carbapenem therapy is associated with better outcomes than non-carbapenem β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor (BL/BLI) therapy in sepsis remains uncertain. We examined this association overall and across simplified Sepsis Endotyping in Emergency Care (SENECA) phenotypes. METHODS: This retrospective study included 4,091 patients from MIMIC-IV and 405 patients from a single-center hospital cohort. Initial therapy was defined by the first eligible carbapenem or BL/BLI regimen initiated within 24 h of admission. The primary outcome was 28-day mortality. Secondary outcomes included selected clinical and in-hospital microbiological detection outcomes. Each cohort was analyzed separately using inverse probability of treatment weighting and weighted logistic regression. RESULTS: After weighting, no overall association with lower 28-day mortality was observed in MIMIC-IV (OR 0.91, 95% CI 0.71-1.17) or the hospital cohort (OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.48-1.16). However, evidence of treatment-by-phenotype interaction was observed in both cohorts (P for interaction = 0.039 and 0.019, respectively), with lower odds of 28-day mortality among patients with the γ phenotype in MIMIC-IV and the hospital cohort (OR 0.66, 95% CI 0.44-0.97, and OR 0.13, 95% CI 0.04-0.46, respectively). A similar direction was observed among mechanically ventilated patients. In MIMIC-IV, carbapenem therapy was associated with longer hospitalization and more frequent detection of fungal organisms and Clostridioides difficile; these associations were not observed in the hospital cohort. CONCLUSION: Initial empiric carbapenem therapy was not significantly associated with lower 28-day mortality overall. Consistent findings in the γ phenotype suggest possible treatment heterogeneity. These findings should be considered alongside patient characteristics and potential clinical and microbiological trade-offs.

A multivalent CPS-CRM197 conjugate vaccine protects against severe/fatal Klebsiella pneumoniae disease in a mouse infection model.
Klebsiella pneumoniae is an important cause of human infections and is often resistant to multiple antibiotics. Most infections occur in individuals with co-morbidities and/or those who have risk factors for infection. Although progress has been made, new therapeutics and preventive measures are needed. To that end, we developed a mouse model of severe/fatal K. pneumoniae infection (intraperitoneal inoculation that leads to bacteremia) to evaluate strain virulence and test protection conferred by a multivalent CPS-conjugate vaccine. We first compared the virulence of four clinical isolates representative of important K. pneumoniae clones globally (ST23/KL1, ST86/KL2, ST11/KL64, and ST147/KL64), each of which harbors a virulence plasmid. The ST11 and ST147 isolates are additionally multidrug resistant, including resistance to carbapenem antibiotics. Compared with ST23 and ST86 isolates, the ST11 and ST147 isolates were less virulent in the mouse infection model. Moreover, numbers of viable ST11 and ST147 organisms recovered from blood decreased over time, whereas those of ST23 and ST86 increased. As a step toward evaluating the ability of a CPS-CRM197 conjugate vaccine to protect against lethal infection, we immunized CD-1 outbred mice with a cocktail of eight selected CPS conjugates, boosted them twice, and then challenged those mice with one of the two most virulent isolates (ST23/KL1 or ST86/KL2) by intraperitoneal inoculation. Mice receiving the CPS-CRM197 conjugate vaccine were protected against lethal infection caused by KL1 and KL2 isolates, whereas all sham-immunized mice developed fatal disease within 96 h. These results underscore the potential of a standard CPS-conjugate approach for development of a multivalent K. pneumoniae vaccine.

Expanding threat of carbapenemase-producing Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae in Peru: genomic and phenotypic evidence of high-risk clones dissemination.
Carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales represent a growing global threat due to their extensive antimicrobial resistance and rapid dissemination. This study characterized the phenotypic and genomic features of Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates collected between 2020 and 2022 from four healthcare institutions in Lima, Peru. A total of 320 non-redundant isolates (61 E. coli and 259 K. pneumoniae) were analyzed through antimicrobial susceptibility testing, polymerase chain reaction, and whole-genome sequencing. The most frequent carbapenemase gene was blaNDM (69%), followed by blaKPC (16.9%) and blaOXA-48-like (4.6%). Eleven K. pneumoniae isolates co-produced NDM and KPC, and one E. coli isolate co-harbored NDM and OXA-48-like. All isolates were multidrug-resistant, and 5% were resistant to all agents included in the routine panel; however, aztreonam/avibactam and cefiderocol retained complete in vitro activity among tested isolates. Novel β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations such as aztreonam/avibactam and cefiderocol showed complete activity against all classes of carbapenemases. Genomic analysis revealed predominant E. coli sequence types ST167 and ST410 and K. pneumoniae lineages ST147, ST15, ST45, and ST273. The blaNDM-5 allele was detected for the first time in Peru, mostly in E. coli ST167, and was carried on multireplicon IncF-type plasmids. In K. pneumoniae, ST147 was identified as a dominant clone associated with blaNDM-1, indicating sustained local dissemination of high-risk clonal groups. The coexistence of multiple carbapenemases and plasmid backbones highlights the ongoing evolution of resistance mechanisms. This work provides the first integrative genomic overview of carbapenemase-producing E. coli and K. pneumoniae in Peru and underscores the need for continuous genomic surveillance and antimicrobial stewardship to mitigate their clinical and epidemiological impact.

Group A Streptococcus in an Unexpected Site: Temporal Pyomyositis in 2 Children.
BACKGROUND: Pyomyositis is an uncommon bacterial infection of skeletal muscle. Group A Streptococcus (GAS) accounts for a smaller proportion of pediatric cases, and temporal muscle involvement is exceptionally rare. CASE DESCRIPTION: We report 2 previously healthy children, a 7-year-old boy and a 6-year-old girl, who presented with acute otitis media (AOM) and painful unilateral temporomandibular swelling. Computed tomography revealed AOM with temporal myositis, complicated by mastoiditis in the first case. Both were treated with intravenous antibiotics, and the first case required drainage and mastoidectomy, with full recovery. GAS was isolated in both cases. CONCLUSIONS: GAS temporal pyomyositis should be considered in children presenting with AOM and painful temporal swelling. Imaging is crucial for diagnosis and assessment of disease extent. Surgical management should be individualized.

Purification and mechanistic characterisation of bacillomycin D homologues from Bacillus velezensis PD9 with antibiofilm activity against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.
Antimicrobial resistance continues to undermine treatment of multidrug-resistant infections, necessitating new antimicrobial agents with distinct mechanisms of action. Bacillus velezensis PD9 (BvPD9), isolated from Heterotrigona itama propolis, produces antibacterial lipopeptides; however, the active bacillomycin D homologues and their mechanisms remain insufficiently characterised. Here, an optimised extraction and chromatographic purification workflow was developed, enabling selective enrichment of two bioactive fractions putatively assigned by LC-TOF-MS/MS as C14-enriched bacillomycin D and a C14/C15-bacillomycin D homologue mixture. The C14-enriched bacillomycin D fraction exhibited selective activity against Staphylococcus spp. and vancomycin-sensitive Enterococcus faecium (VSEF), with minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of 16-32 µg/mL, whereas the C14/C15 homologue mixture demonstrated broader antibacterial activity against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and selected ESKAPE pathogens (Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterobacter spp.) (MICs 16-512 µg/mL), with the lowest MIC (16 µg/mL) observed against VSEF. Both compounds retained activity following heat exposure (40-80 °C), wide pH variation (4-12), and proteolytic enzymes. The C14/C15 homologue mixture was prioritised for further evaluation because of its broader antibacterial spectrum and displayed concentration-dependent inhibition of biofilm formation, membrane permeabilisation, and ultrastructural alterations, together with changes in bacterial DNA-content distribution without detectable direct DNA binding. Preliminary safety evaluation demonstrated concentration-dependent haemolysis and cytotoxicity at higher concentrations, while zebrafish embryos showed concentration-dependent mortality with an LC50 of 109.54 µg/mL at 120 hpf. Serial passaging resulted in a four-fold MIC increase only during the final passages, whereas chloramphenicol showed no detectable MIC change under the same conditions. Overall, the findings demonstrate antibacterial and membrane-associated activities of PD9-derived bacillomycin D-enriched fractions and provide a basis for further investigation of individually purified homologues.

Travel-associated Staphylococcus aureus infections: a global perspective from the GeoSentinel Surveillance Network.
BACKGROUND: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global health threat, and Staphylococcus aureus is among the leading contributors to the global AMR-attributable disease burden. Data on the clinical presentation and antimicrobial susceptibility patterns of Staphylococcus aureus infections in returning travellers remain scarce. METHODS: We described the clinical presentation, travel characteristics, and antimicrobial susceptibility of travellers and migrants diagnosed with Staphylococcus aureus infection through the GeoSentinel network between January 2014 and December 2022. Because no consensus definition exists for travel-associated infections, we included all cases recorded in the GeoSentinel database as travel-associated. We evaluated patients during travel or after return. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) was performed according to routine laboratory practice at participating sites. RESULTS: We retrieved 740 travellers and migrants with Staphylococcus aureus infection diagnosed at 50 GeoSentinel sites. Four hundred thirty-eight (59.2%) were male, and the median age was 32 years (IQR 23-48). The most frequently visited regions were Southeast Asia, sub-Saharan Africa, and South-Central Asia. Most patients presented after travel (576/740; 77.8%). Skin and soft tissue infections were the predominant diagnosis (670/740; 90.5%), and most patients were managed as outpatients (579/740; 78.2%). Overall, 406/740 (54.9%) isolates showed resistance or reduced susceptibility to at least one antimicrobial class, including methicillin (224/656; 34.1%), lincosamides (144/627; 23.0%), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (129/597; 21.6%). Demographic characteristics and hospitalization frequency were similar between patients with MSSA and MRSA infections. CONCLUSIONS: Most Staphylococcus aureus infections in international travellers presented as skin and soft tissue infections and were managed in outpatient settings. Resistance or reduced susceptibility to at least one antimicrobial class was common, with one-third of isolates identified as methicillin-resistant. These findings support the importance of AST to guide management of skin and soft tissue infections in internationally mobile populations and reinforce the need for standardized definitions of travel-associated bacterial infections and continued global surveillance.

Solving the Staphylococcus aureus puzzle: lessons to guide future MRSA vaccine development.
SUMMARYThe broad-spectrum use of antibiotics allows for the development of resistance in symptomatically and asymptomatically carried pathogenic bacteria. Antibiotic-resistant bacteria, with this review focusing on Staphylococcus aureus, cause significant morbidity and mortality and put considerable strain on the global healthcare system. In a vaccinated individual, bacteria are less likely to develop resistance mechanisms compared to an individual treated with antibiotics, highlighting a potential method for conserving antibiotic use. However, despite over a century of research, a S. aureus vaccine candidate is yet to progress past phase III clinical trials, and to develop a successful S. aureus vaccine, the shortcomings of previous attempts require critical analysis. After consideration of the five most successful S. aureus vaccine programs, it is identified in this review that future attempts should (i) be polyvalent to circumvent immune evasion, (ii) include carefully chosen antigens to avoid maladaptive memory, (iii) include T cell targeting to provide a comprehensive immune response, (iv) utilize multiple measures of preclinical efficacy in pre-exposed models, and (v) implement considered clinical study design, including appropriate vaccine formulation for the target population. By combining these attributes, such as in the form of epitope-based or nanoparticle vaccines, there is a promising future for the development of S. aureus vaccines that circumvent the issues that caused the downfall of previous vaccine programs, thereby protecting the global population from development toward a future where bacteria are resistant to all antibiotic treatments.

Wildlife-associated ecosystems in Algeria harbor internationally distributed ESBL-producing clones and plasmids, including a CTX-M-15 Klebsiella pneumoniae ST17 lineage associated with a conserved IncFIB(K) resistance plasmid.
UNLABELLED: Expanded-spectrum cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales (ESC-R-E) have disseminated beyond clinical settings, but their occurrence and genomic epidemiology in wildlife remain poorly characterized, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. ESC-R may result from the production of extended-spectrum β-lactamases (ESBLs) or AmpC-type cephalosporinases. We investigated the prevalence, resistance mechanisms, and population structure of ESC-R-E in free-ranging wildlife, captive wild animals, and zoo workers in Algeria. Between October 2021 and June 2023, 1,899 fecal samples were collected across six Algerian provinces. ESC-R-E isolates were recovered by selective culture and characterized by antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and whole-genome sequencing. Overall, 73 ESC-R-E isolates (3.9%) were identified, including seven OXA-48-like carbapenemase co-producers (0.4%). Carriage was significantly higher in captive animals (13.5%) than in free-ranging wildlife (1.6%) or zoo workers (7.7%). Among the 66 ESBL-producing isolates analyzed, CTX-M enzymes predominated (n = 61), particularly CTX-M-15 (n = 53). Klebsiella pneumoniae was the predominant species (n = 33), with ST17 accounting for 27/33 isolates. Closely related CTX-M-15-producing ST17 isolates were recovered from captive animals, free-ranging wildlife, and a zoo worker and carried an IncFIB(K) plasmid harboring blaCTX-M-15 within a multidrug resistance region closely related to globally disseminated plasmids. Globally disseminated high-risk Escherichia coli clones were also detected, namely ST167, ST361, ST410, and a persistent ST38 lineage in Algerian wildlife since 2016. These findings demonstrate the circulation of high-risk Enterobacterales lineages and mobile resistance plasmids in Algerian wildlife-associated ecosystems and highlight the need for integrated One Health surveillance of antimicrobial resistance at the human-animal-environment interface. IMPORTANCE: Wildlife is increasingly recognized as a potential reservoir and sentinel for antimicrobial resistance, yet genomic data from low- and middle-income countries remain scarce. This study provides one of the largest genomic investigations of expanded-spectrum cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales in wildlife from North Africa. We demonstrate that internationally disseminated high-risk Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli lineages, together with globally distributed CTX-M-15-carrying plasmids, are circulating among captive animals, free-ranging wildlife, and humans in zoological environments. The recovery of closely related K. pneumoniae ST17 isolates from different host species highlights the potential for antimicrobial resistance dissemination across the human-animal-environment interface. These findings extend the known ecological range of clinically important resistant Enterobacterales beyond healthcare settings and identify wildlife-associated ecosystems as part of the broader antimicrobial resistance network. Our study underscores the value of integrating wildlife into One Health surveillance programs to better understand and mitigate the environmental spread of antimicrobial resistance.

Targeting the proteasome in Leishmania donovani: developments from preclinical to Phase I and II trials.
INTRODUCTION: Visceral leishmaniasis (VL), a neglected tropical disease caused by Leishmania donovani and L. infantum, which affects poor areas of South Asia, East Africa, and Brazil, and is fatal if left untreated. Current treatments, including liposomal amphotericin B, miltefosine, paromomycin, and pentavalent antimonials, are limited by emerging resistance, high cost, cold storage, and need for parenteral administration. These drawbacks of the currently available therapy entail the development of a safe, short, and oral therapy for VL treatment. AREA COVERED: This review summarizes current knowledge of the Leishmania 20S proteasome as a therapeutic target, as it maintains protein homeostasis and exhibits structural variances from the human proteasome that allow selective, parasite-specific inhibition. It covers the preclinical story of GSK3494245 to the story of proteasome inhibitors, especially LXE408, which has progressed from Phase I evaluation to Phase II clinical trials in India and Ethiopia. Collectively, these results place proteasome inhibition as a promising clinical approach that may revolutionize the VL treatment. EXPERT OPINION: Proteasome inhibitors provide strong antiparasitic activity, high selectivity and a potential for oral treatment. If the ongoing clinical trials show safety, efficacy and durable cure rates, proteasome-targeting drugs will revolutionize VL therapy and be a model for drug development against other neglected tropical diseases.

Burnout Syndrome in Palliative Care Professionals: A Systematic Review of Prevalence, Associated Factors, and Coping Strategies.
This systematic review aims to evaluate the prevalence of burnout, its associated determinants, and the coping strategies employed by palliative care professionals. Burnout, characterized by emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and diminished personal accomplishment, poses a significant threat to clinician well‑being and the quality of care delivered to patients with life‑limiting illnesses. A comprehensive search of PubMed and Embase identified eleven eligible studies published between 2021 and 2025. Following thematic synthesis, four overarching themes were identified: (1) work-related stress: heavy workloads, emotional demands and lack of support, (2) burden of burnout: the unique stressors facing palliative care professionals, (3) impact of the COVID-19 pandemic: increased workloads and exposure to high-risk environments, and (4) coping strategies: symptom recognition and etiological factors, organizational support and resilience factors. CONCLUSION:: Burnout remains a pervasive challenge in palliative care, and sustained, evidence‑based organizational strategies are essential to protect clinician well‑being and ensure high‑quality patient care. Future research should determine the long‑term effectiveness of these interventions and assess whether tailored approaches are required for specific professional groups and care settings.

Unmasking healthcare disparities: the underreporting of gender, race, and ethnicity data in high-impact factor minimally invasive surgery journals.
BACKGROUND: Diverse representation in clinical research is essential for equitable healthcare. Despite mandates from organizations like the NIH and ICMJE, race and gender remain underreported in surgical research, raising concerns about the generalizability of findings. This study examines demographic reporting trends in minimally invasive surgery (MIS) and advanced endoscopy publications before and after the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. METHODS: A systematic review of Surgical Endoscopy, Journal of Robotic Surgery, and Surgical Innovation was conducted, analyzing articles published between January 1, 2018, and December 31, 2023. 472 studies were included. For each study, study type, journal, date, geographic origin, and reported demographic data were recorded. Reporting rates across time periods (pre- vs. post-March 2020), region of origin, study design, and journal were analyzed via Chi-square, Fisher's exact tests, and Cochran-Armitage trend tests. RESULTS: Of the 472 studies, 61.2% were randomized controlled trials, with geographic representation from Asia (37.7%), Europe (34.8%), and North America (22.3%). Only 21 North American studies (20 U.S., 1 Canada) reported race; no studies from Asia or Europe did so. Among U.S. studies, race reporting did not differ significantly pre- vs. post-COVID (22.2% vs. 21.8%; p = 0.25), nor did gender reporting (p = 0.07). Regional differences in U.S. race reporting were significant (p = 0.003), with the Midwest having the lowest rate. Post-2020, gender reporting was significantly higher in Asia (94.9%) compared to Europe (84.7%) and North America (80.9%) (p = 0.005). CONCLUSIONS: Demographics remain underreported in MIS and advanced endoscopy research, particularly outside North America. Despite increased attention to health equity during the COVID-19 pandemic, reporting practices have not significantly improved. Broader adoption of standardized demographic reporting is needed to ensure evidence-based surgical care for all populations.

Observation versus maintenance immunotherapy after PD-1-induced clinical complete response in dMMR/MSI-H colorectal cancer managed non-operatively: a multicenter cohort study.
BACKGROUND: Whether maintenance immunotherapy is necessary after clinical complete response (cCR) to programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) inhibition in mismatch repair-deficient/microsatellite instability-high colorectal cancer remains unclear. We evaluated its associations with survival and treatment-related toxicity. METHODS: This multicenter cohort study included patients treated at five hospitals in China between January 2018 and March 2025 who achieved cCR after PD-1 inhibitor therapy and entered non-operative management. All patients underwent endoscopy and site-appropriate cross-sectional imaging to confirm cCR; 62.0% also underwent biopsy. Patients were categorized into observation and maintenance groups according to whether they received maintenance immunotherapy after cCR, defined as at least two additional treatment cycles. The primary endpoint was disease-free survival (DFS) from cCR; secondary endpoints were overall survival (OS), locoregional regrowth, distant metastasis, and treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs). Overlap weighting addressed measured confounding, with 6-week landmark and strict per-protocol analyses assessing robustness. RESULTS: Among 318 patients treated with PD-1 inhibitors, 173 (54.4%) achieved cCR; 129 (74.6%) entered non-operative management (observation, n=66; maintenance, n=63), while 44 underwent surgery. The analytic cohort included 58 patients with a single rectal primary, 61 with a single colon primary, and 10 with synchronous colorectal primaries; 115 (89.1%) had stage I–III disease. Median follow-up from cCR was 32.2 months (IQR 20.4–44.4). Both locoregional regrowths occurred in the observation group within 2 years after cCR; both patients underwent salvage treatment and remained alive. No distant metastases occurred, and the only death was due to COVID-19 without recurrence. 3-year DFS was 96.2% with observation and 98.3% with maintenance (log-rank p=0.508); corresponding OS was 100.0% and 98.3% (p=0.321). Overlap weighting did not materially alter the DFS comparison (p=0.192), and sensitivity analyses yielded similar estimates. Across the entire treatment and follow-up, any TRAE was numerically more frequent in the maintenance group than in the observation group (65.1% vs 59.1%); 15.9% of patients in the maintenance group experienced grade ≥2 TRAEs during maintenance therapy. CONCLUSIONS: Findings suggest that discontinuation after cCR may be reasonable within a watch-and-wait strategy for rectal cancer and provide preliminary support for non-operative management of colon cancer; prospective validation is warranted.

Protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis of long influenza following the last five influenza pandemics.
INTRODUCTION: Influenza pandemics have been evaluated in terms of acute disease, while giving limited attention to long-term consequences. Renewed interest in postviral conditions following the COVID-19 pandemic highlights the need to reassess earlier influenza pandemics from a long-term perspective. This protocol describes a forthcoming systematic review and meta-analysis examining long-term health outcomes following exposure to five influenza pandemics. The aim is to assess the magnitude, consistency, mechanisms and determinants of postpandemic health outcomes. METHODS AND ANALYSIS: This protocol followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P) 2015 checklist. The planned systematic review and meta-analysis resulting from the protocol will follow the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 checklist. Nine databases were searched using the PEO (Population, Exposure and Outcome) framework. Eligible studies include peer-reviewed quantitative observational and clinical follow-up studies reporting long-term outcomes. Two investigators will independently screen and select studies, extract data and assess quality. Study quality and risk of bias will be evaluated using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) and publication bias will be assessed using Egger’s and Begg’s tests. Narrative synthesis will be conducted before quantitative pooling. Fixed- and random-effects meta-analysis, meta-regression and Bayesian models will be applied to examine heterogeneity across populations, pandemics and outcomes. ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: This systematic review and meta-analysis do not require ethical approval, as it uses data from previously published studies (Head of department e-mail: elno@oslomet.no). The results will be published as a peer-reviewed article. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: This systematic review protocol was registered in PROSPERO under registration number CRD420251267816.

TeleBACK clinical trial: comparing the effectiveness of telerehabilitation and in-clinic physical therapy for patients with chronic low back pain - protocol for a multicentre, pragmatic, individually randomised group treatment trial.
INTRODUCTION: Chronic low back pain (LBP) is a leading cause of disability and healthcare spending in the USA. While physical therapy (PT) has been shown to improve disability and pain as well as decrease the cost of care associated with LBP, only a small portion (<15%) of eligible patients with LBP ever attend PT. These low utilisation rates are likely influenced by logistical barriers to attending visits (eg, transportation, missed work time). Patients with chronic pain may also struggle to attend frequent clinic visits because of their symptoms. Telerehabilitation, which expanded substantially during the COVID-19 pandemic, can potentially address these barriers by allowing patients to receive PT remotely. However, the effectiveness of telerehabilitation for chronic LBP is unclear. METHODS AND ANALYSIS: This multicentre, pragmatic, individually randomised group treatment, non-inferiority clinical trial will compare synchronous, video-based telerehabilitation with standard in-clinic PT in 1000 adults with chronic LBP (≥3 months duration) receiving primary or specialty care across three healthcare systems in Maryland and Utah. Participants will be randomised 1:1 to receive eight PT sessions over 8 weeks via either video conferencing or in-clinic visits and will be assessed at baseline, 3 months, 6 months and 1 year. The primary outcome is 3-month change in LBP-related disability as measured by the Oswestry Disability Index using a non-inferiority margin of 6 points, based on the minimal clinically important difference for this measure. Secondary outcomes include changes in pain intensity, pain interference and physical function, and LBP-related opioid and healthcare utilisation. Exploratory measures include treatment satisfaction and therapeutic alliance. ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: This study was approved by the Johns Hopkins Medicine Institutional Review Boards (IRB), which serves as the single IRB for this study. Once the study is complete, study data will be shared in compliance with guidelines from the Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute. TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: NCT06821607.

Adoption Strategies and Workarounds in the Evolution of Information Infrastructures Integrating Health and Social Care Providers in Scotland: Multimethod Qualitative Case Study of the Key Information Summary.
BACKGROUND: care records are digital technologies designed to support information sharing and care coordination across fragmented health and social care systems. However, adoption and use of these technologies can vary across diverse health and care settings, with users using workarounds and other strategies to meet their specific information needs. In Scotland, the Key Information Summary (KIS) has been in use for over 13 years, sharing key patient information from general practitioners (GPs) with other health and care providers for future care planning. OBJECTIVE: Using the KIS as a case study, this study examines how various adoption strategies and workarounds have shaped the evolution of regional information infrastructures integrating health and social care in Scotland over time. METHODS: This multimethod qualitative study examined the various contextual factors influencing adoption and use of the KIS across diverse health and care settings. Data collection included interviews with KIS users from health and care settings, implementers, and vendors; documentary analysis of user guides, websites, reports, and policies; and observation of multidisciplinary team meetings and technology use. Data analysis involved a hybrid approach. The technology-people-organization-macroenvironment framework was applied to code interview, documentary, and observational data, followed by an inductive analysis informed by science and technology studies theories of information infrastructures, domestication, and workarounds to examine strategies and workarounds for adapting the KIS to local contexts and evolving needs. RESULTS: Data comprised 54 qualitative interviews, 59 documents, 2 websites, and 20 hours of observational field notes collected between April 2024 and March 2025. Findings indicate that adoption of the KIS varied across settings and over time due to misalignment between system design, evolving expectations of integrated care, and national initiatives during the COVID-19 pandemic that repurposed its use. Professional roles and associated information needs shaped differing expectations of what constituted useful information, generating tensions between users who relied on the KIS and GPs responsible for maintaining it. Formal workarounds enabled the extension of the health care-centric infrastructure into nonclinical settings to facilitate information sharing with GPs and, in some cases, supported clinician access to the KIS during system outages. Across settings, informal user-driven repair practices enabled diverse professionals to adopt and realign the KIS with its intended use. CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates how regional information infrastructures integrating health and care evolve incrementally as they become embedded within local routines, practices, and existing systems. Adoption was shaped by professional roles, information needs, and users' capabilities, with formal workarounds extending infrastructures into new settings and informal, user-driven repair practices supporting ongoing use and maintenance. Policymakers and vendors must recognize that workarounds and user-driven repair practices are central to infrastructural growth and sustainability, and understanding these strategies can inform future technology development and innovation.

Effects of prolonged SARS-CoV2 spike protein exposure in long COVID and a mouse model of the disease.
We addressed the question: can the SARS-CoV2 spike protein persist in ACE2+ endothelia in the CNS/other sites and induce a prolonged microvasculature injury syndrome? People who died from COVID-19, with age-matched controls, and people with long COVID with symptoms persisting from 1-5 years, with controls of people who had recovered from COVID-19, were studied. Also compared were WT mice injected with the spike protein sacrificed at day 5 versus 1.5 months. The ACE2+ microvasculature density in the CNS increased 19-fold in the mice exposed to spike for 1.5 months. Human fatal COVID-19 cases showed an ACE2+ CNS density of 13.2/3.9 versus 2.1/0.9 for the controls. Long Covid cases showed an ACE2 microvasculature density of 11.9/3.0 versus 3.5/0.9 for the people who recovered from COVID (each p value < 0.001). Viral spike microvasculature density in the CNS was similar in the fatal COVID-19 cases (6.9/2.1) and mice (7.0/4.0) and in the skin of long-COVID cases (6.0/1.9) and less in people who recovered from COVID-19 (0.9/0.3) (each p < 0.001). Microvasculature collagen 1 deposition was only evident in fatal COVID, long COVID, and in the mice exposed to S1 for 1.5 mo. Thus, SARS-CoV2 spike (S1) protein can persist for months/years with an associated microvasculature pro-inflammatory state and a restrictive fibrosing microangiopathy; and exposure to high dose S1 markedly increases ACE2 endothelial density.

Patient-month modeling for longitudinal blood culture contamination surveillance during a major healthcare-system disruption: a single-center interrupted time-series study.
INTRODUCTION: Blood culture contamination (BCC) is an important diagnostic quality indicator, but crude temporal comparisons may be misleading when repeated sampling within patients is not considered. We evaluated longitudinal changes in BCC rates before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic using patient-month Poisson generalized estimating equations (GEE). METHODS: This single-center retrospective study included blood culture sets obtained at a tertiary hospital in Japan from April 2017 to June 2025. Eligible episodes had at least two sets drawn within 24 h. Interrupted time-series analysis estimated incidence rate ratios (IRRs) for level and slope changes at pandemic and post-reclassification transitions, with the number of sets as an offset and adjustment for seasonality and within-patient correlation. RESULTS: Among 85,955 blood culture sets, 84,213 sets from 41,732 episodes in 23,705 patients were analyzed. Crude BCC rates were 1.05%, 1.55%, and 1.49% in the prepandemic, pandemic, and post-reclassification periods. No significant overall level or slope changes were observed: prepandemic-to-pandemic level-change IRR, 1.23 (95% CI, 0.93-1.62); slope-change IRR, 1.00 (95% CI, 0.99-1.01); pandemic-to-post-reclassification level-change IRR, 0.88 (95% CI, 0.68-1.14); and slope-change IRR, 0.99 (95% CI, 0.98-1.01). Exploratory subgroup analyses suggested setting-specific post-reclassification changes in the intensive care unit. Sensitivity analyses were generally consistent, although the Omicron-era breakpoint analysis suggested sensitivity to breakpoint specification. CONCLUSION: Patient-month Poisson GEE-based analysis showed that crude increases in BCC rates were not accompanied by statistically significant overall level or slope changes after accounting for repeated patient-level sampling and seasonality. Crude BCC trends should therefore be interpreted cautiously in longitudinal microbiology surveillance.

Pandemic Politics: Developing Vaccines in Canada's Anti-vax Heartland.
The COVID-19 pandemic in Saskatchewan is a story of extremes. Through most of 2020, low case numbers, effective policy, and broad agreement among government officials, health care workers, and the public sustained a consensus that strict measures and vaccination offered the best responses; however, that consensus collapsed. The province shifted from a focal point for Canadian vaccine development to a staging ground for an anti-vaccine movement that took root on social media and then in street protests. Premier Scott Moe moved from a pro-vaccine, pro-consensus stance to a confrontational position questioning federal policies, public health measures, and vaccines. Combining traditional news sources, social media, and interviews with residents and VIDO-InterVac researchers, we track this shift. We argue that the pandemic fostered unmoderated social media discourse that overwhelmed collective responses, shaped health policies, and politicized vaccines as pro-government. Influencers inflated the movement's threat and aligned vaccine uptake to trust in science, with significant political consequences.

Applying normalized p-control charts for early detection of local COVID-19 outbreaks.
The COVID-19 pandemic underscored the urgent need for early detection of local outbreaks to enable better resource allocation and effective mitigation. Outbreak identification largely depended on local infection rates, which were highly variable and influenced by daily testing volumes. Effective pandemic management requires accurate, adaptive methods that reflect the dynamic and localized nature of these rates, ensuring timely and appropriate interventions. This study seeks to improve the early detection and localization of COVID-19 outbreaks through Statistical Process Control (SPC) and health data analytics. We propose an adaptive outbreak-detection framework that combines a normalized p-control chart with an Amplitude-based labeler (ABL). For each area and day, the monitored statistic is a standardized positivity-rate score, computed from the observed daily positivity rate, the number of tests performed that day, and an area-specific baseline positivity estimate derived from recent historical observations. This calibration is followed by Phase II sequential monitoring using fixed three-sigma limits on the normalized scale and Western Electric decision rules. The framework accommodates varying daily sample sizes, captures regional interconnectedness, and supports parameter tuning using a temporally ordered train/test design. Accounting for daily testing fluctuations and spatial variability, it enhances the accuracy of local outbreak detection. Compared with the benchmark outbreak-detection methods considered in this study, the proposed framework was evaluated on its ability to predict outbreak onset within the following three days, achieving overall accuracy of 0.81 and averaged precision and recall of 0.83 and 0.79, respectively. Performance was further evaluated using the Fβ-measure, enabling a flexible trade-off between precision and recall depending on the relative cost of errors. SPC-based methods like ours can significantly improve early outbreak detection and localization. In the post-vaccination era, when targeted responses are key to controlling localized spread while avoiding widespread restrictions, health data analytics offer a valuable tool for informed decision-making.

New Nurse Graduate Readiness for Medication Administration Within the Context of the COVID-19 Pandemic.
Medication administration (MA) has significant implications for patient safety. This qualitative descriptive study, using semistructured interviews, explored the MA experiences of nine newly graduated registered nurses (NGRNs) whose undergraduate studies were primarily undertaken during the pandemic. Two themes were identified: work readiness and transitioning. NGRNs felt that pandemic restrictions, including condensed content delivery and delayed clinical placements, led to curriculum concerns and impeded MA learning. NGRNs valued structured hospital graduate programs and the support received from colleagues and preceptors. Longitudinal studies of the career impact of nurses whose education was disrupted during the pandemic are recommended.

Epidemiology of MERS-CoV in Saudi Arabia, 2012-2025: a nationwide surveillance analysis.
BACKGROUND: Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS), caused by MERS coronavirus (MERS-CoV), is a severe zoonotic respiratory illness first identified in Saudi Arabia in 2012. Dromedary camels are the recognised reservoir, with human transmission occurring through animal exposure and, less commonly, person-to-person spread, particularly in healthcare settings. OBJECTIVE: To characterise all laboratory-confirmed MERS-CoV cases reported in Saudi Arabia from September 2012 to August 2025, examine trends across four periods defined by suspected-case definitions, and identify factors independently associated with mortality. METHODS: We analysed laboratory-confirmed cases in the national surveillance database by period and probable infection source. Case-fatality ratios (CFRs), 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and unadjusted odds ratios were calculated. Multivariable logistic regression assessed independent mortality associations using a prespecified model including period, age, sex, and infection source, and a fuller model additionally considering nationality, comorbidities, and pregnancy. Seasonality of primary cases was assessed using an annual harmonic term. RESULTS: Among 2,219 cases, 1,545 (70%) were male, 1,566 (71%) Saudi nationals, and 608 (27%) aged ≥65 years. Overall, 1,211 (55%) were primary cases, including 172 (14%) reporting camel contact; 737 (33%) were healthcare-associated and 271 (12%) household- or community-associated. There were 867 deaths (CFR, 39%; 95% CI, 37%-41%). CFR declined from 65% in the earliest period to 32% in the most recent, although changing testing eligibility and ascertainment limit temporal comparisons. Older adults had the highest crude CFR. In the prespecified model, healthcare-associated infection among patients was associated with higher odds of death (aOR, 1.74; 95% CI, 1.15-2.65), while odds were lower among healthcare workers (aOR, 0.09; 95% CI, 0.05-0.17) and household contacts (aOR, 0.29; 95% CI, 0.18-0.48). No consistent seasonality was observed. CONCLUSIONS: MERS-CoV epidemiology in Saudi Arabia reflects persistent zoonotic spillover, episodic healthcare-associated transmission, and substantial mortality, particularly among older adults. Sustained One Health surveillance, rapid detection, and rigorous infection prevention and control remain essential.

Genomic analysis and antimicrobial resistance profiling of Klebsiella pneumoniae clinical isolates from urinary tract infections in India: prevalence of class A β-lactamase with molecular docking and simulation insights.
Urinary tract infections are a major global health concern, with Klebsiella pneumoniae emerging as a prominent multidrug-resistant uropathogen. The increasing prevalence of extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing strains has reduced the effectiveness of β-lactam antibiotics. In this study, 87 clinical K. pneumoniae isolates from India were analysed using whole-genome sequencing, MLST and antimicrobial resistance profiling. β-Lactam resistance was the dominant phenotype, with blaSHV and blaCTX-M identified as the most prevalent class A β-lactamase genes. Molecular docking and 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations were conducted to examine enzyme-antibiotic interactions. Meropenem exhibited the lowest binding affinity with both proteins (-2.695 kcal mol-1 for blaSHV and -1.849 kcal mol-1 for blaCTX-M), forming unstable complexes, particularly with blaCTX-M. These findings highlight the growing challenge of β-lactam resistance and emphasize the need for genomic surveillance and alternative therapeutic strategies against multidrug-resistant K. pneumoniae.

Finding a needle in a haystack: Evaluation of Cartridge-Based Nucleic Acid Amplification Test in comparison with microscopy and culture for diagnosis of Extrapulmonary Tuberculosis - A study from a tertiary care centre, Kerala.
Introduction. Mycobacterium tuberculosis has held an exceptional presence in medical research, especially in recent years (1). While pulmonary infections largely remain the focus of literature and public health initiatives (2), extrapulmonary tuberculosis (EPTB) infections have been gaining prominence due to their increasing prevalence, particularly in populations characterized by a low incidence of tuberculosis (2-4). Although EPTB infections, such as tuberculous meningitis, carry a high mortality risk (5), delays in diagnosis and treatment persist. These delays are driven by their diverse, non-specific clinical presentations, coupled with the variable performance of diagnostic modalities like the Cartridge-Based Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (CBNAAT) (6-10). While general literature regarding the use and efficacy of CBNAAT in diagnosing EPTB exists (2,11-15), studies focusing on its sensitivity and specificity in paucibacillary specimens are an evolving niche (16). Since there is a greater prevalence of paucibacillary EPTB specimens in our setting, where such an analysis has not been conducted, we performed a retrospective study to understand the overarching diagnostic performance of our existing modalities in EPTB specimens. Methods. An observational retrospective study was conducted with the data collected between 2019 and 2022 at a tertiary care centre in central Kerala, India. A total of 105 specimens - categorized as pleural, lymph node, pus, tissue, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), peritoneal and others - from presumptive EPTB cases were included in the study. The samples underwent acid-fast bacilli staining microscopy, liquid culture and CBNAAT utilizing the GeneXpert platform. The results were recorded, and the data were analysed with P<0.05 considered statistically significant. Observations and Results. In the 105 samples collected for the study, 6 (5.7%) were positive on Ziehl-Nielsen staining, 26 (24.8%) samples grew M. tuberculosis complex on liquid culture and CBNAAT detected M. tuberculosis in 16 (15.2%) specimens. The sensitivity and specificity of CBNAAT, with culture as the gold standard, were found to be 50.0 and 96.2%, respectively. The sensitivity and specificity of CBNAAT for pus, peritoneal (including tissue and fluid aspirate), pleural fluids, CSF, lymph nodes and other miscellaneous sample types ranged from 33.3 to 100% and 85.7 to 100%, respectively. Among smear-negative specimens, the sensitivity and specificity of CBNAAT were 42.9 and 96.2%, respectively, whereas in smear-positive specimens, the sensitivity increased to 80.0%. Conclusion. CBNAAT is a viable tool for the detection of M. tuberculosis; however, in paucibacillary specimens, its use along with other methods like smear and culture could lead to better identification of the mycobacteria.

A Multifunctional Bacillus-Nanozyme Biohybrid for Control of Tobacco Crown Rot Through Cuproptosis-Like Antifungal Activity and Rhizosphere Regulation.
Tobacco crown rot caused by Fusarium oxysporum is difficult to control because the pathogen persists in soil and disrupts both plant physiology and rhizosphere function. Herein, we developed a multifunctional bacteria-nanozyme biohybrid by immobilizing copper-piceatannol-functionalized mesoporous silica nanoparticles on Bacillus subtilis (BS@MCP). The composite retained bacterial viability while exhibiting peroxidase-like catalytic activity and cuproptosis-like antifungal effects. BS@MCP showed broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity against F. oxysporum, Candida albicans, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and carbapenem-resistant Escherichia coli, with H2O2 further enhancing microbial inhibition. Mechanistic analyses indicated that BS@MCP disrupted fungal membrane integrity, promoted ROS accumulation and lipid peroxidation, increased intracellular copper content, impaired respiratory-chain activity, depleted ATP and induced pyruvate accumulation. Antioxidant and copper-chelation rescue experiments further supported the cooperative involvement of oxidative damage and copper-dependent cell death. In non-sterile soil, BS@MCP/H2O2 reduced the disease index from 91.0% in infected plants to 24.7%, while increasing plant height by 63.5%, root length by 120.7%, fresh biomass by 99.7%, and dry biomass by 225.6%. The treatment enhanced antioxidant and defense-related responses, as well as rhizosphere soil organic matter and total nitrogen. Together, BS@MCP integrates nanozyme-mediated pathogen suppression with microbial biocontrol, host defense activation and rhizosphere improvement, providing a multifunctional strategy for managing soil-borne crop disease.

High-risk antimicrobial resistance genomic traits in multidrug-resistant Salmonella across China's food chain: projections to 2050.
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is rising globally, yet factors shaping its genomic evolution remain poorly understood. We investigated how socioeconomic, climate, and health factors are associated with AMR spread in multi-drug resistant (MDR) Salmonella enterica across China's food chain, mapped hotspots and forecasted genomic trait prevalence to 2050. We analysed 2,536 MDR genomes from 15 provinces over 16 years, covering patients, food and non-food workers, meat, livestock, and environmental sources. A machine learning framework integrated genomic surveillance with risk assessment to identify high-risk AMR traits (clinically relevant, MDR, mobile). Regression models linked trait prevalence to socioeconomic, climate, health, and antimicrobial consumption data, informing projections to 2050. Eighty-four high-risk traits, including carbapenem, colistin, and β-lactam resistance, are projected to rise, with antibiotic use, population growth, healthcare spending, and urbanisation. Projections were trait-specific: blaCTX-M-64 and blaTEM-1 may increase up to 20%, while blaCTX-M-65 and blaCTX-M-14 remain below 5%. A mechanistic shift in fluoroquinolone resistance is projected: mutation-based resistance (gyrA 87) declines while plasmid-mediated genes (qnrB17, qnrS1) rise. Food workers emerged as a potential reservoir, showing higher trait prevalence than food sources, uniquely carrying last-resort antibiotic-resistance genes (blaTEM-30, blaNDM-5, blaCTX-M-64). Integrating genomic with socioeconomic surveillance could shift AMR interventions from reactive to preventive.

The Evolution of Shiga Toxin-Producing Escherichia coli Characterization and Risk Categorization Strategies.
Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) are a group of E. coli that cause food and waterborne enteric illness. STEC are genotypically and phenotypically diverse as they do not have a single evolutionary origin, instead multiple STEC lineages have appeared independently following horizontal gene transfer events. The diversity of STEC is also reflected in an apparent variability in the potential of individual STEC strains to cause severe illness (bloody diarrhea or hemolytic uremic syndrome) or be involved in large foodborne outbreaks. In the context of food safety decision making, the variable characteristics of STEC strains and their potential health outcomes have resulted in an ongoing debate on how STEC should be categorized into risk groups. The aim of this review is to clarify that debate by examining how STEC characterization and risk categorization strategies have evolved over time in response to changes in analytical techniques, understanding of STEC epidemiology, and pathogenicity mechanisms. The origin of established perspectives and practices is explored, from the recognition of STEC O157:H7 as an emerging pathogen in the 1980s, through serotype-based identification and characterization of STEC, to contemporary approaches based on molecular markers for virulence. The evidence for the role of specific virulence factors in STEC pathogenicity is reviewed and their utility in STEC risk categorisation assessed. Finally, a binary categorization scheme is proposed, based on evidence for the correlation of hemolytic uremic syndrome, with the presence of Shiga toxin subtypes Stx2a, Stx2c, Stx2d, and colonisation factors including the Locus of Enterocyte Effacement (intimin/eae) and Enteroaggregative attachment (aggR/aaiC).

Genomic epidemiology of Salmonella from retail chicken meat in Japan: decline in pESI-like plasmid-harboring S. Infantis ST32 and predominance of S. Schwarzengrund ST241.
Salmonella is a major foodborne pathogen, and chicken meat is an important source of infection. This study investigated Salmonella prevalence, serovar distribution, antimicrobial resistance, and genomic characteristics in 150 retail chicken meat samples collected in Japan in 2023. The predominant serovar was S. Schwarzengrund (42.7%), followed by S. Infantis (7.3%), which has long been the predominant serovar in Japan. The globally expanding S. Infantis sequence type (ST) 32 harboring pESI-like plasmids has declined in Japan. In contrast, S. Schwarzengrund ST241 was isolated more frequently in winter (66%) than in summer (31%, P < 0.001) and more often from chicken meat produced in eastern Japan (47.1%) than in western Japan (29.4%, P = 0.042). Antimicrobial resistance was most common to tetracycline (50.6%) and streptomycin (45.7%), whereas kanamycin resistance (33.3%) had declined compared with 2015 to 2019, consistent with reduced use of this antimicrobial in broiler production. Moreover, the proportion of S. Schwarzengrund isolates lacking antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) increased markedly from summer (19.4%) to winter (45.5%). cgMLST analysis revealed that antimicrobial-susceptible S. Schwarzengrund isolates formed the largest clade and, notably, retained pESI-like plasmids despite apparent loss of ARG-containing regions from these plasmids. These findings demonstrate ongoing genomic shifts in Salmonella populations in Japan and underscore the need for continuous genomic surveillance to mitigate their public health impact.

Tracking Illnesses Caused by Four Foodborne Pathogens Over Four Decades of the Healthy People Initiative.
The Healthy People (HP) Initiative, a collaboration between the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and various public and private organizations, aims to improve the health and well-being of all Americans. HP consists of national health objectives with 10-year targets to achieve by the end of the decade. Since HP2000, progress toward goals on four foodborne pathogens (Campylobacter, Listeria monocytogenes, Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli, and Salmonella) has been primarily tracked using data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's Foodborne Diseases Active Surveillance Network (FoodNet). The data used to inform the HP food safety goals spans nearly four decades from 1987 (HP2000) to 2024 (the most recent HP2030 data point). Each decade, measuring foodborne pathogen objectives has become more rigorous and target-setting methods have evolved. HP2000 objectives aimed at a reduction in infections to no more than a set value and, most recently, HP2030 objectives were developed to align with key regulations or targeted a percent improvement in foodborne illness infections. Progress toward these targets has been monitored and categorized (getting worse, no detectable change, improving, or met target) for these pathogens. This article details the advancements made to more accurately establish targets, assess the data, and measure progress at the end or most recent data point of each decade. Each decade, measurement of objectives, baseline-setting methods, target-setting methods, and reporting progress methods have evolved. For this reason, caution must be taken when attempting to compare data across decades.

Epidemiological Characteristics of Pertussis in Hainan Province, 2023-2025.
OBJECTIVE: To analyze the epidemiological characteristics of pertussis in Hainan Province from 2023 to 2025, describe the outbreak trajectory and patterns of population susceptibility, and provide evidence for optimizing pertussis prevention and control strategies. METHODS: Clinically diagnosed and confirmed pertussis cases reported in Hainan Province between January 1, 2023, and December 31, 2025, were retrieved from the China Information System for Disease Control and Prevention; suspected cases were excluded, yielding a total of 2,927 eligible cases.Descriptive epidemiological methods were used to analyze the temporal, geographic, and population distributions of the cases; piecewise linear regression was employed to characterize monthly trends in case counts; and multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify risk factors for hospitalization. RESULTS: The incidence of pertussis in Hainan Province exhibited an outbreak-and-decline pattern from 2023 to 2025, increasing from 4.29 per 100,000 population in 2023 to 22.26 per 100,000 in 2024 before declining to 1.37 per 100,000 in 2025, with a statistically significant difference across the three years (χ2 = 2,888.2, P < 0.001).Piecewise linear regression showed that the monthly number of cases increased significantly during the ascending phase (β = 21.82, P < 0.001) and decreased significantly during the descending phase (β = -11.41, P < 0.001).The age distribution shifted significantly toward older children: the proportion of infants aged <1 year decreased from 43.1% to 27.3%, whereas that of individuals aged ≥1 year increased from 56.9% to 72.7%.Among cases with complete severity records after July 2024, infants aged 0-2 months had the highest risk of hospitalization and accounted for 90.0% of intensive care unit admissions. CONCLUSION: This study shows that the 2024 pertussis outbreak in Hainan was followed by a rapid decline in 2025, with a shift toward older children and a persistently high hospitalization risk in infants aged 0-2 months. These findings support strengthening surveillance in schools and childcare institutions and evaluating the effectiveness of the 6-year DTaP booster policy, while maintaining maternal and infant protection strategies.

Refractory Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome Supported by Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation due to Leptospirosis at Réunion Island and a Literature Review.
Leptospirosis is a zoonosis prevalent on Réunion Island. Severe forms with acute respiratory failure can lead to refractory hypoxemia, requiring the use of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). The aim for the present study was to describe all cases of leptospirosis complicated by refractory acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) requiring veno-venous ECMO on Réunion Island and to conduct a literature review. This retrospective observational study was conducted in a multidisciplinary intensive care unit of the University Hospital of Réunion Island. The aim was to describe the clinical, biological, and prognostic characteristics of patients who developed leptospirosis complicated by refractory ARDS requiring ECMO between January 2011 and December 2024. A total of 14 patients with a median age of 38 years and few comorbidities were included. The organ failure most commonly associated with respiratory involvement was acute kidney injury (93%). The median delay between mechanical ventilation and ECMO support was 0 (0-1) days. The median duration of ECMO support was short (7 [4-12] days). The mortality rate in this population was 29%. A systematic literature review revealed 50 cases of patients with leptospirosis requiring ECMO, with a median age of 34 years and a mortality rate of 20%. The favorable prognosis of patients with refractory ARDS due to leptospirosis justifies the use of ECMO. Early referral to a center equipped with ECMO is essential, given the rapid decline in respiratory function.

Validation of a Rapid Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification-Based Test for the Detection of Shigella from Rectal Swab.
The rapid loop-mediated isothermal amplification-based diagnostic test (RLDT) has been validated as a simple, sensitive, and rapid tool for detecting Shigella spp. from fresh or frozen stool. When stool is unavailable or difficult to transport, rectal swabs (RSs) in Cary-Blair medium, stool collected in buffered glycerol saline (BGS), or stool-dipped swabs (SDSs) in Cary-Blair medium offer alternatives that can be easily collected and transported without maintaining a cold chain. This study evaluated the performance of RLDTs for detecting Shigella spp. from RSs, stool collected in BGS, and SDSs compared with fresh stool (FS). Paired RSs and FS were collected from 105 children younger than 5 years old at two hospitals in Bangladesh. Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and accuracy were determined along with the agreement between assays using kappa statistics. The RLDTs detected Shigella in approximately 38-40% of samples across all sample types. Rectal swabs in Cary-Blair medium and SDS each showed 97.6% sensitivity and 100% specificity, with PPVs of 100% and NPVs of 98.5% (RSs) and 98.4% (SDSs) compared with FS; stool collected in BGS samples demonstrated the highest sensitivity (100%) and NPV (100%), with 98.4% specificity and 97.6% PPV. All alternative specimen types showed almost perfect agreement with FS. The RLDT performed well using RSs, indicating a practical alternative to stool for detecting Shigella. The assay was also reliable with stool collected in BGS and SDSs. Broader adoption of RLDTs could improve diagnostic capacity and strengthen surveillance and control efforts.

Latent Melioidosis Reactivation Following Immunosuppression in Malaysia: A Report of Two Cases.
Melioidosis, caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, is endemic in Southeast Asia. Over 90% of cases present acutely. The reactivation of latent melioidosis in endemic regions is difficult to diagnose, and the incidence is unknown. We report two previously healthy middle-age women from Limbang, Malaysian Borneo, who were newly diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus. They developed fulminant sepsis due to culture-confirmed melioidosis 4 to 8 weeks after starting immunosuppressive therapy. They had pneumonia and multiorgan microabscesses. One patient survived, whereas the other succumbed to illness. Diagnosing the reactivation of latent melioidosis in endemic regions is impeded by substantial gaps in clinical evaluation and laboratory diagnostic capacity, particularly within resource-limited health care systems. Maintaining high clinical vigilance for reactivation, promptly identifying disseminated disease, and initiating targeted therapy early are critical during the initiation and administration of immunosuppressive treatment. Pre-immunosuppression risk assessment and potential prophylactic strategies in high-risk individuals may help reduce the associated morbidity and mortality.

Clinical characteristics and prognosis of central nervous system Klebsiella pneumoniae infection: a focus on hypervirulent and classical strains.
OBJECTIVE: To investigate the clinical characteristics, diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis of 20 cases of central nervous system (CNS) Klebsiella pneumoniae infection diagnosed by metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), and to compare the differences between classical Klebsiella pneumoniae (cKP) and hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae (hvKP) in central nervous system infections. METHODS: Retrospective single-center study of 20 mNGS-diagnosed CNS K. pneumoniae infections (January 2022 - March 2026). Univariate analysis compared hvKP and cKP groups. RESULTS: Among 20 patients, 19 were diagnosed by CSF mNGS and 1 by abscess fluid mNGS. The cKP group had a higher proportion of tumor history (P = 0.029) and a marginally higher rate of neurosurgery history (P = 0.082). Type 2 diabetes was common in both groups (66.7% vs. 62.5%). The hvKP group had higher rates of focal neurological deficits (77.8% vs. 12.5%, P = 0.015) and bacteremia/sepsis (66.7% vs. 37.5%, P = 0.009), while the cKP group had more delirium (62.5% vs. 11.1%, P = 0.050). CSF mNGS positivity (95%) surpassed culture (23.5%, P < 0.001). Radiologically, hvKP showed more brain abscesses (P = 0.015). hvKP had worse modified Rankin Scale scores (P = 0.002) and higher mortality (44.4% vs. 0%, P = 0.002). No cKP deaths occurred. CONCLUSION: hvKP and cKP CNS infections differ significantly. hvKP is associated with community-onset severe disease (multiple brain abscesses, pyoventricle, focal deficits) and high mortality, while cKP links to nosocomial factors and better outcomes. mNGS is key for diagnosis, offering high CSF positivity and concurrent virulence/resistance profiling. Potential prognostic factors identified include high CSF mNGS reads, resistance genes, early liver abscess drainage, timely intravitreal injection, and combination therapy.

Birth and clinical outcomes of pregnant participants with advanced HIV disease.
INTRODUCTION: Clinical trials for the evaluation of novel diagnostics and treatments for HIV-associated opportunistic infections have historically excluded pregnant persons. Little information is available regarding the clinical outcomes and pregnancy outcomes of pregnant persons with advanced HIV disease while taking opportunistic infection prophylaxis for tuberculosis (TB) and cryptococcosis. In this study, we describe characteristics at enrollment, clinical outcomes, and birth outcomes of pregnant people with advanced HIV in Uganda. METHODS: We prospectively enrolled pregnant adults with advanced HIV disease within an on-going pragmatic cluster randomized clinical trial evaluating an enhanced screening and prophylaxis package for opportunistic infections (NCT05085171). The trial began enrollment in May 2022 and continues in 26 outpatient HIV clinics in the Kampala and Wakiso districts of Uganda. We present an analysis of pregnant participants enrolled through April 30, 2025, including their characteristics at study enrollment, opportunistic infections, and birth outcomes. RESULTS: Overall, 15% (114/766) of female participants with advanced HIV disease were pregnant. Median CD4 cell count was 124 cells/µL (IQR: 82-170). Median time since HIV diagnosis was 7 days, and 45% were ART-naive at enrollment. Compared with non-pregnant female participants, pregnant participants were less likely to have a positive cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) test (2% vs 7%, p=0.023), to have a positive Alere tuberculosis (TB) lipoarabinomannan (LAM) test (11% vs 28%, p<0.001), and to be receiving active TB treatment (14% vs 39%, p<0.001).
