Overall, 18% (21/114) experienced at least one opportunistic infection during the study, of which 71% (n=15) were attributed to TB. Eighty-six percent (98/114) of pregnancies were carried to term. Participants on TB preventive therapy (TPT) had 94% of deliveries at term (51/54), compared with 80% (36/45) among participants who did not receive TPT (OR = 4.25, 95%CI:1.07-16.80), and 67% (8/12) among participants on active TB treatment (OR = 8.50, 95%CI: 1.60-45.25). CONCLUSIONS: Although the incidence of opportunistic infections is less commonly reported among pregnant women with advanced HIV disease, TB is the most frequent opportunistic infection. Participants on TPT had 4-fold higher odds of having a term delivery compared with those not on TPT and 8-fold higher odds compared with those with active TB.

Ligand Binding Remodels the Oligomeric State and Active Site of Klebsiella pneumoniae Azoreductase.
Azo dyes are widespread in the environment, and humans ingest a range of these dyes present in food and drugs. The human gut microbiome significantly impacts the fate of ingested azo dyes primarily through the reduction of the azo bond (R-N = N-R'). Flavin-dependent azoreductases have been considered the key enzymatic drivers of this process. To challenge this paradigm, we constructed a sequence similarity network of known azoreductases and focused on AzoA of Klebsiella pneumoniae, a central representative within the gut microbiome cluster. Unexpectedly, K. pneumoniae AzoA displayed relatively low in vitro activity against a range of azo compounds. While the physiological implications remain unclear, these findings are consistent with the possibility that nonenzymatic mechanisms contribute substantially to azo compound reduction in the gut. Furthermore, structural characterization of AzoA, as a holoenzyme and in its ligand-bound state, revealed a previously unrecognized ligand-coupled mechanism involving remodeling of the active site and oligomeric state.

Carbapenem resistance and mortality in pediatric Acinetobacter bloodstream infections: determinants from a 12-year tertiary-care cohort study.
UNLABELLED: Carbapenem-resistant (CR) Acinetobacter spp. bloodstream infections (BSIs) are difficult to treat in children, yet pediatric data on factors associated with resistance and mortality remain limited. We aimed to identify factors associated with carbapenem resistance and 30-day mortality in pediatric Acinetobacter BSIs. We retrospectively analyzed children with monomicrobial Acinetobacter BSIs at a tertiary-care university hospital between January 2014 and September 2025. Factors associated with carbapenem resistance were assessed using co-primary logistic regression analyses in the full cohort and within A. baumannii; 30-day mortality was assessed using Cox regression. Among 128 episodes, median age was 2.0 years (IQR 0.76-8.01), 60.2% (77/128) were male and 90.6% (116/128) had comorbidities. Carbapenem resistance was identified in 54/128 episodes (42.2%), all caused by A. baumannii (54/87, 62.1%). Increasing age, longer hospitalization before BSI onset, mechanical ventilation (MV), and prior meropenem exposure were associated with resistance in both co-primary models. Adjusted ORs for MV were 23.77 (95% CI, 7.54-74.92) in the full cohort and 23.20 (95% CI, 5.39-99.95) within A. baumannii. Overall 30-day mortality was 13.3% (17/128) and was higher in CR than carbapenem-susceptible episodes (22.2% versus 6.8%; p = 0.011). Exploratory comparisons across CR A. baumannii treatment categories were inconclusive (exact p = 0.256). Thrombocytopenia (aHR, 6.12; 95% CI, 2.13-17.61) and carbapenem resistance (aHR, 3.01; 95% CI, 1.04-8.71) were associated with mortality in the primary Cox model. CONCLUSION: Thrombocytopenia and carbapenem resistance were associated with 30-day all-cause mortality in the primary adjusted analysis; the resistance association was not statistically significant in A. baumannii-restricted and first-episode-only sensitivity analyses. WHAT IS KNOWN: • Acinetobacter BSIs mainly affect medically complex hospitalized children. • Pediatric evidence on factors associated with carbapenem resistance and mortality remains scarce. WHAT IS NEW: • Increasing age, longer hospitalization before BSI onset, mechanical ventilation, and prior meropenem exposure were associated with carbapenem resistance in both the full Acinetobacter cohort and within A. baumannii. • Carbapenem resistance was associated with 30-day mortality in the primary model, but this finding was not consistently supported in sensitivity analyses; thrombocytopenia remained associated with mortality.

Australian Gonococcal Surveillance Programme Annual Report, 2025.
The Australian Gonococcal Surveillance Programme (AGSP) has continuously monitored antimicrobial resistance in Neisseria gonorrhoeae (NG) for more than 45 years through the system of jurisdictional Neisseria reference laboratories, the National Neisseria Network (NNN). In 2025, a total of 10,204 isolates across Australia, from public and private sectors, were tested for in vitro antimicrobial susceptibility by standardised methods. In 2025, the AGSP captured antimicrobial susceptibility data for 23.9% of all gonococcal infection notifications nationally. The current treatment recommendation for gonorrhoea, for the majority of Australia, continues to be dual therapy with ceftriaxone and azithromycin. In 2025, of NG isolates tested, 0.73% (74/10,204) met the World Health Organization (WHO) criterion for decreased susceptibility (DS) to ceftriaxone, defined as a minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) ≥ 0.125 mg/L. This proportion of isolates meeting the ceftriaxone DS criterion was greater than that reported in 2024 (0.51%), with the majority from New South Wales and Victoria. Genomic analysis indicated that 64.9% of these isolates (48/74) possessed the mosaic penA 60.001 allele, the key target associated with ceftriaxone resistance. Resistance to azithromycin was reported in 7.1% of NG isolates nationally, increasing from being proportionally stable (3.9% to 4.7%) since 2019. Of NG isolates tested, 0.20% (20/10,204) exhibited high-level resistance to azithromycin (MIC value ≥ 256 mg/L), with cases reported across Australia, predominantly in New South Wales, Victoria and non-remote Western Australia. There were ten isolates detected in 2025 that had an extensively drug-resistant (XDR) phenotype: i.e., displaying both high-level resistance to azithromycin and decreased susceptibility to ceftriaxone (MIC ≥ 0.125 mg/L). When added to the 14 XDR isolates reported during 2022-2024, this brings the total to 24 XDR NG isolates reported in Australia since 2022. Genomic analyses of the ten XDR isolates reported in 2025 indicated all harboured the mosaic penA 60.001 allele, with several differing sequence types (ST) identified. By contrast, during 2022 and 2024, XDR NG sequence types were limited to ST-16406, consistent with reports from Europe and England. Travel information, where available, indicates infections in 2025 were associated with travel to Southeast Asia but also arose where no travel was involved. In 2025, penicillin resistance was found in 23.4% of gonococcal isolates, and ciprofloxacin resistance in 59.3% of isolates where tested, although there was variation by jurisdiction particularly in remote settings, where acquisition of cultures for antimicrobial susceptibility testing is low. Tetracycline resistance has been included in surveillance in the AGSP in recent years, coincident with increasing use of doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis for syphilis and chlamydia. Nationally 36.2% of NG isolates in 2025 were tetracycline resistant, with variation by jurisdiction. No isolates were resistant to spectinomycin; data for gentamicin, whilst no breakpoints are defined, are reported by the AGSP as these data are reportable to the WHO Global Antimicrobial Resistance and Use Surveillance System (GLASS). The emergence of antimicrobial resistant NG in Australia has largely occurred through importation, spread and local transmission. In 2025, in Australia and overseas, increased detection of drug-resistant NG isolates is of significant concern as the threat for the future of the current recommended therapeutic agents is increasingly evident, and no ideal alternate therapeutic agent has been identified. Disease prevention strategies under investigation for the future have included the MenB-4C vaccine, designed to protect against meningococcal disease. Despite early promise, recent results from a large Australian trial indicate the MenB-4C vaccine is not effective at preventing gonorrhoea in men who are at high risk of infection. The AGSP continues to monitor antimicrobial resistance and to identify emerging resistant clones by enhanced surveillance approaches, to inform strategies for disease management and treatment of gonorrhoea in Australia.

Epidemiology of malaria in the Torres Strait Islands, Australia, 2000-2025 and the public health response to three recent outbreaks.
BACKGROUND: Australia was declared malaria free in 1981. However, the proximity of Australia's Torres Strait region to malaria-endemic Papua New Guinea (PNG), and the presence of the Anopheles mosquito across Northern Australia, means there is an ongoing risk of malaria for many Australian residents. This paper describes the epidemiology of malaria in the Torres Strait region between 2000 and 2025 and reports the public health response to three malaria outbreaks between 2023 and 2025. METHODS: Case data from 1 January 2000 to 31 December 2025 were extracted from the Queensland Notifiable Conditions System to describe the epidemiology of malaria in the Torres Strait. The public health responses to each of the three recent outbreaks were reported against the Queensland Health Public Health Unit Guidelines for Malaria. RESULTS: During the period 2000-2013, there were 171 cases of malaria reported in the Torres Strait region. Of these, 89 (52%) were positive for Plasmodium falciparum and 82 (48%) for P. vivax. Of cases during this period, 130 (76%) were imported from PNG; 13 (8%) were acquired in Australia; and 28 (16%) had an unknown place of acquisition. After a nine-year period without any confirmed malaria cases in the region, eight cases were reported across three outbreaks between 2023 and 2025. In all six of the outbreak cases in which a species could be confirmed, P. vivax was identified. The three outbreaks were managed effectively in partnership with local leaders, and included active case finding and vector control activities. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION: The public health response successfully halted transmission of malaria during three separate outbreaks in the Torres Strait Islands. However, there is an ongoing local risk due to the high incidence of malaria in PNG and cross-border movement under the Torres Strait Treaty. Ongoing collaboration with PNG stakeholders and enhanced local surveillance are essential to minimise the future importation of malaria, and other potentially life-threatening pathogens, into mainland Australia.

Analysis of factors associated with death in critically ill patients with COVID-19.
OBJECTIVES: to assess the factors associated with death in critically ill COVID-19 patients. METHODS: retrospective cohort of critically ill patients admitted to the Intensive Care Unit and infected with SARS-CoV-2, followed for 30 days, ≥ 18 years old, with a positive nasopharyngeal RT-PCR test for SARS-CoV-2. Descriptive analysis regarding the outcome, chi-square test, and backward stepwise multiple logistic regression model were used to describe predictor variables of sociodemographic and clinical characteristics. RESULTS: 715 patients were analyzed, of whom 70.8% (n=507) died and 29.1% (n=209) survived. In the multivariate analysis, death outcome dependent variables, such as age range of 61-80 years, > 80 years, invasive mechanical ventilation, dialysis, corticosteroids, vancomycin, platelets after 24 hours, and other antibiotics, were identified as risk factors, and the ROC curve (AUC=0.904) predicted the proposed model. CONCLUSIONS: the multivariate model showed good discriminatory capacity, identifying independent factors associated with death in critically ill COVID-19 patients.

Use of COVID-19 Detection Tests in the Mexican Population from 2020-2022: Frequency and Distribution.
OBJECTIVE: Analyze the frequency and distribution of COVID-19 diagnostic testing (RT-PCR and Ag-RDT) in Mexico during 2020-2022, and identify the sociodemographic and regional factors associated with their use. METHODS: Ecological and cross-sectional study using secondary data from the National Epidemiological Surveillance System for Respiratory Diseases (SISVER). Approximately 15 million tests performed in public and private institutions between June 2020 and April 2022 were analyzed at individual and municipal levels to describe distribution by sex, age, social security coverage, and regional marginalization. RESULTS: Ag-RDT was the most frequently used test nationwide, with testing concentrated in Mexico City and other economically developed regions, while marginalized and predominantly indigenous areas showed the lowest testing rates. CONCLUSION: Significant inequalities were found in access to COVID-19 testing in Mexico, highlighting the influence of socioeconomic and territorial disparities and the need for equity-oriented public health and nursing strategies.

The Impact of the COVID-19 Pandemic on Oral Cancer Screening: Real-World Data From Taiwan.
BACKGROUND: The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted cancer screening services worldwide, but its impact across multiple screening indicators remains unclear. METHODS: This population-based interrupted time series study evaluated the impact of COVID-19 on oral cancer screening in Taiwan. Two intervention points were defined: January 2020 and May 2021. Four indicators were assessed: screening rate, screening positivity rate, incidence, and mortality. Segmented regression analyses were performed across six National Health Insurance divisions, and changes in stage at diagnosis (2018-2022) were examined. RESULTS: At baseline, screening rates declined, screening positivity rate and mortality increased modestly, and incidence remained stable. After the first outbreak, screening positivity rate showed a significant immediate decrease (OR = 0.86, 95% CI: 0.81-0.92, p < 0.001), whereas screening rate, incidence, and mortality showed no significant changes. Advanced-stage diagnoses increased, while early-stage diagnoses declined. Regional analyses demonstrated similar patterns. No significant slope changes after the first outbreak or level/trend changes after the second outbreak were observed. Incidence and mortality remained stable throughout the study. CONCLUSIONS: The first outbreak had the greatest impact on screening-related indicators, with findings consistent with possible delays in cancer detection. Maintaining organized screening services during public health emergencies is essential to minimize delayed cancer detection.

Disparities in the Epidemiology of COVID-19 in Irish Travellers in the Republic of Ireland.
INTRODUCTION: Irish Travellers, a distinct minority ethnic group, make up 0.64% of the population in the Republic of Ireland (n = 32,949) according to the national census. Major health disparities exist between Travellers and the general population including shorter life expectancy and higher mortality rates from respiratory and cardiovascular disease. METHODS: Here, the epidemiology of COVID-19 in Irish Travellers was investigated. Public health surveillance data on 238,907 notified COVID-19 cases in Ireland from March 2020 to April 2021 were analysed. RESULTS: The crude incidence rate (CIR) of recorded COVID-19 infections in Irish Travellers was the highest of any ethnic group in Ireland during the study period. The one-year CIR/100,000 population was 11,094.34 (95% CI:10755.73-11436.95) for Irish Travellers in contrast to 3,213.00 (95% CI:3196.54-3229.53) for the White population and 4,233.77 (95% CI:4216.40-4251.20) for the general population. The mean age of COVID-19 cases was 27.24 years (95% CI:26.66-27.81) in Irish Travellers versus 39.10 (95% CI:39.00-39.21) and 39.65 years (95% CI:39.56-39.73) in the White and general populations, respectively. Age-specific incidence rates were higher in Irish Travellers across each age group ranging from 2.52-fold higher (95% CI:2.34-4.01) in the 20-29 age group to 4.70-fold higher (95% CI:4.36-7.47) in the 0-9 age group relative to the White population. CONCLUSIONS: In this study, a higher incidence rate for notified COVID-19 was observed for Irish Travellers compared to the White and general populations in Ireland across all age groups. This highlights ongoing health disparities experienced by Irish Travellers and the need to further address respiratory illnesses in this marginalised ethnic minority.

Recent National Trends in Time to Breast Cancer Surgery Before and After the COVID-19 Pandemic Onset and Predictors of Failure to Receive Timely Surgery.
BACKGROUND: Time to surgery (TTS) for breast cancer has been increasing for decades, with delays associated with worse survival. A 2022 Commission on Cancer (CoC) quality measure requires upfront surgery within 60 days after diagnosis (BCSdx). The long-term effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on TTS and compliance with BCSdx are unknown. METHODS: Using the National Cancer Database, the study identified 520,967 women with a diagnosis of clinical stages I to III invasive breast cancer from 2014 to 2023 who underwent upfront surgery. Time to surgery was defined as days from diagnosis to definitive surgery. Diagnosis year was modeled continuously and categorically (pre-pandemic 2014-2019, pandemic onset 2020, post-pandemic onset 2021-2023). Linear and logistic regression were used to identify factors associated with TTS and odds of not having surgery in ≤ 60 days. RESULTS: Between 2014 and 2023, the mean TTS increased from 37 to 50 days (+ 13 days). Compared with 2014-2019, the 2021-2023 period was associated with + 7.51 mean days (95% confidence interval [CI], 7.35-7.67 days) and 1.90 times (95% CI, 1.87-1.94 times) increased odds of not meeting BCSdx in the multivariable analysis. Longer TTS also was associated with immediate reconstruction (β = + 8.27 days), uninsured status (β = + 7.99 days), and diagnosis at another facility (β = + 6.55 days). The proportion of patients with a TTS of ≤ 60 days declined from 88% to 74%. The strongest predictors of noncompliance were uninsured status (odds ratio [OR], 2.10), diagnosis at another facility (OR, 1.81), immediate reconstruction (OR, 1.81), black race (OR, 1.72), and Hispanic ethnicity (OR, 1.70). CONCLUSIONS: The increase in TTS for breast cancer accelerated after the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, with a concomitant decrease in BCSdx compliance. Strategies to improve care coordination, particularly for at-risk populations, are needed to address this quality measure.

COVID-19 pandemic-era changes in non-SUID infant mortality in the United States.
INTRODUCTION: The COVID-19 pandemic has been associated with increases in sudden unexpected infant death (SUID), but less is known about other causes of infant mortality (referred to here as non-SUID). We examined pandemic-era changes in non-SUID mortality by gestational age, age at death and cause of death. METHODS: We conducted a nationwide cohort study using Centers for Disease Control and Prevention National Center for Health Statistics data for US births from 2016 to 2021, including deaths in 2022. We focused on non-SUID mortality by excluding International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision codes for SUID. Pandemic-era births were those between April 2020 and December 2021. Interrupted time series analyses were used to determine prepandemic mortality trends and assess whether there were level or trend changes associated with the COVID-19 pandemic. RESULTS: Overall non-SUID infant mortality rates consistently trended downwards with no pandemic-associated change. However, stratified analyses showed that trends differed by subgroup. While mortality rates among preterm infants continued their prepandemic declines, rates among full-term infants reversed their prepandemic declines. Postneonatal deaths similarly reversed their prepandemic decline, with statistically significant increases during the pandemic. Estimated monthly mortality rates for infants born at the end of the study period were 8.7% and 16.5% higher than expected for term births and postneonatal deaths, respectively. In contrast, the decline in early neonatal mortality rates became more pronounced during the pandemic, with a 7.2% reduction in observed versus expected monthly mortality rates. Infection-related mortality initially declined but later returned to prepandemic levels. Rates of mortality due to external causes increased during the pandemic. Mortality rates for perinatal conditions and congenital malformations continued their prepandemic declines. CONCLUSIONS: Declining overall non-SUID infant mortality masked pandemic-era increases among full-term infants, postneonatal infants and deaths from external causes. These findings support prioritising preventive paediatric care and injury-prevention strategies during future public health emergencies.

Composition-aware and leakage-controlled sparse log-ratio learning for mortality classification from respiratory microbiome profiles.
BACKGROUND: Respiratory microbiome profiles contain compositional information that may complement clinical variables for mortality classification in hospitalized patients with COVID-19. However, microbiome-based classifiers remain vulnerable to compositional artifacts, patient-level leakage, and cohort-specific feature construction. OBJECTIVE: To develop and externally evaluate a leakage-controlled sparse log-ratio learning framework for mortality classification using respiratory microbiome profiles. METHODS: This retrospective secondary analysis used three public COVID-19 respiratory microbiome cohorts. The Sparse Log-Ratio Risk Network (SLRRN) was developed using patient-level nested validation, with genus filtering, zero replacement, balance construction, model tuning, and threshold selection restricted to training partitions. The model learned 16 signed genus balances and integrated four clinical covariates available at the first eligible respiratory sampling landmark. The final specification and threshold were frozen before external evaluation. RESULTS: The development cohort included 82 patients (20 deaths) from PRJNA678105 and PRJNA683617, and frozen external evaluation included 76 independent patients (38 fatal and 38 severe nonfatal cases) from PRJNA726205. Internal AUROC was 0.838 (95% CI, 0.765-0.911), and AUPRC was 0.674 (0.577-0.771). The paired AUROC difference versus XGBoost was 0.041 (0.009-0.073). Without refitting or threshold revision, external AUROC was 0.821 (0.738-0.904), with sensitivity of 0.816 and specificity of 0.842 at the frozen threshold of 0.37. In the outcome-enriched external cohort, the Brier score was 0.166 and the ECE was 0.065; these estimates describe the selected study sample. CONCLUSION: SLRRN provides a composition-aware and leakage-controlled framework for respiratory microbiome-based mortality classification. The findings support further prospective evaluation with standardized sampling and direct comparison with established clinical models before clinical translation.

Comparison of Laboratory- Versus Home-Based Assessments for Infants at Elevated Likelihood for Neurodevelopmental Disabilities.
OBJECTIVE: While many studies pivoted to telehealth and distance methods in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, few studies have directly and systematically compared data obtained from home and lab settings. Our goal was to evaluate the impact of these contextual and methodological differences across multiple developmental domains. METHOD: Participants included 111 infants (33 infants with a family history of autism, 51 with a family history of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), and 27 infants with no family history of either diagnosis) who participated in a laboratory-based assessment and a paired telehealth session at 6 or 9, 12 and/or 18 months of age. Both sessions included multiple measures of infant skills across multiple developmental domains (e.g. receptive and expressive language, play, cognition), and autism- and ADHD-specific measures. Mixed models for repeated measures compared scores across contexts and timepoints and validity was evaluated via multitrait-multimethod matrix. Caregiver ratings of representativeness and acceptability were also evaluated. RESULTS: Convergent validity was supported by significant positive correlations between language, social-communication, and developmental measures across the two contexts, ranging from moderate (0.37) to high (0.80). Multilevel models revealed that developmental trajectories were broadly comparable across settings, though significant cross-context differences were observed, particularly for the 18-month timepoint. CONCLUSIONS: We found broad consistency in scores obtained across the two contexts, suggesting that remote assessments can provide valid and reliable developmental data. The high parent satisfaction ratings also suggest remote assessments are feasible and acceptable to families.

Lessons learned from the COVID-19 pandemic for future cochlear implant service preparedness: a multicenter study.
BACKGROUND: Cochlear implantation (CI) is a highly effective intervention for severe-to-profound hearing loss; however, the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted established CI service delivery worldwide. Maintaining access to this resource-intensive procedure during public health emergencies is critical, particularly for pediatric patients in whom delays may compromise auditory and language development. METHODS: This multicenter retrospective comparative study analyzed CI service delivery across seven centers in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia, comparing pre-pandemic and pandemic periods over six months. Data included procedural volumes, waiting lists, committee activity, surgical workflows, intraoperative testing, and adoption of telehealth for fitting and rehabilitation.Generalized estimating equations were used to account for center-level clustering. RESULTS: A total of 984 CI procedures were analyzed. Overall implant volume was preserved during the pandemic, while waiting lists increased by 31%. Telehealth adoption expanded markedly, with all remote fitting sessions and nearly all remote rehabilitation sessions occurring during the COVID-19 pandemic. Unilateral operating time decreased significantly, reflecting streamlined surgical workflows. Committee activity and intraoperative testing practices demonstrated center-specific adaptations. CONCLUSION: CI services demonstrated resilience during the COVID-19 pandemic through rapid telehealth integration and surgical workflow optimization. However, increased waiting lists highlight critical vulnerability, particularly for pediatric candidates. Hybrid care models and contingency planning should be formally integrated into future CI service frameworks.

Changing Patterns of Diagnostic Testing in Children With Asthma: Evidence of Redistribution, Overuse, and Recovery After the COVID-19 Pandemic.
BACKGROUND: Real-world implementation of diagnostic strategies in pediatric asthma remains heterogeneous, and the long-term impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on diagnostic practice patterns is incompletely understood, particularly in middle-income countries. Guideline-recommended objective testing (e.g., spirometry) is inconsistently applied in pediatric asthma worldwide, and whether the COVID-19 pandemic produced a transient disruption or a lasting restructuring of diagnostic practice across testing domains remains unclear. We aimed to characterize longitudinal trends in diagnostic testing among children with asthma, examining pre-pandemic trajectories, COVID-associated changes, and post-pandemic recovery. METHODS: We conducted a nationwide population-based interrupted time-series study using Colombia's mandatory healthcare registry (2015-2024). Asthma encounters were identified using ICD-10 codes (J45-J46). Diagnostic procedures were classified into nine clinically defined domains. Diagnostic intensity was calculated as tests per 100 asthma encounters. Segmented regression estimated pre-pandemic trends, immediate 2020 level changes, and post-pandemic slope modifications. RESULTS: A total of 1,954,680 asthma encounters generated 117,324 diagnostic tests. Pre-pandemic trajectories diverged across domains. Pulmonary function testing (PFT) declined before 2020 (IRR 0.80; 95% CI 0.74-0.86) but showed a significant immediate increase in 2020 (IRR 1.42; 95% CI 1.28-1.57) and sustained post-pandemic acceleration (IRR 1.17; 95% CI 1.09-1.26). Imaging and sleep studies exhibited sharp pandemic-associated declines with partial or full recovery. Cardiopulmonary testing demonstrated marked pre-pandemic expansion (IRR 1.96). CONCLUSIONS: Pediatric asthma diagnostic practice underwent domain-specific restructuring rather than uniform disruption, consistent with a process of diagnostic redistribution across testing domains. Post-pandemic intensification of PFT may reflect improved adherence to objective diagnostic confirmation, whereas persistent contraction in selected domains warrants continued monitoring.

Effect of telemedicine-delivered lifestyle interventions in older adults during the COVID-19 pandemic: a nationwide two-arm randomized trial (PROACTIVE-19).
Older adults are at increased risk of severe COVID-19 outcomes, yet randomized evidence on structured lifestyle interventions in this context remains limited. We aimed to evaluate the effects of a personalized lifestyle intervention on health-related behaviors and adverse outcomes among adults aged ≥ 60 years during the COVID-19 pandemic. PROACTIVE-19 was a nationwide, open-label, randomized trial initiated in Hungary in March 2020, during the first wave of the COVID-19 pandemic. Participants aged ≥ 60 years were randomly assigned (1:1) to general (group A) or personalized (group B) lifestyle counselling delivered via telephone, targeting mental health, smoking, physical activity, diet, and alcohol consumption. The primary planned endpoint was a composite of COVID-19 severity outcomes; however, due to infection rates, all-cause mortality was assessed. Longitudinal lifestyle changes were evaluated using linear mixed-effects models with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs) in a modified intention-to-treat population. A total of 441 participants were analyzed (214 group A; 227 group B). All-cause mortality did not differ significantly between groups (HR = 0.66, 95% CI 0.28-1.53). Significant overall time effects were observed for fruit and vegetable consumption (β = 0.052, CI 0.026-0.074), smoking reduction among current smokers (β = - 0.372, CI - 0.528 to - 0.222), and psychological variables. A significantly greater reduction in estimated alcohol consumption was observed in group B among baseline drinkers compared with group A (β = - 1.357, CI - 2.425 to - 0.187), particularly in women. However, BMI among participants with obesity increased in group B (β = 0.068, CI 0.013-0.119). Seasonal and pandemic-wave effects significantly influenced physical activity and psychological distress. The personalized intervention was not associated with a significant reduction in all-cause mortality. Several lifestyle behaviors improved over time; however, the additional benefit of personalization was limited (Supported by the Semmelweis University Research, Development and Innovation Fund, ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04321928).

A Cohort Retrospective Observational Study of Hospital Accreditation Influence on Medication Safety in Saudi Hospitals.
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Medication errors remain a leading cause of adverse events globally and in Saudi Arabia, accounting for up to 45% of reported medical errors. Despite accreditation programs aiming to improve patient safety, evidence of their impact on medication management (MM) standards is limited. This study addresses this gap by evaluating MM compliance in Saudi hospitals from 2016 to 2023, post-implementation of the Central Board for Accreditation of Healthcare Institutions' Essential Safety Requirements (ESR). METHODS: This retrospective cohort study analyzed ESR survey data from 454 hospitals nationwide. Of these, 161 hospitals met the inclusion criteria by completing all 6 annual ESR surveys (2016-2019, 2022-2023); 293 hospitals were excluded due to incomplete longitudinal data. Scores for 3 MM standards: MM5 (high-alert medication safety), MM6 (look-alike and sound-alike medication safety), and MM41 (medication error monitoring) were extracted. Statistical analysis included descriptive statistics, repeated measures analysis of variance, and independent t tests comparing 2016-2019 and 2022-2023 periods. MM compliance was not reported during the COVID pandemic period (2020-2021). RESULTS: Significant improvements were observed across all MM standards over time. Mean MM5 scores increased from 69.56 in 2016 to 95.66 in 2023, MM6 from 40.79 to 96.10, and MM41 from 61.13 to 93.27 (all P .05), and hospital bed size had no meaningful impact on MM5 and MM6, with a minor trend for MM41 (P = .001 but not statistically significant). CONCLUSIONS: The period after implementation of the Central Board for Accreditation of Healthcare Institutions ESR standards saw significantly improved medication safety compliance in Saudi hospitals, suggesting the effectiveness of accreditation in promoting patient safety. Policymakers should sustain these efforts to maintain progress. Future research should evaluate patient outcomes, cost-effectiveness, and adopt mixed-methods approaches to explore contextual factors influencing compliance.

Multiplexed Nucleic Acid Detection Using Sequence-Specific Cleavage Mediated by Repair Endonucleases.
Rapid, portable detection of multiple nucleic acid targets is essential for infectious disease surveillance and precision oncology. CRISPR-based diagnostics have set a high bar for sensitivity and single-base specificity, yet their reliance on collateral nuclease activity complicates multiplexing, integration with amplification, and point-of-care deployment. Here, we present TIMBER (templated incision mediated by endonucleases of repair), a non-CRISPR platform that achieves comparable performance without nonspecific nuclease activity. TIMBER uses a repair endonuclease to cleave probes containing abasic sites only when they are hybridized to a matched target. The system exhibits strong specificity, enabling single-nucleotide polymorphism discrimination. TIMBER provides an analytical limit of detection of 12 pM without preamplification or one copy per μL (1.6 aM) with preamplification through RT-PCR or RT-LAMP, with results observable by visual fluorescence or on lateral flow. We deploy TIMBER to detect SARS-CoV-2 in clinical saliva samples and further demonstrate multiplex detection of four targets, enabling identification of EGFR mutations in lung cancer samples. This approach offers a flexible, rapid, and low-instrument-ready solution for diverse nucleic acid diagnostics, from viral detection to cancer genotyping.

Transcription Regulatory Sequences in Coronaviruses: Mechanistic Foundations for Antivirals and Vaccines.
Coronaviruses employ a distinctive discontinuous transcription mechanism to generate a nested set of subgenomic mRNAs (sgRNAs) from a single large positive-strand RNA genome. Transcription regulatory sequences (TRSs)-comprising a leader TRS (TRS-L) near the 5' end and multiple body TRSs (TRS-Bs) upstream of downstream open reading frames-serve as the primary cis-acting signals that direct polymerase pausing and template switching during negative-strand synthesis. The COVID-19 pandemic spurred intensive investigation of SARS-CoV-2 gene expression, yielding high-resolution transcriptome maps, genome-wide RNA structure data, and detailed structural models of the replication-transcription complex (RTC). TRS function is therefore best understood as a multi-scale property determined not by the core motif alone, but by the integration of primary-sequence complementarity, local RNA secondary structure, long-range RNA-RNA interactions, and RTC dynamics. This review provides an integrated view of TRS structure-function relationships, with emphasis on how these features collectively shape sgRNA abundance, junction diversity, recombination potential, and prospects for diagnostic and antiviral applications, including vaccines and therapeutics.

TasTY: Development and evaluation of a taste test for quantifying taste sensitivity among preschool children-test-retest reliability, application, and comparison between children with and without prior SARS-CoV-2 infection.
UNLABELLED: Taste dysfunction gained attention during the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic; however, validated objective tests for preschool children remain limited. We aimed to develop a feasible, reliable test quantifying taste sensitivity among children aged 3-6 years and to compare performance between children with and without prior SARS-CoV-2 infection. We included 68 symptom-free children (median age 5.1 years; interquartile range (IQR) 3.9-5.9): 36 without known SARS-CoV-2 infection (control group, CG) and 32 with confirmed prior infection (SARS-CoV-2 infection group, C19-G), tested 79 days after infection (median; IQR 56-112). Children completed a self-developed Taste Test for Young Children (TasTY), a double-blind, playful two-alternative forced-choice test with 10 samples in randomized order (sweet, sour, and salty at three concentrations each; water served as a control). Twenty controls were retested a median of 62 days later (IQR 38-64). Outcomes were total score (0-10), feasibility, task comprehension, and test-retest reliability, assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), standard error of measurement (SEM), and smallest real difference (SRD). Feasibility was high (3% dropout), and 89.4% correctly classified water. Total score test-retest reliability was good (ICC = 0.73; pooled SEM = 0.76; SRD = 2.11). Total scores were similar between CG and C19-G (8.37 ± 1.5 vs. 8.19 ± 1.5; p = 0.63). Descriptively, three-year-olds (n = 17) had lower, more variable scores. CONCLUSION: TasTY provides an age-appropriate, reliable, objective method for quantifying taste sensitivity among preschoolers, supporting standardized group comparisons and longitudinal assessment. WHAT IS KNOWN: • COVID-19 increased awareness of taste dysfunction; however, evidence among young children relies mainly on surveys and parental reports. • Objective taste tests for preschool children remain limited. WHAT IS NEW: • TasTY is a feasible, standardized, and objective test for quantifying taste sensitivity among children aged 3-6 years and goes beyond parental and subjective reports. • Its standardized 0-10 score showed good test-retest reliability and may support group comparisons and longitudinal assessment of preschool children with taste-related conditions.

Impact of COVID-19 on Childhood Obesity in South Korea: Variations by Age and Sex.
BACKGROUND: The prevalence of overweight and obesity among children and adolescents has risen over recent decades, although the increase has recently stabilized. The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic was accompanied by substantial weight gain among Korean children. We examined changes in the prevalence of overweight and obesity among South Korean children from 2017 to 2021, including the pandemic period. METHODS: We analyzed data from the Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey from 2017 to 2021 to compare the prevalence of overweight and obesity before and during the COVID-19 pandemic. The study included 6,249 participants, with subgroup analyses by sex and age (2-9 and 10-18 years). Changes in lifestyle among adolescents aged 12-18 years were assessed using survey responses. RESULTS: Mean body mass index increased significantly during the COVID-19 period among boys in both age groups (P<0.05). The prevalence of obesity among Korean children also increased markedly (P<0.05). Among children aged 10-18 years, boys had a notable increase in obesity prevalence during the pandemic, whereas girls did not have a statistically significant increase. CONCLUSION: The COVID-19 pandemic period was associated with a marked increase in the overall prevalence of obesity and extreme obesity among Korean children, particularly boys aged 10-18 years. Differences in lifestyle factors by sex and age may have contributed to the observed variation in obesity prevalence.

Unravelling the transmission dynamics and evolutionary trajectory of mpox in South Korea: 2022-2025 outbreak.
The 2022 monkeypox (mpox) outbreak, driven by clade IIb monkeypox virus (MPXV), was facilitated by human-to-human transmission, particularly within heavy-tailed sexual networks. APOBEC3-associated mutations have been a prominent feature of MPXV genomic evolution during the global outbreak. National genomic data were collected from clinical samples by the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency to examine the transmission dynamics and molecular evolution of MPXV. Target enrichment-based next-generation sequencing was used to generate high-quality genomes. Mutation profiling was used to identify key genetic changes; clustering based on common variants provided insights into national transmission dynamics and molecular evolution. Analysis of mpox-positive samples revealed the linkage of most cases to sub-lineage C.1 and a few cases to C.1.1. Genomic clustering revealed an uneven distribution of cases, with a dominant cluster accounting for a substantial proportion of domestic transmission while most other cluster remained relatively limited in size, consistent with heterogeneous transmission patterns. APOBEC3-associated mutations progressively accumulated during the outbreak and were frequently observed in genomic regions associated with viral structural integrity and cell-to-cell transmission and host-modulation, indicating continued genomic diversification during human-to-human transmission. Together with the dominance of localized clusters, these findings suggest heterogeneous transmission patterns and the possible contribution of epidemiologically unrecognized transmission to the spread of MPXV in South Korea. These results underscore value of integrating genomic surveillance and targeted interventions to characterize transmission patterns and monitor viral genomic changes of potential biological or public health relevance.

Genotypic and Phenotypic Characterization of MRSA Colonization and Persistence in Residential Aged Care Facilities in Adelaide, Australia.
BACKGROUND: Residential aged care facilities (RACFs) are potential reservoirs for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), with residents at increased risk due to compromised immunity, comorbidities, frequent hospital visits, and close living quarters. OBJECTIVES: This study is aimed at assessing MRSA prevalence in RACFs and analyzing antimicrobial resistance mechanisms both phenotypically and genotypically. METHODS: A total of 106 participants were recruited: 84 from three RACFs and 22 from retirement villages (as control samples). MRSA was isolated from nasal, wound, and urine samples using selective media. Identification was confirmed via MALDI-TOF MS. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing and MRSA screening were conducted using ISO broth microdilution and EUCAST disc diffusion. Whole-genome sequencing and bioinformatics were used to explore resistance mechanisms and clonal transmission. RESULTS: Nasal carriage of MRSA was 8.2% (n = 7/85) among RACF residents; none were found in retirement village participants. All isolates formed strong biofilms, and 66.6% (10/15) showed multidrug resistance. Genotypic analysis revealed ST22 as the predominant clone. Genotypic resistance largely matched phenotypic profiles, except for unexplained tetracycline resistance. No isolates carried Panton-Valentine leukocidin (PVL), consistent with previously reported data on MRSA in long-term care facilities. SNP-based phylogenetic analysis indicated persistent colonization and circulation of multidrug-resistant clones within the facilities. Nasal carriage of MRSA was associated with UTIs and/or wound infections in some cases, whereas a UTI caused by the same clone in a resident within the same facility without nasal carriage indicates possible intrafacility clonal dissemination. CONCLUSION: This study highlights persistent colonization with hospital-associated MRSA and potential clonal transmission among residents of aged care facilities despite several courses of antibiotics. The predominance of the epidemic ST22 clone and high rates of multidrug resistance underscore the urgent need for targeted infection control, routine genomic surveillance, and antimicrobial stewardship in long-term care settings to prevent MRSA dissemination.

NIR-triggered gelatin-based hydrogel for ion-mechanical synergistic antibacterial therapy and infected wound closure.
Bacterial infection and impaired wound closure remain the leading causes of refractory cutaneous wound healing disorders, inflicting substantial global morbidity and mortality while exacerbating the crisis of antibacterial resistance. Infected cutaneous wounds present a persistent clinical difficulty, given that bacterial infection and inadequate wound closure exacerbate one another. Here, we constructed a hydrogel platform that integrates antibacterial activity and active wound closure through ion-mechanical coupling. The system combines thermoresponsive, catechol-functionalized network with core-shell nanoparticles consisting of a metal-organic framework shell (MOF) encapsulating a liquid metal core (LM). Under near-infrared (NIR) irradiation, the liquid metal generates heat that triggers network contraction to mechanically close the wound. Simultaneously, sustained release of Zn2+ and Ga3+ from the nanoparticles provides continuous, antibiotic free antibacterial activity. In a mouse MRSA infected wound model, this hydrogel achieves complete closure within 14 days with improved tissue regeneration. By integrating ion mediated antibacterial action, photothermal bacterial inactivation, and active mechanical contraction in a single platform, this design addresses the intertwined challenges of infection and impaired closure without the compromises of conventional approaches.

Comparative Seroprevalence of Brucella Antibodies in Apparently Healthy Sheep and Goats in a Rural District of Central Nigeria.
BACKGROUND: Brucellosis, caused by bacterial pathogens of the genus Brucella, is a chronic zoonotic disease affecting small ruminants such as sheep and goats. This study evaluated and compared the seroprevalence of Brucella antibodies among apparently healthy sheep and goats in Vwang District, Jos South Local Government Area, Plateau State, Nigeria. METHODOLOGY: A cross-sectional study design was employed from May to June 2024. A total of 140 serum samples collected from goats (n = 77) and sheep (n = 63) using systematic random sampling across four administrative wards were screened for Brucella antibodies using the Rose Bengal Plate Test (RBPT) and confirmed via the Complement Fixation Test (CFT). RESULTS: Overall, 8 out of 140 samples (5.71%, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.50%-10.95%) were reactive on RBPT screening. Upon confirmatory testing with CFT, 6 samples were validated, yielding an overall CFT-confirmed seroprevalence of 4.29% (95% CI: 1.59-9.09%). Seroprevalence was higher in sheep (6.35%, 95% CI: 1.76-15.47%) than in goats (2.60%, 95% CI: 0.32-9.07%); higher in females (4.95%, 95% CI: 1.63-11.18%) than in males (2.56%, 95% CI: 0.06-13.48%); and restricted to animals older than 18 months (6.74%, 95% CI: 2.51-14.10%) compared with younger ones (0.00%, 95% CI: 0.00-6.98%). Geographically, the Turu B Ward recorded the highest seroprevalence (5.88%, 95% CI: 0.72-19.68%). None of the demographic associations reached statistical significance (p > 0.05). CONCLUSION: This study provides serological evidence of Brucella exposure among apparently healthy sheep and goats in Vwang District, Central Nigeria. Although seroprevalence differences across species, sex, age, and location were not statistically significant, the detection of antibodies in nonvaccinated, clinically healthy livestock highlights the value of routine serological monitoring in rural agrarian communities.

Antibacterial and antibiofilm activities of ZnO-NPs against Streptococcus suis serotype 9 in vitro.
Streptococcus suis is an important swine pathogen and an emerging zoonotic threat, with serotype 9 (SS9) increasingly recognized as an important pathogenic serotype. Biofilm formation contributes to the persistence, antimicrobial tolerance, and pathogenicity of S. suis, yet effective strategies for controlling biofilm-associated infections caused by SS9 remain limited. In this study, we evaluated the antibacterial and antibiofilm activities of zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO-NPs) against SS9 and investigated whether their effects were associated with oxidative stress, biofilm formation, and alterations in virulence-associated genes. The minimum inhibitory concentration and minimum biofilm eradication concentration of ZnO-NPs against SS9 were both 49 μg/mL. ZnO-NPs exhibited potent antibacterial and antibiofilm activities, significantly inhibiting biofilm formation and reducing biofilm viability in a dose-dependent manner. Crystal violet staining demonstrated a marked reduction in biofilm biomass, while SEM analysis revealed substantial disruption of bacterial morphology and biofilm architecture following ZnO-NPs treatment. In addition, ZnO-NPs markedly increased intracellular reactive oxygen species levels, indicating the induction of oxidative stress in SS9. ZnO-NPs treatment also reduced the major extracellular matrix components of the biofilm, including extracellular proteins and extracellular DNA. Furthermore, RT-qPCR analysis showed that ZnO-NPs downregulated the expression of biofilm- and virulence-associated genes, including ef, fbps, gdh, and luxS. Collectively, these findings indicate that ZnO-NPs exert antibacterial and antibiofilm effects against SS9, accompanied by oxidative stress induction, disruption of biofilm architecture and extracellular matrix, and modulation of biofilm- and virulence-associated genes. ZnO-NPs may, therefore, represent a promising candidate for controlling SS9-associated infections.IMPORTANCEStreptococcus suis serotype 9 (SS9) is an important pathogen associated with disease in pigs and represents a potential zoonotic threat. The increasing prevalence of antimicrobial resistance highlights the need for alternative approaches to control SS9 infections. In this study, zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO-NPs) showed antibacterial and antibiofilm activity against SS9, including disruption of established biofilms. These findings provide evidence for further exploring ZnO-NPs as a non-antibiotic strategy for controlling SS9 infections and support future studies evaluating their safety and efficacy in animals.

Human Antibody Responses to Group A Streptococcus Infection: A Systematic Review.
OBJECTIVES: Group A Streptococcus (GAS) is a leading global cause of infectious disease morbidity and mortality. A major barrier to GAS vaccine development is our incomplete understanding of human immunity. We undertook, to our knowledge, the first systematic review describing human antibody responses following GAS infection. METHODS: Eligible studies were publications reporting human antibody responses to any GAS antigen in individuals with microbiologically confirmed GAS infection. Case reports and studies primarily describing post-streptococcal autoimmune complications were excluded. Databases were last searched on 15th November 2025. Risk of bias was assessed using the relevant tools from the Joanna Briggs Institute. Results are presented in narrative form as meta-analysis was not appropriate. RESULTS: A total of 143 studies spanning 1948-2025 met inclusion criteria. Most studies (83%) were conducted in the Global North and focused on tonsillopharyngitis (79·4%). Antibody responses were measured in serum (99·3%) and/or saliva (2·1%), targeting 116 distinct GAS antigens. The proportion of individuals exhibiting an antibody response to five antigens (SLO, DNase B, GAC, M protein and Streptokinase) was significantly greater in cases when compared with healthy controls. In longitudinal studies, the peak antibody titres were detected at a median of 28 days post-infection. Higher pre-infection titres of some antibodies (M protein, SpyCEP, SpyAD, SLO, DNase B, SpnA, T25, K4S2) correlated with subsequent protection from GAS infection or reduced severity of disease in three separate studies. Heterogeneity across studies prevented clear conclusions regarding how post-infection antibody responses vary by GAS serotype, participant age, infection site, or disease severity. CONCLUSIONS: This review synthesizes 77 years of heterogenous studies describing antibody responses to GAS infection. Limitations of this review arise from the heterogeneity between studies and study risk of bias. Despite this, we identify major gaps in our understanding of the magnitude, kinetics, and protective role of antibody responses. Our synthesis uncovers information that will support GAS vaccine development including: guidance on sampling time points and the identification of antibodies that may be associated with protection from disease, as well as the need for standardisation of laboratory methodology and minimally-biased antigen discovery approaches.

A Carbapenem-Resistant Acinetobacter baumannii Outbreak in an Intensive Care Unit: Detection Before Recognition and Persistence After Containment.
BACKGROUND: We analyzed a carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB) outbreak in an intensive care unit (ICU) to improve insight into how this pathogen spreads within health care facilities and to inform the development of targeted control procedures. METHODS: A CRAB outbreak in a tertiary referral center was investigated over a 5-month window with clinical data, molecular typing (AP-PCR, PFGE), and one month of environmental sampling. All ICU patients (n=31) were compared-epidemic-clone-positive (n=7) versus -negative (n=24)-using Mann-Whitney/Fisher tests and Firth penalized logistic regression. RESULTS: Although the outbreak spanned 6 days clinically, index patients had been colonized up to 41 days earlier. CRAB was recovered from high-touch surfaces; 6/7 patients developed pneumonia/VAP and 6/7 died (4 CRAB-attributable). Prior A. baumannii isolation (57% vs 0%) was the only independent risk factor (Firth odds ratio 34.7; P=.004). Despite treatment, infected patients redeveloped epidemic-clone infection up to 3.5 months later. CONCLUSIONS: In CRAB outbreaks, spread may begin weeks before clinical recognition, and-even months after the outbreak is contained-the epidemic clone can cause reinfection in previously treated patients; only high-resolution analyses spanning an extended period can document this. Multidisciplinary and administrative collaboration, extended and effective environmental disinfection, and effective isolation of positive patients are important for containing CRAB outbreaks.

The perceived impact of extreme weather events on care for people with HIV or tuberculosis and HIV in Zimbabwe: a survey-based multicentre cross-sectional observational study and formative evaluation.
BACKGROUND: The growing threat to health systems posed by extreme weather events (EWEs) disproportionately affects people living with HIV and tuberculosis disease in high-burden, low-resource settings. In Zimbabwe, for example, the 2023-24 El Niño-induced drought intensified food insecurity and reduced access to clinics and medication for such vulnerable populations. We aimed to conduct a formative evaluation to assess the perceived impact of climate change and EWEs on HIV and tuberculosis determinants and service delivery and identify potential climate-adaptive health-service strategies. METHODS: In this survey-based multicentre cross-sectional observational study with a formative evaluation supplemented by qualitative data, we surveyed people living with HIV from Sept 19 to Dec 19, 2024, across 321 clinics in Zimbabwe to describe their perceived impact of EWEs on their health. Participants were recruited using convenience sampling. The inclusion criteria were being diagnosed with HIV, being older than 18 years, and receiving HIV care at Organization for Public Health Interventions and Development (OPHID) clinics during the study period. Individuals who were not receiving HIV care at an OPHID clinic or who were younger than 18 years were excluded. A client satisfaction survey was used to collect data from in-person surveys. The survey included questions related to the general effects of EWEs, such as drought, extreme heat, and flooding; how EWEs had affected HIV or tuberculosis care; and what, if any, services were currently available or should be made available to mitigate climate impacts on health. We also conducted six focus group discussions (FGDs; five to eight participants per group) between March 12 and May 12, 2024, across the Bulilima, Mangwe, and Matobo districts. We used a convenience sampling approach to select patients who had visited the health facility for medical check-ups, medication resupply, or viral load testing, as recorded in clinical registers and verified by clinical staff. Eligible participants for the FGDs were adults (≥18 years) with HIV, or with current or previous tuberculosis treatment, receiving care at the study facility during the recruitment period; those under 18 years or not receiving care at the facility were excluded. Participants' sex was self-reported at enrolment. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively, whereas FGD data were analysed using a modified framework approach. The main outcomes were the perceived impact of climate change and EWEs on HIV and tuberculosis determinants and service delivery outcomes, as reported by affected communities, and community-prioritised mitigation strategies to feasibly address climate-sensitive determinants and barriers to care. FINDINGS: Among 1804 eligible participants approached across 15 districts, all completed the survey and were included in the analysis. Most survey participants (1363 [75·6%] of 1804 participants) reported noticing changes in climate over the past 5 years; of these 1363 participants, 900 (66·0%) were female and 1024 (75·1%) participants reported disruptions to their HIV care during the time they noticed changes in climate. Survey respondents reported that climate-related disruptions were associated with increased food insecurity (reported by 877 [85·6%] of 1024 participants) and water shortage (667 [65·1%] of 1024 participants). Qualitative analysis confirmed that the barriers to HIV and tuberculosis care from EWEs included widespread food insecurity, crop failures, and livestock deaths, with consequent effects on income leading to challenges in paying for food and transportation to clinics. Participants highlighted the need for expanded services that facilitate social and economic wellbeing, including nutrition support, water access, transportation, and income-generating activities, and decentralised models of health-care delivery. INTERPRETATION: Extreme heat and drought affect food and water security and have financial implications, creating challenges for patients to access care in Zimbabwe. Our findings underscore the urgent need for integrated, climate-adaptive strategies to maintain HIV and tuberculosis care in such climate-vulnerable regions. FUNDING: Nina Ireland Program in Lung Health.

Designing sero-epidemiological studies to explore immune markers associated with a reduced risk of invasive Klebsiella pneumoniae disease.
Klebsiella pneumoniae (Kpn) is a leading cause of neonatal invasive bacterial disease especially in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), with 20-30% of culture-confirmed neonatal sepsis caused by Kpn. This, coupled with the rapid emergence of multidrug-resistant strains, calls for additional therapeutic options. Maternal vaccination represents a promising strategy to confer protection to neonates through transplacental transfer of antibodies, with modelling suggesting a vaccine of moderate efficacy (~70%) could avert over 80,000 neonatal deaths annually. Advancing Kpn vaccine development requires identification and validation of serological thresholds of risk reduction (SToRR), or immune markers associated with a reduced risk of invasive Kpn disease (IKpnD). However, no standardized framework currently exists for this purpose. Drawing on lessons from other pathogens, this review outlines key methodological considerations for designing rigorous sero-epidemiological studies to establish such markers. We address three critical domains: (i) study design and population selection, including the rationale for nested case-control designs within birth cohorts enriched for high-risk neonates; (ii) statistical approaches for threshold estimation, including covariate-adjusted logistic regression and Bayesian frameworks; and (iii) laboratory standardization and assay validation, encompassing binding and functional antibody assays. Addressing these considerations systematically will accelerate the development and deployment of a Kpn vaccine capable of reducing neonatal mortality globally.

Tuberculosis Among Artisanal Miners in the Mulongo Health Zone, Democratic Republic of Congo: Unmatched Case-Control Study.
BACKGROUND: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major global health challenge, with 10.6 million new cases and 1.3 million deaths reported in 2022. Artisanal miners in sub‑Saharan Africa are particularly vulnerable due to poverty, overcrowded living conditions, and high HIV prevalence. In the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), TB prevalence among miners is high, yet determinants remain insufficiently studied. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to identify sociodemographic, behavioral, and clinical factors associated with TB among artisanal miners in the Mulongo health zone, Haut‑Lomami Province, DRC. METHODS: We conducted an unmatched case-control study among miners aged ≥15 years. Data were collected using a validated questionnaire covering socioeconomic, behavioral, and biomedical variables. Interviewers were blinded to TB status to minimize bias. Determinants were assessed using bivariate and multivariable logistic regression. RESULTS: Poverty was strongly associated with TB (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 3.16, 95% CI 1.95-5.11; P<.001). Primary education was associated with increased TB risk (aOR 2.78, 95% CI 1.04-7.44; P=.04), while secondary education showed a borderline association (aOR 2.53, 95% CI 0.93-6.89; P=.07). Higher education was protective (aOR 0.62, 95% CI 0.40-0.95; P=.03). Poor knowledge of TB transmission (aOR 2.11, 95% CI 1.16-3.83; P=.02), cause (aOR 1.79, 95% CI 1.00-3.20; P=.049), and diagnosis (aOR 2.49, 95% CI 1.48-4.17; P=.001) were consistently linked to higher vulnerability. HIV infection was significantly associated with TB (aOR 4.65, 95% CI 1.00-21.74; P=.049). Overcrowding was more frequent among TB cases, but in adjusted models, the association was borderline (aOR 1.65, 95% CI 0.95-2.85; P=.07). Tobacco use (aOR 1.47, 95% CI 0.83-2.61; P=.18), alcohol consumption (aOR 1.18, 95% CI 0.70-1.98; P=.54), and nutritional status (aOR 1.36, 95% CI 0.78-2.37; P=.28) were not significantly associated with TB. CONCLUSIONS: TB among artisanal miners appears to be driven primarily by poverty, limited education, poor knowledge, and HIV infection. Overcrowding showed a suggestive but nonsignificant association. Integrated interventions should prioritize poverty alleviation, improved housing, tailored health education, and strengthened TB and HIV services, while further studies are needed to clarify the role of overcrowding and other contextual factors.

Not All Extrapulmonary Tuberculosis Is Equal: Site-Specific Mortality in a National Indian Cohort.
Among 777,512 Indian adults with extrapulmonary tuberculosis, in-treatment mortality varied over tenfold by site, highest for tuberculous meningitis (adjusted odds ratio 12.48 vs. lymph node TB), miliary (5.17), and pericardial TB (3.86). Associations of HIV, diabetes, alcohol, and tobacco use with mortality varied across sites. Risk-stratified, comorbidity-aware care is warranted.

Simplifying Adult Pneumococcal Vaccination in India: A Cost-Effectiveness Analysis of the 20-Valent Conjugate Vaccine.
INTRODUCTION: In India, adult pneumococcal disease prevention relies on the 23‑valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) and the 13‑ and 20‑valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCV13, PCV20). Before PCV20 introduction, adults at older age or high risk typically received PCV13 followed by PPSV23, although no national recommendation exists and uptake has been low. This study evaluated the cost‑effectiveness of a single‑dose PCV20 strategy compared with the sequential PCV13→PPSV23 regimen from private and public perspectives. METHODS: Incremental cost‑effectiveness ratios (ICERs) per quality‑adjusted life‑year (QALY) gained were estimated for PCV20 versus PCV13→PPSV23. Analyses were conducted from the private perspective for high‑risk adults aged 18-49 years and all adults aged ≥ 50 years, and from the government perspective for high‑risk adults aged 18-59 years and all adults aged ≥ 60 years. RESULTS: Compared with PCV13→PPSV23, PCV20 was projected to reduce pneumococcal disease cases and deaths and was cost‑effective under the 3× GDP per capita threshold. PCV20 generated 18,186 and 44,659 additional QALYs from the private and public perspectives, with incremental costs of ₹2.0 billion (Indian Rupees; medical: -₹17.4B; vaccine: ₹19.4B) and ₹25.5B (medical: -₹3.6B; vaccine: ₹29.1B), yielding ICERs of ₹110,790 and ₹570,327 per QALY, respectively. PCV20 was cost‑effective in 92.4% and 75.0% of probabilistic simulations from the private and government perspectives. Extending vaccination to at‑risk adults aged 18-49 years remained cost‑effective from the private perspective (ICER: ₹292,531/QALY). CONCLUSIONS: A single‑dose PCV20 strategy for high‑risk and older adults in India is cost‑effective compared with the current sequential regimen and may simplify pneumococcal vaccination and potentially improve uptake.

Protein malnutrition facilitates intestinal colonization with highly resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae through disrupted intestinal microbial metabolism.
Pediatric infections with highly resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (HR-Kp) disproportionately affect low-income countries where childhood malnutrition is prevalent. Malnutrition is an identified risk factor for infection with HR-Kp and other antimicrobial-resistant Enterobacterales, but the mechanistic underpinnings of this link and independence from other common exposures, like antibiotics, in children are unclear. Using a murine model of pediatric malnutrition, we found that mice fed a protein-deficient diet (PD) were more susceptible to colonization with HR-Kp at a 4-log lower challenge inoculum and developed a 3-log higher intestinal burden in comparison to adequately nourished mice. HR-Kp colonization in PD-fed mice persisted beyond 5 weeks, and colonization was transmitted to diet-matched cage mates. Antibiotic treatment resulted in similar HR-Kp colonization burdens regardless of diet, suggesting that nutrition-dependent colonization risk is driven by altered intestinal microbiota. Despite reduced dietary protein intake, intestinal amino acid content was maintained in PD-fed mice, supporting optimal HR-Kp growth. Furthermore, secondary bile acids, prototypic intestinal microbiota-derived molecules, were reduced in PD-fed mice, demonstrated an inverse correlation with HR-Kp burden in vivo, and partially inhibited the growth of HR-Kp in vitro. Collectively, these findings reveal a role for dietary protein intake in determining nutrition-dependent colonization resistance to HR-Kp.IMPORTANCEAntimicrobial-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae are responsible for a growing mortality burden worldwide, with disproportionate rates of infection in low-income countries where childhood malnutrition is prevalent. Several publications have demonstrated high rates of intestinal colonization with antimicrobial-resistant K. pneumoniae in children admitted with severe malnutrition in sub-Saharan Africa. However, numerous confounding risk factors in malnourished children (antibiotic use, healthcare exposure, and immune dysfunction) make it difficult to assess the direct impact of nutrition on K. pneumoniae colonization. In this study, we utilized a novel mouse model of protein malnutrition to demonstrate that dietary protein deficiency renders mice susceptible to a higher burden of intestinal colonization at a lower inoculating dose of K. pneumoniae. Furthermore, reduced microbiota-derived bile acid metabolites correlate with increased burden of colonization in protein-deficient mice. These results are the first to establish a direct mechanistic link associating dietary protein deficiency, bile acid metabolism, and intestinal colonization with antimicrobial-resistant K. pneumoniae.

Activity of manogepix and comparator antifungal agents against uncommon filamentous fungal isolates collected in a global surveillance program.
Fosmanogepix (prodrug of manogepix) is a novel antifungal agent targeting the Gwt1 enzyme. This agent has activity against a diverse spectrum of fungal species, including species refractory to other antifungal classes or multidrug-resistant fungi. A total of 332 molds from a worldwide surveillance study were susceptibility tested for manogepix and comparator antifungal agents by the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) reference broth microdilution method. Wild-type upper limit (WT-UL) values were determined for manogepix against organism groups using cumulative surveillance data. Isolates were collected from 20 countries, 41 hospitals, and 7 different infection sources. Eighteen genera were represented. Isolates included 208 non-fumigatus Aspergillus spp.; 37.3% (124 isolates) were non-Aspergillus molds. The manogepix minimum effective concentration (MEC50/90) was lower than the MIC50/90 for azole comparators or amphotericin B against all Aspergillus spp., Fusarium spp., Scedosporium spp., Lomentospora spp., Mucor spp., and Penicillium spp. Only Rhizopus spp. had higher MEC50/90 values for manogepix than the MIC50/90 values of the comparators. The WT-UL values reflected this, with the highest values for Rhizopus spp. at 16 mg/L and Mucor spp. at 4 mg/L, while they were ≤0.12 mg/L for all other organisms. Between 2023 and 2024, there were no organisms with MECs for manogepix above the WT-UL value. Manogepix displayed robust in vitro activity against contemporary non-Aspergillus fumigatus mold isolates. This agent was more potent than azole comparators or amphotericin B against most organism groups. Historically, less than 5% of isolates tested (n = 19) had MECs above the WT-UL cutoff values. These data support the continued development of manogepix for the treatment of mold infections.IMPORTANCEFosmanogepix (prodrug of manogepix) is a novel antifungal agent with a new mechanism of action and broad-spectrum activity, including against yeasts and molds. It is currently in two Phase 3 clinical trials for the treatment of invasive candidiasis and invasive mold infections and has previously been used for the treatment of Fusarium spp. infections during an outbreak. There are three main antifungal classes (echinocandins, azoles, and polyenes), but only azoles and amphotericin B have activity against non-Aspergillus molds; therefore, novel antifungal agents are urgently needed because invasive fungal infections have high morbidity and mortality rates. Here, we look at the in vitro activity of manogepix and comparator antifungal agents against non-Aspergillus fumigatus mold isolates collected from patient infections in 2023 and 2024. Manogepix showed potent in vitro activity against these organisms, with similar to or better activity than that of the comparators against most organism groups, and represents a promising potential future treatment option.

A novel mycovirus identified in clinical isolates of Cryptococcus neoformans.
Mycoviruses are widespread throughout the fungal kingdom and are known to infect diverse fungal taxa, including fungal species that are important plant and human pathogens. Although many mycoviruses have been found to have minimal effects on their host, several viruses have been found to modulate fungal physiology, and, as a result, impact fungal virulence. Screens for mycoviruses in clinically relevant fungi have identified numerous mycoviruses within several important human pathogens, but mycoviruses remain uncharacterized in the clinically relevant human pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans. C. neoformans is an opportunistic encapsulated yeast responsible for life-threatening cryptococcal meningitis, a leading cause of mortality among immunocompromised individuals, particularly those with HIV/AIDS. We performed a search for viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP) signatures in publicly available C. neoformans transcriptomic data. This search identified Totiviridae viral genomes within six clinical isolates of C. neoformans from Botswana. All six isolates originated from the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of HIV-positive individuals with cryptococcal meningitis. Reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR) independently validated the continued presence of the virus in three of these clinical isolates. Subsequent analysis of the viral genome identified two genotypes of a single species of Totivirus. This new species possesses canonical features of the Totiviridae family, including a slippery heptamer and a predicted RNA pseudoknot structure involved in programmed -1 ribosomal frameshifting for RdRP expression. Taken together, these results provide evidence of a mycovirus capable of infecting C. neoformans.IMPORTANCEWe report the identification of a mycovirus capable of infecting Cryptococcus neoformans. While mycoviruses inhabit diverse fungal taxa, they have previously remained uncharacterized in this clinically significant fungal pathogen. The identification of the mycoviruses within C. neoformans isolated from the cerebrospinal fluid of individuals with cryptococcal meningitis places emphasis on the potential role of mycoviruses in the pathogenesis of C. neoformans.

The presence of Histoplasma capsulatum in environments from the state of Nayarit, Mexico, reveals a potential risk of infection for human populations.
The Histoplasma capsulatum complex clusters cryptic species with genetic diversities linked to their geographic distribution and virulence. The American continent harbours its highest diversity, making this region the main axis for H. capsulatum spread. Species of this complex cause respiratory-systemic mycosis known as histoplasmosis. Infection occurs through the inhalation of fungal propagules that grow in sites such as caves, mines, and abandoned buildings, where environments rich in organic matter containing micronutrients present in bat and bird guano favour the development of these fungal pathogens. This research was conducted in the state of Nayarit, Mexico, where the combination of environmental factors and the constant occurrence of bats in urban and rural areas contributes to the proliferation of H. capsulatum. The presence of the fungus was detected by nested-PCR using a specific marker (Hcp100) for H. capsulatum, either in guano or in bat organ samples collected in the municipalities of Tepic, Santa María del Oro (SAMAO), and La Yesca, Nayarit. Out of 27 guano samples analysed by nested-PCR, 21 were positive for H. capsulatum, while of the 12 bats studied, only five revealed infections. The fungus was isolated from a lung sample of a nectarivorous bat (Glossophaga mutica) by culture. The results suggest a potential risk to exposed populations, including different specialized workers and tourists who explored bat roosts. Avoiding guano accumulation, restricting access to bat roosts, and implementing bat-exclusion strategies in homes are general recommendations to prevent fungal infections.

Respiratory mortality in prisons during the 1918-1919 influenza pandemic.
Prisons are among the most controlled human environments, and prisoners often suffer epidemic disease when influenza is introduced into these restricted populations. A review of contemporary records of five prison systems during the 1918-1919 influenza pandemic showed that most prison populations did remarkably well under lockdown, with few resulting respiratory deaths. Exceptional prisons with high respiratory mortality included the Andaman Islands prison colony (17.3/1000) and the US Army Disciplinary Barracks (42/1000) at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. Factors that likely resulted in high respiratory mortality included the absence of earlier waves of influenza-like illness and increased prisoner turnover introducing additional respiratory bacteria strains. Prison staff often had influenza rates that were very different to those of the prisoners they were guarding. Although free populations resented social restrictions during the COVID-19 pandemic, controlling population movements can serve to limit respiratory pathogen spread while waiting for alternative public health measures such as immunisations to arrive.

Management Strategies and Clinical Outcomes of Methicillin Resistant Staphylococcus Aureus Native Vertebral Osteomyelitis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
BACKGROUND CONTEXT: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a major cause of native vertebral osteomyelitis (NVO) and is associated with persistent infection, complications, prolonged hospitalization, and increased mortality. PURPOSE: We conducted this systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the antimicrobial and surgical approaches used for MRSA NVO and their associated clinical outcomes. STUDY SETTING: Systematic review and meta-analysis. METHODS: A systematic literature search of MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science was conducted on November 27, 2025. Studies were eligible if they included adults with MRSA NVO, evaluated medical or surgical treatment strategies, reported clinical outcomes, and included at least five patients. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data. Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and the Murad et al. tool. Random-effects models were used to pool proportions of treatment success, reinfection, and mortality. RESULTS: Thirty studies including 677 patients were included. Treatment strategies were heterogeneous and included prolonged anti-MRSA antimicrobial therapy and surgical approaches ranging from debridement and drainage to decompression and spinal stabilization or fusion. Vancomycin-based regimens were the most frequently reported antimicrobial strategy. Among studies reporting treatment duration, intravenous therapy commonly ranged from 4 to 8 weeks, with some patients receiving oral step-down or suppressive therapy.
