METHODS: A cross-sectional study was conducted among residents of a rural community. Serum samples from 90 residents were tested for anti-HEV immunoglobulin G. Participants completed structured questionnaires and residential addresses were georeferenced to evaluate exposures and spatial distribution. RESULTS: Rural residents reported greater exposure to homemade pork and wild boar sausages, wastewater, untreated well water, agricultural settings, livestock, rodents and flood-prone areas compared with levels previously documented in the urban population of the same region. The overall seroprevalence was 23.3% (95% confidence interval 14.0 to 32.6). Age and history of constipation were related with seropositivity. Rodent presence was more frequent in households of seropositive individuals, while feline contact coincided with reduced rodent occurrence. Spatial analysis identified one high-risk cluster (71.4% [5/7], p>0.05) of seropositivity and one low-risk cluster (0% [0/14], p>0.05), the latter corresponding to areas where contact with felines is greater. CONCLUSIONS: HEV exposure may be substantial in this Argentine rural community, supporting the need for integrated One Health surveillance targeting sanitation, reservoirs and food safety. Larger studies are warranted to validate these findings and better define transmission pathways.

Preferences for treatment for latent tuberculosis infection in primary care among people in the USA at increased risk of tuberculosis: a pilot survey.
OBJECTIVES: Tuberculosis (TB) in the USA disproportionately affects non-US-born individuals. While testing this population for TB infection is recommended, little is known about individuals’ willingness to take treatment for latent TB infection (LTBI). To understand which factors and perspectives around TB and LTBI treatment most influence individuals’ willingness to take LTBI treatment, we conducted a pilot preference survey among individuals from countries with high TB incidence. DESIGN: Cross-sectional survey supported by language concordant community health workers. SETTING: Consecutive recruitment at a federally qualified health centre, serving a primarily Asian immigrant community, in San Francisco. PARTICIPANTS: Adults seeking primary care, eligible for risk-based LTBI testing based on place of birth. OUTCOME MEASURES: Perspectives on TB disease, risk of reinfection, and willingness to accept treatment if diagnosed with LTBI conditional on different factors, such as side effects, costs and other treatment burden. RESULTS: Among 60 participants, the median age was 48 years (IQR 35–63 years), 52% were women and 100% spoke Chinese. Infecting others (n=35, 58%), risk of death (n=30, 50%) and potential isolation (n=25, 42%) were the most worrisome consequences of TB disease. Reinfection risk, risk of liver damage, cost, TB progression risk, clinic visits and blood draws were most often rated moderately or very important when considering LTBI treatment (n=53 to 57, 88–95%). While most participants (n=56, 93%) were willing to take treatment if diagnosed with LTBI even at a 10-year TB progression risk below 1% and willing to accept a risk of liver damage (n=41, 68%), less than half would accept LTBI treatment if there were any associated cost (n=28, 47%). Finally, many participants had concerns about their reinfection risk after completing LTBI treatment (n=34, 57%). CONCLUSIONS: Among surveyed participants, TB disease and its consequences such as hospitalisation, death and infecting others were worrisome, and participants had a high level of willingness to take treatment if diagnosed with LTBI. Future assessments of how people weigh trade-offs regarding LTBI diagnosis and treatment could inform interventions to increase LTBI treatment acceptance and completion.

Novel Target for Pathogenic Leptospira Detection via Colorimetric Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP): Development, Validation, and Comparative Analysis.
BACKGROUND: Leptospirosis is a globally prevalent zoonotic disease that remains challenging to diagnose due to its nonspecific symptoms and the limitations of current diagnostic methods and targets. To address these challenges, we developed and validated a naked-eye loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) assay targeting the newly identified orpH region for the rapid detection of pathogenic Leptospira species. METHODS: Comparative genomic analysis identified orpH as a conserved sequence among pathogenic Leptospira. A colorimetric LAMP assay (LAMP-orpH) was developed and evaluated using reference strains and serum samples obtained from patients with suspected leptospirosis. The diagnostic performance of the assay on these serum samples was evaluated in comparison with conventional PCR and the microscopic agglutination test (MAT), with the real-time PCR assay targeting lipL32 designated as the reference standard. RESULTS: The LAMP-orpH assay demonstrated 87.2% sensitivity and 94.8% specificity among 76 suspected cases and 29 controls, showing strong agreement with real-time PCR (κ = 0.826). It outperformed MAT (63.8% sensitivity) and conventional PCR (23.4% sensitivity), achieving a detection limit of 102 cells/mL in spiked serum. CONCLUSION: The LAMP-orpH assay offers a rapid, sensitive, and specific tool for early leptospirosis diagnosis. Its simple colorimetric readout and minimal equipment requirements make it ideal for use in rural and resource-limited settings, providing a practical alternative to MAT, conventional PCR, and qPCR.

FDG-PET in Infection Imaging of Immuno-compromised Patients.
Infectious syndromes represent a monumental challenge in the management of immunocompromised patients, directly driving high rates of morbidity and critical mortality. This clinical cohort comprised oncological populations undergoing aggressive cytoreductive chemotherapy, end-stage renal disease patients dependent on specialized long-term dialysis access networks, and individuals undergoing treatment with advanced antiretroviral regimens. Because these individuals suffer from blunted or suppressed cellular immune mechanisms, standard structural imaging methodologies (such as standard digital radiography and cross-sectional computed tomography) exhibit prolonged diagnostic latency, frequently remaining negative or ambiguous during the crucial early windows of active pathogen replication.

Identifying overlooked factors associated with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis: an ecological study across 201 countries and regions, 1990-2021.
BACKGROUND: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) is a critical global health challenge. Whether environmental, nutritional, and socioeconomic factors are associated with MDR-TB remains insufficiently investigated. METHODS: We analyzed outcome and exposure data from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) Study and four additional databases covering 201 countries and territories from 1990 to 2021; the primary analyses included 4,019 country-years from 186 countries. Sex ratio, diabetes prevalence, and HIV/AIDS burden were regressed out of each outcome before analysis. Every candidate exposure was then both regressed against the confounder-adjusted outcome and correlated with it. Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted P values, together with correlation strength, determined which factors were retained for display. Effects are expressed as the absolute change per interquartile range (IQR) increase in exposure. Drug-susceptible tuberculosis served as a control outcome. RESULTS: Per IQR of exposure, unsafe sanitation was associated with 13.9 more prevalent cases per 100,000 (95% CI 13.0-14.7) and 2.87 more deaths per 100,000 (2.72-3.03); unsafe water source with 11.2 (10.5-12.0) and 2.64 (2.49-2.78); and polluting fuels for cooking with 10.7 (9.8-11.6) and 2.74 (2.58-2.89). After further adjustment for GDP per capita and health expenditure, six of the thirteen principal exposures remained significantly associated with MDR-TB prevalence, including unsafe sanitation, unsafe water source, absence of handwashing facilities and underweight (e.g., unsafe sanitation 2.8 per 100,000 per IQR, P < 0.001). Most of these associations were stronger for drug-susceptible disease than for MDR-TB, with the exception of diet low in fruits. CONCLUSIONS: Unsafe sanitation, unsafe water source, and polluting fuels for cooking are the population-level factors most strongly associated with MDR-TB burden. These associations are largely shared with drug-susceptible tuberculosis, supporting their integration into tuberculosis control efforts as a whole.

Genomic epidemiology reveals niche specialization and a virulence-resistance trade-off in ST23 and ST11 hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae.
OBJECTIVES: The convergence of hypervirulence and carbapenem resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae poses a critical public health threat, yet the comparative genomic characteristics and adaptation patterns of dominant clones ST23 and ST11 in clinical settings remain unclear. This study aimed to characterize their divergent adaptive strategies. METHODS: We performed whole-genome sequencing on 824 hvKP isolates derived from 2,193 clinical Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates collected at a National Regional Medical Center in Central China. Among these, ST23 (n=199) and ST11 (n=140) represented the two predominant sequence types and were compared regarding antimicrobial resistance profiles, resistance determinants, virulence determinants, plasmid replicon types, and phylogenetic relationships using comparative genomic, phylogenetic, and co-acquisition analyses. RESULTS: ST23-hvKP was primarily associated with surgical and medical departments, largely antibiotic-susceptible (MDR 33.7%, CR 1.0%), with near-complete virulence gene profiles (iuc 99.5%, iro 97.5%). Conversely, ST11-hvKP was predominantly ICU-associated and extensively drug-resistant (MDR 97.9%, CR 93.6%), characterized by frequent blaKPC-2 carriage (95.7%) and a highly prevalent IncFII(pHN7A8) replicon (98.6%), with blaKPC-2 strongly associated with IncFII(pHN7A8), but with an incomplete virulence profile (iro 0.7%). Resistance-hypervirulence convergence was markedly higher in ST11 (92.1%) than ST23 (9.5%). Plasmid ecology and co-acquisition analysis revealed a negative correlation between resistance-associated (IncFII/IncR) and virulence-associated (IncFIB(K)) replicons, suggesting that convergence in ST11 involves coexisting distinct plasmid systems rather than detectable plasmid fusion events. Phylogenetic analysis demonstrated distinct clustering patterns between ST23 and ST11. CONCLUSIONS: ST23 retains a classic hypervirulent phenotype, whereas ST11 represents a hospital-adapted convergent clone characterized by a complex resistome, an incomplete canonical virulence repertoire, and separate plasmid systems. This niche-specialized resistance-virulence trade-off underscores the need for clone-tailored surveillance and management strategies.

Construction, expression, and immunogenicity analysis of a fusion gene based on the PE/PPE family in combination with adjuvants.
Tuberculosis (TB) remains the leading global cause of death from a single infectious agent and a major fatal infectious disease worldwide. However, the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine-currently the only licensed TB vaccine in clinical practice-has critical limitations in preventing latent infection and disease reactivation, failing to deliver comprehensive protective immunity. Given these gaps, targeting Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M.tb) antigens with strong immunogenic potential is a key strategy for next-generation TB vaccine development. The pathogenic M.tb harbors the Pro-Glu (PE) and Pro-Pro-Glu (PPE) motif gene families, named for their N-terminal conserved proline (P) and glutamic acid (E) residues, which are increasingly recognized as promising vaccine targets due to their roles in host-pathogen interaction and immune modulation. To address BCG's limitations, this study selected the PE/PPE family members Rv0832 and Rv3653 for full-length gene synthesis to construct a fusion antigen designated ZMM6, which was expressed using the pET-28a vector. The immunogenicity of the ZMM6 subunit vaccine was then evaluated in M.tb-infected human cohorts and animal models. The results showed that the fusion protein ZMM6 induced peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from M. tb-infected individuals to secrete high levels of IFN-γ, IL-2, and IL-6 cytokines. Moreover, the levels of cytokine secretion induced by the fusion protein were higher than those induced by the individual subunit proteins, suggesting that the fusion protein possesses higher immunogenicity. In mice immunized with the protein vaccine (adjuvant formulation) ZMM6/MnJ, high titers of various IgG subclass antibodies were elicited, with the immune response skewed toward a Th1-type profile, accompanied by robust induction of multiple Th1-type cytokines. Flow cytometry (FCM) analysis further revealed a significant increase in CD4+IFN-γ+ single-positive T cells in ZMM6/MnJ-immunized mice. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the protein vaccine (adjuvant formulation) ZMM6/MnJ exhibits strong immunogenicity.

Genomic surveillance-guided phage repository construction and rational cocktail design for carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae.
OBJECTIVES: Given the treatment delays inherent in reactive phage matching, we aimed to develop a preparedness-oriented strategy linking genomic surveillance of carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) to targeted phage-resource development and rational cocktail design. METHODS: We analysed >64,000 K. pneumoniae genomes to characterize the geographical and temporal representation of KL types within the genomic dataset. Phages were isolated and prioritized according to host-range profiles, genomic nonredundancy, receptor-binding protein diversity and morphology. Quantitative inhibition profiling and principal component analysis guided the selection of candidate combinations targeting KL64 isolates, followed by in vitro, in vivo, and resistance analyses. RESULTS: A limited number of KL types were frequently represented among the analysed CRKP genomes and showed regional variation. From a nonredundant repository of 33 phages, 10 were selected to target 10 frequently represented KL types. In a KL64 clinical isolate panel, selected combinations broadened and prolonged bacterial suppression. The phage cocktail significantly prolonged survival in mice under lethal CRKP challenge and phage-resistant derivatives showed restored susceptibility to multiple antibiotics. CONCLUSIONS: This study presents a framework for using genomic data to prioritize phage-resource development and guide cocktail design for KL-defined CRKP groups.

Shelter dogs harbor diverse tick species and demonstrate high exposure to tick-borne pathogens in a zone of tick range expansion.
OBJECTIVE: To characterize ticks and tick-borne pathogens (TBPs) among Ohio shelter dogs and identify factors associated with canine exposure. METHODS: This cross-sectional study included dogs admitted to an Ohio shelter partner between January 2020 and January 2021. Paired tick and blood samples were collected at intake. Ticks were identified and tested for TBPs by PCR; dogs underwent serologic testing and PCR. Logistic regression assessed associations between demographic and clinical variables and seropositivity. RESULTS: A total of 273 dogs were enrolled. Four tick species, including Haemaphysalis longicornis, were found on 22% of dogs. Overall, 43.9% were seropositive for ≥ 1 TBP and 24% for multiple TBPs. Seroprevalence was highest for Borrelia burgdorferi (33.5%) followed by Ehrlichia spp (24.4%) and Rickettsia spp (19.8%). Few dogs were PCR positive, and clinical signs were uncommon (3.7%). Tick PCR detected several relevant pathogens. Tick presence and host factors were associated with increased odds of seropositivity. CONCLUSIONS: Ohio shelter dogs demonstrate high exposure to diverse TBPs despite few PCR-positive results and infrequent clinical signs. Paired testing of dogs and attached ticks provides integrated information relevant to veterinary and public health surveillance in a region experiencing increasing tick abundance and pathogen prevalence. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Tick presence at intake may help prioritize testing when universal screening is infeasible. Rickettsia seropositivity should be interpreted cautiously because serologic cross-reactivity complicates clinical interpretation and species-level attribution.

Antimicrobial resistance and antibiotic therapy in patients with urinary tract infections and asymptomatic bacteriuria: A Peruvian perspective.
Overdiagnosis and overtreatment of urinary tract infections (UTIs) and asymptomatic bacteriuria (AB) increase antimicrobial resistance. The aim of this study was to evaluate resistance patterns and antibiotic therapy in patients with UTIs and AB in Peru. Cross-sectional study based on 164 urine cultures and antimicrobial susceptibility testing. A total of 62 cases of AB and 102 of UTI were identified. Women (116, 70.7%) and older adults (60, 36.6%) predominated. A total of 4582 antibiotic prescriptions were recorded, with a therapeutic pattern in both UTI and AB centered on the use of meropenem (540, 21.3%) and (333, 16.3%), vancomycin (221, 8.7%) and (454, 22.2%), ceftriaxone (369, 14.5%) and (176, 8.6%) and ceftazidime (227, 8.9%) and (274, 3.4%), respectively. In general, antibiotic therapy was bactericidal in (87, 53.0%) cases, from the surveillance group in (98, 59.8%) cases, monotherapy in (112, 68.3%) cases, and in cycles of ≤7 days. UTI was associated with a higher burden of comorbidities, including chronic renal failure, hypertension, and diabetes. Fifteen bacterial species were isolated in both clinical entities, with a predominance of Gram-negative bacilli, mainly Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae, both of which exhibited high resistance to cephalosporins, sulfonamides, and ampicillin/sulbactam. Among Gram-positive bacteria, Enterococcus faecalis and E. faecium showed resistance to erythromycin, tetracycline, and quinolones. The widespread use of antibiotics from the surveillance group and similar antibiotic therapy in AB and UTI, revealed a critical gap in the implementation of clinical guidelines and the urgent need to accurately differentiate between the two diagnoses to avoid overprescribing and help contain bacterial resistance.

Maternal vaccination with capsular polysaccharide bioconjugates protects against murine Klebsiella pneumoniae neonatal sepsis.
Klebsiella pneumoniae is the leading cause of neonatal sepsis in low- and middle-income countries and the foremost cause of infectious deaths in young children. K. pneumoniae isolates are becoming increasingly resistant to antibiotics, creating a great need for additional therapies or preventative strategies. Maternal vaccination serves as an attractive approach to protect from K. pneumoniae neonatal sepsis. Herein, we report a murine model of maternal immunization followed by pup challenge to evaluate putative K. pneumoniae vaccines. Dams were immunized with capsular polysaccharide bioconjugate vaccines at mating and boosted with two different immunization schedules throughout the gestational period. After parturition, offspring were tested for antigen-specific antibody levels and later challenged with a lethal dose of K. pneumoniae. Pups born to dams immunized with K1- and K2-conjugate vaccines demonstrated significant protection from sepsis relative to control pups. Antibodies transferred from vaccinated dams persisted and remained protective in pups for at least six weeks after birth. Collectively these results demonstrate a feasible and reproducible murine model of maternal immunization verifying the efficacy of bioconjugate vaccines in protecting against lethal neonatal K. pneumoniae infection.

Integrative multi-omics reveals CUL4B as a modulator of macrophage pyroptosis and innate defense against Staphylococcus aureus.
Staphylococcus aureus (SA) causes a broad range of invasive human diseases, increasingly complicated by antibiotic resistance. Macrophages (MΦ) play a central role in innate immunity, yet key aspects of their interaction with SA remain incompletely understood because of the pathogen's diverse immune evasion strategies. Using multi-omics and systems-level analytics, we identified the E3 ubiquitin ligase cullin 4B (CUL4B) as a host factor that modulates MΦ responses to SA infection. CRISPR-mediated deletion of CUL4B in human THP-1 MΦ enhanced intracellular bacterial killing, reduced cell death, decreased caspase-1 activation, and lowered interleukin-1β production, consistent with altered inflammasome signaling. In a murine methicillin-resistant SA (MRSA) pneumonia model, CUL4B deficiency improved pulmonary bacterial clearance, reduced bacteremia, and decreased inflammatory tissue injury. Whole-lung and serum proteomics further revealed increased antimicrobial protein abundance and reduced markers of inflammatory damage. Together, these findings identify CUL4B as a regulator of MΦ inflammatory responses during MRSA infection and suggest a potential host-directed pathway that could be leveraged to improve outcomes against this major pathogen.

Subnational spatial co-distribution of tuberculosis and diabetes mellitus across Ghana's 16 regions following administrative reorganisation: An ecological analysis.
BACKGROUND: National administrative boundary reorganisations, increasingly common across sub-Saharan Africa, create discontinuities in surveillance data alignment that complicate subnational burden estimation for infectious and non-communicable diseases alike. Ghana's expansion from 10 to 16 administrative regions in 2019 provides a tractable case for demonstrating how publicly available surveillance and survey data can be used to characterise subnational co-distribution of tuberculosis and diabetes mellitus (DM) under a revised boundary structure. DM is an established risk factor for active TB, yet population-level evidence on their geographic co-distribution at the subnational level in West Africa remains scarce, and no prior study has characterised this co-distribution at the subnational level across Ghana's current 16-region structure-a gap this study addresses directly by leveraging the post-2019 administrative framework to generate region-specific evidence for programme planning. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional ecological analysis using 16 administrative regions in Ghana as the unit of analysis. TB case notification rates (per 100,000 population, 2022) were obtained from the Ghana Health Service's DHIMS2, with the Ministry of Health 2022 Holistic Assessment and WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2025 used as independent consistency checks. Regional DM prevalence estimates were drawn from the Ghana STEPS 2017 survey and published scoping literature. Sociodemographic covariates included urbanisation, a DHS-derived wealth index, mean body mass index, and smoking prevalence. Spatial autocorrelation was assessed using Moran's I with queen contiguity weights. Bivariate associations were estimated using Spearman and Pearson correlations. Negative binomial regression with log-population offset examined the adjusted association between DM prevalence and TB notification rates. A sensitivity analysis excluded the three regions created by the 2019 reorganisation. RESULTS: TB notification rates ranged from 18.9 to 58.3 per 100,000 (mean 32.0, SD 10.1) and DM prevalence from 1.8% to 6.3% (mean 3.5%, SD 1.3). DM prevalence showed moderate positive spatial autocorrelation (Moran's I = 0.40, p = 0.004); TB notification rates did not (Moran's I = -0.16, p = 0.272). Bivariate correlation between the two outcomes was moderately positive (Spearman rho = 0.638, p = 0.008; Pearson r = 0.762, p = 0.0006). In adjusted negative binomial regression, DM prevalence showed a positive but statistically imprecise point estimate (IRR = 3.62; 95% CI: 0.47 to 27.9; p = 0.217), consistent with limited power at n = 16 ecological units. CONCLUSIONS: DM prevalence shows moderate positive spatial autocorrelation across Ghana's 16 regions, concentrated in the southern urban belt, and is moderately correlated with TB notification rates at the regional level; TB notification rates themselves did not show significant spatial clustering when tested with real-boundary contiguity weights, elevated TB notification alongside low DM prevalence, suggests that drivers other than DM dominate in that zone and that uniform national TB-DM programme approaches may be suboptimal. These methods and findings provide a reproducible template for subnational TB-DM surveillance in other post-reorganisation African programme contexts. Individual-level causal inference is not possible from this ecological design.

Identification and Characterization of Patient Populations at High Risk for Clostridioides difficile Infection (CDI): A Narrative Review.
Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) is a major cause of infections worldwide and can lead to life-threatening complications and a severe impact on patients' quality of life (QoL). CDI can affect anyone, but it is generally accepted that those at greatest risk include people receiving antibiotics, of older age, and with a compromised immune system. However, beyond these broad categories, specific populations at high risk for CDI are not clearly defined. We performed a literature search to identify and characterize patients at high risk for CDI. We found that those at high risk for CDI include patients undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplant, solid organ transplant or chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy, or with chronic kidney disease/end-stage kidney disease, hematological malignancies or inflammatory bowel disease, or who are older and frail with comorbidities. In the identified patient populations, CDI was associated with significantly worse clinical outcomes, increased healthcare resource utilization and costs, and generally an increased risk of mortality compared with those without CDI. Patients at high risk for CDI have multiple risk factors for infection that further complicate management of their disease. Apart from older patients, there is a lack of information on the impact on QoL in high-risk populations. Prevention strategies for CDI in high-risk populations are lacking and are based on the general population. As such, there is a need to increase understanding of those at high risk for CDI and the significant impact infection has in these populations, and to identify preventive therapies to alleviate the burden on both patients and healthcare systems.

The PVL threat: A multicenter, single-cohort retrospective study of Panton-Valentine leukocidin staphylococcal infections in critically ill children.
UNLABELLED: Staphylococcus aureus carrying the Panton-Valentine leukocidin (PVL) genes, in both methicillin-susceptible (MSSA) and methicillin-resistant (MRSA) strains, causes severe infection in previously healthy children. We described critically ill children with PVL-positive infection and explored predictors of prolonged intensive care. In this multicenter, single-cohort retrospective study, we included 44 consecutive children aged 0-16 years with PVL-producing S. aureus infection admitted to a neonatal or pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) at 13 Italian centers between 2022 and 2025. The primary outcome was PICU stay above the cohort median. We used Fisher exact tests and exploratory Firth penalized logistic regression, overall and within age strata, with sensitivity analyses. Median age was 22 months (interquartile range [IQR] 11-123); 5 children (11%) were neonates. MSSA caused 25 cases (57%) and MRSA 19 (43%). Necrotizing pneumonia predominated, with excavation in 34 children (77%). Empyema (52%), acute respiratory distress syndrome (41%), pneumothorax (36%) and septic shock (34%) were the leading complications; 41 children (93%) required respiratory support and 4 (9%) extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Median PICU stay was 17 days (IQR 10-28); 2 children died (5%). Septic shock was associated with prolonged stay (odds ratio 7.2; 95% CI 1.5-49.3), also after adjustment in children ≥ 1 year (adjusted odds ratio 8.0; 95% CI 1.3-49.8), with consistent but imprecise sensitivity analyses. CONCLUSION: PVL-producing S. aureus caused life-threatening infection at all pediatric ages. Methicillin resistance was not associated with prolonged stay, supporting PVL testing of S. aureus isolates from critically ill children. Predictors of prolonged stay are exploratory and need prospective confirmation. WHAT IS KNOWN: • PVL-producing S. aureus causes necrotizing pneumonia and disseminated infection in previously healthy children. • Evidence rests largely on case reports and small series, and infants are underrepresented. WHAT IS NEW: • In 44 critically ill children, including 5 neonates, MSSA and MRSA produced comparable critical illness. • In exploratory analyses, septic shock was associated with prolonged intensive care; mortality was 5%.

Twenty-Four Month Clinical and Laboratory Follow-Up of Children Infected During a Shiga toxin-Producing Escherichia coli Outbreak.
BACKGROUND: Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) infections can cause significant long-term renal sequelae. Intermediate-term outcomes for patients who do not develop hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) remain unclear. We evaluated clinical and laboratory outcomes in children with laboratory-confirmed STEC O157 infection in a large childcare outbreak. METHODS: This prospective longitudinal cohort study enrolled children aged 9 months to <6 years attending childcare centers in Calgary, Alberta, Canada during an STEC outbreak in September 2023. Among cases, clinical presentation was categorized as: asymptomatic, mild-moderate (diarrhea, no HUS), and severe (HUS). Cases were STEC-infected children confirmed by stool molecular testing; controls were exposed children whose stool tested negative by the same method. Outcome measures assessed at 6-, 12-, and 24-months post-exposure included: general assessments, inflammatory markers, hematologic parameters, renal function, gastrointestinal outcomes, and cardiometabolic markers. RESULTS: Of 932 eligible children, 145 (16%) participated: 72 cases (4 asymptomatic, 59 mild-moderate infection, 9 HUS) and 73 controls. Median age was 3.3 (IQR: 2.3, 4.2) years. After adjustment for multiple comparisons, no laboratory parameters or clinical outcomes differed between groups at any timepoint. Functional gastrointestinal disorders occurred at similar rates across groups, except functional dyspepsia was more common among STEC-infected children at 6-month follow-up. At 24 months, median eGFRs were similar across groups. One of 9 (11%) children with HUS had proteinuria and hematuria at 24 months. CONCLUSIONS: Among children with STEC infection without HUS, no evidence of persistent clinical symptoms or laboratory abnormalities emerged during 24-month follow-up compared with controls, providing reassurance regarding intermediate-term outcomes.

blaIMP-4-associated imipenem susceptibility discordance in the Klebsiella pneumoniae complex: characterization and a phenotype-guided confirmatory workflow.
Automated antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) may generate carbapenem minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) results differing from reference methods, complicating recognition of carbapenemase-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae complex isolates. We characterized carbapenem susceptibility discordance in a retrospective discovery cohort of 133 carbapenemase-producing isolates collected in Shenzhen (2004-2017) by comparing imipenem (IPM) and meropenem (MEM) MICs obtained by VITEK 2 and broth microdilution (BMD). Confirmed discordance was defined as repeat-confirmed raw MIC differences of ≥2 log2 dilutions. Features were assessed by whole-genome sequencing, mCIM/eCIM, and exploratory phenotypic assays. Cross-card reproducibility was assessed using an alternative VITEK 2 AST card. A separate retrospectively enriched cohort of 166 K. pneumoniae isolates (2018-2024) was used to evaluate a phenotype-guided reflex-testing workflow. Twenty-nine isolates showed confirmed carbapenem AST discordance, including 28 with IPM discordance. Of these, 27 had raw VITEK 2 IPM MICs at least 2 log₂ dilutions higher than those obtained by BMD, whereas one was reported as resistant after system adjustment despite a low raw MIC. All discrepant isolates carried blaIMP-4 as the sole detected carbapenemase gene, had relatively low carbapenem MICs by BMD, and were distributed across 14 sequence types. Cross-card retesting reproduced the direction of IPM elevation, although the magnitude varied. In a combined internal analysis set of 275 isolates, the phenotype-guided workflow identified unflagged ≥2 log₂ MIC discrepancies with 81.4% sensitivity (95% CI, 67.4%-90.3%) and 92.2% specificity (95% CI, 88.1%-95.0%). These findings define a repeat-confirmed blaIMP-4-associated, IPM-predominant discordance between VITEK 2 and BMD and support phenotype-guided reflex-testing to identify unflagged MIC discrepancies and prioritize confirmatory testing in routine laboratories.IMPORTANCEClinical microbiology laboratories rely on automated systems to support antimicrobial susceptibility interpretation, but these systems may not always recognize method-dependent carbapenem susceptibility discordance. In this study, we show that a specific group of bacteria carrying the blaIMP-4 gene can produce potentially misleading carbapenem susceptibility results, particularly for imipenem, when tested by automated methods. These discrepancies may not be flagged by the instrument and could therefore be overlooked in routine practice. By combining routine laboratory data with genetic analysis and additional testing, we identify a recognizable pattern associated with these hidden discrepancies and examine a phenotype-guided confirmatory workflow to support their laboratory recognition. Our findings highlight the importance of targeted confirmatory testing and provide a framework for local validation of laboratory-actionable carbapenem susceptibility discrepancies, thereby supporting more reliable AST interpretation and antimicrobial resistance surveillance.

Invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella disease in the vaccine-development era: diagnostic blind spots, antimicrobial resistance, genomic transmission, and prevention.
SUMMARYInvasive non-typhoidal Salmonella (iNTS) disease is a severe bloodstream and focal invasive infection caused by non-typhoidal serovars of Salmonella enterica, especially S. Typhimurium and S. Enteritidis. Its clinical importance is disproportionate to its routine visibility because disease often presents as undifferentiated fever, sepsis, meningitis, severe anaemia-associated deterioration, recurrent bacteraemia, or focal infection, while definitive recognition depends on blood or other sterile-site microbiology. Global estimates indicate substantial mortality, but the true incidence remains uncertain because blood-culture access, prior antimicrobial exposure, specimen volume, and surveillance intensity vary widely. The vaccine-development era has intensified the need for a unified clinical microbiology framework. Prevention of invasive disease requires host-risk recognition, laboratory-confirmed endpoints, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, lineage-aware genomic surveillance, reservoir assessment, and post-introduction systems able to detect residual disease, breakthrough infection, non-target serovars, lineage shifts, and resistant invasive clones. This narrative review synthesizes the clinical, immunological, genomic, diagnostic, antimicrobial resistance, and vaccine era evidence relevant to iNTS control. Emphasis is placed on immune evasion, macrophage survival, T-cell dysfunction, immunosuppressed hosts, diagnostic blind spots, treatment under uncertainty, and the integration of laboratory systems with surveillance and prevention policy.

County-level differences in Salmonella incidence across urban and rural United States, 2011-2023.
Salmonella is a leading cause of foodborne illness in the United States, yet rural-urban differences in incidence and their underlying drivers remain poorly characterized. We conducted an ecological analysis of deidentified probable and confirmed Salmonella cases from the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System (NNDSS), 2011-2023, to evaluate temporal, regional, and population-level determinants of Salmonella incidence. Multivariable negative binomial models assessed rural-urban differences nationally and by U.S. Census region, and Blinder-Oaxaca decomposition quantified contributions of demographic, socioeconomic, healthcare access, and health-related factors. Age-adjusted incidence was consistently higher in rural than in urban counties. After adjustment, rural counties had higher incidence nationally and separately in all four regions (Northeast, Midwest, West, and South). County-level factors explained 66% of the national rural-urban gap, driven primarily by age structure, income, education, and food environment. Adults aged ≥65 years accounted for approximately 60% of the explained difference and were the dominant contributor in some regions. Regional variation was evident, with age predominating in the Midwest and West and education contributing more in the Northeast and South. A substantial unexplained component remained. These findings highlight persistent, regionally heterogeneous disparities and underscore the need for targeted, region-specific surveillance and prevention strategies.

Whole-Genome Sequencing-Based Characterization and Antimicrobial Resistance Analysis of Shiga Toxin-Producing Escherichia coli Isolated from Retail Meat Products.
Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC), a zoonotic foodborne pathogen, has become a critical global public health issue. This study investigates molecular traits and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) mechanisms of STEC strains derived from retail meat products sourced from domestic production in Liaocheng city, Shandong province, China, to inform health risk assessment. Using quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR), phenotypic AMR testing, and whole-genome sequencing (WGS), 38 STEC isolates were identified from 400 retail meat products, with an isolation rate of 9.5%. Significant differences in STEC isolation rates were detected among different meat types, and mutton exhibited a relatively high isolation rate of 26.09%. Genomic virulence analysis showed that there were higher proportions of single stx2 (58.33%) and dual stx1/stx2 genotypes (33.33%) in mutton isolates than in beef (stx2: 48.00%, dual stx1/stx2: 12.00%), and only the stx2 gene was found in pork isolates. STEC isolates exhibited marked serotypic diversity, including O128ac:H2, O168:H7, O178:H7, O2:H25, and O6:H10. Multilocus sequence typing analysis revealed heterogeneous sequence type (ST) distributions among isolates, with ST10, ST25, and ST2722 as dominant STs, suggesting diverse contamination sources. STEC isolates exhibited high phenotypic resistance to tetracycline (TET) (68.42%), which corresponded to the highest detection rate of the TET resistance gene tet(A) at the genomic level. All isolates were susceptible to ertapenem, meropenem, ceftazidime, ceftazidime-avibactam, ciprofloxacin, and amikacin. Multidrug resistance (MDR) analysis indicated that 16 STEC isolates were MDR strains, with beef-derived isolates having relatively high MDR rates. This study verifies the occurrence of STEC in retail meat, highlighting prevalent AMR and substantial genetic heterogeneity among isolates. The findings underscore the necessity of systematic surveillance to limit STEC transmission along the meat supply chain and facilitate targeted food safety interventions.

The emergence and spread of third-generation cephalosporin-resistant Neisseria Meningitidis in China.
Neisseria meningitidis is the causative agent of invasive meningococcal disease. Although third-generation cephalosporins remain the recommended empirical therapy, there has been a growing number of globally reported isolates with resistance. This study aims to elucidate the genetic and evolutionary mechanisms underlying third-generation cephalosporin resistance in N. meningitidis. Whole-genome sequencing and phenotypic antibiotic susceptibility testing were performed, and the potential resistance determinants, genomic features, and evolutionary trajectories of resistant strains were comprehensively characterized. Seven PBP2 mutation sites potentially associated with resistance were identified, including A311V, R468K, E469K, D/N472E, L/P480A, T483S, and G545S. Genomic analysis revealed that strains possessing these seven potential resistance determinant mutations emerged within the past two decades and exhibited an increasing trend. The majority of these strains were isolated from northern regions of China. The predominant mutation strains were located in mainly epidemic strains, like cc4821, cc23, serogroup B and serogroup Y, respectively. Systematic phylogenetic analysis revealed that there has been a phenomenon of cross-regional transmission. Three potential cross-regional transmission third-generation cephalosporin-resistant strain types were identified, namely cc4821-ST-8920-NEIS1753_3923-penA795, ST-14760-NEIS1753_3652-penA1357, and cc23-ST-18108-NEIS1753_5058-penA1258. This study systematically analyzed the phenotypic and genetic characteristics of third-generation cephalosporin-resistant N. meningitidis strains. It not only deepened the understanding of the resistance mechanism but also provided a scientific basis and practical guidance for rapid clinical detection, laboratory monitoring, as well as the prevention and control of cross-regional transmission risks.

Toxoplasmosis: Epidemiological Significance, Economic Burden, and Emerging Directions in Drug Discovery and Artificial Intelligence.
Toxoplasmosis, a parasitic disease caused by Toxoplasma gondii, affects a wide range of warm-blooded hosts and remains most prevalent in tropical regions, with distribution shaped by climate, cultural practices, and environmental conditions. Clinical severity varies across susceptible populations, generating substantial economic burdens through medical costs and agricultural losses. Given this global health impact, a comprehensive, up-to-date understanding of the disease is essential. However, significant gaps persist. While diagnostic techniques and epidemiological surveillance have advanced considerably, treatment protocols have remained largely unchanged for decades, revealing a disconnect between diagnostic innovation and therapeutic progress. Moreover, existing literature lacks an integrative synthesis connecting these advances to their broader significance, leaving researchers without a unified framework for understanding where the field stands and where it should go next. To address these gaps, this narrative review draws on peer-reviewed literature and institutional reports across major biomedical databases, synthesizing findings descriptively and thematically rather than through statistical meta-analysis. It critically examines toxoplasmosis across several dimensions. It first considers geographical distribution and the cultural, environmental, and economic factors shaping its epidemiology. It then turns to the parasite's biochemical and molecular characteristics, using this foundation to evaluate persistent limitations in treatment and vaccine development, an area where progress has stalled. In response, the review explores emerging alternatives, including plant-based compounds, as avenues beyond conventional pharmacological strategies. Finally, it examines artificial intelligence as an underexplored but promising tool for improving diagnosis and treatment, an area with limited application to toxoplasmosis specifically. By consolidating these threads, this review clarifies not only what is known about toxoplasmosis but also where critical gaps in treatment innovation and integrative understanding continue to hinder effective prevention and control.

Abattoir Surveillance of Suspected Cystic Echinococcosis in Cattle: Insights From Molecular Analysis in a Hypoendemic Area.
Cystic echinococcosis (CE) is a zoonotic disease of global public health impact. In hypoendemic regions, the epidemiological role of cattle as intermediate hosts remains unclear, and routine abattoir-based surveillance may overestimate prevalence due to diagnostic limitations. This study integrated a retrospective and prospective study of CE in cattle from the hypoendemic areas of Emilia-Romagna and Lombardy regions (northern Italy) based on postmortem surveillance at slaughterhouses. Retrospective data were analyzed over four years (2021-2024), and the prospective study was performed in 2025, combining macroscopic inspection with anatomopathological and molecular analyses to evaluate diagnostic accuracy. The retrospective analysis revealed a low mean prevalence of suspected CE (0.32%), while prospective evaluation showed an apparent prevalence of 0.08% based on macroscopic inspection. However, molecular analyses revealed the absence of Echinococcus granulosus and E. multilocularis DNA, while 50% of isolated lesions were caused by Taenia hydatigena. The integration of molecular diagnostics with in-depth anatomopathological evaluation improves diagnostic accuracy, reduces misclassification, and allows risk-targeted control strategies. Prioritizing confirmatory diagnostics and targeted interventions is recommended in a One Health approach.

Global trends in the burden of malaria: mapping the prevalence, incidence and mortality of Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax in the era of climate change and emerging drug resistance.
INTRODUCTION: Malaria remains a major global health challenge, with Plasmodium falciparum and P. vivax showing marked geographical and biological differences. Climate variability and change, antimalarial drug resistance, insecticide resistance and vector adaptation increasingly complicate malaria control and elimination. MATERIALS AND METHODS: We systematically reviewed evidence on the global epidemiology of P. falciparum and P. vivax, focusing on prevalence, incidence, mortality, geographical distribution, climate-related transmission, antimalarial drug resistance, insecticide resistance and vector adaptation. Searches of major bibliographic databases were complemented by authoritative malaria surveillance and modelling sources. Evidence was synthesised according to species, geographical region, epidemiological outcome, environmental determinants and resistance characteristics. RESULTS: Malaria burden showed substantial geographical heterogeneity, with P. falciparum predominating in sub-Saharan Africa and P. vivax contributing substantially outside this region. Temperature, precipitation and humidity influenced vector and parasite biology and transmission suitability, although projected climate-related changes remained subject to substantial uncertainty. Artemisinin and partner-drug resistance in P. falciparum, chloroquine resistance and radical-cure challenges in P. vivax, and insecticide resistance and behavioural adaptation in vectors emerged as major threats. DISCUSSION: Sustainable malaria elimination requires integrated, species-specific, resistance-informed and climate-sensitive strategies combining surveillance, effective treatment, adaptive vector control and resilient health systems.

Toxoplasma gondii prevention literacy and self-reported preventive practices among online respondents in China: a cross-sectional survey.
Toxoplasma gondii is a widespread zoonotic parasite, yet prevention literacy and protective practices among online respondents in China remain poorly characterized. We conducted a cross-sectional survey from April to November 2025 using a purpose-designed questionnaire distributed through WeChat and QQ. Knowledge and preventive-practice items contributed 23 and 10 points, respectively; a composite score of ≥20/33 represented meeting the prespecified 60% threshold. Among 622 valid respondents, 56.8% had heard of Toxoplasma gondii, the mean composite score was 14.22 ± 6.69, and 21.4% met the threshold. Undercooked meat consumption was reported by 8.2%. Separate utensils for raw and cooked foods were always used by 40.5%, sometimes by 45.2%, and never by 14.3%; 65.6% reported immediate handwashing after handling raw meat, whereas 31.2% did so inconsistently and 3.2% never did so. Regular or occasional contact with stray cats was reported by 31.4%, and 17.2% owned pets, predominantly cats. Among cat owners, 19.6% never sought veterinary care for their pets. In exploratory multivariable logistic regression, occupation remained associated with meeting the threshold; medical staff had higher odds than the reference group (adjusted odds ratio 3.39, 95% confidence interval 1.82-6.30). Short-video popular science was the most frequently reported information source, and 73.0% expressed moderate-to-high willingness to share health information. By jointly examining prevention literacy, practices, information channels, and dissemination willingness, this study provides a multidimensional baseline for toxoplasmosis education in China. The findings identify modifiable behavioral gaps and support evidence-based education that communicates foodborne, environmental, and cat-associated risks through short-video and social-media platforms.

Temperature seasonality and spatially structured variation in cutaneous leishmaniasis in Algeria: A source-verified national panel, 2000-2024.
Algeria carries one of the highest cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) burdens worldwide, yet the climatic structure of its provincial distribution has not been quantified nationally with year-specific covariates. We assembled a balanced panel of all 48 wilayas over 2000-2024 (1200 province-years), linking notified CL counts to annual ERA5-Land bioclimatic indicators, and verified the case series province-by-province against the primary national epidemiological bulletins. Counts were strongly overdispersed and modelled by negative binomial regression with a log-population offset and province-clustered standard errors, then extended with year fixed effects, a within-between decomposition, and BYM2 spatially structured area effects on a shared-border contiguity graph. Temperature seasonality was the dominant bioclimatic correlate (incidence rate ratio 4.28 per standard deviation, 95% CI 2.91-6.29) and the only term robust across non-spatial specifications, concentrated in the between-province component (7.64, 2.71-21.55) with no detectable within-province association (0.92, 0.77-1.10). Spatially structured area effects left the point estimate positive but its interval spanning the null (1.07, 0.93-1.22), confirmed by an independently coded full-posterior cross-check. Annual precipitation was inversely associated under naive standard errors but did not survive province clustering (p=0.063); precipitation seasonality was null under province-clustered inference, but showed a modest inverse association in its within-province component (0.90, 0.82-0.99) and under spatial adjustment (0.91, 0.83-0.98), an exploratory finding. Incidence declined 3.4% per year (0.966, 0.945-0.987), consistent with the separately curated World Health Organization series. The climatic signal in these data is a persistent geographical gradient that spatial adjustment substantially reshapes rather than an identified driver of year-to-year change.

Leishmania tarentolae as a potential disease-modifying agent in dogs infected with Leishmania infantum.
Canine leishmaniosis (CanL), by Leishmania infantum, is a global zoonotic disease with complex immune interactions. The non-pathogenic Leishmania tarentolae emerged as a candidate for immunoprophylaxis, yet in vivo evidence demonstrating natural cross-protection in dogs remains scarce. This experimental study evaluated the immunological and clinical outcomes of co-exposure to both parasites. Fourteen purposedly breed dogs were allocated into three groups: Group 1 (G1) and Group 2 (G2) were previously exposed to L. tarentolae, then challenged with L. infantum intravenously (G1) or intradermally (G2). Group 3 (G3) served as unimmunized L. infantum-infected control group, with three dogs challenged intravenously and two intradermally. Animals were longitudinally monitored for 13.5 months through clinical, molecular and serological assessments. While prior exposure to L. tarentolae did not confer sterilizing immunity against L. infantum, differences in clinicopathological and immunological parameters were observed among experimental groups. Unimmunized controls (G3) developed higher UPC values during the later stages of the study, whereas pre-exposed dogs (G1 and G2) generally showed lower UPC values, although considerable inter-individual variability was observed. The intravenous challenge group (G1) developed high parasite burdens, hyperglobulinemia, and inflammatory alterations, whereas intradermally challenged group (G2) showed comparatively lower parasite burdens and fewer clinicopathological alterations. Additionally, in vitro stimulation with L. infantum, on peripheral blood monocytic cells from pre-immunized dogs, revealed a cytokine profile characterized by intermittent pro-inflammatory activation and variable regulatory interleukin-10 expression (IL-10). Overall, this is the first study detailing the longitudinal clinicopathological and immunological profile of L. infantum infection in the canine model, which suggests that prior exposure to L. tarentolae may influence the subsequent course of L. infantum. Hence, further studies are advocated to investigate the potential disease-modifying effect herein observed.

Profile and classification of invasive fungal disease in patients with haematologic malignancies using microscopy, culture, biomarkers and polymerase chain reaction.
BACKGROUND: Invasive fungal diseases (IFDs) are significant causes of morbidity and mortality in patients with haematologic malignancies (HM). This study aimed to classify IFD using integrated diagnostic methods according to European Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer/Mycoses Study Group Education and Research Consortium (EORTC/MSGERC) criteria. METHODS: A prospective observational study was conducted in 100 adult HM patients not on antifungal prophylaxis. Diagnosis included microscopy, culture, galactomannan (GM) enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), Candida mannan immunoglobulin M (IgM) lateral flow assay (LFA), Aspergillus IgM assay, cryptococcal antigen LFA, (1,3)-β-D-glucan (BDG) assay and panfungal polymerase chain reaction (PCR), along with high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT). RESULTS: Probable IFD was observed in 51%, possible in 24%, proven in 12% and no IFD in 13%. Acute leukaemia predominated, with invasive aspergillosis (IA) and candidiasis being the most common infections. Fever was the most frequent presentation, while respiratory symptoms were associated with invasive aspergillosis. PCR showed the highest sensitivity (88.8%), followed by BDG (87.3%). Microscopy and culture were positive in 25% cases, Aspergillus fumigatus being the most common isolate. HRCT was normal in 56%, with ground-glass opacities and consolidation as the most frequent abnormalities. CONCLUSION: Integrated diagnostic approaches improve classification and early detection of IFD in HM patients and support timely antifungal management.

Proteome-based computational identification of cathepsin B as a TLR1/2-binding virulence factor in Naegleria fowleri and design of a novel multi-epitope vaccine candidate.
Primary Amoebic Meningoencephalitis (PAM), also known as Naegleriasis, has historically been rare but is re-emerging as a major public health concern. This acute, often fatal infection is caused by a free-living freshwater amoebic protozoan Naegleria fowleri, which invades the host central nervous system (CNS), inducing severe neuroinflammation. The immunopathogenesis of PAM remains poorly understood. Herein, the entire N. fowleri proteome was computationally analyzed, revealing Cathepsin B as a putative virulence factor with a potential to form a stable complex with human TLR1/2. This finding was further supported by molecular dynamics simulation analyses of the complex. Interestingly, Cathepsin B has been reported to mediate amoebic invasion of the host nasal mucosa, which reinforces our prediction. Based on these findings, a novel vaccine construct was designed using immunoreactive T and B cell epitopes from Cathepsin B and coupled with different TLR adjuvants. Computational analyses demonstrated the strong binding affinity of TLR4 adjuvant-coupled multi-epitope vaccine with TLR4, forming the most stable interactions. Theoretical immune simulation studies revealed that this vaccine elicits robust IgM and IgG responses upon triple administration, maintains B cell memory and triggers the expression of IFN-γ. Our data thus provide insight into the pathogenesis of PAM and offer a promising lead toward the development of an effective vaccine to combat the disease, which currently lacks reliable and effective treatments.

Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis as a poor prognostic factor in cystic fibrosis patients with atelectasis.
INTRODUCTION: Pulmonary atelectasis is the least studied pulmonary complication in cystic fibrosis (CF). The following objectives have been proposed: 1) to determine whether allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) acts as a factor associated with a poor prognosis in patients who subsequently developed atelectasis (decline in lung function, exacerbations, transplantation, lung surgery and death), 2) to identify factors associated with the onset of APBA prior to the diagnosis of atelectasis, 3) therapeutic management, and 4) the clinical and radiological course of both conditions in combination. PATIENTS AND METHODS: A longitudinal, retrospective, multicentre study involving 14 national cystic fibrosis (CF) specialist units, including cases of persistent atelectasis and a minimum follow-up of two years. Data were collected on anthropometric measurements, genetics, imaging tests, placement on the transplant list, lung transplantation/surgery or death, extrapulmonary comorbidities, other pulmonary complications (infectious or non-infectious), lung function closest to the onset of atelectasis (baseline) and the most recent recorded value, number of mild-to-moderate or severe exacerbations in the year prior to and following the atelectasis and in the final year of follow-up, medical treatment, indications for flexible bronchoscopy and subsequent course. RESULTS: 55 patients with atelectasis (3.9%; 95% CI=3-5.1) were included, with a mean age of 25±10 years. Thirteen patients had ABPA (23.9%). Patients with ABPA had a higher number of mild-to-moderate exacerbations in the year prior to developing atelectasis, as well as in the final year of follow-up; and a higher total number of exacerbations in the year before and after the complication. CONCLUSION: Patients with atelectasis who had previously presented with ABPA had a poorer prognosis due to an increase in exacerbations.

Proteotyping reactivant toxoplasmic encephalitis reveals virulence-associated dense granule protein GRA5 polymorphisms.
BACKGROUND: A fatal case of toxoplasmic encephalitis has caused microbiologists and clinicians to question whether different strains of Toxoplasma gondii have more pathogenic potential than others. This is concerning, as T. gondii is a widely spread parasite presumed to lie dormant in a third of the world's population. METHODS: Here, we expand on a previous proteomic analysis of toxoplasmosis and have identified T. gondii-specific peptides in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of three cases of toxoplasmic reactivation. Multilocus PCR-restriction fragment-length polymorphism (PCR-RFLP) genetically identified the T. gondii strain responsible for a fatal case as ToxoDB PCR-RFLP genotype #7. Using other T. gondii strains of this genotype, we performed bioassays to compare the pathogenicity of this genotype to the Type II strain, ME49. RESULTS: Both tested genotype #7 strains have greater pathogenic potential, although likely through different mechanisms. Of the most abundant T. gondii-specific CSF peptides across multiple patients, we identified a polymorphic region of the dense granule protein GRA5 with strain specificity. CONCLUSIONS: This approach could represent a "proteotype" that allows for T. gondii strain identification. Ultimately, CSF could be a valuable tool for distinguishing strains among T. gondii-exposed individuals with toxoplasmic encephalitis and may prove useful for future identification of the presence of T. gondii in clinically silent patients.

A protective hybrid protein vaccine informed by mapping major histocompatibility class II epitopes in Cryptococcus neoformans chitin deacetylases that stimulate CD4+ T-cell responses.
UNLABELLED: Infections due to Cryptococcus species are estimated to cause over 100,000 deaths a year. No cryptococcal vaccines are approved for human use. We have shown that vaccine formulations consisting of C. neoformans chitin deacetylase 2 (Cda2) and Cda1 adjuvanted with Cationic Adjuvant Formulation 01 (CAF01) protect mice against experimental cryptococcosis by a mechanism dependent upon CD4+ T cells. Here, using overlapping peptide libraries, we mapped epitopes in Cda2 and Cda1 that stimulated interferon-gamma (IFNγ) release from splenocytes of C57BL/6 and DR4 mice immunized with these proteins. DR4 mice lack mouse major histocompatibility class II (MHC-II) proteins and express chimeric MHC-II proteins with the specificity of the human HLA-DR allele, HLA-DRB1*04:01. Experimental results were then compared with MHC-II binding predictions using the Immune Epitope Database NetMHCIIpan 4.1 BA MHC-II epitope prediction tool. Unique epitopes in Cda2 and Cda1 were discovered for each mouse strain, some of which were not predicted to bind well to MHC-II. CD4+ T cells were responsible for cytokine release as IFNγ production was lost if CD4+ T cells were depleted from the splenocyte population. Finally, we tested a hybrid recombinant protein that consisted of portions of Cda2 and Cda1 containing the MHC-II/CD4+ T-cell epitopes that induce CD4+ T cells in DR4 mice. When administered as a CAF01-adjuvanted vaccine, the hybrid protein protected DR4 mice from an otherwise lethal C. neoformans pulmonary challenge. These results provide a proof of principle regarding the utility of MHC-II/CD4+ T-cell epitope mapping in cryptococcal vaccine development. IMPORTANCE: The development of vaccines to prevent cryptococcosis, a fungal disease which causes over 100,000 deaths annually, is a public health priority. We have demonstrated that adjuvanted vaccines containing two Cryptococcus neoformans protein antigens, chitin deacetylase (Cda)2 and Cda1, protect mice against experimental cryptococcosis by a mechanism dependent upon CD4+ T cells. In this study, we determined which 15-amino-acid peptides of Cda2 and Cda1 stimulate CD4+ T cells in C57BL/6 and DR4 mice; the latter mouse strain has human major histocompatibility class II (MHC-II) specificity. We then synthesized a small hybrid protein containing those portions of Cda2 and Cda1 that strongly stimulated CD4+ T-cell responses in DR4 mice. As an adjuvanted vaccine, the hybrid Cda2/1 protein protected DR4 mice from a C. neoformans pulmonary challenge. Thus, CD4+ T-cell/MHC-II epitope mapping experimentally validated the design of a protective multi-epitope protein for use in cryptococcal vaccines.

Global Genomic Surveillance of Middle East Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus.
Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV) is a persistent zoonotic and epidemic threat. We analyzed 807 publicly available human- and camel-derived MERS-CoV genomes collected during 2012-2024 to assess global genomic surveillance. Most sequences originated from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Major gaps in surveillance persist across Africa and South and Central Asia despite large camel populations, active trade, and evidence of viral circulation. Phylogenetic analysis confirmed predominance of clade B in the Arabian Peninsula and clade C in East Africa, consistent with regional patterns. We identified uneven sampling, incomplete metadata, and long delays between sample collection and public sequence submission, often spanning years. Those limitations reduce the value of genomic data for timely situational awareness. Integrating genomic with population and trade data supports timelier, more representative, and coordinated One Health surveillance for MERS-CoV but reveals major blind spots.

Impact of the 2017 secured-prescription regulation of zolpidem on hypnotic dispensing in France: a nine-year interrupted time-series analysis.
BACKGROUND: In April 2017, France required a secure prescription, normally reserved for narcotics, for all zolpidem prescribing, because of its misuse. Published evaluations covered the first years after the measure, before or at the start of the COVID-19 period. METHODS: Interrupted time series of national open reimbursement data (Médic'AM; all schemes, community pharmacies) from January 2015 to February 2026 (134 monthly points). Reimbursed boxes per day of zolpidem, zopiclone and all hypnotics combined were modelled by segmented regression with seasonality and Newey-West standard errors. The pre-intervention model, projected forward with its 95% prediction interval, served as the counterfactual. Two sensitivity analyses tested dependence on the pandemic months. RESULTS: Zolpidem fell abruptly in April 2017 (-22,186 boxes/day, p < 0.001) and kept declining, reaching 59% below the expected level by 2026 (-72% in 2025 versus 2015-2016). Zopiclone rose (+9147 boxes/day, p < 0.001), offsetting 39% of that fall, but the substitution faded: it exceeded the counterfactual prediction interval in 50 months between May 2017 and June 2023 and in none since, annual dispensing returning from 16.6 (2018) to 14.3 million boxes (2025). All hypnotics stood 14% below expectation. Deviations in 2020-2021 stayed within pre-pandemic dispersion (zolpidem -5.0%, all hypnotics -0.5%), and the April 2017 estimates were unchanged when those months were excluded or modelled. CONCLUSIONS: Nine years on, a molecule-specific measure was followed by a durable reduction in zolpidem and in hypnotics overall (59% and 14% below expectation), and the displacement toward zopiclone has receded. Such measures deserve long follow-up, and reimbursed access to cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia.

Viral load measurements and viral suppression in a cohort of acutely treated people living with HIV during the COVID-19 pandemic in Bangkok, Thailand: a longitudinal cohort analysis.
INTRODUCTION: Lockdowns during the COVID-19 pandemic decreased disease transmission by reducing social interactions but also potentially hindered access to medical care. For individuals who face social and structural barriers to healthcare, such as people with HIV, the overall effect on medical care is unclear. METHODS: Using data from the RV254/SEARCH010 study, a cohort of people with acutely treated HIV, we examined changes in HIV care during the COVID-19 pandemic. Participants with at least one suppressed viral load measurement (≤1000 copies/mL) after 24 weeks on antiretroviral therapy (ART) between 1 January 2018 and 30 September 2023 were included to assess maintenance of HIV care. Time periods were defined as pre-COVID-19, COVID-19 and post-lockdown. COVID-19 was further divided into lockdown 1 (16 March to 3 May 2020), lockdown 2 (1 May to 6 June 2021) and the open inter-lockdown period. Generalised estimating equations were used to calculate prevalence ratios (PRs) of measurements/year and ORs of viral suppression, with 95% CIs. Analyses were adjusted for demographic factors, ART regimen and enrolment status (newly enrolled or established in care). RESULTS: Among 606 participants, 591 (97.5%) were male with a median age of 26.9 years. Participants had 3.50 measurements/year in the pre-COVID-19 period, which decreased to 2.36/year (aPR 0.67 (95% CI 0.65 to 0.70)) during the COVID-19 period and 2.56/year (aPR 0.73 (0.71-0.75)) in the post-lockdown period. Older participants also had fewer measurements/year compared with those 18-19 years of age (20-29 years, aPR 0.90 (0.82-0.98); ≥30 years, aPR 0.88 (0.80-0.97)), as did sex workers (aPR 0.91 (0.85-0.96)). Viral suppression remained unchanged during the COVID-19 (aOR 0.95 (0.43-2.07)) and post-lockdown (aOR 0.95 (0.48-1.88)) periods compared with pre-COVID-19. During the COVID-19 period, there were fewer measurements in lockdowns 1 and 2 (0.34/year and 0.14/year) than the inter-lockdown period (2.82/year). CONCLUSIONS: Lockdowns during COVID-19 reduced HIV care engagement, particularly among participants established in care, without affecting viral suppression.

Feasibility of implementing a mindfulness-based program for paediatric intensive care unit staff.
BACKGROUND: Paediatric intensive care unit (PICU) clinicians are particularly susceptible to workplace stress due to frequent ethical dilemmas (for example, perceptions of futile or unethical treatment), patient morbidity and mortality, sleep disruption, and emotional exhaustion, putting them at increased risk of anxiety, depression, and burnout. The psychological well-being of these healthcare professionals is vital for maintaining high standards of patient care and safety. OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to evaluate the feasibility of implementing a mindfulness-based program among PICU staff, with a focus on acceptability and barriers to participation. METHODS: Weekly 20-min guided group-practice sessions in mindfulness, with both in-person and virtual attendance options, were held over a 6-month period. These sessions were offered to medical, nursing, and allied health staff working in the PICU of a specialist paediatric hospital in Queensland, Australia, serving families from Queensland and northern New South Wales. The program was offered during a period of increased personal and occupational stress arising from the delivery of high-acuity care during the global COVID-19 pandemic. FINDINGS: The program was successfully delivered within the PICU setting, with most participants expressing interest in continuation of the program (72%). Qualitative responses suggested perceived individual and collective well-being benefits, alongside generally positive perceptions of the program. However, participants also identified important barriers to participation, including workload pressures and rostering constraints. CONCLUSIONS: This study suggests that implementation of a mindfulness-based program within a PICU setting may be feasible while also highlighting important operational barriers to participation in high-acuity healthcare environments. Qualitative findings indicated generally positive staff perceptions and perceived acceptability of the program. Further research using longitudinal designs is recommended to better understand implementation considerations and potential longer-term outcomes associated with mindfulness-based interventions in PICU settings.

Pentosan polysulfate sodium limits pulmonary inflammation in a SARS-CoV-2 mouse model.
UNLABELLED: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection remains prevalent globally, causing severe pulmonary inflammation and mortality in up to 10% of patients. While the introduction of effective vaccines has substantially reduced the number of severe coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) cases, there are currently few available therapeutics that have been developed. Pentosan polysulfate sodium (PPS) has been shown to possess potent anti-inflammatory activity in influenza infection and allergen-induced rhinitis models and was recently demonstrated to inhibit SARS-CoV-2 infection in vitro. As such, we hypothesized that PPS may represent an attractive therapeutic that could be utilized for SARS-CoV-2 infection and COVID-19. Using the K18-hACE2 mouse model of SARS-CoV-2 infection, we administered PPS (6 mg/kg) from either 1 (early) or 3 (late) days post-infection via intranasal instillation and then examined the efficacy in mitigating viral-induced inflammation and severe disease outcomes. We found that the early administration of PPS was accompanied by significant improvements in weight loss, clinical disease presentation, and neutrophilic airway inflammation. Early PPS administration also significantly reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine production at both the mRNA and protein levels while having no impact on viral titers or interferon and antiviral gene expression. Histologically, early treatment significantly prevented severe pulmonary inflammation and tissue remodeling. Comparatively, late administration of PPS worsened weight loss and clinical disease presentation following SARS-CoV-2 infection. Moreover, late administration was unable to prevent significant increases in pro-inflammatory cytokines and was further associated with significantly downregulated antiviral-associated genes. Histological examination also showed no protection in the late PPS administered groups. Taken together, these findings underscore the significance of time-dependent administration and demonstrate the therapeutic potential of PPS for treatment of SARS-CoV-2-induced inflammation. IMPORTANCE: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) continues to cause infections globally, with most cases resulting in mild to moderate disease outcomes. However, approximately 10% of patients experience virally induced hyperinflammation leading to poor outcomes. As such, new or repurposed therapeutics need to be rapidly implemented to address this urgent medical need. Here, we show that pentosan polysulfate sodium (PPS) is a leading Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved therapeutic that significantly mitigates SARS-CoV-2-induced pulmonary inflammation. Critically, timing of PPS during the infection establishment and progression is critical for PPS efficacy, highlighting time-dependent responses that must be considered for further human clinical implementation. The findings from this study demonstrate that PPS holds significant promise as a repurposed anti-inflammatory agent for SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Correction to: Prevalence of Endemic Respiratory Viruses During the COVID-19 Pandemic in Urban and Rural Malawi.
[This corrects the article DOI: 10.1093/ofid/ofad643.].

Personalizing digital mental health: a micro-randomized trial analysis of cognitive behavioral therapy/dialectical behavioral therapy text messages to improve mood.
PURPOSE: Digital mental health interventions could improve population health. However, our understanding of how to improve their effectiveness through personalization is limited. We describe the outcomes of a micro-randomized trial (MRT) of a 60-day text messaging program, delivered during the final stages of the COVID-19 pandemic. We analyze the effects of 6 different types of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and dialectical behavioral therapy (DBT) messages, and examine whether socio-demographic, health-related, and contextual factors (eg, timing of sending a message) moderate effectiveness. METHODS: This secondary analysis included 373 adults aged 18 years or older (mean = 38.07), mostly English-speaking female, highly educated White individuals who reported being in good health, but having high stress and struggling to get their basic needs met. Participants were recruited between December 2021 and September 2022 through social media and a recruitment service (Health Match). We used the weighted and centered least squares method to examine the proximal effects of the text-message categories on daily mood, and whether sociodemographic, health-related factors, and the timing of message delivery moderated effectiveness. RESULTS: None of the 6 CBT/DBT-message categories significantly improved mood ratings marginally. However, their effectiveness varied based on the time of day and self-reported health. Overall, sending a message in the afternoon was more effective. However, certain message categories showed significant effects when sent in the morning among participants with poorer self-reported health, while some showed lower effectiveness when sent in the late afternoon for participants with better health. CONCLUSION: Our analysis underscores the importance of considering the time of day and individual health status when developing digital mental health interventions. These insights can help in designing more personalized, adaptive, and effective digital interventions.

Navigating Infection Control and Dialysis Delivery in Nursing Homes: Organizational Perspectives From 2020 to 2025.
OBJECTIVES: Nursing home (NH) residents with end-stage kidney disease requiring thrice-weekly hemodialysis faced challenges during the COVID-19 pandemic, as infection control imperatives conflicted with access to life-sustaining care. This study examines how NHs and dialysis organizations navigated dialysis care for NH residents from 2020 to 2025, exploring how pandemic-era adaptations continue to shape care delivery. DESIGN: Descriptive qualitative study that synthesized interview data from the qualitative arms of three mixed-methods studies conducted between 2020 and 2025. SETTING AND PARTICIPANTS: Participants included NH administrators, clinical staff, and residents, as well as Medicare Advantage plan executives, kidney care management company leadership, and dialysis organization administrative leadership and staff across diverse US health care markets. METHODS: Semistructured interviews were conducted. Interview transcript coding used a modified grounded theory approach. Theme and subtheme development used thematic and content analysis. RESULTS: Three hundred nine interviews were conducted with representatives from 66 NHs, 8 Medicare Advantage plans, 5 kidney care management companies, and 6 dialysis organizations. Three themes were identified, reflecting varied perspectives on the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on dialysis care for NH residents. First, during the pandemic, NHs and dialysis centers prioritized infection mitigation through spatial distancing, cohorting, extended quarantine protocols, and reduced admissions of residents requiring dialysis. Second, NH residents experienced significant barriers to dialysis access, including transportation and schedule disruptions. Third, the pandemic continues to affect dialysis care for this population: although infection control practices have become routine, transportation challenges remain unresolved, and many NHs have reduced admissions of dialysis-dependent residents, threatening access for this vulnerable population. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: Although the COVID-19 pandemic prompted more rigorous infection control practices at NHs and dialysis centers, it also intensified longstanding vulnerabilities in cross-sector health care coordination for NH residents requiring dialysis. Insights from this study's findings could inform efforts to design more resilient, better coordinated models of care.

Post-Master's Psychiatric/Mental Health Nurse Practitioner Students' Perspectives on Addressing Mental Health Stigma in the Post-COVID-19 Era: A Qualitative Description Study.
