Many people with mental health disorders experience mental health related stigma. This type of stigma may impact mental health care and treatment. The COVID-19 pandemic further impacted mental health stigma, indicating a need for psychiatric/mental health nurses to become involved in efforts to address mental health stigma. The purpose of this study was to understand psychiatric/mental health nurse practitioner (PMHNP) students' perspectives on how to address and reduce mental health stigma in the post-COVID era. A qualitative description design was used to collect data from a formal writing exercise with 29 PMHNP students at the end of a one-semester course on theories and psychotherapy modalities. Responses were analyzed with qualitative rigor to form categories. Participants identified six major categories, such as the responsible use of social media and the use of destigmatizing language, and five minor methods, such as partnering with primary care providers and mental health providers' self-care, to address and reduce mental health stigma. This study's results have implications for psychiatric/mental health nursing education, practice, and research.

Between Postmodernism and Medical Populism: Cultural Determinants of Conspiracy Theories on Vaccination After Experience of the COVID-19 Pandemic.
The primary objective of the study was to analyse the correlations between belief in and acceptance of vaccine-related conspiracy theories and prevailing cultural models. The authors emphasise that not only right-wing populism and fundamentalist beliefs, but also postmodern relativism, may contribute to the rejection of established medical knowledge and practices. Drawing on a survey conducted among a representative sample of 1000 members of the Polish population using random-quota sampling, the authors offer an analysis at the level of preferred models of knowledge and the epistemological conditions that contribute to the rejection of contemporary medical knowledge on vaccination in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic. The article is inspired by the theoretical concepts of Ernest Gellner. This cultural and epistemological analysis of knowledge models that support the rise of vaccine hesitancy across different societies may contribute to a better understanding of the anti-vaccination movement and cultural trends that fuel belief in conspiracy theories and medical populism. The authors argue that the principles of Enlightenment rationalism - grounded in knowledge verified through transparent and testable procedures - provide essential cognitive support in countering vaccine-related myths, rumours, and conspiracy theories.

From the operating room to the cloud: the evolving continuum from live surgical broadcasting to remote tele-surgery.
In the last four decades, the transmission of a live surgical operation to a remote audience has evolved from closed-circuit educational broadcast into a fully remote, robot-assisted surgery performed across different continents. This review maps that journey systematically, defining a six-rung Digital Surgical Spectrum - from passive live broadcast to artificial-intelligence-augmented autonomous surgery - grounding each stage in published clinical evidence across multiple surgical domains. We demonstrate that each rung of this spectrum is no longer theoretical. Live broadcasts have reached audiences across multiple countries. Tele-proctoring was validated at scale during the COVID-19 pandemic, and tele-mentoring has been shown in systematic review to produce a safety and efficacy profile broadly comparable to on-site supervision. True remote tele-surgery has been accomplished over distances exceeding 8,000 km with latencies well within established procedure specific safety thresholds. We also present a case timeline and an Institutional Readiness Framework specifying the technical, regulatory, and other prerequisites for each rung, organized visually as a Digital Surgical Spectrum. Importantly, nuances such as the performance paradox of observed surgery, consent frameworks, cybersecurity risk, regulatory fragmentation, and the threat of entrenching rather than correcting global surgical inequity are examined. As the field advances, the growth of tele-surgical technologies will depend on international regulatory harmonization and equity-centered deployment, supported by prospective multi-specialty outcome registries.

A comparative analysis of cell death signalling in RNA and DNA virus infections and potential inhibitory strategies.
The recent COVID-19 pandemic and the epidemic outbreak of Mpox have demonstrated that viruses, despite their apparently simple structure, are sophisticated microorganisms that have evolved complicated pro-survival mechanisms. Their potential to manipulate cell death pathways can affect and determine the outcome of the infection cycle and the host's immune response. RNA viruses typically display a more acute and aggressive nature, as they often promote cell death. In this way, they proliferate and release their virions to infect adjacent cells and perpetuate their life cycle. Common consequences of RNA virus infection include hyperinflammatory responses in hosts, typically leading in damage to the epithelial barrier. Conversely, DNA viruses modulate these pathways to sustain a balance between the lytic cycle, during which they replicate, and latency, wherein they remain inactive until an appropriate stimulus triggers reactivation. Achieving this balance and transitioning between stages of infection requires the inhibition of cellular death processes. In both instances, the viruses seem to respond to the cellular context, enhancing their adaptability through mutations, so to deceive host defenses and therefore secure their survival. This highlights the necessity to comprehend the processes via which these biological threats induce cell death, thereby facilitating the development of broad-spectrum or targeted antiviral treatments.

"It's quite a dark, long journey to the light at the end of the tunnel": a qualitative study of children's experiences of living with Long COVID.
OBJECTIVES: The COVID-19 pandemic had a significant impact on global health, with some individuals experiencing long-term health effects known as Long COVID. This study explored the lived experiences of children with Long COVID, providing further insight into the impacts and needs within this group. METHODS AND MEASURES: Semi-structured interviews, facilitated by children's drawings, were conducted with 15 children. Thematic analysis was used to analyse the data. RESULTS: Four themes were identified: (1) 'I feel completely different': the physical and emotional burden of Long COVID (2) 'Like the buzz of people speaking and I can't concentrate': education challenges created by Long COVID, (3) 'I'm on my third friend group since I've had COVID': disrupted relationships and fractured connections and (4) 'What can I do now to get myself better?': managing life with Long COVID. These findings reveal a narrative of loss and change during key developmental periods. CONCLUSION: This research illustrates the life-altering impact of Long COVID on children across many domains. Despite these challenges children were hopeful for the future. A multi-faceted approach to management is needed, including utilising technology to aid self-management strategies such as pacing and to support social connection, as well as psychological support and school adjustments.

Visual Biopolitics in Crisis: Multimodal Analysis of Tuberculosis in the Early Republican Period and COVID-19 Health Communication in Turkey.
This study investigates how visual materials used during tuberculosis (1930s-1940s) and COVID-19 in Turkey, supported and reflected evolving forms of biopolitical governance. Drawing on data from the state-funded project "Analysis of Public Health Visual Communication Methods" (TÜBİTAK Project No. 123K980), we apply critical multimodal discourse analysis to explore how visual campaigns shaped public perceptions of health, risk, responsibility, and citizenship. Our source materials include archival visuals from Yaşamak Yolu, a journal published by the Istanbul Anti-Tuberculosis Society, illustrations from contemporary newspapers such as Cumhuriyet, and digital COVID-19 media, including the Ministry of Health's Twitter posts, the HES (Life Fits Home) mobile app, TRT Çocuk (Turkish Radio Television Child) content, and materials by Yeşilay (Green Cross). We identify seven key thematic domains ("citizen - population-state," "patient-healthy," "microbe," "hope," "expertise-knowledge," "education-school," "family/child.") that structure these campaigns. Findings indicate a historical continuity in the use of visual communication to guide health behavior and intensified state-defined norms of well-being. Yet significant ruptures emerge in representational strategies and media technologies. In the tuberculosis era, visuals highlighted medical paternalism, pedagogical authority, and individualized care, whereas COVID-19 visuals underscored emotional labor, collective responsibility, and digital engagement. Key discursive shifts include the transformation of the medical authority figure from a rational, commanding presence to a self-sacrificing, emotionally expressive one and the evolution of the child figure from a symbolic national emblem to an agentive, responsible actor. Depictions of contagion also transformed, shifting from minimalist, scientific imagery to colorful digital infographics. While the mother figure remained central across both periods, her portrayal grew more emotionally complex during the COVID-19 pandemic. Mental health also gained increased visibility as a domain of both individual vulnerability and national concern. By tracing these visual shifts, the study highlights how health communication mediates the intersection of biopolitical control, emotional appeal, and national identity. We argue that visual discourse is constitutive, reshaping the public's sense of care, risk, and belonging during times of crisis.

Suicide in South Wales: comprehensive review of suicides reported to the South Wales Central Coroner's Service, 2016-2023.
AIMS AND METHOD: An analysis of coronial inquest data provides contextual information rarely available in routine surveillance systems, including a nuanced understanding of proximal circumstances preceding death of value to mental health services. Inquest records of more than 750 suicides occurring within the South Wales Central Coroner's jurisdiction between 2016 and 2023 were reviewed, including the COVID-19 pandemic years, to assess the effects of lockdown and social isolation. Detailed information was extracted, including medical records, toxicology, police reports, witness statements and suicide notes. RESULTS: Several patterns emerged relating to age, gender, method of death, trigger factors, local authority area, and engagement with mental health services. Hanging was the predominant method, particularly among men. Depression was the most common trigger factor, followed by relationship problems, alcohol/drug misuse, health concerns, psychotic illness and bereavement. CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS: Key structural and psychosocial risk factors identified highlighted the need for tailored, context-specific suicide-prevention strategies, with circumstances preceding suicide integrated into public health planning.

Circulating SARS-CoV-2 RNA detection in acute COVID-19 disease and post-COVID condition.
OBJECTIVES: The study aimed to determine the clinical significance of circulating plasma SARS-CoV-2 RNA across acute COVID-19 and post-COVID condition (PCC) by investigating prevalence, determinants, and kinetics in a large longitudinal cohort, accounting for hospitalization and vaccination. METHODS: We consecutively enrolled individuals with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection. Acute COVID-19 was classified as mild, severe, or critical per WHO criteria. PCC was assessed 3 months after symptom onset, and plasma SARS-CoV-2 RNA (RNAemia) was quantified during acute infection (T0) and at follow-up (T1) by RT-qPCR. Associations between RNAemia and acute disease severity or PCC were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression. RNAemia was analysed as tertiles, binary detectability, and continuous levels. RESULTS: A total of 442 individuals with COVID-19 were included, of whom 195 (44.1%) had mild disease, 161 (36.4%) had severe illness, and 86 (19.5%) had critical illness. At a median of 3.2 (interquartile range, 2.7-3.9 months) months from symptom onset, 184 of 442 patients were followed up, and 144 of 184 (78.3%) reported at least one persistent symptom compatible with PCC, most commonly asthenia (22.9%), myalgic pain (26.4%), brain fog (19.4%), dyspnoea (31.3%), and cough (42.4%). RNAemia was detected in 67.4% of participants at baseline and in 53.6% at follow-up. RNAemia in the II-III tertiles or any detectable RNAemia was associated with critical COVID-19. Neither baseline nor follow-up RNAemia was associated with PCC, and results were unchanged in a sensitivity analysis excluding vaccinated individuals. RNAemia trajectories were not associated with PCC, PCC clusters, or upper respiratory tract viral clearance. CONCLUSIONS: SARS-CoV-2 RNAemia was closely linked to acute COVID-19 severity but showed no association with PCC or PCC phenotype, which were assessed at 3 months from symptom onset in a cohort predominantly experiencing severe COVID-19 and hospitalization during acute infection. This dissociation may suggest that viral RNA in the peripheral blood is primarily involved in acute pathogenesis, whereas PCC likely arises from distinct biological mechanisms.

Routine laboratory data are decoupled from symptom phenotype and prognosis in Long COVID: within-cohort variation is dominated by age.
OBJECTIVES: Long COVID is defined by persistent multi-organ symptoms without an alternative diagnosis. This study evaluated whether routine laboratory data collected under real-world conditions differentiate symptom-defined subgroups within an outpatient cohort and predict the course. METHODS: In this single-center cohort study of 564 Long COVID patients (1,452 visits), symptom phenotypes were derived by latent class analysis of 19 organ-system domains at baseline. Structure in 89 routine analytes was sought by k-means clustering, confirmed with alternative algorithms, and repeated after age residualization. Analytes were compared across phenotypes using Kruskal-Wallis tests with false-discovery-rate control and adjustment for confounders. Equivalence testing was performed against reference change values. The course was modeled by count models. Prediction of improvement used a nested cross-validated elastic net with a baseline-independent endpoint. RESULTS: Clustering showed no convincing structure (silhouette ≤0.09, two to eight clusters); the weak split tracked age (50.5 vs. 38 years) and vanished after residualization. Three age-independent phenotypes (n=503) had no laboratory correlate: none of 89 analytes survived FDR correction, with or without adjustment, or across 50 pseudo-class draws. Equivalence held for 86/89 analytes within ±0.5 SD and 63/70 within the reference change value. Symptom burden declined (median 4 to 2 organ systems, p=2.5 × 10-19); however, no analyte predicted the course (AUC 0.46). CONCLUSIONS: Routine laboratory variation in this cohort was dominated by age and decoupled from symptom phenotype in both directions. Routine testing in a real-world setting could not provide an age-independent diagnostic, subtyping, or prognostic signature in a cohort of patients suffering from Long COVID.

Heterogeneous co-circulation of multiple DENV-1 and DENV-2 genotypes in Vung Tau during the 2023 dengue outbreak in Vietnam.
Dengue virus (DENV) remains a significant global health threat, particularly in hyper-endemic regions like Vietnam, where the co-circulation of multiple serotypes and genotypes complicates disease control. In 2023, 6.5 million dengue cases and 6,800 deaths were reported globally, marking the largest dengue outbreak in the world. Vietnam recorded 149,557 dengue cases and 36 deaths, with a notable dominance of the DENV-2 serotype. This study provides a comprehensive genomic characterization of the 2023 outbreak using isolates collected from hospitalized patients (n = 148; 66.89% adults). To ensure robust viral recovery, we propagated 90 isolates using a low-passage, antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE)-based system. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) of 53 isolates yielded 47 consensus sequences, including 26 complete genomes. Phylogenetic analysis revealed the simultaneous co-circulation of diverse DENV-1 and DENV-2 genotypes. DENV-1 isolates were predominantly genotype I (86%), clustering closely with prior Vietnamese strains and suggesting sustained endemic maintenance, while genotype IV (14%) was detected sporadically. Among DENV-2 isolates, the Cosmopolitan genotype was predominant (98%), with a smaller proportion (2%) belonging to the Asian 1 genotype. Both genotypes clustered with previously reported Vietnamese and regional Southeast Asian strains, indicating ongoing local circulation and regional viral exchange. Comparative mutational analysis of DENV-2 Cosmopolitan isolates identified multiple non-synonymous amino acid substitutions across the viral genome. Fourteen substitutions were shared between Vietnamese historical (2019-2022) and 2023 isolates, while 24 substitutions were unique to the 2023 outbreak strains. The majority of amino acid changes were concentrated within the NS5, E, NS1, and NS3 proteins, suggesting continued genetic diversification within the circulating Cosmopolitan lineage. Overall, these findings demonstrate the persistence of established DENV lineages alongside ongoing viral evolution during the 2023 outbreak in Vietnam. This study highlights the value of whole-genome surveillance for monitoring dengue virus genetic diversity and provides insight that may support future epidemiological surveillance, vaccine evaluation, and outbreak preparedness.

rVSV-ΔG-EBOV-GP-Nipah-G (also designated PHV02) replication-competent, recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus vaccine for prevention of Nipah virus disease: Standardized template with key considerations for a risk/benefit assessment.
A recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (rVSV) expressing the glycoprotein (GP) of Ebola virus (rVSV-EBOV GP) has been approved for preventive immunization against Ebola (Ervebo®, Merck & Co.). The rVSV-EBOV vector was modified to express an additional glycoprotein (G) of Nipah virus (NiV), a bat-borne henipavirus endemic/epidemic in South and Southeast Asia that causes fatal encephalitis and pneumonia. The rVSV-EBOV-GP-NiV G vaccine candidate ("PHV02") is a unique chimeric virus with tropism and immunological properties derived from the wild-type (wt) vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) parent, the rVSV-EBOV-GP vector and the NiV G transgene donor. The EBOV GP enables fusion with the cell membrane and virus entry, whereas the NiV G protein mediates attachment to cells and serves as the antigen for stimulating NiV-specific immunity. This review focuses on the characteristics of the vector and vaccine candidate relevant to clinical and environmental safety, immunogenicity and efficacy. The Brighton Collaboration Benefit-Risk Assessment of VAccines by TechnolOgy (BRAVATO) standardized template is used to update the key characteristics and risks of the rVSV-EBOV vector (previously published [1]) and the novel PHV02 NiV vaccine candidate which is now in clinical trials. The template provides a rich source of information and guide to the supporting literature. While analogies of the PHV02 NiV vaccine to the backbone rVSV-EBOV vector are useful given the more extensive data available on the vector, the template emphasizes that PHV02 is a novel construct from a regulatory perspective and targets a different disease with unique characteristics and pathogenesis. Where similarities and parallels are drawn between nonclinical and clinical outcomes of rVSV-EBOV (vector) and PHV02 (vaccine), the reader should be cognizant of the limitations of these conclusions. The intended use of the standardized template is to provide a cohesive reference allowing vaccine developers and regulatory reviewers to understand characteristics, benefits and risks of a new vaccine candidate against NiV relevant to its future use in human populations, and to compare and contrast these characteristics to an approved vaccine constructed from the same (rVSV) vector system against a different indication (ebolavirus). The systematized template structure should facilitate utility of the paper.

Entomological response to control interventions during the first chikungunya and dengue outbreak in White Nile, Sudan.
BACKGROUND: White Nile State in south-central Sudan experienced its first documented outbreak of dengue and chikungunya in 2022. The present study evaluates the entomological response following an integrated vector management package implemented during the outbreak in Tandalti town. METHODS: Longitudinal entomological surveillance across 10 clusters encompassing 600 households and 2500 containers was conducted from July to December 2022. Stegomyia indices together with per-container productivity of larvae and pupae were calculated to quantify container infestation and evaluate entomological changes following the intervention. RESULTS: Widespread Aedes aegypti infestation was documented across all clusters, with clay pots (zeers) and barrels accounting for 97.1% of positive containers. Following the implementation of control interventions, Stegomyia indices decreased substantially from September to December (house index by 78.2%, container index by 35.1%, Breteau index by 92.8% and pupal/demographic index by 94.1%) and total immatures decreased by 89.5% (larvae) and 95.5% (pupae). The few residual containers remaining in December were still producing pupae at per-container rates comparable to baseline, with barrels sustaining higher productivity than zeers. CONCLUSIONS: The decrease in vector density is a combined effect of the control interventions and the wet to dry seasonal transition. Combining Stegomyia indices with per-container productivity identifies and quantifies residual containers sustaining the vector population. Sustained post-outbreak surveillance is needed, as these residual containers may contribute to vector population resurgence during subsequent transmission seasons.

A rare case of ultrastructurally proven toxoplasmic myositis masquerading as necrotizing myopathy with emphasis on pathobiology.
Toxoplasmosis is a zoonotic infection caused by the obligate protozoan Toxoplasma gondii. In an immunocompetent human host, the parasite forms bradyzoites (tissue cysts), mainly in skeletal muscle, eye, brain, or cardiac muscle, and remains latent. Once cysts are established, type 1 cytokine-based immunity controls the conversion to tachyzoites from bradyzoites. We propose that short-term immunosuppression can only cause a transient defect in this cycle of conversion control. The temporary lapse in conversion control releases few tachyzoites, and the host immunity in response gives rise to cytokines that can cause polymyositis. Myositis and the presence of a parasite in the muscle biopsy are very rare, even in immunosuppressed patients. We present a case of a young man with quadriplegia after immunosuppression for dengue-associated hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. We report a rare case of toxoplasmic myositis in a patient masquerading as necrotizing myopathy, with emphasis on the possible pathomechanism of myositis and ultrastructure of toxoplasma. We recommend that toxoplasma myositis should be included among the differentials of sudden muscular weakness, especially in an immunocompromised host. Our case highlights the crucial role of muscle biopsy in the diagnosis of toxoplasmic myositis. For early diagnosis, a systematic search for toxoplasmosis should be formulated in case of polymyositis, especially in immunocompromised patients, as a quicker identification of the parasite is possible and treatment response is also better in the early, acute phase of toxoplasmic myositis.

Cross-sectional study on norovirus genotyping and epidemiology among hospitalised children with acute gastroenteritis in Tianjin, North China, 2020-2023.
PURPOSE: To understand the molecular epidemiological and clinical characteristics of norovirus in children with acute gastroenteritis in Tianjin from 2020 to 2023. METHODS: A total of 6714 faecal samples were collected from children aged 0–17 years with acute gastroenteritis who visited Tianjin Children’s Hospital from August 2020 to July 2023. All samples were initially screened for norovirus using reverse transcription PCR. The polymerase region and capsid protein region of the initially screened positive samples were amplified using reverse transcription PCR, the sequences were aligned and a phylogenetic tree was constructed. RESULTS: Of the 6714 children with acute gastroenteritis, 1395 (20.78%) tested positive for norovirus in stool samples. Among them, 810 were male (20.62%, 810/3929) and 585 were female (21.01%, 585/2785). Norovirus detection rate showed seasonal differences, with the detection rates of norovirus-RNA in spring, summer, autumn and winter being 27.97% (605/2163), 11.04% (195/1767), 12.04% (141/1171) and 28.15% (454/1613), respectively. 155 norovirus-positive specimens were subjected to dual-region typing and clinical symptom-related information was collected. They were divided into nine genotypes, all of which were GII type. The three most prevalent genotypes were GII.4(P16), GII.3(P12) and GII.2(P16). The GII.4(P16) genotype accounted for 38.06% (59/155), the GII.3(P12) genotype for 27.74% (43/155) and the GII.2(P16) genotype for 19.35% (30/155). CONCLUSION: From 2020 to 2023, the main age of onset of diarrhoea in children in Tianjin was 13–36 months, with a higher incidence in spring and winter. The most susceptible genotypes were GII.4(P16), GII.3(P12) and GII.2(P16). Abdominalgia, aminotransferase, C-reactive protein, procalcitonin and neutrophil count are statistically associated with norovirus genotypes in paediatric patients. Close monitoring of the norovirus’s spread in the population is crucial to prevent outbreaks in childcare facilities, schools and other places where children congregate, which could increase the risk of severe cases, burden family care and strain public health control efforts.

Forecasting of infectious disease epidemics in sexual networks using attenuated renewal processes.
Forecasting emerging infectious disease outbreaks is particularly challenging for sexual networks of men who have sex with men (MSM), where transmission can be shaped by heterogeneous and overdispersed contact structures, mixing assortativity, and both one-time and recurrent partnerships. Using stochastic epidemic simulations on synthetic MSM networks and empirical mpox case data from major cities, we systematically evaluated five classes of short-term forecasting models, from random walk approaches to semi-mechanistic attenuated renewal processes. Model performance was assessed using the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS). Across both simulated and empirical epidemics in heterogeneous networks, renewal models attenuated by a reverse-sigmoid curve, to account for early depletion of highly-connected nodes, consistently outperformed alternatives, achieving more balanced and reliable forecasts. Our findings suggest a practical approach for robust forecasting in highly overdispersed networks, where distinguishing network effects from other factors remains challenging and usually requires additional data.

Prevalence and genotype distribution of norovirus and rotavirus among children under five with diarrheal infection in lower-middle-income countries after Rotavirus vaccine introduction: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
BACKGROUND: Rotavirus and norovirus are the leading viral causes of acute diarrheal disease worldwide. Both viruses encompass multiple genotypes and subgenotypes, and this genetic diversity presents a significant challenge to rotavirus vaccine effectiveness and development. High-quality evidence on the prevalence and circulating genotypes of these enteric viruses among children under five years of age remains limited, particularly following the introduction of rotavirus vaccination in low and middle-income countries (LMICs). Therefore, this systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to synthesizes available evidence on the prevalence and genotype distribution of norovirus and rotavirus in this population. METHODS: A systematic literature search was conducted across five major databases PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect, Embase, and Web of Science between February 20 and 28, 2026. Duplicate removal, title and abstract screening, full-text review and data extraction were performed independently by two investigators using the Rayyan web-based platform. STATA version 17 software was used for statistical analysis. A random-effects model was applied to estimate pooled prevalence and effect sizes. Heterogeneity was evaluated using Cochran's Q statistic, the I2 statistic, forest plots, and Galbraith plots. Publication bias was assessed using both graphical (funnel plots) and statistical methods. RESULTS: A total of 35,704 children under five years with diarrheal infection from LMICs were included across eligible studies. The overall pooled prevalence of norovirus and rotavirus combined was 18% (95% CI: 15-21%). Rotavirus had a higher pooled prevalence than norovirus, at 24% (95% CI: 19.6-28.3%) and 13% (95% CI: 11-15%), respectively. Substantial heterogeneity was observed across studies (I2 = 98.72%, p < 0.001). Among norovirus genotypes, GII was predominant (76%), with subgenotype GII.4 accounting for 53% of cases, followed by GI (23%). The most frequently identified rotavirus genotypes were G3[P8] (39%) and G1[P8] (17%). CONCLUSIONS: Norovirus and rotavirus remain significant causes of diarrheal disease among children under five in LMICs, even after the introduction of rotavirus vaccination. Approximately one in five children with diarrheal illness were infected with at least one of these virusesGII, particularly subgenotype GII.4, was the dominant norovirus strain, while G3[P8] and G1[P8] were the most prevalent rotavirus genotypes. These findings underscore the need to strengthen surveillance systems, consider circulating genotypes in vaccine formulation, and continuously monitor genotype shifts within the population.

Delay in initiation of rabies post-exposure vaccination and influencing factors in Gondar zones of Ethiopia.
Rabies is a viral zoonotic disease of warm-blooded animals, which is preventable through proper administration of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). In controlling rabies, delays in initiating post exposure vaccination (PEV) are a challenge in endemic regions. A study was conducted to assess the delay in initiation of PEV and identify associated factors in Ethiopia. Data was collected by face-to-face interviews from 260 dog bite victims or their guardians between January and June, 2025 using a questionnaire. Post exposure vaccination was considered delayed if it was initiated after 48 hours of the exposure incident. The prevalence of delayed initiation of PEV was calculated as a percentage from the number of individuals who initiated PEV after 48 hours and the total number of individuals exposed to rabies. Factors associated with delay were identified using logistic regression models. The prevalence of delayed in initiation of rabies PEV was 86.1% (224/260); 13.9% (36/260) of participants commenced vaccination within 48 hours of exposure. Severity of bite and ownership of biting animal were factors associated with the outcome. Deep bite (OR = 0.22, 95% CI: 0.07 - 0.66, P = 0.008) and bitten by stray dogs (OR = 0.51, 95% CI = 0.27 - 0.95, P = 0.033) reduced delay in initiation of PEV. Majority of respondents (88.5%) are aware of the existence, the signs (71.5%), the way of transmission (75.4%), and the fatal nature (96.5%) of rabies, and the need for PEV (95.4%). Another majority believe that the cost of the vaccine is fair and PEV is effective (95%), and and costs of the vaccination (76.2%) was not a reason for delay. In conclusion, the study outlined that respondents know many aspects of rabies control and had fewer barriers to uptake the PEV; however, the delay in initiating PEV was high. This underscores that respondents may not be aware of the risk of delay. Therefore, interventions focusing on the risk of delayed PEV initiation are needed.

Predicting Measles Vaccination Defaulting in Uganda and Kenya: Comparative Evaluation of Custom Soft Voting and TabNet Stacked Ensemble Architectures.
BACKGROUND: Measles is a major cause of death among infants despite free routine immunization (RI) in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Vaccination defaulting contributes to measles outbreak occurrences. Conventional immunization defaulter identification methods are expensive to implement, prone to data falsification, reactive, and overestimate uptake. Several machine learning studies leveraged the use of child and maternal characteristics as predictors of immunization defaulting, overlooking community, demographic, and socioeconomic factors. Similarly, there is limited research regarding the use of interpretable deep learning and advanced ensemble methods to improve model performance in predicting RI defaulters and establishing significant predictors at the national level in the LMIC context, like Uganda. OBJECTIVE: This study predicts infants at a risk of defaulting on measles vaccination in Uganda and Kenya using advanced ensemble learning architectures. METHODS: The study benchmarked classical and deep learning models using Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) datasets (2016-2022) with child, maternal, community, social-economic, and demographic characteristics as predictors. The robust modeling pipeline began with feature selection according to the literature and the expert domain. It was followed by vaccination eligibility, missing value handling, and feature elimination using the phi-k correlation framework. To mitigate class imbalance, synthetic minority over-sampling technique for nominal continuous features was used in a training pipeline after the RobustScaler. Nine baseline classifiers, including Tabular Network (TabNet), multilayer perceptron (MLP), random forest (RF), gradient boosting (GB), adaptive-boosting (AB), among others, underwent stratified k-fold cross-validation and hyperparameter optimization via grid search. Custom soft voting was evaluated alongside TabNet stack architecture for superior ensemble prediction. Models were evaluated for accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. Model explainability was decoded using Shapley additive explanations (SHAP), while Streamlit and SQLite formed the tool architecture. RESULTS: The proposed TabNet+GB+RF custom soft voting achieved significant, nonrandom performance over tuned base models with an F1-score of 0.7111, area under the curve (AUC) of 0.8847 for Kenya. Conversely, for Uganda, the TabNet hybrid ensemble (GB+RF+ AB→TabNet) was the best with AUC of 0.8862 and F1-score of 0.6756, which was statistically insignificant. SHAP identified child's age and vitamin A1 as universal key predictors in both countries; others varied. In Kenya, time to water source, respondents' education, district lived previously, and current district were the most influential global features, respectively. In Uganda, Polio inactive, Pentavalent3, current district, and respondents' education were the most influential factors to defaulting, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: The proposed advanced ensemble learning models improved the classification of measles vaccine defaulters compared to individual models. The study recommends distinct country-tailored strategies. In Kenya, outreaches are recommended to areas with low literacy, distant water sources, and mobile populations. Conversely, in Uganda, the study recommends reminders to avoid missing preceding vaccines and outreaches to high-default districts.

Dual-mechanism adjuvant catharanthine restores β-lactam efficacy against Staphylococcus aureus infections.
Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) remains a major global health threat with high mortality, causing both community-associated and hospital-acquired infections. Consequently, resistance mechanisms, notably β-lactamase production and biofilm formation, are considered promising therapeutic targets. In this study, Catharanthine, a plant-derived alkaloid extracted from Catharanthus roseus (Madagascar periwinkle), is a potent adjuvant that restores the efficacy of β-lactam antibiotics against S. aureus. This study aimed to investigate resistance mechanisms, notably β-lactamase production and biofilm formation, which are considered promising therapeutic targets. Molecular docking was performed to evaluate the binding interaction between catharanthine and β-lactamase. Metabolomic analysis was used to investigate the effect of catharanthine on bacterial metabolic pathways, particularly those associated with biofilm formation. In addition, murine models of S. aureus pneumonia and skin infection were established to assess the therapeutic efficacy of combination treatment with catharanthine and cefixime in vivo. Catharanthine showed high-affinity binding to β-lactamase in molecular docking analysis, supporting its potential role as a β-lactam antibiotic adjuvant. Metabolomic profiling revealed that catharanthine perturbed glutamate-associated amino acid metabolism involving the arginine biosynthetic network, thereby impairing biofilm development. In vivo, combination therapy with catharanthine and cefixime effectively alleviated infection in murine models of S. aureus pneumonia and skin infection. This study demonstrates that catharanthine enhances the therapeutic efficacy of β-lactam antibiotics through dual targeting of β-lactamase-associated resistance and biofilm formation. These findings identify catharanthine as a promising preclinical β-lactam adjuvant candidate and support further pharmacological and translational evaluation against MRSA infections.

The Impact of Empiric Linezolid Compared With Vancomycin on Inpatient Outcomes.
BACKGROUND: Vancomycin and linezolid are commonly used for empiric treatment of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), but differences may influence the preferred agent. Vancomycin requires individualized dosing and drug monitoring, possibly delaying initiation. Linezolid offers fixed dosing, and potentially lower costs, which may improve time to first dose. This study compares clinical, operational, and cost outcomes associated with empiric vancomycin and linezolid use. METHODS: This single-center, retrospective chart review included a convenience sample of 100 hospitalized adults receiving more than 1 dose of empiric vancomycin or linezolid, stratified by level of care (intensive care unit [ICU] vs non-ICU). The primary endpoint was 30-day all-cause mortality. Secondary endpoints included time to first dose, adverse events, therapy changes, treatment duration, length of stay (LOS), cost, and vancomycin dosing characteristics. RESULTS: A convenience sample of 100 patients (50 per group) was analyzed. Thirty-day all-cause mortality was 22% with vancomycin versus 12% with linezolid (P = .183). No statistically significant differences were observed in time to first dose (2.03 ± 1.51 hours vs 1.6 ± 1.66 hours, P = .180). No statistically significant difference was detected in therapy changes, treatment duration, hospital/ICU LOS, treatment failure, and adverse events. Vancomycin had a higher medication cost ($46.59 vs $29.52, P = .012). Patients receiving vancomycin had an average of 2.8 levels, requiring a median of 54.6 hours to reach therapeutic range, maintaining it for 29.5% of treatment duration. This study is limited by its retrospective design and small sample size. CONCLUSION: No statistically significant differences in clinical outcomes were detected between patients receiving empiric linezolid and vancomycin. Linezolid was associated with lower drug acquisition cost.

Coxiella burnetii exposure at the human-livestock interface in Southern Punjab, Pakistan: A serological one health investigation.
Coxiella burnetii, the causative agent of Q fever, is an important zoonotic pathogen affecting livestock and humans worldwide. In Pakistan, epidemiological evidence remains limited, particularly at the human-livestock interface. This study aimed to determine the seroprevalence of C. burnetii and identify associated risk factors among livestock and livestock-exposed humans in Southern Punjab, Pakistan. A cross-sectional study was conducted across six districts, including 4758 livestock comprising goats, sheep, cattle, buffaloes, and camels, and 1019 humans with livestock-associated exposure. Serum samples were tested for the presence of antibodies against C. burnetii using an ELISA assay. Overall 17.65% and 21.98% seroprevalence rates were observed among livestock and humans, respectively at individual-level while 67.3% and 32.3% seroprevalence rates were observed at the herd- and household-level, respectively. Tick infestation, larger herd size, extensive husbandry, transhumant production, and reproductive problems were associated with higher odds of seropositivity. Among humans, livestock ownership, raw milk consumption, placenta handling, family history of abortion, and uncertainty regarding tick exposure were associated with seropositivity. These findings provide evidence of substantial prior exposure to C. burnetii among livestock and humans and highlight Q fever as an underrecognized zoonotic health concern. Integrated One Health surveillance combining serology with molecular and environmental testing, together with improved farm biosecurity and targeted public awareness, is warrant to reduce occupational exposure and ultimately strengthen disease prevention strategies.

Trends in Pseudomonas aeruginosa Resistance After a Four-Dimensional Antimicrobial Stewardship Intervention.
This single-center retrospective study analyzed de-duplicated Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates collected at Huaian Municipal Infectious Diseases Hospital from 2023 to 2025. A total of 121 unique isolates were included, of which 83.5% were from sputum. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) was performed using an automated microbiology system, and minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) results were interpreted according to CLSI M100, 33rd edition. In early 2024, a four-dimensional linkage-targeted antimicrobial stewardship intervention was implemented in the Respiratory and Tuberculosis Department (Resp-TB) (n = 97), comprising: (1) dynamic antimicrobial resistance surveillance with quarterly feedback; (2) risk-stratified antimicrobial prescribing based on local susceptibility data; (3) standardized specimen collection protocols; and (4) enhanced infection prevention and control measures. In the Resp-TB, the overall resistance rates were 74.19% in 2023, 81.63% in 2024, and 82.93% in 2025, with no significant reduction after the intervention (p ≈ 0.37). By 2025, resistance to tobramycin was 0/41 (0.00%), cefepime was 1/41 (2.44%), and piperacillin-tazobactam was 0/41 (0.00%); levofloxacin resistance reached 15/41 (36.59%). Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole resistance remained high across the study period. These findings show persistent antimicrobial resistance in the Resp-TB after implementation of the intervention, while resistance to selected agents, including tobramycin, cefepime, and piperacillin-tazobactam, remained low in 2025.

BCG vaccination and first hospitalization in children younger than 5 years: a nationwide cohort study in Portugal.
BACKGROUND: The BCG, used to prevent tuberculosis, has been associated with beneficial non-specific effects (NSEs), including reduced childhood morbidity and mortality. In Portugal, universal neonatal BCG vaccination was discontinued in 2016 and replaced by a selective, risk-based strategy. This policy transition resulted in substantial variation in BCG vaccination status and provides an opportunity to examine the association between BCG vaccination and hospitalization in children. OBJECTIVE: The primary objective was to estimate the association between BCG vaccination and the risk of first hospitalization, with secondary analyses examining cause-specific hospitalizations. METHODS: We conducted a nationwide retrospective cohort study including all children younger than 5 years born in mainland Portugal between July 1, 2010 and June 30, 2021. Data were obtained from linked national health registries. Follow-up began at day seven of life and continued until first hospitalization, age 5 years, or end of study. BCG vaccination was categorized according to age at vaccination (unvaccinated, 7-90 days, 3-12 months, and 1-5 years) and Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate hazard ratios for first hospitalization. Kaplan-Meier curves were used to describe cumulative incidence. Models were adjusted for sex, birth year, birth season, comorbidities, and child health surveillance visits. Cause-specific analyses and hospitalization duration (≥3 days) were also examined. Sensitivity analyses addressed calendar-period effects, geographic adjustment, and adjustment for child health surveillance visits. RESULTS: Among 544,794 children, 66.5% received BCG vaccination. Over 1,781,194 child-years of follow-up, 169,286 first hospitalizations were recorded. After adjustment, associations between BCG vaccination and first hospitalization varied according to age at vaccination. Compared with unvaccinated children, adjusted hazard ratios for first hospitalization were 0.15 (95% CI: 0.14-0.16) for vaccination between 7-90 days, 0.16 (95% CI: 0.15-0.16) for vaccination between 3-12 months, and 0.42 (95% CI: 0.41-0.43) for vaccination between 1-5 years. Similar associations were observed for respiratory, other medical, and neurological hospitalizations. For respiratory hospitalizations, adjusted hazard ratios were 0.56 (95% CI: 0.51-0.61), 0.57 (95% CI: 0.55-0.59), and 0.81 (95% CI: 0.78-0.83) for vaccination at 7-90 days, 3-12 months, and 1-5 years, respectively. Most hospitalizations were short, with stays lasting ≥3 days occurring slightly less frequently among BCG-vaccinated than unvaccinated children (7.1% vs 8.0%). CONCLUSIONS: BCG vaccination was associated with a lower hazard of first hospitalization in this setting, particularly among children vaccinated during early infancy. However, given the observational design and the selective vaccination strategy implemented after 2016, these associations should not be interpreted as evidence of a causal protective effect. The variation in effect estimates according to age at vaccination and hospitalization outcome highlights the potential influence of contextual factors, healthcare utilization, and residual confounding.

Blocking Extracellular Cyclophilin A-Mediated Adhesion Protects Against Bacterial Infection.
Bacterial pneumonia remains a leading cause of mortality and morbidity worldwide and is primarily managed through antibiotic therapy. However, the increasing threat of antimicrobial resistance underscores the urgent need for alternative strategies. In this study, we identify extracellular cyclophilin A (eCypA) as a key host factor that promotes the adherence of bacteria such as group A Streptococcus (GAS) and Streptococcus pneumoniae (S. P.). Using single-nucleus RNA sequencing of mouse lung tissue, we demonstrate that eCypA upregulates the expression of integrin/extracellular matrix adhesion receptors, including integrin α5, fibronectin, and mucin, an effect largely mediated by enhancing the transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) signaling. Mechanistically, eCypA interacts with TGF-β receptor II, acting as a coactivator to increase its binding to TGF-β1 and amplify downstream signaling. Notably, administration of an anti-CypA monoclonal antibody yields both prophylactic and therapeutic effects against GAS-induced lung damage in mice by reducing bacterial adhesion and suppressing proinflammatory cytokine production. Collectively, these findings identify eCypA as a critical regulator of infection exploited by diverse bacteria that rely on integrin/extracellular matrix for adherence, highlighting eCypA as a promising target for host-directed therapies designed to mitigate bacterial attachment and subsequent inflammation.

Drug-resistant tuberculosis in Nepal: the sixth national prevalence drug-resistant survey, 2024.
BACKGROUND: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major public health challenge in Nepal, characterized by increasing drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) and constrained surveillance capacity. The sixth national DR-TB prevalence survey was therefore implemented to address this gap. This study aimed to estimate the national prevalence of DR-TB and identify risk factors among new and previously treated pulmonary TB patients. METHODS: A national cross-sectional survey was conducted from December 2022 to January 2024, enrolling bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB patients using stratified cluster sampling at 49 diagnostic centers. Phenotypic and genotypic drug sensitivity testing was performed on 1768 Mycobacterium tuberculosis-confirmed samples. Logistic regression analysis estimated DR-TB prevalence and its associated risk factors. RESULTS: Rifampicin resistance was identified in 2.2% [95% confidence interval (CI) 1.4-3.6] of new TB patients and 10.1% (95% CI 5.1-19) of previously treated patients. In total, 9.4% exhibited resistance to at least one first-line drug, with isoniazid exhibiting the highest resistance rate. Within the rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) group, resistance to moxifloxacin was more prevalent among newly diagnosed patients than previously treated patients at both critical concentrations (55.3% vs. 33.3% at 0.25 µg/ml; 34.2% vs. 11.1% at 1 µg/ml). Previous TB treatment emerged as the strongest predictor of rifampicin resistance [adjusted odds ratio (aOR) = 4.1, 95% CI 2.6-6.4]. CONCLUSIONS: The prevalence of RR/multidrug-resistant (MDR)-TB in Nepal remains stable compared with previous surveys. However, a high rate of fluoroquinolone resistance among new patients underscores the urgent need for improved antibiotic stewardship and expanded drug-susceptibility testing services. These findings provide essential evidence to guide national TB control strategies.

Clonal outbreak of mecC-MRSA carriage linked to phage-mediated acquisition of immune evasion cluster genes.
OBJECTIVES: mecC-carrying methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (mecC-MRSA) are predominantly animal-associated pathogens that rarely cause human infections and have not been linked to hospital outbreaks. We investigated a suspected cluster of mecC-MRSA in a Belgian hospital and contextualised the outbreak isolates within the global mecC-MRSA population using whole-genome sequencing. METHODS: Seven mecC-MRSA isolates from screening samples from patients hospitalised in a single unit between September 2024 and January 2025 underwent whole genome sequencing alongside 16 unrelated human and 3 bovine mecC-MRSA from Belgium. Core-genome MLST (cgMLST) was performed to assess clonality. These were compared with 571 publicly available mecC-MRSA genome assemblies from NCBI. Immune evasion cluster (IEC) genes were sought. Associated prophage regions were characterised using PHASTEST. RESULTS: All seven outbreak isolates belonged to ST599, shared the same complex type (CT47051), and differed by a maximum of 4 cgMLST allelic differences, confirming clonal transmission. Six of seven were detected within 48 hours of admission; all patients resided in a semi-rural area within a 23 km radius. The outbreak isolates harboured IEC genes sak and sea on a ΦSa3-like prophage, a novel IEC variant lacking scn and chp, while an unrelated CC599 Belgian human isolate harboured sak and scn. Among publicly available mecC-MRSA assemblies, CC599 represented only 16 isolates (2.8%), and IEC genes were carried only by 6 isolates (0.9%)- none within CC599. The outbreak cluster was most closely related to an unrelated historical Belgian bovine ST599 isolate (75 allelic differences). CONCLUSIONS: This first documented clonal mecC-MRSA outbreak was caused by a rare ST599 clone that acquired IEC genes through phage-mediated horizontal transfer, a feature associated with human adaptation and enhanced transmissibility in other S. aureus lineages. These findings highlight the need for mecC-capable diagnostic assays and One Health genomic surveillance to detect emerging human-adaptive mecC-MRSA clones.

Characterization of the Growth Variability of Multiple Listeria monocytogenes Strains on Smoked Salmon.
Listeria monocytogenes poses a significant food safety risk in ready-to-eat products like smoked salmon, which support bacterial growth during refrigerated storage and have been linked to several listeriosis outbreaks. Product manufacturers rely on challenge tests and predictive microbiology (PM) to ensure product safety, and strain variability is an important consideration for both of these approaches. In this study, we reported a detailed analysis of strain variability in challenge tests and compared results to the outputs of common PM tools. Detailed growth data were generated on a commercial smoked salmon product stored at refrigeration (4.1 °C), temperature abuse (9.6 °C), and room temperature (19.8 °C) with nine individual L. monocytogenes strains. Strains were selected based on differences in lineage, strain origin, cold/salt tolerance in laboratory media, and included strains recommended in the European Union Reference Laboratory for L. monocytogenes (EURL-Lm) technical guidance document. The growth rates were compared to predictions from well-established PM tools (ComBase, Food Spoilage and Safety Predictor, Pathogen Modeling Program) as well as a smoked salmon-specific secondary model. Growth rates of all strains were below predictions of tertiary models at 9.6 °C and 19.8 °C, but some strains had higher estimated growth rates than predicted rates at 4.1 °C. Cluster analysis also demonstrated no significant correlation between growth rates and strain origin or salt/cold tolerance, although strains from lineage II were clearly associated with higher growth rates at 4.1 °C and 19.8 °C. Overall, this study presents detailed strain-specific growth rate data of genetically diverse L. monocytogenes strains on a smoked salmon product and highlights the importance of considering strain variability when designing challenge tests and interpreting predictive microbiology outputs.

Unexplained Colistin Resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae: Insights into sRNA-Mediated Post-Transcriptional Regulation.
Colistin is a last-resort antibiotic used to treat infections caused by multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens, including Klebsiella pneumoniae. Resistance to colistin can be explained by canonical mechanisms involving chromosomal mutations that activate lipid A modification pathways or by acquisition of plasmid-mediated mcr genes. These mechanisms modify the net charge of the bacterial outer membrane, reducing the binding affinity of colistin. However, an increasing number of genomic surveillance studies report colistin-resistant K. pneumoniae isolates that lack detectable alterations in known resistance mechanisms. This genotype-phenotype discordance suggests that additional regulatory mechanisms may contribute to colistin resistance. This review evaluates the hypothesis that mutation-independent regulatory changes within the PhoP/PhoQ-PmrA/PmrB-CrrA/CrrB signaling network may alter the output of lipid A modification pathways in isolates lacking detectable canonical resistance determinants. This model remains to be experimentally validated. The role of small regulatory RNAs (sRNAs) as potential post-transcriptional modulators of regulatory networks involved in envelope remodeling and antimicrobial susceptibility is explored as a potential explanation for this genotype-phenotype discordance. Finally, experimental approaches including transcriptomics, RNA-RNA interaction mapping, and functional validation are discussed as strategies to study sRNA-mediated regulatory networks. Understanding these regulatory mechanisms may help explain unresolved resistance phenotypes and refine antimicrobial resistance surveillance frameworks.

Outcomes in Patients with Tuberculous Meningitis: A Prospective Cohort Study in North India.
Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) is the most severe form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis, carrying the highest mortality among all forms. This multicentric prospective cohort study conducted in North India aimed to determine the incidence of complications, functional outcome (modified Rankin scale [mRS]), and mortality in TBM. Patients 12 years old and older with TBM were followed up until completion of 9 months of antitubercular treatment. Patients with concomitant HIV infection, other infections causing meningitis, or multidrug-resistant tuberculosis were excluded. The primary outcome was mRS at 9 months. Secondary outcomes included mRS at 6 months, poor mRS (>2), Barthel Index, and mortality at 6 and 9 months. Between October 1, 2019 and March 31, 2024, 585 eligible patients were enrolled, of whom 495 (84.6%) completed follow-up. The median age was 24.0 years old, and the majority were female (n = 304/495; 61.4%). Complications were present in 377 patients (76.2%): focal neurological deficits (41.6%), seizures (38.6%), immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (32.7%), hydrocephalus (24.8%), and drug-induced liver injury (14.1%). Complications were associated with worse mRS on unadjusted analysis (odds ratio [OR]: 2.5 [1.7-3.7]; P <0.001); however, this association was no longer statistically significant after adjustment for age, sex, baseline mRS, study center, and disease stage and category (OR: 1.3 [0.8-2.0]; P = 0.30). The median mRS improved from 4.0 at presentation to 2.0 at 6 months and 1.0 at 9 months. Death occurred at a median of 91.0 days after presentation. Mortality at 6 months was 9.3% and at 9 months was 10.7%.

Tick-borne pathogens in Finnish wildlife: The role of non-native raccoon dog and European hare.
The role of different host species in the circulation dynamics of tick-borne pathogens (TBPs) in northern ecosystems remains insufficiently characterized, despite the widespread distribution of these pathogens in European wildlife. In particular, the contribution of medium-sized mammals, including non-native species, to TBP circulation is poorly understood. We screened 446 skin samples from nine wildlife species in Finland for multiple zoonotic TBPs to assess pathogen occurrence across host species with particular emphasis on the invasive raccoon dog (Nyctereutes procyonoides) and non-native European hare (Lepus europaeus). Borrelia burgdorferi s.l., Anaplasma phagocytophilum, and Rickettsia helvetica were the most frequently detected pathogens, with prevalence varying among host species. Babesia spp. was predominantly detected in ungulates, whereas Spiroplasma ixodetis and Borrelia miyamotoi were rare. Raccoon dogs and European hares showed generally low pathogen prevalence, while the highest TBP prevalences were observed in squirrels, hedgehogs, and ungulates. We also screened for two Ixodes-associated endosymbionts (Rickettsiella spp. and Midichloria mitochondrii) as potential indicators of tick exposure. Although Rickettsiella spp. was associated with TBP infections, the low prevalence of both endosymbionts suggests their limited utility as tick bite markers. These findings provide a cross-sectional overview of TBP occurrence in Finnish wildlife and demonstrate that host-pathogen associations vary among species. The relatively low pathogen prevalence observed in the raccoon dog and European hare suggests that these species are unlikely to play a major role in maintaining TBP transmission in northern ecosystems, although they may contribute to tick abundance and dispersal.

Investigation on the use of ceftazidime-avibactam at a national hospital in Vietnam.
OBJECTIVES: To assess the utilization of ceftazidime-avibactam at Thong Nhat Hospital, a national hospital in Vietnam. METHODS: A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted using retrospective data from medical records of inpatients aged ≥ 18 years who received ceftazidime-avibactam for at least 2 days between January 2023 and March 2025 at Thong Nhat Hospital, Vietnam. The appropriateness of ceftazidime-avibactam use was evaluated based on Thong Nhat Hospital's antibiotic use guideline. The backward conditional method was used to identify factors associated with patient treatment outcomes. RESULTS: A total of 101 patients were included, with a median age of 78 years (68-86). Respiratory and bloodstream infections were the most common types, accounting for 84.15% and 44.55% of cases, respectively. Gram-negative bacteria comprised 76.05% of isolates, with Klebsiella pneumoniae (26.47%), Klebsiella aerogenes (18.50%) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (10.50%) being the most frequent. The susceptibility rate to ceftazidime-avibactam was 71.43% for Klebsiella pneumoniae, 95.65% for Klebsiella aerogenes and 42.86% for Pseudomonas aeruginosa. OXA-48 was the most detected carbapenemase gene (37.84%). The overall appropriateness rate of ceftazidime-avibactam use was 70.30%. The treatment success rate was 39.60%. Treatment in the intensive care unit was associated with decreased treatment success, while comorbid heart failure showed a potential association. CONCLUSIONS: The treatment success rate with ceftazidime-avibactam in this study was relatively low. Continuous surveillance of microbiological profiles and antibiotic resistance, particularly to ceftazidime-avibactam, is essential to better guide the management of drug-resistant Gram-negative infections at the hospital.

Draft genome sequence of emerging Salmonella enterica serovar Kentucky ST198 isolated from broiler litter at an integrated poultry-aquaculture marketplace in Bangladesh.
Integrated live poultry-aquaculture marketplaces represent high-risk One Health interfaces where environmental circulation of zoonotic Salmonella poses a threat to public health. Using Illumina NovaSeq, this study delineates genomic features of a Salmonella Kentucky ST198 strain, providing insight into a globally disseminated lineage and a resource for future surveillance and epidemiological investigations.

Operational integration of FT-IR spectroscopy into a genomics-based surveillance algorithm for Listeria monocytogenes.
Rapid and cost-effective tools are needed to complement whole-genome sequencing (WGS) in Listeria monocytogenes surveillance, particularly in settings with limited sequencing capacity. We evaluated the operational integration of Fourier-transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy as a first-line screening method within a genomics-based surveillance algorithm. A total of 24 L. monocytogenes isolates, including two epidemiologically confirmed outbreaks (n = 15) and unrelated sporadic isolates (n = 9), were analyzed. Species identification was performed by matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization-time-of-flight mass spectrometry, and genomic characterization was conducted using WGS, including multilocus sequence typing and single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) analysis. FT-IR spectra were acquired using the IR Biotyper system, and serogroup prediction and clustering were assessed using artificial neural network-based classification and multivariate analysis. FT-IR achieved 100% concordance with WGS for serogroup assignment, with consistently high confidence scores. Clustering analysis generated FT-IR groupings broadly concordant with WGS-defined outbreak clusters, correctly grouping isolates differing by ≤9 SNPs within the same outbreak-associated clusters while differentiating most genetically unrelated strains. FT-IR excluded seven of nine unrelated isolates from outbreak-associated clustering, although partial overlap was observed among highly clonal CC1 isolates. Operationally, FT-IR enabled preliminary results within 48-72 h after isolation, significantly reducing turnaround time compared to WGS. This tiered approach improves cost-efficiency by optimizing sequencing resource allocation, which is particularly relevant for low- and middle-income settings. These findings demonstrate that FT-IR spectroscopy provides rapid and reliable preliminary typing and can be effectively integrated into routine workflows, enhancing early outbreak detection and supporting more efficient measures. To our knowledge, this is among the first studies describing the structured integration of FT-IR into a genomics-based national surveillance workflow for L. monocytogenes, including its use as a real-time triage tool to optimize WGS allocation and accelerate epidemiological response in a public health reference laboratory setting.IMPORTANCEUsing a well-characterized data set, including two epidemiologically confirmed outbreaks and sporadic isolates, we demonstrate complete concordance (100%) between Fourier-transform infrared (FT-IR)-based serogroup prediction and whole-genome sequencing, along with the capacity of FT-IR to support rapid preliminary clustering. Notably, this study was conducted following the implementation of the first FT-IR system installed in Argentina, representing a major step forward in the incorporation of innovative technologies into national surveillance programs. To our knowledge, this is the first manuscript reporting the combined use of FT-IR spectroscopy, matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization-time-of-flight mass spectrometry, and genomics within an integrated surveillance framework for Listeria monocytogenes. This approach provides a novel and pragmatic model for strengthening microbiological surveillance in resource-constrained settings. Beyond analytical performance, this work provides a real-world, operational framework for integrating rapid phenotypic screening with genomic confirmation, enabling earlier outbreak detection, optimized use of sequencing resources, and the potential to accelerate source-tracking investigations.

Genomic diversity of human-associated Mycobacterium bovis in Canada.
Human infections caused by Mycobacterium bovis in Canada are not well documented. The following study analyzed M. bovis (excluding BCG) isolates identified in public health laboratories across Canadian provinces between 2000 and 2025. Whole-genome sequencing was used to catalog mutations linked to antimicrobial resistance and evaluate the genomic relatedness of isolates. The majority of samples in this study were non-respiratory (60%). Of 74 study isolates, 69 (93%) were phenotypically sensitive to first-line drugs isoniazid, rifampin, and ethambutol. The most frequently encountered M. bovis clusters belonged to M. tuberculosis complex lineages La 1.7 and La 1.8. Although some isolates showed phylogenetic clustering, their lack of spatial and temporal relatedness suggested sporadic cases rather than local M. bovis transmission. Of all first-line drugs evaluated, isoniazid showed the lowest concordance (94.4%) between phenotypic and genotypic methods. The isolates in this study harbor some mutations that are not currently documented in the WHO mutation catalog, indicating that these variants may be rare. The findings suggest that the prevalence of M. bovis infection in Canada is low with cases unlikely to be acquired through human-to-human transmission.IMPORTANCEIncidence of human infections due to Mycobacterium bovis in Canada is largely unknown as these data are not collected or annually published. This research is a first effort to identify historical M. bovis isolates that were available for culture, had drug susceptibility testing data, and were analyzed through whole-genome sequencing. The annual reporting of these data in Canada holds value.

Analysis of nontuberculous mycobacteria infection risks from CDC's water-related healthcare outbreak consultations, 2018-2024.
OBJECTIVE: Nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) are commonly found in healthcare facility water systems and can lead to serious and difficult-to-treat infections. We analyzed Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) consultations of water-related healthcare-associated infections (HAI) investigations involving NTM. DESIGN: Retrospective observational study. METHODS: We searched CDC consultation records from January 1, 2018, through December 31, 2024, using water-related terms and organisms, excluding Legionella, to identify and review investigations involving potential or confirmed transmission of water-related organisms; we reviewed investigations that involved NTM. RESULTS: Among 1,458 consultations, we identified 639 (43.8%) water-related investigations involving 4,685 patients and 60 different organisms. Investigations involving NTM accounted for 10.3% (n = 66) with 15 NTM species identified. Among NTM-related investigations, almost half involved M. abscessus (n = 31, 47.0%) and two-thirds (n = 44, 66.7%) involved extrapulmonary infections only. More than half of identified NTM investigations (n = 37, 56.1%) occurred in hospitals and over one-third (n = 23, 34.8%) in outpatient settings. Exposures to surgery (n = 27, 40.9%) and medical products (e.g., medical devices, medications, and biological products) (n = 35, 53.0%) were common. CONCLUSIONS: Over this seven-year period, approximately one-tenth of CDC healthcare water-related consultations involved NTM. The majority involved extrapulmonary infections, with surgery and exposure to contaminated medical products representing the most common exposures of concern. These findings highlight the potential for NTM infections when water-related healthcare exposures occur. Healthcare facilities are encouraged to identify the potential for exposure to nonsterile water during surgery, during the use of medical devices, and during the preparation and administration of medications to reduce the risk from NTM.

Temporal dynamics and forecasting of laboratory-confirmed human nontyphoidal Salmonella cases in Malaysia, 2018-2024: implications for surveillance.
OBJECTIVES: Nontyphoidal Salmonella (NTS) is a major cause of foodborne illness in Malaysia. Time-series modeling can characterize temporal patterns, although structural disruptions, nonlinear dynamics, and regional variability may affect model performance. This study aimed to characterize NTS seasonality in Malaysia, assess temporal stability, and explore model-based approaches for surveillance. METHODS: Monthly laboratory-confirmed human NTS cases from national laboratory surveillance databases for 2018-2024 were analyzed using time-series models, including autoregressive integrated moving-average (ARIMA) models with Fourier terms and an exploratory hybrid ARIMA-long short-term memory (LSTM) model. Interrupted time-series analysis was used to assess structural stability. Anomalies were identified using 95% prediction intervals, and stratified modeling assessed regional heterogeneity. RESULTS: NTS cases showed recurring annual seasonal patterns of moderate strength, with temporal variation over the study period. A significant decline occurred in March 2020 (β=-62.24 cases, p=0.001), followed by gradual recovery (β=2.71 cases/month, p<0.001), suggesting a marked coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic-related disruption and a subsequent positive post-intervention trend. The ARIMA(0,1,1)-Fourier (K=1) model outperformed conventional ARIMA, benchmark, and exponential smoothing models (root mean squared error, 42.9 vs. 51.37-108.79). The hybrid ARIMA-LSTM model provided modest additional improvement, particularly during high-case periods. Model-based anomaly detection identified deviations from expected patterns that coincided with documented outbreak-associated months. Regional heterogeneity in temporal dynamics suggested the need for surveillance strategies tailored to local epidemiological patterns. CONCLUSION: Parsimonious models captured most temporal patterns in NTS cases, with only modest gains from more complex approaches. Context-specific modeling strategies, model-based anomaly detection, and tiered surveillance frameworks may support more proactive NTS surveillance in Malaysia.

From Rare to Rising: A Story of Enterobacter-associated Pneumonia Evolving in the Community.
INTRODUCTION: Pneumonia is a common cause of mortality and morbidity worldwide and is the fifth leading cause of death. It is generally caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and some atypical microorganisms. Interestingly, a member of ESKAPE pathogens, mainly Enterobacter cloacae complex, is increasingly showing its presence in the samples of lower respiratory tract specimens. Emergence of multidrug resistance (MDR) in these bacteria, including resistance to last-resort carbapenems, has led to an increased interest in this organism causing pneumonia. AIMS AND OBJECTIVES: (1) Prevalence of E. cloacae complex among community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) patients and (2) antibiotic resistance pattern of these pathogens. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Respiratory samples from adult patients were processed according to standard microbiological techniques, including direct smear examination, incubation in blood, MacConkey and chocolate agar plates, and Gram staining. Identification of E. cloacae complex and antibiotic susceptibility testing, along with resistance patterns, was performed by automated ID/AST instrument. RESULTS: About 15.7% of E. cloacae complex-associated CAP patients were found over a 1-year study period. Antimicrobial susceptibility tests indicated a MDR profile in 58.3% of isolates. Resistance was mostly to carbapenems (72.73%), followed by aztreonam (69.7%), piperacillin-tazobactam (68%), and fluoroquinolones (63.6%). CONCLUSION: E. cloacae complex is an emerging and clinically significant pathogen causing CAP. Its MDR profile contributes to an increased tendency to intensive care unit admission and the development of sepsis. Hence, detecting this pathogen in lower respiratory tract specimens should be treated as a high alert and should prompt treatment at the earliest.

Pancreatic hydatid cyst with a characteristic "water-lily" sign.
BACKGROUND: Cystic echinococcosis rarely involves the pancreas and may mimic common cystic neoplasms. Recognition of characteristic imaging signs is central to diagnosis; the "water-lily" sign (floating detached endocyst) is a rare and highly characteristic finding in favor of transitional-stage hydatid cyst and, when recognized, can prevent inappropriate cyst puncture and guide stage- and anatomy-based management. CASE: A 34-year-old woman from Iran, an endemic region for cystic echinococcosis, presented with intermittent epigastric/right upper quadrant pain. At an outside institution, endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration had been performed before referral; cyst-fluid amylase was 20 U/L and carcinoembryonic antigen was not detected, arguing against pseudocyst and mucinous neoplasm. Ultrasound and MRI/MRCP performed after EUS showed a unilocular pancreatic head cyst with a floating internal membrane ("water-lily"/"serpent" appearance) and mild upstream pancreatic duct dilatation. Our multidisciplinary team favored pancreatic cystic echinococcosis. The patient underwent surgical cyst excision with avoidance of scolicidal instillation into the biliary tree. Albendazole (400 mg twice daily, ∼ 10-15 mg/kg/day) was given perioperatively and continued for 6 months. Pathology confirmed laminated membranes and protoscolices. She remains asymptomatic on surveillance MRI without recurrence. CONCLUSION: In an endemic region, a pancreatic cyst with a floating membrane and low cyst-fluid amylase should raise suspicion for cystic echinococcosis. Anchoring the diagnosis to WHO staging and resisting routine EUS-FNA can avert spillage and caustic cholangiopathy from scolicidal agents. Radiologists play the key role in making this distinction.

Rethinking CD47 an innate immune checkpoint and immunotherapeutic target in malaria pathogenesis: A narrative review.
Malaria remains a significant global health challenge, particularly in tropical regions, where high morbidity and mortality persist. The need for new therapeutic strategies remains urgent as increasing antimalarial drug resistance threatens treatment efficacy and highlights the need for innovative approaches that target not only the parasite but also host-pathogen interactions. While malaria immunology has traditionally focused on adaptive responses, including T-cell dysfunction, the role of innate immune checkpoints remains underexplored. Among these, CD47- a transmembrane protein best known for delivering a "don't-eat-me" signal to phagocytes has emerged as a potential therapeutic target. This concept is particularly relevant to malaria because Plasmodium infects red blood cells, whose survival and clearance are tightly regulated by CD47-SIRPα signalling. Emerging evidence suggests that CD47 contributes to the regulation of phagocytic clearance of infected red blood cells and may influence inflammatory responses associated with disease severity. Disruption of CD47-SIRPα signalling may enhance host phagocytic responses, promoting clearance of parasitized erythrocytes and potentially improving disease control. This review examines the immunopathological role of CD47 in malaria, evaluates its potential as a host-directed therapeutic target, and discusses the challenges and future directions for translating CD47-targeted strategies into clinical practice. CD47, therefore represents a promising but incompletely validated host-directed therapeutic target, with important translational gaps that must be addressed before clinical application.

Heterologous expression of the Metarhizium anisopliae barc gene cluster reveals a diphenyl ether-to-xanthene transformation in barceloneic acid biosynthesis.
Filamentous fungi generate chemical diversity through several evolutionary strategies, including the elaboration of conserved biosynthetic intermediates into structurally distinct secondary metabolites. Emodin and its corresponding anthrone are central intermediates in fungal aromatic polyketide metabolism, yet the enzymatic logic that remodels these precursors into more complex scaffolds remains incompletely understood. To investigate this process, we examined an infection-responsive non-reducing polyketide synthase biosynthetic gene cluster (barc) from the entomopathogenic fungus Metarhizium anisopliae predicted to encode an emodin-derived aromatic polyketide pathway. Heterologous reconstruction of the barc cluster in Aspergillus nidulans led to the production of the previously reported diphenyl ether barceloneic acid A (1) and the xanthene barceloneic acid C2 (2), together with two new compounds derived from 2, barceloneic acids D and E (3 and 4). Compound 3 is a cyclopentanone adduct of the xanthene 2, whereas 4 is a polyketide-indole hybrid, highlighting the chemical reactivity of the xanthene 2 scaffold. Through combinatorial heterologous expression and feeding assays, we identified a predicted glucose-methanol-choline oxidoreductase (BarcL) as the enzyme responsible for converting diphenyl ether 1 to xanthene 2.
