This defines a previously uncharacterised oxidative scaffold-remodelling step in barceloneic acid biosynthesis, revealing how an emodin-derived pathway can access a xanthene scaffold. Deletion of the backbone gene barcB in M. anisopliae did not significantly alter virulence towards Tenebrio molitor (mealworm) under the conditions tested, suggesting that barceloneic acids are not essential for pathogenicity in this insect model.

Plasmodium vivax Malaria in Afghanistan: A Scoping Review of Epidemiology, Relapse, Treatment and Elimination Challenges.
BACKGROUND: Plasmodium vivax predominates in Afghanistan. Recurrent disease and the safety requirements of anti-relapse treatment complicate elimination, while routine case counts provide limited information about completed radical cure. OBJECTIVE: To synthesize Afghanistan-specific evidence on P. vivax epidemiology, recurrence, treatment, G6PD safety, diagnosis, resistance and elimination, and translate it into measurable service priorities. METHODS: This JBI- and PRISMA-ScR-guided nested scoping review reassessed 287 publications and 45 reports from a parent evidence map using a vivax-focused population-concept-context framework. The core search ended on 12 August 2026; 40 publications and 10 institutional reports were included. Two reviewers independently assessed eligibility and charted data, with third-reviewer verification. RESULTS: WHO reported 247,100 P. vivax cases among 257,524 confirmed malaria cases in 2024 (96.0%). An independent national series recorded 887,227 vivax episodes in 2018-2023, peaking in September. In a 593-patient Afghan trial, chloroquine plus 14-day primaquine reduced 1-year recurrence compared with chloroquine alone (hazard ratio: 0.37, 95% CI: 0.25-0.54). Paired primaquine comparisons support an important relapse contribution, but their attribution estimate is assumption-dependent and is not a national relapse rate. Historical treatment studies, G6PD surveys, and molecular findings support continued efficacy and safety surveillance. Evidence is geographically uneven, and supported refugee-camp treatment outcomes do not establish feasibility in contemporary routine services. CONCLUSIONS: The priority is to link case characterization to a measurable radical-cure cascade: diagnosis, G6PD assessment, regimen selection, initiation, completion, safety monitoring and recurrence investigation. Phased delivery should combine district- and season-specific targeting with clinical efficacy monitoring and documented cross-border referral.

Strengthening geospatial surveillance for malaria control and elimination in Indonesia: a meeting report.
As Indonesia progresses toward malaria elimination, geospatial analysis offers opportunities to strengthen surveillance, improve intervention targeting, and support data-informed decision-making. However, despite increasing availability of georeferenced surveillance data, the routine use of geographic information systems (GIS) within malaria programs remains uneven. A three-day consultation and GIS training workshop was conducted in Jakarta, bringing together 25 representatives from National and Sub-National Malaria Programs and other disease control units. The workshop included hands-on R-based spatial analysis, followed by semi-structured focus group discussions exploring current practices, barriers, and potential strategies for strengthening geospatial surveillance. Participants reported growing recognition of the value of geospatial data and described surveillance platforms that routinely capture spatially referenced information; however, these data were often used primarily for basic visualization. Key challenges included limited capacity in advanced GIS and spatial modelling, high staff turnover, data quality concerns, fragmented health information systems, and infrastructure constraints, particularly in remote settings. Participants identified opportunities to strengthen applied training and mentorship, improve data quality and interoperability across platforms, and gradually integrate geospatial analysis into routine planning and resource allocation. The consultation highlighted both progress and continuing challenges in operationalizing geospatial analysis within Indonesia's malaria surveillance system. Continued investment in workforce capacity, data quality, infrastructure, and system integration may help strengthen the translation of routinely collected geospatial data into programmatic decision-making for malaria elimination.

Diagnostic Value of Skin Biopsy in Fatal Histoplasmosis-Associated Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis: A Case Report.
INTRODUCTION: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) is a rare, life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome most commonly triggered in adults by infection, malignancy, or autoimmune disease. Disseminated histoplasmosis is an uncommon but recognized infectious trigger, particularly in immunosuppressed patients. Its cutaneous manifestations may be subtle and nonspecific but can provide accessible tissue for diagnostic evaluation. CASE REPORT: A 41-year-old man with psoriasis treated with adalimumab presented with 5 months of progressive constitutional and abdominal symptoms followed by fever, shock, pancytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, coagulopathy, hypertriglyceridemia, and extreme hyperferritinemia (> 89,000 ng/mL). Bone marrow biopsy demonstrated hemophagocytosis but was negative for fungal organisms on Grocott methenamine silver staining. Punch biopsy of scattered pink-to-violaceous acneiform papules on the forehead and scalp demonstrated numerous tissue-invasive microorganisms, and subsequent molecular testing identified Histoplasma capsulatum. He received dexamethasone, ruxolitinib, and liposomal amphotericin B; etoposide was withheld because of ongoing hemorrhage. Despite treatment, he succumbed to hemorrhagic shock and multiorgan failure and died. Autopsy demonstrated widespread histoplasmosis. CONCLUSIONS: In patients with HLH, subtle skin lesions may provide accessible tissue for demonstrating invasive infection and obtaining organism-specific confirmation, even when fungal staining of another tissue is negative. Careful skin examination and targeted biopsy of new, atypical, or evolving lesions should be considered in immunocompromised adults with unexplained systemic inflammation, particularly those receiving tumor necrosis factor-alpha inhibitors.

Mosquito-based malaria control through genetic, microbial and immunological innovations.
Malaria remains a major global health challenge, causing approximately 600,000 deaths annually despite decades of progress using insecticide-based and drug-based interventions. These core tools are increasingly compromised by widespread insecticide resistance in mosquitoes, drug resistance in parasites, adaptive vector behaviours and the lack of highly effective vaccines, together with logistical and sustainability constraints. Complementary strategies, including larval source management, environmental modification and novel insecticide formulations, also require sustained investment and strong community engagement. Novel Plasmodium transmission-blocking and Anopheles population-suppressing technologies, based on transgenic gene drives, natural and engineered microorganisms, and transmission-blocking vaccines and drugs, have the potential to redefine malaria control by providing parallel, sustainable, mosquito-targeted interventions. In this Review, we synthesize scientific advances underpinning these innovations, identify key knowledge gaps and discuss the science-based safeguards necessary for the responsible implementation of these malaria control strategies.

Detection of Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium falciparum using colorimetric loop-mediated isothermal amplification from dried blood spots collected in active and passive malaria surveillance in the Peruvian Amazon.
BACKGROUND: As malaria transmission declines in regions approaching elimination, highly sensitive diagnostic tools are needed to detect low-density infections, particularly in active and passive surveillance settings. Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) is a promising molecular alternative to conventional diagnostics. This study evaluated the performance of a colorimetric LAMP (cLAMP) assay for detecting Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium falciparum from dried blood spots (DBS) in the Peruvian Amazon. METHODOLOGY/PRINCIPAL FINDINGS: The cLAMP assay was applied to DNA extracted from DBS collected through active case detection (ACD; n = 574) and passive case detection (PCD; n = 431). Two extraction methods were compared: mini spin column (MSC DNA) and a boil-and-spin (BS DNA) method. Diagnostic performance was evaluated against microscopy and real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR). In ACD samples, qPCR identified 125 malaria-positive cases (117 P. vivax, 8 P. falciparum). Microscopy showed a sensitivity of 57.6%, compared with 63.2% for cLAMP using BS DNA and 82.4% using MSC DNA. In PCD samples, qPCR detected 140 positives (129 P. vivax, 9 P. falciparum, and 2 mixed infections). Microscopy sensitivity was 72.9%, while cLAMP reached 77.1% with BS DNA and 82.1% with MSC DNA. Specificity remained high (> 99.0%) across methods. CONCLUSIONS/SIGNIFICANCE: cLAMP improved the detection of malaria infections from DBS compared with microscopy when combined with column-based DNA extraction in active surveillance activities. While the boil-and-spin method showed performance comparable to microscopy, column-based extraction substantially increased sensitivity, especially for low-density infections identified through active surveillance. These findings support cLAMP as a practical and sensitive complementary tool for malaria surveillance in low-transmission and elimination settings.

Travel history and occupation among diagnosed Cutaneous Leishmaniasis cases in Guyana: A multi-site retrospective case series, 2017-2021.
BACKGROUND: Cutaneous Leishmaniasis (CL) in Guyana has not been systematically characterised in the peer-reviewed literature for several decades. This study aimed to describe the demographic, occupational, geographic, and clinical profile of diagnosed CL cases at Guyana's principal diagnostic sites, and to test, within this case series, whether field-based occupation is associated with reported interior travel and whether travel history is associated with time to presentation. METHODOLOGY/PRINCIPAL FINDINGS: Retrospective case series (chart review) of CL diagnoses recorded at three facilities in Georgetown and the interior (2017-2021). Of 223 available case records, a random subsample of 170 was abstracted. Occupation and interior travel were patient-declared; their association was tested directly, then via adjusted logistic regression. Most patients (61.8%) reported interior travel, and 45.3% held field-based occupations, chiefly mining and military. Interior travel was more common among field-based than non-field workers (84.4% vs 43.0%; OR = 7.18 [95% CI, 3.42-15.04]; p < .001), and this association persisted after adjustment for age and sex (OR = 7.08 [3.07-16.30]). Younger age was associated with interior travel (OR = 0.96 [0.94-0.98]; p = .001), whereas sex was not. The sample was predominantly male (81.8%; median age 33 years). Patients with interior travel presented earlier than those without (Mdn = 61 vs 243 days; p < .001). CONCLUSIONS/SIGNIFICANCE: Most diagnosed CL cases in this series occurred in people reporting interior travel, predominantly those in field-based occupations, and this travel history was associated with earlier presentation. All participants had CL and there was no comparison group, so these findings describe the case population and associations within it rather than risk factors for acquiring infection; they also rest on a single, retrospectively recorded travel variable. They nonetheless indicate where pre-deployment prevention, occupational screening, and traveller advisories could be focused, and they support a case-control study with validated exposure measurement.

Multifactorial Contributors to Diagnostic Delay in a High-Risk Patient with Hepatocellular Carcinoma: A Case Report with Clinical Lessons.
BACKGROUND: Patients at high risk for primary liver cancer (PLC) are recommended to undergo PLC surveillance at least every six months. Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is a commonly used biomarker; however, approximately 15-30% of PLC cases remain AFP-negative throughout their course. Therefore, surveillance in high-risk populations should be based on liver imaging. Any newly detected or progressive lesion should be further characterized by contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT), contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), or contrast-enhanced ultrasound, following guideline-based classification and follow-up recommendations. CASE PRESENTATION: This case details a 45-year-old Chinese male with hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and a family history of PLC. As a high-risk individual for PLC, he did not undergo regular PLC surveillance for three years. During opportunistic encounters for acute myocardial infarction and abdominal pain, the attending specialists failed to appreciate the progression of liver imaging findings. In addition, the COVID-19 pandemic may have further aggravated pre-existing difficulties with follow-up and access to care, contributing to a delayed diagnosis of PLC. CONCLUSION: This case illustrates how a combination of physician-related, patient-related, and social-environmental factors contributed to surveillance failure and diagnostic delay in a high-risk patient with PLC. It reflects on why guideline-recommended interventions were not implemented at each healthcare encounter, how to correctly interpret AFP, and how to improve adherence to surveillance among high-risk populations for PLC. The insights from this case aim to inform systematic improvements in PLC monitoring for patients with chronic HBV infection.

Post-COVID-19 changes in the epidemiology of group A Streptococcus infections in Taiwan: A retrospective study.
BACKGROUND: Temporal changes in group A Streptococcus (GAS) infections have been reported worldwide, but long-term data from Taiwan remain limited. This study evaluated temporal patterns, age-specific disease characteristics, antimicrobial susceptibility, and factors associated with invasive GAS infection. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective study that included patients with GAS infection at a tertiary referral center in Taiwan from 2015 to 2024. Monthly hospital-identified case counts were described, and multivariable logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with invasive disease. RESULTS: Among 454 patients, 33 (7.3%) had invasive disease. Monthly case counts declined markedly during the COVID-19 period (2020-2022), remained low in 2023, and increased to 45 cases in 2024, still below pre-pandemic annual levels. Adults aged ≥65 years accounted for 14 of 33 invasive cases (42.4%). Age ≥18 years (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 11.6; 95% confidence interval [CI], 4.4-30.9; p < 0.001) and the presence of two or more underlying disease categories (aOR, 29.7; 95% CI, 10.4-84.5; p < 0.001) were associated with invasive disease. All isolates were susceptible to penicillin. Invasive isolates showed higher susceptibility to clindamycin and erythromycin but lower susceptibility to tetracycline than noninvasive isolates. CONCLUSION: Hospital-identified GAS cases showed substantial temporal variation. Older age and greater underlying disease burden were associated with invasive infection. These findings may support clinical risk assessment and institutional surveillance.

Hematological indices as predictors of in-hospital adverse outcomes in patients with COVID-19.
The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic required medical teams to make rational decisions with limited resources, especially in Brazil. Various diagnostic tools, clinical guidelines, and existing indices were adopted to predict the risk of death and other adverse outcomes. The objective of this study was to validate three hematological indices [neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), and lymphocyte-monocyte ratio (LMR)] for predicting adverse hospital outcomes in patients with COVID-19 in an observational cohort at a hospital in northeastern Brazil between April 2020 and October 2021. Hematological indices were calculated based on admission blood counts and correlated with hospital outcomes: in-hospital death, invasive mechanical ventilation, and renal replacement therapy. The analysis determined the frequencies of outcomes, established index thresholds, and assessed their association and accuracy and factors associated with hospital survival. Intra-hospital outcomes reflected disease severity; 34.62% of patients required admission to the ICU, 26.21% invasive mechanical ventilation, 4.2% renal replacement therapy, and 21.04% died. Advanced age, ICU requirement, and higher NLR were associated with higher risk of death. Multivariate analysis identified NLR as the only index associated with worse prognosis, with a cutoff point of 5.24 at hospital admission, showing a sensitivity of 84.0% and accuracy of 86.9%. The negative predictive value of 95.52% was highly significant, assisting hospital management by focusing efforts on higher-risk patients. These findings highlight the predictive value of the NLR, PLR, and LMR indices as valuable markers for risk stratification in patients hospitalized with COVID-19, offering a broader view of prognosis and guiding more personalized management and care strategies.

Large-scale COVID-19 asymptomatic testing using lateral flow devices (LFDs) in reducing nosocomial infections and healthcare worker absenteeism: an observational study and cost-effectiveness analysis in NHS acute trusts in England.
INTRODUCTION: Twice-weekly lateral flow device (LFD) testing for asymptomatic healthcare workers (HCWs) was introduced in the National Health Service (NHS) in England in November 2020. We retrospectively examine associations between LFD testing, nosocomial infections and HCW absenteeism at NHS acute trusts. METHODS: We collected 16 million LFD testing results reported by NHS acute trusts from 1 October 2020 to 30 March 2022 and estimated the prevalence of nosocomial COVID-19 infections in NHS acute trusts using data from the International Severe Acute Respiratory and Emerging Infection Consortium (ISARIC). We used a mixed-effects linear model to examine the association between full-time equivalent (FTE) days lost due to COVID-19 and LFD test coverage. The relationship between weekly prevalence of nosocomial infections and LFD test coverage in the previous week was modelled using logistic regression weighted by the number of new COVID-19 cases reported in the ISARIC dataset for that week. We conducted an analysis of cost-effectiveness of testing for nosocomial infections. RESULTS: Increased LFD test coverage was associated with decreases in FTE days lost due to COVID-19 from November 2020 to July 2021, with no association observed from August 2021 to March 2022. The proportion of nosocomial infections among new weekly cases in hospitalised patients was negatively associated with reported LFD testing levels. CONCLUSIONS: Higher LFD test coverage was associated with lower HCW absenteeism (November 2020-July 2021) and with a lower proportion of nosocomial infections among hospitalised patients. Given the retrospective, ecological design, these are associations rather than causal effects, and the cost-effectiveness estimates are valid only if the observed association reflects a causal effect of testing rather than confounding by co-occurring interventions or temporal trends in the pandemic. Under that assumption, LFD testing would have been a cost-effective measure for reducing nosocomial infections in NHS acute trusts.

Infant vaccination coverage trajectories and immunisation system archetypes in the WHO African region, 2019-2024: a longitudinal analysis of 47 countries.
INTRODUCTION: COVID-19 disrupted childhood vaccination, but country-specific heterogeneity in diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis-containing vaccines (DTP3) coverage across the WHO African region remains poorly understood. This study addressed this gap by quantifying temporal trajectories and identifying latent structural patterns in DTP3 coverage across all 47 countries in the WHO African region from 2019 to 2024, spanning the onset and recovery phases of the COVID-19 pandemic. METHODS: Country-level DTP3 coverage data from 2019 to 2024 were extracted from the WHO/United Nations Children's Fund Estimates of National Immunisation Coverage, published in July 2025. Country-specific ordinary least squares regression models estimated annual rates of change (slopes) in DTP3 coverage, while linear mixed-effects modelling decomposed within-country and between-country variance components. Principal component (PC) analysis (PCA) was then applied to the 6-year coverage matrix to derive two dominant, uncorrelated components capturing coverage level (PC1) and temporal trajectory (PC2). K-means clustering of PC scores grouped countries into empirically distinct immunisation system archetypes. RESULTS: Between 2019 and 2024, the estimated annual rate of change in DTP3 coverage was positive in 21 countries and negative in 24; Eritrea and Burkina Faso showed no evidence of a linear trend. The fixed-effect slope was 0.07 percentage points per year (95% CI -0.34 to 0.47; p=0.75), indicating no statistically significant net regional change, while between-country heterogeneity was substantial (random-intercept variance, 188.18; random-slope variance, 1.18). PCA showed that PC1 dominated, explaining 93% of variance (capturing sustained coverage level), with PC2 contributing an additional 3% (capturing temporal trajectory). K-means clustering of PC scores yielded four archetypes: cluster 1 (high coverage, consolidating; n=15), cluster 2 (chronically low coverage, divergent trajectories; n=9), cluster 3 (mid-low coverage, predominantly improving; n=11) and cluster 4 (mid-high coverage, erosion risk; n=12). CONCLUSION: This study generated an empirically derived, model-driven typology of immunisation system performance across the WHO African region, characterised by four distinct DTP3 coverage archetypes. The typology provides decision-makers with a granular basis for differentiating programmatic strategies, prioritising resource deployment and designing cluster-specific implementation research rather than applying uniform regional solutions.

Gendered forms of intergenerational solidarity in the COVID-19 pandemic: an intersectional perspective on the public renegotiation of a moral resource for future health crises in Germany.
BACKGROUND: During the COVID-19 pandemic, 'intergenerational solidarity' became a prominent buzzword in public debates. At the same time, a resurge of ageist stereotypes could be observed that proved to be a constant structuring element in the public renegotiation of intergenerational solidarity. Despite a growing body of research indicating that the COVID-19 pandemic also had a significant impact on inequalities related to other social categories, such as gender, the interplay between appeals for intergenerational solidarity and other social inequalities in public debates has received limited attention. METHODS: To examine how appeals to intergenerational solidarity and gender-related aspects are intertwined in times of crisis, we provide an intersectional perspective on the public renegotiation of intergenerational solidarity during the COVID-19 pandemic, using the example of the German media debate. Based on a qualitative content analysis of articles from two major German weekly newspapers, Die Zeit and Welt am Sonntag, published between March 2020 and June 2022 (n = 351), we identified two paradigmatic cases for an intersectional in-depth-analysis, focusing primarily on the categorial intersection of age and gender within the material. RESULTS: We can observe not only a resurge of ageism and age-related stereotypes in these media representations regarding various aspects of intergenerational solidarity, but also their entanglement with gender norms. Prevailing notions of intergenerational solidarity in the media continue to rely on gendered and age-based assumptions that shape how the moral actors, the basis, contributions, and normative goals of intergenerational solidarity are elucidated. We critically discuss these claims against the backdrop of broader intersectional feminist philosophy literature on structural social inequities and injustices. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings illustrate the significance of a gendered and heteronormative generational divide in appeals for intergenerational solidarity that include pertinent gender and age stereotypes. Intergenerational solidarity proves to be a moral resource in times of crisis, even though it often runs the risk of reiterating and perpetuating gendered ageism. However, approaches from intersectional feminist philosophy can help to conceptualize intergenerational solidarity as a diversity-sensitive moral resource in impending health crises in Germany and beyond.

A global community of practice to improve public-private engagement in TB: the TBPPM Learning Network.
BACKGROUND: In many high-TB-burden settings, most people seek initial care from private providers who are often not integrated into national TB programmes. Public-private mix (PPM) strategies are therefore critical, yet difficult to operationalise. Communities of Practice (CoPs) can act as health system enablers and facilitate knowledge exchange, but empirical evidence on their long-term function in disease specific contexts is limited. METHODS: We conducted a mixed-methods descriptive analysis of the TBPPM Learning Network (LN) from 2019 to 2025. Quantitative data from routine platform analytics were triangulated with thematic analysis of 53 webinars and 9 Friday Forum topics. RESULTS: The LN engaged over 6,000 TB professionals across more than 130 countries, with over 75% from low- and middle-income countries. It adapted rapidly during the COVID-19 pandemic, strengthened South-South exchange, and supported leadership development among frontline implementers. Six key lessons were identified, including the importance of sustained facilitation, community-building, and adaptability, alongside persistent challenges in translating learning into action in resource-limited settings. CONCLUSION: A global virtual CoP can function as a scalable mechanism to support knowledge translation, capacity strengthening, and collaboration in complex TB health systems, but sustained investment is required to translate learning into policy and practice.

Epidemiology, risk factors and clinical outcome of community-acquired pneumonia in severely immunosuppressed patients: a comprehensive analysis from the multinational, prospective CAPNETZ Cohort.
PURPOSE: Despite growing evidence that immunosuppression (IS) influences aetiology and prognosis of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), there remains a lack of data from representative multicentre studies. METHODS: The multinational prospective CAPNETZ study includes patients with CAP and HIV since 2017, and with other causes of IS since 2020. We present the first comprehensive analysis of patients with CAP and IS (HIV with low CD4 cells, systemic steroids, immunosuppressive drugs, antineoplastic treatment, neutropenia, primary immunodeficiency, transplantation, haematological neoplasia) included within CAPNETZ until December 2023. IS cases were matched 1:1 with non-IS patients. The primary end-point was 30-day mortality and/or organ replacement therapy. Additionally, cases of CAP caused by non-core respiratory pathogens (NCRPs) according to an international consensus were evaluated. Univariate and multivariate risk factor analyses and evaluation of predictive scores by receiver operating characteristic analysis were performed. RESULTS: We included 232 patients with IS, most commonly after antineoplastic therapy (37.5%), systemic steroids (36.2%) and immunosuppressive drugs (35.8%). 10.3% reached the primary end-point. Overall, IS was not associated with prognosis compared to matched non-IS patients, but patients with immunosuppressive drugs had a significantly lower risk. The qSOFA, CRB-65 and CURB-65 scores showed limited prediction (area under the curve 0.57-0.64) and insufficient sensitivity for the primary end-point. CAP caused by NCRPs occurred in 16.4% in IS and was associated with transplantation, previous anti-infective treatment and intensive care unit admission, but SARS-CoV-2, Haemophilus influenzae and Streptococcus pneumoniae were the most common pathogens in both groups. CONCLUSION: This study demonstrates the relevance and heterogeneity of CAP in IS and highlights the need for individualised risk stratification and treatment.

Long-term trends in pediatric intussusception in Hokkaido, Japan, 2007-2024 across the rotavirus vaccination era.
OBJECTIVES: Pediatric intussusception is the most common cause of acute intestinal obstruction in young children. We investigated long-term epidemiological trends in pediatric intussusception before and after rotavirus vaccine introduction and during the COVID-19 pandemic in Hokkaido, Japan. METHODS: A retrospective multicenter surveillance study was conducted at 17 hospitals in Hokkaido between 2007 and 2024. Clinical characteristics, management, outcomes, and viral antigen test results were collected. Only cases fulfilling Brighton Level 1 diagnostic certainty were included. Annual incidence rates were calculated using regional population statistics. RESULTS: A total of 513 children met the inclusion criteria, with 93.0% aged 0-4 years. Non-surgical reduction was successful in 94.0% of cases, and no deaths or long-term sequelae were observed. Among infants aged <1 year, incidence decreased from 99.4 per 100,000 person-years during the pre-vaccination period (2007-2011) to 69.9 during the voluntary vaccination period (2012-2019), and was 79.7 during the universal vaccination/COVID-19 period (2020-2024). Corresponding incidence rates among children aged 0-4 years were 55.4, 36.7, and 38.1 per 100,000 person-years, respectively. CONCLUSION: Among children aged 0-4 years, intussusception incidence was lower during the period following rotavirus vaccine introduction than during the pre-vaccine period and remained broadly stable during the universal vaccination and COVID-19 period. The observed changes cannot be attributed to rotavirus vaccination alone because of concurrent changes in infectious disease circulation and other population-level factors. Continued surveillance is warranted to further clarify the epidemiology of pediatric intussusception.

Drawing on lessons from the COVID-19 pandemic and seizing the opportunity for health promoting prisons.
Health promoting prisons is an approach that emphasises structural and whole of system response to health promotion in correctional settings. Three decades on since its initiation in 1995, progress in the health promoting prisons agenda has remained limited. This commentary takes a strengths-based stance to provide some insights from the COVID-19 pandemic to help progress the health promoting prisons agenda.

Residential setting as an effect modifier of intellectual and physical disability associations with COVID-19 infection, hospitalisation and mortality in Scotland.
BACKGROUND: People with intellectual and physical disabilities experienced disproportionately adverse COVID-19 outcomes, and communal residential settings were major sites of transmission. However, whether residential setting modifies the associations of these specific disability groups with recorded infection, hospitalisation and mortality has not been examined at population scale. We assessed interaction on both multiplicative and additive scales. METHODS: We conducted a population-wide retrospective cohort study of 3,719,651 adults aged 16 years or older who were alive and resident in Scotland on 1 March 2020. Disability status was derived from the 2011 Scottish Census and classified as intellectual disability, physical and/or sensory disability without intellectual disability, or no recorded intellectual or physical disability. The latter category was the prespecified comparison group and could include people with other long-term conditions. Residential setting was classified as private dwellings, small communal establishments (<50 residents) or large communal establishments (50 or more residents). Outcomes were first laboratory-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection, first COVID-19 hospitalisation and COVID-19-related mortality from 1 March 2020 to 30 April 2022. Cox proportional hazards models estimated joint category hazard ratios and departures from multiplicative and additive no-interaction models. RESULTS: For recorded infection, interaction was positive on both scales. Multiplicative interaction was significant (χ²(4) = 541.42, p < 0.001), with joint hazard ratios for intellectual disability increasing from 2.54 (95% CI 2.46-2.62) in private dwellings to 9.42 (95% CI 8.08-11.00) in large communal establishments; corresponding estimates for physical disability increased from 1.55 (95% CI 1.53-1.57) to 5.67 (95% CI 5.37-5.98). RERI was 6.09 (95% CI 4.63-7.54) for intellectual disability and 3.31 (95% CI 3.00-3.62) for physical disability in large communal establishments. For hospitalisation, there was no clear evidence of interaction (χ²(4) = 9.32, p = 0.050; all RERI confidence intervals included zero). For mortality, interaction was negative on both scales (χ²(4) = 106.58, p < 0.001), with predominantly negative RERI estimates in communal establishments, most notably for intellectual disability in small communal establishments (RERI -2.07, 95% CI -3.21 to -0.93). CONCLUSIONS: Residential setting modified associations between intellectual and physical disability and COVID-19 outcomes, with positive interaction for infection, no clear interaction for hospitalisation, and negative interaction for mortality. These findings support pandemic preparedness that considers disability and residential setting together, including tailored infection prevention in communal settings.

Sustained type I interferon activity and N-antigenemia form a vicious cycle during severe COVID-19.
BACKGROUND: Although antigenemia is associated with poor outcomes in respiratory viral infections, the underlying mechanisms driving viral bloodstream dissemination remain not fully understood. Herein, we aimed to characterise SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid (N)-antigenemia kinetics in patients with severe COVID-19. We also sought to identify host and viral determinants associated with viral dissemination through a multiparametric integrated analysis and assess the associated risk of death. METHODS: This observational study included hospitalised patients with severe COVID-19 across three independent cohorts (discovery, n = 66; confirmation, n = 137; validation, n = 27), used respectively for identification, replication, and validation of findings, along with patients with mild COVID-19 and with severe influenza infection, as a disease severity and non-COVID-19 control group. From blood and nasal samples, N-antigenemia levels were analysed in relation to 45 host/viral parameters. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to assess the association with in-hospital mortality. Single-cell RNA sequencing was used to identify host determinants, and in vitro primary human airway epithelial models were used to assess epithelial barrier integrity and viral translocation. FINDINGS: Across cohorts, we observed a significantly higher detection rate and concentration of N-antigenemia in patients with severe COVID-19 at admission compared to those with mild COVID-19 or controls (fold change [FC] >54.7, p < 0.001 [Kruskal-Wallis, Dunn post-hoc]). Type-I interferon (IFN-I) activity was the strongest correlate of N-antigenemia (ρ = 0.72, p.adj < 0.001 [Spearman, Benjamini-Hochberg]), and longitudinal analyses revealed a strong positive sigmoidal relationship (p < 0.001 [approximate Wald test]). Patients with severe COVID-19 with neutralising autoantibodies against IFN-I lacked detectable N-antigenemia, further supporting a link between systemic viral dissemination and IFN-I activity. Single-cell RNA sequencing showed higher expression of interferon-stimulated genes in monocytes and dendritic cells in patients with a high N-antigenemia level. Furthermore, high N-antigenemia at hospital admission was independently associated with an increased risk of death (aOR 2.6, 95% CI 1.0-6.7; p = 0.042 [Wald test]). Finally, we demonstrated that prolonged IFN-I exposure in vitro appears to impair epithelial barrier integrity. INTERPRETATION: These findings suggest that sustained IFN-I activity is associated with systemic viral dissemination and epithelial barrier dysfunction in patient with severe COVID-19. The concordance between clinical observations and in vitro data supports a potential link between prolonged IFN-I responses and these processes, although causality remains to be established. These results highlight the potential importance of the timing and duration of IFN-I immunity and warrant further investigation of its clinical relevance. FUNDING: Agence Nationale de Recherches sur le Sida et les Hépatites Virales (ANRS), ANRS Maladies Infectieuses Émergentes (ANRS MIE), Agence Nationale de la Recherche (ANR), Institut National de la Santé et de la Recherche Médicale (INSERM), European Union Horizon 2020 Research and Innovation Programme, CAPNET, and Klinbeforsk.

From behavioural insight to system design: Reframing the role of psychology in public health.
Contemporary public health challenges, including non-communicable diseases, persistent inequalities, misinformation, and complex organisational systems, are fundamentally shaped by behavioural, social, and psychological processes. Although this is increasingly recognised, psychological science remains unevenly integrated into public health and is often confined to individual-level interventions rather than embedded in system design, governance, and policy. A more fundamental shift is required. Psychology should be understood not as an adjunct to public health but as one of its foundational disciplines. Drawing on behavioural science, social identity research, and systems thinking, this commentary argues that psychological processes operate across multiple levels, from individual behaviour and community participation to organisational practice, leadership, implementation, and collective action. The COVID-19 pandemic illustrated this clearly: psychologically informed approaches supported public adherence, effective communication, trust, and community resilience. However, a broader conception of psychology, encompassing social identity, organisational behaviour, implementation, and structural pathways, is needed. Psychology should be recognised as a foundational contributor within the wider public health sciences ecosystem. Embedding psychological insight within the infrastructure of public health is essential if public health systems are to address the growing complexity of protecting and improving population health. A mature partnership between psychology and public health requires the systematic integration of psychological expertise into the design, implementation and governance of public health systems if they are to respond effectively to the complexity of twenty-first century population health challenges.

COVID-19 and thrombotic risk in patients with active cancer: a matched cohort study.
COVID-19 has been associated with an increased thrombotic risk, potentially exacerbated in patients with active cancer. We conducted a retrospective cohort study including 119 cancer patients with COVID-19 and 214 matched pre-pandemic controls. Patients with COVID-19 had poorer performance status and were more frequently treated with palliative intent. After a median follow-up of 32.7 months, overall thrombotic event rates did not differ between groups. However, after adjustment for clinically relevant covariates and accounting for death as a competing event, COVID-19 status and palliative treatment intent remained independently associated with a higher cumulative incidence of thrombotic events. In conclusion, COVID-19 may increase thrombotic risk in patients with cancer and occurs more frequently in patients with poorer clinical status. These findings are exploratory and require confirmation in larger prospective studies.

Co-occurrence of viral respiratory pathogens: prevalence, seasonal distribution, and symptomatology in outpatients in Bavaria, Germany, from April 2025 - March 2026.
PURPOSE: The Bavarian Influenza Sentinel (BIS + C) monitors the circulation of respiratory viruses in outpatients in Bavaria, Germany. After the Covid-19 pandemic, the molecular surveillance program was expanded for improved insight into the rate of viral infections. Only limited information on viral co-infections is yet available, so this study provides an insight into their co-occurrence, seasonal distribution, and symptomatic outcome. METHODS: From calendar week 15/2025 to 14/2026, general practitioners and pediatricians collected swab samples from outpatients with acute respiratory diseases, that were tested for twelve viral pathogens using qPCR multiplex systems. RESULTS: At least one virus was found in 58.8% of the outpatients (n = 7,416/12,614) including 4.1% (n = 520) multiple viral detection, primarily in patients younger than 5 years and more frequent in males. The frequency of multiple virus detection ranges from 6.7% in influenza A (n = 118/1,761) to 43.3% in adenoviruses (n = 154/356) positive tested samples. The most common pathogens in multiple detections were entero-/rhinoviruses involved in 11.9% (n = 292/2,459). Differences in the reported symptoms between single- and co-infections have been found, including less muscle/joint pain in influenza A co-infections. The detected Ct values in co-infections compared to mono-infections were lower for SARS-CoV-2, adenoviruses, entero-/rhinoviruses, and coronaviruses. CONCLUSION: The frequency of multi-infections follows the seasonality of the corresponding viruses. Especially children under 5 years of age are affected by co-infections. Among the studied viruses, influenza A showed the lowest relative rate of co-detection, in line with its pronounced seasonality - a pattern that warrants further investigation.

VITALITY - a longitudinal cohort established to assess the role of postnatal vitamin D supplementation in atopic disease and immune health.
VITALITY was established as a single-centre, doubleblind, randomised controlled trial (RCT) to determine whether daily supplementation of 400 International Units (IU) of vitamin D in the first year of life reduces the prevalence of food allergy at 12 months of age, compared to placebo. It recruited 2739 healthy, term, breastfed infants from 2014 to 2022 in Greater Melbourne, Australia. With an overall high retention rate despite the COVID-19 pandemic of over 83%, VITALITY is a rich cohort with extensive samples and data at baseline (six-12 weeks) and at six-, nine- and 12-months of age. Questionnaires collected information on demographics and environmental exposure, allergic diseases, infant feeding and factors thought to influence vitamin D levels at all timepoints. The majority of participants had a family history of allergic disease (89.2%) and 61.2% had both parents born in Australia. The standardized clinic visit at 12 months of age, attended by 79% of participants, included skin prick tests (SPT) +/- oral food challenges (OFC) and eczema assessment. Biospecimen collection included blood, skin and nasal swabs, stool and breastmilk which can be used for multi-omics profiling. Overall we performed SPTs on 2151 infants and undertook 612 OFCs. A six year follow up of VITALITY participants is underway and will determine the effect of early-life vitamin D supplementation on outcomes of asthma and other allergic diseases, lung function, infection and oral health. VITALITY is a large longitudinal cohort with data collected at multiple timepoints in childhood on a range of health outcomes. It provides a unique opportunity to explore early-life risk factors including genetic and environmental markers for food allergy, asthma, other atopic and non-communicable diseases as the cohort matures, in addition to establishing the role of vitamin D as an early-life strategy for prevention of disease and sustaining immune health.

Vaccination for girls and women across the life course: Evidence-based recommendations for clinical practice and policy.
Vaccination across the life course is a cornerstone of preventive health care for girls and women. Although WHO recommends completion of essential vaccines by adolescence, global coverage remains suboptimal. Vaccine-preventable diseases-including HPV-related cancers, vaginal, vulvar, anal, oropharyngeal, influenza, pertussis, hepatitis B, herpes zoster, and pneumococcal disease-continue to impose a disproportionate burden on girls and women, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) and migrant populations. Key life stages, such as childhood (early and middle), adolescence, preconception, pregnancy, postpartum, midlife, and beyond, offer critical opportunities for immunization. Obstetricians, gynecologists, midwives, and other women's healthcare providers are uniquely positioned to integrate vaccination into routine care in all settings and influence vaccine acceptance. Strengthening vaccine advocacy within women's health care is essential to reduce preventable morbidity and mortality and advance health equity for girls and women globally. This paper presents evidence-based recommendations for equitable vaccination across the life course of girls and women, synthesizing guidance from WHO, the Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization (SAGE), the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), and national immunization technical advisory groups. Vaccines reviewed include HPV, tetanus-diphtheria-pertussis (Tdap), influenza, hepatitis B, measles-mumps-rubella (MMR), varicella, herpes zoster, pneumococcal, Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), and COVID-19. A life-course framework is proposed, emphasizing maternal immunization, cervical cancer prevention, and integration of regular and opportune vaccination into routine obstetric and gynecologic services. Practical implementation strategies and policy recommendations are outlined to support FIGO member societies.

Temporal Associations Between Nonpharmaceutical Interventions and COVID-19 Transmission in Delaware.
BACKGROUND: Understanding how nonpharmaceutical interventions temporally align with changes in COVID-19 transmission remains important for public health monitoring and evaluation. However, substate-level evidence remains limited. Delaware provides a useful setting for such analyses due to its small population and largely uniform statewide policy implementation during 2020. METHODS: We analyzed COVID-19 transmission dynamics in Delaware and its 3 counties (Kent, New Castle, and Sussex) between March 2020 and March 2023, with policy-focused analyses restricted to major statewide interventions implemented in 2020. Incident infections were reconstructed using a deconvolution-based approach, and the time-varying reproduction number (Rt) was estimated using the EpiEstim R package. RESULTS: Rt estimates varied across policy periods and revealed substantial spatial heterogeneity. The most consistent increases in Rt were associated with the transition to hybrid school reopening, while decreases in Rt were associated with limits on social gatherings, the public mask mandate, and the stay-at-home advisory and overnight curfew. During Phase 1 reopening, Rt changes were small statewide, while Sussex County exhibited a larger increase than other counties. CONCLUSIONS: COVID-19 transmission dynamics in Delaware during 2020 varied across policy periods and counties, illustrating substate heterogeneity under uniform statewide interventions and the use of Rt-based estimates for monitoring epidemic dynamics.

Knowledge and Preventive Practices as Potential Factors of Empowerment Against Dengue in Córdoba, Colombia.
INTRODUCTION: Given the growing health impact of dengue fever in recent years, which primarily affects Latin American countries and Colombia in particular, interdisciplinary studies and scientific and technological advances to combat it, such as vaccines, mosquito genetic modification techniques, vector control using drones, and digital surveillance systems, among others, are becoming increasingly important. However, despite these achievements, little is known about the disease itself. The relationship between knowledge, sanitation conditions, and the preventive actions against dengue can be understood as part of the whole process of construction of community empowerment. Rather than acting solely as external factors, these dimensions constitute interrelated components that reflect the individuals and communities' capacity to understand, confront, and actively participate in dengue prevention and control. Against this background, the main contribution of this study lies in addressing community empowerment in the face of dengue as a multidimensional construct comprised of dimensions of knowledge, sanitation, and preventive practices, allowing us to explore its internal structure and understand how these dimensions relate within a common analytical framework. METHOD: A quantitative approach with an observational, cross-sectional, and analytical design was used. A total of 352 people infected with dengue during 2019 in the department of Córdoba, Colombia, were surveyed. Each response was assigned a score using the Likert scale question technique. Subsequently, a composite empowerment index was constructed. This index was conceptualized as a multidimensional construct consisting of domains related to knowledge, sanitation, and preventive practices against dengue. Consequently, the analysis did not aim to evaluate external predictive relationships between these components and empowerment, but rather to explore the relative contribution of the dimensions that internally comprise the construct and its association with different levels of empowerment. RESULTS: The analysis revealed differences in the relative contribution of the components making up the empowerment construct. The higher index levels were associated with higher scores in the dimensions related to knowledge and preventive practices. In contrast, profiles characterized by favorable sanitation conditions, but lower levels of knowledge and preventive skills, tended to be located in lower categories of the empowerment index. This indicates that there is heterogeneity in the internal construct structure and reflects the relative importance of its constituent dimensions. CONCLUSION: It is concluded that empowerment has to be understood not only as the result of an individual effort or purpose but also as a complex and multidimensional process whose levels of development reflect the individual, relational, and collective capacity to act together and achieve significant changes.

Design and in silico evaluation of PV-GNProtecta: an mRNA multi-epitope vaccine candidate against Puumala virus using immunoinformatics and structural analysis.
Puumala virus (PUUV), the principal causative agent of nephropathia epidemica (NE), poses a significant public health threat due to its zoonotic transmission, renal complications, and the lack of an approved vaccine. In this study, an immunoinformatics-driven mRNA multi-epitope vaccine, PV-GNProtecta, was designed using conserved regions of the viral glycoprotein (G) and nucleoprotein (N). Highly antigenic, non-allergenic, and non-toxic T-cell and B-cell epitopes were identified and assembled with appropriate adjuvants to enhance immunogenicity. Population coverage analysis suggested broad HLA responsiveness across diverse populations. The vaccine construct exhibited favorable physicochemical properties, including stability, solubility, and antigenicity. Structural validation predicted high model quality, with 95.5% of residues located in favored Ramachandran regions and an ERRAT score of 91.4. Molecular docking and MM-GBSA analyses predicted favorable computational interactions between PV-GNProtecta and TLR4, while a 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation provided computational insights into the dynamic behavior of the vaccine-TLR4 complex. Codon optimization suggested compatibility of the designed sequence with an Escherichia coli-based expression framework. Immune simulation predicted potential humoral and cellular immune response patterns, including changes in IgG, IFN-γ, and IL-2 levels. The designed mRNA sequence exhibited favorable predicted secondary structural characteristics; however, further experimental evaluation is required to assess translational efficiency and stability. Although this study is limited to computational analyses and requires experimental validation, the findings suggest that PV-GNProtecta may represent a potential candidate for further investigation against PUUV infection.

Building equitable epidemic response: the Interdisciplinary Consortium for Epidemics Research (ICER) position on Bundibugyo ebolavirus and regional preparedness in sub-Saharan Africa.
The 2014-16 West African Ebola epidemic exposed consequences of weak regional preparedness and limited local scientific leadership. The Bundibugyo ebolavirus (BDBV) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), with spill over into Uganda threatens to follow the same trend. Beyond the immediate response, this crisis is a defining moment for a question the region can no longer defer: who leads the science when Africa faces epidemics? As a scientific response, we argue for an immediate, regionally led research programme. To do this, ICER makes five priority positions: 1) Conduct of hypothesis-driven research as BDBV is understudied and yet is a high-risk and not a benign strain pathogen, 2) Rapid regional expansion is a realistic scenario, hence respective governments' preparedness frameworks must expedite to accommodate such an expansion, 3) African-led science is essential to an effective response, not merely an equity aspiration but a preparedness imperative, 4) Diagnostic, therapeutic, and vaccine development for BDBV cannot await commercial incentives and must be initiated proactively by public institutions, 5) An equitable partnership encompassing local leadership, fair authorship, capacity enhancement, and benefit sharing, is a prerequisite to be negotiated before research begins, and not an afterthought.

Zika virus produces two isoforms of the NS2A protein that play mutually exclusive roles in viral replication and virion assembly.
Zika virus (ZIKV), dengue virus, and several other orthoflaviviruses cause disease outbreaks in human and animal populations worldwide. The orthoflaviviral nonstructural protein 2A (NS2A) is critical for both viral replication and virion assembly. However, due to its small size, hydrophobicity, and the absence of structural information or protein-specific antibodies, we lack a clear understanding of how NS2A participates in these disparate processes. Here, using endogenously tagged NS2A-containing viral RNAs, we reveal that two NS2A isoforms are present during ZIKV infection, including both full-length NS2A and a C-terminally truncated isoform, termed NS2Aα. Phylogenetic and conservation analyses combined with polyprotein cleavage assays suggest that both NS2A isoforms are generated via the viral protease and are conserved across the Orthoflavivirus genus. Finally, using assays for viral replication and infectious particle production, we demonstrate that the two distinct NS2A isoforms function at different stages of the viral life cycle, with full-length NS2A required for viral RNA replication and NS2Aα important for virion assembly. Taken together, our data helps shed light on the form(s) and function(s) of the NS2A protein and suggests that each NS2A isoform plays a mutually exclusive role in the orthoflaviviral life cycle.

Species breadth is a preparedness metric: lessons from the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak.
Recent outbreaks of non-Zaire orthoebolaviruses have exposed a persistent weakness in outbreak preparedness: diagnostic, vaccine, therapeutic, regulatory, and research systems remain disproportionately optimized for Ebola virus (EBOV). The 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda illustrates the consequences of this species restriction. Initial testing with an EBOV-focused assay was negative, whereas broader molecular testing and genomic sequencing subsequently confirmed Bundibugyo virus, highlighting a gap between clinical suspicion and species coverage. This Commentary proposes an auditable species-breadth profile across four preparedness domains: diagnostics, vaccines, therapeutics, and evidence generation. For a minimum audit covering EBOV, Sudan virus, and Bundibugyo virus, each domain can be scored from 0/3 to 3/3 using predefined criteria for deployable detection, countermeasure availability, access pathways, and the capacity to initiate rigorous research during an outbreak. Species-breadth assessments should be integrated with specimen referral, genomic sequencing, cross-border surveillance, responder protection, community engagement, and contingency financing. Preparedness should, therefore, be judged not only by the availability of tools for one Ebola virus species, but by the ability of surveillance, diagnostics, countermeasures, and research systems to respond rapidly to whichever pathogenic orthoebolavirus emerges next.

High-risk extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae ST307 in a neonatal sepsis outbreak in Zambia: a secondary genomic analysis.
Neonatal sepsis caused by multidrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae contributes substantially to neonatal morbidity and mortality, especially where treatment options and genomic surveillance are limited. Phenotypic microbiology defines susceptibility, whereas Illumina short-read whole-genome sequencing (WGS) links phenotypes to lineage, capsule, resistome, virulome and mobilome contexts. However, complete characterization of mobile genetic element (MGE) structure remains inferential. This secondary analysis re-examined 411 public K. pneumoniae genomes from the University Teaching Hospital neonatal outbreak in Zambia. The population was dominated by ST307/KL102/OL2α.2, a comparatively recent but globally expanding high-risk clone, accounting for 284 out of 411 genomes (69.1%). Minority genomes included established resistance or virulence-associated high-risk backgrounds, including carbapenemase-positive KL15/OL4 lineages and yersiniabactin-positive ST147/ST985. Extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL) genotypes were widespread (396 out of 411; 96.4%) and mainly driven by blaCTX-M-15 (406 out of 411; 98.8%), whereas carbapenemase carriage was restricted to blaNDM-5-positive ST5856/ST340 (11 out of 411; 2.7%). Plasmids were the principal acquired resistance layer, as most AMR genes were plasmid-associated, and similarity analysis revealed a cohesive ST307-linked IncFIB/IncFII AA277 ESBL background, in contrast to distinct minority ESBL and IncX3 blaNDM-5 architectures. This pattern supports clonal maintenance of a stable ESBL plasmid background within ST307, while identifying IncX3 blaNDM-5 plasmids in minority lineages as a key convergence risk. Resistance genes were further structured by integron cassettes, insertion-sequence modules and plasmid cargo containing metal-, biocide- or stress-response genes. Virulence was limited and mainly ICEKp/ybt-associated, and widespread predicted prophages did not carry priority determinants. These findings show that WGS can add mechanistic resolution to routine phenotypic surveillance by identifying clone-MGE configurations that warrant targeted monitoring in neonatal K. pneumoniae outbreaks in Zambia.

Sulbactam-Durlobactam for Carbapenem-Resistant Acinetobacter baumannii in a Child: A Novel Application of Adult Pharmacokinetics.
There are limited antimicrobial options for the treatment of carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB). Sulbactam-durlobactam was recently approved for the treatment of CRAB in patients 18 years and older. However, CRAB infections can have mortality rates up to 80% in the intensive care unit. We describe the successful novel use of sulbactam-durlobactam in a pediatric patient using available adult pharmacokinetic data and preliminary pediatric dosing suggestions from a phase 1b trial.

Molecular Recognition and Immunopharmacological Implications of Serratiopeptidase Targeting Snake Venom Bradykinin-Potentiating Peptides.
PURPOSE: Bradykinin-potentiating peptides (BPPs), found in snake venom, are known to modulate cardiovascular functions, but their susceptibility to enzymatic degradation remains poorly understood. METHODS: Models were generated using AlphaFold-Colab for five small BPPs ( 80) were used for docking studies. Protein-peptide docking experiments were done using HADDOCK for studying the interaction between wild-type (WT) and mutant serratiopeptidase with BPPs. After selecting the best complex, simulation of the complex was done using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations for 100 ns and binding energy determination using MM/PBSA analysis. For checking the mechanical stability of the protein-peptide complexes, Steered MD was performed. RESULTS: HADDOCK docking identified BPP-4 as a favorable binder of WT and mutant serratiopeptidase supported by a HADDOCK score of -109.1 ± 5.2 and minimal restraint violations. MD simulations revealed greater stability in the mutant complex supported by persistent hydrogen bonds, reduced RMSD/RMSF fluctuations, restricted conformational sampling in PCA, favorable MM/PBSA energy contributions, and a more stable conformational ensemble in cluster analysis. The Steered MD simulation showed a higher rupture force in the mutant BPP-4-serratiopeptidase complex compared to the WT. CONCLUSIONS: Computational analysis identified BPP-4 as a promising serratiopeptidase-binding peptide, with differences in binding affinity and mechanical stability between WT and mutant complexes. The results offer insight into BPP-serratiopeptidase recognition at the molecular level and set the basis for future experiments on peptide binding.

Establishing a human co-infection challenge study of Streptococcus pneumoniae (Spn) and live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV) in older healthy adults: Exploring Co-infection with Live Attenuated Influenza Vaccine and PneumococcuS in healthy oldEr adults (ECLIPSE), a UK-based single-centre, single-blind randomised controlled trial.
INTRODUCTION: Secondary bacterial pneumonia following influenza is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in older adults. The Exploring Co-infection with Live Attenuated Influenza Vaccine and PneumococcuS in healthy oldEr adults study investigates how the order of exposure to Streptococcus pneumoniae serotype 6B (Spn6B) and live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV) affect mucosal immunity, pathogen load and respiratory symptoms in adults over 55 years of age. Immunisation with LAIV is a safe alternative to nasal challenge with live influenza virus because it is cold-adapted and cannot replicate in the lower respiratory tract, reducing the risk of disease in older study participants. METHODS AND ANALYSIS: This is a single-centre, single-blind randomised controlled human co-infection study (protocol V.4.2, 20 January 2026). Up to 60 healthy adults aged between 55 and 80 years will be randomised 1:1 for intranasal immunisation with LAIV first followed by inoculation with Spn6B or intranasal inoculation with Spn6B first followed by immunisation with LAIV with a 3-day interval between exposures. Throughout the study, we will collect samples from the nose, throat, saliva and blood to analyse how the immune system responds. Participants will also complete a daily symptom diary. Participants will collect saliva and nasosorption samples at home. A control cohort of up to 20 participants (up to 10 adults aged 18–49 years and up to 10 adults aged 55–80 years) will enable age-stratified comparisons of viral load and mucosal immune responses to immunisation with LAIV only. This cohort will not be randomised. The primary outcome is feasibility of the study and the safety of participants. The secondary outcomes include respiratory symptoms, how the order of exposure affects pneumococcal carriage, LAIV viral load and nasal immune responses over time as well as the impact of asymptomatic infection with other respiratory pathogens at baseline on these parameters. The study will improve our understanding of immune responses to co-infection with bacterial and viral pathogens in the upper respiratory tract in older adults and why they are at increased risk of pneumonia. ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: Ethical approval for this study has been obtained from the East Midlands–Leicester South Research Ethics Committee (REC reference 24/EM/0200). The results will be disseminated via publication in a peer-reviewed journal and presentation at international conferences. TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: ISRCTN13284643.

High burden of Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales: A prospective cross-sectional study at a tertiary hospital in Morocco.
OBJECTIVES: The present study aimed to determine and update the prevalence of Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales, to characterize carbapenemase production, and to assess antimicrobial susceptibility in a Moroccan tertiary hospital. PATIENTS AND METHODS: A prospective cross-sectional study was conducted from January 2021 to December 2022, during which time 6672 Enterobacteriaceae isolates were recovered from clinical specimens from patients with suspected bacterial infections. Species were identified using MALDI-TOF-MS and the BD Phoenix® M50 for antimicrobial susceptibility according to EUCAST screening criteria. NG-Test® CARBA 5 assay was used for carbapenemase detection and characterization. RESULTS: Among the 6672 Enterobacteriaceae isolates, 1289 showed decreased susceptibility to ertapenem (19.3%). Klebsiella pneumoniae was the predominant species (47.4%), followed by Enterobacter cloacae complex (20.8%). The neonatal intensive care unit was the main reservoir of cases (22.0%). Blood and purulent specimens were the most frequent sources of isolation (62.8% combined). Among the 322 non-duplicate isolates tested, 252 (78.3%) were carbapenemase producers. Antibiotic susceptibility profile displayed high rates of resistance to ciprofloxacin (91.0%), gentamicin (85.1%), and cotrimoxazole (86.6%). NDM (34.8%) and OXA-48-like (30.1%) were the predominant enzymes. NDM and OXA-48-like co-production was observed in 12.1% of isolates. A novel VIM + OXA-48-like combination was detected in an Enterobacter cloacae complex isolate. CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates an alarming increase in the proportion of Enterobacterales exhibiting decreased susceptibility to carbapenems, highlighting a need for robust infection prevention measures, rapid diagnostics, and continuous epidemiological surveillance in high-dependency units.

Mixed strain infections and microevolution of Mycobacterium tuberculosis: Genetic diversity in a high-burden setting of Northeastern Brazil.
BACKGROUND: Tuberculosis (TB) control in high-burden settings is complicated by the genetic diversity of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), which influences transmission. This study assessed the prevalence of mixed strain infections (MSIs) and microevolutionary events, analyzing their association with biosocial and clinical variables in Fortaleza, northeastern Brazil. METHODS: This prospective study included 168 patients with pulmonary TB from two referral hospitals serving socioeconomically vulnerable populations. Mtb isolates were subjected to drug resistance testing using Xpert MTB/RIF, MGIT 960, SIRE kit, and 24-locus mycobacterial interspersed repetitive unit-variable number tandem repeat typing. Genetic diversity was classified as MSI when multiple alleles were detected at two or more loci, or as a microevolutionary event when multiple alleles were detected at a single locus. Clinical and socioeconomic data were correlated with the genotypic profiles of the patients. RESULTS: Genetic diversity was observed in 10 isolates (6%), comprising three (1.75%) MSIs and seven microevolutionary events. Among the 10 patients with genetic diversity, the median age was 46 years, and illicit drug use was reported in this subgroup. All MSIs were rifampicin-sensitive; four of the seven cases with microevolution showed rifampicin resistance. Half of the patients with genetic diversity showed poor treatment outcomes in the form of death, failure, and loss of follow-up; comorbid conditions such as diabetes, syphilis, and previous TB were common in this subgroup. CONCLUSIONS: The patterns of Mtb genetic diversity in this high-burden setting coexist with conditions of social vulnerability and complex disease presentations. These findings highlight the coexistence of Mtb genetic diversity with social and clinical vulnerability in this setting and support further investigation using larger cohorts and higher-resolution genomic approaches.

Comparative evaluation of classical and modified Tamra Bhasma: Acute oral toxicity, antimicrobial, and antioxidant profiles.
BACKGROUND: Tamra Bhasma, a traditional Ayurvedic copper-based formulation, has been used for its antimicrobial and therapeutic benefits. However, its complex preparation and the risk of toxicity when not made according to classical methods have limited its broader clinical use. Recent efforts aim to simplify its preparation and scientifically validate its safety and efficacy. OBJECTIVE: The present study aimed to evaluate and compare the acute oral toxicity of two Tamra Bhasma preparations viz. Classical Tamra Bhasma I (CTB I) and a chemically processed form (CTB II) in comparison with synthetic copper oxides (A-CuO and S-CuO). The antimicrobial and antioxidant profiles are also compared between CTB I and CTB II. MATERIALS AND METHODS: CTB I and CTB II were prepared using standard Ayurvedic protocols with different raw materials. Acute oral toxicity was tested in female rats using OECD guideline 425 at a limit dose of 2000 mg/kg, followed by a two-week observation period. Hematological, biochemical, and histopathological analyses were performed. Antimicrobial activity was assessed against Enterococcus faecalis, Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Klebsiella pneumoniae using the disk diffusion method. Antioxidant activity was measured by DPPH radical scavenging assay. RESULTS: No mortality, behavioral abnormalities, or significant weight changes were observed at the test dose. Hematological and biochemical parameters remained within normal ranges. Histopathological findings showed mild liver congestion in the CTB I group and increased sinusoidal space in the S-CuO group, with normal architecture in other organs. CTB I exhibited stronger antibacterial activity against Gram-positive bacteria, whereas CTB II was more effective against Gram-negative strains. CTB I also showed higher antioxidant activity than CTB II, though less potent than ascorbic acid. CONCLUSION: CTB I and CTB II have LD50 more than 2000 mg/kg and demonstrate differing antimicrobial and antioxidant effects depending on preparation methods. These results support further investigation into their therapeutic mechanisms and potential applications.

Identifying counties at elevated acarological risk for reporting high incidence of Lyme disease in the eastern United States.
Lyme disease, caused primarily by the bite of a nymphal blacklegged tick (Ixodes scapularis) infected with Borrelia burgdorferi sensu stricto (Bbss), is the most common vector-borne disease in the United States. Counties reporting high Lyme disease incidence (LDI) continue to expand beyond historic foci in the Northeast and Upper Midwest. Identifying areas of expansion aids in targeting efforts to improve Lyme disease awareness in affected communities. Tick surveillance is conducted to track changes in acarological risk for tickborne diseases; the density of host-seeking Bbss-infected I. scapularis nymphs (DIN) is considered the most predictive metric for human LDI. We aimed to identify a threshold in DIN that accurately separated high (≥10 average annual cases/100,000 and ≥3 cases/year; 2022-2023) from low LDI counties in the eastern US. Using previously reported model-derived DIN, we identified 0.98 Bbss-infected nymphs per 1000 m2 as the threshold. Based on this threshold, we classified 18% of eastern counties (487/2695), primarily in the Northeast and Upper Midwest, with both high LDI and elevated acarological risk and 72% (1935/2695) with both low LDI and acarological risk. Another 8% of counties (220/2695), primarily in Michigan, Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio, were predicted to pose elevated acarological risk, but reported low LDI and may reflect areas of emergence that could benefit from expanded tick surveillance and public health outreach. The remaining 2% of counties (53/2695), mainly along the Appalachian Mountains, reported high LDI, but were misclassified as low acarological risk, highlighting the need for additional tick surveillance to improve acarological risk assessments.

Immunogenicity and Safety of Single-Dose MenACYW Conjugate Vaccine in Vietnamese Participants Aged ≥ 12 Months: A Phase III, Open-Label Study.
INTRODUCTION: Invasive meningococcal disease (IMD) is a progressive condition commonly presenting as septicemia and meningitis, with significant mortality and morbidity. Vietnam reports high incidence rates among military populations and young infants. Despite this burden and unpredictable outbreaks, meningococcal vaccination in Vietnam is offered primarily to high-risk individuals and travelers rather than as routine childhood immunization. MenACYW-TT, a quadrivalent meningococcal polysaccharide tetanus toxoid-conjugate vaccine with licensure in > 80 countries, is approved for toddlers aged ≥ 12 months and for infants aged ≥ 6 weeks. This Phase III, open-label study evaluated the immunogenicity and safety of a single dose of MenACYW-TT in healthy Vietnamese participants aged ≥ 12 months. METHODS: This study (NCT06228586) was conducted in Vietnam among healthy participants aged ≥ 12 months (five age groups) who received a single dose of MenACYW-TT. Functional antibody activity against all four meningococcal serogroups was measured using serum bactericidal assay with human complement (hSBA) at baseline (Day 1) and after vaccination (Day 31). Safety data were collected up to 30 days (+ 14 days) after vaccination. RESULTS: Among the 447 enrolled participants, seroprotection rates (hSBA titers ≥ 1:8) were high and comparable across all age groups for each serogroup, i.e., 88.8% for serogroup A to 100% for serogroup C. Overall, the seroresponse rates were high for serogroups C: 98.6%, Y: 96.0%, W: 95.0%, and A: 73.6%, with higher seroresponse to serogroup A in the 12- to 23-month group (81.5%) versus the ≥ 24-month group (66.5%). No safety concerns or vaccine-related serious adverse events were observed. CONCLUSIONS: A single dose of MenACYW-TT induced robust immunogenicity against all four serogroups and demonstrated an acceptable safety profile across all age groups of Vietnamese participants. Given the high burden of meningococcal disease in Vietnam, these findings support the potential inclusion of MenACYW-TT in Vietnam's National Expanded Program on Immunization. TRIAL REGISTRATION: clinicaltrials.gov, NCT06228586.

Paradoxical reactions during treatment of miliary tuberculosis: a 25-year single-centre case series and literature review.
BACKGROUND: Paradoxical reactions during otherwise effective anti-tuberculosis treatment can resemble treatment failure or drug resistance. Their frequency and clinical spectrum in miliary tuberculosis are incompletely characterised. AIMS: To describe the timing, manifestations, management and outcomes of paradoxical reactions identified in a defined cohort of patients with miliary tuberculosis and to place these events in the context of the published literature. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed the records of 63 patients with miliary tuberculosis managed at a single centre between 1981 and 2005. A paradoxical reaction was defined as clinical or radiological worsening of an initially improving lesion, or development of a new lesion during appropriate therapy, after reasonable exclusion of treatment failure, drug resistance and alternative diagnoses. RESULTS: Five of 63 patients (7.9%) developed six paradoxical reaction episodes. Manifestations included multiple subcutaneous abscesses, two small-intestinal perforations, two spontaneous pneumothoraces and progression of miliary nodules with new cavitary lesions. Reactions occurred 10-240 days after treatment initiation (median, 108 days). Five episodes required surgical or interventional management. The anti-tuberculosis regimen was continued without modification in every episode. One patient developed two reactions despite corticosteroid treatment for systemic lupus erythematosus. All patients recovered, with no recurrence during 4-24 months of follow-up. CONCLUSIONS: Paradoxical reactions in miliary tuberculosis may be anatomically diverse and life-threatening. Recognition of this pattern, together with careful exclusion of microbiological failure, can prevent unnecessary alteration of effective treatment while ensuring timely management of site-specific complications.

Comparative genomics of hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates from Brazil.
Klebsiella pneumoniae represents a major public health threat at the convergence of antimicrobial resistance and hypervirulence. While classical K. pneumoniae (cKp) is a leading cause of healthcare-associated infections, hypervirulent K. pneumoniae (hvKp) causes severe invasive disease in otherwise healthy individuals. We performed a comparative genomic analysis of hvKp (n = 8) and cKp (n = 17) isolates recovered in Salvador, Brazil. The eight Brazilian hvKp isolates displayed the canonical hypervirulence genotype, encoding the five major biomarkers (iroB, iucA, peg-344, rmpA, and rmpA2) while carrying only a limited repertoire of intrinsic antimicrobial resistance genes. These isolates belonged to sequence types ST23, ST65, ST86, ST3690, and ST5750 and were associated with K1 or K2 capsular types and the O1 antigen. In three isolates, iroB was detected in both chromosomal and plasmid-associated regions, a dual localization reported at low frequency among hvKp. The predominant plasmid replicons were IncHI1B (pNDM-MAR) and repB_KLEB, with IncFIB (K) in two isolates. Screening for mobile genetic elements recovered an F-type conjugative transfer locus in these two isolates only. Chromosomes and plasmids showed high similarity with well-characterized reference hvKp strains, including SGH10 and NTUH-K2044, as well as the pLVPK virulence plasmid. Comparative proteomics analysis identified 53 protein clusters conserved across hvKp strains examined.
