Among these were four hypothetical proteins previously associated with invasive liver infection, containing DUF1471, DUF417, and carboxymuconolactone decarboxylase-related domains, suggesting potential roles in pathogenicity. Collectively, these findings expand current knowledge of hvKp genetic diversity in Salvador, Brazil and highlight genomic features that may contribute to the emergence and maintenance of the hypervirulent phenotype.

From overcoming to exploiting hypoxia: a metronidazole-armed type I photosensitizer for septic arthritis therapy.
Septic arthritis is a life-threatening joint infection with high mortality, yet clinical antibiotic and surgical treatments usually cause increasing drug resistance and irreversible tissue damage. Photodynamic therapy (PDT) offers a non-invasive alternative with low drug resistance. However, its efficacy in septic arthritis is severely hampered by the intra-articular hypoxia. To address this issue, we propose an innovative strategy that shifts from overcoming hypoxia to fully exploit hypoxia. Accordingly, we developed a metronidazole-functionalized Type I cationic photosensitizer (PS), ACR-DM-MNZ. It anchors onto bacterial surfaces via electrostatic interactions and, importantly, leverages hypoxia-overexpressed nitroreductase to reduce its nitro group, thereby enhancing bacterial membrane binding and toxicity. Upon white light irradiation, it generates hydroxyl radicals (˙OH) to kill bacteria and eliminate biofilms. In a murine model of MRSA-induced septic arthritis, under light irradiation, ACR-DM-MNZ effectively eradicated intra-articular pathogens, alleviated joint swelling, modulated inflammation, reduced histopathological damage, and promoted joint repair. This work presents an efficient strategy that transforms the hypoxic barrier into a therapeutic asset, offering a promising platform for the treatment of septic arthritis.

Invasive Bacterial Infections Other Than Escherichia coli and Streptococcus agalactiae in Febrile Infants Younger Than 90 Days: A Multicenter Emergency Department Study.
BACKGROUND: Invasive bacterial infections (IBIs) in febrile infants ≤90 days are mostly caused by Escherichia coli and Streptococcus agalactiae. However, data on IBIs caused by other pathogens remain limited. METHODS: We conducted a multicenter retrospective study of febrile infants aged ≤90 days diagnosed with IBI between 2008 and 2022 at 12 Spanish pediatric emergency departments. Epidemiology, clinical features, microbiology and outcomes of cases caused by pathogens other than E. coli/S. agalactiae were analyzed. Adverse outcomes included death, inotropic or respiratory support, acute complications, or sequelae. RESULTS: Among 375 infants with IBI, 106 (28.3%) had infections caused by pathogens other than E. coli/S. agalactiae. The most frequent pathogens were Staphylococcus aureus (n = 30, 8.0%), Streptococcus pneumoniae (n = 15, 4.0%) and Enterococcus faecalis (n = 14, 3.7%). Most cases presented as isolated bacteremia (65.1%), followed by bacteremic urinary tract infection (18.9%) and meningitis (12.3%); 46.2% of infants with meningitis had a concomitant urinary tract infection. The distribution of pathogens varied according to age, with S. aureus being more frequent among younger infants and S. pneumoniae accounting for 8.6% of IBIs in infants aged 61-90 days. Listeria monocytogenes caused 1.3% of IBIs, with only 1 case identified in the last decade. Adverse outcomes occurred in 7.5% of infants with infections caused by other pathogens and 8.6% of those with E. coli/S. agalactiae (absolute risk difference, -1.0% [95% confidence interval, -7.1 to 5.0]). CONCLUSIONS: IBIs caused by pathogens other than E. coli/S. agalactiae accounted for a substantial proportion of cases and showed an age-dependent distribution. Most presented as isolated bacteremia, while meningitis was associated with a higher observed frequency of adverse outcomes.

Severe Congenital Pneumonia Associated With Probable Vertical Transmission of Mycoplasma pneumoniae During a UK Epidemic Surge.
Congenital Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP) is rare. During the United Kingdom's 2023/2024 MP epidemic, we encountered a fatal case of probable vertically transmitted MP in a preterm infant. This report highlights the need to consider MP during incidence surges, reviews existing literature, and examines whether congenital MP cases cluster around epidemic peaks.

The Utility of Microbial Cell-Free DNA in the Rapid Diagnosis of Chagas Disease: Chagas Disease Case Series.
BACKGROUND: Chagas disease (CD) is a leading tropical disease and the most prevalent parasitic infection in Latin America, affecting >7 million people globally and ∼240 000-350 000 individuals within the United States. Though known to be endemic to Latin America, prevalence in the United States is also increasing with improved recognition of locally acquired cases, especially in Texas. Autochthonous cases occur throughout the Southern United States, but the geographic range is anticipated to shift northwards as a result of climate change. Chagas disease is referred to as a "silent and silenced disease" by the World Health Organization as most people show no signs or symptoms for years following acute infection, and it primarily affects individuals who are socioeconomically disadvantaged. Historically, Chagas disease has been underrecognized. In the absence of treatment, infected individuals progress to a clinically silent or "indeterminate form" of infection that persists for life. While most patients with indeterminate Chagas disease do not have long-term sequelae, ∼30%-40% will develop end-organ cardiac or gastrointestinal disease decades after infection. Due to its protean clinical presentations, diagnosis requires a high clinical index of suspicion and knowledge of the epidemiology. Traditionally, the diagnosis is based on serology, visualization of the parasite in blood, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR), all of which require suspecting the infection. Microbial cell-free DNA (mcfDNA) of blood can serve as a useful tool for detection of Trypanosoma cruzi even when Chagas disease is not suspected. RESULTS: Here we present 7 cases, 3 children and 4 adults, who presented with nonspecific manifestations; CD was not in the initial differential diagnosis in 5 of them. Chagas disease was ultimately diagnosed by Karius Spectrum test. In 1 case, the test was sent to expedite diagnosis in the setting of suspected Chagas reactivation.

Early Invasive Fungal Infections in Liver Transplant Recipients Receiving Risk-Stratified Echinocandin Prophylaxis: A Descriptive Single-Center Cohort Study.
BACKGROUND: Invasive fungal infection (IFI) remains a cause of morbidity and mortality after liver transplantation; guidelines recommend targeted antifungal prophylaxis in recipients with specific risk factors. METHODS: We retrospectively studied adult liver transplant recipients (LTR) at a single center, 2017-2023. High-risk recipients received a planned 14-day course of echinocandin prophylaxis, caspofungin in 97.6%. The primary endpoint was IFI within 30 days of transplantation, a window spanning the planned prophylaxis and the 2 weeks after it. Secondary endpoints were fungal etiology and factors associated with IFI. We also examined the temporal distribution of early aspergillosis across the whole institutional registry to 2025. RESULTS: Of 286 recipients, 85 (29.72%) were high risk. IFI was more frequent in high-risk than non-high-risk LTR (8/85, 9.41% vs. 4/201, 1.99%; p = 0.0077); most were breakthrough (7/8) mold infections. In exploratory analyses, IFI was associated with high-risk status (unadjusted odds ratio: 5.12, 95% CI: 1.50-17.49), MELD > 30 (4.67, 1.25-17.41) and diabetes (4.64, 1.37-15.79); with 12 events, these estimates are imprecise, and no multivariable model was fitted. Among 452 transplants performed in 2017-2025, seven developed early aspergillosis across four calendar years, with no significant variation in annual incidence (p = 0.146), never more than two cases in any 90-day window (Monte Carlo p = 0.82) and none among the 117 transplants of the following 28 months. CONCLUSION: Early IFI under risk-stratified echinocandin prophylaxis concentrated in the sickest recipients and was dominated by mold disease. No clear temporal pattern suggestive of a sustained common-source outbreak was identified, although environmental transmission cannot be excluded.

A national spatial prioritisation framework for the targeted expansion of essential sickle cell disease services across health-facility catchments in Uganda.
BACKGROUND: Sickle cell disease causes substantial childhood morbidity and premature mortality in sub-Saharan Africa, while access to essential services remains uneven. In Uganda, geographic variation in inherited SCD risk supports spatially targeted service planning. METHODS: We conducted a national facility-linked ecological spatial planning analysis using 280 eligible higher-level public facilities. Populated cells were assigned to the nearest eligible facility within a modelled 60-minute travel-time boundary. Epidemiological context was represented by a study-specific co-risk index combining standardised haemoglobin S (HbS) allele frequency and Plasmodium falciparum parasite rate among children aged 2 to 10 years (PfPR2-10). Reported availability was assessed for newborn screening, hydroxyurea, blood transfusion, and specialised SCD clinic care. We derived service-deficit, structural-vulnerability, programme-priority, service-specific priority, and coverage-to-need measures and assessed sensitivity to alternative weighting specifications. RESULTS: Among 280 planning zones, 122 (43.6%) had none of the four reported services and 205 (73.2%) had no more than one. Co-risk ranged from 0.003 to 0.934 and service-mediated SCD structural vulnerability from 0.000 to 0.905. Higher programme-priority scores were concentrated mainly in northern, north-eastern, eastern, and parts of central Uganda, while lower-priority tiers were more common in the south-west. Newborn-screening and hydroxyurea priorities were closely aligned, transfusion priorities extended more broadly into northern and central Uganda, and specialised-clinic priorities were more spatially mixed. The overall coverage-to-need gap had a mean of 0.190 and median of 0.205. The 56 zones comprising the national top 20% of programme priority contained approximately 7.0 million people, representing 17.3% of the population within the analytic framework. Priority concentration was strongest in Lango, Teso, Acholi, Karamoja, and Busoga. CONCLUSIONS: The framework identified a concentrated set of candidate service-strengthening nodes under the specified assumptions, mainly in northern, north-eastern, and eastern Uganda. The findings can support further programme assessment and stakeholder review for phased, regionally coordinated, and service-specific expansion of SCD care.

Malarial anemia: an interplay between impaired erythropoiesis and uninfected erythrocyte clearance.
Malaria-associated anemia is a major cause of morbidity and mortality, affecting young children and pregnant women in endemic regions. This review synthesizes current evidence on the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying malaria-associated anemia, emphasizing impaired erythropoiesis and increased destruction of uninfected erythrocytes. Ineffective erythropoiesis may result from the presence of parasites within the bone marrow, hemozoin accumulation, inflammatory cytokine responses, and altered iron availability. Persistent inflammation and oxidative stress promote erythrocyte shrinkage, with consequent eryptosis and premature clearance by splenic macrophages. Plasmodium-induced immune responses promote anti-erythrocyte antibody production, which further contributes to erythrocyte removal. Malaria-associated anemia arises from interconnected alterations in erythrocyte production, survival, and clearance, highlighting its multifactorial nature and the need for more integrated studies to better characterize these mechanisms.

Immunoinformatics-based design and in silico evaluation of a multi-epitope vaccine candidate against Naegleria fowleri.
Primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM) is caused by Naegleria fowleri, a free-living amoeba. It is a fatal infection with more than 95% mortality rate. Even though several combinations of antimicrobial agents were used to treat the condition, the overall survival remains poor and no effective vaccine is currently available. In this study, an immunoinformatic approach was utilized for designing a multi-epitope vaccine against N. fowleri. The sequences of antigenic proteins were retrieved for epitope prediction. The computational prediction identified 400 CTL, 590 HTL, and 65 B-cell high-binding epitopes. After evaluating their antigenicity, allergenicity and toxicity, 5 CTL, 5 HTL and 3 B-cell epitopes were selected and assembled into a multi-epitope vaccine construct using linkers and a human β-defensin-3 adjuvant. The 3D structure of the vaccine was predicted using AlphaFold and refined with GalaxyRefine. Ramachandran plot analysis indicated that 96.5% of the residues of the refined vaccine are present in the most favored regions, indicating good stereochemical quality. The molecular docking analysis was performed using HADDOCK to evaluate the interaction between the vaccine and the Toll-like Receptors (TLRs), which predicted favorable binding affinities of -15.6 kcal/mol, -14.2 kcal/mol, and - 13.1 kcal/mol for TLR1 & 2, TLR3, and TLR4, respectively. The codon was optimized using JCat and cloned into the pET-28a(+) plasmid. The in silico immune simulation analysis predicted potential humoral and cellular immune responses to the vaccine construct. Overall, the proposed multi-epitope vaccine represents a promising computational candidate, however, further experimental validations have to be performed to confirm its efficacy against the pathogen.

A multiscale framework for heme crystallization inhibition: From single-molecule step-capping to parasite suppression.
Heme crystallization is central to malaria parasites' survival during the erythrocytic stage of the disease, yet how clinically relevant antimalarial drugs modulate this process at the molecular level remains unclear. Here we employ stage-resolved parasite assays and multiscale in vitro approaches to explore the interactions between lumefantrine (LF), one of the popular components of current combination therapies, and hematin crystallization. Pulse LF suppresses Plasmodium falciparum during both ring and trophozoite stages. Under biomimetic conditions, LF markedly reduces β-hematin crystal growth rates. High-resolution atomic force microscopy reveals that individual LF molecules bind directly to crystal steps, physically constraining step motion through a previously unreported step-capping mechanism. This localized inhibition propagates to the mesoscale, producing step broadening, reduced interstep spacing, and causing surface kinetic roughening. In contrast to its strong inhibition of crystal growth, LF enhances hematin nucleation by promoting the formation of mesoscopic hematin-rich clusters, as detected by a combination of scattering and microscopy techniques. Attachment of the nucleated crystallites to larger crystal surfaces initiates a nonclassical inhibition sequence by straining the crystal interface, which further impedes step growth.

Long-term Outcomes in Previously Healthy non-HIV Individuals with Cryptococcal Meningitis Treated with Pulse-taper Corticosteroids for Post-infectious Inflammatory Syndrome.
BACKGROUND: Post-infectious inflammatory response syndrome (PIIRS) is an increasingly recognized complication of cryptococcal meningoencephalitis (CM) in non-HIV infected hosts with significant morbidity and mortality. Data describing long-term outcomes following immunomodulatory therapy are limited. METHODS: We conducted a prospective observational study of 15 immunocompetent adults with CM-PIIRS treated with a pulse corticosteroid taper (PCT) regimen. Performance status, neurocognitive, ophthalmologic, audiologic, and radiologic assessments were performed at greater than one year following CM diagnosis. RESULTS: After one year, performance status continued to improve from both baseline and the post-pulse periods. Neurocognitive testing revealed mild residual deficits, within the limits of normal, most prominently in information processing and psychomotor speed. Ocular abnormalities were frequent at baseline but showed substantial and sustained reductions following PCT, particularly in retinal nerve fiber layer thickness. Visual field deficits improved by 40% and remained stable thereafter. Evidence for changes in hearing sensitivity at post 1-year follow-up was mixed with 44.5% of ears meeting criteria for improvement, 11% for worsening, and 44.5% being stable. Radiologic abnormalities improved in 79% of patients, although intermittent inflammatory flares occurred during PCT but responded to dose escalation. A prolonged corticosteroid taper may be helpful, and MRI imaging can be used to evaluate response to taper. CONCLUSIONS: In immunocompetent patients with CM-PIIRS, adjunctive corticosteroid therapy was associated with sustained improvement in neurologic, visual, and radiologic outcomes with mixed improvement in hearing after a year of therapy, with mild residual deficits.

Acute Inner Foveal Toxoplasmic Maculopathy: An Atypical Manifestation of Ocular Toxoplasmosis.
PURPOSE: To describe the clinical and multimodal imaging characteristics of an atypical clinical and imaging presentation of ocular toxoplasmosis. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed six eyes of five immunocompetent patients (including one patient with bilateral involvement), with clinically diagnosed ocular toxoplasmosis. Diagnosis was based on compatible clinical findings, multimodal retinal imaging, positive Toxoplasma gondii serology, and exclusion of alternative infectious etiologies. Intraocular PCR and Goldmann-Witmer coefficient analysis were not available. Clinical presentation, multimodal imaging findings, treatments and outcomes were reviewed. RESULTS: Six eyes of five patients were included. All eyes demonstrated a consistent inner foveal SD-OCT imaging pattern characterized by focal inner retinal cavitation, ellipsoid zone disruption, and outer nuclear layer involvement, with variable but generally limited intraocular inflammation. Two eyes (Case 1 OD and Case 3) presented with predominantly macular involvement without adjacent active retinochoroiditis. Following treatment with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and systemic corticosteroids, all eyes showed anatomical improvement, although residual inner retinal thinning persisted in several eyes. CONCLUSIONS: This case series described an atypical clinical and imaging presentation of ocular toxoplasmosis characterized by a distinctive inner foveal SD-OCT imaging pattern (acute inner foveal toxoplasmic maculopathy). Although the absence of intraocular microbiological confirmation limits diagnostic certainty, recognition of this presentation may facilitate earlier diagnosis and appropriate treatment in selected patients. The term "acute" refers to the active ocular presentation and does not imply recently acquired systemic infection. Further studies are warranted to validate these findings and clarify their underlying pathophysiology.

Five ways to find a parasite: comparison of five molecular assays for the detection of Strongyloides spp.
UNLABELLED: Strongyloidiasis, caused by nematodes of the genus Strongyloides, is a neglected tropical disease with significant public health implications. Accurate diagnostics are essential for disease surveillance and control, yet traditional stool-based and serological methods have limitations in sensitivity and specificity. Molecular assays offer an alternative diagnostic approach. In this study, we compared four probe-based real-time PCR (qPCR) assays and one loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) assay using human fecal DNA samples from Gabon and Papua New Guinea with both Strongyloides stercoralis and Strongyloides fuelleborni infections. Our results revealed discordance between assays, with no single primer set identifying all positive samples across all assays. One assay was identified as specific for S. stercoralis only, while other assays amplify other Strongyloides spp. This may impact the specificity of molecular diagnostics in epidemiological surveys, particularly with increasing identifications of S. fuelleborni infections in humans from Asia and New Guinea. Of the assays examined, four were probe-based qPCR assays and a LAMP assay. On sequencing positive amplicons, enteric bacterial sequences were identified for two assays. However, subsequent testing and BLAST results identified that including a probe, as the assays were designed, would increase specificity, so that the bacterial sequences would not be amplified. These findings provide a context for the interpretation of results from various Strongyloides molecular assays. IMPORTANCE: Strongyloidiasis is an underdiagnosed neglected parasitic infection that poses a growing challenge for public health surveillance and control, particularly in regions where multiple Strongyloides species exist and clinical case detection is challenging. Molecular assays are increasingly used as reference diagnostic tools, yet their performance and species specificity have not been systematically evaluated across diverse endemic settings. In this study, we tested the hypothesis that commonly used molecular assays differ in their ability to accurately and consistently detect and discriminate Strongyloides stercoralis and Strongyloides fuelleborni in human fecal samples. By comparing five molecular assays using samples from Gabon and Papua New Guinea, we demonstrate discordance between tests, including species-dependent detection biases. These findings provide evidence that molecular diagnostics may misrepresent species distribution. Our results highlight the necessity for awareness of target species specificity and for regionally validated molecular tools to ensure the reliable interpretation of assay results.

Increased Risk of Thyrotoxicosis After COVID-19 in Adolescents and Young Adults During the Omicron-Predominant Period: A Nationwide Matched Study.
OBJECTIVE: Thyroid dysfunction has been increasingly reported after the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic. To date, no population-based study has examined this association using more than 10 million matched pairs. We compared the risk of documented thyroid outcomes after COVID-19 with that after influenza during the Omicron-predominant period. METHODS: We conducted a nationwide retrospective cohort study using the Japanese National Database of Health Insurance Claims, including patients with COVID-19 between January 2022 and March 2023, and those with influenza between September 2017 and March 2023. Individuals with pre-existing thyroid disease were excluded. After 1:1 propensity score matching, 24,173,646 pairs were analysed. Database-recorded outcomes assessed within 90 days of documented COVID-19 infection included diagnoses of thyrotoxicosis, hypothyroidism and subacute thyroiditis, as well as initiation of antithyroid drugs (ATDs) and thyroid hormone replacement therapy (THRT). RESULTS: Among database-recorded outcomes, COVID-19 was associated with higher risks of thyrotoxicosis diagnosis (risk ratio [RR], 1.08), hypothyroidism diagnosis (RR, 1.12), ATD initiation (RR, 1.06) and THRT initiation (RR, 1.22) than influenza, but not subacute thyroiditis diagnosis. Age-stratified analyses showed markedly higher risks in individuals aged 0-19 years for thyrotoxicosis diagnosis (RR, 1.38) and ATD initiation (RR, 1.77). CONCLUSIONS: In this nationwide cohort, COVID-19 was associated with higher risks of database-recorded diagnoses of thyrotoxicosis and hypothyroidism than influenza during the Omicron-predominant period. The strongest association was observed for thyrotoxicosis diagnosis and ATD initiation in younger individuals, underscoring the importance of post-COVID-19 thyroid monitoring in adolescents and young adults.

Racial and Socioeconomic Inequities in COVID-19 In-Hospital Mortality in Brazil in the Post-Emergency Era: A National Cohort Study of 19,718 Hospitalized Adults in 2024.
BACKGROUND: In 2024, COVID-19 entered a post-emergency phase, but in-hospital mortality remains a relevant public health concern in Brazil. As population immunity, vaccination, and clinical management evolved, the hierarchy of mortality predictors may have shifted from traditional metabolic risk factors toward clinical severity and social vulnerability. This study aimed to identify sociodemographic, clinical, management, and vaccination-related variables associated with in-hospital COVID-19 mortality among adults in Brazil in 2024, with emphasis on racial and socioeconomic inequities. METHODS: A retrospective national cohort study was conducted using the SIVEP-Gripe surveillance database. Adults aged ≥ 18 years hospitalized with laboratory-confirmed COVID-19 between January and December 2024 were included. The primary analysis was restricted to patients with observed hospital outcomes, resulting in an analytical sample of 19,718 individuals. Crude and adjusted associations were estimated using binary logistic regression. Race/color was modeled using White patients as the reference category. Robustness to unmeasured confounding was assessed using E-values, and model performance was evaluated using AUC-ROC. RESULTS: The in-hospital fatality rate was 23.5% (n = 4,633). Invasive ventilatory support was the strongest predictor of death (aOR: 7.574; 95% CI: 6.801-8.435; E-value: 4.95). Black patients had higher odds of death compared with White patients (aOR: 1.506; 95% CI: 1.233-1.838; E-value: 1.76), as did Pardo/mixed-race patients, although with lower magnitude (aOR: 1.103; 95% CI: 1.006-1.209). A strong educational gradient was observed, with illiterate patients having more than twice the odds of death compared with those with higher education (aOR: 2.148; 95% CI: 1.628-2.833). Incomplete COVID-19 vaccination was also associated with increased mortality, while influenza vaccination was associated with lower odds of death. Diabetes, obesity, and chronic cardiovascular disease were not independently associated with mortality after adjustment. CONCLUSIONS: In-hospital COVID-19 mortality in Brazil in 2024 was shaped by respiratory severity, incomplete vaccination, and persistent racial and socioeconomic inequities. Although structural racism was not directly measured, the persistence of racialized mortality differences after adjustment is compatible with structural barriers in the healthcare pathway. Equity-oriented strategies should complement vaccination and clinical management to reduce preventable mortality among socially vulnerable populations.

[Predictors of willingness for COVID-19 vaccination in patients with inflammatory rheumatic diseases at the beginning of the vaccination rollout].
INTRODUCTION: In January 2021 the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) was coupled to high case numbers and mortality worldwide and in Germany. The start of the vaccination campaign was initially characterized by limited availability and uncertainty but rapidly gained momentum. Patients with inflammatory rheumatic diseases (IRD) were prioritized at an early stage due to the high risk for a severe disease trajectory. In this group vaccination proved to be effective and greatly reduced the risk of a severe course. The aim of the study was to ascertain the willingness for vaccination and the influencing factors in patients with IRD in order to optimize vaccination strategies and to reach vulnerable groups more easily. METHODS: Between January and April 2021 a nationwide survey was carried out in Germany among N= 3661 patients with IRD and N=381 control patients with other chronic internal diseases. The questionnaire covered willingness to undergo vaccination against COVID-19 and demographic and disease-related variables. For the analysis, "willing to be vaccinated" and "already vaccinated" were pooled ("vaccination willingness") and compared the unwilling. The statistical evaluation was carried out using χ2-tests, odds ratio (OR) analyses and logistic regression to identify independent influencing factors. RESULTS: The proportions of those willing to be vaccinated were comparable in both groups with 90% very high (IRD 89.2% and control group 93.9%). They continually increased in both groups during the observational period and with increasing age. Another strong predictor was a previously carried out simultaneous vaccination for influenza, which was associated with a significantly higher willingness to be vaccinated in both groups. CONCLUSION: The willingness to be vaccinated against COVID-19 at the time of the vaccination rollout in Germany was high. For patients with IRD, it was predicted by age, previous vaccination against influenza and the timing of vaccination but not the subtype of IRD or the type of immunomodulatory medication. Young patients with IRD in particular should be systematically identified as a risk group with a low willingness to be vaccinated. For this patient group an intensified target group-specific vaccination counselling should be integrated into the clinical care, which specifically addresses suitable information channels for those affected.

A grounded theory of compassionate care among clinical nurses.
BackgroundCompassionate care is a core ethical obligation in nursing, yet the processes through which nurses enact and sustain it remain insufficiently theorized. Existing grounded theory models have not examined an East Asian care context in which nursing staff may assume both clinical and daily living care.Research question/aim/objectivesHow do clinical nurses experience, construct, and sustain compassionate care, and what ethical challenges shape this process?Research designA grounded theory design following Strauss and Corbin was employed. Semi-structured interviews were analysed using open, axial, and selective coding with constant comparison. Ethics of care and moral distress served as sensitizing concepts, while categories were generated inductively. Trustworthiness followed Lincoln and Guba's criteria.Participants and research contextParticipants were thirteen female nurses from tertiary and secondary hospitals in South Korea, working across intensive care, hospice and palliative care, general and haematology wards, and emergency settings (mean clinical experience 14.9 years). Interviews were conducted from July 2020 to February 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic.Ethical considerationsInstitutional Review Board approval was obtained, and all participants provided written informed consent.Findings/resultsThe core category-comprehensive care grounded in an understanding of the illness trajectory-described compassionate nursing as a practice in which anticipating where a patient stands in the illness course shaped responses to present and emerging needs. Workload and time pressure constrained compassionate engagement, while collegial support helped nurses sustain it. Professional fulfilment and emotional depletion appeared as consequences that could influence subsequent care.ConclusionsCompassionate care was shaped by the integration of clinical understanding, relational engagement, and organizational conditions. Sustaining this practice may require workload governance and structured collegial support rather than reliance on individual resilience alone.

Outbreak of BA genotype-derived RSV-B lineages in Northeast India: Molecular epidemiology and phylogenetic insights from Dibrugarh, 2022.
Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a major cause of respiratory illness in children, but molecular data from Northeast India remain limited. We investigated an RSV-B outbreak among 239 children aged <5 years in Dibrugarh, Assam, during November-December 2022. RSV-B was detected in 67 (28.0%) samples by real-time RT-PCR. G-gene sequencing of 43 isolates and phylogenetic analysis identified three BA genotype-derived lineages: B.D.E.1 (48.8%), B.D.E.1.2 (37.2%), and B.D.4.1.1 (14.0%). B.D.E.1 and B.D.E.1.2 predominated, comprising 86.0% of sequences. The conserved G:I252T substitution was present across all lineages, with predicted glycosylation differences. These findings provide evidence of RSV-B lineage circulation in Northeast India.

Scrub Typhus in Pregnancy: A Retrospective Observational Study From Primary Hospital of Southwest China.
BACKGROUND: Scrub typhus is an acute zoonotic disease caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi. There are limited reports on scrub typhus in pregnancy, and the misdiagnosis rate is relatively high, potentially leading to adverse maternal and fetal outcomes. METHODS: This retrospective observational study analyzed 19 pregnant patients with scrub typhus admitted to the People's Hospital of Ximeng Wa Autonomous County, Southwest China, from August 2023 to November 2025. Epidemiological, clinical, test, treatment, and outcome data were collected and descriptively analyzed. RESULTS: All patients were farmers, with 73.68% reporting a history of outdoor activities. Common symptoms included fever (100%), myalgia (78.94%), headache (57.89%), and eschar (94.74%). Laboratory findings revealed elevated transaminases (ALT or AST 94.74%) and decreased eosinophil percentages (89.47%). Initial misdiagnosis occurred in 10.53% (upper respiratory infection). Among the 18 patients treated with azithromycin, fever resolution occurred within 1 to 5 days. No maternal deaths occurred. However, adverse fetal outcomes included spontaneous miscarriage (n = 1), embryonic arrest (n = 1), and embryo demise (n = 3). Among 19 cases, 14 resulted in live births; 2 premature infants required pediatric care, and all live-born newborns showed normal development at six-month follow-up. CONCLUSIONS: Scrub typhus in pregnancy poses serious maternal-fetal risks. Early clinical recognition and prompt azithromycin therapy are crucial for improving maternal and perinatal outcomes, especially in resource-limited settings.

Molecular detection of mecA and mecC-Mediated MRSA nasal carriage among healthcare workers in a tertiary care hospital.
BACKGROUND: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) remains a major cause of healthcare-associated infections worldwide. Healthcare workers (HCWs) colonized with MRSA may act as reservoirs for transmission, contributing to hospital- and community-acquired infections. Early detection of MRSA carriage is essential for effective infection-prevention and control. METHODOLOGY: This cross-sectional study was conducted at a tertiary care hospital. A total of 407 HCWs were screened for MRSA colonization using anterior nasal swab specimens. Staphylococcus aureus was identified using standard microbiological techniques. Methicillin resistance was determined phenotypically by the cefoxitin disc diffusion method according to Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) guidelines. Genotypic confirmation was performed using real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) to detect the mecA and mecC genes. MRSA carriers received 2% intranasal mupirocin followed by repeat screening. RESULTS: Among 407 HCWs screened, 96 S. aureus isolates were recovered, of which 80 (83.3%) were phenotypically confirmed as MRSA. The overall MRSA nasal carriage rate was 19.65%, with the highest prevalence among interns (40.62%). Male gender was significantly associated with MRSA carriage (p < 0.05). Among the 80 MRSA isolates, mecA was detected in 55 (68.75%), including 30 (37.5%) co-harbouring mecC. No isolate carried mecC alone, while 25 (31.25%) lacked both genes. All carriers became culture-negative after decolonization. CONCLUSION: A substantial proportion of HCWs were colonized with MRSA, highlighting their role in nosocomial transmission. Combined phenotypic and genotypic methods improved MRSA detection. Routine surveillance, strict infection-control measures, and targeted decolonization are essential to reduce MRSA transmission.

Innate immune response to Streptococcus suis infection: advances and future challenges.
Streptococcus suis is a pathogenic bacterium primarily found in pigs, where it causes sudden death and meningitis, but it is also capable of causing septic shock and meningitis in humans, being the most important cause of adult bacterial meningitis in Southeast Asia. As the host's innate immune system serves as the first line of defense against microbial invaders, it is crucial to understand the intricate relationship between the bacterium and this system. Despite an increasing number of studies performed in the last 20 years, the pathogenesis of S. suis infection is not fully understood, and there is still an absence of effective vaccines on the market. Recent population-genomic studies have further highlighted that pathogenic S. suis is not a single uniform entity but comprises multiple lineages with distinct genome content and disease associations, raising the possibility that innate immune evasion mechanisms may not be equivalent across lineage. In the current article, we conducted a comprehensive review of the literature, focusing on the innate response developed mainly by phagocytes against this Gram-positive bacterium. Our aim was to summarize the last findings and to identify the main gaps in knowledge to guide future research efforts toward areas that require further investigation.

A staged clinical development and evidence-generation framework for Group A Streptococcus vaccines.
Group A Streptococcus (Strep A) causes substantial global morbidity and mortality, yet vaccine development faces scientific, regulatory, and strategic challenges. We propose a platform-agnostic, staged clinical development and evidence-generation framework aligning trial feasibility with public health priorities. Laboratory-confirmed symptomatic pharyngitis could provide a feasible pivotal efficacy endpoint for initial licensure, subject to regulatory agreement. Complementary efficacy, effectiveness, and implementation studies could then generate evidence across diverse populations and outcomes.

Penicillin susceptibility in Staphylococcus aureus from blood isolates- a multicentre surveillance study in Denmark, Iceland, Norway and Sweden.
BACKGROUND: Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia (SAB) remains associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Interest in penicillin-susceptible S. aureus (PSSA) has re-emerged, but robust epidemiological data and reliable susceptibility testing are needed to guide antibiotic choice. METHODS: In this multicentre observational study, clinical microbiology laboratories in Sweden, Denmark, Norway, and Iceland contributed antibiotic susceptibility testing (AST) data for S. aureus blood culture isolates collected over six consecutive months in 2024. All laboratories followed EUCAST breakpoints, with additional confirmatory testing in selected centres. RESULTS: A total of 2,203 isolates were included. SAB incidence ranged from 34.0 to 62 per 100,000 inhabitants annually. Median patient age was 73 years (IQR 59-82), and 63.8% were male. PSSA constituted 32.2% of isolates, methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) 2.2%, while methicillin-susceptible, penicillin-resistant isolates comprised 65.6%. Among isolates with penicillin zone diameter ≥26 mm, 97.7% were penicillin-susceptible; 2.3% were resistant based on zone edge characteristics and/or blaZ detection. Resistance to non-β-lactams was low overall but higher among MRSA isolates. CONCLUSIONS: PSSA comprises a substantial proportion of SAB isolates in the Nordic countries, supporting routine susceptibility testing and more targeted use of benzylpenicillin.

Clinical burden and outcomes of pediatric carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae bloodstream infections in a tertiary care center.
BACKGROUND: Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) is an emerging threat in pediatric healthcare settings because of limited treatment options and high morbidity and mortality. However, data regarding pediatric CRKP bloodstream infection (BSI) remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate the clinical characteristics and outcomes of CRKP BSI in children. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was conducted among children hospitalized with Klebsiella pneumoniae BSI between 2020 and 2025. Demographic characteristics, healthcare exposures, laboratory findings, antimicrobial therapy, and clinical outcomes were analyzed. RESULTS: A total of 86 children were included; the median age was 12 months, and 50% were male. Overall, 91.9% had at least one underlying comorbidity, 89.5% had a history of previous hospitalization, 83.3% had prior antibiotic usage, and 25.9% had undergone surgical intervention. During the index hospitalization, 57.0% required intensive care unit admission and 77.6% had at least one invasive device. Fifteen children (17.4%) had CRKP BSI. Prior carbapenem exposure and longer antibiotic use were more frequent in the CRKP group, although the differences were not statistically significant. White blood cell, neutrophil, lymphocyte, and platelet counts were significantly lower in patients with CRKP BSI. Three-month mortality was 40.0% in the CRKP group and 15.9% in the CSKP group, with no statistically significant difference (p = 0.069). Length of hospital stay was also similar between the groups. CONCLUSION: CRKP accounted for 17.4% of K. pneumoniae BSIs in this pediatric cohort. No independent factor associated with carbapenem resistance was identified. The small number of CRKP cases limited the statistical power of the study. Larger multicenter studies are needed to better define factors associated with CRKP and its clinical outcomes in children.

The gene expression signature of multinucleated giant cells in the spleens of Leishmania donovani-infected mice.
Multinucleated giant cells (MGCs) are associated with chronic inflammation and infectious diseases, but their biological characteristics in vivo remain poorly understood because intact cells are difficult to isolate from tissues. In visceral leishmaniasis, heavily parasitized, hemophagocytic MGCs are observed in the spleens of Leishmania donovani-infected mice, suggesting that these cells may contribute to parasite persistence and disease pathology. In this study, we established a method for isolating intact MGCs from the spleens of chronically infected BALB/c mice and performed transcriptomic analysis of manually collected single cells. Gentle enzymatic digestion of infected spleens enabled the recovery of large, multinucleated, F4/80-positive cells, indicating that size-based manual selection efficiently enriched for MGCs. Principal component analysis of single-cell RNA-seq data from 10 isolated MGCs showed that most MGCs formed a cluster distinct from those of naïve and infected bulk-spleen samples and RAW264.7 macrophage cells. Differential expression analysis identified genes that were upregulated during infection and further enriched in MGCs, including Ccl8, Cd63, Cebpb, and Fabp5, which are associated with macrophage activation and immune regulation. These findings provide a practical approach for isolating splenic MGCs and offer preliminary insight into the transcriptional features of L. donovani-induced MGCs in vivo.

[Study on infectious disease outbreak detection methods based on simulation experiments and case validation].
Objective: By constructing infectious disease scenarios with different outbreak characteristics, this study systematically compared the performance of six outbreak detection methods and validated them using real epidemic data, providing scientific evidence for optimizing surveillance and early warning models and enhancing epidemic response capacity. Methods: Time series with baseline and outbreak periods were simulated by adjusting three parameter types: sequence length (long/short), baseline level (low/medium/high), and linear trend (small/medium/large), yielding 12 outbreak scenarios. Outbreak detection was performed using six methods: cumulative sum control chart (CUSUM), exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA), moving percentile method (MPM), Farrington flexible algorithm, Bayesian outbreak detection algorithm (BODA), and autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA). The performance of each method under different scenarios was compared. Furthermore, the methods were validated using COVID-19 data from Shanghai between November 2021 and March 2022. Results: In simulation experiments, CUSUM performed best in most scenarios, particularly in long sequences with high baseline levels (sensitivity 0.88, specificity 0.93), followed by BODA and the Farrington flexible algorithm. EWMA showed high sensitivity (0.97) in short sequences with low baseline levels. MPM and ARIMA exhibited relatively limited ability to detect sudden outbreak signals. Validation with real epidemic data yielded results consistent with the short-sequence, low-baseline simulation scenario: CUSUM achieved the highest sensitivity (1.00) and F1 score (0.84), while BODA showed a high specificity (0.97), effectively controlling false alarms. Conclusions: CUSUM and BODA are effective primary methods for infectious disease outbreaks. The Farrington flexible algorithm provides supplementary value in seasonal or long-term surveillance; EWMA is suitable for short-term monitoring, whereas MPM and ARIMA demonstrated relatively limited detection performance in this study. These findings provide empirical evidence for optimizing infectious disease surveillance and early warning systems and have important implications for enhancing early warning and emergency response capacity in public health events in China.

Trends in past-year suicidal ideation and planning among U.S. adolescents: 2021-2024, USA.
INTRODUCTION: Although youth mental health concerns intensified during the COVID-19 pandemic, national post-pandemic trends in suicidal thoughts and behaviors remain unclear. This study examined trends in suicidal ideation and suicide planning among adolescents from 2021 to 2024 and identified demographic, substance use, and mental health correlates. METHODS: Data were drawn from the 2021-2024 National Survey on Drug Use and Health for adolescents aged 12-17 years (N = 36,372). Weighted prevalence estimates were calculated, and multivariable logistic regression models examined associations between substance use, demographics, and suicidal ideation/planning. Adjusted odds ratios (AORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported. RESULTS: Suicidal ideation increased from 12.8% in 2021 to 13.2% in 2022 before declining to 11.8% in 2023 and 10.0% in 2024. Suicide planning followed a similar pattern (7.41%, 7.46%, 6.02%, and 5.13%, respectively). Compared with 2021, adjusted models showed no significant differences in suicidal ideation across years, whereas suicide planning was significantly lower in 2024 (AOR = 0.76, 95% CI: 0.61-0.96). Female sex, alcohol, tobacco, and marijuana use were associated with greater odds of both outcomes, while past-year major depressive episode demonstrated the strongest associations (ideation AOR = 20.4; planning AOR = 19.4). Adolescents aged 15-16 years had lower odds than those aged 12-13 years. CONCLUSIONS: Persistent disparities in suicidal ideation and planning highlight the continued need for targeted prevention and early intervention efforts.

County-level context and differential policy impacts on buprenorphine use among medicaid enrollees with opioid use disorder in Kentucky, 2018-2025.
PURPOSE: To estimate changes in buprenorphine use among Kentucky Medicaid enrollees with opioid use disorder (OUD) after policy changes and pandemic disruptions, and whether impacts differed by county-level context, primarily rurality and, secondarily, opioid treatment program (OTP) availability. METHODS: We analyzed Kentucky Medicaid claims from January 2018 through June 2025, identifying enrollees with diagnosed OUD to construct 10,800 county-month observations. Logistic regression fitted with weighted generalized estimating equations was used for statistical modeling of an interrupted time series (ITS) design to assess changes in the monthly proportion of enrollees with OUD receiving buprenorphine. Interruptions included removal of prior authorization (PA) requirements for transmucosal buprenorphine, methadone coverage initiation, COVID-19-related policy changes, and federal X-waiver elimination. Rurality and OTP availability were evaluated as effect modifiers. RESULTS: The proportion of enrollees with OUD receiving buprenorphine increased from 0.29 to 0.45 across the study period. PA removal was associated with an immediate increase in the odds of buprenorphine use (odds ratio [OR]=1.043; 95% confidence interval [CI]=1.025, 1.061), corresponding to a 1.4-percentage-point increase. X-waiver elimination was associated with a sustained increase in trend (OR 1.007; 95% CI 1.004-1.010). Differential effects by rurality were limited to the COVID-19 period. Counties without an OTP responded more strongly to PA removal than counties with an OTP (P = 0.037). CONCLUSIONS: Removal of administrative and regulatory barriers was associated with increased buprenorphine use among Kentucky Medicaid enrollees with OUD, with effects varying by county-level context, particularly OTP availability.

How Swedish healthcare workers managed the early weeks of the COVID-19 pandemic: sensemaking across organisational, interpersonal and individual levels.
BACKGROUND: In times of crisis the need to make sense of the situation becomes particularly evident. The perspective of sensemaking captures how individuals seek to clarify and understand what is going on when they encounter ambiguous, unexpected or confusing events, such as the COVID-19 pandemic. Sensemaking may occur at different but mutually interrelated organisational, interpersonal and individual levels. During the COVID-19 pandemic, healthcare workers (HCWs) faced multifaceted challenges related to their work. This study aimed to explore how HCWs managed their daily work during the early weeks of the COVID-19 pandemic through the perspective of sensemaking across organisational, interpersonal and individual levels. METHOD: The data was collected through individual interviews with 18 nurses and physicians between March and May 2020, and analysed using a reflexive thematic analysis. FINDINGS: The analysis revealed an overarching pattern of sensemaking as a way of holding clinical practice together throughout uncertainty. At an organisational level, sensemaking included how organisational structures contributed to stability in the organisation of work. The interpersonal level captured how understanding of uncertain circumstances was grounded in a collective understanding wherein HCWs reflected together and in relation to others. The individual level of sensemaking captured HCWs´ capability and commitment to continuing to provide care, despite uncertain circumstances. CONCLUSIONS/IMPLICATIONS: The findings imply that sensemaking at organisational, interpersonal and individual levels is an important consideration for healthcare organisations when facing future crisis or other uncertain events. Clear organizational directives are important for fostering a shared understanding of how uncertain situations should be interpreted and managed in practice. Furthermore, HCWs need opportunities and time for interaction with colleagues, enabling them to collectively construct meaning and maintain a sense of stability when managing uncertainty. It is also important to acknowledge HCWs´ individual knowledge, experiences and capability to sustain clinical practice despite conditions of uncertainty.

Adaptation and Translation of the Brain Fog Scale into the Indian Psycho-Socio-Cultural Context.
BACKGROUND: Brain fog is a subjective experience characterised by forgetfulness, poor concentration, mental slowness, dissociation and fatigue, with individuals describing experiences such as a 'mental wall' over formerly simple tasks. During and after the 2019 pandemic, scientific enquiry into brain fog was revived, explored and studied worldwide. Specifically, a large number of studies focused on the COVID-19 population and established strong associations with long COVID. Further, this in-depth research interest has led to the emergence of brain fog as a transdiagnostic factor. PURPOSE: Over the past half-decade, given the said and established facts, the majority of scientific evidence has been contributed by researchers outside India. This highlights that brain fog is subjectively experienced worldwide, but its objective expression varies. Given the existing literature gap, the present article focuses on developing the psychometric properties of the Brain Fog Scale (BFS) and on adapting and translating it into Hindi. METHODS: For this purpose, a set of data was collected from participants (N = 159) with a mean age of 32.5 years, including representation from both genders. Standardised measures, the original and translated forms of the BFS, along with quality of life (QoL), were administered. RESULTS: Principal component analysis revealed a refined 26-item, two-component structure comprising Psychophysiological Brain Fog (PsyPhyBF) and Cognitive Brain Fog, accounting for 52.8% of the total variance. The adapted scale demonstrated excellent internal consistency, with Cronbach's alpha coefficients of 0.91 and 0.92 for the two components, respectively, and 0.95 for the overall scale. Both dimensions of brain fog demonstrated significant negative associations with QoL, with PsyPhyBF emerging as a significant predictor of poorer QoL. CONCLUSION: The findings support the reliability and construct validity of the adapted Hindi version of the BFS and highlight the importance of culturally sensitive assessment tools for understanding subjective cognitive experiences in diverse populations.

SARS-CoV-2-Streptococcus pneumoniae Coinfection: A Narrative Review of Pathogenesis, Synergy, and Clinical Impact.
Bacterial coinfection following a respiratory viral infection is one of the main causes of morbidity and mortality during viral pandemics. However, the specific interaction between S. pneumoniae and SARS-CoV-2 remains scattered and poorly understood. In this narrative review, current evidence regarding the pathogenesis, synergistic effects, and clinical impact of this coinfection was collected and reviewed. Peer-reviewed literature published between January 2020 and January 2026 was retrieved from PubMed, Scopus, and ScienceDirect, and the evidence is presented separately according to its source, namely, experimental animal-model data, clinical observations, antimicrobial-resistance surveillance, and vaccine-related observational findings. From experimental studies in human angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (hACE2) mouse models, direct SARS-CoV-2 with S. pneumoniae coinfection caused lethal synergy via alveolar macrophage depletion, cytokine storm, and increased mortality. From clinical observations, coinfection was associated with poor outcomes, especially in the elderly and patients with comorbidities, although reported coinfection rates and effect sizes vary considerably between cohorts. Although global nonpharmacologic interventions (NPIs) temporarily reduced pneumococcal transmission, a concerning rise in antimicrobial resistance due to empiric antibiotic use during the pandemic had been observed. Additionally, several observational studies suggest that the 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13) may be associated with more favorable COVID-19 outcomes, potentially through the reduction of pneumococcal carriage, although this evidence remains susceptible to residual confounding. Despite evidence of synergism in animal models, clinical mechanisms remain inconclusive. Therefore, future research is required to validate these findings in clinical settings and to provide stronger evidence regarding cross-protection of the PCV to support valid recommendations.

Molnupiravir, first small molecule therapeutic to demonstrate therapeutic efficacy against Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus in the cynomolgus macaque model.
Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus (VEEV) is an emergent arbovirus of major epidemic concern. Associated with periodic outbreaks in Central and South America, VEEV has a high morbidity rate in humans due to a 1:1 clinical-to-subclinical ratio and can cause neurological disease in up to 14% of cases. Concerningly, no FDA-approved vaccines or therapeutics for VEEV exist. Molnupiravir, an isopropyl ester prodrug of β-D-N4-hydroxycytidine, has previously showcased notable antiviral activity against VEEV in vitro and in rodents. While molnupiravir emergency use authorization has been granted for SARS-CoV-2, drug efficacy against VEEV in a translational model of human disease has yet to be investigated. We therefore performed the first study examining molnupiravir efficacy against VEEV in cynomolgus macaques, a non-lethal animal model known to reiterate clinical hallmarks of VEEV human disease. Animals treated twice-daily with 150 mg/kg molnupiravir approximately 8 h post-VEEV exposure demonstrated improved human-relevant clinical parameters, including reduced viremia, febrile illness, and lymphopenia, as well as diminished histopathological evidence of encephalitis and cerebral RNA persistence. We additionally showcased that the calculated human equivalent dose of molnupiravir (97 mg/kg BID) was insufficient in decreasing viremia or improving clinical parameters. Our study is the first to characterize a small molecule therapeutic as an effective treatment against VEEV in a macaque model accurately recapitulating human VEEV disease [Words: 215].

Beyond the Room: Bed-Level Isolation as Surge-Capable Infrastructure for Pandemics and Disasters-A Conceptual Framework.
The COVID-19 pandemic exposed a structural limit of hospital isolation infrastructure: airborne infection isolation and protective-environment rooms are fixed assets that cannot be multiplied at the speed of a respiratory surge, and the constraint is more severe in field hospitals after disasters. Pandemic workarounds (ward conversion, portable negative-air machines, and modular container construction) each addressed part of the problem at the cost of bed capacity, sustained containment, or deployment speed. This concept paper aims to synthesize the failure modes of room-scale isolation into a device-agnostic set of clinical and engineering criteria for deployable bed-level single-patient isolation with switchable pressure polarity, in-enclosure air-quality monitoring, and on-board between-patient decontamination. These criteria are summarized in a requirements matrix, and one illustrative implementation is outlined. The intended contribution is a framework to guide future design, testing, and evaluation, not a validated solution; no validation data are presented, and none should be inferred.

Seroepidemiological investigation and risk factors of Q fever and Rift valley fever in livestock in Bangladesh.
Rift Valley fever (RVF) is an emerging and re-emerging mosquito-borne zoonosis of major economic, public health, and veterinary importance, often causing great population-level impact. Q fever remains a neglected zoonotic disease of considerable public health and veterinary significance, responsible for notable economic losses for livestock farmers. Despite their significance, the epidemiology of RVFV and Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) remains poorly understood, with little evidence on their seroprevalence and associated risk factors. We conducted a cross-sectional study to estimate the seroprevalence of RVFV and C. burnetii, and to identify associated risk factors in domestic livestock. We collected a total of 568 blood samples from domestic livestock across three different districts using convenience sampling. Individual animal and herd-level data were obtained through a pre-tested structured questionnaire. Serum samples were tested for antibodies against RVFV and C. burnetii using a competitive Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (cELISA). While none of the animals tested positive for RVFV antibodies, the overall seroprevalence of C. burnetii antibodies was 9.7% (95% CI: 7.4-12.4), which was highest in sheep (5.8%), followed by goats (2.1%), camels (1.1%), and cattle (0.7%). Animals from households (OR = 0.19, p = 0.04) and young livestock (OR = 0.10, p < 0.01) had lower odds of C. burnetii seropositivity than those from farms and adults, respectively, whereas animals with moderate BCS (OR = 3.1, p < 0.01), poor BCS (OR = 8.8, p < 0.01), and clinical signs (OR = 3.01, p < 0.01) had higher odds of seropositivity. These findings indicate the circulation of C. burnetii among livestock population of this country. Although no serological evidence of RVFV was detected in the studied animals, the possibility of exotic vector-borne disease being introduced into the country cannot be ruled out. Therefore, we recommended establishing a sustainable surveillance program in both livestock and vector populations to monitor and mitigate the burden of Q fever while maintaining vigilant for potential RVF emergence and other vector-borne viruses in regions where they are not currently endemic at the animal-human interface.

From Ebola response to adaptable preparedness beyond a single virus.
The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has been an important setting for Ebola innovation, including ring vaccination with recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus-based Ebola vaccine and the integration of clinical research into emergency response. These advances strengthened preparedness for Zaire ebolavirus (EBOV), but the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak highlights a remaining limitation: many preparedness capabilities remain closely linked to individual pathogens. Unlike EBOV, Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) has no licensed vaccine specifically indicated for prevention, and current evidence is insufficient to establish clinically meaningful protection from Ervebo against BVD in humans. Operational constraints documented in the current response, including a temporary Ervebo stock-out, limited mobility for vaccination teams, absent vaccination microplans, shortages of personal protective equipment, and gaps in triage and isolation capacity in the Bas-Uélé province, further illustrate that biomedical tools alone cannot ensure effective outbreak control. We propose extending pathogen-specific preparedness through adaptable, platform-based outbreak infrastructure encompassing four linked domains: scientific readiness, research and regulatory readiness, operational readiness, and community readiness. Such platforms should enable rapid evidence generation while retaining pathogen-specific diagnostics, clinical management, vaccines, and epidemiological knowledge. Global preparedness should therefore support transition from uncertainty to evidence and equitable action before transmission outpaces response capacity.

Human febrile illness associated with Yanggou tick virus: Clinical characteristics and epidemiological links to rodents.
OBJECTIVES: We identified Yanggou tick virus (YGTV), a segmented flavivirus previously unrecognized as a human pathogen, in a patient presenting with fever and headache. This study aims to characterize the epidemiology and clinical manifestations of YGTV infection in patients with fever of unknown origin (FUO). METHODS: We conducted a surveillance study at the First Hospital of Jilin University (2020-2025) involving 1011 patients with FUO. Concurrently, ticks and rodents in the vicinity of the patients' residences and workplaces were collected for viral detection. YGTV infection was confirmed via PCR assays. Positive samples were used for viral isolation, genome amplification, and phylogenetic characterization. An Apodemus agrarius challenge model was established to evaluate viral persistence and shedding. RESULTS: Of the 30 confirmed cases of YGTV infection, 10 were co-diagnosed with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS). The patients showed no clear seasonality or geographic bias. Notably, rodent contact (43.3%) was a more frequent risk factor than tick bites (6.7%). While clinical presentations were non-specific, nearly 50% of the patients presented with gastrointestinal and neurological symptoms. YGTV was isolated from patients, ticks, and A. agrarius (the latter often co-infected with Hantaan virus). Animal models confirmed persistent splenic infection and viral shedding via oral and fecal routes. CONCLUSION: Our findings establish YGTV as an underdiagnosed cause of human febrile illness, underscoring the transmission risks posed by tick vectors and rodent reservoirs. These results highlight the urgent need for enhanced clinical surveillance and diagnostic screening among patients presenting with FUO, particularly in regions where the virus is endemic.

Community views of factors influencing participation in dengue research: Fuzzy cognitive mapping in Dhaka, Bangladesh.
BackgroundBangladesh is among the countries most affected by dengue, the fastest spreading vector-borne disease worldwide. Engaging communities in designing and implementing solutions is a promising strategy for dengue control. However, collaborating with communities in urban settings like Dhaka presents challenges. As part of a pilot study for a cluster randomized controlled trial testing participatory interventions, we aimed to understand factors influencing community participation in dengue research in Dhaka.MethodsWe used fuzzy cognitive mapping to explore perceived barriers and enablers of participation. We engaged 97 participants (community members and leaders, community health workers, personnel from NGOs, public health actors, and local researchers) in 28 participatory mapping sessions. We analyzed maps using tools from graph theory, fuzzy logic, and thematic and social network analysis. Composite maps compared community and non-community perspectives.ResultsParticipants identified 223 factors influencing participation, grouped into 22 categories. Composite maps highlighted the five most influential. Both community and non-community participants emphasized positive community perceptions of dengue, involvement of community leaders, and logistical challenges as important determinants of participation. Community participants also stressed receiving benefits and innovative information sharing, while non-community participants focused on Dhaka's sociopolitical context.DiscussionAddressing barriers and leveraging enablers to community participation before beginning research is essential. Fuzzy cognitive mapping not only identified key factors, but also revealed which were most important, to whom, and why. This approach can guide researchers and others in building more equitable partnerships with communities - a step towards inclusive and decolonizing global health research.

Hepatitis A-Associated Very Severe Aplastic Anemia in a Young Adult Female: A Case Report.
BACKGROUND: Hepatitis‑associated aplastic anemia (HAAA) is a rare but life‑threatening immune‑mediated complication of acute viral hepatitis, and hepatitis A virus is an uncommon cause of this syndrome. CASE PRESENTATION: We report the case of a 24‑year‑old woman who developed acute hepatitis A followed by rapidly progressive pancytopenia fulfilling the criteria for very severe aplastic anemia. Her clinical course was complicated by febrile neutropenia, transfusion dependence, gastrointestinal bleeding, and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia bacteremia. Bone marrow biopsy demonstrated marked hypocellularity with severe trilineage suppression. Despite intensive supportive care including broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy and transfusion support, her clinical condition deteriorated, and she died from infectious and hemorrhagic complications before definitive therapy could be initiated. This case emphasizes the importance of early recognition of cytopenias during the acute phase of hepatitis and prompt hematology referral for definitive management. CONCLUSION: Aplastic anemia following acute hepatitis A infection is rare but potentially fatal. Early recognition of cytopenias during or following acute hepatitis, prompt bone marrow evaluation, and urgent hematology referral is essential for timely definitive treatment and improved outcomes.

Rat Hepatitis E Virus (RHEV) in Mus musculus and Rattus norvegicus in Northwestern Italy.
INTRODUCTION: Hepatitis E virus (HEV) represents a major public health concern. Beyond the main zoonotic genotypes HEV-3 and HEV-4, with pigs and wild boars recognized as the primary reservoirs of infection, a genetically distinct hepevirus of rodent origin (species Rocahepevirus ratti, genotype C1) (rat HEV, RHEV) has recently been implicated in human hepatitis cases worldwide. Although several risk factors have been proposed, contact with rats has been documented in one human case only, and the sources and transmission routes of RHEV remain largely unclear. Of interest, RHEV RNA has recently been detected in farmed pigs, highlighting livestock environments as potential interspecies transmission interfaces. In light of these findings, we performed a molecular investigation for RHEV in rodents captured on farms raising different livestock species in Northwestern Italy (Piemonte region). METHODS: A total of 98 rodents, collected on 32 livestock farms, were tested for RHEV by a combined molecular approach based on RHEV specific real-time reverse transcription (RT)-PCR assay and a pan-hepevirus heminested RT-PCR. Positive samples were further processed to attempt full-genome amplification. RESULTS: RHEV RNA was identified in a Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus) and in house mice (Mus musculus), with detection rates of 16.6% (1/6; 95% CI: 0.41-64.1) and 7.0% (6/86; 95% CI: 2.6-14.5), respectively. The positive rodents were captured in five livestock farms, raising cattle, goats, and poultry, located across three municipalities. The nearly full-length genome of a rat strain (RHEV/Rattus norvegicus/38129-22/ITA) was reconstructed. Pairwise nucleotide alignment showed high genetic relatedness of RHEV/Rattus norvegicus/38129-22/ITA with sequences previously identified in rodents and human patients, including those from European countries. CONCLUSIONS: The identification of infected rodents in livestock farms highlights RHEV circulation in rural environments, where interactions among rodents, domestic animals, and humans may be facilitated. Additional studies are necessary to elucidate RHEV transmission dynamics and assess public health implications.

Heart-to-kidney signal by extracellular vesicles promotes kidney injury in cardiorenal syndrome.
AIMS: Cardiorenal syndrome type-1 (CRS1), defined as acute kidney injury occurring in the setting of acute cardiac illness, is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Our objective was to determine whether extracellular vesicles (EVs) derived from the injured heart localize to the kidneys and contribute to renal injury in CRS1, and to elucidate mechanisms by which cardiac-derived EVs mediate kidney damage. METHODS AND RESULTS: Using cardiomyocyte-specific EV reporter mice, we characterized the release of cardiac-derived EVs and their biodistribution to the kidneys. Acute myocardial infarction increased circulating levels of these EVs and enhanced their uptake by proximal tubular epithelial cells. To directly assess their impact on the kidney, EVs derived from cardiomyocytes cultured under normoxic (N-EV) or hypoxic (H-EV) conditions were injected into the renal arteries of wild-type mice. H-EV, but not N-EV, induced proximal tubular epithelial cell injury and worsening of kidney function. To identify EV biomarkers, we performed proteomic profiling of cargo from N-EV and H-EV, and validated the muscle-specific protein TRIM72 as a biomarker of EVs originating from injured cardiomyocytes. In a porcine CRS1 model, plasma levels of TRIM72 positive-EVs were increased, and we demonstrate their delivery to the kidney. Similarly, in CRS1 patients, higher plasma levels of TRIM72-positive EVs correlated with the development of acute kidney injury. Mechanistically, uptake of H-EVs by proximal tubular epithelial cells induced transcription of lipogenic genes and caused lipid accumulation, whereas lipogenesis blockade protected these cells from H-EV-induced injury. We subsequently found that reduced expression of the transcription factor FOXO3 drove H-EV-induced transcriptomic reprogramming. H-EV cargo was enriched with specific Foxo3-targeting miRNAs, whose delivery promoted proximal tubular epithelial cell cytotoxicity, oxidative stress, and suppressed FOXO3 levels. CONCLUSIONS: Overall, this work demonstrates that a Foxo3-targeting miRNA heart-to-kidney signal mediated by injured cardiac-derived EVs contributes to kidney injury in CRS1.

Cold-induced transcriptomic responses are associated with strain-dependent Salmonella enterica persistence in refrigerated lettuce leaves.
Salmonella enterica is a leading cause of foodborne outbreaks linked to leafy greens. Refrigerated storage is a cornerstone of leafy-green safety, yet strain-level variation in the persistence of internalized S. enterica under these conditions remains poorly understood. Screening of eleven S. enterica strains revealed marked differences in their persistence within detached romaine lettuce leaves stored at 10 °C. Two isolates, belonging to serovars Montevideo and Newport, displaying contrasting persistence phenotypes were selected for detailed analysis, and these differences were confirmed at 4 °C. To investigate transcriptional responses associated with this variation, we profiled transcriptomic responses to cold stress in nutrient-rich medium by RNA-seq and evaluated post-cold recovery. Both isolates grew similarly at 28 °C but diverged at 4 °C, with the Montevideo strain maintaining higher growth capacity. Functional enrichment of KEGG pathways and Gene Ontology terms revealed shared repression of central metabolic and energy-producing pathways, coupled with induction of stress-response processes. Genes associated with general stress responses, cold-shock functions, and envelope integrity were more prominently represented among the induced responses of the Montevideo strain after cold exposure. These findings indicate that strain-dependent differences in Salmonella persistence during refrigerated lettuce storage are associated with distinct transcriptional responses to cold stress and post-cold recovery phenotypes observed in cultured bacteria. Consideration of strain-level variation may improve interpretation of pathogen persistence during leafy-green storage and inform future microbial risk assessments.

Genomic Epidemiology and Antimicrobial Resistance Analyses of bla KPC-2-Producing Pseudomonas aeruginosa in Zhejiang, China.
INTRODUCTION: Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase (KPC)-producing carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a global health burden due to its multidrug resistance. However, the resistance characteristics, molecular epidemiology, and dissemination mechanisms of bla KPC-2-producing carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa in China remain limited. METHODS: A total of 23 bla KPC-2-producing carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa isolates were collected in a hospital in Jiaxing, Zhejiang, from February 2021 to January 2025. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing and whole-genome sequencing were performed. Multilocus sequence typing, antimicrobial resistance genes, and virulence factors were identified. Phylogenetic analyses were performed, and genetic context analyses were conducted. RESULTS: Six sequence types (STs) were identified among 23 isolates, with ST463 accounting for 56.5%. All isolates exhibited multidrug-resistant phenotypes and were identified as carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa. 17.4% of isolates showed resistance to ceftazidime/avibactam (CZA). All ST463 isolates co-harbored exoS and exoU. The core-genome MLST analysis identified two clusters within ST463 isolates, and the core-genome single-nucleotide polymorphism analysis revealed close genomic relatedness among ST4424 and ST4526 isolates. The bla KPC-2 genetic context was mainly associated with an ISKpn27-bla KPC-ISKpn6-like structure and IncU-related sequences. CONCLUSION: ST463 was identified as the predominance lineage among bla KPC-2-producing carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa in this study, and multidrug resistance genes and multiple virulence factor genes in the ST463 were demonstrated. Genomic analyses identified closely related isolates consistent with potential nosocomial transmission in the hospital. These findings highlighted the importance of continuous genomic surveillance, susceptibility monitoring, and strengthened infection control strategies for limiting the persistence and potential nosocomial spread of high-risk bla KPC-2-producing carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa.

Molecular Characterization of Listeria monocytogenes Associated with Adverse Pregnancy Outcomes in Iraq with Whole-Genome Analysis of a Representative Isolate.
BACKGROUND: Pregnancy-associated listeriosis can cause severe fetal and obstetric complications, yet molecular epidemiological data from Iraq remain limited. This study integrated clinical and epidemiological data with PCR-based virulence profiling of Listeria monocytogenes isolates and whole-genome sequencing (WGS) of one representative clinical isolate. METHODS: In this prospective cross-sectional study, 150 pregnant women presenting with spontaneous abortion, stillbirth/intrauterine fetal death, or preterm labor were enrolled. L. monocytogenes isolates were characterized by culture, biochemical testing, 16S rRNA PCR, and PCR screening of hlyA, actA, inlA, and inlB. One representative isolate (A125-2) was subjected to WGS on the BGISEQ-500 platform for sequence typing, virulence and antimicrobial-resistance gene profiling, and phylogenomic placement. RESULTS: L. monocytogenes was isolated from 18/150 participants (12.0%; 95% CI, 7.3-18.1%), with the highest positivity among spontaneous abortion cases (14.3%). PCR detected hlyA, actA, and inlA in all 18 isolates and inlB in 12/18 (66.7%). The sequenced representative isolate A125-2 was assigned to Sequence Type 1 (ST1) and Clonal Complex 1 (CC1) and carried LIPI-1, LIPI-3, multiple internalin genes, stress-response determinants, and several antimicrobial-resistance-associated genes. WGS also detected inlB in A125-2 despite the PCR discrepancy. Descriptively, 28.7% of participants reported unpasteurized dairy exposure, and 61.1% of L. monocytogenes-positive cases occurred during winter. CONCLUSION: The clinical and PCR findings support an association between L. monocytogenes and adverse pregnancy outcomes in this Iraqi cohort. Genomic characterization of one representative isolate demonstrated an ST1/CC1 background with multiple virulence and stress-adaptation determinants and illustrated the added resolution of WGS for investigating PCR discrepancies. Because only one isolate underwent WGS, the genomic findings should be interpreted as isolate-specific and not as population-level evidence for Iraqi L. monocytogenes strains. Broader multi-isolate genomic surveillance is warranted.

Recent advances in antituberculosis drugs and therapeutics: from mechanistic breakthroughs to clinical translation.
