Tuberculosis (TB), caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, reclaimed its status as the deadliest single-pathogen infectious disease globally in 2023, accounting for 10.8 million new cases and 1.25 million deaths in 2023. The escalating crisis of drug-resistant TB, suboptimal BCG vaccine efficacy in adults, and persistent treatment gaps for vulnerable populations collectively drive an urgent shift toward mechanism-driven, precision-oriented therapeutic strategies.This review presents a critically integrated appraisal of anti-TB research advances spanning 2020 to 2025, drawing on structural biology, multi-omics, and real-world clinical evidence. It distinguishes itself from conventional descriptive literature compilations through systematic cross-population efficacy comparisons, in-depth dissection of translational bottlenecks, and explicit maturity stratification of emerging biotherapies. We synthesize progress across six interconnected domains: mechanistic insights into drug targets and spatiotemporal resistance evolution, novel short-course therapeutic regimens, precision medicine strategies, host-directed therapies, targeted delivery systems for extrapulmonary TB, and next-generation vaccine development. Three transformative breakthroughs are particularly highlighted: structural biology-guided rational drug design, spatial immune profiling of tuberculous granulomas, and AI-assisted diagnostic pipelines.We conclude by delineating priority research directions aligned with the WHO End TB Strategy, providing a translational roadmap to advance global TB elimination efforts. This rigorous, multi-dimensional synthesis offers an authoritative reference for advancing basic and translational anti-TB research and informing global public health strategy.

Development of a multiplex PCR for detection of pathogenic Mycobacterium orygis in cattle tissues harboring tuberculous-like lesions: a pilot study.
Mycobacterium orygis, a member species of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC), is emerging as a major threat to the control of zoonotic tuberculosis. The lack of low-cost diagnostic assays to differentiate M. orygis from other MTBC members has created a critical data gap in estimating its true burden in human and animal populations, especially in the Asian subcontinent. In this study, a multiplex PCR assay was developed to distinguish M. orygis from other MTBCs, based on two M. orygis-specific non-synonymous point mutations in the mbtG and fadD23 genes. The assay exhibited a limit of detection (LOD) of 32 pg for M. orygis DNA and demonstrated high specificity by amplifying a 434 bp IS1081 gene fragment from common members of the MTBC, including M. orygis. Also, 240 bp and 181 bp fragments of the mbtG and fadD23 gene fragments were amplified exclusively from M. orygis. Conversely, the assay showed no amplification with non-tuberculous Mycobacterium or other non-mycobacterial pathogens. Furthermore, tuberculous-like lesions in the different tissues (n = 135) of slaughtered cattle were tested for the identification of M. orygis. An established TaqMan real-time PCR assay carried out to validate the result by targeting regions of difference in the M. orygis genome of the assay showed high accuracy of the in-house developed multiplex PCR.

Risk and determinants of tuberculosis recurrence: a 12-year population-based cohort study.
OBJECTIVES: Tuberculosis recurrence remains a challenge to elimination efforts in high-burden settings. We aimed to estimate the incidence and timing of tuberculosis recurrence and to identify its risk factors to inform post-treatment care. METHODS: We conducted a population-based cohort study of tuberculosis survivors successfully treated for a first tuberculosis episode from 2013 through 2024 in São Paulo state, Brazil. Data were obtained from the state tuberculosis surveillance system (TBweb), and deaths were identified through linkage with the national mortality database. We applied competing risks survival analysis to estimate incidence and assess risk factors for recurrence. Covariates included demographic, clinical, behavioral, and social vulnerability indicators, measured at treatment initiation for the first tuberculosis episode. Risk factor models were stratified by age (<15 vs. ≥15 years). RESULTS: Among 154,579 individuals who completed treatment for a first episode of tuberculosis, we identified 9,464 first recurrences over a median follow-up of 5.4 years (IQR 2.5-8.2). The overall recurrence incidence was 1,127.2 per 100,000 person-years. Rates were highest between 3-12 months after treatment completion, yet recurrence incidence remained over 1,000 per 100,000 person-years in the 2-5 years after treatment completion. In adults, hospitalization (adjusted subdistribution hazard ratio [aSHR] 2.53, 95%CI 2.36-2.71), and incarceration during the initial episode (aSHR 2.30, 2.13-2.48), together with pulmonary tuberculosis as initial diagnosis (aSHR 2.10, 1.87-2.35) were the strongest independent risk factors for recurrence. In children, HIV (aSHR 6.38, 2.64-15.40) was the strongest predictor. CONCLUSIONS: The high and persistent risk of tuberculosis recurrence reinforces the importance of post-treatment care with risk-based follow-up strategies.

Effects of Immune-Modulatory Nutrients as Host-Directed Therapy in Pulmonary Tuberculosis Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
CONTEXT: Tuberculosis (TB) remains the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent worldwide, and treatment outcomes remain suboptimal. Host-directed therapies, including immunonutrients, have gained attention for their potential to support immune function and modulate inflammation. OBJECTIVE: To determine the effects of adjunct immunonutrients (omega-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids [n-3 LCPUFAs]; vitamins A, C, D, and E; selenium; zinc; arginine; glutamine; iron; and nucleotides) on early sputum conversion (sputum smear or culture negative at 4-8 weeks); and culture time to conversion, inflammation, mortality, and TB score in adults (aged ≥15 years) with drug-sensitive pulmonary TB. DATA SOURCES: Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane, and PubMed were searched from March 19, 2024, to May 2026. The review was performed according to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA). guidelines and was registered on PROSPERO. DATA EXTRACTION: Two authors independently screened articles, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using RoB 2.0. Certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) methodology. The review included 44 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and 1 quasi-experimental trial. DATA ANALYSIS: Vitamin D lowered TB scores at 8 weeks (standardized mean difference [SMD], -0.83; 95% CI, -1.09 to -0.57; P < .001), and C-reactive protein (CRP) at 6 weeks (SMD, -0.43; 95% CI, -0.83 to -0.03; P = .03), but did not improve sputum smear conversion (odds ratio [OR], 1.05; 95% CI, 0.99-1.10; P = .098). Arginine and vitamin C pooled effects on sputum smear conversion were not robust in sensitivity analyses or based on only 2 trials. Arginine reduced CRP at 8 weeks (OR, 0.55; 95% CI, 0.40-0.75; P < .001). Vitamin A, zinc, and their combination showed no significant effects. Certainty of evidence was low to very low. CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest a potential but unconfirmed benefit of selected adjunct immunonutrients, most notably vitamin D. Routine supplementation cannot be recommended. Large, well-designed RCTs with standardized dosing and outcomes are needed, including for those with no eligible trials identified (vitamin E, selenium, n-3 LCPUFAs, nucleotides, iron, and glutamine). SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: PROSPERO registration No. [CRD42024567237].

Taking a BREATH (Bayesian Reconstruction and Evolutionary Analysis of Transmission Histories) to simultaneously infer phylogenetic and transmission trees for partially sampled outbreaks.
We introduce and apply Bayesian Reconstruction and Evolutionary Analysis of Transmission Histories (BREATH), a method to simultaneously construct phylogenetic trees and transmission trees using sequence data for a host-to-host outbreak. BREATH's transmission process that accounts for a flexible natural history of infection (including a latent period if desired) and a separate process for sampling. It allows for unsampled individuals and within-host evolution. It also accounts for the fact that an outbreak may still be ongoing at the time of analysis, using right truncation adjustment. We perform a simulation study to verify our implementation and explore sensitivity to unknown or misspecified parameters. We then apply BREATH to a previously-described 13-year outbreak of tuberculosis. We find that using a transmission process to inform the phylogenetic reconstruction results in better resolution of the phylogeny (in topology, branch length and tree height) and a more precise estimate of the time of origin of the outbreak. Considerable uncertainty remains about transmission events in the outbreak, but our reconstructed transmission network resolves two major waves of transmission consistent with the previously-described epidemiology, estimates the numbers of unsampled individuals, and describes some high-probability transmission pairs. An open source implementation of BREATH is available from https://github.com/rbouckaert/BREATH as the BREATH package to BEAST 2.

Impact of Reduced Clinical Practicum Duration on the Clinical Competence, Communication Confidence, and Retention of New Nurses-A Follow-Up Study.
BACKGROUND: Clinical practicums provide essential learning experiences for nursing students and are critical in preparing these students to enter the workforce. The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted nursing education worldwide, leading to reduced clinical practicum opportunities for graduates. Research on how shorter/abbreviated clinical practicums affect the competence of newly graduated nurses is lacking. PURPOSE: The purpose of this research was to explore the impacts of reduced clinical practicum duration and content on the clinical competence, communication confidence, and retention rate of newly hired nurses over a 6-month follow-up period. METHODS: A follow-up design incorporating a retrospective baseline assessment of clinical practicums was used to track outcomes at three time points during June 12, 2023 and June 11, 2024. The sample included 133 newly hired nurses at a medical center in northern Taiwan. Data on clinical practicum experience and clinical nursing competence, communication confidence, and retention rate outcomes at the commencement of employment and after 3 and 6 months were collected. RESULTS: The results showed the average percentage of overall clinical practicum completed was 80.78% and that actual durations ranged from 37.5% to 100% of the normal (nonpandemic) duration. Clinical practicum experience was found to significantly influence nursing competence at the start of employment (p=.004) and at 3 (p=.002) and 6 months (p=.023) of employment. In addition, clinical practicum experience was also shown to affect communication confidence at the start of employment (p=.035). No correlation was observed between clinical practicum experience and retention rates at 3 and 6 months of employment. Finally, newly graduated nurses without licenses exhibited significantly less nursing competence than their licensed counterparts (p=.001). CONCLUSIONS/IMPLICATIONS FOR PRACTICE: Nursing education programs should assess the clinical practicum experience of newly hired nurses and provide support for those with less experience to enhance their nursing competence and communication confidence. Future research should address the challenges associated with unlicensed nursing graduates.

Innate immune response in COVID-19 pneumonia during the pandemic: a prospective cohort study.
BACKGROUND: Dysregulated innate immunity contributes to COVID-19 severity, but its evolution over the periods of the pandemic is undefined. The aim of the study was to compare ex vivo innate immune responses in COVID-19 and non-COVID-19 community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) and assess associations with pandemic period, severe respiratory failure (SRF), mortality, and circulating microRNA patterns. METHODS: In this prospective cohort study conducted at 2 tertiary hospitals in Athens, Greece, 102 hospitalized patients with COVID-19 pneumonia and 28 with non-COVID-19 community-acquired pneumonia were enrolled. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells were isolated during the first 24 hours before any immune intervention other than dexamethasone and stimulated for cytokine production. SRF was defined as a PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio <150 mmHg necessitating invasive or non-invasive ventilation. Exploratory serum microRNA sequencing was performed in a small subset. RESULTS: On Day 1, release of TNFα and IL-6 was higher by the PBMCs of patients with COVID-19 pneumonia than non-COVID-19 CAP; the opposite was found for IL-1RA. Patients infected by the Omicron variant had higher production of TNFα and lower of IL-6. Using multivariate logistic regression analysis, it was confirmed that over-time decrease of the production of IL-6 by the PBMCs of patients with COVID-19 was a risk factor for progression into SRF and 28-day mortality. CONCLUSION: COVID-19 pneumonia and non-COVID-19 CAP exhibited distinct patterns of ex vivo PBMC responsiveness, characterized by higher TNF-α and IL-6 production in COVID-19. Functional cytokine responses also varied across pandemic periods.

[Maternal death due to abortion in the states of the Northern region: an analysis from 2012 to 2022].
The study analyzed the ratio of maternal mortality due to abortion in the northern region of the country, using a retrospective sectional method with analysis of data from the Mortality Information System, Live Birth System and Hospital Information System. From 2012 to 2022 there were 174 maternal deaths due to abortion in the region, in 106 (61%) cases it was registered as the principal cause and in 68 (39%) it was registered as a cause associated with death. The most prevalent ICD 10 codes as the principal cause of maternal death were unspecified abortion (54.7%) followed by the ICD codes for Spontaneous abortion (18%) and failed abortion attempt (14.1%). Less than 2% of cases were abortions for medical and legal reasons. The socioeconomic profile was women aged 20 to 29 years (45.3%), black (68.8%) and education was between 8 and 11 years of study (40.6). In the COVID-19 pandemic, RMMA increased by 4.27%. The North region is the one with the highest MMR in the country and abortion continues to be one of the main causes of death. The women who die most are young, black, with low education and without a partner, confirming the characteristics that predict death from abortion. The reduction in maternal deaths in the North region and in Brazil continues to be a challenge for public health and a debt society owes to women.

Actions and financing of renal replacement therapy during the COVID-19 pandemic in Paraná, Brazil: a documentary study.
The aim of this study was to identify actions and funding allocated to renal replacement therapy (RRT) for patients with chronic kidney disease in the state of Paraná, Brazil during the COVID-19 pandemic. We conducted a documentary study using data extracted from six official health platforms in Brazil. Of the 17 documents published between January 2020 and May 2023 selected for analysis, seven (41.18%) addressed financial resources allocated to RRT during the pandemic and 10 (58.82%) described RRT actions. The data were analyzed according to the care quality assessment triad structure, process and outcomes. The findings indicate that both funding and actions implemented during the pandemic focused on expanding installed capacity, adapting infrastructure and reorganizing services to ensure the continuity and quality of care provided to patients undergoing RRT.

Memorialization practices in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic in Brazil: the online wake ritual.
This study aimed to understand the online wake ritual as a virtual Memorialization practice in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic in Brazil. This is an exploratory and descriptive qualitative study, with document analysis as the main study design. A search was conducted on the Google platform, with links published between March 11, 2020 and July 27, 2021, in Portuguese, with "Brazil" as the geographic definition. Among the 4924 links identified, 162 links referred to online news articles published in the context of the pandemic and available for full and free access. Among these, 65 were selected as they mentioned the online wake ritual, and were analyzed through content analysis. Significant transformations were identified in the topography of the wake ritual in order to respond to sanitary restrictions and social distancing measures. These were related, for instance to: the form and diversity of people involved in the offering; the transmission mode; and aspects related to spatiality and temporality. The presence of singularized symbolic elements concerning belongingness gave visibility to the leading role of the bereaved in the design of the wake ritual.

[Securitisation of health and the production of neglect: the case of the United Nations Mission for Ebola Emergency Response (2014-2015)].
This study aims to analyze the international community's response to the health crisis caused by the Ebola virus outbreak in West Africa (2014-2015), addressed through the establishment of the United Nations Mission for Ebola Emergency Response (UNMEER). This unprecedented mission resulted from a process of securitisation of Ebola by the United Nations, in that it transformed the response to the disease into a form of threat containment through immediate medical care, rather than addressing the socioeconomic factors related to the emergence and recurrence of the illness. Through a narrative literature review on the securitisation of health within Critical Security Studies, as well as documentary research on the international response to Ebola, this research concludes that the securitisation of the disease resulted in neglectful outcomes in the international community's response to the outbreak, failing to reduce vulnerabilities faced by affected populations.

Impact of temperature on patient-derived dengue virus breakthrough infections in wMel-infected Aedes aegypti.
The wMel strain of the insect endosymbiont Wolbachia reduces the potential for Aedes aegypti to transmit mosquito-borne viruses such as dengue (DENV). Field trials that have introgressed wMel into Ae. aegypti populations have shown this approach significantly reduces dengue incidence. In a laboratory, setting some wMel-Ae. aegypti develop infectious saliva following a viremic blood meal. Additionally, studies have demonstrated that exposing wMel-Ae. aegypti to heat treatment, particularly during the larval stage, reduces wMel density in key tissues such as the ovaries, midgut and salivary glands. Here we build on these studies, using viremic blood collected from 13 dengue inpatients at the Hospital for Tropical Diseases in Ho Chi Minh City (Viet Nam), to assess how temperature affects the protection afforded to Ae. aegypti by wMel. We found that, compared to wMel-Ae. aegypti reared at 28 ± 4°C, those reared at 31 ± 4°C developed infectious saliva more frequently, but the risk of this occurring was still reduced compared to WT mosquitoes reared at the same temperature. Heat treatment reduced the density of wMel in all tissues tested, and significantly increased the amount of DENV-1 and DENV-4 replication in wMel-Ae. aegypti. When comparing cohorts of wMel-Ae. aegypti that did or did not develop infectious saliva, DENV levels in the head/thorax were associated with increased odds of mosquitoes developing infectious saliva, but wMel density was not. Overall, these findings show that elevated rearing temperatures increase the risk of patient-derived DENV breakthrough infections in wMel-Ae. aegypti, potentially due to increased DENV replication in these mosquitoes. This limitation suggests it would be prudent to increase surveillance in regions using wMel for dengue control when daily mean temperatures remain above 30°C for multiday periods.

An immunoinformatics-driven multiepitope subunit vaccine targeting Oropouche virus: Molecular docking, immune and dynamics simulation approaches.
The Oropouche virus (OROV) is an emerging zoonotic orthobunyavirus responsible for recurring outbreaks of febrile illness and neurological disorders in South and Central America. Despite its growing public health issues, no FDA-approved vaccines or antiviral therapies currently exist. To address this gap, a multiepitope subunit vaccine was designed to target OROV glycoproteins G1 (Gn), G2 (Gc), and the nucleocapsid (N) protein using a reverse-vaccinology (RV) approach. For vaccine construction, suitable epitopes (MHC-I, MHC-II, and linear B-cell) were selected based on percentile rank, antigenicity, allergenicity, and toxicity. However, the biophysical attributes demonstrated advantageous characteristics, including stability and solubility (GRAVY score: -0.432). The structural modelling exhibited a Ramachandran and Z scores of 91.86% (most favoured regions) and -1.81, respectively. However, the molecular docking with TLR-2 and TLR-4 receptors showed probable interactions (-1126.8 kJ/mol) and (-1239.4 kJ/mol), respectively. Moreover, dynamics simulation of the vaccine and Vaccine-TLR-4 complexes confirmed probable dynamic stability and compactness. The codon optimisation for Escherichia coli K12 expression yielded a CAI value of 1.0 and a GC content of (30-70) %, indicating optimal expression. The immune simulation predicted strong antibody-mediated and T cell-mediated immunity, including elevated IFN-γ, IgG, and memory cell populations. These findings suggest the potential of multiepitope subunit vaccines as a promising preventive candidate against OROV. However, additional experimental verification is required to confirm its immunogenicity and safety in experimental settings.

Characterization of acute dengue immune status and serotype surveillance in three regions of Burkina Faso: a hospital-based cross-sectional study.
INTRODUCTION: In recent years, dengue has become a significant public health concern in Burkina Faso, associated with severe disease and death. Rapid characterization of acute dengue serostatus is useful for identifying patients at risk, informing transmission dynamics, and supporting public health decision-making. This study aimed to characterize dengue immune status in three regions of Burkina Faso to inform pre-vaccination screening, evaluate a commercial combined DENV NS1, IgM, and IgG rapid diagnostic test (RDT) kit, and investigate DENV serotype circulation. METHODS: A multicenter study was conducted between 2023 and 2025 in Bobo-Dioulasso, Houndé, Ouagadougou, and Gaoua. Blood samples were collected from patients with suspected dengue. Acute DENV infections and serotypes were identified using real-time RT-PCR, and immune status was characterized by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) according to WHO criteria. Serum samples were screened using the reference standard (RT-PCR combined with ELISA) to evaluate the performance of a commercial DENV NS1, IgM, and IgG RDT kit in characterizing dengue immune status. RESULTS: Primary dengue accounted for 75.9%, 80.4%, and 71.4% in 2023, 2024, and 2025, respectively. The sensitivity of the RDT for determining primary and post-primary dengue during the first 5 days of illness was 93.3% and 94.7%, respectively. DENV-1, DENV-2, and DENV-3 accounted for 47.0%, 5.6%, and 47.4% of cases, respectively. DENV-4 was not detected. The diagnostic specificity of the RDT for both primary and post-primary dengue was 100%. CONCLUSIONS: Primary dengue cases predominated, while severe dengue was associated with post-primary infection. The RDT proved to be a useful point-of-care tool for discriminating dengue immune status. DENV-3 and DENV-1 were the predominant serotypes driving recent transmission dynamics. The findings may help inform future vaccination strategies.

Informing an mpox stockpile investment case: epidemiological modelling and cost-benefit analysis.
BACKGROUND: In response to ongoing mpox outbreaks, Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, was considering funding the establishment of an mpox vaccine stockpile. To support their decision making, Gavi commissioned the Center for Outbreak Response Innovation at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health to estimate the optimal size, impact, health benefits, and monetised net benefits of different mpox vaccine stockpile sizes for an effective global stockpile to support outbreak containment and prevention of widespread mpox transmission. We aimed to quantify the potential impact of vaccination on future mpox outbreaks to inform Gavi's decision making for investing in an effective mpox vaccine stockpile. METHODS: A deterministic compartmental model of mpox transmission with vaccine interventions was developed, including intervening rapidly-at 20 cases reported-versus at 100 cases reported. The model was used to assess potential vaccine-based mitigation strategies for mpox outbreaks in Gavi-eligible countries by simulating mpox transmission and control dynamics, given two vaccination strategies (one dose and two doses) compared with no intervention in high-risk groups and contacts of cases, across four distinct subpopulations: (1) children younger than 5 years, (2) men who have sex with men, (3) female sex workers, and (4) the remaining general population. The findings from this model were incorporated into a Monte Carlo cost-benefit analysis of different stockpile sizes. FINDINGS: Rapid response (ie, intervening at 20 cases reported) using a single-dose vaccination strategy provided the greatest benefits relative to costs compared with a two-dose strategy. Using a one-dose strategy, expected net benefits were estimated to be over US$81 million to $220 million higher when responding to outbreaks rapidly than when responding after 100 cases. Furthermore, the total cost per disability-adjusted life-year (DALY) averted with rapid response using a one-dose vaccine strategy responding at 20 cases was 18% to 53% lower than a one-dose strategy introduced at 100 cases. A stockpile of 1 000 000 doses had the highest ratio of benefits to costs. INTERPRETATION: A stockpile calibrated to attain a high ratio of benefits to costs can be effective in controlling outbreaks and reducing overall negative health impacts. The cost-effectiveness of mpox vaccine stockpiles could be further maximised with reduced vaccine pricing and dose-sparing strategies. FUNDING: Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance.

Why does rotavirus vaccine effectiveness vary around the globe?
Rotavirus vaccines have transformed the prevention of severe childhood diarrhea globally, yet their effectiveness remains markedly lower in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where rotavirus mortality is greatest. Understanding the biological and environmental determinants of this disparity is critical for optimizing existing vaccination strategies and informing next-generation vaccine development. This review examines the factors contributing to variable rotavirus vaccine effectiveness across different settings, with a focus on maternal antibodies, infant gut health, co-infections, co-vaccinations and human genetic polymorphisms. Maternal antibodies, transferred transplacentally and through breast milk, can inhibit vaccine replication in the infant gut. Maternal antibody interference may be exacerbated in LMICs due to higher maternal antibody levels, driven by increased rates of natural rotavirus exposure and prolonged breastfeeding. Malnutrition, disruption of the gut microbiome, and environmental enteric dysfunction collectively impair intestinal immune responses, with their relative contributions also varying by geography. Co-administration of the oral poliovirus vaccine and concurrent enteric infections represent additional sources of interference that are more prevalent in resource-limited settings. Host genetic factors, particularly polymorphisms in fucosyltransferase genes governing histo-blood group antigen expression, further modulate vaccine immunogenicity across populations. These factors do not act in isolation; rather, they interact to shape the gut environment and collectively limit oral vaccine replication. Addressing rotavirus vaccine inequity will require context-specific strategies that combine optimized vaccine scheduling, nutritional and microbiome-targeted interventions, and the development of novel vaccine platforms capable of overcoming the unique immunological challenges of LMICs.

Factors associated with measles infection during the 2025-6 outbreak in Burao, Somaliland: a case-control study.
OBJECTIVES: Somaliland has recurrent measles transmission, but outbreak-specific evidence on modifiable child, household, and health-service factors is limited. We examined factors associated with measles case status during the 2025-6 Burao outbreak. METHODS: We conducted a community-based unmatched case-control study among children aged <15 years from 14 June to 8 July 2026. Cases were enrolled consecutively and controls sampled systematically from households using a random start and every fourth household. Cluster-robust logistic regression estimated adjusted ORs (aORs), with indeterminate responses modeled separately. RESULTS: Among 804 children (290 cases, 514 controls), case status was associated with non-vaccination (aOR 2.12, 95% CI 1.02-4.42), close contact (3.00, 1.72-5.25), reported health-facility attendance (2.79, 1.91-4.06), vaccine unavailability (2.62, 1.17-5.85), and trucked/vendor water (2.98, 2.03-4.36). Prior malnutrition, large-gathering attendance, household vaccination-refusal history, and poor ventilation were also associated. Health-facility attendance referred to the 21 days before rash onset/reference date, but exact visit dates were not collected. CONCLUSION: Measles case status was associated with immunity gaps, contact, household conditions, and service-related factors. Response priorities include reliable vaccine availability, catch-up vaccination, and contact-based action. The health-facility attendance association is temporally ambiguous and does not establish healthcare-associated transmission.

Safety of nirsevimab in children aged 0-24 months: Analysis based on EudraVigilance data (2023-2025).
Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a cause of severe lower respiratory tract infections in infants, and it is associated with substantial morbidity, including hospitalization and death. After European Medicine Agency approval of nirsevimab, a monoclonal antibody against RSV, immunization campaigns have been implemented in several European Union countries for administration to children as preventive intervention against severe RSV disease during RSV epidemic season. Monitoring its safety in routine healthcare practice is also important. We described suspected adverse drug reactions (ADRs) following nirsevimab administration in children aged 0-24 months, reported in the EudraVigilance system between 2023 and 2025. There were 1,923 ADRs, corresponding to 808 cases. By System Organ Class, ADRs mainly included general disorders and administration site conditions, which include nonspecific systemic manifestations and administration-site reactions that cannot be readily assigned to a single organ system (28.4%), infections and infestations (23.3%), respiratory, thoracic, and mediastinal disorders (12.2%); by Preferred Terms most frequent were drug ineffective (12.6%), and RSV bronchiolitis (9.6%). In addition, pyrexia, rash, and injection site reactions were also common. This study offered systematic characterization of ADRs following administration of nirsevimab. It found that the reported ADRs are consistent with the safety results from pre- and real-world safety studies. Our study can support the continue monitoring of the real-world safety and guide the planning of analytical observational studies on the safety profile of nirsevimab.

Occurrence and characterization of biofilm-forming and multidrug-resistant Shigella spp. in retail poultry meat and associated environments in Sylhet, Bangladesh.
Shigella spp. are important foodborne pathogens increasingly associated with antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and contamination within retail poultry-handling environments. This study investigated the prevalence, antimicrobial resistance profiles, extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL) determinants, virulence-associated genes, efflux pump genes, and biofilm-forming ability of Shigella spp. isolated from retail poultry meat and associated environments in Sylhet, Bangladesh. A total of 300 samples, including cloacal swabs, meat, handler hand swabs, utensil swabs, and wastewater samples, were collected and analyzed using culture-based methods, biochemical tests, and species-specific PCR. We also performed antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) and molecular characterization. Overall, 50.0% (150/300) of samples were culture-positive for Shigella. Among the 150 culture-positive samples, 144 (96.0%) were confirmed by species-specific PCR, including 98 Shigella flexneri and 46 S. dysenteriae isolates. When calculated against the total number of samples tested, Shigella flexneri and S. dysenteriae were present in 32.67% (98/300) and 15.33% (46/300) of samples, respectively, with the highest prevalence observed in cloacal swabs (46.38% and 21.74%, respectively). AST revealed high resistance to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (92.9% and 84.8%), tetracycline (87.7% and 87.0%), azithromycin (86.7% and 76.1%), and levofloxacin (76.5% and 56.5%) among S. flexneri and S. dysenteriae, respectively. In contrast, cefixime and gentamicin remained the most effective agents, showing susceptibility rates of 82.7% and 80.6% in S. flexneri and 67.4% and 58.7% in S. dysenteriae. The predominant resistance genes were tetA (72.45; 78.26%), qnrS (80.61; 89.13%), sul1 (50.0; 69.57%), and blaTEM (38.78; 45.65%), while efflux pump genes acrAB (60.20; 80.43%) and tolC (77.55; 86.96%) were widely distributed. Biofilm formation was detected in 37.76% and 56.52% of isolates by Congo red agar and in 27.55% and 36.96% by microtiter plate assay for S. flexneri and S. dysenteriae, respectively. All isolates exhibited MAR indices >0.20, while MDR and possible XDR (P-XDR) phenotypes were detected in 38.78% and 61.22% of S. flexneri and 58.70% and 41.30% of S. dysenteriae isolates, respectively. These findings highlight the occurrence of antimicrobial-resistant and biofilm-forming Shigella spp. within the investigated retail poultry-handling environment and underscore the need for strengthened biosecurity, antimicrobial stewardship, and One Health surveillance strategies.

Clinical and biochemical determinants of critical deterioration in paediatric scrub typhus: a retrospective study from a tertiary care centre in South India.
Scrub typhus causes substantial morbidity and mortality in children across South Asia, yet admission-time predictors of critical deterioration remain poorly characterized in the paediatric population. This study aimed to identify independent predictors of critical deterioration in hospitalized children with confirmed scrub typhus. A retrospective observational cohort study was conducted at a tertiary-care teaching hospital in South India over 6 years. Children aged 1-14 years with immunoglobulin M enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay-confirmed scrub typhus were included. Critical deterioration, a pre-specified composite of shock, acute respiratory distress syndrome, multiple organ dysfunction syndrome, mortality, or high-flow respiratory support requirement, constituted the primary outcome. Independent predictors were identified by multivariable logistic regression, and discriminatory performance was assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). One hundred and eighty-one children were enrolled (median age 6.0 years; 50.3% male). Critical deterioration occurred in 62 children (34.3%), with a case fatality rate of 12.9% among those affected. Serum albumin demonstrated the highest univariable discriminatory performance (AUROC 0.973), followed by neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) (0.945), total bilirubin (0.929), and lactate dehydrogenase (0.902). Four variables independently predicted critical deterioration on multivariable analysis: NLR [adjusted odds ratio (aOR) 3.811, 95% confidence interval (CI): 2.119-6.857; P < .001), C-reactive protein (CRP) (aOR 1.052, 95% CI: 1.018-1.089; P = .003), doxycycline delay (aOR 1.829, 95% CI: 1.146-2.920; P = .011), and serum sodium (aOR 0.689, 95% CI: 0.523-0.909; P = .008). The model demonstrated excellent discrimination (apparent AUROC 0.986, 95% CI: 0.971-0.997; optimism-corrected AUROC 0.982, 95% CI: 0.978-0.987) and satisfactory calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow P = .997). NLR, CRP, serum sodium, and doxycycline delay independently predict critical deterioration in paediatric scrub typhus at hospital admission, with serum albumin demonstrating the highest univariable discriminatory performance. Serial biomarker trajectories demonstrated sustained inflammatory and haemodynamic perturbation through 72 hours in deteriorating children, in contrast to the rapid biochemical resolution observed in those who recovered. These findings require external prospective validation before application to clinical risk stratification.

Severe strongyloidiasis and Gram-negative bacterial superinfections: epidemiology, clinical implications, and therapeutic strategies.
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Strongyloidiasis is a neglected tropical disease affecting over 600 million people worldwide. Its severe forms carry a fatality rate exceeding 60%, yet death is rarely attributable to the parasite alone: the terminal event is often bacterial sepsis or meningitis of enteric origin. We review recent evidence on Gram-negative and other bacterial superinfections in severe strongyloidiasis, and their diagnostic and therapeutic implications. RECENT FINDINGS: Cohort studies show that bacteraemia is the commonest complication of severe disease, affecting 38.3% of cases against 4.1% of uncomplicated infections, and is predominantly Gram-negative, with Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli most often isolated; Gram-positive and polymicrobial infections also occur. Beyond corticosteroids, targeted immunosuppressants and transplantation are increasingly implicated. Recognition is difficult, as eosinophilia is frequently absent and serological tests, including recent rapid assays, perform poorly in immunocompromised patients. Diagnostic delay is associated with higher risk of sepsis and mortality. Emodepside and moxidectin show promise in chronic infection but remain untested in severe disease. SUMMARY: Enteric Gram-negative bacteraemia or meningitis in an at-risk patient, particularly if recurrent or polymicrobial, should prompt parasitological investigation. As treatment of established disease is unproven, detecting and treating chronic infection before immunosuppression, including transplant donors and recipients, remains the intervention most likely to reduce mortality.

Bayesian estimation of true herd-level prevalence and spatial distribution of Salmonella Dublin-seropositive dairy herds in Alberta, Canada.
Salmonella Dublin, a cattle-adapted serovar of Salmonella enterica ssp. enterica with zoonotic potential, has become a pathogen of increasing concern for the dairy industry in Canada and beyond. A comprehensive understanding of its epidemiology is crucial to guide effective surveillance and control. The objectives of this serial cross-sectional study were to estimate the true herd-level seroprevalence of Salmonella Dublin and to characterize the spatial distribution of Salmonella Dublin-seropositive dairy herds in Alberta, Canada. Bulk tank milk (BTM) samples were collected from all active dairy herds in Alberta, Canada, in June (n = 462) and December (n = 451) 2024, and PrioCHECK ELISA was used to detect antibodies against Salmonella Dublin. Herds were classified as positive if ≥ 1 sample had a percent positivity ≥ 35. True seroprevalence was estimated using a Bayesian latent class model accounting for imperfect sensitivity and specificity. Spatial patterns were evaluated using a Bayesian geostatistical model, and a spatial scan statistic was used to detect localized clusters. The estimated true prevalence of Salmonella Dublin-seropositive herds in Alberta was 14.9% (95% Bayesian credible interval: 7.3-28.2%), with regional estimates of 8.0% (95% BCI = 1.6-22.6%), 13.9% (95% BCI = 4.2-31.8%), and 20.9% (95% BCI = 8.5-42.5%) for the north, central, and south regions of Alberta, respectively. The continuous spatial risk surface revealed that the true herd seropositivity varied markedly across Alberta, with some areas having much higher predicted seropositivity probabilities than others. Furthermore, 2 localized clusters of higher seropositivity were detected: a prominent cluster (95-km radius) in southwestern Alberta and a relatively smaller cluster (19-km radius) in a high-density dairy corridor in the central region. These findings indicate that Salmonella Dublin exposure is moderate in Alberta, with marked regional heterogeneity and pronounced spatial gradients in herd-level seropositivity. Incorporating spatial context into surveillance and control may improve targeting of interventions aimed at reducing within-region transmission. These findings also illustrate the value of Bayesian latent class modeling for generating bias-adjusted true seroprevalence estimates in the absence of a gold-standard diagnostic test.

The future of cholera genomics through the lens of clinical, public health, and research practitioners in Africa.
Cholera remains a persistent public health threat, complicating efforts to track transmission across borders and undermining control measures. Surveillance systems often remain fragmented and reactive, and many aspects of Vibrio cholerae evolution continue to be challenging, restricting the development of effective, data-driven interventions. Although genomics is increasingly transforming our understanding of cholera by revealing new insights into pathogen biology, transmission dynamics, and evolution, its routine integration into public health practice remains low. In this Personal View, we present the perspectives of those working at the frontline of cholera control in Africa (clinicians, public health practitioners, and researchers) who are rarely heard from, yet who actively shape strategies, navigate technological hurdles, and address system-level challenges to incorporate genomics into routine practice. These insights emerged through the Vibriowatch and Cholera Genomics Course, funded by the Gates Foundation and hosted by the Centre for Infectious Disease Research in Zambia in Lusaka, Zambia, on Feb 9-14, 2025. The course convened 36 participants from 18 African countries to exchange practical experience on how genomic data can be translated into public health decision making. A key outcome of this convening was the establishment of the Community of Practice for Cholera Genomics, which has since evolved into a sustained and structured platform for collaboration, peer learning, and collective problem solving, bringing together practitioners working across cholera surveillance, genomics, and response systems, ensuring that genomic approaches are grounded in local realities and appropriately embedded within cholera-control approaches. The thematic workstreams of the Community of Practice for Cholera Genomics meet regularly to deliver defined technical priorities, with seminar sessions bringing the whole community together to review progress, align priorities, and engage external experts. Accountability is embedded through shared ownership of workplans within each thematic team, with members jointly responsible for tracking progress. Grounded in real-world experience, in this Personal View, we offer timely, policy-relevant recommendations to strengthen genomic approaches, centring African leadership, equity, and long-term sustainability.

Community-acquired Acinetobacter baumannii pneumonia in Southern Vietnam: A retrospective cohort study.
Acinetobacter baumannii has traditionally been considered a nosocomial pathogen, but cases of community-acquired A. baumannii pneumonia have increasingly been reported in tropical Asia, including Vietnam. Data on its clinical characteristics, antimicrobial resistance, and patient outcomes remain limited. This study aimed to describe the clinical profile, resistance patterns, and outcomes of community-acquired A. baumannii pneumonia in southern Vietnam. We performed a single-center retrospective cohort study at Nhan Dan Gia Dinh Hospital, a 1500-bed tertiary center in Ho Chi Minh City (January 2021-December 2023). Adults (≥18 years) with community-acquired pneumonia and a positive sputum, endotracheal aspirate, or blood culture for A. baumannii obtained within 48 hours of admission were included. Patients with cultures >48 hours after admission, hospitalization in the prior 90 days, residence in/transfer from another facility ≥48 hours preadmission, polymicrobial cultures, or incomplete records were excluded. Thirty-one patients were identified (median age 69.0 years (interquartile range 64.0-84.0); 83.9% male; 83.9% current/former smokers). No clear seasonal predominance was observed within the study window after month-level normalization. On admission, 87.1% had hypoxemia (peripheral oxygen saturation<90%) and nearly half (45.2%) were severe community-acquired pneumonia. Antibiotic escalation was required in 61.3% after a median of 4 days (interquartile range 3-5). Resistance was approximately 69%-83% across the routinely tested β-lactams and fluoroquinolones, whereas aminoglycosides showed comparatively higher in vitro activity than the other tested antibiotic classes but susceptibility remained suboptimal (amikacin 50%, tobramycin 46%, gentamicin 36%). Initial empiric therapy was active against the index isolate in 4/25 patients (16.0%) with available susceptibility results. In-hospital mortality was 13/31 (41.9%). Community-acquired A. baumannii pneumonia is associated with severe disease, extensive antimicrobial resistance, frequent empiric treatment mismatch, and high mortality. In resource-constrained settings, limited therapeutic options highlight the importance of early microbiological diagnosis, comprehensive susceptibility testing, and locally informed treatment strategies.

Heterogeneity in Mycobacterium tuberculosis immunoreactivity in young children in Blantyre, Malawi: A community-based survey.
As tuberculosis (TB) incidence declines, transmission becomes increasingly concentrated in vulnerable populations and neighbourhoods. There is an urgent need for affordable surveillance strategies to monitor trends, identify high-risk groups and target interventions. TB disease prevalence surveys are no longer cost-effective in monitoring epidemiological trends as countries target TB elimination, while passive surveillance methodologies such as case-notification rates (CNRs) are biased by healthcare access disparities. Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) immunoreactivity surveys indirectly measure transmission and therefore undiagnosed infectious TB, and may provide valuable information to TB programmes globally. We conducted a pragmatic hybrid clinic- and household-based cross-sectional interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) survey in healthy children aged 1-4 years in 33 high-burden neighbourhoods Blantyre, Malawi. Participants were recruited using novel convenience sampling in health facilities, alongside random household sampling guided by satellite imagery, and tested for Mtb immunoreactivity using QFT-Plus IGRA. We constructed hierarchical Bayesian logistic regression models for IGRA positivity, with neighbourhood-level random effects. Of 1,545 participants, 102 (6.6%) had a positive IGRA: an annual risk of Mtb infection (ARTI) of 2.7% (95% CrI 2.2-3.2%). Immunoreactivity was higher in the poorest third of households (8.7% vs 4.9%; adjusted odds ratio: 1.88, 95% CrI 1.08-3.01) compared to the richest, but was not associated with HIV exposure, malnutrition or reported household TB exposure. There was substantial between-neighbourhood heterogeneity (ARTI range 1.1-4.1%). There was no association between neighbourhood-level TB case notifications and ARTI. Measuring Mtb immunoreactivity in young children, using innovative recruitment strategies, revealed a high burden of immunoreactivity suggestive of recent TB transmission. Children in the poorest households were at highest risk, highlighting the importance of social and economic inequity in driving the TB epidemic. Case notification rates may not reflect the areas with the highest transmission, and Mtb immunoreactivity surveillance may support identification of high-risk populations, monitoring of trends and targeting of public health interventions.

Tuberculosis disease burden trends, drivers, and projections to 2050 in China and the wider Central Asian region, 1990-2023.
BACKGROUND: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a leading infectious killer, with high burden concentrated in China and wider Central Asia. Integrated long-term trend analysis and forecasting for this region are scarce. We aimed to quantify TB burden trends, drivers, inequalities, and 2050 projections across China and wider Central Asia (1990-2023). METHODS: We used Global Burden of Disease 2023 data to estimate age-standardized incidence, prevalence, mortality, and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs). Joinpoint, age-period-cohort, decomposition, and Bayesian APC models were applied. Socioeconomic inequalities were assessed via Socio-demographic Index (SDI) and Concentration Index. RESULTS: China achieved steep declines in age-standardized mortality (-94.2%) and DALYs (-92.4%), driven by epidemiological gains offsetting population growth and aging. Central Asia improved moderately but heterogeneously; population growth diluted gains, with Tajikistan showing rising absolute burden. TB burden correlated negatively with SDI; socioeconomic inequality fell markedly, especially for mortality (-69.0%), but persisted among low-SDI groups. By 2050, model projections suggest that mortality targets may be achievable under current trends, although uncertainty remains substantial. CONCLUSIONS: China has undergone a substantial TB epidemiological transition characterized by marked declines in mortality and DALYs. Targeted interventions-latent TB treatment in China, accelerated case finding and cross-border collaboration in Central Asia-and strengthened regional cooperation are critical to advance regional TB elimination.

One Health genomic surveillance of ticks found on community-dwelling non-human 'farm' animals to identify microbes associated with tick borne illnesses in Eastern Ontario.
Companion animals, such as dogs and cats, and wildlife are recognized as sentinel species in One Health surveillance due to periodic exposure to ticks and infection by tick-borne pathogens (TBPs). Surveillance of this type is a strategy that captures a broad range of genetic, immunological, and behavioral factors that affect tick and disease dynamics. In contrast, non-human animals (hereafter referred to as 'animals') that are traditionally farmed for their meat and other products have been largely overlooked as sentinel species. Community-dwelling farm sanctuary residents, such as cattle, pigs, horses, and other traditionally 'farmed' animals have close daily contact with human caregivers, making them excellent candidates for One Health surveillance. These animals, often free-range in pastures and/or woodlands, bridging the territory inhabited by wildlife and that occupied by humans. This study collected 67 ticks, from bovines (n = 22), equines (n = 35) and canines (n = 6) residing in a farm animal sanctuary and screened them for microbes associated with tick borne illnesses using 16S rRNA V4 amplicon targeted sequencing (515F/906R) with custom Rickettsia buchneri blocking primers to boost sensitivity. Only 60 ticks were viable for analysis, 59 were of Ixodes species and one was Dermacentor variabilis. Of these, 31.6% (n = 19) tested positive for potential pathogens, including 21.6% (n = 13) for the causative agent of Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi) and 15% (n = 9) for Anaplasma phagocytophilum, with a co-infection rate of five percent (n = 3). Utilizing community dwelling sanctuary residents allowed us to detect potential threats to both animal and human health and was instrumental in the rapid diagnosis of anaplasmosis in two study participants (a horse and a pony) who showed symptoms of lethargy and inappetence after being bitten by ticks.

Functional Divergence of Regulatory and Conventional Bovine Neutrophils following Mycobacterium bovis Infection.
INTRODUCTION: Bovine tuberculosis (bTB), due to Mycobacterium bovis (Mb) infection, is a chronic cattle disease and neglected cause of zoonotic tuberculosis. The role of neutrophils in bTB is overlooked. We recently identified a new neutrophil subset in cattle and mice with a similar morphology to conventional inflammatory neutrophils (Nconv). However, unlike Nconv, these regulatory neutrophils (Nreg) express MHC-II at their surface and can suppress lymphocyte proliferation. METHODS: In this study, we compared the responses of bovine Nconv and Nreg to infection with a virulent Mb strain circulating in France and the attenuated Mb BCG vaccine. RESULTS: Nreg and Nconv had different transcriptional profiles and were differentially activated by Mb infection. Both Nreg and Nconv efficiently killed Mb, but Nreg had higher levels of phagocytosis activity (2-fold difference) and ROS production (2.3-fold difference). Nreg had higher levels of mitochondrial activity and an ultrastructural organization different from that of Nconv. CONCLUSION: Our results provide the first insight into the functional characterization of bovine neutrophil subsets during Mb infection and highlight a new layer of complexity in their functional diversity that must be taken into account to improve our understanding of bTB pathophysiology, which is urgently required to improve the management of this costly disease.

Retrospective two-centre study of human tularemia, Austria.
PURPOSE: Tularemia, a zoonotic bacterial infection has re-emerged in many European countries over the last years. Data on the management of tularemia are scarce. METHODS: In this two-centre retrospective cohort study, we describe real-world data on the clinical manifestations, diagnostic procedures and management of 51 tularemia patients in East Austria. RESULTS: The patients showed heterogeneous clinical presentation, including glandular infection (n = 17, 33.3%), ulceroglandular infection (n = 23, 45.1%), pulmonary infection (n = 10, 19.6%) and typhoidal infection (n = 1, 2%). Notably, seven cases were culture positive, including one case with positive blood culture. Time to achieve the correct diagnosis was associated with the duration of treatment (β = 0.89, p < 0.001), as well as the need for a surgical intervention (OR 1.04, 95%CI 1.01-1.09, p = 0.04). Moreover, we demonstrate a high rate of treatment failure in patients receiving monotherapy (27%). CONCLUSION: We highlight the heterogeneous clinical presentation of tularemia patients in Austria. Further we demonstrate that timely diagnosis and a prompt implementation of an appropriate antimicrobial therapy may contribute to shorter treatment durations and a reduced need for surgical intervention.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae infections in the Post-COVID era: recent advances from pathogenesis to clinical management.
M.pneumoniae is a major cause of human respiratory infection whose pathogenicity relies on adhesion proteins, secreted virulence factors, and immune evasion mechanisms. This review contextualizes these strategies within the broader phylogeny of clinically relevant Mycoplasma species while addressing the diverse extrapulmonary manifestations of M. pneumoniae. Current challenges in managing M. pneumoniae infections are multifaceted. The post-pandemic resurgence reflects a population-level immune debt resulting from prolonged non-pharmaceutical interventions, with test positivity rising sharply after restrictions were lifted and driving pneumonia outbreaks across age groups. Macrolide resistance remains persistently high in East Asia and is emerging at variable rates in other regions; routine diagnostics cannot detect resistance in real time, complicating first-line empirical therapy. Vaccine development continues to face obstacles including antigenic variation mediated by recombination between repetitive genomic sequences, the IL-17 A paradox wherein protective Th17 responses also drive vaccine-enhanced disease, and the inability of systemic vaccines to induce mucosal secretory IgA and tissue-resident memory T cells. In response, we evaluate emerging diagnostics-including metagenomic sequencing, CRISPR-Cas platforms, and host biomarkers-and discuss resistance-guided therapies involving doxycycline, quinolones, and novel agents like lefamulin and omadacycline. We further analyze vaccine development hurdles alongside the potential of mRNA-LNP platforms targeting conserved adhesin epitopes. Our findings indicate that the lag between mechanistic insight and clinical implementation remains the most pressing challenge. Future research must shift from simple mechanistic elucidation to addressing real-world clinical dilemmas, including distinguishing colonization from infection through integrated pathogen-host evaluation, exploring synergistic use of antibiotics and immunomodulators targeting the IL-17 A pathway, advancing vaccine design that circumvents IL-17 A-mediated immunopathology via conserved epitope selection and mucosal delivery, and establishing real-time surveillance networks integrating genomics and clinical phenotypes. Collectively, this work provides a practical roadmap spanning molecular pathology to clinical practice for the precise management of M. pneumoniae infections.

Listeria monocytogenes septicemia and fetal maceration in long-tailed chinchillas (Chinchilla laniger) in Argentina.
Listeria monocytogenes is a zoonotic bacterium widely distributed in the environment and capable of infecting a broad range of animal species, including humans, usually as a food-borne disease. Although listeriosis is well recognized across multiple hosts, information in small mammals such as rodents and lagomorphs remains comparatively limited, with most reports describing sporadic systemic disease. This study describes two cases of septicemic listeriosis with reproductive involvement in pregnant long-tailed chinchillas (Chinchilla laniger) from a breeding facility in Argentina. Both animals developed depression, anorexia, prolonged gestation, and died. Grossly, both animals had mucosanguineous vaginal discharge and fetal maceration; one also showed multifocal random hepatic necrosis. Histopathology revealed severe multifocal necrosuppurative hepatitis, enteritis, endometritis and placentitis, and pulmonary thromboembolism. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated abundant intralesional Listeria spp. antigen in the liver and uterus. L. monocytogenes DNA was detected in the liver by real-time PCR. The present work expands the knowledge of listeriosis in chinchillas by providing detailed documentation of systemic infection with reproductive involvement. Given the zoonotic nature of L. monocytogenes, early recognition of infection in captive animal populations is relevant for both animal and public health.

Adrenal Infections: An Underrecognized Cause of Primary Adrenal Insufficiency.
INTRODUCTION: Adrenal infections are an underrecognized but clinically significant cause of primary adrenal insufficiency (PAI). OBJECTIVES: This review proposes a diagnostic algorithm for the evaluation of suspected cases. RESULTS: The most common causative pathogens are Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Histoplasma capsulatum; however, bacterial infections and viral pathogens such as cytomegalovirus (CMV) and SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) have also been reported. These infections, particularly in tuberculosis and histoplasmosis, can induce granulomatous inflammation, tissue necrosis, and destruction of the adrenal glands, leading to systemic symptoms and hormonal deficiency. The prevalence of adrenal insufficiency varies widely, ranging from 14% to 100%, depending on the study population and diagnostic criteria. Affected patients may present across a broad clinical spectrum, from chronic adrenal insufficiency to adrenal crisis, and some patients may be identified incidentally through imaging performed for unrelated indications. Computed tomography is the primary imaging modality for diagnosing adrenal infection, typically demonstrating bilateral adrenal lesions characterized by hypodensity with central necrosis, peripheral rim enhancement, and calcification. In contrast, during the late phase, the adrenal glands progressively decrease in size and may become atrophic, particularly in tuberculosis, and often with persistent calcifications. Tissue biopsy with histopathological examination and culture remains the definitive diagnostic tool to confirm the infectious etiology. CONCLUSIONS: Early recognition is essential, as management requires two complementary approaches: 1. antimicrobial therapy directed at the causative pathogen, and 2. hormonal replacement in patients with established adrenal insufficiency and longitudinal hormonal surveillance in those with preserved adrenal reserve at initial presentation.

Detection of Candidatus Rickettsia andeanae in ticks from sympatric canids in northeastern Argentina.
In northeastern Argentina, wild canids such as the pampas fox (Lycalopex gymnocercus) and the crab-eating fox (Cerdocyon thous) coexist with domestic dogs (Canis lupus familiaris) across rural and peri-urban landscapes, creating opportunities for tick and pathogen exchange. Characterizing tick assemblages and associated pathogens in these hosts is essential to assess potential public health risks at the wildlife-domestic interface. Ticks were collected opportunistically from domestic dogs and road-killed foxes near two protected areas in Corrientes Province. Specimens were identified using morphological and molecular approaches and screened for Rickettsia spp. by PCR. A total of 30 adult ticks were obtained from 12 dogs and 8 foxes, representing four species: Amblyomma tigrinum, A. ovale, A. dubitatum and Rhipicephalus sanguineus. Amblyomma tigrinum was the most frequent species (50%). Seven individual ticks were confirmed as Candidatus Rickettsia andeanae in A. tigrinum, while one pooled sample was positive by screening only and was not confirmed. These findings expand the known geographic distribution of Ca. R. andeanae and provide molecular evidence of its circulation in ticks collected from both wild and domestic canids in northeastern Argentina. Our results highlight the importance of these hosts as sentinels for tick-borne pathogens and underscore the need for integrated One Health surveillance to better anticipate emerging potential risks in interface areas.

Hospital wastewater-based antimicrobial resistance epidemiology: a scoping review.
INTRODUCTION: Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) offers pooled biological samples of defined populations, complementing clinical surveillance for infectious diseases. Hospitals are hotspots for antimicrobial resistance (AMR). We performed a scoping review assessing hospital wastewater for AMR monitoring. METHODS: We searched Medline, Embase, Biosis, Web of Science, and biorxiv.org from inception to May 5, 2026, for studies using hospital wastewater to monitor AMR. The primary outcome was AMR detection and concordance with traditional surveillance. Concordance was reported by resistance class, and reported as strain- or gene-level, as discordant, or as not assessed. Secondary outcomes included sampling methods, and laboratory techniques. RESULTS: Of 4,695 screened studies, 36 from 22 countries met inclusion criteria (high-income 53%, upper-middle-income 42%, and lower-middle-income 5%). Traditional surveillance used mostly routine diagnostics (58%); only 39% of studies aligned temporally with wastewater sampling. Extended-Spectrum Beta-Lactamase-producing organisms showed strain-level concordance in 2/6 studies, and gene-level concordance in 4/6; carbapenem resistance showed strain-level concordance in 2/9 and gene-level concordance in 4/9. Concordance was present for vancomycin-resistant enterococci (2/3), while inconsistent for Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (0/2) and Candida auris (1/2). One study quantified correlation statistically, finding strong association (Spearman's rho = .88). Wastewater sampling methods included grab sampling (39%), composite sampling (36%), and was unreported (25%). Most studies combined culture-based (89%) and molecular methods (PCR 75%, WGS 42%, metagenomics 17%), mostly targeting Gram-negatives (83%). CONCLUSION: Hospital WBE showed variable concordance with traditional surveillance, but methodological heterogeneity and limited temporal alignment constrain comparisons. Standardized frameworks and patient-level studies, particularly from low- and middle-income countries, are needed.

Māori notified with tuberculosis in one public health region of Aotearoa New Zealand: a document review.
AIM: Among Aotearoa New Zealand-born people with tuberculosis (TB), half are Māori. TB is preventable, and Aotearoa New Zealand has signed up to the global strategy to end the TB epidemic. TB among Māori has endured since the late 1800s and occurs in a complex political, social and wellbeing context. We aimed to review current public health practices used for contacting and following up Māori with TB and their contacts. METHODS: We undertook a retrospective case review of Māori notified with pulmonary TB (2018- 2023) in the Waikato Region. Data included TB notification, treatment start and end dates, number and type of contacts, latent TB infection (LTBI) testing, screening and support for wellbeing issues. RESULTS: Seventeen Māori were identified with pulmonary TB (aged 23-81 years). Sixteen started and 13 completed treatment. One died prior to formal TB notification; two died during treatment. A total of 182 contacts were identified-mostly household contacts (42%) and hospital staff (25%). Sixty-four percent (n=117) of contacts were screened for LTBI: 15 (11%) tested positive and were referred for follow-up. Health navigator support was noted for two patients only. CONCLUSION: A new model of care is required for contacting and following up Māori with TB and their contacts to end the Māori TB epidemic.

Epidemiology and social factors of malaria in the Yanomami Indigenous Territory: a critical review of the challenges of control and elimination.
Malaria in the Yanomami Indigenous Territory (YIT) constitutes a serious public health concern and has been hyperendemic since 1987, following the arrival of illegal gold miners in the area. Disease transmission has steadily increased since 2013, particularly among children. It escalated into a crisis in 2019, driven by the intensification of illegal mining and environmental, sociocultural, and political factors, and reached approximately 33,000 cases in 2024. Although the declaration of a Public Health Emergency in 2023 led to advancements in surveillance and diagnosis, the incidence of cases remains elevated. Nevertheless, there was a remarkable reduction in malaria-related mortality, evidenced by a 42% decrease in deaths and a 47% decline in the case-fatality rate, even in the context of persistently high notification rates. Barriers to control include limited access to remote communities, ecological degradation that favours vector proliferation, a high prevalence of submicroscopic infections, and sociocultural constraints. Expanded diagnostic capacity and a reinforced workforce are essential but insufficient without addressing the underlying structural causes. This mini-review summarises and critically discusses the epidemiological trends of malaria in YIT, as well as the social, environmental, cultural, and operational factors that sustain transmission.

A Case of Neurohistoplasmosis Successfully Treated With Single High-Dose Liposomal Amphotericin B.
Disseminated histoplasmosis is a leading AIDS-related opportunistic mycosis and carries high mortality risk. A simplified induction strategy using single high-dose of liposomal amphotericin B (L-AmB) has shown promise for disseminated disease, but persons with central nervous system (CNS) involvement were excluded from the clinical trial. We describe a 35-year-old man with advanced HIV disease (CD4 24 cells/µL) and a high fungal burden who was diagnosed with disseminated histoplasmosis and, subsequently, culture-confirmed CNS involvement. He was administratively withdrawn from the trial when CNS involvement was noted. He was treated within a randomized trial with a single 10 mg/kg dose of L-AmB, followed by antiretroviral therapy (ART) and itraconazole consolidation therapy, with full clinical recovery, normalization of cerebrospinal fluid biochemistry findings, and microbiological clearance. This suggests that a single high-dose L-AmB induction strategy, combined with effective ART and azole consolidation therapy, may be viable in selected patients with CNS involvement.

Chronic Wasting Disease Exposure Risk to Male Cervids During the Mating Season in A Multi-Host Community.
Multi-host infectious diseases present myriad challenges to wildlife managers due to variation in spatial overlap, contact rates, and host competence that complicate understanding of exposure risk and transmission dynamics. These challenges are present in cervid systems impacted by chronic wasting disease (CWD), where CWD prevalence tends to be highest in male cervids. This study focuses on male cervids during the mating season in a multi-host system where CWD is enzootic. We used wildlife camera traps placed at two types of potential local infectious zones-water tanks and scrape sites-and reference sites to measure spatial overlap and duration of contact behaviors for three susceptible cervid species: mule deer (Odocoileus hemionus); white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus); and elk (Cervus canadensis). For each species, we evaluated differences in intraspecific, interspecific, and total environmental exposure risk, along with direct exposure risk, at each site type. We also explored how varied assumptions of host competence across species affected interspecific exposure risk. For mule deer and white-tailed deer, interspecific environmental exposure risk was 100 and 6 times higher at local infectious zones than at reference sites, and exclusively occurred at water tanks for elk. Interspecific environmental exposure risk occurred entirely at local infectious zones, but the proportion of total risk attributed to intraspecific vs. interspecific contributions depended greatly on whether we considered mule deer and elk to have equal host competence or used prevalence within a species as a proxy for variable host competence. Mule deer engaged in direct contact behaviors for similar durations across all site types, with no significant differences in direct exposure risk across sites. Our study highlights the potential central role of mule deer in multi-host cervid communities impacted by diseases transmitted horizontally such as CWD, and provides insight for CWD surveillance and management during a period of particularly high male-male contact that is relevant to CWD epidemiology.

Inferring Geographic Origin of White-Tailed Deer (Odocoileus virginianus) Using Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms in a Region Experiencing Long-Term Effects of Chronic Wasting Disease.
Chronic wasting disease (CWD) is a contagious, 100% fatal disease affecting North American cervids. White-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) is the most abundant host, and movements of this species, either natural or human-mediated, have been considered primary drivers of CWD spread. Inferring the geographic origin of CWD-positive individuals can help identify source-sink dynamics of disease spread and anthropogenic translocation of carcasses. We explored two approaches to infer origin of wild white-tailed deer: (1) a combination of genetic structure inference and categorical assignment tests, and (2) continuous assignment methods (SPA and LOCATOR) to infer coordinates of origin, based on comparisons between test and reference genotypes. We analyzed 1749 samples genotyped using a recently developed single nucleotide polymorphism panel, retaining > 63,000 markers. Genetic structure analyses identified four, five, or ten clusters, with barriers to gene flow that were consistent between the different analyses and explainable by landscape features. We used the ten-cluster configuration to perform categorical assignment tests, but these tests showed low-moderate performance (assignment accuracy ranged between 41% and 100% among clusters, average was 71%). SPA produced a high level of inaccuracy in inferred origins. In contrast, LOCATOR assigned most individuals (82%) to an origin < 50 km from their sampling coordinates. Given the species' life history traits (e.g., vagility, overlapping generations, polygamy), this level of accuracy suggests that continuous assignment tests may be a valuable tool for wildlife managers. Additionally, the inferred genetic structure can inform the delineation of management units, with implications for population control and mitigation of contagious diseases.

Over-dispersion in malaria-schistosoma co-infection: insights from a meta-analytical approach and systematic review.
BACKGROUND: Malaria and schistosomiasis are two major parasitic diseases that are co-endemic in many regions of sub-Saharan Africa. Despite their frequent geographical overlap, the potential epidemiological patterns and potential interactions associated with Plasmodium--Schistosoma co-infection remain poorly characterized. This study aimed to systematically assess the epidemiology of malaria-schistosomiasis co-infection and to quantify whether co-infections occur more frequently than expected under an assumption of independence between the two infections. METHODS: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. A total of 192 studies published between 1996 and 2023 were included in the qualitative synthesis, of which 59 studies involving 73,383 individuals were included in the meta-analysis. Pooled odds ratio (ORs) were estimated to compare observed and expected co-infection prevalence. RESULTS: The pooled analysis showed that Plasmodium-Schistosoma co-infection occurs more frequently than expected by chance (overall OR = 1.20, 95% CI 1.02-1.40), despite substantial heterogeneity across studies (I2 = 89%). Reported co-infection prevalence ranged from 1.1% in Benin to 36.6% in Mali. School-age children and pregnant women were disproportionately affected. Subgroup analyses revealed no consistent differences according to sex or parasite species. CONCLUSIONS: These findings indicate a non-random distribution of malaria-schistosomiasis co-infection in sub-Saharan Africa, consistent with epidemiological over-dispersion. Although the underlying biological and immunological mechanisms remain uncertain, the widespread co-occurrence of these parasites highlights the importance of integrated surveillance and control strategies that account for polyparasitism in endemic settings.

Risk factors of imported malaria in Bhutan: A retrospective analysis (2013-2024).
BACKGROUND: Bhutan's malaria elimination is constrained by imported malaria. Hence, this study aimed to quantify the risk factors of imported malaria in Bhutan. METHODS: Individual malaria data for the period 2013 - 2024 were obtained from the Bhutan National Malaria Control Programme. Seasonal trend decomposition and hotspot analysis were conducted to explore trends and high-risk areas of imported malaria. Multivariable Bayesian logistic regression was used to quantify risk factors of imported malaria. RESULTS: Imported malaria made up 81% (563/693) of total cases and 61.8% (348) originated from India. Imported malaria did not show significant trend; however, hotspots were observed in major points of entry, in the capital city, and at hydropower projects sites. Malaria cases recorded after 2018 were eight times (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] = 8.0 (95% credible interval [CrI] 4.9 - 13.0) more at odds of being imported than those reported before 2018. Districts without borders with India had higher odds of reporting imported malaria (AOR 4.4, 95% CrI 1.2 - 24.7) compared to districts sharing a border with India. Labourers (AOR = 38.1; 95% CrI 10.5 - 187.1) and military personnel (AOR = 5.0; 95% CrI 1.5 - 20.3) were 38 and five times more likely of being imported malaria compared to public servants. CONCLUSION: The imported malaria poses significant threat to national elimination plan. The interior non-border districts, migrant labourers and security force personnels were significantly associated with increased odds of imported malaria. Therefore, surveillance and response strategies should be targeted to these hotspots and hotpops to reduce importation risks and sustain malaria-free status.

Allergic bronchopulmonary mycosis associated with Talaromyces boninensis: A case report.
Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is a chronic inflammatory pulmonary disorder characterized by type I and III hypersensitivity reactions to Aspergillus fumigatus in the airways of patients with asthma or cystic fibrosis. However, other filamentous fungi can cause similar pathophysiological changes, a condition referred to as allergic bronchopulmonary mycosis (ABPM). Data on ABPM involving non-Aspergillus fungi remain limited. To the best of our knowledge, we present the first case of ABPM associated with Talaromyces boninensis. The patient met the diagnostic criteria proposed by the Japan ABPM Research Program, and T. boninensis was isolated from bronchial lavage fluid and identified by molecular analysis.

Evaluation of Active Surveillance Testing for Candidozyma (Candida) auris and Impact on Infection Control Behaviors in an Acute Healthcare System.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the impact of active surveillance testing (AST) for Candidozyma auris on healthcare system epidemiologic trends and infection prevention and control (IPC) behaviors. DESIGN: Explanatory sequential mixed methods study using retrospective electronic medical record review, hand hygiene observations, and healthcare personnel focus groups. SETTING AND PATIENTS: Five acute care hospitals within a suburban healthcare system. Chart reviews included 3,688 patients who underwent AST for C. auris or had positive clinical cultures for C. auris from 2020-2023. METHODS: Incidence and prevalence were calculated by year and location. Logistic regression examined associations with C. auris events. Observations and focus groups explored barriers and facilitators to IPC behaviors. RESULTS: AST volume increased from 66 tests in 2020 to 1,619 in 2023, while positivity decreased from 7.58% to 2.47%.
