Concurrent increases in community-onset and hospital-onset prevalence were observed over time. Focus groups identified barriers including fatigue and accountability, and facilitators including role modeling and supply accessibility. CONCLUSIONS: AST facilitated early identification of colonized or infected patients and supported systemic surveillance of C. auris, while behavioral assessment identified opportunities to strengthen adherence to core IPC practices. These findings demonstrate the value of integrating epidemiologic and behavioral evaluation when assessing IPC programs.

Novel EG95-based mRNA vaccines induce long-term protective immunity against echinococcosis.
Cystic echinococcosis (CE), a neglected zoonotic disease caused by Echinococcus granulosus sensu lato, remains a significant public health and veterinary concern worldwide. Despite efforts to develop recombinant protein-based vaccines against EG95, a key protective antigen, existing platforms suffer from limited immunogenicity, short-lived immunity, and complex production processes. Here, we designed and evaluated three novel mRNA-LNP vaccines, including EG95 mRNA-LNP vaccine, IL-4-EG95 mRNA-LNP vaccine encoding EG95 fused with IL-4 via a flexible linker to enhance immune stimulation, and EG95-EC95 mRNA-LNP vaccine that multivalent formulation incorporating EC95 antigens from Echinococcus canadensis. The vaccine candidates were efficiently encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles and demonstrated robust target expression in vitro and in vivo. Immunization induced significantly stronger, more durable humoral and cellular immune responses compared to a commercial EG95 subunit vaccine both in mice and lambs. Notably, high levels of specific antibodies persisted for over 12 months post-vaccination. Parasites infection challenge experiments confirmed that these three mRNA-LNP vaccines, especially the IL-4-EG95 vaccine conferred superior protection, inhibited protoscolex survival and cyst growth. These results highlight the advantages of mRNA-based vaccines in safety, scalability, and flexibility over conventional approaches, offering a promising strategy for controlling E. granulosus sensu lato transmission and reducing the zoonotic burden of CE.

Outdoor attractive targeted sugar bait Phase III trials for malaria control in Kenya, Mali, and Zambia: An individual participant data meta-analysis.
Attractive targeted sugar baits (ATSB) are a potential new class of vector control tool that act through an "attract and kill" mechanism on mosquitoes. We conducted a meta-analysis using data from three large-scale Phase III trials of the Westham Sarabi v1.2 ATSB (0.11% dinotefuran) conducted in Kenya, Mali, and Zambia, to determine the effect of the intervention on clinical malaria incidence in children, Plasmodium falciparum infection prevalence, and dominant vector species parity, abundance, landing rate, and sporozoite positivity. The Sarabi ATSB was deployed on exterior walls at the rate of two per residential structure. Aggregated and individual-level meta-analyses were completed for each of the six trial outcomes, comprising 6981 person-years of follow-up for clinical malaria incidence (primary epidemiological outcome) and 19443 Anopheles for parity assessment (primary entomological outcome). Post-hoc analyses included assessment of dose-response relationships between coverage-adjusted intervention density and clinical malaria incidence. There were no statistically significant differences between arms in any of the epidemiological or entomological outcomes. There was statistically significant evidence of a 19% reduction in clinical malaria incidence for every 10 bait stations per hectare increase observed in spatial density (IRR 0.81, 95% CI 0.74-0.89, p < 0.001), provided that the ATSB were in good condition. This finding suggests that there may be deployment approaches or dosing strategies under which ATSB tools could be efficacious, although threshold spatial densities could not be determined from available data. This meta-analysis furthermore highlights important recommendations for future cluster-randomized trials of vector control interventions, including conducting comprehensive baseline data collection to identify cluster outliers or sites with differences in vector bionomics, and collecting a limited set of entomological outcomes in all trial clusters to ensure an adequately powered and balanced analysis of entomological effects.

Development and effectiveness test of an internet-based real-time monitoring device for malaria parasite vector mosquitoes.
BACKGROUND: Malaria remains a major global health threat, and effective vector surveillance is essential for timely vector control. However, surveillance systems are challenged by behavioral shifts in Anopheles mosquitoes, labor-intensive procedures, and delays in real-time data transmission. Existing electronic monitoring tools often suffer from low sensitivity and specificity, creating an urgent need for automated, high-precision alternatives. METHODS: We developed the "Black Box," a 3D-printed, internet-enabled device integrating multispectral light, thermal simulation, chemical attractants, and photocatalytic materials with automated counting and wireless data transmission. Laboratory trials demonstrated trapping rates of 94.00%-95.00% for Anopheles sinensis, An. stephensi, and An. anthropophagus, with data consistency exceeding 97.00%. Semi-field tests yielded trapping rates of 73.60%-90.80% and consistency above 92.00%. In field deployments, the device captured 5,109 mosquitoes with a 94.17% consistency rate and captured more Anopheles than the light trap during the field observation period. Real-time data revealed distinct bimodal activity peaks at dawn and dusk. Among the 112 field-captured female An. sinensis, 21 (18.75%; exact 95% CI, 12.60%-26.97%) were blood-fed, indicating that blood-fed mosquitoes may occur in outdoor collections. CONCLUSIONS: The Black Box provides a highly efficient, automated solution for real-time malaria vector surveillance. By delivering accurate, timely ecological data, it supports dynamic risk assessment and enables targeted interventions, addressing key limitations of current control programs.

Social determinants of partner and non-partner sexual violence against women in Chile: a population-based multilevel analysis.
BACKGROUND: Sexual violence against women is a major public health problem in Latin America, yet evidence on its social determinants is scarce and often conflates partner and non-partner forms. We characterised determinants of intimate partner sexual violence (IPSV), non-partner sexual assault (NPSA), and non-partner sexual harassment (NPSH) in Chile and compared their risk profiles. METHODS: We analysed pooled 2017 and 2020 rounds of the Chilean National Survey on Violence in the Family and Other Settings, representative of urban women aged 15 years or older; fieldwork preceded Chile's first COVID-19 case. We fitted multilevel logistic regression for past-year outcomes, women nested in municipalities. FINDINGS: The sample comprised 13,128 women (8335 for IPSV models). Past-year prevalence was 2.8% (95% confidence interval [CI] 2.4-3.3) for IPSV, 2.5% (2.1-3.0) for NPSA, and 11.3% (10.4-12.3) for NPSH. IPSV was associated with relational factors: dominant relationship (adjusted odds ratio [OR] 6.40, 4.68-8.76) and partner violence elsewhere (2.79, 1.75-4.43); between-municipality variance was negligible. NPSA and NPSH concentrated in younger women and the Metropolitan Region (OR 2.92 [2.00-4.28] and 2.29 [1.77-2.96]); both were associated with social participation (1.49 [1.11-2.00] and 1.26 [1.09-1.46]). Childhood sexual abuse was associated with all three (OR 2.05 [1.45-2.89], 3.03 [2.20-4.20], and 2.06 [1.72-2.46]). Reported non-partner victimisation rose between 2017 and 2020, pre-pandemic. INTERPRETATION: Risk profiles differed: relational and life-course for IPSV, age-graded and metropolitan for NPSA and NPSH; childhood sexual abuse was common to all three, supporting trauma-informed responses. FUNDING: Agencia Nacional de Investigación y Desarrollo, Chile (Doctoral Scholarship 21212141).

What you saw was what you got? Correcting reported incidence data for testing intensity.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, non-pharmaceutical interventions were employed to limit the spread of the SARS-CoV-2 virus. In some countries, this included large-scale voluntary testing of non-symptomatic individuals to gauge the prevalence in the general population and to identify asymptomatic and pre-symptomatic infections in order to reduce disease spread. Differences between the intensity of testing means that comparing case-counts across borders may be deceptive. In this work, we use mathematical modeling to investigate the dynamics of both observed and unobserved infections as a function of the rate of voluntary testing. The model indicates that increasing the rate of testing causes the number of observed cases to increase, despite a decrease in prevalence due to testing. For large testing rates, the observed case-counts also decrease. The non-monotonicity of the observed cases explains some discrepancies seen when comparing uncorrected case-counts between countries. One such example was observed during the winter 2020/2021 COVID-19 epidemics in Denmark and Hungary, where reported case-counts were comparable, despite differences in prevalence. We determine a quantitative measure for the ascertainment ratio between observed cases and all infections, allowing for test-intensity correction of case-counts. This measure allows us to correct case-counts for testing intensity during the winter 2021/2022 epidemic of the Omicron variant (BA.1 and BA.2) in Denmark, showing good agreement with results from serology-studies. While the model does not capture the full complexity of epidemic dynamics, it provides a simple way to correct case-counts for differences in testing, simplifying comparison across international borders and testing activities.

Pathogen and Testing Profiles in Post-Infectious Irritable Bowel Syndrome Across the COVID-19 Public Health Emergency: A Retrospective Case Series.
Background/Objectives: The COVID-19 public health emergency altered enteric infection surveillance, diagnostic testing, and antibiotic prescribing. We compared pathogen/testing composition among post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome (PI-IBS) cases stratified by whether index gastroenteritis occurred before, during, or after the emergency. Methods: This single-centre retrospective case series included 138 adults with clinician-diagnosed PI-IBS classified as Rome IV-compatible by chart adjudication. Index gastroenteritis occurred from January 2019 to December 2024; existing clinical records were reviewed retrospectively. The primary comparison was a five-category pathogen/testing profile. Results: The profile differed across pre-pandemic (n = 30), pandemic (n = 39), and post-emergency (n = 69) periods (χ2 = 35.56, p < 0.001; Cramér V = 0.36, 95% CI 0.30-0.48). Bacterial/protozoal cases represented 63.3%, 7.7%, and 33.3%, respectively; SARS-CoV-2-associated cases represented 0%, 35.9%, and 13.0%. Antibiotic exposure was 56.7%, 12.8%, and 33.3%. In an exploratory adjusted model, confirmed enteric pathogens were associated with antibiotic exposure (OR 16.28, 95% CI 3.03-87.35), whereas period was not. Sensitivity analyses excluding SARS-CoV-2 cases and period-crossing diagnoses were concordant. Conclusions: Pathogen/testing and antibiotic-exposure profiles differed across periods among diagnosed PI-IBS cases. These data describe case composition, not incidence or causal risk, and cannot separate infection ecology from diagnostic behaviour.

Factors Associated with Depressive Symptoms Among Korean Young Adults by Sex in the Third Year of the COVID-19 Pandemic.
Background/Objectives: This study analyzed factors associated with depressive symptoms by sex among Korean young adults in the third year of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic. Methods: The subjects of this secondary data analysis were 47,353 young adults (23,407 men and 23,946 women) aged 19-39 years from the nationwide 2022 Community Health Survey. Depressive symptoms were defined as a Patient Health Questionnaire-9 score ≥ 6. Complex sample multiple logistic regression analyses were performed for the total sample (adjusted for sex) and separately for men and women. Results: The proportion of participants with depressive symptoms was 16.3% in women and 10.1% in men, and women had higher odds of depressive symptoms than men (adjusted odds ratio = 1.89, 95% confidence interval: 1.72-2.07). In both sexes, high subjective stress, poor subjective health status, short or long sleep duration, perceiving oneself as obese, living alone, low household income, and smoking were associated with depressive symptoms, whereas a higher body mass index (obesity in men and overweight in women) was associated with lower odds. Lower education; being separated, widowed, or divorced; having no occupation; and perceiving oneself as skinny were associated with depressive symptoms only in men, whereas binge drinking was associated with depressive symptoms only in women. Conclusions: Korean young adults showed both common and sex-specific correlates of depressive symptoms in 2022. Screening and intervention programs for depressive symptoms in young adults may need to consider psychological stress, sleep, and economic and household conditions, as well as sex differences.

Mandatory reporting of healthcare-associated infections: a global comparative policy analysis using Kingdon's multiple streams framework.
BACKGROUND: Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) impose a substantial burden on healthcare systems worldwide. Despite strong evidence of their impact and preventability, national infection prevention and control (IPC) surveillance systems remain inconsistently implemented. In contrast, the COVID-19 pandemic catalyzed rapid surveillance reforms, highlighting policy conditions that facilitate surveillance-based IPC strategies. OBJECTIVE: To examine policy factors influencing the implementation of national HAI surveillance and compare the policy window created during COVID-19 with the more limited political attention devoted to HAI surveillance. METHODS: A qualitative comparative policy analysis was conducted using Kingdon's Multiple Streams Framework. World Health Organization policy documents, peer-reviewed literature, reports from international public health organizations, and selected national policy documents were synthesized to examine how the problem, policy, and political streams influenced the implementation of HAI surveillance. RESULTS: The problem stream was well established, with extensive evidence of the burden of HAIs. The policy stream was similarly well developed through established surveillance frameworks, whose feasibility was demonstrated during the COVID-19 pandemic. In contrast, the political stream remained comparatively weak, characterized by fragmented political commitment, inconsistent legal mandates, limited public visibility, and variable implementation across countries. Consequently, convergence of the three streams required to sustain a policy window for HAI surveillance remained incomplete. CONCLUSION: The principal barrier to national HAI surveillance is insufficient alignment of the problem, policy, and political streams rather than a lack of evidence or technical solutions. Strengthening political commitment through legal mandates, sustained investment, governance, and advocacy is essential to institutionalize surveillance systems and strengthen long-term IPC.

Prioritizing Risk Factors for Nosocomial COVID-19 Infection in a Taiwanese Hospital: An Integrated DEMATEL-ANP-IPA Approach.
OBJECTIVE: During the COVID-19 pandemic, the rapid influx of patients with undiagnosed or confirmed infection increased the risk of healthcare-associated transmission and nosocomial infection. Identifying and prioritizing risk factors is essential for strengthening infection prevention and supporting hospital risk management and resource allocation. This exploratory study aimed to prioritize factors associated with nosocomial COVID-19 infection from an expert-based perspective. METHODS: An integrated multicriteria decision-making (MCDM) framework combining the decision-making trial and evaluation laboratory (DEMATEL), analytic network process (ANP), and importance-performance analysis (IPA) was used to examine the relative importance, interrelationships, and intervention priorities of risk factors. Eight experts from five hospitals in Taiwan participated in the assessment. One hospital in Taipei City was selected as the case hospital for exploratory evaluation and prioritization. RESULTS: "Lack of hospital protective equipment" and "Superspreading event" were identified as the most influential attributes, while "Patients with high viral load" and "Close contact" were the key risk factors associated with nosocomial COVID-19 infection. The integrated MCDM analysis also revealed interrelationships among risk factors and identified priorities of risk factors of infection-control intervention for the case hospital. CONCLUSION: The case hospital should prioritize adequate hospital facilities and infection risks associated with patients with chronic diseases when developing nosocomial infection prevention strategies. The proposed framework may support hospital risk assessment, infection-control planning, and resource allocation during infectious disease outbreaks. Given the exploratory and single-hospital design, the findings should be validated in other hospital settings.

[Preparedness for summer illnesses and emergencies in Chile, 2024-2025: lessons from an innovative policyPreparação para doenças e emergências no verão de 2024-2025 no Chile: lições de uma política inovadora].
Climate change and the increasing frequency of extreme heat events have heightened the importance of health issues during the summer season. This season is also associated with greater population mobility, outdoor recreational activities, and exposure to biological and environmental risks, all of which require coordinated responses from health systems. Within this context, the Ministry of Health of Chile implemented the summer seasonal illness and emergency preparedness plan 2024-2025, with the goal of strengthening surveillance, intersectoral coordination, and risk communication in response to priority threats to population health.This article describes the design, implementation, and key results of this first national initiative to prepare for diseases occurring during the summer season. The strategy was based on a multilevel governance model that liaised between the central, regional, and local levels of the health system through national coordination meetings, integrated surveillance, strengthening of technical capacities, and public communications. During the season covered by the plan, detection of Aedes aegypti remained confined to areas where it was previously known to occur; 395 outbreaks of foodborne illnesses affecting 2618 people were investigated; 8 cases of hantavirus were reported, with no deaths; and environmental risks and emergencies were monitored, including 4330 forest fires, none of which affected health facilities.This experience demonstrates the feasibility of implementing integrated disease preparedness strategies during the summer season and provides lessons for their consolidation as public policy, including the formalization of coordination mechanisms, the systematic assessment of implementation, and the incorporation of new hazards, such as drowning and injuries associated with recreational water activities.

[Sociodemographic factors associated with yellow fever mortality in Colombia, 2024-2026Fatores sociodemográficos associados à letalidade por febre amarela na Colômbia, 2024-2026].
OBJECTIVE: To analyze the sociodemographic factors associated with case fatality rates for yellow fever in Colombia between January 2024 and January 2026. METHODS: A retrospective observational analytical cohort study was conducted based on records from the national public health surveillance system (Sivigila). Probable and confirmed cases of yellow fever reported between 1 January 2024 and 31 January 2026 were included. Quantitative variables were described using the median and interquartile range, and categorical variables using absolute and relative frequencies. Cumulative survival was estimated using Kaplan-Meier curves, and factors associated with case fatality were evaluated using Cox proportional hazards models. RESULTS: A total of 164 cases were included, with a predominance of men and a median age of 45 years. There were 70 deaths attributable to yellow fever, with a case fatality rate of 42.7%, showing a marked geographical concentration in the department of Tolima and a higher incidence among men, older adults, and people involved in agricultural and livestock activities. Age over 60 years was associated with a higher risk of death (adjusted HR = 5.45; CI 95%: 1.13-26.2.). CONCLUSIONS: Yellow fever had a high case-fatality rate among cases reported as probable and confirmed in Colombia, in particular among older adults. The findings support the need to strengthen vaccination strategies, epidemiological surveillance, and early detection in areas with active virus circulation.

Post-Dengue Deep Vein Thrombosis Complicated by Pulmonary Embolism: A Case Report.
Dengue fever is commonly associated with bleeding complications, particularly in patients with thrombocytopenia. However, thrombotic events, such as venous thromboembolism, are rare and under-recognized manifestations, particularly during the recovery phase, posing diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. We report the case of a 25-year-old previously healthy male who presented with high-grade fever, myalgia, and headache and was diagnosed with dengue fever based on positive NS1 antigen testing. Dengue infection was confirmed by a positive NS1 antigen test performed on Day 3 of illness, consistent with early acute dengue infection. The diagnosis was further supported by the patient's clinical presentation, including high-grade fever, myalgia, and headache in the appropriate epidemiological context of a dengue-endemic region. During the recovery phase of the illness, he developed painful swelling of the right lower limb and progressive dyspnea. Investigations revealed markedly elevated D-dimer levels, right lower limb deep vein thrombosis on Doppler ultrasound, and bilateral pulmonary emboli with right ventricular strain on CT pulmonary angiography images. Although dengue-associated thrombosis has been reported in the setting of thrombocytopenia, as described by Ghatak et al., the present case demonstrates that thrombotic complications may also occur despite preserved platelet counts, highlighting the potential contribution of endothelial dysfunction and inflammatory activation. This case highlights the paradoxical coexistence of thrombosis and bleeding risk in dengue fever. To avoid potentially fatal thromboembolic complications in patients with dengue, early diagnosis, prompt anticoagulation, and a high index of suspicion are crucial.

Laboratory-based trends in dengue and other arboviruses in the Caribbean: Analysis of surveillance data, 2018-2024.
OBJECTIVE: To describe laboratory-based patterns of arboviral circulation, including serotype distribution and temporal trends, and their contribution to regional situational awareness in the Caribbean. METHODS: This was a retrospective analysis using clinical samples submitted to the Caribbean Public Health Agency Medical Microbiology Laboratory for suspected arboviral infection. Samples were tested using Trioplex real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction and immunoglobulin M and G enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Data were analyzed by virus type, serotype, age group, sex, and seasonality. Statistical associations were assessed using Pearson's chi-square tests. Because the dataset is based on submitted samples, findings are presented as proportions among tested samples rather than population-level estimates. RESULTS: Dengue virus (DENV) accounted for the largest proportion of confirmed arboviral infections (34.7%) among tested samples, with DENV-3 as the most frequently detected serotype (65.5%), followed by DENV-2 (26.8%), DENV-1 (4.3%), and DENV-4 (0.17%). Significant associations were observed between serotype and age group (χ² = 201.88; P < 0.001) and sex (χ² = 22.15; P = 0.036). Seasonal peaks were observed primarily between August and November, although an atypical increase in early 2024 was noted. Chikungunya (0.2%) and Zika (0.1%) viruses were infrequently detected. CONCLUSIONS: In this retrospective analysis, DENV was the most frequently detected arbovirus among tested samples in the Caribbean, with dynamic serotype distribution and marked seasonal variability. These findings highlight the value of laboratory-based surveillance in strengthening regional situational awareness and informing public health responses, while recognizing limitations related to representativeness and the absence of population denominators.

Rethinking Clinical Trial Design to Accelerate Therapeutics for Arboviral Epidemics.
Arboviral diseases represent an escalating global health threat, yet therapeutic development has been markedly slower than for other viral illnesses. Key barriers include the unpredictability and variability of arbovirus transmission, which complicate site selection, limit recruitment, and increase delays and the risk of inconclusive trials. Additional challenges include maintaining trial-ready sites, recruitment within the narrow therapeutic window, ensuring rapid diagnostics, and including high-risk groups. To address these barriers, we propose several innovative strategies based on a Clinical Experts meeting convened by the Dengue Alliance. These include pre-activated trial networks for rapid initiation during outbreaks; early-warning surveillance to guide geographic activation using real-time transmission signals; decentralized trial models to expand recruitment beyond major research centers; platform trial designs that allow treatment arms to be added or discontinued adaptively; and participant inclusion based on clinical syndrome supported by rapid diagnostics. Their successful adoption requires regulatory harmonization, ethical oversight, and emphasis on equity.

Neutralizing antibody evidence of dengue and chikungunya virus exposure in macaques from an urban-forest fringe in Peninsular Malaysia.
Arboviruses such as dengue virus (DENV), chikungunya virus (CHIKV), Zika virus (ZIKV), and Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) circulate between mosquito vectors and vertebrate hosts, with non-human primates (NHPs) playing an important role in sylvatic transmission cycles. In Malaysia, frequent interactions between long-tailed macaques (Macaca fascicularis) and humans at the Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia (UKM) Bangi campus provide an opportunity to investigate arbovirus exposure at the human-wildlife interface. Forty free-ranging macaques were sampled from five locations within the UKM Bangi campus. Serum samples were screened for neutralizing antibodies against DENV, CHIKV, ZIKV, and JEV using the 90% focus reduction neutralization test (FRNT90), while whole blood was tested for viral RNA by RT-qPCR. Seventeen macaques (42.5%) had neutralizing antibodies, indicating previous arbovirus exposure. Specifically, 16 (40.0%) had neutralizing antibodies against DENV and one (2.5%) against CHIKV. Neutralizing antibodies against DENV-1, DENV-2, and DENV-3 were detected, whereas DENV-4, ZIKV, and JEV antibodies were not detected. No viral RNA was identified in any sample. To our knowledge, this is the first study in Malaysia to investigate arbovirus exposure in free-ranging macaques using FRNT90 neutralizing antibody assays. These findings provide updated evidence of DENV and CHIKV exposure in macaques at the human-wildlife interface and highlight the need for integrated longitudinal surveillance of NHPs, mosquito vectors, and humans to better understand arbovirus ecology and transmission dynamics.

Filovirus reactive antibodies in wildlife hunting communities suggest ongoing zoonotic spillover in forested Guinea.
Forested Guinea has been the site of multiple high-consequence viral spillover events, including the index case of the 2013-16 West African Ebola epidemic. Deforestation and wildlife hunting rapidly expand the human-animal interface, increasing opportunities for transmission. Here we integrate serologic, spatial and questionnaire data to characterize zoonotic filovirus spillover events and risk factors amongst wildlife hunter communities in Forested Guinea. Hunters and close contacts from 43 villages in 2017 (n = 511) and 2023 (n = 648) were screened using a multiplex microsphere-based immunoassay panel of 9 filoviruses, identifying IgG binding against Ebola virus (EBOV) in 57/1159 individuals (4.9%), as well as species-specific binding against Bundibugyo (BDBV) (49/1159, 4.2%), Taï Forest (TAFV) (13/1159, 1.1%), Reston (4/1159, 0.3%), Měnglà (MLAV) (8/1159, 0.7%), Lloviu (LLOV) (8/1159, 0.7%) and Bombali (BOMV) (1/1159, 0.1%) viruses. Parallel pseudotyped virus neutralization assays identified species-specific neutralization of EBOV, BDBV and TAFV, as well as likely cross-neutralization of BOMV, LLOV and MLAV, suggesting multiple zoonotic virus spillover events. Mixed-effects regression analyses of satellite-derived land-cover data identified environmental risk factors (including forest fragmentation) reflecting potential pathways of exposure. Together, our data suggest multiple ongoing zoonotic filovirus spillover events in wildlife hunting communities and highlight the importance of landscape configuration in driving pathogen spillover.

Pre-travel medical consultation patterns among older adults before, during, and after Taiwan's COVID-19 border quarantine period: A repeated cross-sectional study at a medical center.
BACKGROUND/PURPOSE: Older adults encounter increased health risks during international travel due to higher burden of comorbidities. The COVID-19 pandemic further imposed additional challenges on pre-travel risk assessment and preventive care. This study aimed to characterize elderly travelers attending a travel medicine clinic and to examine age-related differences in travel patterns and pre-travel healthcare needs across the COVID-19 pandemic era. METHODS: A retrospective observational study of individuals attending a travel medicine clinic in northern Taiwan was conducted between 2015 and 2024. A total of 50,661 travelers were included and categorized into two age groups: <60 years (n = 45,968) and ≥60 years (n = 4693). De-identified data on demographics, travel destinations, travel purposes, prescribed vaccines and prophylactic medications were obtained from administrative visit records and the National Taiwan University Hospital Integrated Medical Database(NTUH-iMD). RESULTS: Travelers younger than 60 years accounted for most of the clinic attendees (86.0-95.4% annually). Elderly travelers most frequently visited Africa (20.3%) and Central and South America (17.5%), whereas younger travelers predominantly traveled to the United States of America (USA) (40.3%) and Southeast Asia (9.0%). Group package tours (42.3%) and visiting friends and relatives (20.0%) were common among elderly travelers, while education (49.6%) and business travel (19.8%) predominated in the younger group. Yellow fever immunization was most prevalent among elderly travelers (25.7%), whereas hepatitis A vaccination predominated in the younger cohort (15.0%). CONCLUSION: Substantial age-related differences were observed in travel destinations, purposes, and preventive interventions. These findings underscore the importance of age-specific pre-travel consultations.

Design and preliminary analytical evaluation of an in-house primer panel for dengue virus whole-genome sequencing: Evidence from Chhattisgarh, India.
Next-generation sequencing offers higher resolution than targeted gene sequencing for genomic surveillance and phylogenetic analysis of dengue virus (DENV). However, limited availability of commercial whole genome sequencing assays restrict comprehensive DENV genomic analysis. This study thus aimed to design, develop and evaluate an in-house DENV NGS primer panel and workflow, compatible with all four DENV serotypes, to investigate the circulating serotypes and genotypes in Chhattisgarh, India. The in-house primers panels were used to generate library and subsequent sequencing in Illumina MiniSeq using paired-end sequencing. A total of 30 archived DENV positive serum samples confirmed by NS1/Dengue IgM/IgG assay were included to check efficacy of in-house primer panel. Complete genome consensus sequences were successfully obtained for all 30 samples using the in-house DENV NGS primer panel and workflow processed in repetition. Sequencing-based serotyping demonstrated 100% concordance with RT-PCR results, without observing any discrepancies. Phylogenetic analysis revealed the circulation of DENV-1 (n = 1, 3.3%), DENV-2 (n = 23, 76.6%), and DENV-3 (n = 6, 20.0%) in Chhattisgarh. Notably, DENV-2 strains exhibited 20 distinct amino acid substitutions in the E protein, indicating potential genetic diversity within circulating strains. The docking analysis suggests that mutations within the DENV-2 E protein may induce structural changes capable of modulating interaction with DC-SIGN. The developed in-house DENV WGS primer panel provides a cost-effective, high-resolution approach enabling comprehensive genomic surveillance, mutation analysis, and epidemiological insights in resource-limited settings with reliable sequencing depth and coverage. Mutation-induced structural changes in the E protein alter receptor-binding interfaces and conformation, potentially affecting viral attachment and host-cell entry.

Facilitators and barriers to community-based livestock abortion reporting for Rift Valley Fever surveillance in Uganda: A COM-B analysis.
Rift Valley Fever Disease (RVFD) causes substantial economic losses via livestock abortion storms, yet community-based abortion reporting for early warning remains suboptimal in endemic settings. This study analysed the behavioural determinants of livestock abortion reporting to inform RVF surveillance interventions in Uganda. We conducted a cross-sectional study using qualitative data collection methods in Isingiro District, Uganda, employing the Capability, Opportunity, Motivation-Behaviour (COM-B) framework. We conducted 29 key informant interviews with national/district policymakers and technical officers and 17 focus group discussions involving livestock owners, abattoir operators, and local leaders. Transcripts underwent deductive thematic analysis using NVivo-12, with independent coding verification and member checking. Barriers and facilitators were ranked by frequency and thematic emphasis, and a comparative analysis was conducted across participant groups. The most frequently cited barrier was poor community knowledge about RVF, while the most powerful demotivator was the absence of post-reporting feedback. Key facilitators included mobile phone platforms, community governance structures, and fear of economic and cultural loss. Our study recommends that sustainable abortion reporting requires simultaneous intervention across capability, opportunity, and motivation domains. Priority interventions could include: integrating reporting into Uganda's electronic surveillance platforms, co-developing local RVF names with communities, establishing reliable feedback mechanisms, addressing veterinary staffing gaps in remote areas, and implementing no-blame reporting protocols. Effective RVF surveillance depends on reinforcing existing community structures while ensuring responsive feedback that validates reporters' contributions.

Household representatives' understanding of dengue solutions and larval indices surveillance systems in southern Thailand: A mixed methods study.
BACKGROUND: Dengue fever remains a major public health concern in tropical regions, particularly in Southeast Asia. Effective prevention depends on the community's understanding of both dengue control measures and vector surveillance systems. This study assessed and explored household representatives' understanding of dengue solutions (care and preventive measures) and the Aedes larval index surveillance system in southern Thailand. METHODS: A community-based convergent mixed-methods study was conducted among 824 household representatives selected through stratified random sampling. Quantitative data were collected using a structured questionnaire and analyzed using logistic regression to identify factors associated with understanding. Qualitative data were collected through in-depth interviews with 13 purposively selected participants and analyzed using thematic analysis. Findings were integrated using a joint display approach. RESULTS: Only 28.9% of participants demonstrated a high understanding of the dengue solution, and 1.2% had a high understanding of the larval indices surveillance system. Training attendance (AOR 2.01, 95% CI: 1.45-2.78), fewer water containers (AOR 2.06, 95% CI: 1.20-3.54), and higher larvae-positive containers (AOR 0.64, 95% CI: 0.43-0.97) were significantly associated with lower understanding. Qualitative findings revealed the following key themes: recognition of dengue fever, awareness of preventive practices, risky season, and the importance of training. Training was identified as a key factor in improving understanding and practices. CONCLUSION: Household heads' understanding of dengue prevention is limited, particularly regarding larval surveillance systems. Household representatives were familiar with dengue symptoms; they lacked technical knowledge of surveillance systems. Strengthening community-based training and improving the communication of technical concepts are essential to enhance dengue prevention and control efforts.

Zoonotic arboviruses and associated risk factors in donkeys from northeastern Algeria.
Rift Valley fever virus (RVFV), Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV), and several zoonotic flaviviruses represent an emerging threat to animal and human health. In Algeria, particularly in the northern regions, data on the circulation of these viruses remain limited, especially for RVFV and CCHFV. In this context, we aimed to assess the seroprevalence of these arboviruses among donkeys across three provinces in northeastern Algeria and to identify factors associated with seropositivity. Between 2019 and 2024, 183 serum samples were collected and analyzed by ELISA. Binary logistic regression was used to evaluate potential factors associated with CCHFV and flavivirus seropositivity. The overall seroprevalence was 31.7% (95% CI: 25.0-39.0) for CCHFV, 2.2% (95% CI: 0.6-5.5) for RVFV, and 18.0% (95% CI: 12.8-24.4) for flaviviruses. In the multivariable analyses, age group was significantly associated with both CCHFV and flavivirus seropositivity, while geographic origin, sampling season, and donkey mobility were independently associated only with CCHFV seropositivity. To the best of our knowledge, this study provides the first serological data documenting exposure of donkeys to CCHFV and RVFV in Algeria. These findings provide evidence of prior exposure to these arboviruses in the study area and highlight the importance of integrating donkeys into epidemiological surveillance programs. Further large-scale studies encompassing vectors, animals, and humans are needed to better characterize the epidemiology of these zoonotic pathogens and assess their potential public health impact in Algeria.

Powassan virus LB neuroinvasion and lethality are determined by envelope protein domain III residues.
Powassan viruses (POWVs) are tick-borne orthoflaviviruses that cause lethal encephalitis and long-term neurologic sequelae. POWVs are divided into two lineages that share 86% genetic identity. POWV-LB (Lin I) was isolated from a fatal case of encephalitis, while POWV-LI9 (Lin II) is a tick-derived isolate that causes age-dependent lethality in mice. Domain III of orthoflavivirus envelope proteins (EDIII) directs cell attachment and determines murine neuropathology and lethality. Here, we developed POWV LB reverse genetics, analyzed brains of LB- and recLB mutant-infected mice, and assessed the role of EDIII residues in LB pathogenesis. LB infection of 50-week-old B6 mice focally activated microglia in the midbrain and cerebellum, discrete from and independent of the location of envelope protein in the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, and thalamus. Reverse genetic analysis of LB EDIII residues revealed that mutating D308N only partially reduced LB neuropathology and lethality. However, mutating D308N along with an adjacent EDIII residue, A310T, completely abolished LB-D308N/A310T neuroinvasion and lethality, yet elicited neutralizing antibody responses that protected mice from a lethal WT LB challenge. Signifying a change in neuroinvasion, LB-D308N/A310T failed to activate microglia or yield detectable POWV RNA and antigen in the CNS. Overall, recombinant LB-D308N/A310T mutants fail to induce neurologic symptoms or neuropathology while eliciting a protective immune response. These findings reveal that EDIII residues determine the neuroinvasion and lethality of lineage I POWVs and that genetically modifying EDIII provides a mechanism for POWV attenuation and vaccine development.IMPORTANCEPowassan virus causes lethal encephalitis and long-term neurological sequelae in survivors; however, there are currently no licensed POWV vaccines or therapeutics. POWVs are comprised of two genetic lineages (LB-Lin I and LI9 Lin II) that are derived from discrete ticks and small mammal hosts. Orthoflavivirus envelope proteins determine cell attachment, viral tropism, and neurovirulent spread and lethality in mice. Here, we created a POWV LB reverse genetics system and assessed mutations that determine LB neuroinvasion in 50-week-old mice. Studies reveal novel LB neuropathology with divergent patterns of gliosis and POWV antigen expression within the CNS. Mice subcutaneously infected with an LB-D308N/A310T envelope mutant elicited responses that protect mice from a lethal LB challenge and failed to enter the CNS or cause neurologic symptoms, CNS pathology, or lethality. LB reverse genetics permits defining the determinants of LB neuroinvasion that are required for rational vaccine development.

Rickettsia rickettsii encephalitis in Brazilian spotted fever: a case report.
Brazilian spotted fever, caused by Rickettsia rickettsii, is a life-threatening tick-borne disease endemic to southeastern Brazil and is associated with high mortality when treatment is delayed. Central nervous system involvement poses a particular diagnostic challenge because of nonspecific early symptoms and frequent misdiagnosis as dengue or leptospirosis. We report a case illustrating characteristic neuroimaging findings and therapeutic considerations in rickettsial encephalitis. We describe the clinical course, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings, serologic results, and treatment response in a 23-year-old man who presented with febrile encephalopathy in an endemic region of Brazil. The patient had a five-day history of fever, erythematous macules, and progressive encephalopathy. CSF analysis showed elevated protein and lymphocytic pleocytosis. MRI showed T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities with restricted diffusion involving the bilateral corticospinal tracts and the splenium of the corpus callosum, forming a "boomerang" pattern. Clinical improvement followed initiation of empirical doxycycline and pulse methylprednisolone. Serologic testing supported the diagnosis of R. rickettsii infection with a positive immunoglobulin M titer of 1:512. Follow-up MRI showed near-complete lesion resolution at 4 months, with a residual splenial lesion persisting at 18 months. This case illustrates the importance of recognizing characteristic MRI patterns, including the "starry sky" and "boomerang" signs, as diagnostic clues in rickettsial encephalitis, even when the classic triad is incomplete. Early empirical doxycycline remains critical for neurologic outcomes, and adjunctive corticosteroids may have a role in selected cases when immune-mediated central nervous system injury is suspected.

Appropriateness of respiratory virus screening among hospitalized patients with respiratory symptoms: A retrospective observational study.
BACKGROUND: Respiratory viruses such as SARS-CoV-2, influenza, and RSV place considerable pressure on healthcare systems. Inconsistent respiratory virus screening among hospitalized patients with respiratory symptoms may delay recognition of respiratory viral infections and implementation of appropriate infection prevention and control measures. OBJECTIVE: To assess the appropriateness of respiratory virus screening among hospitalized patients with respiratory symptoms and to identify factors associated with inappropriate screening. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective observational study in a 2500-bed tertiary hospital in Belgium during three periods of the 2022-2023 influenza epidemic. Medical records were reviewed for demographic and clinical characteristics, respiratory symptoms, and respiratory virus screening practices. Screening was classified as appropriate or inappropriate (delayed or absent despite indication) based on prevailing guidelines. Determinants of inappropriate screening were explored using univariable analyses. RESULTS: Of 743 hospital admissions assessed for eligibility, 345 (46%) involved patients with respiratory symptoms and constituted the primary analysis population. Respiratory virus screening was appropriate in 75% (258/345) and inappropriate in 25% (87/345) of cases. Appropriate screening was more frequent among patients admitted for respiratory conditions and among those meeting criteria for severe acute respiratory infection (SARI). Screening appropriateness was significantly lower among patients who developed respiratory symptoms during hospitalization than among those with symptoms documented at admission (37% vs. 77%, p < 0.001). Isolation status could not be reliably determined for 44% of patients and was therefore considered descriptive only. CONCLUSION: Gaps remain in appropriate respiratory virus screening among hospitalized patients with respiratory symptoms, particularly among patients who develop symptoms during hospitalization. Systematic symptom-based screening and standardized decision-support tools may help improve adherence to respiratory virus screening recommendations.

A three-generation mpox cluster in Chongqing, 2024: transmission chain investigation and phylogenetic characterization.
BACKGROUND: In recent years, mpox has emerged as a significant public health concern, with the potential for both local and international spread. This study aimed to describe a three-generation mpox cluster and characterize its epidemiological features. METHODS: A three-generation mpox cluster was reported between August 19 and 23, 2024, in Chongqing China. Field epidemiology investigations were conducted to identify high-risk exposures and transmission routes and to guide the public health response. Rash lesion samples, anal swabs, pharyngeal swabs, and blood samples were collected from the cases for real-time polymerase chain reaction testing. Genome sequencing was performed to determine the MPXV clade. RESULTS: The cluster comprised three men who have sex with men, aged in their 40s, 30s, and 20s, respectively. All cases had mild symptoms, including perianal or genital rashes. .Case B was exposed to Case A through condomless sexual intercourse four days before symptom onset in Case A. Epidemiological investigation supported transmission through condomless sexual contact along the Case A → B → C chain in August 2024. Samples from Cases A and C were successfully sequenced and identified as MPXV clade IIb, lineage E.3. CONCLUSIONS: This three-generation mpox cluster was caused by MPXV clade IIb and was transmitted through condomless sexual contact. The findings suggest possible pre-symptomatic transmission of MPXV. Health education and sustained surveillance are essential for mpox prevention and control.

Identification of a putative novel rotavirus A VP4 genotype in bats from an urban Atlantic Forest, in the metropolitan region of Rio de Janeiro State, Southeastern Brazil.
Cross-species transmission occurs in rotaviruses, and human infection by animal strains is possible. We investigated the occurrence and genetic diversity of Rotavirus A (RVA) in bats from urban Atlantic Forest remnants under intense anthropogenic pressure in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Bats were captured between September 2020 and March 2022, totaling 240 samples (rectal swabs and feces) from 16 species. The RVA infection rate was 1.25% (3/240; Artibeus lituratus and Carollia perspicillata) using RT-qPCR targeting the NSP3 gene. A complete genomic constellation was attempted for positive samples. Phylogenetic analyses were performed, and homology-based three-dimensional modeling was applied to proteins encoded by genes showing low similarity to GenBank sequences. Partial VP4 sequences were successfully obtained from all three RVA-positive samples. Molecular characterization identified distinct genotypes: Gx-P[26]-I5, G20-P[unclassified*]-I13-T15, and G20-P[unclassified*]-I13-R13-C13-M12-A23-N13-T15-Ex-H15. The latter two harbored a putative novel VP4 genotype (P[unclassified*]) with <75% nucleotide identity to known genotypes and formed a distinct, well-supported phylogenetic clade. The Gx-P[26]-I5 strain showed highest identity to porcine RVA strains, representing the first detection of VP4 genotype P[26] in bats. Except for VP4, both G20P[unclassified*] strains were most closely related to a human G20P[28] strain from Suriname, suggesting a shared genomic constellation and possible reassortment between bat and human viruses. 3D structural analyses revealed conserved VP4 conformation among animal and human strains, suggesting structural compatibility across host species. These findings highlight bats as reservoirs of diverse RVA lineages and their role in viral evolution, reassortment, and zoonotic emergence, reinforcing the need for continuous One Health surveillance.

Intersecting threats: Brucella spp. and nematodes in small cetaceans of the California coast.
Brucella is a genus of zoonotic, intracellular alphaproteobacteria known to cause disease in marine mammals as well as livestock and companion animals. Specifically, Brucella ceti may be associated with severe neurological, respiratory, and reproductive disease in small cetaceans. Nematodes, particularly members of the Pseudaliidae, are common in small cetaceans and may harbor Brucella ceti, although the nature of this relationship remains unclear. This study investigated the prevalence of Brucella spp. in nematodes collected at necropsy from 64 small cetaceans that stranded on the central California coast between 2017 and 2023, to better document this host-parasite-pathogen relationship and its potential implications for cetacean population health. A total of 2703 nematodes were analyzed using real-time PCR to identify Brucella at both the genus and marine mammal specific species level. Five individual nematodes of three separate species collected from five individual animals were found to have marine brucellae and from one of these, sequencing confirmed the identity as B. ceti. The pooled prevalence of marine mammal Brucella spp. in all parasites was estimated at 0.18%. No significant associations were found between marine mammal Brucella-positive parasites and host demographics, Brucella-clinical hosts, parasite species, or tissue location. While no associations existed between the presence of Brucella within host parasites and host Brucella infection status, demographic features, or parasite characteristics, this is the first time marine Brucella has been detected within parasites from cetaceans in this geographic region. This, along with the novel finding of a Brucella-positive parasite within cetacean mammary tissue, suggests that marine mammal brucellosis and parasitism may coexist within hosts and brucellosis may be more prevalent than anticipated, highlighting the need for additional research to clarify the dynamics between Brucella, parasites, and vulnerable small cetaceans.

The Patients' Voice in Clostridioides difficile Infection: Large Language Model-Assisted Thematic Analysis of Patient Testimonials.
BACKGROUND: Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) imposes a burden that extends well beyond the gastrointestinal tract, yet existing outcome measures only partially capture the patient experience. We used frontier large language models (LLMs) on patient and caregiver narratives at scale to describe how burden shifts with disease course. METHODS: We analyzed 189 testimonials from the Peggy Lillis Foundation corpus, sorted into 4 cohorts with recurrence (r) and fulminant (f) severity as axes (rfCDI, fCDI, rCDI, non-rfCDI). Two independent LLMs coded 8 thematic domains, 4 fulminant flags, 13 emerging semantic fields, the dominant dimension, and narrative arcs. Two physicians independently coded a subset for inter-rater reliability (PABAK, Gwet's AC1). RESULTS: Treatment trajectory was the dominant theme in recurrent disease, whereas death and near-death dominated nonrecurrent fulminant narratives. Psychological burden was near-universal in fulminant disease (98.0% in rfCDI, 97.2% in fCDI). Caregiver and bereavement content concentrated in fCDI (66.7%). Diagnostic failure was frequent across recurrent cohorts (47.6-56.1%). Mentions of bacteriotherapy (fecal microbiota transplantation) concentrated in recurrent cohorts (60.2% rfCDI versus 5.6% fCDI). Financial, mental-health, and caregiver burdens were prominent and remain largely unaddressed by guidelines. Human-human reliability was substantial (PABAK 0.79 for semantic fields, 0.76 for domains); arc coding was least reliable. CONCLUSIONS: Patient narratives reveal a course-dependent, multidimensional burden in CDI. Concrete gaps exist between what patients prioritize, what guidelines recommend, and what therapy access provides. Frontier-LLM coding, validated against clinicians, offers a reproducible route to translate these priorities into research, care, and policy.

High-dose sulbactam for extensively drug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii infection in patients with critical illness.
OBJECTIVES: The therapeutic effect and tolerability of sulbactam, at a daily dose of at least 9 g, were assessed in critically ill individuals who acquired extensively drug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (XDR-AB) infection. METHODS: This single-center retrospective cohort evaluated a primary composite endpoint of death from any cause or invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) within 28 days. Secondary endpoints comprising the 14-day composite outcome, IMV-free and ICU-free days through day 28. RESULTS: The study cohort comprised 114 patients diagnosed with XDR-AB infection, of whom 72 (63.2%) received high-dose SBT-containing therapy. The high-dose SBT group showed a lower incidence of the composite outcomes, a higher IMV-free rate, and more IMV-free days through 28 days, with consistent results after adjustment using inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) or the overlap weighting (OW) approach. The observed association of high-dose SBT did not differ significantly by concomitant antibiotic regimen. Within-regimen analysis showed that patients receiving polymyxin B plus high-dose SBT had more IMV-free days through day 28 (mean difference 4.0 days, P = 0.025). No increased signal of nephrotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, or other SBT-related adverse events was observed during the 7-day monitoring period. CONCLUSIONS: With both high-dose and low-dose SBT combined with comparable antimicrobial regimens, the high-dose group was associated with potentially better outcomes, with no increased signal of adverse events. The observed association was independent of concomitant antibiotic choice, with more IMV-free days in the polymyxin B subgroup. These findings suggest high-dose SBT could serve as a therapeutic option in patients with critical illness who have XDR-AB infection.

Whole-genome insights into a multidrug-resistant, biofilm-forming, and pathogenic Salmonella Umbilo isolate and molecular characterization of rare Salmonella serovars from poultry.
Salmonellosis is one of the leading foodborne zoonoses worldwide, with contaminated poultry products representing a major source of human infection. This study characterized rare Salmonella serovars circulating in poultry flocks with respect to biofilm formation, virulence, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), CRISPR loci diversity, and genomic features. Salmonella isolates were conventionally isolated from drug swap samples and serotyped. Biofilm- (csgA, csgB, csgD, ompR, adrA, rpoS, and fimH) and virulence-associated genes (sipA, sipD, sopB, sopD, sopE, sopE2, sitC, sifA, ssaR, spvC, and pefA) were investigated. CRISPR loci and phenotypic AMR were examined. The Salmonella isolate, which exhibited the highest MAR index, was analyzed by whole-genome sequencing (WGS). Bioinformatic analyses were conducted to determine its plasmid, AMR, and virulence capacity. Thirty rare Salmonella serovars were identified including, Aba, Atento, Ball, Blegdam, Bonariensis, Bradford, Chandans, Fallowfield, Ferruch, Idikan, II (1,9,12:g,m,s,t:e,n,x), Inganda, Korbol, Leeuwarden, Menden, Naestved, Ohlstedt, Papuana, Petahtikve, Sandow, Schwarzengrund, Svedvi, Telaviv, Thompson, Tinda, Tsevie, Tumodi, Umbilo, Uppsala, and Vejle. CsgA-B-C (100.0%) and sipA (96.7%) were the most prevalent genes. S. Sandow harbored all examined genes. CRISPR2 locus (23.3%) was more prevalent than the CRISPR1 locus (3.3%). Resistance to streptomycin (56.7%) and sulfonamides (46.7%) was most common, whereas 40.0% of the isolates were MDR. WGS of the S. Umbilo isolate, which exhibited the highest MAR index (0.48), identified the IncHI2A plasmid (a key factor in horizontal transfer of AMR genes), 12 AMR genes (responsible for resistance to beta-lactams, aminoglycosides, phenicols, and lincosamides), and 181 virulence-associated genes (involved in adhesion, invasion, chemotaxis, intracellular survival, and environmental persistence). The detection of highly resistant and potentially pathogenic S. Umbilo, previously linked to a multinational foodborne outbreak in Europe, highlights its potential public health significance. MLST further proved useful for serovar prediction, with ST2014. Rare Salmonella serovars circulating in poultry flocks possess substantial virulence, biofilm-forming, and AMR potential. These findings highlight the importance of including rare serovars in surveillance and control programs to mitigate foodborne transmission and the spread of AMR.

Clinical Characterization and Outcomes of Pneumonic Plague in Madagascar: A Case Series.
Pneumonic plague is rare compared to bubonic plague; data on clinical presentation and treatment outcomes are scant. We report on 13 prospectively-enrolled suspected pneumonic plague cases (7 laboratory-confirmed, one probable, 5 not-plague) treated with aminoglycoside plus ciprofloxacin for 10 days and discuss findings in the context of the available literature.

[Translated article] The "Trojan horse" against antimicrobial resistance: Siderophore conjugates and public health.
OBJECTIVE: Antimicrobial resistance, particularly in carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales such as KPC-type, represents a critical threat to public health in Latin America, associated with high mortality rates and increased healthcare costs. This systematic review aims to evaluate the therapeutic potential of siderophore-drug and siderophore-peptide conjugates against priority multidrug-resistant pathogens, including Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Acinetobacter baumannii, analyzing their efficacy, mechanisms of action, and implementation challenges. METHOD: A systematic search was conducted in the PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science databases up to August 2025. Key terms such as "siderophore conjugates", "Trojan horse antibiotics", "antimicrobial resistance", and "Gram-negative bacteria" were used. Preclinical and clinical studies, reviews, and meta-analyses published between 2019 and 2025 were included, selecting 55 references based on relevance to the topic, currency, and methodological quality. This review is a narrative review with a systematic literature search, developed in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. RESULTS: Siderophore conjugates, via the "Trojan horse" mechanism, effectively exploit bacterial iron uptake systems to deliver antimicrobial agents in a targeted manner. They overcome key resistance mechanisms such as β-lactamase production, porin alterations, and efflux pump activity, while reducing systemic toxicity and preserving commensal microbiota. Clinical evidence (e.g., cefiderocol) and preclinical studies confirm their efficacy against multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) strains, achieving significant reductions in minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs). However, critical challenges were identified: optimization of chemical stability and intracellular drug release, complexity in synthesis and industrial scaling under Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standards, and regulatory and logistical barriers in resource-limited settings. CONCLUSIONS: Siderophore conjugates offer a targeted therapeutic approach against multidrug-resistant pathogens by exploiting the bacteria's own iron-uptake systems. The available evidence ranges from clinical results with cefiderocol to preclinical developments with other platforms. Their application, however, faces challenges that span chemical optimization, manufacturing, regulation, and access in clinical settings.

Direct Lateral Flow Detection of Carbapenemase-producing Acinetobacter baumannii From Screening Samples Using the RESIST ACINETO Lateral Flow Assay: A Proof-of-Concept Study.
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the lateral flow assay (LFA) RESIST ACINETO targeting the Acinetobacter baumannii-associated carbapenemases, applied directly to screening swabs and compare this culture-independent approach with conventional culture-based diagnostics during a suspected outbreak. METHODS: We analysed 106 screening swabs from 35 patients. Routine diagnostics included culture, species identification, antimicrobial susceptibility testing and carbapenemase detection from isolates, while the LFA was applied directly to eSwab transport medium without prior culture. Samples positive by both methods were classified as true-positives. Discordant results were resolved by enrichment culture. A confirmation set of 24 swabs from nine known CRAB carriers was analysed to assess sensitivity, and the analytical detection limit was determined using serial dilutions of a blaOXA-23-carrying A. baumannii reference strain. RESULTS: Routine diagnostics detected CRAB in six samples from two patients. Direct LFA identified these samples and yielded positive results in five additional samples from three patients. Enrichment culture confirmed three of the five discordant samples as CRAB positive, resulting in nine true positive samples. The LFA achieved 100% sensitivity (9/9) and 97.9% specificity (95/97). One false-positive result was caused by an NDM-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae, while one remained unexplained. LFA results were available at least 24 hours earlier than routine diagnostics. In the confirmation set, the direct LFA was positive in all 24 swabs from nine CRAB carriers. The analytical limit of detection was 107 CFU/mL. CONCLUSIONS: Direct LFA application enabled the rapid, culture-independent detection of carbapenemase-producing A. baumannii and provided results earlier than culture. As an adjunct to conventional screening, it may support earlier infection-control decisions.

Fate of Listeria monocytogenes on Chopped Citric Acid-Treated Hard-Cooked Eggs During Storage.
A multistate outbreak of Listeria monocytogenes linked to commercially prepared peeled hard-cooked eggs (HCEs) occurred in the U.S. in 2019. HCEs are commonly treated with citric acid to extend shelf life and inhibit postcontamination bacterial growth. However, no information is currently available on the efficacy of citric acid treatment to control L. monocytogenes when HCEs are chopped and stored. This study evaluated the survival and growth of L. monocytogenes on chopped HCEs treated previously with 2% citric acid or water during storage at 5, 10, or 25 °C for up to 14 days. Whole HCEs were treated with citric acid or water for 24 h, inoculated with L. monocytogenes at approximately 4 log CFU/HCE, chopped, and stored. Citric acid treatment maintained chopped HCE pH at 4.11 to 4.44 throughout storage, while water-treated chopped HCEs had higher pHs (6.1 to 7.9). At 5 °C, no significant increase in populations of L. monocytogenes was detected on citric acid-treated chopped HCEs. Water-treated eggs at 5 °C supported slow growth (0.08 log CFU/g per day; a 1 log CFU/g increase in 12.5 days). At 10 and 25 °C, citric acid treatment reduced L. monocytogenes growth rates on chopped HCEs, compared to the water controls (0.54 vs 1.03 log CFU/g per day at 10 °C; 1.40 vs 4.38 log CFU/g per day at 25 °C). These results demonstrate that 2% citric acid treatment prevented significant increases in populations of L. monocytogenes on chopped HCEs during refrigerated storage, and that temperature control remains critical for safety.

Combating antimicrobial resistance: Emerging non-traditional therapeutics, clinical translation challenges, and future perspectives.
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has emerged as one of the most severe global health threats. The rapid expansion of multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) pathogens compromises the effectiveness of conventional antibiotics. Globally, ESKAPE organisms (Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterobacter spp.) have led to therapeutic failure, prolonged hospitalization, and increased mortality rates. This review identifies the molecular mechanisms, including enzymatic antibiotic inactivation, efflux pump overexpression, biofilm formation, and horizontal gene transfer, that underlie the resistance of disseminated pathogens to antibiotics in clinical, agricultural, and environmental settings. Antibiotic overuse and pharmaceutical and agricultural discharges create persistent reservoirs for the dissemination of AMR genes. Furthermore, we evaluated the non-traditional antibacterial efficacy of antimicrobial peptides, bacteriophage therapy, monoclonal antibodies, probiotics, fecal microbiota transplantation, anti-virulence agents, CRISPR-Cas precision antimicrobials, and nanotechnology-based drug delivery platforms. Current preclinical and clinical evidence indicates the eradication of resistant pathogens, disruption of biofilms, and preservation of host microbiota, thereby reducing the selective pressure associated with broad-spectrum antibiotics. Despite these advances, major translational barriers, such as pharmacokinetic instability, manufacturing limitations, and insufficient clinical validation, restrict the implementation of the framework. In the future, the AMR management framework will require precision medicine, artificial intelligence, and One Health-based integration via multidisciplinary collaboration.

Outbreak of Salmonella Agona linked to cross-contamination via doner kebab and electric knives in Hesse and Baden-Wuerttemberg, Germany, January 2022 - December 2024.
OBJECTIVES: Following an increase in Salmonella enterica spp. enterica (S.) serovar Agona notifications in Hesse and Baden-Wuerttemberg, Germany, 2022-2024, we investigated to identify the outbreak vehicle and source to implement control measures. METHODS: Outbreak cases included laboratory-confirmed S. Agona cases defined as (1) probable (no isolate) or (2) confirmed cases (whole genome sequencing assigned outbreak strain, complex type 20182), residing in Hesse and Baden-Wuerttemberg. We analysed epidemiologic data, including food consumption histories, and compared isolates from clinical, food, and environmental samples. RESULTS: Sixty S. Agona outbreak cases were identified (Hesse: 25 confirmed, 16 probable; Baden-Wuerttemberg: 15 confirmed, 4 probable), with 83% (40/48) of sequenced isolates closely linked genetically. The median age of cases was 21 years (range: 0-76 years) and 63% (38/60) were male. Cases were more likely to have consumed doner kebab compared to a population-based food survey (OR 6.7, CI 2.66-16.9). In three identified doner restaurants, the outbreak strain was detected in doner meat and on electric knives. CONCLUSION: Inadequate cleaning of knives due to improper disassembly may have contributed to sustained transmission over the three-year outbreak period. Improved hygiene measures, targeted sampling, and enhanced surveillance are essential to prevent similar foodborne outbreaks.

Dynamics of emm types in invasive Streptococcus pyogenes isolates from Argentina, 2018-2024.
Group A Streptococcus (GAS) is a major cause of invasive bacterial infections worldwide, making molecular surveillance essential for monitoring strain dynamics and detecting emerging lineages. We conducted nationwide molecular surveillance of invasive GAS (iGAS) infections in Argentina between July 2018 and December 2024, analyzing 1127 isolates from confirmed cases. emm typing was performed using Sanger sequencing (2018-2020) and whole-genome sequencing (WGS) (2022-2024), enabling multilocus sequence typing (MLST), virulence and antimicrobial resistance profiling. Surveillance was interrupted during 2020-2021 due to the COVID-19 pandemic but was strengthened thereafter when iGAS became nationally notifiable. Overall, 59 emm types and 61 sequence types were identified. emm1 predominated across the study period (42.4%), followed by emm12, emm3, and emm4, with marked temporal shifts. In 2023, clonal diversity declined, with emm1 and emm12 accounting for 72% of isolates and the emergence of hypervirulent M1 lineages. In 2024, emm diversity increased, with expansion of emm3, emm4, emm49, and emm87.

Optimizing pneumococcal prevention in South African older adults: Cost-effectiveness of PCV20 versus PPSV23 in the context of HIV-associated risk.
Pneumococcal disease remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality among older adults in South Africa, particularly among people living with HIV. Evidence on the cost-effectiveness of Prevnar 20 (PCV20) vs. Pneumovax 23 (PPSV23) vaccine in this setting remains limited. This study was conducted to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of PCV20 compared with PPSV23 vaccine among adults aged ≥65y in South Africa, and to assess the impact of HIV stratification on economic outcomes. A static decision-tree model was developed from the South African public healthcare payer perspective. The analysis incorporated invasive pneumococcal disease, pneumococcal community-acquired pneumonia, quality-adjusted life-years, maximum acceptable price, and 5y budget impact. HIV-stratified incidence and CD4-adjusted vaccine effectiveness were included. In the general population, PCV20 provided greater health benefits than PPSV23 but was not cost-effective at the current base-case price (USD 20.00/dose), with an ICER of USD 17,323/QALY. Price was the main driver of cost-effectiveness. In contrast, targeted vaccination of older adults living with HIV was economically favorable, with an ICER of USD 2,104/QALY under national incidence assumptions, and even stronger results in high-burden settings. The cost-effectiveness of PCV20 in South Africa is contingent upon the price of vaccine and risk-based targeting. Vaccinating all older adults universally may not be cost-effective at current prices, suggesting that targeted vaccination of older adults with HIV represents a more efficient strategy.

Implementing computer‑aided detection for TB active case finding: A qualitative study of feasibility and acceptability in Tondo, Manila.
Tuberculosis (TB) remains the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent, with over 1.23 million deaths globally in 2024. Despite available treatment and prevention strategies, timely and accurate detection remains challenging, particularly in high-burden settings such as the Philippines, which accounted for 6.8% of the global burden of TB in 2024. Computer-aided detection (CAD) software integrated with digital chest X-ray offers enhanced screening capacity, but its success depends on feasibility and acceptability within local health systems. This qualitative study explored perceptions and experiences of CAD integration during a Médecins Sans Frontières community-based TB active case finding campaign (ACF) in Tondo, Manila. In-depth interviews, focus group discussions, and direct observations were conducted with MSF staff, health center physicians, TB program personnel, ACF participants, and community leaders between January and April 2023. Thematic analysis identified four main themes: (1) Operational functionality and efficiency: Staff reported CAD increased screening capacity, supported clinical decision-making, and streamlined workloads; ACF participants reported a convenient process. (2) Human resources and role adaptation: Staff perceived role redistribution as initially challenging, highlighting the need for adequate capacity building and technical support; (3) Technical feasibility and system design: project managers and staff emphasized understanding CAD's capabilities and limitations to plan infrastructure, set thresholds, and compensate for inherent limitations. (4) Community acceptability and ethical considerations: community participants expressed mixed views on the reliability of novel "high-tech" tools and stressed the importance of aligning with local healthcare needs. This study demonstrates that implementing CAD in TB ACF is both feasible and acceptable when supported by careful planning and adaptation to local contexts. Sustainable implementation hinges on technical support and the meaningful involvement of healthcare workers and communities, whose insights help ensure ethical and effective digital health innovation. The experience in Tondo offers lessons on deploying CAD in high-burden, resource-constrained settings.

A Recyclable Coconut-Shell-Carbon-Based Photocatalyst for Robust Antimicrobial Activity and Enhanced Wound Repair.
Acinetobacter baumannii (A. baumannii) is a notorious nosocomial pathogen for its extensive drug resistance and adaptability. This study developed a novel heterojunction photocatalyst (PC), PTQ10-SY1, supported on coconut shell charcoal (CSC), a carbon material derived from natural biomass. The CSC matrix ensures efficient dispersion of PTQ10-SY1 and enhances its recoverability, thereby synthesizing the reusable, environmentally friendly, white light-responsive material CSC@PTQ10-SY1. Under 13.2 mW/cm2 of light excitation, the material efficiently generates reactive oxygen species (ROS), which disrupt the cell wall and membrane integrity of A. baumannii, inhibit ATP synthesis, and leading to bacterial death. It achieves significant elimination of A. baumannii within 30 min and also demonstrates effective activity against Methicillin-resistance Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (P. aeruginosa). In mammalian safety assessments, CSC@PTQ10-SY1 shows minimal adverse effects under the tested conditions. In a wound-associated infection model, topical application of CSC@PTQ10-SY1 significantly reduces bacterial burden and inflammation, resulting in improved wound healing outcomes compared to the control group. Furthermore, the material retains its composition and shows no evidence of tolerance to photodynamic therapy (PDT) after 10 cycles. This work highlights an innovative strategy for designing antimicrobial PC materials and promotes the application of antimicrobial PDT for the A. baumannii.

Pathogen and host biomarkers to aid early diagnosis and prognosis of tuberculous meningitis.
BACKGROUND: Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) is the most sinister form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis (EPTB), associated with high mortality due to delayed diagnosis and limited sensitivity of conventional and molecular tests. Current study evaluated the diagnostic utility of Lipoarabinomannan antigen (LAM) detection in CSF and urine and explored host inflammatory biomarkers for diagnosis and prognosis of TBM. METHODS: This prospective observational cohort study enrolled 80 HIV-negative adults with presumptive TBM at a tertiary care center. Patients were classified according to the uniform TBM case definition, based on clinical, CSF, radiological, and microbiological findings. CSF samples were subjected to AFB microscopy, liquid culture (MGIT-960), GeneXpert MTB/RIF (GX), and LAM lateral flow assay. Urine LAM was performed at baseline. Serum and CSF levels of IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, IFN-γ, IL-17 A, and IP-10 were measured at baseline and after 1 month of treatment. RESULTS: Among 80 HIV-negative participants, 23 (28.7%) had definite TBM and 46 (57.5%) had probable TBM. CSF LAM sensitivity and specificity against microbiological reference standards were 43.5% and 80.7%, while urine LAM sensitivity (60.9%) and specificity 82.5% were higher. Against composite reference standards, both CSF and urine LAM showed reduced sensitivity but achieved 100% specificity. Serum IL-1β demonstrated the highest diagnostic performance for distinguishing TBM from non-TBM patients (AUC 0.943; sensitivity 88.9%, specificity 90.9%). Elevated serum and CSF IP-10 levels were associated with on-treatment mortality, whereas declining IL-6 and TNF-α levels correlated with treatment response. CONCLUSION: LAM detection in CSF and urine may serve as a useful adjunct to existing diagnostic approaches for TBM when interpreted alongside clinical, radiological, and microbiological findings. Host inflammatory biomarkers, especially IL-1β and IP-10, show additional diagnostic and prognostic value. Combining LAM testing with cytokine biomarkers may improve early diagnosis and efficient clinical management of TBM. However, larger multicentre studies are required to validate these findings before routine clinical implementation.

Detection characteristics and antimicrobial resistance profiles of Salmonella spp. isolated from fecal cultures of inpatients at a maternal and child healthcare hospital in Shenzhen: a 5-year retrospective study.
UNLABELLED: Salmonella spp. remain an important cause of bacterial gastrointestinal infection, but local data from maternal and child healthcare hospitals remain limited. This retrospective study analyzed Salmonella spp. isolated from fecal cultures of inpatients at Longgang District Maternity and Child Healthcare Hospital of Shenzhen City from 2021 to 2025.
