These findings support the implementation of dengue vaccination programs while reinforcing the importance of ongoing surveillance to identify rare safety signals and reduce preventable immunization errors.

Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome: an emerging fatal zoonotic infection.
Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome is a potentially fatal respiratory zoonotic infection caused by New World hantaviruses, and it is acquired mostly via inhaling aerosolized excreta from infected rodents. Over the past 30 years, HCPS has expanded beyond its initial foci, and recent events suggest a potential for spread beyond traditionally endemic regions. The disease rapidly progresses from a vague prodrome to acute cardiopulmonary failure with a high fatality rate despite optimum supportive treatment. Pathophysiology involves endothelial failure, increased vascular permeability, acute thrombocytopenia and excessive immunological responses resulting in capillary leak syndrome and cardiogenic shock. It is still hard to clinically suspect early since the prodromal symptoms are vague and mirror common viral infections and respiratory disorders. Diagnostic confirmation needs serological testing or genetic approaches, which are typically unavailable in resource-limited endemic situations, leading to considerable diagnostic delays. Management is generally supportive, with early ICU admission, judicious hydration management, mechanical breathing and cardiopulmonary support including extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in refractory patients. The recent multi-country Andes virus epidemic on a cruise ship in May 2026 highlights the potential for fast worldwide transmission of HCPS outside of usual endemic settings. This review summarizes the current information on the epidemiology, pathophysiology, clinical presentation, diagnostic techniques, and treatment options for HCPS. We also highlight the pressing need for improved global surveillance, rapid point-of-care diagnostics, global awareness among health care workers, and ongoing development of preventive vaccines and effective antiviral therapies to address this significant public health threat.

A Kidney Transplant Patient Suffering From Multiple Colonic Ulcers and Hepatic Abscess: A Case Report and Literature Review.
We present a rare case of colonic mucormycosis with hepatic dissemination after kidney transplantation. Early diagnosis was achieved through rapid metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of blood and liver abscess samples, enabling timely intervention. The patient achieved complete clinical recovery with preserved allograft function. Gastrointestinal mucormycosis is extremely rare, reported cases frequently require colectomy (83.3%) and carry a mortality rate approaching 50%. This case highlights key management principles for intestinal mucormycosis in transplant recipients: rapid pathogen identification via mNGS, prompt initiation of dual antifungal therapy against Mucorales, and urgent surgical debridement of necrotic tissue.

Candidozyma auris: "The Silent Colonizer" mapped through 15-month surveillance in a North Indian tertiary-care hospital.
BACKGROUND: Candida auris (reclassified as Candidozyma auris) is an emerging multidrug-resistant fungal pathogen associated with healthcare-associated outbreaks. Its persistence in healthcare environments and frequent misidentification pose challenges for infection prevention. This study aimed to estimate ICU colonisation prevalence, reassess non-albicans Candida (NAC) isolates using molecular diagnostics, and conduct targeted ward surveillance. METHODS: A prospective surveillance study was conducted from September 2022 to December 2023 across six ICUs of a tertiary care hospital in Jammu & Kashmir. Monthly axilla-groin composite swabs were collected, with rescreening of patients remaining admitted during subsequent rounds. Targeted surveillance was undertaken in wards where C. auris was recovered from sterile-site specimen. Identification used HiCrome Candida differential agar (HCDA), VITEK® 2 Compact, and species-specific PCR. Antifungal susceptibility testing (AFST) was performed by E-test. RESULTS: Twenty unique patients were colonised with C. auris, giving an overall ICU colonisation prevalence of 4.1%. Ten additional unique patients were identified through targeted surveillance and were not included in the ICU denominator. Thus, 30 unique patients were identified. Of 120 non-albicans Candida isolates, PCR confirmed 54 C. auris, including eight misidentified by VITEK 2. All isolates met the CDC tentative resistance threshold for fluconazole, while no echinocandin resistance was detected. Amphotericin B resistance occurred in 4/54 (7.4%) isolates. Voriconazole MICs >32 μg/mL occurred in 7/54 (13.0%) isolates and were reported descriptively. Sixteen (53.3%) patients with C. auris expired. CONCLUSION: Fifteen-month surveillance identified ICU colonisation and highlighted limitations of phenotypic identification. Molecular confirmation and continued surveillance are important for early recognition of C. auris and infection control.

Multidrug Resistance and Host Adaptation in Candida Auris: From Molecular Mechanisms to Emerging Therapeutic Frontiers.
C. auris is an emerging multidrug-resistant (MDR) fungal pathogen that poses an urgent threat to global public health. It is characterized by rapid nosocomial transmission, persistent environmental survival, and extensive cross-resistance to conventional antifungal therapies. This comprehensive narrative review bridges the fundamental molecular mechanisms of intrinsic and acquired antifungal resistance with host adaptation strategies and emerging clinical interventions. C. auris resistance is driven by a highly sophisticated network of genetic mutations and metabolic reprogramming distributed across six geographically distinct clades (I-VI), including the newly identified Clade VI from the Indomalayan zone. Azole resistance primarily relies on clade-specific point mutations in the target gene ERG11, synergistically amplified by TAC1b-driven transcriptional upregulation of the CDR1 efflux pump. Echinocandin resistance is predominantly mediated by conformational reshaping across three distinct hotspot regions of the FKS1 gene, bolstered by Hsp90-mediated stress compensatory networks. For polyenes, while clinical resistance is frequently overestimated by commercial assays, true tolerance mechanisms involved the depletion of target ergosterol and profound non-sterol-dependent sphingolipid remodeling. Beyond genomic modifications, C. auris exhibits significant phenotypic plasticity, forming robust, polysaccharide-rich biofilms on indwelling medical devices that confer profound physical drug tolerance. Clinically, the fungus demonstrates a strong cutaneous tropism-predominantly colonizing the axilla and groin-which acts as the primary reservoir for hospital outbreaks. Furthermore, experimental models reveal that C. auris actively exploits host immune deficiencies, specifically subverting the IL-17A/neutrophil/S100A8 axis, to evade immune clearance and establish persistent colonization. To overcome these formidable MDR bottlenecks, therapeutic paradigms are rapidly evolving. The integration of next-generation antifungals such as the long-acting echinocandin rezafungin, fosmanogepix, and ibrexafungerp, synergistic combination therapies, quorum-sensing inhibitors such as farnesol, and experimental nanocarrier delivery systems could represent promising frontiers to effectively dismantle the complex defense networks of C. auris.

30-day mortality and antifungal resistance in confirmed Candida auris bloodstream infections (BSI): a systematic review and meta-analysis.
BACKGROUND: Candida auris is a potentially multidrug-resistant nosocomial fungus that was classified as a WHO critical priority pathogen in 2022. Individual cohort studies report 30-day bloodstream infection mortality; however, prior meta-analyses have not restricted their primary pool to confirmed bloodstream infection cases. METHODS: A PROSPERO-registered systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted (CRD420261418844). Studies enrolling patients with confirmed C. auris bloodstream infection and reporting 30-day or in-hospital all-cause mortality were included. Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation with DerSimonian-Laird random-effects modelling was applied to all proportion pools. Fluconazole and amphotericin B resistance were combined. Echinocandin resistance was synthesised narratively because of the zero-event problem. Subgroup analyses were pre-specified by geographic region and study designs. RESULTS: Sixteen studies (N = 1,069 patients; 2016-2026) met the inclusion criteria. Pooled 30-day mortality from 13 studies (N = 813) was 39.6% (95% CI 32.4-47.0%; I2 = 75.5%). In-hospital mortality from three studies (N = 256) was 45.1% (95% CI 30.9-59.7). Pooled fluconazole resistance was 95.0% (95% CI 86.7-99.7%; I2 = 92.6%). Pooled amphotericin B resistance was 45.5% (95% CI 22.6-69.4%; I2 = 97.5%), with extreme heterogeneity driven by clade-specific variations. Echinocandin resistance ranged from 0 to 16% across the individual cohorts. Multinational consortia showed the highest regional mortality estimate (52.4%, 95% CI 41.4-63.3%). CONCLUSIONS: Confirmed C. auris bloodstream infections have a pooled 30-day mortality rate of approximately 40%, along with near-universal fluconazole resistance. Echinocandins remain the first-line therapy, although mortality rates remain high. Susceptibility-guided therapy and enhanced infection control are essential.

Local Wealth Inequality and Working-Age Mortality in US Counties.
IMPORTANCE: Household wealth is associated with health and survival, but little is known about whether wealth inequality is associated with mortality as a contextual exposure. OBJECTIVE: To examine the association between local wealth inequality and age-adjusted all-cause mortality across US counties over 5 decades. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This longitudinal, county-level study of up to 18 344 county-year observations from 1970 to 2019 linked restricted-access, all-cause mortality data from the US National Center for Health Statistics with county-level population and sociodemographic information and commuting zone estimates of household wealth inequality from the GEOWEALTH-US database. US counties were observed at decennial intervals from 1970 to 2019, with 2019 mortality used for the final period to avoid distortion from the COVID-19 pandemic. After listwise deletion, the estimation sample included up to 18 344 county-year observations nested in 732 commuting zones. EXPOSURE: Commuting zone Gini index score of household net wealth inequality. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: County-specific, sex-specific, age-adjusted all-cause mortality rates for ages 25 to 44, 45 to 54, and 55 to 64 years, modeled on the natural log scale. RESULTS: In adjusted 2-way fixed-effects models with county, year, and state by year fixed effects, higher local wealth inequality was associated with higher mortality across all sex-age groups. Unstandardized regression coefficients (b) were 1.72 (95% CI, 0.99-2.45), 1.57 (95% CI, 0.96-2.18), and 1.11 (95% CI, 0.65-1.57) for female individuals aged 25 to 44, 45 to 54, and 55 to 64 years, respectively, and 0.75 (95% CI, 0.12-1.37), 0.71 (95% CI, 0.27-1.14), and 0.66 (95% CI, 0.24-1.08), respectively, for male individuals in the same age groups. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this aggregate longitudinal cross-sectional study, increases in local wealth inequality were associated with within-county increases in working-age mortality. These findings suggest that wealth inequality may be relevant to population health beyond income inequality, although mechanisms and causality require further study.

A systematic review to characterize functional tic-like behaviors.
BACKGROUND: Functional tic-like behaviors (FTLBs) have emerged as a prominent clinical presentation within the context of the COVID-19 pandemic. Although FTLBs share phenomenological overlap with Tourette Syndrome and other tic disorders (collectively Tourette Syndrome, TS), evidence suggests that differences exist in demographics, phenomenology, clinical course, psychiatric comorbidity, and response to intervention. Given the rapid rise in the incidence of FTLBs-along with their complex clinical presentation-we provide a systematic review and integrated synthesis of the extant literature. METHODS: We conducted a systematic review following PRISMA guidelines. PubMed and PsycINFO databases searches were completed in June 2026, using terms related to functional tics and TS. Inclusion criteria were English-language studies reporting clinical data on FTLB with sample sizes of 8 or greater. Case reports, non-human studies, and commentaries were excluded. Thirty-nine studies were included. Data were extracted on demographics, phenomenology, clinical course, psychiatric comorbidity, and treatment responsiveness. Since multiple reports originated from the same data repositories, information was synthesized qualitatively by study sample and conceptual domain. RESULTS: The results of our review suggest that FTLBs predominantly affect adolescents and young adults and exhibit a strong female predominance-with higher than anticipated representation of gender-diverse individuals. Compared with TS, the onset of FTLB symptoms was abrupt and characterized by complex motor movements and vocalizations that cause functional impairment. While there is a considerable overlap between FTLBs and TS, there were distinctions in patterns of psychiatric comorbidities. Pharmacological and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) provided some benefit for individuals with FTLBs, but the therapeutic target of these interventions was not specified. CONCLUSIONS: While sharing some similarities, FTLBs have a distinct clinical presentation from TS. There is some evidence to inform treatment approaches, but findings are complicated by the retrospective nature of most extant reports. Future research is essential to characterize longitudinal trajectories, underlying mechanisms, and evaluation of targeted interventions in randomized clinical trials.

Comparative serum cytokine and chemokine profiles across tuberculosis, latent TB, HIV, and COVID-19 infections in Namibian adults.
BACKGROUND: The devastating pandemic of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) highlighted the importance of early detection and global collaboration in combating infectious diseases. Namibia is one of the countries that bears a high burden of tuberculosis (TB) and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. The overlap of these diseases underscores the need to better understand host immune responses, which play a critical role in disease pathogenesis and may differ across infections. This study aimed to profile selected cytokines and chemokines among Namibian individuals with TB, latent TB infection (LTBI), COVID-19, and HIV infection. METHODS: A cross-sectional study was conducted between August 2022 and May 2023 among adults (≥18 years) recruited from two clinics in Namibia. 222 participants were categorized into multiple clinical groups, including mono- and co-infections of COVID-19, active TB, LTBI, HIV, and control participants. Serum concentrations of 23 cytokines and chemokines were measured using the LEGENDPlex™ multiplex immunoassay. Differences, discriminations and correlations in biomarker levels between groups were analysed using non-parametric statistical tests with adjustment for multiple comparisons. Statistical significance was defined as an adjusted p < 0.05. RESULTS: MCP-1 demonstrated consistent upregulation across active TB, COVID-19, COVID-19/LTBI, and HIV/LTBI groups. In contrast, free active transforming growth factor beta 1 (TGF-β1) was significantly downregulated in both TB and LTBI participants. Individuals with TB exhibited elevated MCP-1 and macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) levels compared to those with LTBI, with both analytes demonstrating discriminatory performance between TB and LTBI. Multiple moderate and weak positive correlations among inflammatory markers were observed in individuals with LTBI and HIV/LTBI but were absent in active TB and COVID-19/LTBI participants. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings demonstrate distinct serum cytokines and chemokines across TB, LTBI, HIV, and COVID-19 in a Namibian cohort. MCP-1 emerged as a consistent marker associated with inflammation. MIF was detected as a potential differentiating marker for TB and LTBI. Larger studies are needed to evaluate the diagnostic potential of these biomarkers and their incorporation into clinical diagnostic algorithms. The results also suggest a possible role for LTBI-associated immune activation in HIV co-infection, which warrants further investigation.

High-throughput screening to identify inhibitors of the MTB CARD•RNA polymerase protein-protein interaction.
In 2023, tuberculosis (TB) once again became the world's deadliest infectious disease, overtaking COVID-19 as the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent, Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB). The World Health Organization (WHO) reports that the COVID-19 pandemic has reversed years of progress in providing essential TB services and reducing TB disease burden. In 2025, TB was responsible for an estimated 1.23 million deaths globally (95% uncertainty interval: 1.13-1.33 million), and there were 400 K cases of rifamycin resistant/multidrug resistant TB (RR, RIFR, MDR). While treatment success for drug susceptible TB remains high (88%), outcomes for MDR/RR-TB are lower but improving, reaching 71% globally. Clearly, there is a critical unmet need for novel antibiotics against MTB, exacerbated now due to COVID-19. The limited success in pursuing novel targets underscores the urgent need to revisit and reevaluate the mechanisms of action behind existing and once effective drugs, a strategy that may hold untapped potential in the fight against growing antibiotic-resistant TB. The MTB RNA polymerase (RNAP) is a proven target for TB treatment by rifampin (RMP), which kills both active and latent MTB. However, RMP suffers from several drawbacks including: long treatment times, activation of hPXR (inducing Cyp3A4 which is problematic for HIV-TB coinfection), and resistant mutations within RNAP. Two newer treatments with novel mechanisms of action include bedaquiline and delamanid, the former has been approved by the FDA for the treatment of multiple-drug resistant tuberculosis (MDR-MTB); however, even these new drugs already have incidences of acquired resistance. Our goal is to develop novel drug candidates for TB treatment that: target RNAP, have the potential to shorten treatment times, and have activity against RIFR mutants. Our approach, orthogonal to the rifamycins, is to target the interaction of MTB RNAP with the required transcription factor CarD. We have previously labeled CarD with the BODIPY-FL fluorophore via engineered cysteine mutations and developed a fluorescence polarization assay to monitor its interaction with RNAP and promoter DNA. Leveraging this target, we screened a 24 K small molecule library against CarD binding to MTB RNAP. We have now extended this screening to∼88,000 additional molecules.

Burden of dermatology outpatient and inpatient services in China, 2011-2023.
BACKGROUND: This study aimed to describe the temporal trends, regional distribution of dermatology services, and the hospitalization burden of common skin diseases in China (2011-2023) and provide reference for the government about resource allocation. METHODS: Data on dermatology outpatient visits and discharges from public hospitals by age and provinces were sourced from the China Health Statistics Yearbook. RESULTS: From 2011 to 2023, the total number of dermatology outpatient visits and inpatient discharges from public hospitals in China were 1.36 billion and 7.38 million, respectively. Both the number and rate of outpatient and inpatient increased until 2019, declined in 2020, and rebound after 2021. Outpatient visits were highest in the eastern region, whereas inpatients were highest in the western region. The top five provinces for total outpatient visits were Guangdong, Zhejiang, Jiangsu, Shanghai, and Sichuan, for inpatient discharges from public hospitals: Hubei, Sichuan, Shandong, Guangdong, and Henan. Among four skin diseases, eczema/dermatitis had the most hospitalizations (1,209,754), followed by urticaria (719,610), benign skin tumors (653,036), and psoriasis (370,409). Total hospitalization cost for the four diseases was 14.66 billion RMB, with eczema/dermatitis accounting for the largest share (6.23 billion). Psoriasis had the longest hospital stay (median 11.58 days) and highest cost (median 8,880.66 RMB) per patient. Hospitalized for benign skin tumors, psoriasis, eczema/dermatitis, and urticaria were mainly in the 15-44, 15-44, ≥60 and 5-44 age group, respectively. CONCLUSION: The burden of skin diseases in China showed an increased trend before the COVID-19 pandemic. Dermatology service in China showed an east-west inverse pattern between outpatient and inpatient care. Resource allocation should consider both outpatient and inpatient data. Eczema/dermatitis had the highest hospitalization burden, while psoriasis had the longest stays and highest costs. Meanwhile, age-stratified strategies should be implemented in skin diseases clinical management.

Pre-Analytical Errors Before, During, and After the COVID-19 Pandemic: A Multi-Year Retrospective Observational Study.
OBJECTIVE: The pre-analytical phase is the stage at which laboratory errors most frequently occur and is therefore of critical importance for patient safety. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the marked increase in workload, organizational restructuring, staff and resource redeployment, changes in patient volume and clinical workflows, and disease-related pathophysiological alterations affecting specimen characteristics created unprecedented conditions that could influence laboratory quality indicators. This study aimed to characterize changes in specimen rejection rates across the pre-pandemic, pandemic, and normalization periods between 2018 and 2023, and to determine whether pandemic-related disruptions in health care delivery were associated with differences in the number, rate, and distribution of specimen rejections according to clinical unit, rejection reason, and time interval, with emphasis on the magnitude of these differences rather than statistical significance alone. The study also sought to generate evidence that could inform the development of preventive systems and strengthen laboratory preparedness for future large-scale disruptions to health care services. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective observational study used routinely collected, aggregated laboratory information system (LIS) data from the Central Laboratory of Istanbul Atlas University Hospital for 1 January 2018 through 31 December 2023. The LIS extract was restricted to eligible specimen types, including spot and 24 h urine, serum, and whole-blood or plasma specimens collected in EDTA-, citrate-, or heparin-containing tubes; all other specimen types were excluded. Specimen rejection rates were evaluated by study period, clinical unit, time interval, and rejection reason. For cross-period comparisons, the total number of specimens within each respective study period was used as the denominator for calculating rejection rates, whereas for rejection-reason-specific analyses, the number of specimen types relevant to each rejection category was used as the denominator. Negative-binomial regression with denominator-based offsets estimated adjusted rejection-rate ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), with Bonferroni adjustment for selected pairwise comparisons. No missing or unclassifiable values were identified; no imputation was required. Reporting follows STROBE and the RECORD extension for studies using routinely collected health data. RESULTS: The overall rejection rate increased progressively from 0.23% in the pre-pandemic period to 0.49% during the pandemic and 0.65% in the normalization period, and monthly observed rates supported this progressive increase. In adjusted terms, the rejection rate was 2.20-fold higher during the pandemic than in the pre-pandemic period (95% CI: 1.96-2.46) and increased a further 1.42-fold in the normalization period compared with the pandemic period (95% CI: 1.27-1.59). Across clinical units, the emergency department had the highest observed rejection rate, whereas intensive care units showed the highest adjusted rejection rates during the pandemic (RR = 1.34 versus the emergency department, 95% CI: 1.00-1.80) and normalization periods. Hemolysis and clotting were the dominant rejection reasons; although clotting had the highest observed rates in the pre-pandemic and pandemic periods, hemolysis ranked highest after adjustment in all periods and separated significantly from clotting only in the normalization period (RR = 1.97, 95% CI: 1.65-2.35). Time-interval effects were context-dependent rather than uniform and became informative mainly in combination with clinical unit or rejection reason: intensive care unit rejections peaked in the daytime interval during the pandemic (RR = 1.84 versus the evening interval, 95% CI: 1.06-3.19), and in the normalization period emergency department-hemolysis emerged as the leading adjusted clinical unit-rejection reason combination (RR = 1.89 versus intensive care unit-hemolysis, 95% CI: 1.19-3.00), while clotting remained centered on intensive care units and became more concentrated in the overnight and early-morning interval. CONCLUSIONS: Pre-analytical specimen rejection increased progressively across the pre-pandemic, pandemic, and normalization periods, with adjusted effect sizes indicating a substantial and sustained deterioration rather than a transient pandemic-related disturbance, and with persistent differences in rejection patterns according to clinical unit, time interval, and rejection reason. The further increase observed in the normalization period suggests that pandemic-related disruptions were associated with sustained changes in pre-analytical performance but were unlikely to be the sole explanation. Emergency department-hemolysis during the normalization period and intensive care unit-related clotting emerged as the most concrete quality-monitoring targets. Integrating rejection rates and counts with stratified monitoring by clinical unit, time interval, and rejection reason in combination may support earlier identification of emerging risks, more targeted preventive interventions, and stronger laboratory preparedness for future large-scale disruptions to health care services.

Development of a Single Thermal Cycling Multiplex RT-qPCR Assay for Rapid Arbovirus Detection.
Background: The co-circulation of multiple arboviruses with similar clinical presentations poses a significant challenge for public health surveillance. This study aimed to develop and clinically validate a novel multiplex RT-qPCR assay for the simultaneous detection of five arboviruses in three reactions. Methods: A diagnostic accuracy study was conducted in Salvador, Brazil. Evaluation was performed using 254 prospective serum samples and 34 archived positive samples. The primers and probes for the assay were designed in silico, all targeting highly conserved regions of Dengue (DENV), Zika (ZIKV), Chikungunya (CHIKV), Oropouche (OROV), and West Nile (WNV) viruses. The protocol was optimized in three reactions with a single thermal cycle, comprising a tetraplex reaction (DENV, CHIKV, ZIKV, and hRNAseP, an endogenous control) and two singleplex reactions (OROV and WNV). Results: In prospective analysis, the assay identified 45 DENV, 3 CHIKV, and 9 OROV-positive cases. Diagnostic accuracy for DENV and CHIKV was 96% (95% CI: 93.3-98.0%), successfully detecting four DENV cases missed by the reference standard. Furthermore, incorporating OROV enabled the identification of nine cases that conventional triplex protocols would have overlooked. Conclusion: This single-cycling multiplex RT-qPCR assay enhances epidemiological surveillance by expanding detection beyond traditional triplex targets to include OROV and WNV. This operational optimization reduces turnaround times and prevents the underdiagnosis of emerging arboviruses, serving as a robust diagnostic tool for endemic regions.

Sentinel surveillance of acute febrile illness in a Brazilian Amazon region: laboratory findings and epidemiological implications.
The Amapa State, Brazil, in the Amazon region and bordering French Guiana, is a strategic sentinel location for infectious disease surveillance. Ecological pressures such as deforestation, artisanal gold mining, and high human mobility contribute to complex transmission dynamics of arboviruses, bacterial infections, and other pathogens. This study aims to characterize the etiologies of acute febrile illness (AFI) reported in Amapa State in 2018-2020, focusing on arbovirus circulation, bacterial contributions, and emerging pathogens. A retrospective analysis was carried out with 727 AFI cases. Laboratory diagnoses were established using molecular and serological assays, with systematic testing for different pathogens. Definitive diagnoses were obtained in 185 individuals (25.4%), yielding 209 positive results and including 23 cases of co-infection. Dengue virus was the predominant etiological agent (n=109, 52%), followed by leptospirosis (n=20, 9.5%), chikungunya virus (n=16, 7.6%), parvovirus B19 (n=16, 7.6%), measles (n=15, 7.1%), zika virus (n=10, 4.8%), mayaro virus (n=1,0.5%), and other bacterial infections (n=5, 2.4%). Isolated cases of hepatitis A and B, malaria, SARS-CoV-2, enterovirus, and acute Chagas disease were also identified. No hepatitis E virus or oropouche cases were detected. Dengue virus was the leading cause of AFI. Leptospirosis, chikungunya virus, and parvovirus B19 were other prevalent and often underrecognized contributors. The detection of additional viruses highlights Amapa State as a potential zone of "silent expansion" for emerging arboviruses. Co-detection of multiple pathogens underscores diagnostic complexity in regions with overlapping transmission. Strengthening surveillance, expanding laboratory capacity, and prioritizing differential diagnostics are essential to capture epidemiological dynamics and guide public health interventions.

Measles outbreak in a unique sociocultural context: epidemiological investigation and control measures in Northern Brazil, 2025.
After the recertification of measles elimination in Brazil, outbreaks associated with imported cases may occur in pockets of susceptible individuals, including communities with low vaccination coverage. This study describes an outbreak investigation conducted in 2025 in Campos Lindos, Tocantins State, Brazil. In total, 25 cases were confirmed, mostly among unvaccinated Old Believers (a traditional community of Russian origin) following viral introduction linked to international travel, with transmission occurring predominantly within the community. Outbreak response measures, including ring vaccination and active case finding, interrupted transmission after 12 weeks with no new cases. The rapid response was effective and reinforces the importance of identifying susceptibility pockets in the population to prevent measles reintroduction.

Identifying Risk Factors for PICU Mortality in Pediatric Cancer Patients: A 10-Year Retrospective Study.
This 10-year retrospective study of pediatric cancer patients requiring intensive care evaluates mortality risk factors. The data included patients' demographics, cancer types, admission reasons, treatment modalities, and laboratory results. Standardized mortality ratio (SMR), mortality at different intervals, length of stay, and risk factors for death were analyzed. The most common malignancy was leukemia (n=116, 37.0%), followed by noncentral nervous system solid tumors (n=71, 22.6%). The acute kidney injury (AKI) rate was 23.7% (n=74), with 55.4% requiring renal replacement therapy (RRT). RRT indications included tumor lysis syndrome, AKI, fluid overload, and treatment toxicity. 66.7% of leukemia patients and 64.7% of lymphoma patients needed RRT (P=0.012). Three patients underwent extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, one of them was successfully weaned; however, died later due to sepsis. The crude mortality rate was 17.6% (n=47). SMR was 0.51. The highest PICU mortality rate occurred among leukemia patients (19.1%). Multivariate analysis showed that age and invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) were significantly associated with PICU mortality. NIV was used in 25 patients, and only one patient required intubation. IMV was independently associated with increased mortality (OR: 9.029, 95% CI: 2.921-27.914, P<0.001).

Small quantity lipid-based nutritional supplementation and measles vaccination coverage in children aged 6-23 months: a pragmatic cluster-randomized trial.
Undernutrition and infectious diseases pose a double threat to child survival, especially in areas with a high malnutrition burden and low vaccination coverage. In this study, we evaluated whether distributing preventive small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) alongside routine immunization services may increase vaccine uptake in a pediatric, pragmatic, cluster-randomized controlled trial in northern Nigeria. Twenty geographically defined clusters across two Local Government Areas were randomized 1:1 to the NutriVax strategy (intervention) or standard National Program of Immunization (NPI) services (control). NutriVax provided a monthly ration of SQ-LNS to children aged 6-23 months after routine NPI delivery at primary healthcare centers. The primary outcome was coverage of the first dose of measles-containing vaccine (MCV1) verified by vaccination card among children aged 12-23 months, assessed in an endline population-based household cross-sectional survey 12 months after conducting a similar baseline survey. The endline survey included 1,604 children (801 control, 803 NutriVax); 48% of children surveyed in intervention clusters had ever received SQ-LNS. The odds of receiving card-verified MCV1 were two times higher in the NutriVax arm than in the control arm (odds ratio = 2.08, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.30-3.35, P = 0.004). The difference-in-differences, cluster conditional analysis indicated a 20.1 percentage-point (pp) increase in MCV1 coverage from baseline (95% CI: 13.7-26.5 pp, P < 0.0001) relative to the control arm. Co-delivering SQ-LNS with routine immunization substantially improved card-verified MCV1 uptake, supporting a scalable strategy to make progress toward targets set by the World Health Organization's Immunization Agenda 2030 in similar settings. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT06387511 .

Whole-brain cortical morphometry and structural covariance network disruption in subacute sclerosing panencephalitis.
BACKGROUND: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a progressive, fatal encephalitis caused by persistent measles virus infection. Quantitative cortical imaging in SSPE remains poorly characterised, and the topology of the cortical structural covariance network (SCN) has not been examined. OBJECTIVE: To characterise whole-brain cortical structural alterations in SSPE using surface-based morphometry (SBM) and voxel-based morphometry (VBM), evaluate their clinical correlates, and describe the topology of the cortical SCN. METHODS: Twenty-eight patients with SSPE and 48 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent 3.0 T volumetric T1-weighted MRI. SBM was performed in FreeSurfer using the Desikan-Killiany (DK) atlas, adjusted for age and sex; VBM used the FSL-VBM pipeline with threshold-free cluster enhancement, adjusted for age, sex and total intracranial volume. Clinical associations used Pearson correlation with false discovery rate (FDR) correction and Spearman sensitivity analyses; severity was quantified with the Neurological Disability Index. Group-level SCNs were constructed from age- and sex-adjusted regional thickness correlations; graph metrics were computed across 16 network densities and summarised as the area under the metric-versus-density curve, so that findings do not depend on a single arbitrary threshold. Group differences were assessed by subject-label permutation testing with bootstrap confidence intervals. RESULTS: VBM identified widespread bilateral grey matter volume reduction extending from cortex into deep grey matter and cerebellum, with additional right-lateralised clusters in the planum temporale and frontal pole. Vertex-wise SBM demonstrated 35 bilateral cortical thickness clusters and 21 cortical volume clusters; in the covariate-adjusted regional analysis, 38 of 68 DK regions showed significant thinning after FDR correction, and 18 of 68 regions showed significant volume reduction, most prominently the bilateral frontal pole and posterior cortices. Cortical thickness and volume correlated negatively with disease duration across most regions, but not with clinical severity. SCN metrics differed consistently in direction across all densities - longer characteristic path length, higher modularity and local efficiency, and loss of degree assortativity in patients - but no metric difference survived subject-label permutation testing after FDR correction (smallest adjusted p = 0.24); SCN findings are therefore reported as descriptive. CONCLUSIONS: SSPE produces widespread, duration-dependent cortical thinning and grey matter volume loss involving association, limbic and primary cortices. Group-level SCN topology showed a consistent directional pattern of network reorganisation that did not reach corrected statistical significance at this sample size. Prospective, longitudinal and multi-centre studies are required before any clinical application of these measures can be considered.

The Impermanence of Public Health Gains-Lessons Learned from Measles Resurgence, Bangladesh, 2026.
The global resurgence of measles is a major public health concern. After the success of its Expanded Programme on Immunization, Bangladesh experienced a measles resurgence in 2026. The country faced major setbacks after measles vaccination coverage declined because of political instability, discontent among field-level staff, change in procurement policy, COVID-19-related service disruptions, and delayed supplementary immunization campaigns. During March 15-September 13, 2026, Bangladesh reported 170,638 suspected and 20,006 confirmed measles cases, including 919 deaths among suspected and 100 deaths among laboratory-confirmed cases. The outbreak disproportionately affected unvaccinated and underimmunized children. Political turmoil during 2024-2025 disrupted vaccine procurement, delayed mass vaccination campaigns, weakened the health workforce, and compromised financial and logistic continuity. Simultaneously, disruptions in vitamin A supplementation and worsening child malnutrition amplified disease severity. To prevent future resurgence, immunization programs must be depoliticized, supported by buffer vaccine stocks, strengthened through microlevel surveillance, and integrated with nutrition and primary healthcare services.

Nationwide Surveillance and Control Measures during Large Measles Outbreak, Bangladesh, 2026.
Nationwide surveillance in Bangladesh during April 2-May 27, 2026, identified a total of 67,079 suspected and 8,834 confirmed measles cases across 8 administrative divisions. Among suspected cases, 472 deaths were reported, and 88 deaths were reported among confirmed cases. Despite high reported vaccine coverage, transmission persisted amid residual immunity gaps. Vaccine stockouts, discontinued vaccination campaigns, and coverage overestimation likely contributed to Bangladesh's largest recorded measles outbreak.

Genomic Epidemiology and Antimicrobial Susceptibility of Human Brucellosis - Shenzhen City, Guangdong Province, China, 2005-2024.
WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ABOUT THIS TOPIC?: Brucellosis is a zoonotic disease historically concentrated in pastoral regions of China; however, an increasing number of cases have been reported in large urban centers in recent years. WHAT IS ADDED BY THIS REPORT?: Analysis of 191 human-derived Brucella isolates collected in Shenzhen between 2005 and 2024 showed that Brucella melitensis predominated and that Shenzhen isolates were interspersed with strains from multiple provinces, suggesting repeated introductions from other regions. Most cases occurred in working-age adults, and both imported cases and Shenzhen-resident cases without documented external exposure were identified. WHAT ARE THE IMPLICATIONS FOR PUBLIC HEALTH PRACTICE?: These findings suggest that brucellosis control in highly urbanized settings should prioritize surveillance for imported infections, improved traceability and regulation of animal-derived food products, targeted protection of high-risk occupational groups, and continued genomic and antimicrobial susceptibility surveillance.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae PCR positivity rate among children in Chengdu, China: a retrospective cross-sectional epidemiological study.
BACKGROUND: Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP) is one of the most common pathogens responsible for respiratory infections in children. The objective of this study was to investigate MP positivity rate and its distribution characteristics across different clinical diagnostic groups among children in Chengdu, China. METHODS: A retrospective cross-sectional study was conducted at a single center in Chengdu, China, involving children aged 0-18 years who underwent MP polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing based on clinician requisition or self-requested laboratory testing (SRLT) between January 1 and December 31, 2024. χ2 tests and multivariable logistic regression models were applied for statistical analyses. RESULTS: Among 94,889 children (51,105 males and 43,784 females), the overall MP positivity rate was 12.3%, with no significant difference between sexes. Across five clinical diagnostic groups, MP positivity rate was highest in the acute lower respiratory tract infections (ALRTIs) group (13.9%), followed by the SRLT group (12.8%); both were significantly higher than those in the chronic respiratory diseases (CRDs) group (8.8%), the acute upper respiratory tract infections (AURTIs) group (6.6%), and the non-respiratory diseases (NRDs) group (4.8%). MP positivity rates in the ALRTIs, AURTIs, NRDs, and SRLT groups showed significant seasonal variation, peaking in winter, followed by spring; both seasons exhibited significantly higher positivity rates than summer and autumn. Monthly MP positivity rate peaked in January and February across all groups, after which it generally decreased with mild fluctuations, with the ALRTIs group consistently exhibiting the highest positivity rate. Among children with ALRTIs and AURTIs, MP positivity rates were significantly higher in school-aged, preschool, and adolescent children than in toddlers, infants, and newborns (p < 0.001). Multivariable logistic regression analysis revealed that MP positivity was independently associated with healthcare setting (inpatient vs. outpatient/emergency, OR: 1.24, 95% CI: 1.15-1.35), and PCR assay type (multiplex vs. singleplex, OR: 2.45, 95% CI: 2.25-2.67). CONCLUSIONS: Among children in Chengdu in 2024, MP PCR positivity peaked in winter (January-February) and was highest in school-aged children. These single-year findings may help inform local surveillance and guide future long-term epidemiological monitoring.

Immune mechanisms underlying endothelial and placental dysfunction in leptospirosis during pregnancy.
Leptospirosis is a zoonotic disease caused by pathogenic bacteria of the genus Leptospira and represents a major public health concern worldwide. Although its systemic manifestations are well documented, the consequences of leptospirosis for reproduction and pregnancy, particularly in humans, remain poorly understood. This narrative review summarizes the principal reproductive outcomes associated with leptospirosis and examines the mechanisms that may contribute to pregnancy complications. In livestock, leptospirosis is a well-established cause of reproductive failure, including abortion and infertility, and is frequently associated with persistent infection and colonization of the genital tract. In humans, where available evidence remains limited, adverse pregnancy outcomes may be mediated predominantly by systemic endothelial injury, inflammatory activation, and immune dysregulation leading to impaired placental perfusion, rather than solely by direct infection of placental tissues. We therefore integrate evidence from veterinary research and human studies to examine the biological mechanisms through which leptospirosis may contribute to pregnancy complications and potentially overlap with other pregnancy-related disorders. A One Health approach that combines human, animal, and environmental data is essential to improve disease prevention, reduce its reproductive burden, and protect the health of pregnant individuals and their developing fetuses.

Safety of PCV13 with Different Carrier Proteins (CRM197, TT, and TT/DT) - Jiangsu Province, China, 2022-2024.
INTRODUCTION: This study aimed to evaluate the safety of three kinds of 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCV13) with different carrier proteins - cross-reactive material 197 (CRM197), tetanus toxoid (TT), and a novel tetanus toxoid/diphtheria toxoid (TT/DT) dual-carrier - by monitoring adverse events following immunization (AEFI) in Jiangsu Province, China. METHODS: The Chinese National Adverse Events Following Immunization Information System and Jiangsu Province Vaccination Integrated Service Management Information System were used. Reporting rates (RR) per 100,000 doses were calculated and stratified. Chi-square tests with Bonferroni correction and disproportionality analyses were performed. RESULTS: A total of 1,734,810 PCV13 doses were administered, with 5,195 AEFI reports (RR=299.46 per 100,000 doses). RR was highest for TT/DT-carrier (399.84 per 100,000 doses) versus CRM197-carrier (286.69 per 100,000 doses) and TT-carrier (286.01 per 100,000 doses). Common adverse reactions accounted for 98.23% (5,103/5,195) of all AEFIs, with fever, local redness, and induration being the most common. Disproportionality analysis revealed positive signals for general reactions. CONCLUSION: All three PCV13 carrier protein types demonstrated acceptable safety profiles in Jiangsu Province from 2022 to 2024. Despite a higher RR for TT/DT-carrier PCV13 than for the other two PCV13 carrier protein types, most AEFIs were mild and common reactions.

Distinct time-dependent S. Typhi-specific CD8+ T cell programs are associated with clinical outcome following Ty21a immunization and wild-type S. Typhi challenge in humans.
INTRODUCTION: CD8+ T cells are essential components of the adaptive immune system that play a critical role in determining the clinical severity of typhoid disease by directly killing Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (S. Typhi)-infected cells, producing cytokines, chemokines, and establishing memory responses that have been linked to clinical outcome in a controlled human infection model (CHIM) of typhoid. Despite decades of extensive research, the role of memory CD8+ T (TM) cells and its subsets as correlates of protection against S. Typhi infection and typhoid disease remains incompletely understood. METHODS: In this study, we used specimens from a typhoid CHIM study in which participants who were immunized with live attenuated S. Typhi vaccine, Ty21a, were subsequently challenged with virulent S. Typhi. Some participants developed typhoid disease (TD) and some did not (NoTD), allowing us to assess the immune program of CD8+ TM subsets involved in the prevention of typhoid disease using mass cytometry, CyTOF. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION: Our high-dimensional profiling data showed that TD and NoTD participants followed divergent memory CD8+ T cell trajectories. We observed that CD8+ T clusters from NoTD participants are enriched for early multifunctional, protection-associated programs while TD participants exhibited a distinct clustering associated with susceptibility states. Specifically, using unsupervised dimensionality reduction and clustering analysis, T-REX, and feature-ranking analyses, we identified memory CD8+ T cell subsets including effector/memory (TEM), T central/memory (TCM) and CD45RA+ TEM (TEMRA) associated with clinical outcomes. CD8+ TEM from NoTD participants were generally characterized by stronger effector-associated signatures such as CXCR3, IL-17A, TNFα, and MIP1b. In contrast, CD8+ TEM from TD participants showed CCR6- and integrin α4β7-biased immune profiles. Detailed analysis revealed that CD8⁺ TCM and TEMRA subsets also contained distinct outcome-associated states. These patterns were confirmed by conventional supervised gating that validated both protection-associated and susceptibility-associated marker combinations across CD8+ TEM, TCM and TEMRA subsets. These data suggest that: 1. Protection and susceptibility are not restricted to one CD8+ T cell subset but rather are distributed across the broader CD8+ T memory landscape and, 2. Typhoid clinical outcome is associated with qualitatively distinct CD8+ T memory programs rather than differences only in the magnitude of the overall anti-S. Typhi immune response.

Zinc Homeostasis in Brucella ovis Under Zinc Scarcity: Characterization of the ZnuABC Zinc Import System and of a Newly Identified Gene of the Zur Regulon.
The zinc import system ZnuABC is essential for the virulence of smooth (bearing O-polysaccharide chains) zoonotic Brucella species but remains uncharacterized in the non-zoonotic rough (lacking O-chains) species Brucella ovis, the causative agent of a type of ovine brucellosis of veterinary and economic importance. In this study, we constructed a panel of B. ovis mutants for genes of the znuACB locus that were characterized by evaluating growth, gene expression, protein abundance, metal content, and virulence in mice. We identified a ZigA ortholog (uncharacterized in the genus Brucella but linked to zinc homeostasis and histidine metabolism in other bacteria) that belongs to the Zur regulon and is transcriptionally modulated in a zinc-dependent manner as the ZnuABC system. A potential link of B. ovis ZigA with histidine catabolism and a crosstalk between the homeostasis of zinc and other metals have been identified as areas for further exploration. Remarkably, the znuA, zigAznuA and znuACB mutants of B. ovis displayed wild-type virulence in mice, which contrasts with the reported attenuation for the znuA mutant of smooth zoonotic Brucella species sharing a high degree of DNA homology. These results significantly enlarge the knowledge about the metallobiology of the genus Brucella, providing new perspectives for related research.

Changing Burden of Opportunistic Infections in the New ART Era.
INTRODUCTION: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) remains a major global health challenge, characterized by progressive CD4⁺ T-cell depletion leading to opportunistic infections (OIs) and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). Despite widespread antiretroviral therapy (ART) coverage, significant disparities persist, particularly in resource-limited settings. This review critically appraises the evolving burden and spectrum of OIs in the pre- and post-ART eras. METHODS: A comprehensive literature search for this narrative review was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Google Scholar using the most relevant keywords focused on epidemiological trends, clinical manifestations, and outcomes of OIs across ART eras, combined with the Boolean operator "AND". Studies published in English from inception through April 5, 2026, were included. RESULTS: The pre-ART era was marked by a high incidence of severe, disseminated OIs. The advent of combination ART, particularly highly active ART (HAART), led to substantial immune restoration and a marked decline in the incidence and severity of most OIs. Notably, CMV disease, Kaposi's sarcoma, tuberculosis, and Pneumocystis pneumonia have significantly decreased in PLWH in the post-ART period. However, OIs persist in individuals with delayed diagnosis, poor adherence, or treatment failure. Additionally, the post-ART era has seen emerging challenges, including immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS), antimicrobial resistance, chronic viral co-infections, and a rising burden of non-AIDS-defining malignancies. DISCUSSION: ART has transformed HIV into a chronic, manageable condition for most patients. Most studies show an ART-associated decline in the epidemiology of OIs in HIV, shifting the pattern from acute, life-threatening infections to a manageable chronic infectious condition, with or without immune-mediated complications such as IRIS. However, persistent inequities in ART access, late presentation, and incomplete immune recovery sustain the global burden of OIs. CONCLUSION: Although ART has dramatically reduced OI-related morbidity and mortality, these infections remain a significant concern. Strengthening early diagnosis, ensuring universal ART access, and improving adherence are essential to further reduce the burden of HIV-associated OIs.

Mortality of Candida auris candidemia compared with non-auris candidemia: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
BACKGROUND: Candida auris has emerged as a globally significant healthcare-associated fungal pathogen. Although descriptive studies have reported high mortality for candidemia caused by C. auris, whether the mortality differs from non-auris candidemia remains unclear. We conducted this meta-analysis to compare the mortality between patients with C. auris and non-auris candidemia. METHODS: We searched PubMed (including MEDLINE), Embase, and Web of Science databases for relevant studies published before June 2026. A random-effects model was used for meta-analysis. RESULTS: A total of 16 articles were included in this meta-analysis. In the pooled crude analysis, mortality was significantly lower in patients with C. auris candidemia than in those with non-auris candidemia (OR = 0.77, 95% CI 0.67-0.90). Subgroup analyses showed significant geographic variation (P for interaction = 0.019), with lower mortality observed in studies from Turkey, the Middle East and the Americas, but not in South Asia and Africa. Despite lower mortality, C. auris candidemia was associated with prolonged hospitalization in descriptive analysis. CONCLUSION: In this meta-analysis of crude estimates, mortality was significantly lower in patients with C. auris candidemia than in those with non-auris candidemia. However, prolonged hospitalization in C. auris infection highlights its medical resource burden. For clinicians, management of C. auris candidemia should focus on timely diagnosis, appropriate antifungal therapy, and strengthened infection prevention, especially in cases of long-term hospitalization.

Leishmania respiration profiling as a One Health functional marker associated with antimony resistance in human and canine leishmaniases.
Rapid functional tools for assessing antimony susceptibility in Leishmania are needed to strengthen resistance surveillance across human and veterinary settings. We developed a real-time oxygen-consumption assay using the Resipher analyzer and evaluated normalized oxygen-consumption rate (OCR) as a functional correlate of antimony (Sb) resistance in Leishmania infantum and Leishmania donovani. A density of 1 × 107 parasites/mL and a 48-h readout provided the most robust analytical window, and rotenone markedly reduced OCR, demonstrating assay responsiveness to respiratory perturbation. Antimony-resistant laboratory lines showed lower OCR/proliferation ratios than the wild-type strain. This phenotype was reproduced in ten canine L. infantum field isolates and ten human L. donovani clinical isolates. OCR/proliferation ratio was inversely correlated with promastigote (L. infantum: r = -0.8930, p = 0.0008; L. donovani: r = -0.8470, p = 0.0019) and intracellular-amastigote Sb EC50 values (L. infantum: r = -0.8787, p = 0.0008; L. donovani: r = -0.7964, p = 0.0058). Under isolate-specific Sb EC90 exposure, resistant isolates accumulated less ROS, which was positively associated with OCR/proliferation ratio (L. infantum: r = 0.6927, p = 0.0390; L. donovani: r = 0.7560, p = 0.0114). Low-OCR isolates were also less sensitive to rotenone and antimycin A, indicating broader bioenergetic remodeling. Normalized OCR is a functional correlate of Sb susceptibility and a complementary phenotypic screening approach for One Health surveillance. Future studies incorporating larger and more genetically diverse isolate collections, prospective susceptibility testing, and inter-laboratory standardization will enable the definition of robust analytical thresholds and facilitate implementation in resistance-surveillance programs.

Investigation of suspected Candidozyma auris outbreaks in Malaysia using integrated genomic, clinical, and antifungal susceptibility analyses.
Candidozyma auris (formerly Candida auris) is an emerging multidrug-resistant fungus with limited genomic epidemiological data from Malaysia. This study investigated the genomic epidemiology, clinical characteristics and antifungal susceptibility of C. auris outbreak isolates using an integrated whole-genome sequencing (WGS) approach. Eleven clinical C. auris isolates from five healthcare facilities across three Malaysian states were analysed alongside clinical and epidemiological data. Antifungal susceptibility testing was performed for azoles, echinocandins, amphotericin B, flucytosine, and manogepix. Among 11 patients, seven had candidemia and four were colonized. Median age was 48 years, with diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, and hypertension as the most common comorbidities. All candidemia patients had urinary and central venous catheters; 71% required mechanical ventilation, 43% had haemodialysis and recent surgery, respectively. Recent antibiotic exposure was common, whereas none had prior antifungal therapy. All isolates belonged to Clade I but separated into distinct genomic clusters, supporting healthcare-associated transmission within clusters and simultaneous circulation of multiple genomic groups. All Johor-associated isolates were fluconazole resistant and carried ERG11 K143R and CDR1 V704L substitutions. An ERG5 variant was detected in non-Johor isolates with amphotericin B minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) ≥ 1 µg/ml. The MICs for other antifungals remained low across isolates. Echinocandin therapy was initiated in 27% of patients, with one survivor. Our C. auris showed genomic diversity, distinct healthcare-associated clustering, and variable antifungal susceptibility. Integrating WGS with clinical and susceptibility data enhanced outbreak investigation of C. auris.

Gastrointestinal and hepatic endoparasites of domestic guinea pigs (Cavia porcellus (Linnaeus, 1758)): Diversity, diagnosis, epidemiology, and clinical relevance.
The guinea pig (Cavia porcellus (Linnaeus, 1758)) is a popular companion animal and an important laboratory model. Gastrointestinal and hepatic endoparasites are documented in this host across companion, laboratory and production settings, but the available evidence is methodologically heterogeneous and should be interpreted at study level. This structured narrative review summarizes parasite diversity, host-specific clinical evidence, diagnostic approaches and epidemiological findings. Particular emphasis is placed on separating parasite detection from infection intensity and attributable clinical disease, and on avoiding zoonotic inference without species-, genotype- or assemblage-level evidence. Across the reviewed literature, Paraspidodera uncinata and Eimeria spp. are recurrent findings, while molecular studies have refined interpretation of Cryptosporidium, Giardia and Balantioides. A source-level audit of epidemiological studies highlights substantial variation in analysis units and diagnostic methods, including pooled farm samples, individual fecal samples, post-mortem examinations and molecular assays. These differences preclude direct regional prevalence comparisons. Future studies should report explicit numerators, denominators, units of analysis, diagnostic endpoints and molecular resolution to improve comparability and One Health interpretation.

Evaluation of a multiplex qPCR assay for rapid diagnosis of fungal pneumonia and tuberculosis in people with advanced HIV disease.
Fungal pneumonias and tuberculosis (TB) remain major causes of mortality among people living with advanced HIV disease (PLWHA). Their overlapping clinical manifestations delay diagnosis in developed and resource-limited settings, with greater impact where access to rapid diagnostic tools is limited. This study evaluated the performance of a multiplex quantitative PCR (qPCR) assay for simultaneous detection of Histoplasma capsulatum, Cryptococcus neoformans, Pneumocystis jirovecii, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex in respiratory samples from PLWHA. A cross-sectional study was conducted at the Instituto Nacional de Infectologia Evandro Chagas (Rio de Janeiro, Brazil) between December 2023 and March 2025. Adults with HIV infection (CD4 < 200 cells/mm³) and clinical or radiological evidence of pulmonary infection were enrolled. Standard diagnostic methods included culture, microscopy, antigen detection (CrAg-LFA, urinary Histoplasma antigen, TB-LAM), GeneXpert® MTB/RIF, and commercial qPCR for P. jirovecii. The multiplex assay targeted the ITS region (H. capsulatum and C. neoformans), mtLSU (P. jirovecii), and IS6110 (M. tuberculosis). Among 198 screened participants, 88 met inclusion criteria (mean CD4 count: 56 cells/µl). Diagnosis included TB (56.8%), pneumocystosis (34.1%), histoplasmosis (10.2%), and cryptococcosis (11.4%); 25% presented coinfections. The multiplex qPCR showed 100% sensitivity for histoplasmosis, 80% for pneumocystosis, and 40% for both cryptococcosis and TB, with specificities ≥ 82% and 100% for TB. Overall accuracy ranged from 66% to 86%. Mortality was 12.5%, highest among cryptococcosis cases (20%). The assay provided accurate detection of H. capsulatum and P. jirovecii, although performance was limited for TB and cryptococcosis, supporting its use as a complementary molecular tool for differential diagnosis in PLWHA.

Pulmonary cryptococcosis mimicking metastatic progression despite systemic disease stability in advanced colon cancer: A case report and literature review.
RATIONALE: In patients with advanced cancer, newly detected pulmonary nodules are often interpreted as metastatic progression. The distinctive feature of this case was the appearance of multiple new lung nodules during otherwise controlled systemic disease: the primary colonic lesion and hepatic metastases remained stable while tumor marker levels declined. This radiologic-clinical discordance prompted reconsideration of metastatic progression and broadened the differential diagnosis. PATIENT CONCERNS: A patient with advanced colon cancer, who was undergoing systemic chemotherapy and had otherwise stable disease, was found to have developed new pulmonary nodules on routine surveillance imaging. The patient was entirely asymptomatic from a respiratory standpoint. The primary clinical concern was the discordance between the radiologically suspicious findings and the patient's overall stable clinical condition. DIAGNOSES: The initial radiologic impression favored pulmonary metastases. However, multidisciplinary review recognized the discordance between the new lung lesions and the otherwise stable systemic disease and raised concern for an opportunistic infection. Serum (1,3)-β-D-glucan and qualitative cryptococcal capsular polysaccharide antigen tests were positive, supporting a diagnosis of pulmonary cryptococcosis. INTERVENTIONS: After cerebrospinal fluid evaluation excluded central nervous system involvement, fluconazole 400 mg once daily was initiated. The anticancer strategy was not escalated on the basis of the pulmonary findings alone. OUTCOMES: Follow-up chest computed tomography demonstrated marked regression of the pulmonary nodules. LESSONS: When new pulmonary lesions arise despite stability or response at established tumor sites, apparent radiologic progression should not automatically be equated with oncologic progression. Integrating the longitudinal treatment response, tumor marker trends, clinical symptoms, imaging features, and targeted infectious testing can prevent unnecessary changes in cancer therapy and may avoid invasive procedures when a sufficiently supported alternative diagnosis is available.

Candidozyma auris (Candida auris) as a harbinger of novel fungal pathogens.
Mammals are protected from fungal pathogens by two evolutionary pillars: adaptive immunity and elevated body temperature. Anthropogenic climate change is eroding this thermal barrier, while a concurrent decline in human basal body temperature accelerates convergence from both directions. Candida auris, a thermotolerant, multidrug-resistant pathogen, arose independently as genetically distinct clades on multiple continents, a pattern implicating shared selective pressures rather than clonal spread. Unlike its closest relatives, which grow poorly at mammalian temperatures, it thrives at 37°C, tolerates up to 47°C, persists on hospital surfaces, resists all three major antifungal classes, and causes invasive infections with 30-60% mortality. We review its evolutionary biology, ecology, and clinical significance, evaluating hypotheses for its origin, and the mechanisms underlying its thermotolerance and virulence. C. auris may be the first of many fungi adapting to breach mammalian thermal defenses, making predictive frameworks for fungal disease emergence an urgent priority.

Antenatal interventions to support newborn survival: updates for the Lives Saved Tool.
BACKGROUND: Antenatal care strategies encompass a series of interventions delivered to expectant mothers to optimise both their health outcomes and those of their neonate. We summarise the most recent effect estimates for maternal immunisation, screening and management of infections, pre-existing chronic diseases such as hypertension and diabetes, nutrition, psychosocial interventions for smoking cessation, pre-term pre-labour rupture of membranes, administration of corticosteroids for foetal lung maturation, and induction of post-term labour. METHODS: We synthesised effect estimates for antenatal and intrapartum interventions using PubMed and CENTRAL searches (2022-2023) and in consultation with a technical advisory group to determine whether and how new meta-analysed effect estimates could be incorporated into the Lives Saved Tool (LiST) model, as well as which of these estimates should be updated and which should be retained. RESULTS: Tetanus toxoid vaccination during the antenatal period lead to a significant reduction in neonatal mortality. Antibiotics for pre-term pre-labour rupture of membranes and administration of corticosteroids for foetal lung maturation lead to significant reductions in neonatal mortality due to sepsis and prematurity, respectively. Nutritional interventions including balanced protein and energy supplementation and multiple micronutrient supplementation reduced the risks of small-for-gestational-age babies. Insecticide-treated bed-nets for malaria, antibiotic treatment of syphilis, and post-term induction of labour demonstrated significant reductions in the risks of stillbirth. The effect estimates for preterm births contributed to the LiST model for interventions including treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria, omega-3 fatty acid supplementation, calcium supplementation, and provision of low-dose aspirin for pre-eclampsia, which projected significant reductions in the risks of small-for-gestational-age babies. CONCLUSIONS: The evidence described here highlights the potential impact of implementing high-yield healthcare packages in context-specific settings to effectively improve neonatal survival. These estimates can be used as inputs to model the impact of antenatal care interventions using the LiST.

Mucormycosis outbreak caused by Rhizomucor pusillus in a Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplant Unit, Brazil.
Mucormycosis is a severe fungal infection with high mortality in immunocompromised patients. Although most cases occur sporadically in the community setting, there are reports of healthcare-associated outbreaks of mucormycosis. We describe the investigation and clinical features of an outbreak of mucormycosis caused by Rhizomucor pusillus in a hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) unit in Brazil. Cases were screened through the hospital records, defined according to the European Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer and the Mycoses Study Group Education and Research Consortium criteria, and classified as HSCT unit-acquired or not. Mucormycosis incidence was monitored from 2 years before the index case until 2 years after the last case. The clinical course of identified cases and potential environmental exposure data were recorded. Microbiological samples were identified with conventional methods and internal transcribed spacer sequencing; whole genome sequencing was performed for phylogenetic analysis. Potential source investigation was conducted according to the US Centers for Disease Control recommendations. Four proven cases of HSCT-unit-acquired mucormycosis were identified over a 10-month period. Rhizomucor pusillus was identified in three of the four patients. Disseminated disease, beginning with pulmonary infection, was the most common clinical presentation. Survivors (75%) received treatment with lipid complex amphotericin B, isavuconazole, and/or surgical resection. Environmental investigation was negative and phylogenetic analysis demonstrated that isolates were not clonal. Following air system maintenance, no further cases were identified. We characterize the first reported outbreak investigation of mucormycosis caused by R. pusillus in a Brazilian HSCT unit, with favorable outcomes in most cases despite aggressive clinical presentation. Despite the lack of clonality and negative environmental investigation, epidemiological evidence strongly suggests nosocomial transmission.

Clinical management, antifungal susceptibility, and predictors of 28-day mortality in Candidozyma auris candidemia: A single-center cohort study.
Candidozyma auris (Candida auris) candidemia is a serious healthcare-associated infection with substantial mortality and limited treatment options. We retrospectively evaluated adult patients with C. auris candidemia at a tertiary care center between June 2022 and December 2025 to describe clinical management, microbiological outcomes, antifungal susceptibility, and factors associated with 28-day mortality. The descriptive cohort included 108 patients; mortality status was available for 107. Most patients (92.6%) were in intensive care at candidemia onset, and among evaluable patients, 76.1% had prior C. auris colonisation detected. Twenty-eight-day mortality was 41.1% (44/107). Non-survivors were older and had higher Charlson Comorbidity Index, Pitt bacteremia, and Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) scores. Central venous catheter removal was more frequent among survivors (72.7% vs. 45.0%; P = .012), although removal timing and time to initiation of effective antifungal therapy did not differ significantly between groups. In multivariable analysis, Charlson Comorbidity Index (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.22; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.02-1.44) and SOFA score (aOR, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.05-1.27) were independently associated with 28-day mortality. Resistance rates were 95.1% for fluconazole, 31.2% for amphotericin B, and 1.3% for both anidulafungin and micafungin; multidrug resistance rate was 28.6%, and no isolate met the definition of pandrug resistance. Mortality in C. auris candidemia was mainly associated with baseline comorbidity burden and acute organ dysfunction. Local susceptibility surveillance and early recognition of high-risk patients may support treatment and infection-control strategies.

A pragmatic approach to investigating nosocomial acquisition of rare and emerging molds.
Invasive mold disease is associated with high mortality in immunosuppressed patients. While Aspergillus spp. and the Mucorales are well known, several other molds have emerged that cause infections and even outbreaks in susceptible hosts. These include Fusarium spp., Scedosporium spp., Lomentospora prolificans, and several others. The principles of preventing nosocomial mold infections include use of high-efficiency particulate air filters, removal of any potential sources of contamination, and risk-assessment of construction sites in adjacent areas. However, there is limited information on the approaches to assessment and management of outbreaks when there is a cluster of rare mold infections. The incubation period of rare and emerging molds is unknown and ascertaining whether the origin is nosocomial or community-acquired is difficult. Surveillance may be required to determine whether cases are part of an ongoing problem. The environmental niches of the rare molds are unique; e.g., Fusarium spp. are associated with hospital water distribution systems. They also cause outbreaks of fungal keratitis. Many rare molds are seen in cases of medicinal product contamination and managing such outbreaks requires support from and coordination by national agencies. Environmental precautions around patients and construction activities should be reassessed during outbreaks. A systematic approach is required when evaluating a cluster or even an isolated nosocomial case. Surveillance systems should be strengthened. This review summarizes the information available on outbreaks of rare and emerging molds. We further discuss a set of actions that may be undertaken in the event of an outbreak.

Transferrin Receptor as a Target for Regulation of Ferroptosis and Some Viral Infections.
This review is devoted to molecular mechanisms of ferroptosis, a type of programmed cell death dependent on lipid peroxidation and limited by iron influx, mediated by the transferrin receptor (TfR1 or CD71). In addition to the iron-saturated transferrin, ligands of transferrin receptor also include its homologues lactoferrin and melanotransferrin, as well as heavy-chain ferritin and heme complex with human serum albumin. Activation of ferroptosis, including by increasing the labile pool of iron in tumor cells, is considered a promising strategy for combating cancer. However, a number of pathogenic human viruses, including influenza virus, SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus, and rabies virus, use binding with TfR1 to infect cells and affect ferroptosis. The review summarizes information on natural and synthetic TfR1 regulators, including the mechanisms of their influence on the development of ferroptosis and the prospects for their use as antiviral agents.

Emotion-Focused Behavioral Weight Loss Treatment for Adolescents: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
IMPORTANCE: Family-based behavioral treatment (FBT) efficacy decreases in adolescence, a developmental period of gradual maturation and increasing autonomy during which emotion regulation skills develop. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the feasibility and efficacy of FBT alone compared with FBT plus emotion regulation across 6 months of treatment and 12 months of follow-up on adolescent weight change, emotion regulation, emotional eating, and parent weight change. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This parallel-group randomized clinical trial of adolescents 13 to 16 years of age with body mass index (BMI) in the 85th percentile or higher but less than the 99.9th percentile was conducted from August 29, 2019, to January 4, 2024, at 2 university clinics. Central randomization was completed by a statistician, and outcome assessors were blinded to treatment condition. The majority of treatments and assessments were delivered remotely via video conference due to the COVID-19 pandemic. INTERVENTIONS: FBT plus emotion regulation vs traditional FBT skills alone for weight loss. FBT included nutrition and physical activity education, behavior change strategies, and parenting skills. Both treatments had 6 months of adolescent and parent groups and behavior coaching sessions. The combined group included FBT skills and added dialectical behavior therapy and emotion-focused therapy. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The main outcomes were adolescent weight (body mass index [BMI] z score (BMIz) and BMI as a percentage of the 95th BMI percentile [%BMIp95]), emotion regulation skills (measured by Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale [DERS] scores), emotional eating behaviors (measured by Emotional Eating Scale [EES] scores), parent weight, and feasibility and acceptability of treatment. Primary outcome analyses used an intention-to-treat approach. RESULTS: A total of 166 (FBT plus emotion regulation = 84; FBT = 82) dyads (adolescents: mean [SD] age, 14.3 [1.2] years; 95 [57%] female; mean [SD] BMIz, 2.2 [0.6]; mean [SD] %BMIp95, 120.4 [21.4]; parents: mean [SD] age, 45.3 [6.5] years; 141 [85%] female; mean [SD] BMI, 32.6 [7.0]) were assessed at baseline, midtreatment, posttreatment, and 6- and 12-month follow-up visits. There were no statistically significant differences in posttreatment weight loss among adolescents receiving FBT plus emotion regulation compared with FBT (difference in BMIz, 0.03 [95% CI, -0.05 to 0.10]). However, adolescents in FBT plus emotion regulation did not regain as much weight at the 12-month follow-up (difference in BMIz, -0.09 [95% CI, -0.17 to -0.02]). At the 12-month follow-up, 4% (95% CI, 1%-12%) of adolescents in FBT and 22% (95% CI, 8%-48%) of adolescents in FBT plus emotion regulation lost a clinically significant amount of weight (≥0.20 BMIz). At 12 months' follow-up, parent weight (difference in BMI, 0.51 [95% CI, -0.03 to 1.05]) and adolescent emotion regulation (difference in DERS scores, -0.06 [95% CI, -0.25 to 0.50]) did not differ by treatment. By contrast, the FBT plus emotion regulation group had lower scores than the FBT group on emotional eating (difference in EES scores, -0.39 [95% CI, -0.63 to -0.15]). CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this randomized clinical trial of 166 parent-adolescent dyads, adding emotion regulation skills to FBT did not improve weight loss during treatment but was associated with less weight regain and lower emotional eating through the 12-month follow-up. These findings suggest that adding emotion regulation skills to an FBT program may attenuate weight regain and decrease emotional eating among adolescents. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03674944.

Risk and Protective Factors for Youth Deviance After a Large-Scale Crisis: A General Strain Theory Approach.
OBJECTIVE: deviant behaviors comprise a broad range of actions that violate the norms of the society to which individuals belong. Contemporary research drawing on General Strain Theory argues that macro-level disruptions represent strain-inducing contingencies that may precipitate deviant behaviors and highlights lack of family support and deviant peer association as variables contributing to engagement in deviance.
