METHODOLOGY: Demographic and clinical data were obtained from hospital records. The isolates were identified using matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization-time of flight (MALDI-TOF) mass spectrometry and serotyped at the National Public Health Laboratory. Antimicrobial susceptibility was determined by gradient diffusion. The results were interpreted according to the European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing clinical breakpoints. RESULTS: Of the 58 included patients (62.1% male; median age 42.8 years), 96.4% had at least one comorbidity; most commonly solid organ malignancies (21.4%). Salmonella Enteritidis was the predominant serotype (82.8%), followed by S. Infantis (3.4%). The cases were most frequent in autumn (41.4%). The rates of resistance were 29.3% for ampicillin, 13.7% for ciprofloxacin, and 1.8% for trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. All the isolates were susceptible to ceftriaxone and azithromycin, while 12.0% exhibited multidrug resistance. The overall mortality was 25% (14/56), with ampicillin resistance detected in 6 fatal cases. CONCLUSIONS: This long-term single-center study demonstrates that S. Enteritidis is the leading cause of NTS BSIs in Antalya and is associated with seasonal clustering and notable AMR. The substantial burden of comorbidities and mortality underscores the importance of continued regional AMR surveillance and appropriate empirical treatment strategies.

Research trends in minimally invasive partial splenectomy: a bibliometric mapping review with cross-database comparison.
BACKGROUND: Minimally invasive partial splenectomy (MIPS) is used for hereditary hematologic disorders, splenic cysts, hydatid disease, benign tumors, and selected traumatic lesions. However, its literature remains dispersed across patient groups, indications, and surgical specialties. This study mapped the development, contributors, knowledge base, and thematic structure of MIPS research and examined the concordance of its principal patterns across databases. METHODS: Articles and reviews published from 1 January 1995 to 29 August 2026 were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC), Scopus, and PubMed. WoSCC supported the primary bibliometric and knowledge-mapping analyses; Scopus and PubMed supported cross-database comparisons. Bibliometrix, VOSviewer, and CiteSpace were used to analyze publication output, contributors, keywords, co-cited references, and citation bursts. Database overlap, annual-output correlations, and journal and theme descriptive agreement were also assessed. RESULTS: The final datasets comprised 150 WoSCC, 154 Scopus, and 161 PubMed publications. WoSCC output increased after 2015 and reached 15 publications in 2024, the highest total among complete years. China contributed the most publications (n = 53), while the United States had the highest country-level total link strength. Surgical Endoscopy, Journal of Pediatric Surgery, and Journal of Laparoendoscopic & Advanced Surgical Techniques were the leading sources. Keyword analysis identified eight moderately coherent clusters (Q = 0.4383; mean silhouette = 0.6477), covering partial splenectomy, laparoscopic surgery, hydatid disease, hereditary spherocytosis, pediatric surgery, and operative techniques. Cross-database linkage identified 183 unique publications; 122 (66.7%) occurred in all three databases. Annual publication counts were strongly correlated for 1995-2025 (Spearman's ρ = 0.960-0.979) and after inclusion of partial-year 2026 data (ρ = 0.963-0.978; all P < 0.001). Eight journals appeared in all three database-specific Top-10 lists, and the leading thematic distributions were broadly similar across databases. CONCLUSION: MIPS research has expanded but remains relatively small, institutionally dispersed, and focused on operative feasibility, technical refinement, and perioperative outcomes. These broad patterns were consistent across the three databases, although the comparisons do not constitute independent external validation. Disease-stratified multicenter studies with standardized long-term assessment of splenic function are needed.

Bacillus velezensis 802 with antagonistic activity against Aspergillus flavus: genome characterization, secondary metabolites and antifungal mechanism.
BACKGROUND: Aspergillus flavus causes severs postharvest spoilage and aflatoxins contamination of agricultural commodities, posing major threats to food safety and human health and underscoring the need for safe, effective biocontrol strategies. This study aimed to identify an antagonistic endophytic bacterium against A. flavus and to integrate whole-genome mining, metabolomics, and mechanistic assays to elucidate the molecular basis of its antifungal activity. METHODS: An endophytic isolate was identified as Bacillus velezensis 802. Its crude extract was evaluated in vitro, and SEM, CLSM, and physiological assays were used to assess hyphal morphology, membrane integrity, mitochondrial function, energy metabolism, and apoptosis. Bioinformatic analysis of the whole-genome sequence was used to predict biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) and their associated pathways. UHPLC-MS/MS was used to identify metabolites in the active extract. RESULTS: Bacillus velezensis 802 inhibited A. flavus by 70.16%. The crude extract induced hyphal wrinkling and swelling, disrupted membrane integrity, reduced mitochondrial membrane potential, suppressed key energy-metabolism enzymes, and activated the Caspase-9-mediated apoptotic pathway. Genome analysis revealed a 3,951,806 bp circular chromosome containing 13 BGCs. Metabolomics identified six secondary metabolites, among which isobutyric acid showed the strongest antifungal activity. CONCLUSION: By coupling whole-genome mining with metabolomic profiling and mechanistic validation, this study demonstrates that B. velezensis 802 suppresses A. flavus through multi-target interference with cell structure, energy metabolism, and apoptosis. The strain and its metabolites, especially isobutyric acid, are promising biocontrol candidates for improving grain storage safety.

Antifungal susceptibility and genomic profile associated with biosynthetic gene clusters of bovine mastitis-derived Aspergillus fumigatus DAH1043FM.
The most frequently isolated fungus from mycotic mastitis in cattle is Aspergillus fumigatus, which can cause infection by germinating on the animal's surface to form hyphae that penetrate epithelial and endothelial barriers and initiate mastitis. In this study, the fungal strain DAH1043FM was isolated from the milk of a cow with mastitis and identified as Aspergillus fumigatus by internal transcribed spacer (ITS) region sequencing. Species identity was further confirmed by whole-genome Average Nucleotide Identity (ANI) analysis. A. fumigatus DAH1043FM showed minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) values of 0.5 μg/mL for amphotericin B and itraconazole, 0.12 μg/mL for posaconazole and voriconazole, 128 μg/mL for fluconazole, and >8 μg/mL for caspofungin, micafungin, and anidulafungin. Comparative Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) with two reference genomes of A. fumigatus, Af293 and A1163, was used to identify genetic variants, such as single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and other mutations, in genes associated with antifungal resistance, including those involved in drug efflux, ergosterol biosynthesis, echinocandin target pathways, and other resistance-related processes. Furthermore, genome mining identified biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) showing substantial similarity to characterized pathways associated with fumiquinazoline (100%), gliotoxin (84%), fumagillin (80%), and trypacidin (71%). These results demonstrate that strain DAH1043FM carries predicted genetic variants in target pathways while exhibiting wild-type susceptibility to azoles alongside off-scale endpoints for echinocandins. Genome analysis of strain DAH1043FM identified predicted secondary metabolite BGCs, highlighting the value of genome-level surveillance for fungal isolates recovered from bovine milk.

The mosquito gut microbiome and Plasmodium development: a scoping review of molecular approaches and implications for malaria vector control.
BACKGROUND: Malaria remains a major health burden, with an estimated 282 million cases and approximately 610,000 deaths recorded in 2024. The increasing prevalence of insecticide-resistant Anopheles vectors and drug-resistant Plasmodium strains has substantially eroded the efficacy of conventional control strategies, underscoring the critical need for innovative approaches. Accumulating evidence suggest that the mosquito midgut microbiome exerts a significant influence on Plasmodium sporogonic development; however, no scoping investigation has fully mapped the metagenomic evidence base in this field. METHODS: Adhering to the Arksey and O'Malley framework and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, a systematic search was conducted across PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for publications from January 2000 to April 2026. Studies that used microbiological, molecular, or metagenomic techniques to study the gut microbiota of mosquito species related to Plasmodium were included. Descriptive mapping was used to synthesize the data in a thematic manner. RESULTS: Thirteen primary studies met the inclusion criteria, comprising both observational field surveys and experimental infection studies. Four themes emerged: (1) gut microbiota diversity and composition are associated with Plasmodium infection status, though the direction varies by mosquito species, geography, and season; (2) several taxa, including Burkholderia, Asaia, Sphingomonas, Pseudomonas, and Serratia, are consistently associated with reduced infection or are experimentally inhibitory; (3) the Enterobacteriaceae and Serratia spp. show context-dependent, bidirectional relationships with Plasmodium that are best explained by strain-level variation; and (4) a smaller set of taxa, including Elizabethkingia, Chryseobacterium, Methylobacterium, and Pantoea, is positively associated with infection, on observational evidence only. The evidence relied predominantly on 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, with a minority of studies adding whole-genome sequencing, transcriptomics, or metabolomics; none used shotgun metagenomics. CONCLUSIONS: The mosquito gut microbiome exerts a net inhibitory effect on Plasmodium development, with translational potential for microbiome-based vector control, including paratransgenesis. However, the microbiota is not uniformly antagonistic to the parasite, and taxa positively associated with infection remain observational. The field is limited by a near-exclusive reliance on 16S rRNA profiling, few functional and longitudinal studies, and geographically narrow evidence. Multi-omics approaches, longitudinal designs, and broader geographic coverage will be essential to translate these associations into sustainable malaria control.

Diagnosis and treatment of four cases of pulmonary cryptococcosis: case report and literature review.
INTRODUCTION: Cryptococcosis has attracted global attention due to its high mortality rate, unique geographical distribution, and tendency to cause severe and rapid disease progression. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) is a novel detection technology that provides diagnostic insights for identifying pathogens, particularly rare ones. The present article describes 4 individuals diagnosed with pulmonary cryptococcosis (PC) using mNGS of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF). CASE PRESENTATION: Among these patients, 3 had cancer, 1 had sarcoidosis and diabetes, and 2 were exposed to pigeons and/or pigeon droppings. These patients experienced symptoms, including fever, cough, and chest pain. They were diagnosed with PC after mNGS of BALF. The patient was diagnosed based on mNGS test results. Subsequently, the patient was treated with fluconazole, and the patient's chest computed tomography scan showed significant absorption of the lung lesions. CONCLUSIONS: mNGS of BALF can quickly diagnose PC. This diagnostic method has minimal trauma to the body and is worthy of clinical promotion. Fluconazole remains the preferred and best therapeutic drug for PC treatment.

Whole-genome characterization of Plasmodium falciparum population structure and drug resistance across Uganda and neighboring countries.
Uganda has one of the world's highest malaria burdens, but parasite population structure and connectivity have not been characterized nationally with whole-genome data. We analyzed 249 monoclonal Plasmodium falciparum genomes from 26 sentinel sites across Uganda in 2023 and compared them with publicly available genomes from five neighboring countries. Genetic diversity was high and differentiation low in Uganda, but identity-by-descent detected limited structure. This was most pronounced in the low-transmission southwest, where parasites shared ancestry and recent relatedness with isolates from western Tanzania. Selection scans identified signals at loci associated with resistance to artemisinins and their partner drugs, and to chloroquine and antifolates. The strongest signal was at PfPX1 where the PIN haplotype (L1222P, M1701I, D1705N) reached 70% prevalence nationwide, but selection was carried by PIN haplotypes that had additionally acquired D384A, largely confined to northern and eastern Uganda. A second substitution at the same codon, D384Y, formed a haplotype shared across the Tanzanian border. PfKelch13 variants were partitioned across multiple backgrounds, consistent with repeated independent emergence, and C469Y was enriched on the PfPX1 D384A-PIN background. These genomes provide a 2023 baseline for tracking potential mediators of drug resistance and support coordinated genomic surveillance across Uganda and its neighbors.

A rapid sporozoite viability assay identifies leads and targetable enzymatic activities against the zoonotic Cryptosporidium parvum.
Current phenotypic screens for anti-Cryptosporidium compounds typically quantify intracellular parasite growth in host cell cultures after two days of infection. Here, we developed a rapid, host cell-free phenotypic assay that directly measures compound-induced loss of viability in excysted Cryptosporidium parvum sporozoites, the invasive stage that initiates infection. We first compared qRT-PCR, luminescence ATP, and resazurin fluorescence readouts for detecting viable sporozoites. The luminescence ATP assay provided the best balance of linear dynamic range, assay time, parasite input, and cost, and was therefore adapted for high-throughput screening. Screening 5000 bioactive compounds at 40 μM identified 28 primary hits with ≥50% inhibition of sporozoite viability, including 14 with >60% inhibition. Secondary screening of these 14 compounds at 4 μM identified five hits retaining >50% inhibition: ZL0420, sulbactam, abexinostat, kojic acid, and SIB-1757. All five showed submicromolar to low-micromolar activity against free sporozoites, with EC50 values of 0.420-3.114 μM. Four compounds, abexinostat, ZL0420, SIB-1757, and sulbactam, also inhibited intracellular parasite growth in vitro, with EC50 values of 0.316-11.87 μM and selectivity indices from >17 to >107. In an IFN-γ-knockout mouse model, these four compounds reduced oocyst shedding over the 35-day experiment by 53.7-79.0% based on area-under-the-curve analysis of fecal nanoluciferase activity and improved body-weight trajectories and ileal histopathology. Biochemical assays further showed that abexinostat inhibited native parasite HDAC activity at low nanomolar concentrations, while sulbactam inhibited a β-lactamase-like activity in sporozoite lysates. These findings establish sporozoite viability as a rapid screening endpoint and identify anti-Cryptosporidium leads associated with targetable enzymatic activities in the invasive stage.

Assessing the impact of routine malaria vaccination on total disease burden in Cameroon: a nationwide difference‑in‑differences analysis using health district surveillance data (2023-2025).
BACKGROUND: Cameroon introduced the RTS, S/AS01 malaria vaccine into routine expanded immunisation (EPI) in 2024, targeting 42 priority health districts. We assessed changes in total malaria burden between intervention and non-intervention districts over 2023-2025. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective, quasi-experimental, ecological longitudinal study using a difference-in-differences (DiD) approach on routine district-level surveillance data from 206 districts (42 intervention, 164 non-intervention) for 2023-2025. Outcomes included severe malaria rate (per 1,000 children < 5), uncomplicated malaria rate, all malaria-related hospitalisations, and malaria mortality rate (per 100,000). Crude pre-post changes and DiD were calculated. Adjusted linear DiD models with district and year fixed effects and cluster-robust standard errors were also fitted. Subgroup analyses examined interactions with seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC), intermittent preventive treatment in infants (IPTi), insecticide-treated nets (ITNs), and ecological region. RESULTS: Baseline characteristics differed significantly: intervention districts had higher ITN coverage (60.2% vs. 45.5%, p = 0.006), higher IPT coverage (35.1% vs. 24.4%, p = 0.001), and larger populations (median 121,284 vs. 89,592, p = 0.029). From 2023 to 2025, intervention districts experienced larger declines in all outcomes. Crude DiD showed a 2.6 per 1000 (15%) reduction in severe malaria, 8.1 per 1000 (22%) reduction in uncomplicated malaria, 5.3 per 1000 (28%) reduction in hospitalisations, and 4.1 per 100,000 (26%) reduction in malaria deaths. Adjusted linear DiD estimates were not statistically significant (e.g., severe malaria coefficient - 0.54, 95% CI - 11.07 to 9.99, p = 0.920). Subgroup analyses indicated the largest effects in the Sahel (crude rate ratio 0.78) and added benefit when the vaccine was combined with SMC (additional - 5.6 per 1000 reduction). In 2025 alone, vaccination averted an estimated 7,200 severe cases, 12,800 uncomplicated cases, 5,300 hospitalisations, and 77 deaths. CONCLUSION: Crude trends show favourable declines in malaria burden in intervention districts, but adjusted estimates were null, likely due to selection bias and low power. These findings support continued vaccine scale-up and use of routine data for monitoring, while acknowledging the limitations of non-randomised evaluations.

A community-based participatory research and community health workers-led health education strategy for schistosomiasis control among schoolchildren in Pemba Island, Zanzibar: a cluster-randomized trial.
BACKGROUND: Schistosomiasis remains an intractable public health challenge in sub-Saharan Africa. While mass drug administration (MDA) has been the cornerstone of control, its limited impact on sustained behavioral change and persistent transmission in high-intensity transmission areas underscores the urgent need for complementary strategies. We aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of a community-based participatory research (CBPR) approach led by community health workers (CHWs), compared to conventional health education, in achieving sustainable schistosomiasis control among schoolchildren in Pemba, Zanzibar. METHODS: A pilot, cluster-randomized controlled trial (cRCT) was conducted from February 2024 to February 2025. Since the screening revealed that the infection rates in all six local schools exceeded 3%, we randomly selected two of them and randomized them 1:1 to receive either a CBPR-CHW health education (1 intervention school) or conventional health education (1 control school). A total of 650 eligible school children aged 11-13 years were initially enrolled. After screening, 602 children completed the baseline survey and were assigned to either the CBPR-CHW intervention group (n = 278) or the control group (n = 324). After accounting for attrition, the final analytical sample at the 12-month follow-up (T3) consisted of 540 participants. The CBPR intervention was developed through a structured process of community needs assessment and co-design culminating in six culturally adapted educational modules delivered by trained CHWs. Primary outcomes were Schistosoma haematobium infection prevalence (urine egg positivity) and comprehensive knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) scores, assessed at baseline (T1), 6 months (T2), and 12 months long-term follow-up (T3). Analyses utilized two-way repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni correction for KAP score comparisons, supplemented by Kruskal-Wallis tests for non-normal data. Missing values (< 5%) were addressed via multiple imputation. RESULTS: Loss to follow-up was low across all time points, ranging from 8.5 to 11.9%. At the 12-month follow-up (T3), the CBPR-CHW group demonstrated a significantly greater reduction in infection prevalence (from 19.18 to 0.82%) (P < 0.001) compared to the control group (from 11.86 to 1.02%). The CBPR-CHW group also showed sustained, significant improvements in KAP scores, significantly outperforming the control group at T3 (e.g., knowledge scores: 7.11 ± 1.35 vs. 6.56 ± 1.70; P < 0.05). In contrast, the control group showed transient or non-significant improvements. High student satisfaction was reported (total score: 5.28 ± 1.28/6), and household latrine usage increased by 56.3%. CONCLUSIONS: The CBPR-CHWs-led strategy was significantly more effective than conventional education in achieving sustainable reductions in schistosomiasis infection and improvements in KAP outcomes. This model represents a highly effective, scalable complement to MDA, directly addressing gaps in the WHO's 2030 elimination roadmap by fostering community ownership and cultural relevance. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06312462. Registered on February 28, 2024. Available at: https://register. CLINICALTRIALS: gov/.

Temporal and spatial patterns of malaria in Somalia, 2021-2025: a district-level analysis of routine surveillance data.
BACKGROUND: Malaria has increased across the Horn of Africa, where invasive urban mosquito vectors have been established. Somalia's sub-national epidemiology, surveillance completeness, and care cascade have not been evaluated in recent years. METHODS: Routine national malaria surveillance data for Somalia from 2021 to 2025 were analyzed using a retrospective observational design, organized as a district-level annual panel of the same administrative units observed repeatedly each year. All 20 regions and 125 district reporting units were included, yielding 625 district-year records. Test positivity, annual parasite index, treatment coverage, and reporting completeness were calculated by reporting area and year, and the 2024 increase was disaggregated into testing and positivity components against the means for 2021 to 2023. RESULTS: Confirmed cases remained near 13,000 per year from 2021 to 2023, rose to 32,030 in 2024, and then fell to 25,586 in 2025. The 2024 figure was 142.8% above the 2023 figure, while testing rose by only 8.9%, and test positivity rose from 4.3% to 9.5%. Nine neighboring north-western districts contributed 14,238 cases (90.0% of the district-level increase of 15, 828), with Borama alone contributing 47.7%. Cases treated without a parasitological test fell from 26,493 in 2021 to none, and reporting completeness rose from 76.1% to 99.9%. CONCLUSION: The 2024 increase appears to reflect a genuine rise in transmission concentrated in north-western Somalia rather than wider testing alone. Expanding entomological surveillance for invasive vectors, aligning vector control with district-level burden, and improving data quality on parasite species and disease severity are urgent priorities for the disease.

Burden of asymptomatic malaria among school-aged children: Protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis.
BACKGROUND: Asymptomatic malaria infection remains a major challenge for malaria control and elimination efforts, particularly in endemic settings such as Ethiopia. School-aged children are increasingly recognized as a potential reservoir for malaria transmission due to frequent exposure to infection and the development of partial immunity that allows infections to remain clinically silent. However, available evidence on the burden, species distribution, and determinants of asymptomatic malaria in this population is fragmented and inconsistent. This systematic review and meta-analysis aim to synthesize evidence on the prevalence, Plasmodium species distribution, and risk factors of asymptomatic malaria among school-aged children in Ethiopia. METHODS: This protocol was developed in accordance with the PRISMA-P guidelines. A comprehensive literature search will be conducted in electronic databases (PubMed, Scopus, CINAHL, and ScienceDirect) and additional sources, including Google Scholar and African Journals Online. Eligible studies will include observational studies reporting asymptomatic malaria among school-aged children in Ethiopia. Two independent reviewers will conduct study selection, data extraction, and quality assessment using the Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tool for prevalence studies. A random-effects meta-analysis will be performed using R software to estimate the pooled prevalence. Heterogeneity will be assessed using Cochran's Q test and I2 statistics, and subgroup analyses will be conducted by diagnostic method, study area, study design, years of actual data collection, and transmission season during data collection. Where sufficiently comparable adjusted estimates are available, associations between prespecified factors and AMI will also be quantitatively synthesized. CONCLUSION: The findings will generate comprehensive evidence to support malaria control and elimination strategies in Ethiopia by highlighting the epidemiological importance of school-aged children as a potential reservoir for infection. The results are expected to inform targeted interventions and strengthen school-based malaria surveillance and prevention programs.

Excess p50 induces Arp1-dependent dynactin clusters containing the assembly factor VezA.
Dynactin, a complex essential for cytoplasmic dynein function, contains an Arp1 mini-filament with a pointed-end sub-complex including Arp11 and a shoulder sub-complex including p50 and p150. We recently identified in Aspergillus nidulans a vezatin homolog VezA that enhances dynactin assembly, but VezA does not co-localize with dynactin, suggesting a transient interaction. It was found that overexpression of p50 separates the shoulder from the mini-filament and causes late-onset neurodegeneration in mice, but its cellular effects in the context of VezA need to be studied. Here, we surprisingly found that p50 overexpression in A. nidulans causes Arp11, p50 (but not p150), and VezA to form co-localized clusters whose presence depends on Arp1. Formation of the VezA cluster also depends on Arp11, and VezA significantly enhances the intensity of Arp11-GFP clusters but not that of p50-GFP clusters. Moreover, an evolutionarily conserved region of p50 (aa17-25) forming a beta-sheet structure with Arp1 as revealed in previous cryo-EM studies is critical for the formation of Arp11, p50 and VezA clusters. These results suggest that excess p50 induces cluster formation driven by p50-Arp1 interactions, and that this assembly intermediate lacking the intact shoulder traps VezA, which participates in the Arp11-Arp1-p50 interactions. Molecular types, clinical profile, and exploratory virulence-associated phenotypes of clinical Cryptococcus isolates from Amazonas, Brazil.
BACKGROUND: Cryptococcosis remains a severe systemic mycosis, especially among people living with HIV/AIDS, and culture-based molecular data from Amazonas remain limited. OBJECTIVES: The aim was to identify which Cryptococcus molecular types circulated among clinical isolates from Amazonas between 2020 and 2024; what were the main clinical characteristics and outcomes of patients infected with Cryptococcus neoformans molecular type VNI and Cryptococcus gattii molecular type VGII; and whether these molecular types differed in selected susceptibility-related and virulence-associated phenotypes. METHODS: We analyzed 70 culture-confirmed clinical isolates from patients treated at the Dr. Heitor Vieira Dourado Tropical Medicine Foundation, Manaus, Brazil. Molecular types were assigned by URA5 PCR-RFLP using reference strains. Demographic and clinical variables were retrieved from medical records. A stratified 30-isolate subset comprising 24 VNI and 6 VGII isolates was evaluated for phospholipase activity and melanization. Fluconazole MICs were analyzed for the complete 70-isolate dataset and were determined by broth microdilution according to CLSI M27-A4. RESULTS: VNI predominated (64/70; 91.4%), whereas VGII accounted for 6/70 isolates (8.6%). The series was predominantly composed of men, young adults, and HIV-positive patients. HIV infection was more frequent among VNI cases, whereas VGII included proportionally more HIV-negative patients. In-hospital death occurred in 17/70 patients (24.3%). Fluconazole MICs, phospholipase activity, and melanization were broadly comparable between VNI and VGII, although the small VGII subgroup precluded robust genotype-associated inference. CONCLUSION: VNI was the dominant molecular type in this severe reference-center cryptococcosis series from Amazonas. Phenotypic findings should be interpreted as exploratory and hypothesis-generating.

Artificial Intelligence-Supported Automated Microscopy for Malaria Diagnosis: A Multicenter Study.
BACKGROUND: Accurate malaria diagnosis is key for patient management, surveillance, and control. Automated microscopy can overcome the variation observed among microscopists and is a promising new tool for diagnosis. The Noul miLab integrates smear preparation, staining, imaging, and artificial intelligence-supported parasite detection in a portable device. METHODS: A total of 2201 samples were collected from febrile patients across 2 sites in Ethiopia, where Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax are frequent, and in Ghana, where P. falciparum transmission is intense. Samples were screened using local microscopy at the health center, miLab, and rapid diagnostic tests. Quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) and expert microscopy were used as gold standards. RESULTS: The miLab reached a sensitivity for P. falciparum diagnosis of 96.3% (335 of 348) using expert microscopy as the gold standard and a sensitivity of 97.4% (298 of 306) using qPCR-positive infections at densities >200 parasites/µL as the gold standard. The sensitivity of miLab for P. vivax was 96.8% (399 of 412) using expert microscopy as the gold standard and 95.9% (419 of 437) using qPCR-positive infections at densities >200 parasites/µL as the gold standard. Compared to qPCR, specificity was 98.8% for P. falciparum and 97.8% for P. vivax. miLab was significantly more sensitive than microscopy conducted at the health center. In Ethiopia, among miLab-positive samples, miLab assigned the correct parasite species to 98.7% of P. falciparum and 96.2% of P. vivax mono-infections. CONCLUSIONS: The miLab automated microscope shows high sensitivity and specificity for P. falciparum and P. vivax diagnosis.

Malaria vaccines are here-can surveillance keep pace?
Malaria vaccines RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M represent a major advance in malaria control, with rapid expansion across Africa. As vaccination scales up, surveillance, programme monitoring, and evaluation will be essential to track disease trends, vaccine delivery, coverage, safety, effectiveness, and impact. Linking immunization, malaria, laboratory, genomic, and geospatial data can help identify breakthrough infections, parasite changes, and populations being missed. Strengthening existing systems and sustained investment in data, laboratory, and workforce capacity will be critical to achieving equitable and lasting vaccine impact.

Permissive versus conventional weaning from venovenous ECMO in patients with ARDS: a retrospective cohort study.
BACKGROUND: Criteria for weaning from venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (V-V ECMO) in acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) remain poorly standardized. Some patients are decannulated despite persistent abnormalities in respiratory mechanics once oxygenation and carbon dioxide clearance are considered adequate. We aimed to compare outcomes associated with permissive versus conventional V-V ECMO weaning. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective single-center cohort study including adult patients with refractory ARDS treated with V-V ECMO between January 2015 and December 2022 who were successfully decannulated while receiving invasive mechanical ventilation. Permissive weaning was defined as ECMO decannulation despite persistence of at least one of the following criteria during the sweep gas-off trial: plateau pressure ≥30 cmH₂O, driving pressure ≥20 cmH₂O, positive end-expiratory pressure ≥15 cmH₂O, or tidal volume ≤5 mL/kg predicted body weight. The primary outcome was 90-day mortality after ECMO decannulation. Secondary outcomes included liberation from mechanical ventilation within 90 days, analyzed using competing-risk models with death as a competing event. Associations with mortality were assessed using landmark Cox proportional hazards models anchored at decannulation. RESULTS: Among 469 patients treated with V-V ECMO, 280 successfully decannulated patients were included; 117 (42%) underwent permissive weaning and 163 (58%) conventional weaning. Baseline characteristics were broadly similar, although body mass index was higher and SARS-CoV-2 ARDS more frequent in the permissive group. Patients undergoing permissive weaning had longer ECMO support (19 [9-37] vs. 12 [6-27] days; p < 0.01). At the sweep gas-off trial, respiratory mechanics remained more impaired in the permissive group, whereas oxygenation parameters were comparable. In landmark analysis, permissive weaning was associated with higher 90-day mortality in both univariable (hazard ratio [HR] 3.53, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.62-7.66; p < 0.01) and multivariable analyses (adjusted HR 4.45, 95% CI 1.98-9.97; p < 0.01). However, permissive weaning was not associated with delayed liberation from mechanical ventilation by day 90 (adjusted subdistribution HR 0.90, 95% CI 0.70-1.17; p = 0.4). CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with severe ARDS successfully decannulated from V-V ECMO, permissive weaning was associated with increased 90-day mortality but not with delayed liberation from mechanical ventilation.

The effect of time-varying left ventricular ejection fraction on clinical outcome in critically ill COVID-19 patients.
BACKGROUND: Although right ventricular (RV) dysfunction and acute cor pulmonale are associated with adverse outcomes in critically ill patients with COVID-19, the prognostic significance of left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction remains insufficiently characterized. In particular, dynamic changes in cardiac function during intensive care has seldom been studied. We therefore investigated the association between time-varying LV systolic function, assessed by LV ejection fraction (LVEF) and intensive care unit (ICU) mortality in patients with COVID-19, taking into account right ventricular function and forward flow. METHODS: This retrospective observational cohort study combined three ICU data repositories comprising 808 patients with 1614 echocardiographic examinations. Time-varying LV systolic function (LVEF ≤ 50%, 51-70%, >70%) was the primary exposure, and ICU mortality was the outcome. Multivariable Cox models with time-varying covariates, including, acute cor pulmonale, left ventricular outflow tract velocity time integral and key clinical characteristics were used to assess associations between LV systolic function phenotypes and outcome. RESULTS: At baseline, 27% of patients had abnormal LV systolic function (LVEF ≤ 50%) and 17% had hyperdynamic LV function (LVEF > 70%). The proportion of patients with normal LV systolic function increased over time. Abnormal LV systolic function was most prevalent at the first echocardiographic examination (27%) and least prevalent at the fifth examination (17%), whereas hyperdynamic LV function became more frequent during ICU stay, peaking at the 4th echocardiographic examination. Abnormal (aHR; 1.174, 95% CI: 0.901-1.531) or hyperdynamic (aHR: 1.041, 95% CI: 0.785-1.379) LV systolic dysfunction was not independently associated with ICU mortality. CONCLUSION: In critically ill patients with COVID-19, LV systolic dysfunction, including both abnormal and hyperdynamic LV phenotypes, were common and dynamic during ICU stay. LV systolic dysfunction was not independently associated with ICU mortality when modelled longitudinally and adjusted for RV dysfunction, forward flow and other clinical covariates. These findings suggest that the prognostic value LVEF phenotypes in severe COVID-19 may be limited. Further studies incorporating more sensitive measures of LV function and biomarkers of myocardial injury may be required to delineate subtle changes not captured by LVEF.

Temporal Trends in Six Major Cancers: Implications for Lifestyle-Based Cancer Prevention and Early Detection Across the Life Course.
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Cancer remains a serious public health challenge in the United States. Six major cancers (female breast, colorectal, liver, lung/bronchus, pancreas, and prostate) account for a substantial proportion of the national cancer burden. Understanding the changes in the incidence of these cancers over time can provide insights for prevention and control. This study examined temporal trends in the cancer incidence according to age at onset and stage at diagnosis. METHODS: This population-based study analyzed data from the United States Cancer Statistics database for 2001-2023, including all 50 states and the District of Columbia. Joinpoint regression was used to estimate annual percent changes (APCs) and average annual percent changes (AAPCs), with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs), based on age-adjusted incidence rates per 100,000 people. Of note, incidence rates from 2020 data were excluded from the Joinpoint models because COVID-19 pandemic disruptions affected cancer screening, diagnosis, and reporting. RESULTS: From 2001 to 2023, the incidence of lung and colorectal cancers declined, particularly among older adults (aged ≥50 years) (lung cancer: AAPC -2.09; 95% CI: -2.27, -1.90; colorectal cancer AAPC -2.70; 95% CI: -2.83, -2.56). In contrast, the incidence of colorectal, pancreatic, and breast cancers increased among younger adults (aged <50 years), whereas the incidence of liver and lung cancer declined. Moreover, prostate cancer incidence declined over time despite modest rebound in recent years (AAPC 1.83; 95% CI: 0.53, 3.14). Stage-specific analyses revealed increasing rates of early-stage diagnoses for several cancers, while late-stage cancer incidence increased for pancreatic and colorectal cancers (especially among younger adults). CONCLUSIONS: Cancer incidence varied substantially by cancer type, age, and stage at diagnosis. The rising incidence of colorectal, pancreatic, and breast cancers among younger adults underscores the need for continued research into risk factors, early detection, and prevention strategies.

Hyperinflammation and immunomodulation in influenza, SARS-CoV-2 and syncytial respiratory virus infection in adults: from innate immune responses and biomarkers to clinical and therapeutic implications.
Influenza, SARS-CoV2-2 and syncytial respiratory virus infection in adults are major causes of morbidity and mortality. However, the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying these infections remain incompletely understood. Disease severity results from an interaction between viral factors and host responses. Lung damage and respiratory failure are produced by hyperinflammation. Understanding these mechanisms is necessary to improve risk stratification and may guide therapeutic decisions. C- reactive protein (CRP), IL-6, ferritin, and ApoH are relevant biomarkers which can identify inflammatory phenotypes. Antivirals and supportive care are the main approaches for these viral infections. From a therapeutic perspective, broad immunosuppression is unlikely to be optimal, and strategies should focus on selectively modulating harmful inflammation while preserving antiviral immunity. Nevertheless, there is scarce evidence of the best choice of treatment based on the patient's clinical profile and further studies are needed.

MERS-CoV accessory ORF proteins in innate immune evasion: an evidence-graded functional framework.
Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV) is a merbecovirus associated with recurrent zoonotic spillover and severe lower-respiratory disease. Research has focused largely on DPP4-mediated entry, spike structure, replicase biology, neutralizing antibodies, and vaccines. However, the 3'-encoded accessory proteins are increasingly recognized as context-dependent modulators of viral fitness and pathogenesis. ORF4a binds double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) and suppresses MDA5- and PKR-dependent antiviral responses; ORF4b antagonizes OAS-RNase L and NF-κB signaling and contributes to inflammatory pathology in defined infection models; ORF5 modulates interferon and inflammatory responses in a genetic-background-dependent manner; and ORF8b interferes with MDA5- and HSP70-IKKϵ-dependent signaling, although its pathogenesis phenotype varies by experimental system and viral background. ORF3 shows HUWE1-regulated pro-apoptotic activity in ectopic-expression systems, but its role during authentic MERS-CoV infection remains unresolved. Our review organizes these findings by evidence type, pathway position, cell or tissue context, sampling time, and genetic-interaction evidence. This framework separates demonstrated mechanisms from inferred biological consequences and identifies the validation required before accessory-ORF biology can inform host-range assessment, therapeutic development, sequence surveillance, or rational attenuation.

Correction: The prolonged health sequelae "of the COVID-19 pandemic" in sub-Saharan Africa: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

Sex and age distribution of schizophrenia admissions at a psychiatric hospital in Morocco (2011-2024).
BACKGROUND: Schizophrenia is a severe psychiatric disorder with a significant social and economic burden, yet epidemiological data on schizophrenia in Morocco remain scarce, particularly regarding long-term patterns of admissions. OBJECTIVE: Our study aims to describe the temporal trends in schizophrenia admissions at Ar Razi Psychiatric Hospital in the Salé-Rabat region of Morocco from 2011 to 2024 and to analyze variations in admissions by age and sex. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective descriptive study using aggregated annual statistical registers from Ar Razi University Psychiatric Hospital (Salé, Morocco) from 2011 to 2024. The registers record, for each calendar year, the number of admissions cross-tabulated by sex (Male, Female) and by age range (0-14, 15-60, 61+ years), with admissions further classified as either first-ever presentations ("new") or returning patients previously seen for the same diagnosis ("old"). The unit of analysis is the admission, and the same patient may contribute admissions in more than one calendar year. Descriptive statistics were computed for sex, age range, and admission type. Annual male and female admission counts were compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. RESULTS: Over the study period, the registers recorded 13,564 schizophrenia admissions at Ar Razi, of which 5028 (37.1%) were first-ever presentations and 8536 (62.9%) were returning patients. Of all admissions, 10,488 (77.3%) were of male and 3076 (22.7%) of female patients, giving an overall male-to-female admission ratio of 3.41. The annual ratio ranged from 2.32 (2018) to 4.59 (2011), and was greater than 2 in every year. The 15-60-year age group accounted for 12,976 admissions (95.7%), with 230 (1.7%) in the 0-14 group and 358 (2.6%) in the 61+ group. The male-to-female ratio was substantially higher at the extremes of age (229:1 in 0-14; 9.85:1 in 61+) than in the 15-60 group (3.27:1). Total admissions declined to 840 in 2013 and to 616 in 2020 (-41.1% relative to 2019), then rose to a peak of 1226 in 2023. CONCLUSION: Schizophrenia hospitalizations in the Salé-Rabat region predominantly affect males in early to middle adulthood. The observed fluctuations highlight the impact of social, cultural, and external factors such as the COVID-19 pandemic on hospitalization rates. These findings describe patterns of psychiatric hospital use rather than population-level prevalence or incidence, and they are consistent with hypotheses about gender-related barriers to psychiatric care in Morocco. They support the need for targeted mental health policies addressing stigma, sex disparities in access, and continuity of care during public-health emergencies.

SARS-CoV-2 seroprevalence and extent of infection under-ascertainment in seven regions of Uzbekistan: a population-based serosurvey, May-July 2022.
Accurate estimation of SARS-CoV-2 transmission was limited in many settings by incomplete diagnostic testing and case reporting. We conducted a population-based cross-sectional serosurvey in seven regions of Uzbekistan between May and July 2022 to estimate SARS-CoV-2 seroprevalence, describe self-reported vaccination coverage, and assess the implications for routine surveillance. A two-stage cluster sampling design was used to randomly select polyclinic catchment areas and registered residents aged ≥5 years. Survey weights accounted for selection probabilities, non-response, and regional population structure. Among 15,000 invited individuals, 13,173 completed both questionnaire and serological testing, corresponding to an 87.8% response rate. Weighted seroprevalence was 98.3% (95% CI 98.0-98.6), indicating extensive cumulative exposure through infection, vaccination, or both. Self-reported vaccination coverage was 59.0% among adults and substantially lower among children. Approximately 243,000 COVID-19 cases had been officially reported nationally by August 2022; however, this national count is not directly comparable with seroprevalence in the seven surveyed regions. Nevertheless, the high seroprevalence, including among groups with low vaccination coverage, is suggestive of substantial transmission not identified by routine case reporting. Population-based serosurveys can therefore complement routine surveillance when interpreted alongside vaccination and epidemiological data.

Living with uncertainty: associations of personal and environmental uncertainty, resilience, and self-efficacy with anxiety symptoms in young adults.
BACKGROUND: Anxiety symptoms are highly prevalent among young adults and remain a major public mental health concern, with national data showing a marked increase during the COVID-19 pandemic. Contrary to expectations, anxiety rates did not decline after the pandemic ended. Persistent high anxiety levels may be contextually linked to an accumulation of concurrent global challenges, including climate change and geopolitical conflicts, that have been described as a "polycrisis" and are characterized by pervasive uncertainty. However, this framework was not directly examined in the present study. This study investigated the association between uncertainty, anxiety symptoms, resilience, and self-efficacy among university students. METHODS: We used two datasets collected in Switzerland: a repeated cross-sectional pandemic study conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic (April 2020 to April 2023), and a post-pandemic cross-sectional study conducted in Fall 2023. First, general linear models were used to examine the trend of anxiety from Spring 2020-Fall 2023, combining data from both studies (Nwave= 1,158). Second, using data from the post-pandemic study (N = 1,001), a hierarchical regression was conducted to examine the relationship between uncertainty, self-efficacy and resilience with anxiety symptoms, and to test for moderation effects of self-efficacy and resilience on the uncertainty-anxiety relationship. RESULTS: A general linear model exhibited significantly better for a quadratic function compared to a linear function, suggesting an increase in anxiety followed by a saturation-plateau post-COVID-19 [β = -0.02, 95% CI (-0.03, -0.01)]. Regression results supported independent relationships [ R ( anxiety ) 2 = 39%], such that uncertainty positively was associated with anxiety [β = 0.50, CI (0.44, 0.56)], whereas self-efficacy [β = -0.22, 95% CI (-0.29, -0.15)], and resilience [β = -0.08, 95% CI (-0.29, -0.03)] were negatively associated. Moderation results were non-significant. CONCLUSION: Our findings highlight that uncertainty may play a role in sustaining high levels of anxiety among university students. Although high self-efficacy and resilience did not modify the relationship between uncertainty and anxiety symptoms, they were independently associated with lower anxiety levels. Addressing both global and specific facets of uncertainty appears to be highly relevant when designing targeted interventions to support mental health in young adults, particularly university students.

Changes in birth certificate-reported prevalence of congenital anomalies at live birth during the COVID-19 pandemic: a nationwide study of 26 million United States live births.
BACKGROUND: Although the majority of studies have indicated that maternal severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection and coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) vaccination are not associated with neonatal birth defects, it is relevant to examine whether the disease burden changed during the COVID-19 pandemic, as other influencing factors may have also changed. We aimed to compare the birth certificate-reported prevalence of congenital anomalies at live birth before and during the pandemic. METHODS: Using public birth data, all live births from 2016 to 2022 in the United States of America (USA) were retrospectively included. The birth certificate-reported prevalence at live birth of selected congenital anomalies identified from the birth certificate, including anencephaly, meningomyelocele/spina bifida, cyanotic congenital heart disease (CCHD), congenital diaphragmatic hernia, omphalocele, gastroschisis, limb reduction defect, cleft lip, cleft palate, Down syndrome, chromosomal disorder, and hypospadias, was estimated and compared by calendar year of birth using logistic regression. RESULTS: A total of 26,345,765 live-born infants from 2016 to 2022 were included. The mean gestational age of the infants was 38.4 weeks (SD = 2.1 weeks), 48.9% were female babies, and 96.7% were singleton. The overall reported prevalence of congenital anomalies was highest in 2018 (3.51‰, 95%CI = 3.45‰-3.57‰) and has since shown a decreasing trend [3.38‰ (95%CI = 3.32‰-3.44‰) in 2019 and 3.35‰ (95%CI = 3.29‰-3.41‰) in 2022]. Using 2019 as a reference, it did not differ in 2020 and 2021 [odds ratio (OR) = 1.01 (0.98-1.03) and OR = 1.00 (0.98-1.03), respectively, after adjusting for maternal age, ethnicity/race, and socioeconomic status] and was slightly lower in 2022 [OR = 0.97 (0.95-0.99)]. For the majority of the congenital anomalies, the reported prevalence during the pandemic (2020-2022) remained unchanged or showed a decreasing trend (i.e., gastroschisis and Down syndrome) compared with that in 2019. The reported prevalence of CCHD was higher in 2021 and 2022 than in 2019. However, the increase had begun before the pandemic, and after correction for multiple comparisons, only the 2021 contrast remained significant. Segmented regression confirmed a significant pre-pandemic upward trend in CCHD with a level change dated to infants born in March 2020. When exposure was re-indexed by estimated year of conception, neither pandemic conception cohort differed from the 2019 conception cohort [2020: OR = 1.03 (0.97-1.09); 2021: OR = 1.02 (0.97-1.08)]. The direction of these results was consistent when stratified by gestational age (≥37 or <37 weeks), with wider intervals in the preterm stratum. CONCLUSIONS: The birth certificate-reported prevalence of congenital anomalies at live birth did not increase during the COVID-19 pandemic in the USA and decreased for several specific anomalies. The higher reported prevalence of CCHD continues a trend that began before the pandemic and is null once exposure is aligned with organogenesis.

Clinical characteristics, pathogen detection, and severity markers among children with acute respiratory infections during the COVID-19 restriction period: a retrospective hospital-based study.
BACKGROUND: The epidemiology of pediatric acute respiratory infections (ARIs) changed substantially during the COVID-19 (coronavirus disease 2019) pandemic, largely because of school closures, masking, reduced travel, and other non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs). However, hospital-based data from the restriction period remain useful for describing pathogen detection patterns, clinical severity, and markers of adverse clinical course. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective hospital-based study of 62 children aged <18 years who were evaluated for ARI symptoms and underwent real-time fluorescent quantitative nucleic acid testing for common respiratory pathogens, including respiratory viruses and Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Demographic, clinical, laboratory, treatment, severity, and outcome variables were extracted from medical records. Continuous variables were summarized using medians and ranges, and group comparisons used non-parametric tests. Given the small sample size and sparse severe-outcome events, the study was not powered to detect small effect sizes, and regression findings were interpreted conservatively as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. RESULTS: The median age was 9 years (range, 1-17), and 33 patients (53.2%) were female. Most children had mild disease (37/62, 59.7%); 19 (30.6%) had moderate disease and 6 (9.7%) had severe disease. Intensive care unit (ICU) admission was recorded in 6 patients (9.7%), and mechanical ventilatory or noninvasive respiratory support in 9 (14.5%). Fever (43.5%) and cough (22.6%) were the most frequent presenting symptoms. Median oxygen saturation was 94.7% (range, 87.2-97.8). Respiratory virus detection was documented in 15 children (24.2%). Human rhinovirus was detected in 15 children (24.2%), human bocavirus in 9 (14.5%), and Mycoplasma pneumoniae in 10 (16.1%); co-detection was recorded in 14 children (22.6%). Lower SpO2 and longer symptom duration differed significantly across severity categories (both p < 0.001). In exploratory logistic regression, each additional day of symptoms was associated with higher odds of hospital admission/continued inpatient management [odds ratio [OR], 1.4; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.03-1.93; p = 0.022]. Sex was not significantly associated with clinical severity or laboratory parameters. CONCLUSIONS: In this small hospital-based pediatric ARI cohort during the COVID-19 restriction period, severe disease was uncommon, and oxygen saturation and symptom duration were the most clinically coherent markers of greater severity. The observed pathogen detection pattern is compatible with pandemic-era disruption of respiratory pathogen circulation, but causal conclusions about NPIs require larger denominator-based studies with pre-pandemic and post-restriction comparison groups.

Strengthening health system resilience in Somalia: The role of community health workers.
OBJECTIVES: To synthesize global evidence and Somalia-specific reports on the role of community health workers (CHWs) in addressing health vulnerabilities within fragile and conflict-affected settings, and to argue that CHWs represent a primary care response essential for strengthening health system resilience in Somalia. STUDY DESIGN: Narrative synthesis of published literature and selected reports. METHODS: A targeted search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Google Scholar, and institutional repositories (WHO EMRO, World Bank, UNICEF Somalia) was conducted using combinations of terms including ("community health worker" OR "CHW" OR "female health worker") AND ("Somalia" OR "fragile setting" OR "conflict-affected") AND ("health system resilience" OR "primary health care" OR "maternal health" OR "disease surveillance"). Peer-reviewed articles and institutional reports published in English were eligible for inclusion. Sources were excluded if they lacked Somalia-specific data or empirical grounding. As a narrative review, the search was purposive rather than exhaustive, consistent with the interpretive synthesis approach. Two authors independently screened titles and abstracts, with full-text review of potentially eligible sources. Key findings were extracted regarding intervention design, outcomes, and implementation barriers. The synthesis was developed iteratively: all authors reviewed the evidence summary and interpretive framework, and consensus on conclusions was achieved through multiple rounds of written revision and discussion. RESULTS: Somalia faces one of the world's most acute health workforce shortages, with fewer than 0.4 doctors, nurses, and midwives per 10,000 populations-well below the WHO minimum threshold of 23 per 10,000-and over 5.4 million people in urgent need of health services. Global evidence from 55 studies across 19 conflict-affected settings demonstrates that CHW-delivered interventions effectively circumvent access barriers and strengthen disease detection, care-seeking, and treatment adherence. In Somalia, community-based maternal and newborn care programs in rural Galmudug, delivered through 34 CHWs serving 1165 women over 24 months, achieved 88% enrollment coverage, 94% average competency scores, and strong acceptability among participants. CHWs also contributed to COVID-19 surveillance, identifying approximately one-third of suspected cases with higher positivity rates than facility-based surveillance. Mental health represents a substantial and neglected component of Somalia's disease burden, with an estimated one in three Somalis affected by some form of psychological disorder, yet 80-90% lack access to care. CHWs have demonstrated potential to deliver effective mental health care for conflict-affected populations, including PTSD. However, current programs face inconsistent integration into national systems, variable supervision, fragmented external support, and sustainability concerns amid 95% donor-dependent health financing. The Community Health Strategy 2025-2029 represents a landmark policy shift toward professionalizing and integrating the CHW workforce under government leadership. CONCLUSIONS: CHWs are not merely supplementary actors but represent a primary care response essential for addressing Somalia's health vulnerabilities. Deliberate investment in CHW workforce development-through formal recognition within the Essential Package of Health Services, standardized training and certification, sustainable financing, improved supervision linked to district health systems, and strengthened community engagement-is critical to strengthening primary health care and build health system resilience. As Somalia implements its Community Health Strategy, sustained investment, government ownership, and international partnerships will be vital to translating policy into impact for every Somali family.

Association of dengue severity with the serotype of infection: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
BACKGROUND: Dengue is a mosquito-borne infection caused by one of four dengue virus serotypes (DENV1-4) that circulates endemically across the tropics and subtropics. To date, there is contrasting evidence on the relationship between the serotype of infection and disease severity. METHODS: We conducted a systematic review (PROSPERO, CRD42023443101) and meta-analysis to examine the association between the serotype of symptomatic infections with severe disease while accounting for both prior exposure status and geographic region, with severity defined by (i) the 1997 World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines, (ii) the 2009 WHO guidelines or (iii) hospitalisation. We searched the Global Health, Embase Classic + Embase, and Medline databases using Ovid for studies published up to 20 January 2025 and extracted case counts with matched serotype and severity information. We fitted generalised linear mixed models to estimate the proportions of severe cases, running independent analyses per severity definition, and stratifying by prior exposure-serotype combinations (e.g. primary DENV2) and geographic region (Asia versus Americas). Heterogeneity was assessed using the τ and I 2 metrics and risk of bias was assessed by adapting an established tool for risk of bias in prevalence studies. FINDINGS: Our search yielded 4621 unique records, with 71 studies included for the meta-analysis. We found that, on average, DENV3 in Asia resulted in the highest proportion of DHF/DSS (21·00% [95% CrI: 13·02-30·44%]) and hospitalised (22·00% [95% CrI: 0·88-75·31%]) cases among symptomatic primary infections, while also causing the highest proportion of DHF/DSS among secondary infections (37·61% [95% CrI: 24·19-52·32%]). However, conditional on the same prior exposure status (primary/secondary infections), we found no statistically significant differences between serotypes across the three severity definitions. For 1997-type severity, we found some evidence of secondary infections being more severe than primary infections and found that dengue was significantly less severe in the Americas when compared to Asia, though this disparity between regions was sensitive to the inclusion of cases with unknown prior exposure status. There was no significant difference between regions for 2009-type severity and hospitalisations. The paucity of published studies from Africa limited the extent to which we could investigate dengue severity in this region. INTERPRETATION: This study provides evidence that, according to the published literature, prior dengue exposure has a stronger association with the development of severe disease than the serotype of infection. Better characterising the local population-level immunity remains a current priority for outbreak response and healthcare demand planning. FUNDING: UK Medical Research Council, UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office, Wellcome Trust, European Union.

Psychosocial impact of Marburg virus disease on recovered individuals and frontline health workers in Rwanda: a cross-sectional survey.
OBJECTIVES: To examine the psychosocial impact of this disease on recovered individuals and frontline health workers (FHWs) following the 2024 MVD outbreak in Rwanda. DESIGN: a cross-sectional survey. SETTING: Kigali, the capital city of Rwanda, had two treatment centres during the outbreak of the MVD disease from 24 September to 24 October 2024. PARTICIPANTS: All 51 recovered individuals from MVD and 98 FHWs who met the eligibility criteria were involved in the study.Depression was measured using the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9), anxiety with the Generalised Anxiety Disorder (GAD-7) scale and post-traumatic stress disorder using the PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5). Perceived stigma was measured using the adapted Ebola stigma and discrimination questionnaire and the Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support Scale (MPSS) to assess social support. Wilcoxon rank-sum and Kruskal-Wallis tests examined differences in depression, anxiety and PTSD by sex and profession. Spearman correlation assessed relationships between variables. RESULTS: 115 participants, including 29 recovered people and 86 FHWs. 11.8% of FHWs had moderate to severe depression and 20.7% of recovered people had mild to moderate depression. Moderate to severe anxiety was exhibited by 9.4% of FHWs, and mild anxiety was reported by 17.2% of recovered people. 9.3% of FHWs and one recovered individual had a total PCL score above 33 (PTSD). Among recovered people, there was a significant negative correlation between anxiety and social support (r=-0.36, p value=0.05) and a significant difference in PTSD symptom levels between sexes (p value=0.01). Among FHWs, MVD-related stigma was positively correlated with PTSD symptoms (r=+0.23, p value=0.05). Symptoms of depression (β coef.=-0.19, 95% CI -0.32, -0.05) and anxiety (β coef.=-0.16, 95% CI -0.26, -0.06) decreased with age. Married FHWs had lower levels of depression (β coef.=-2.72, 95% CI -4.96, -0.49) and anxiety (β coef.=-2.35, 95% CI -4.07, -0.62) compared with single individuals. CONCLUSION: Six months post-containment of the MVD outbreak in Rwanda, many FHWs were still experiencing depression, anxiety and PTSD. Contextualised and culturally adapted mental health and psychosocial support interventions are highly recommended for integration into infectious disease response plans.

Epidemiology and phylogenomic characterisation of the 2025 Ebola virus disease outbreak in Bulape, Kasaï province, Democratic Republic of the Congo: a retrospective observational study.
BACKGROUND: An Ebola virus disease (EVD) outbreak in Bulape health zone, Kasaï province, DR Congo, was declared on Sept 4, 2025, and ended on Dec 1, 2025. We describe the dynamics of this outbreak and the molecular characteristics of the causative Ebola virus variant (species Orthoebolavirus zairense). METHODS: This retrospective observational study included probable and PCR-confirmed EVD cases reported between Aug 4 and Dec 1, 2025. Individuals who tested PCR-negative for Ebola virus were classified as discarded cases and excluded. Trained field investigators and health professionals recorded epidemiological and clinical data during initial case investigation. The primary outcome was the generation of complete Ebola virus genomes from clinical samples tested PCR-positive. Ebola virus RNA was detected by real-time PCR and subjected to whole-genome sequencing to generate complete Ebola virus genomes. Ebola virus sequences were integrated with detailed epidemiological data to infer case linkages and reconstruct transmission chains. Bayesian analysis was performed to infer time-scaled phylogenetic trees. FINDINGS: In total, 64 EVD cases (53 confirmed and 11 probable) were reported, including 45 deaths, corresponding to a case-fatality rate of 70·3% (45 of 64, 95% CI 57·6-81·1%). The median age of affected individuals was 25 years (IQR 6-51) and 58% (37 of 64) were women. Our analysis identified five generations of transmission originating from an undetected index case, with transmission occurring predominantly in health-care settings. One inferred superspreading patient generated 11 secondary infections, indicating marked heterogeneity in early transmission. The mean serial interval was 15·7 days (95% CI 13·9-17·6 days). Two hypothetical unsampled cases were inferred within the transmission chain: one representing the superspreading patient within the chain, and another representing a case that did not lead to any further secondary human-to-human transmission. Phylogenetic analysis showed two distinct clusters, each likely arising from a single source and both sharing a recent common ancestor. The 2025 Ebola virus lineages are most closely related to genome sequences from the 1976 Yambuku-Mayinga outbreak. INTERPRETATION: The 2025 EVD outbreak likely resulted from a novel zoonotic spillover; health care-associated transmission substantially amplified the outbreak. Delayed recognition and inadequate infection prevention and control capacity likely facilitated superspreading. Integrated genomic and epidemiological investigation strengthens transmission chain inference and supports a rapid public health response. Strengthening infection prevention and control measures in health-care facilities, alongside integrated epidemiological-genomic and ecological surveillance, rapid response, and vaccination among health-care workers, is essential to minimising the effect of future EVD outbreaks. FUNDING: WHO; Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention; Culmen International LLC; and the Belgian Directorate-General for Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid under the extended Framework Agreement 5.

Association of the glucose-to-lymphocyte ratio with short-term mortality in critically ill patients with documented mitral valve disease: A retrospective cohort study.
ObjectiveThe glucose-to-lymphocyte ratio (GLR) integrates metabolic stress and lymphocyte depletion, but its prognostic relevance in critically ill patients with mitral valve disease (MVD) is uncertain. We examined the association between early GLR and short-term all-cause mortality.MethodsWe used MIMIC-IV version 3.0 to identify adults with a documented MVD diagnosis and calculable GLR from the first valid glucose and absolute lymphocyte measurements within 24 hours of ICU admission. Primary analyses used a 24-hour landmark and modeled log2-transformed GLR continuously. Cox regression, restricted cubic splines, multiple imputation, timing and phenotype sensitivity analyses, paired DeLong tests, bootstrap-corrected C-index, calibration, and decision-curve analysis were performed.ResultsAmong 1,538 patients with calculable GLR, seven died by the 24-hour landmark, leaving 1,531 patients; 148 (9.7%) died by day 28 and 203 (13.3%) by day 90. In the primary complete-case model (n=1,245), each doubling of GLR was associated with higher 28-day mortality (HR 1.43, 95% CI 1.22-1.66) and 90-day mortality (HR 1.30, 95% CI 1.14-1.49; both P<0.001). Spline analyses showed no evidence of nonlinearity, and multiple-imputation and major sensitivity analyses were directionally consistent. GLR discriminated mortality better than glucose alone but not significantly better than lymphocyte count. Adding GLR to age, sex, SOFA, and CCI increased optimism-corrected C-index by 0.030 at 28 days and 0.023 at 90 days, with good calibration and modest net benefit.ConclusionsHigher early GLR was independently associated with 28-day and 90-day mortality in critically ill patients with documented MVD and provided modest adjunctive prognostic information.

Summary of National Surveillance Data on Vaccine Preventable Diseases in Australia, 2019-2022.
This summary report on vaccine preventable diseases in Australia is the latest in a series of multi-year surveillance reports that bring together the three most important national sources of routinely-collected data on VPDs (notifications, hospitalisations and deaths) and serve as a resource to support surveillance and control of VPDs in Australia. This report focuses on the four-year period 1 January 2019 to 31 December 2022 with longer term trends also presented. Two VPDs are included for the first time: coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) and Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) infection.

Zika virus in the Americas: transmission dynamics, clinical lessons, and future risk.
INTRODUCTION: The emergence of Zika virus (ZIKV) in the Americas in 2015-2016 transformed a neglected arbovirus into a major public health concern, revealing severe congenital and neurological complications and important weaknesses in surveillance and response. Although epidemic transmission has declined, low-level circulation persists and the risk of resurgence remains uncertain. AREAS COVERED: This review synthesizes current evidence on ZIKV epidemiology, transmission dynamics, molecular evolution, and clinical impact in the Americas. We summarize findings from clinical, epidemiological, and genomic studies, highlighting how phylogenetic and phylogeographic analyses have reconstructed viral spread, revealed cryptic transmission before outbreak recognition, and clarified the roles of human mobility, vector ecology, and population immunity. Persistent diagnostic and surveillance challenges are also discussed. EXPERT OPINION: Continued low-level circulation and major surveillance gaps indicate that ZIKV resurgence cannot be excluded. Integrated genomic, entomological, epidemiological, and clinical surveillance will be essential for early detection of transmission changes and more timely public health responses. Strengthening these systems will also improve preparedness for other emerging and re-emerging arboviruses.

Epidemiological insights into bovine viral diarrhea virus and bovine rotavirus in diarrheic Yaks on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau.
Diarrhea is common in yak calves and causes substantial economic losses to the yak industry on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. Bovine viral diarrhea virus (BVDV) and bovine rotavirus (BRV) are important enteric pathogens in cattle, but their epidemiology and potential association in yaks remain unclear. In this study, 1,623 fecal samples were collected from yaks across different locations, age groups, seasons, and breeds to investigate BVDV, BRV, and BVDV/BRV dual positivity. Viral positivity was detected using PCR amplification, and associated factors were analyzed using chi-square tests and multivariable binary logistic regression. Overall, 277 samples were positive for BVDV, 224 for BRV, and 92 for both viruses, corresponding to positivity rates of 17.07%, 13.80%, and 5.67%, respectively. BVDV positivity differed significantly among seasons (P = 0.0008), with a lower rate in summer than in spring and winter, and was strongly associated with BRV positivity (P < 0.0001). BRV positivity differed significantly by location, age, season, and breed in univariable analyses, and was higher in adult yaks than in calves (16.54% vs. 11.35%, P = 0.0025) but lower in summer than in spring and winter. Multivariable analysis showed that BRV status was the only factor associated with BVDV positivity (OR = 4.277, 95% CI: 3.121-5.861, P < 0.001), whereas age, sampling location, and BVDV status were associated with BRV positivity, with BVDV-positive yaks showing a markedly higher risk of BRV positivity (OR = 4.299, 95% CI: 3.138-5.889, P < 0.001). No factor was significantly associated with BVDV/BRV dual positivity. These findings indicate that BVDV and BRV circulate among yaks and are strongly associated, suggesting possible viral interaction or shared exposure conditions and highlighting the need for integrated surveillance and control strategies targeting multiple viral pathogens.

Application and prospects of veterinary diagnostic techniques in laboratory monkeys.
As the non-human primate models with the closest genetic relationship to humans, laboratory monkeys are indispensable in life sciences research, drug development, and biological product evaluation. However, infectious diseases either endemic in laboratory monkey colonies or acquired during breeding and husbandry-for example, B virus and Mycobacterium tuberculosis-threaten animal welfare and colony security, while also elevating zoonotic transmission risks and compromising the reliability of research data. The diversity, complexity, and clinically insidious nature of diseases in laboratory monkeys impose stringent demands on veterinary diagnostic capabilities. This review summarizes the current status and recent advances in mainstream veterinary diagnostic techniques applied to laboratory monkey disease surveillance. We analyze the specific applications, strengths, and limitations of molecular, immunological, imaging, and conventional microbiological methods for detecting major viral, bacterial, and parasitic pathogens of laboratory monkeys, covering quantitative PCR (qPCR), CRISPR-based assays, ELISA, IFA/IHC, and other established platforms. By comparing these techniques across sensitivity, specificity, cost-effectiveness, and operational feasibility, we delineate their suitability for distinct use cases: high-precision laboratory testing, large-scale colony screening, and point-of-care clinical diagnosis. Current veterinary diagnostic assays for laboratory monkeys achieve robust analytical performance. In several studies, qPCR delivers 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity for B virus detection, digital PCR (dPCR) attains a limit of detection as low as 45 copies/ml for monkeypox virus; and CRISPR/Cas-based assays have demonstrated 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity in clinical validation cohorts. Building on these advances, we further identify practical bottlenecks in diagnostic deployment and propose targeted countermeasures. Finally, we explore emerging trends and application prospects for point-of-care testing, multiplex pathogen detection, and artificial intelligence-assisted diagnosis, which collectively support the development of accurate, efficient, and intelligent disease diagnostics for laboratory monkeys. This work aims to provide a theoretical and practical reference for clinical practice and scientific research focused on laboratory monkey disease prevention and control.

Factors Predicting the Outcome in Patients With Acute Encephalitis Syndrome: A Retrospective Analysis of Surveillance Data in Bangladesh.
INTRODUCTION: Acute encephalitis syndrome (AES) is a severe inflammatory condition affecting the central nervous system, frequently leading to significant morbidity and mortality. Despite advancements in diagnostic techniques, the etiology of AES remains unidentified in a substantial number of cases, particularly in low- and middle-income countries like Bangladesh. Understanding factors that predict outcomes in AES patients is crucial for improving management strategies and patient outcomes. METHODS: We used data from the Nipah surveillance in Bangladesh, analyzing patients admitted with AES to 11 surveillance hospitals across diverse geographical regions in Bangladesh from January 2021 to December 2023. Trained surveillance team members screened patients and collected data through face-to-face interviews using a structured questionnaire, and surveillance physicians made decisions on enrollment as an AES case. Bivariate and multivariable logistic regression analyses were used to identify predictors of mortality. RESULTS: A total of 12,603 AES patients were included, of whom 2,759 (22%) died. Mortality rates varied significantly across different administrative divisions, with the highest rates observed in the Rangpur division. Increased age, female sex, and delayed hospital admission were associated with higher odds of mortality. Patients from divisions like Rangpur and those aged 60 or over had notably higher odds of mortality, with adjusted odds ratios of 2.55 and 4.22, respectively. Clinical factors such as high pulse rate, ronchi, difficulty breathing, altered mental status, stiff neck, paralysis, and unconsciousness at admission were significantly associated with unfavorable outcomes. DISCUSSION: The findings highlight significant geographical, demographic, and clinical predictors of mortality among AES patients in Bangladesh. Older age, delayed hospital admission, and certain reported clinical symptoms on admission increase the risk of death. The study underscores the importance of timely intervention and targeted management strategies, particularly in identified aforementioned high-risk groups. CONCLUSION: Identifying predictors of adverse outcomes in AES patients can aid in developing early warning and triage systems, potentially enabling adequate resource allocation and the delivery of timely, personalized, and higher standard of care.

Predictive Accuracy of the 1-h HACOR Score for Identifying Non-Invasive Ventilation Failure in COPD Patients With Acute Hypercapnic Respiratory Failure: A Prospective Observational Study.
